stories.title: John Cleese is not dead yet
stories.summary: The 89-year-old is travelling on a Canadian tour screening Monty Python and the Holy Grail alongside Q&A sessions
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
A few years ago in Los Angeles, the Monty Python comedian John Cleese had a precancerous growth surgically removed from his arm. It was a minor procedure that required a few stitches.

“As the guy left the room, he said, ‘Tis but a scratch,’” Cleese says, speaking on a video call.

The pop-culture reference “Tis but a scratch” comes from the 1975 British comedy classic Monty Python and the Holy Grail. Cleese, 86, is travelling with the film on a Canadian theatre tour that begins with three screenings and Q&A sessions at Toronto’s Winter Garden Theatre (Sept. 30 to Oct. 2). The tour then moves on to Kitchener, Ont., Hamilton, Ont., Montreal and Ottawa.

The film is a zany parody of the Arthurian legend, written collectively by Cleese and the other Python members: Eric Idle, Terry Gilliam, Michael Palin and the late Terry Jones and Graham Chapman. Idle later adapted the movie for the stage musical Spamalot, also known as Monty Python’s Spamalot: A New Musical (Lovingly) Ripped Off from the Motion Picture Monty Python and the Holy Grail .

The name of Cleese’s tour is Not Dead Yet! , inspired by a memorable scene from the movie. An old man resists being placed on the plague cart because he’s still alive. Other 51-year-old quotes Python aficionados like to throw around include “Just a flesh wound” and “I fart in your general direction.” Who knew flatulence humour would age so well?

“It’s lovely to think that people have these words in their minds,” Cleese says.

He’s speaking from his place in London’s Chelsea neighbourhood. “It’s a 10-minute walk to Harrods, which pleases my wife very much.”

For those keeping track, Cleese is on his fourth wife. He says their flat is relatively small. “It’s all I could afford after the divorce.” (Cleese went on a tour called A Ludicrous Evening with John Cleese − Or How to Finance Your Divorce in 2009 after expensively splitting with his third wife, psychotherapist Alyce Faye Eichelberger. Another series of shows, dubbed The Alimony Tour, followed.)

Jokey online memes or lines from today’s Saturday Night Live don’t quite stick around the way Monty Python ’s catch phrases used to. Comedy fans remember lines from Kids in the Hall , older SNL sketches , SCTV , even the Cleese co-written Fawlty Towers from 1975 like they heard them yesterday. Contemporary equivalents, however, are ephemeral.

“We had much, much better television in England 40 years ago, on just four channels,” Cleese says. “The sad thing about comedy today is that when you come up with something they ask, ‘Can we make it into 12 one-hour segments, and can we put dragons in it?’”

The troupe’s second feature film, 1979’s Monty Python’s Life of Brian , is prescient, even though it was a satire set in biblical times. Cleese wrote a scene − “with a little help from Graham Chapman, who was drinking quite a lot at the time” − in which a man wants to be a woman (named Loretta) and have babies.

Stan/Loretta, played by Idle: “It’s every man’s right to have babies if he wants them.”

Reg, played by Cleese: “But you can’t have babies!”

Stan/Loretta: “Don’t you oppress me!”

It was meant as satire on political thought in the 1970s, when the left in England had become splintered. “What was funny, and is often true, is that they hated the splinter groups more than they hated the original enemies,” Cleese explains.

As for a man wishing to give birth, the idea had to do with the discussion on human rights in the 1970s. “I was trying to think what would be a ridiculous right. Well, it’s the right to have a baby if you were a fellow. So, that got sort of tacked on.”

The troupe released its final feature film, Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life , in 1983. Unlike the narrative-driven absurdity of the previous two movies, it was made up of sketches and musical numbers. Cleese thought it was a backward move and wasn’t happy with some of the sketches and began to branch out on his own.

“My thought was that I didn’t want to go on making other people’s mistakes. I wanted to make my own.”

He first collaborated with British director and editor Charles Crichton on the well-received heist comedy A Fish Called Wanda in 1988. If there were mistakes with the film starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Kevin Kline, Python’s Palin and himself, they weren’t noticed. At the 61st Academy Awards, it was nominated for Best Director and Best Original Screenplay and won a Best Supporting Actor statuette for Kline.

Monty Python last reunited in 2014, when they gave ten concerts at the O2 in London.

“Comedy relies on freshness and newness,” Cleese says. “In the beginning, it was as if were going into a field of flowers nobody had ever been in. We would go around picking flowers, these lovely sketches, but after a time there were fewer and fewer flowers that hadn’t been picked. There’s a certain point where you just run out.”

Contemporary equivalents, however, are ephemeral.

content_blocks.text: “We had much, much better television in England 40 years ago, on just four channels,” Cleese says. “The sad thing about comedy today is that when you come up with something they ask, ‘Can we make it into 12 one-hour segments, and can we put dragons in it?’”

The troupe’s second feature film, 1979’s Monty Python’s Life of Brian , is prescient, even though it was a satire set in biblical times. Cleese wrote a scene − “with a little help from Graham Chapman, who was drinking quite a lot at the time” − in which a man wants to be a woman (named Loretta) and have babies.

Reg, played by Cleese: “But you can’t have babies!”

content_blocks.text: Stan/Loretta: “Don’t you oppress me!”

It was meant as satire on political thought in the 1970s, when the left in England had become splintered. “What was funny, and is often true, is that they hated the splinter groups more than they hated the original enemies,” Cleese explains.

As for a man wishing to give birth, the idea had to do with the discussion on human rights in the 1970s. “I was trying to think what would be a ridiculous right. Well, it’s the right to have a baby if you were a fellow. So, that got sort of tacked on.”

The troupe released its final feature film, Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life , in 1983. Unlike the narrative-driven absurdity of the previous two movies, it was made up of sketches and musical numbers. Cleese thought it was a backward move and wasn’t happy with some of the sketches and began to branch out on his own.

stories.title: Maple Leafs fall to Canadiens as McKenna, Marchenko make their Toronto debuts
stories.summary: Leafs head coach Jim Hiller said it will take some time for the roster to find cohesion, with newcomers Darren Raddysh and Sergei Bobrovsky.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Joshua Clipperton, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 5:57 am.

Gavin McKenna has known for quite some time his NHL debut would come Tuesday night. Kirill Marchenko wasn’t even a member of the Maple Leafs at the start of the week.

The pair were among 10 players to suit up with Toronto for the first time in a 3-2 loss to the Montreal Canadiens as the NHL regular season opened for both teams.

McKenna was selected first overall at June’s draft after the Maple Leafs missed the playoffs for the first time in decade before beating the lottery odds, while Marchenko was acquired from the Columbus Blue Jackets in a blockbuster trade just over 24 hours prior to puck drop that saw Matthew Knies head the other way.

“It’s pretty hard to forget a day like this,” said McKenna, an 18-year-old winger from Whitehorse. “Getting to have that rookie lap, seeing my family on the glass in warm-ups, hearing your name called in player intros — it’s all pretty special.”

Marchenko had a much shorter runway to prepare, and only learned around lunchtime he would be able to suit up after his immigration paperwork was completed.

“It’s crazy,” said the 26-year-old Russian winger, who signed a six-year contract extension worth US$75 million with Toronto. “We packed, we moved with my wife … really busy. But I’m happy it’s done and I’m happy to be here. I hate that we lost, but it’s still a great memory.”

“Dream for everybody being with the Toronto Maple Leafs,” he added. “But it’s happened quick.”

McKenna had a few nice moments, but also had some turnovers he wanted back before finishing a minus-2 with one shot on goal in 15 minutes 19 seconds of action.

“The first exhibition game, he talked to (the media) and said, ‘Ya, it was just an OK night, I’ll learn from it,'” Toronto head coach Jim Hiller said. “He came back and had a really strong game. It’s up another level again. You just keep taking the test, and he’ll be back. I thought he was all right. But he’ll probably want to be better.”

Marchenko was fired out of a cannon in his debut with eight shot attempts, including four on target, in just over 20 minutes of ice time.

He picked up an assist on William Nylander’s opener 48 seconds into the first period and had a couple of great chances on Canadiens goaltender Jakub Dobes.

“A big boy, can make plays, shoots it,” said Maple Leafs centre Auston Matthews, who centred a line with Marchenko and Jack Roslovic. “I thought for what he had to endure the last 24 hours — getting traded, flying here last night, getting here today, new everything, getting a visa, all that stuff — we had some really good opportunities.”

Hiller said it will take some time for the roster to find cohesion with so many new faces, including defenceman Darren Raddysh and goaltender Sergei Bobrovsky, following a truncated training camp and pre-season.

“We looked a little bit like a new team,” said the coach. “We just weren’t connecting with our passes. I don’t know if that has anything to do with nerves or being in the building for the first time, and the first time everybody together.

“We just weren’t clean as a team.”

McKenna, Marchenko and the rest of the Maple Leafs will get another chance Wednesday when they host the New York Islanders.

“It’s pretty special,” McKenna said of his debut. “There’s not much I’ll forget about this day.”

Maple Leafs general manager John Chayka was asked Tuesday morning about his expectations for the club after acquiring Marchenko.

“It’s unchanged … our expectations are always high,” Chayka said. “We’re the Toronto Maple Leafs and ownership’s spared no expense to try to put the best product on the on the ice and support the guys and give us every resource to be successful.

“We think Kirill could be a big part of that. But we felt like we had a good group going in.”

Toronto would have normally paid tribute to Cliff Fletcher following his death in June at age 90, but the former executive’s family was unable to attend Tuesday’s opener.

The Maple Leafs will honour Fletcher, whose first tenure included the franchise-altering trade for Doug Gilmour in 1992, on Oct. 15 when the club hosts the Buffalo Sabres.

stories.title: Western student creates orange shirt design for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: New orange shirt design created by student Kolbi Williams for National Day for Truth and Reconciliation is available at Western University
stories.author: Colleen MacDonald
stories.content:
A fourth-year English and creative writing student crafted a new orange shirt design as part of Western University’s recognition of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, with proceeds from t-shirt sales supporting an Indigenous-led preservation initiative.

Kolbi Williams’ artwork, inspired by Haudenosaunee teachings, is featured on this year’s orange shirts sold at Western.

Kolbi Williams, a member of the Mohawk Nation from Six Nations of the Grand River, created the artwork titled Tewa:aráton and Its Creations, after a call for submissions from Western’s Office of Indigenous Initiatives. Her design illustrates a Haudenosaunee creation story about lacrosse, known in her community as Tewa:aráton, and its origins as a gift from the Creator to bring relief during a time of hardship and conflict.

According to Haudenosaunee tradition, in the first game of lacrosse played between four-legged animals and birds, the mouse and squirrel were ostracized by their own team because of their small size. They asked to join the birds, who accepted them as teammates and fashioned wings for them. With the game tied at nightfall, the mouse – transformed into a bat – ultimately scored the winning goal.

“This story teaches us not to judge another by the way they look because you don’t know what they’re capable of,” Williams said. “It’s the same in the community – you might not know what someone’s teachings and gifts are.”

Williams says this message is at the heart of reconciliation as Canadians reckon with the legacy of the Residential School System for Indigenous children. From the 19th century until 1996, more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were forced to attend church-run residential schools where they were stripped of their languages, cultures and traditions.

(L to R) Mike Cywink, community engagement coordinator for Indigenous Initiatives, Mikayla Antone-Gregory, Indigenous Students’ Association president and Kolbi Williams, student artist, wear orange shirts symbolizing the loss of identity, culture and family experienced by Indigenous children in residential schools, while honouring children who never returned home. (Western Housing and Ancillary Services)

“Coming together to appreciate all people’s gifts is one way to better understand and share the gifts that children in residential schools were denied access to and punished for using,” Williams said.

Survivors have described abuse, neglect, malnutrition, harsh working conditions and unsanitary living quarters. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented thousands of children who died at the schools and says the true number is likely much higher.

Orange Shirt Day began in 2013 as a grassroots movement under the rallying cry “Every Child Matters” to remember the children who never made it home and honour survivors of residential schools. It evolved into the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 to promote awareness of the harms caused by residential schools and grow reconciliation across Canada.

Wearing an orange shirt is considered a way of standing with Indigenous communities in remembrance and healing. Orange shirts with Williams’ design will be sold year-round at the Dellelce Family Bookstore in Western’s University Community Centre. Proceeds will support the Save the Barn campaign, a project to preserve the last remaining building from Mount Elgin Industrial Institute, a residential school on what is now Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, near London, Ont.

Mount Elgin, one of the first residential schools in Canada, operated until 1946. It included a farm where children were forced into labour tending livestock and growing crops, though the harvest was rarely used to supplement their meagre diets. A barn bearing inscriptions students left on the walls is the only structure still standing. The First Nation has been fundraising to restore it as an interpretive centre to document local history and help revitalize the community’s language and culture.

“Our communities did so much work to keep our language, culture and people alive in a time when everything was against them,” Williams said. “It’s a big part of why the Save the Barn campaign is such a vital part of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation here in London. While this city was being developed, the trauma of residential schools was happening just a half hour away to local First Nations children.”

Western supports National Day for Truth and Reconciliation by designating September 30 as a non-instructional day with no regular classes, allowing the campus community to participate in educational and commemorative events. Attendees are encouraged to wear orange. Williams said she hopes her design prompts meaningful reflection on the ongoing responsibility to remember the past, learn from it and carry those lessons forward.

“When people put on an orange shirt, I hope they have reconciliation in mind and put it into action in their daily lives when thinking about and interacting with any Indigenous Peoples.”

Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

Her design illustrates a Haudenosaunee creation story about lacrosse, known in her community as Tewa:aráton, and its origins as a gift from the Creator to bring relief during a time of hardship and conflict.

According to Haudenosaunee tradition, in the first game of lacrosse played between four-legged animals and birds, the mouse and squirrel were ostracized by their own team because of their small size. They asked to join the birds, who accepted them as teammates and fashioned wings for them. With the game tied at nightfall, the mouse – transformed into a bat – ultimately scored the winning goal.

“This story teaches us not to judge another by the way they look because you don’t know what they’re capable of,” Williams said. “It’s the same in the community – you might not know what someone’s teachings and gifts are.”
Orange shirt design supports reconciliation and First Nations’ history near London

Williams says this message is at the heart of reconciliation as Canadians reckon with the legacy of the Residential School System for Indigenous children. From the 19th century until 1996, more than 150,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children were forced to attend church-run residential schools where they were stripped of their languages, cultures and traditions.

content_blocks.alt: an Indigenous Western University staff member and two students, all wearing orange shirts symbolizing remembrance of children who died in residential schools and solidarity with In

content_blocks.text: (L to R) Mike Cywink, community engagement coordinator for Indigenous Initiatives, Mikayla Antone-Gregory, Indigenous Students’ Association president and Kolbi Williams, student artist, wear orange shirts symbolizing the loss of identity, culture and family experienced by Indigenous children in residential schools, while honouring children who never returned home. (Western Housing and Ancillary Services)

“Coming together to appreciate all people’s gifts is one way to better understand and share the gifts that children in residential schools were denied access to and punished for using,” Williams said.

Survivors have described abuse, neglect, malnutrition, harsh working conditions and unsanitary living quarters. The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented thousands of children who died at the schools and says the true number is likely much higher.

Orange Shirt Day began in 2013 as a grassroots movement under the rallying cry “Every Child Matters” to remember the children who never made it home and honour survivors of residential schools. It evolved into the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation in 2021 to promote awareness of the harms caused by residential schools and grow reconciliation across Canada.

Wearing an orange shirt is considered a way of standing with Indigenous communities in remembrance and healing. Orange shirts with Williams’ design will be sold year-round at the Dellelce Family Bookstore in Western’s University Community Centre. Proceeds will support the Save the Barn campaign, a project to preserve the last remaining building from Mount Elgin Industrial Institute, a residential school on what is now Chippewas of the Thames First Nation, near London, Ont.
Preserving Indigenous history and language at former Mount Elgin residential school

Mount Elgin, one of the first residential schools in Canada, operated until 1946. It included a farm where children were forced into labour tending livestock and growing crops, though the harvest was rarely used to supplement their meagre diets. A barn bearing inscriptions students left on the walls is the only structure still standing. The First Nation has been fundraising to restore it as an interpretive centre to document local history and help revitalize the community’s language and culture.

“Our communities did so much work to keep our language, culture and people alive in a time when everything was against them,” Williams said. “It’s a big part of why the Save the Barn campaign is such a vital part of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation here in London. While this city was being developed, the trauma of residential schools was happening just a half hour away to local First Nations children.”

Western supports National Day for Truth and Reconciliation by designating September 30 as a non-instructional day with no regular classes, allowing the campus community to participate in educational and commemorative events. Attendees are encouraged to wear orange. Williams said she hopes her design prompts meaningful reflection on the ongoing responsibility to remember the past, learn from it and carry those lessons forward.
“When people put on an orange shirt, I hope they have reconciliation in mind and put it into action in their daily lives when thinking about and interacting with any Indigenous Peoples.”
Learn more about how Western is navigating new realities.

stories.title: CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette’s fresh start withers in the end
stories.summary: François Legault’s successor tried to set herself apart, and it seemed to be paying off. But she and the Coalition Avenir Québec are now fighting for survival in Monday’s election
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
François Legault’s successor tried to set herself apart, and it seemed to be paying off. But she and the Coalition Avenir Québec are now fighting for survival in Monday's election

Christine Fréchette has done her best to outrun her own party.

Since taking over the Coalition Avenir Québec and becoming Premier in April, she has tried less to rehabilitate a tarnished brand than to erase it.

Her strategy was on display at the launch of the Quebec election campaign in late August, when observers quickly noticed that her bus and election signs did not feature her party’s name. “ Avançons ,” her campaign slogan read. Let’s move forward.

Ms. Fréchette, 56, began the first debate of the campaign by declaring that she is not her predecessor, François Legault.

As she faces a restive electorate looking for change, she has attempted to shed the baggage of her party’s eight years in government. In this election, she is selling herself.

For a moment, voters were buying in. Early in the campaign, which began days after trade talks between Canada and the United States fell apart, Ms. Fréchette invited comparisons to Prime Minister Mark Carney. Like him, she embodied the sort of unflappable technocrat that seemed a welcome contrast to the erratic and hostile behaviour of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Though the Coalition Avenir Québec had spent months circling the drain, Ms. Fréchette, who declined an interview request from The Globe and Mail, orchestrated an unlikely comeback.

It seemed possible she could achieve what Mr. Carney had done in last year’s federal election and turn near-certain defeat into an improbable victory. If she was a touch bland, well, perhaps that was exactly what Quebeckers were looking for.

But then it went away. Days ahead of the vote on Oct. 5, Ms. Fréchette’s campaign has lost its momentum. The winds of change are blowing in the direction of a Parti Québécois government, regardless of Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s unpopular promise to hold a third referendum on independence.

Despite Ms. Fréchette’s best efforts, the legacy of the CAQ has caught up to her. Now, she is fighting for the survival of the party she would prefer not to name.

Christine Fréchette is not the kind of politician who delivers thunderous oratory or inspires breathless excitement, but in a way, that’s what her supporters like about her.

She has had the unenviable task of reshaping a party built in the image of Mr. Legault, who co-founded the CAQ in 2011 and led it to form government in 2018.

Mr. Legault, who announced his resignation in January after more than seven years as premier, had a folksy, plainspoken style and a hair-trigger reaction to negative press. Though he walked on water during the COVID-19 pandemic, a series of controversies and questionable financial decisions had made him one of the least popular politicians in the country by the time he made his exit.

At a September campaign event on Montreal’s South Shore, supporters told The Globe and Mail they’d joined the party specifically because of Ms. Fréchette.

Marie-France Bilodeau, 69, said she previously voted for the CAQ but grew disenchanted with Mr. Legault’s performance. She became a party member to support Ms. Fréchette’s bid for the leadership earlier this year. “She’s really smart. I think she takes the time to think things through before making decisions,” Ms. Bilodeau said. “She’s calm.”

As the room emptied out after the event, she approached the CAQ Leader. “The only thing that brought me back was you,” she told her.

Ms. Fréchette doesn’t stand out as the type of person who would want to be premier, though she showed an interest in public policy and civic life from a young age.

The cut and thrust of partisan politics appealed less to her, said Vicky Trépanier, a long-time friend. “She wants to have in-depth debates.”

Ms. Trépanier, who is not involved in politics, met the future Premier when they were both part of the student movement of the 1990s. Ms. Fréchette earned a Master’s degree in international relations from Laval University in 1994, and went on to work for a provincewide student union.

In those early years, she rubbed shoulders with a group of future politicos, including Martin Koskinen, who would become Mr. Legault’s long-time chief of staff. “She wasn’t someone who wanted to be the centre of attention,” Mr. Koskinen recalled in an interview.

Several years after completing her studies, Ms. Fréchette began organizing annual simulations of a North American parliament attended by university students from Canada, the United States and Mexico.

It was an impressive achievement, said Ms. Trépanier, who helped out with the paperwork and grew close to Ms. Fréchette during that time. “She created an institution that didn’t exist.”

Starting in 2007, Ms. Fréchette worked at a centre for international studies at the University of Montreal, where she met Jean-François Lisée, a future leader of the separatist Parti Québécois. When Mr. Lisée was elected to the National Assembly in 2012 and named minister of international relations, he hired her to work in his office.

Ms. Fréchette had voted “yes” in 1995, but she was never a “militant sovereigntist,” said Ms. Trépanier, her friend.

Her career with the PQ would be short-lived, however. She left the minister’s office in 2014, unable to accept the government’s proposed charter of values, which would have banned religious symbols for many public servants.

Ms. Fréchette would go on to spend nearly five years as the head of the chamber of commerce of eastern Montreal. But there were signs she was looking for a new political home. Ms. Trépanier recalled that after Ms. Fréchette left the PQ, the two of them attended a meeting of a group of so-called “orphelins politiques” (political orphans) organized by none other than Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon, who would seek the PQ leadership for the first time in 2016.

As the CAQ gained prominence, Mr. Legault, who had moved in the same circles as Ms. Fréchette in her younger years, tried to recruit her to the party multiple times, according to her partner, businessman Guy Nadeau. She declined his invitation to run for the CAQ in 2018, having started her position at the chamber of commerce not long before.

But when he came calling again four years later, she was ready to take the plunge. Among other things, she was impressed by how Mr. Legault had handled the pandemic, Mr. Nadeau said. “It took shape slowly in her mind,” he said. “She’s not an opportunist.”

Ms. Fréchette won a seat in the National Assembly as the CAQ formed its second majority government. She was named immigration minister, before being moved to the high-stakes energy and economy portfolio in 2024.

In the fall of 2025, after the CAQ’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.

Mr. Koskinen, Mr. Legault’s chief of staff, hadn’t expected the reserved Ms. Fréchette would want the job.

But he now believes her restraint was part of her appeal to party members. “Quebeckers weren’t going to choose a François Legault 2.0.”

After being sworn in as the province’s second-ever female premier in April, Ms. Fréchette hit the ground running.

Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.

While Mr. Legault had an often adversarial relationship with Ottawa, Ms. Fréchette arranged a meeting with Mr. Carney two days after her swearing-in. The two leaders have since made several joint announcements, and the CAQ enjoyed a modest bump in the polls.

Ms. Fréchette kicked off her campaign in late August as a new round of U.S. tariffs loomed, naming Mr. Trump as her prime adversary. Her party’s fortunes rose again, with one survey putting the CAQ neck-and-neck with the PQ.

But the Trump effect didn’t last, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “People have gotten somewhat used to the tariff crisis.”

Ms. Fréchette has proven less adept at campaigning than at being Premier, Ms. Yaccarini said, and her debate performances were underwhelming. She is also an easy mark for her opponents, given the eight years of unpopular CAQ decisions that are all too easy to dredge up.

The CAQ Leader has also prevaricated repeatedly when asked for her personal position on sovereignty, despite her promise not to hold a referendum.

Back in April, before anyone was comparing Ms. Fréchette to Mr. Carney, some were drawing parallels to a different Canadian prime minister. Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

Ms. Fréchette may share the same fate. Quebec’s governing party is once again looking to save the furniture, with projections suggesting it could lose every one of its 79 seats. A majority may be in reach for the PQ.

In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”

content_blocks.caption: Ms. Fréchette's partner is Guy Nadeau, a businessman based in Montreal. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: As the CAQ gained prominence, Mr. Legault, who had moved in the same circles as Ms. Fréchette in her younger years, tried to recruit her to the party multiple times, according to her partner, businessman Guy Nadeau. She declined his invitation to run for the CAQ in 2018, having started her position at the chamber of commerce not long before.

But when he came calling again four years later, she was ready to take the plunge. Among other things, she was impressed by how Mr. Legault had handled the pandemic, Mr. Nadeau said. “It took shape slowly in her mind,” he said. “She’s not an opportunist.”

Ms. Fréchette won a seat in the National Assembly as the CAQ formed its second majority government. She was named immigration minister, before being moved to the high-stakes energy and economy portfolio in 2024.

In the fall of 2025, after the CAQ’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.
content_blocks.html: In the fall of 2025, after the CAQ’s support had collapsed, colleagues told Ms. Fréchette she should consider running to replace Mr. Legault if he resigned, her partner said. She felt it might be a “unique opportunity” that wouldn’t come along again, he added.

content_blocks.text: Mr. Koskinen, Mr. Legault’s chief of staff, hadn’t expected the reserved Ms. Fréchette would want the job.
But he now believes her restraint was part of her appeal to party members. “Quebeckers weren’t going to choose a François Legault 2.0.”

content_blocks.caption: Ms. Fréchette and her candidates were doing better in the polls this summer, when the Canada-U.S. trade war was heating up. But that momentum has not lasted. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press
Ms. Fréchette and her candidates were doing better in the polls this summer, when the Canada-U.S. trade war was heating up. But that momentum has not lasted. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: After being sworn in as the province’s second-ever female premier in April, Ms. Fréchette hit the ground running.

Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.
content_blocks.html: Political observers suggested the best she could hope for was to save her party from devastation. But ahead of an election set for October that would hinge partly on the question of sovereignty, she took steps to prove she could work within Canada.

content_blocks.text: While Mr. Legault had an often adversarial relationship with Ottawa, Ms. Fréchette arranged a meeting with Mr. Carney two days after her swearing-in. The two leaders have since made several joint announcements, and the CAQ enjoyed a modest bump in the polls.

content_blocks.caption: Ms. Fréchette has been out and about several times with Mr. Carney, such as this August news conference in St. John's with her Newfoundland counterpart, Tony Wakeham. Paul Daly/The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Ms. Fréchette kicked off her campaign in late August as a new round of U.S. tariffs loomed, naming Mr. Trump as her prime adversary. Her party’s fortunes rose again, with one survey putting the CAQ neck-and-neck with the PQ.
But the Trump effect didn’t last, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “People have gotten somewhat used to the tariff crisis.”

Ms. Fréchette has proven less adept at campaigning than at being Premier, Ms. Yaccarini said, and her debate performances were underwhelming. She is also an easy mark for her opponents, given the eight years of unpopular CAQ decisions that are all too easy to dredge up.

content_blocks.caption: Ms. Fréchette says she would not hold a referendum on Quebec independence; Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon says he would, but not while Mr. Trump is in power in Washington. Graham Hughes/AFP via Getty Images

content_blocks.text: The CAQ Leader has also prevaricated repeatedly when asked for her personal position on sovereignty, despite her promise not to hold a referendum.

Back in April, before anyone was comparing Ms. Fréchette to Mr. Carney, some were drawing parallels to a different Canadian prime minister. Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

Kim Campbell, who took over from Brian Mulroney in June, 1993, led the Progressive Conservatives to a devastating defeat in an election that November, from which the party never really recovered.

content_blocks.text: Ms. Fréchette may share the same fate. Quebec’s governing party is once again looking to save the furniture, with projections suggesting it could lose every one of its 79 seats. A majority may be in reach for the PQ.
In the months since becoming Premier, Ms. Fréchette has made it very clear who she is not. She is not François Legault. She is certainly not Donald Trump. And she is not Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

But it is less clear who she is, and that could be her downfall. “The problem is she herself, despite her impressive demeanour, is a bit of an empty shell,” journalist and author Francine Pelletier said in an interview. “What’s the new dream?”

Ms. Fréchette, standing in a tan jacket, spoke during her last Question Period less than two months into her premiership. At dissolution, the CAQ had 79 seats; to win a majority on Oct. 5, a party needs 64 or more. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press
Ms. Fréchette is rallying Quebeckers under the slogan Avançons, let's move forward. Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press

stories.title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation recognized on B.C. election campaign
stories.summary: Kamloops - Politicians in British Columbia's election campaign are paying their respects on National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
NDP Leader David Eby will be marking the day on the Tk’emlups te Secwepemc First Nation, which came under a spotlight on the weekend when an apparent group of white nationalists stood at the reserve and unfurled a banner in reference to what are believed to be unmarked graves on the site.

Eby was invited to mark the day and his campaign says that in light of recent events, the leader wanted to be there.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak will also attend the same event at the Powwow Arbour on the reserve.

The First Nations Leadership Council issued a statement Tuesday condemning what it says is white nationalist activity on the reserve, and Regional Chief Terry Teegee called on the Canadian government to acknowledge residential school denialism as hate speech in the Criminal Code.

B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan said in a statement that on the eve of the day of recognition, her heart goes out to Indigenous nations that oppose the multibillion-dollar LNG Canada 2 project that was announced Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadians mark fifth annual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadians across the country will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday for the fifth consecutive year, honouring the survivors of residential schools and those who never made it home.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
An Every Child Matters flag flies in the breeze during the second annual South Island Powwow at Royal Athletic Park in Victoria on Saturday, Sept. 30, 2023. THE Canadian Press/Chad Hipolito THE Canadian Press

By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

Ottawa — Canadians across the country will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Wednesday for the fifth consecutive year, honouring the survivors of residential schools and those who never made it home.

Beginning in the 19th century, more than 150,000 Indigenous children in Canada were separated from their families and communities and sent to church-run residential schools where abuse, malnutrition and inadequate health care were rampant.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded in its landmark 2015 final report that the school system was a central element of a state-backed policy of cultural genocide.

Between 1857 and 1996, 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend church-run, government-funded residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission initially documented the deaths of 3,200 children at residential schools. However experts at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation — who continue to comb through millions of records — say the actual number could be much higher.

The establishment of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Sept. 30 was among the recommendations in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s report.

CBC/Radio-Canada, Aptn and the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation are hosting their annual Remembering the Children event on Parliament Hill.

The 90-minute ceremony will feature speeches from residential school survivors, elders and Indigenous leaders. Performances by Tia Wood, Soleil Launière, Silla and Adrian Sutherland are also scheduled.

Guests and participants are encouraged to bring a pair of children’s shoes to place at the front of the stage to honour the children who attended residential schools.

Separate events to mark the day are taking place across the country, including in Toronto, Vancouver, Calgary and Iqaluit.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to speak at an event in Edmonton.

“On this day, we gather to honour every child taken by the residential school system and to stand in solidarity with those who survived it. As denialist voices seek to distort the past, our collective responsibility to uphold the truth is more important than ever,” said Stephanie Scott, the executive director of the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation.

“Honouring these children means facing our history with unwavering honesty and ensuring that ‘Never Again’ is not just a phrase, but a binding commitment backed by meaningful action.”

Canadian Heritage Minister Marc Miller said the day is an opportunity for non-Indigenous and Indigenous Peoples to come together and reflect on the legacy of residential schools.

“Reconciliation is a responsibility we all share, and by connecting with each other and our history, we can help build a future grounded in understanding, respect and hope.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mark Carney is banking on economic reconciliation but critics say he’s not on track
stories.summary: Ottawa — When Wilton Littlechild was co-chairing the landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission more than a decade ago, he thought a lot about the idea of economic reconciliation and how it could help transform Indigenous communities.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

OTTAWA — When Wilton Littlechild was co-chairing the landmark Truth and Reconciliation Commission more than a decade ago, he thought a lot about the idea of economic reconciliation and how it could help transform Indigenous communities.

“You may have the best ideas in the world but without a fundamental grounding and foundation to self-determination, you’re missing a very important part,” Littlechild said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

Littlechild said economic reconciliation is still the key to achieving reconciliation between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Canadians — but not in the way Prime Minister Mark Carney sees it.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission, launched out of a legal settlement between the federal government and survivors of residential schools, was tasked with researching the history and legacy of those institutions. It was chaired by Littlechild, Murray Sinclair and Marie Wilson.

Between 1857 and 1996, 150,000 Indigenous children were forced to attend church-run, government-funded schools. They were barred from speaking their languages in institutions often rife with abuse and located far away from their families and communities.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission initially documented the deaths of 3,200 children attending residential schools. Experts at the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation — who continue to comb through millions of records — say the actual number could be much higher.

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission concluded in 2015 the goal of the schools was to erase Indigenous cultures. MPs unanimously voted to recognize residential schools as a form of genocide in 2022.

Economic reconciliation is mentioned twice in the Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s 94 Calls to Action. They call on the corporate sector to engage in meaningful consultations before proceeding with economic development projects, and to ensure Indigenous people have equitable access to jobs in those projects.

The federal government under Carney has made economic reconciliation the focus of its efforts to rebuild relations with Indigenous Peoples as it pushes forward an aggressive major projects agenda in the face of U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Littlechild said that while Carney has been focused on securing overseas investments, he’s ignoring the rights of Indigenous Peoples at home and sidelining their traditional economies by fast-tracking legislation that would allow for quicker project approvals and environmental reviews.

He said Carney’s approach risks alienating Indigenous communities and the federal government’s idea of economic reconciliation falls short of the efforts industry is making to work in partnership with communities. He said he also fears traditional economies — hunting, fishing, trapping — could be damaged by an aggressive approach to resource development.

“Right now, it’s like a four-legged stool with one leg missing,” Littlechild said. That missing leg, he said, is true respect for Indigenous rights.

The federal government’s Bill C-39, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, seeks to approve projects within one year. First Nations chiefs say they worry that will severely compress the timeline for their communities to complete land-use assessments and consultations.

Similar legislation introduced by Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government is being challenged by Indigenous and environmental groups in court.

And while Ottawa’s focus has shifted to economic reconciliation, the TRC’s Calls to Action that touch more on social issues are languishing, Littlechild said.

“(Carney is) approaching things by violating treaty rights, by violating the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and just steamrolling on national interest strategies that completely exclude us by way of disrespect,” he said.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty disagreed with the suggestion that Carney does not prioritize Indigenous rights or the social issues faced by communities.

“There is a lot of institutional reconciliation that’s happening,” Gull-Masty told The Canadian Press, citing work on reforming child and family services.

“And to me, that institutional reconciliation is maybe not language people are familiar with, but it is in progress and it is occurring.”

Hayden King, executive director of the Yellowhead Institute, said he wonders what those institutional commitments are — since First Nations are still waiting for the government to pass clean drinking water legislation, improve their access to health care, address the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, and reduce incarceration and over-policing in their communities.

“All I’ve heard Carney talk about is resource development,” King said.

“You can look at all of the proposals to improve the relationship, institutionally or otherwise, and it’s just a record of neglect.”

Yellowhead released a report last year on major projects and the conflicts that could arise from Indigenous participation — including the prospect of one First Nation violating the rights of another in order to invest in a controversial project.

King said Carney’s approach to relations with Indigenous communities puts him more in line with former prime minister Stephen Harper than with Justin Trudeau. Harper’s government also introduced legislation to speed up project approvals, leading to the Idle No More movement that staged protests across the country in 2012.

“Where Harper was the stick, Carney is the carrot,” King said.

The “carrot” approach can be seen in how Carney’s cabinet is encouraging First Nations to back the Trans Mountain pipeline through a low-cost loan and a $2.5 million payment for willing investors that some are comparing to a bribe.

“The discourse around (economic reconciliation) is most definitely that Indigenous people are going to be formal partners and this is going to breathe life into Indigenous sovereignty,” King said.

“But it’s the reverse of the process that the TRC advocated for — it was, ‘Let’s get this relationship right, and then we can talk about partnerships.'”

King said economic reconciliation can’t be achieved until Indigenous groups no longer have to fight for their rights and their land in court.

“If we’re really interested in holding up sovereignty and jurisdiction, then we have to insist on consent, and consent means knowing all the details before we make decisions.”

Stephanie Scott heads the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, which works to preserve the historical record of residential schools and educate Canadians about what happened in the institutions.

She said while economic reconciliation can help create opportunities, strengthen communities and support Indigenous governance, reconciliation is about people — the survivors, their families, communities and future generations.

She pointed to the growing tide of residential school denialism — which scholars have warned risks unwinding decades of progress in the relationship between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Peoples.

“In a time when truth is being challenged and distorted, the need for trusted institutions to preserve, protect and share the historical record has never been greater,” Scott said.

NDP MP Leah Gazan has put legislation to criminalize residential school denialism before the House of Commons, but the Liberals have not indicated they will support it.

Calls for its passage grew louder this week after a group linked with white nationalism reportedly staged a demonstration in the B.C. interior.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk̓emlups te Secwepemc First Nation, said on Sunday a group of masked individuals dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops, B.C. The banner — bearing the words “Got bones?” — appeared to be questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.

The demonstration happened just days ahead of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, a day to honour the children who attended residential schools and to remember the ones who never came home.

Scott said that while Canada’s future depends on trust, justice and shared prosperity, those things can’t exist without truth.

“Residential school denialism is not harmless dialogue or a difference of opinion. It is a deliberate misinterpretation of the history and is an ongoing source of harm to Indigenous Peoples,” Scott said.

Littlechild said the way forward is to work together — both on the economy and on the social issues that have afflicted Indigenous communities for decades.

“We’re not taking advantage of opportunities because they’re still building a fence between us by not including us,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: From chocolate to coin purses, Lake Ontario merchandise proves a hit with consumers
stories.summary: Toronto — After Tareq Hadhad and his family moved to Antigonish, N.S., as Syrian refugees in 2016, they built a business on the premise that chocolate was so uniting it could create peace.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

Posted September 30, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 30, 2026 6:01 am.

TORONTO — After Tareq Hadhad and his family moved to Antigonish, N.S., as Syrian refugees in 2016, they built a business on the premise that chocolate was so uniting it could create peace.

So when U.S. President Donald Trump renamed Lake Ontario to Lake America in late August, the chief executive of Peace by Chocolate felt he couldn’t ignore the antagonism.

Within a day, his company had created the Lake Ontario bar — 92 grams of milk chocolate and maple cream, made partially with Ontario ingredients, packaged in a Canadian flag wrapper and emblazoned with the body of water’s name and information about its Indigenous origins.

“We wanted to be there for our country, no matter how odd that it sounded,” Hadhad said. “If you showed me a Lake Ontario chocolate bar, even a year ago, I would say, why would we even create one because we have so many great lakes all across Canada? But it meant a big deal.”

The treat quickly became one of the company’s five bestselling bars, generating interest from coast to coast and a flurry of emails from south of the border, where Peace by Chocolate has paused sales because of tariffs on exports to the United States.

The reaction has been just as strong at many other Canadian companies selling Lake Ontario products, ranging from candles and caps to cottage decor and more. One month after the body of water entered the president’s crosshairs, businesses say interest in Lake Ontario merchandise remains high.

Teresa Paul, owner of Rockwood, Ont., leather goods company Hides in Hand, said the Lake Ontario coin purses she started making and selling recently are a “pretty hot” commodity.

Customers have been buying them from a store in Erin, Ont., or craft fairs she participates in, often picking up extra for family members.

“People are like, ‘Yep, I want it. Yep, I’ll take two,'” Paul said. “They love them.”

The zippered pouches come in red or blue leather and are embroidered with the outline of Lake Ontario and the body of water’s name. They’re made with Canadian components and embroidered in Ontario.

Paul designed the pouch in no time after Trump’s lake renaming “rubbed me the wrong way,” she said.

“Because I’m a leather designer, my way of responding was to actually make something. I thought why not put Lake Ontario right there on something that we’re making here in Ontario?” she said.

“It’s that little expression of Lake Ontario and Canadian pride. Nothing angry, nothing over political. Just something practical, something that meant home to me.”

Unlike Paul, when the name swap first bubbled up, Province of Canada wasn’t sure it would wade into the moment. There was no shortage of patriotism in the Toronto-based apparel company’s collections — Le Canadien T-shirts, “Made in Canada” sweatshirts and “I was Canadian before it was cool” crop tops.

“But it really became, I think, a movement and we felt that as a Canadian brand who makes their products in Canada, we really did need to become part of the conversation in some way,” said product and operations manager Alli Piccininni.

The company had been selling prints of the Great Lakes for a few years but decided that wasn’t enough.

It designed a grey fleece sweatshirt with “Lake Ontario” in navy and offered it through preorder with 15 per cent of each purchase being sent to Indspire, an Indigenous education charity.

The sweater sold out “really, really quickly,” Piccininni said.

Another round was made and availability has dwindled down to just a few sizes, so the company prepared a third batch shipping in December and fourth featuring a new colourway scheduled to reach buyers before Christmas.

Even as Province of Canada releases other items, the Lake Ontario sweater remains among its most popular releases.

Piccininni couldn’t be happier with that reception.

“When customers get behind us and support us … it’s a really good feeling,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: The 'Super El Nino' is upon us. What does that mean for Ontario's fall colours?
stories.summary: The phenomenon is expected to bring a warmer-than-normal fall to Ontario.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
What’s expected to be the strongest El Nino on record may delay Ontario’s stunning fall foliage, but experts say there’s no reason to worry – the colour show will go on.

Dubbed by scientists as the “Super El Nino,” the climate pattern is already disrupting global weather with drought striking some parts of the planet, and floods and storms ravaging others.

The phenomenon is expected to bring a warmer-than-normal fall to Ontario and possibly prolong the season’s colour progression.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Experts say the trees will still give Ontarians a show, but they need to be patient and wait for the vibrant mosaic of orange, red and yellow pigments to start appearing in the leaves.

“It’s cold nights or cooler nights that cue the big change in colour, and so that may be a little delayed in some places because of the warmer El Nino weather, or it may mean that there’s just a longer period during which the (leaf) colour changes,” said Susan Dudley, a biology professor at McMaster University in Hamilton.

The hues were duller last fall as the leaves browned before they could change colour due to limited rainfall and hotter-than-normal summer weather that year, Dudley said.

But trees haven’t been as stressed this past summer, she said. “Trees around here, anyway, are keeping their leaves. They’re just starting to turn colours.”

Leaves get their typical green colour from chlorophyll, which helps plants absorb light as part of a process called photosynthesis. The yellow and orange pigments that exist in the leaf become visible in the fall when trees withdraw nutrients from the leaves into their trunks, branches and roots before shedding them, Dudley said. The next step in the process brings red and bright purple hues, thanks to pigments called anthocyanins that help protect plants against ultraviolet light.

“The red colour that we are really inspired by is actually the tree giving itself sunscreen as it takes away the chlorophyll molecules and the resources in chlorophyll,” Dudley said.

The strongest colouration is triggered by the combination of brighter daylight and cooler temperatures, Dudley added.

Since El Nino leads to warmer days, Dudley said the foliage this fall might be “slightly duller” because trees don’t need as much anthocyanins to protect themselves.

Ontario’s fall colours are particularly breathtaking because the province is home to a variety of woody plants, including maple trees, and has enough daylight on cold fall days, experts said.

“It is … just like a painting out there, and we don’t see this in other parts of the world,” said David Phillips, a climatologist with Environment and Climate Change Canada.

Phillips said while the amount of rainfall varied across the province, the trees generally got enough precipitation over the summer. Even though the temperature was warmer than normal, it wasn’t “excoriatingly” warm, he said.

That is the right mix for the trees to remain healthy and produce vibrant foliage, Phillips said.

El Nino’s warmer weather also gives fall admirers an opportunity to go out and view the gorgeous colours without shivering outside, he added.

“The trees are going to co-operate and they’re going to give their beauty and we’re going to be able to enjoy it,” he said. “Doesn’t matter whether you go to the Muskokas or to your backyard or your park area, you’re going see these brilliant colours because the viewing weather is going to be good.”

The fall colours come in different phases, starting from the north, then moving into the Muskoka area, and finally arriving in central Ontario and the Greater Toronto Area, he said.

Algonquin Provincial Park is already blazing. The park said in its latest fall colour report that sugar and red maples are showing off the season’s best foliage at the canopy level.

The normal window for fall foliage spans from mid-September to late October in Ontario, but Phillips said it has been pushed back by a few weeks this season due to El Nino.

Remnants of hurricanes originating from the Atlantic Ocean often bring heavy rainfall, clouds and powerful winds to Ontario during late summer and early fall, causing the trees to either lose or brown their leaves.

The good news is that El Nino has significantly reduced Atlantic hurricanes this year, Phillips said.

“All we need now is a little bit of time and we’ll be rewarded with this thing that we always look forward to.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 30, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Mark Carney’s stand against Trump leads to Nobel Peace Prize and Time Person of the Year buzz
stories.summary: Toronto (AP) — Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine’s Person of the Year.

TORONTO (AP) — Mark Carney built a global profile in 2026 by standing up to U.S. President Donald Trump. If some prediction-market traders and prominent admirers are right, the Canadian prime minister could end the year with the Nobel Peace Prize and Time magazine’s Person of the Year.

Carney briefly became the favorite Monday for the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Kalshi , a U.S.-based prediction market, when traders on the exchange put his chances at 14%. His odds later fell, illustrating the highly speculative nature of the wagering.

There is no public evidence Carney is on the Nobel Committee’s secret shortlist for the prize that will be announced Oct. 9 in Oslo, Norway.

But the buzz about the Canadian leader possibly winning the esteemed peace prize reflects the message that has raised his profile: Middle powers should band together to defend sovereignty as great powers increasingly use economic and military leverage.

Whether that position resonates with the Nobel Committee is impossible to know. One thing is certain, though: the Nobel and Time’s annual award happen to be two honors Trump covets .

Trump believes he deserves Nobel honor

Carney and Trump are locked in an escalating trade war , with 50% U.S. tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods and Canadian retaliation. Trump also has told Canadian leaders to “fall in line” or face consequences “far WORSE” than existing tariffs.

Trump, who has twice been Time’s Person of the Year, has repeatedly complained about not receiving the Nobel, saying in July that he “should have won that award more than anybody.”

“President Trump would be furious, of course,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. “If this ever happens, I would love to be a fly on the wall of the Oval Office to see the president’s face when he learns about it.”

Trump already possesses a Nobel medal, just not one awarded to him.

Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 Nobel laureate, presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Trump accepted it, while the Nobel Committee stressed the prize itself remains hers.

“Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel,” said Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto. “If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are.”

Carney has strong case for Time award

Time already named Carney one of its 100 most influential people of 2026 and specifically noted his popularity increased as he stood up to Trump.

On Tuesday, Carney was the second choice on major prediction markets for Time’s Person of the Year, behind New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. The winner will be announced Dec. 10.

Time has described Trump’s cumulative impact as helping create a “new global order” increasingly shaped “not by systems or institutions, but by the will of a single man.” Carney’s answer has been to urge middle powers to band together rather than bend one by one.

New York University professor Scott Galloway said Carney has it in the bag and called him “the leader that Europe’s been looking for for the last 20 years.”

“I believe, hands down, Time’s Person of the Year has already been decided and it’s going to be Mark Carney,” Galloway said.

On Galloway’s podcast, journalist Fareed Zakaria said Carney is winning admiration abroad and has given countries facing a less predictable United States “a kind of language and a path” to build new alliances rather than simply bend to Washington.

Carney moving to front of a new global order

Carney’s standing abroad took off in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where he declared the old international order was not coming back and urged middle powers to work together rather than wait for its restoration. His speech came as European leaders were confronting Trump’s push to acquire Greenland and tariff threats.

“We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition,” Carney said in his speech, which received a standing ovation.

Carney has since tried to put the argument for a new global order into practice, pushing Canada closer to Europe and seeking new partners in Asia as Trump’s tariffs fractured the old Canada-U.S. relationship.

European lawmakers gave Carney another standing ovation this month as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed opening the door for Canada to become the European Union’s first associate member .

“Carney’s international profile has been driven by his standing up to Trump, unlike the Europeans and Asians who rushed to make deals with him,” Wiseman said. “Trump’s pressure on Canada has helped elevate Carney in the eyes of the world.”

Rob Gillies, The Associated Press

stories.title: Mary Louie recalls leaving residential school and why her band marks Orange Shirt Day a day early
stories.summary: When Mary Louie was at Residential school she remembers wanting only one thing when she was a young girl at residential school: to get home.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
Mary Louie remembers wanting only one thing when she was a young girl at residential school: to get home.

Louie says she did not understand everything happening around her, but she noticed changes in the friends and became increasingly uneasy.

“Well, I did go to residential school, but what I seen, I didn’t quite understand what was happening,” Louie said.

She eventually escaped the school late one night.

“I stayed off the road. I stayed in the mountains and crossed the highway at night. Walked back and walked home” Louie said.

She says fear did not stop her from making the journey.

“I just walked and I wasn’t afraid or anything, so I just wanted to get home,” she said.

Louie’s story was among those remembered Tuesday as the Lower Similkameen Indian Band (LSIB) held its Community Walk close to Keremeos for Truth and Reconciliation, one day before the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.

Organizers wanted the community to come together for a collective remembrance on Sept. 29, leaving the actual National Day for Truth and Reconciliation for people to commemorate in their own way. Darian Ueusta-Che-Peone, who works with the band, says the group activity is meant to happen beforehand so people can spend Sept. 30 reflecting individually.

“That actual day we can kind of rest and like you know think about what happened and today we celebrate it so we have that kind of rest in between of the day,” he said.

For LSIB elder Herman Edward, residential schools took far more than childhoods from Indigenous families.

“We all lost something. It’s not always the orange shirts, but it was our culture, language, way of life,” Edward said.

But the national day of remembrance has also become a point of controversy.

In Kamloops, masked men were seen protesting Truth and Reconciliation events, drawing condemnation and an RCMP investigation.

Janet Cherbaskin, an LSIB council member, says demonstrations like that cannot erase the experiences of residential school survivors.

“You can’t erase history. It doesn’t matter what you say and how you dress. You can be in masks and and try and prove a point. But to our people, we know what the truth is,” Cherbaskin said.

When Louie finally made it home, she never wanted to return to school. Instead, she stayed home to look after her younger siblings and learned from her grandmother.

“Ever since I got home, my place was to take care of my siblings, so I didn’t go back to school. A lot of the things I’ve learned was from my grandmother and the teaching she gave me,” Louie said.

For Louie, seeing children take part carries particular meaning after her own experience at residential school.

“Well, it’s good to see the children and to know and I pray that the parents love their children and start teaching them,” she said.

After walking home from residential school as a young girl, Louie now sees children walking together as a community

stories.title: Fatal shooting investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (September 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section are investigating a fatal shooting in the downtown core.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (September 30, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Major Crime Section are investigating a fatal shooting in the downtown core.

At approximately 5:45 p.m. on Tuesday, September 29, 2026, police responded to the area of Central Avenue and Richmond Street after receiving reports of a possible shooting.

An adult male was located with life-threatening injuries and transported to hospital by paramedic services, where he was later pronounced deceased.

A suspect male has been arrested and the investigation is ongoing.

Officers are actively investigating this matter and will maintain a visible presence in the area as the investigation continues.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:30 p.m. and 6 p.m., and who may have information, dash-cam footage, or residential or business video surveillance, to contact the London Police Service at 519-661-5670.

The investigation is in its early stages, and more information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-TIPS (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.summary: Foreign Minister Anita Anand vowed continued support for Ukrainian children abducted by Russia and pledged $863,000 in new funding for groups.
stories.author: Ben Cohen

ByBen Cohen City Hall Bureau

As a child, Matviy Chos could see the jaws of the Russian war machine snapping ahead of him. Adults waxed patriotic to him about the glory of feeding yourself to it, as soon as you’re able, to spite the enemy in Ukraine.

“One military person came to our school,” the now 19-year-old said in Toronto Monday through a translator. “We were gathered from eight years to 16. He would tell us about the war, freshly off the front-line where he murdered people. If you are a real man, at 18, you too will go to kill people, especially Ukrainians, who are not a nation and who are not people.”

On Monday, Chos spoke at the two-day Pathways to Peace conference in Toronto with his wife of three weeks, Dariia Tomashova, 18, who also just escaped occupied Crimea, about the tens of thousands of Ukrainian children who aren’t as fortunate as them.

Ukrainian survivors of Russian captivity say they endured attempts at brainwashing in schools, while families of civilians taken by Russia say they live in agony. They spoke at a Toronto summit Canada is co-hosting to build momentum on projects that have returned more than 2,000 children taken by Russia, some of whom are supported upon their return thanks to Canadian-funded projects. (Sept. 28. 2026)

The Canadian Press

Canadian and international authorities say there is a crisis of unlawful deportation, indoctrination and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children into Russian-occupied territory. A report in March by the United Nations’ Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine called these acts by Russia crimes against humanity.

Ukraine estimated that more than 20,000 of its children have been moved from their birthplaces and into Russia or Russian territory. Many have been separated from their parents and placed into Russian state or foster care, officials believe, where some have been physically and sexually abused.

The circumstances of Chos’ birth helped inoculate him against the propaganda, he said. He is from the city of Yevpatoria in the Crimean peninsula, which is internationally recognized as part of Ukraine but was seized by Russia in 2014, when he was six years old. He said he doesn’t remember how Russian forces took over the territory. But he knows that he is a person with a homeland, in spite of what he was raised to believe under occupation.

Growing up, he said he underwent “constant military training.” This, he said, included field trips to military bases and classroom weapons drills.

Six months ago, Chos was at university in Moscow, hoping an education would spare him from the front lines. He was able to escape into unoccupied Ukraine with the help of non-profit humanitarian organization Save Ukraine, which receives funding from the Canadian government.

It was a risky procedure, he said, requiring reams of documentation and a “dangerous” trip through Belarus, during which he said he could have been apprehended and conscripted at any time.

At the conference, which was jointly hosted with Ukraine and Norway,Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced $863,000 in new funding for groups including Save Ukraine. With this, Canada has now committed a total of $7 million to helping abducted children and their families.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is co-hosting a global conference in Toronto on the plight of Ukrainian children abducted by Russian officials. In 2024, the Trudeau government co-launched with Ukraine an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia since it began its full-scale invasion in 2022. (Sept. 28, 2026)

Canada is also offering assistance in the form of artificial intelligence technology, Anand said, which can trace missing Ukrainian children, some of whom have had their names changed as part of Russia’s “systematic effort to separate Ukrainian children from Ukraine.” Officials say 2,573 Ukrainian children have been returned to date. Qatar has been successful in negotiating the release of some of them.

“The testimony that we have heard over the past two days underscores the intense and unacceptable suffering that we know exists at Russia’s hands,” said Anand in her concluding remarks on Tuesday. “We have pledged to find Ukrainians who have been taken from their homes. We have pledged to bring them back, knowing that it can be dangerous, complex, difficult, but above all, necessary.”

Anand spoke to a room in the Exhibition Place Automotive Building full of dignitaries from 73 countries and 10 international organizations, including multiple UN high commissions and the European Union.

“Accountability and the safe return of every child must remain at the centre of our common response,” said the Polish delegate,Arletta Brzozowska. “Poland stands ready to contribute to these efforts.”

Ukrainian Canadian Congress president Alexandra Chyczij was also in attendance Tuesday. She told reporters she was grateful for Canada’s support, which she said has grown under Prime Minster Mark Carney. Ottawa and Kyiv are now in talks to strike a deal ensuring Canada’s political, military and economic aid to the embattled nation continue for the next century.

Chyczij cautioned, however, that efforts to bring these stolen children home might be dashed if Russia is allowed to continue its bombardment of Ukraine. Russia hammered Kyiv with ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones this month, which are too fast for Ukraine to intercept. These attacks destroyed, among other things, Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences, killing at least one person in the process. The president of the academy called the attack an act of terrorism.

“We need to bring these children and POWs and civilians home to something,” said Chyczij. “If the wanton bombing and destruction of Ukraine isn’t stopped, they will have no home to return to.”

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says more than 50 countries and organizations have pledged to continue work on returning abducted children from Russia, along with civilians and prisoners of war. Advocates say those held in Russia and the occupied Ukrainian territories experience violence, and are returned to Ukraine amid frequent airstrikes. (Sept. 29, 2026)

Ben Cohen is part of the Star's city hall bureau, based in Toronto. Follow him on X: @bcohenn.

stories.title: Thousands of Indigenous remains and artifacts are in Canadian museums, schools and homes. This archeologist wants them back
stories.summary: Brandy George is working with First Nations to help find sacred objects and remains of ancestors that were stolen.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
Archaeologist and cultural adviser Brandy George is pictured in Springbank Park in London, Ont. on Monday.She’s working on the Help Us Bring Our Ancestors Home project with the Chiefs of Ontario, who are calling on the Ontario government, institutions and individuals to bring sacred artifacts and ancestors home.

Nicole Osborne for the Toronto Star

Twitter

SMS

Print "Print")

Brandy George said she and her partners are not trying to assign blame, as many people inherited artifacts or remains from grandparents and didn’t understand their significance.

Knowledge Keeper Pat Oakes, from the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, said it’s difficult visiting museums and seeing traditional headdresses on display, knowing they hold spiritual and cultural significance.

ByOmar Mosleh Staff Reporter

Early in her career, Brandy George sat with an Elder in Six Nations of the Grand River, who asked her what she could tell him about his people and traditional territory.

“I said actually no, I consider you to be the experts because they’re your people, your ancestors and it’s your territory,” George recalled.

The Elder smiled.

“You know how many years I’ve been waiting for quote unquote professionals to come in and tell me what you just told me?” he said. “We’ve been waiting for you.”

It was a defining moment for George and cemented her commitment to working directly with First Nations to help them find, reclaim and learn more about the sacred artifacts, belongings and remains of ancestors that were stolen from them. She’s now working on the Help Us Bring Our Ancestors Home project with the Chiefs of Ontario, who are calling on the Ontario government, institutions and individuals to bring sacred artifacts and ancestors home.
