stories.title: B.C. top court judge rules in favour of operators of illicit-drug compassion club
stories.summary: Lawyers had argued the pair who tested illicit drugs for fentanyl before reselling them offered a safer alternative to toxic supply
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
A B.C. Supreme Court judge has struck down a provision in Canada’s federal drug law that prohibits possession for the purposes of trafficking, ruling that it violates the Charter rights of people who use drugs by preventing access to safer alternatives to toxic street drugs.

The Tuesday ruling was in response to a constitutional challenge by Jeremy Kalicum and Eris Nyx, who were convicted of trafficking for operating a compassion club in Vancouver that provided drug users with such unadulterated alternatives for more than a year.

B.C. Supreme Court Justice Catherine Murray declared Section 5(2) of the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act (CDSA) to be “of no force or effect,” finding that it infringes on sections 7 and 15 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which guarantee the right to life, liberty and security of the person, and equal protection under the law.

While the trafficking section of the law was declared invalid, Justice Murray suspended that declaration for six months to allow for legislative amendments. She also stayed the pair’s convictions.

The federal Public Prosecution Service of Canada has 30 days to decide whether to appeal the ruling. Prosecutors are reviewing the judgment and assessing “any potential next steps,” the agency’s spokeswoman Alessia Bongiovanni said.

People in the courtroom gallery cried as the judge read her findings and addressed Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx directly.

“I applaud you for what you’ve done,” Justice Murray said. “I think you should be very proud of yourselves, and it’s people like you who make a difference. And you just did.”

For more than a year, the compassion club founders Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx operated as the Drug User Liberation Front (DULF), buying illicit heroin, cocaine and methamphetamine from the dark web and testing the products at university labs for fentanyl and other impurities. They then sold the drugs at cost to their group’s 43 members.

At the heart of the ruling is what Justice Murray found to be a fundamental contradiction in Canada’s drug laws: A prohibition intended to protect public health and safety can also criminalize actions that can reduce the risk of overdose. But a critic of B.C.’s approach to drug use said the decision fails to account for broader societal harms and called the judge’s praise of the pair “insulting” to police combating the criminal organizations behind the illicit drug trade.

During a multiweek trial and constitutional challenge that unfolded over nine months, the court heard that Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx regularly engaged with top health, government and police officials as they pursued legal pathways to operate the club.

Vancouver Coastal Health officials provided letters of support as they applied to Health Canada for an exemption from drug laws required to operate. Mr. Kalicum regularly e-mailed top police brass with updates.

The court also got a window into the pair’s motivations; the two have responded to more than 100 overdoses and described panic and distress from having watched friends and co-workers die from drugs.

Health Canada denied their application in April, 2022, saying that acquiring drugs from the dark web was “not a viable option.” Jennifer Saxe, director-general of the controlled substances directorate, said the department “is committed to supporting efforts to expand access to a safer supply” nonetheless, and conveyed appreciation for the pair’s “willingness to think and act creatively in search of new solutions.”

Despite the denial, DULF began openly operating the compassion club in August, 2022, out of a Vancouver storefront provided by B.C.’s Ministry of Health. The local health authority provided DULF with up to $200,000 in annual funding for drug-checking and overdose prevention services.

The tides turned in September, 2023, when a magazine article on the pair ignited what Justice Murray called “a maelstrom of activity.” Members of the political opposition rebuked the B.C. NDP for supporting the illegal activity, successfully putting pressure on officials to end funding and the site lease.

In October, 2023, Vancouver Police raided the site and arrested Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx. They were each charged with three counts of possession for the purposes of trafficking and found guilty in November, 2025.

Lawyers Stephanie and Tim Dickson, the married co-counsel for DULF, called 14 witnesses, including five experts, who testified to the causes of the toxic drug crisis, the inadequacy of the current response, the efficacy and limitations of existing prescribed alternatives programs, and the urgent need for expanded access.

In her ruling, Justice Murray said there are “no legally and practically available safety valves in the CDSA to support the implementation of a non-medicalized safer supply program,” which she said is “urgently needed to save lives.” She also found that the compassion club “reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.”

Mr. Dickson called the judgment a vindication.

“This case is about the federal and provincial governments’ refusal to implement that life-saving measure, and it is also about how the federal legislation effectively blocks any effort to implement that measure,” he said outside the courthouse.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, who as the former BC United addiction critic in 2023 called for an investigation into the public funding of DULF, called the ruling worrisome. She argued that Justice Murray gave insufficient weight to the broader harms of the program, including its funding of criminal organizations through dark-web drug purchases.

Ms. Sturko, a former RCMP officer, supports providing pharmaceutical alternatives to illicit drugs through medically supervised programs, but rejects models that make them available outside of a health care setting.

She said governments should focus on recovery-oriented systems of care and urged Ottawa to appeal the decision.

“British Columbians have resoundingly said that they do not think that the answer to our drug crisis is more drugs,” she said.

John Conroy is a Vancouver-area lawyer who was involved in successful challenges at the Supreme Court against parts of the federal drug law, first in 2011 in the Insite case over supervised drug injection and then in 2015 in the Smith case over medical marijuana. The top court, in both cases, ruled parts of the drug legislation violated Section 7 of the Charter, similar to Tuesday’s ruling.

“This is very good news,” Mr. Conroy said of the latest judgment. “It is going to be interesting to see what the government does to rectify the unconstitutionality.”

In the Insite case, the Supreme Court ordered Ottawa to allow the facility to keep operating. In the medical marijuana case, the court said the government had to provide reasonable access for patients for possession and use of cannabis through a health care practitioner.

Editor’s note: The headline on this story has been corrected to state that the ruling was made by a B.C. Supreme Court judge. The story has also been corrected to refer to the Controlled Drugs and Substances Act, not the Canadian Drugs and Substances Act, as previously published.

The tides turned in September, 2023, when a magazine article on the pair ignited what Justice Murray called “a maelstrom of activity.” Members of the political opposition rebuked the B.C. NDP for supporting the illegal activity, successfully putting pressure on officials to end funding and the site lease.

In October, 2023, Vancouver Police raided the site and arrested Mr. Kalicum and Ms. Nyx. They were each charged with three counts of possession for the purposes of trafficking and found guilty in November, 2025.

Lawyers Stephanie and Tim Dickson, the married co-counsel for DULF, called 14 witnesses, including five experts, who testified to the causes of the toxic drug crisis, the inadequacy of the current response, the efficacy and limitations of existing prescribed alternatives programs, and the urgent need for expanded access.

content_blocks.text: In her ruling, Justice Murray said there are “no legally and practically available safety valves in the CDSA to support the implementation of a non-medicalized safer supply program,” which she said is “urgently needed to save lives.” She also found that the compassion club “reduced the harms associated with the toxic drug crisis and did not negatively impact the community or public safety.”
Mr. Dickson called the judgment a vindication.

“This case is about the federal and provincial governments’ refusal to implement that life-saving measure, and it is also about how the federal legislation effectively blocks any effort to implement that measure,” he said outside the courthouse.

CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko, who as the former BC United addiction critic in 2023 called for an investigation into the public funding of DULF, called the ruling worrisome. She argued that Justice Murray gave insufficient weight to the broader harms of the program, including its funding of criminal organizations through dark-web drug purchases.

content_blocks.text: Ms. Sturko, a former RCMP officer, supports providing pharmaceutical alternatives to illicit drugs through medically supervised programs, but rejects models that make them available outside of a health care setting.
She said governments should focus on recovery-oriented systems of care and urged Ottawa to appeal the decision.
“British Columbians have resoundingly said that they do not think that the answer to our drug crisis is more drugs,” she said.

John Conroy is a Vancouver-area lawyer who was involved in successful challenges at the Supreme Court against parts of the federal drug law, first in 2011 in the Insite case over supervised drug injection and then in 2015 in the Smith case over medical marijuana. The top court, in both cases, ruled parts of the drug legislation violated Section 7 of the Charter, similar to Tuesday’s ruling.
“This is very good news,” Mr. Conroy said of the latest judgment. “It is going to be interesting to see what the government does to rectify the unconstitutionality.”

In the Insite case, the Supreme Court ordered Ottawa to allow the facility to keep operating. In the medical marijuana case, the court said the government had to provide reasonable access for patients for possession and use of cannabis through a health care practitioner.

stories.title: Mother speaks out after video shows fight at London school
stories.summary: A London mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

A London, Ont., mother says her two children were assaulted during recess at C.C. Carrothers Public School and is raising concerns about what she describes as ongoing bullying.

Sammy Riley shared a video on social media that she says shows her 11-year-old daughter and nine-year-old son being attacked by other youths at the school.

The graphic video appears to show a young girl being hit by several people before a young boy is kicked in the head.

“I was heartbroken, I was sick to my stomach,” Riley said. “That was a vicious and vile attack.”

Riley says she took her son to hospital, where she says he was diagnosed with a minor concussion.

She also alleges her children have experienced ongoing bullying at the school for the past three years.

“I’ve been dealing with this school for the past three years, with the bullying and the constant everything, it’s just getting brushed under the rug,” she said.

‘No place for violence’: school board

Riley says she previously tried to have her children transferred to another school, but that request was denied because of where they live.

She has since contacted the Thames Valley District School Board, London police and other authorities.

The school board declined a request for an interview but said it is aware of the incident and an investigation is underway.

“The school board takes incidents like these very seriously and there is no place for violence inside or outside of TVDSB classrooms,” the board said in a statement.

Police investigating

The London Police Service says it began investigating on Sept. 24 after receiving a report of an assault at a school earlier that day.

Police say the investigation is in its early stages as they gather information and determine the circumstances surrounding the incident. All those involved are youths.

Police say no charges will be laid, if all parties involved are under the age of 12.

Riley says she has removed her children from the school for the time being but remains concerned about the safety of other students.

“I feel that they’re not doing anything to make it better or a safer situation for any of the children, because I’m not just worried about my own children now,” she said. “I’m worried about all those other children there.”

The Thames Valley District School Board says students are subject to its Code of Conduct, which includes policies and procedures related to suspension, expulsion, and other disciplinary measures.

stories.title: Toronto woman says Meta won’t let her talk to a human after killing her accounts
stories.summary: Ottawa — A Toronto woman says Meta permanently shut down her Facebook and Instagram accounts without warning — and her only recourse has been to talk to AI chatbots.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A Toronto woman says Meta permanently shut down her Facebook and Instagram accounts without warning — and her only recourse has been to talk to AI chatbots.

Jasmine Ault told The Canadian Press she has not been able to reach a human being at Meta since the accounts were deactivated on Sept. 24.

She said the company shut down her 20-year-old Facebook account, an Instagram account that dates back to 2011 and another Instagram account dedicated to her dog.

“It’s actually quite scary to think about the trust that we put in the social media platforms that can all be taken away in one day,” she said in an interview.

Ault compared the experience to losing belongings in a fire.

“That’s how it feels. And it’s really upsetting because the hypothetical, the metaphorical fire that I’m referring to, is my memories.”

She said she has lost her social media contacts and is unable to let people know she hasn’t blocked them and isn’t ignoring them.

“There’s a dead end and I can’t even communicate to the people I want to communicate with,” Ault said.

She described the experience as isolating, leaving her unable to look back at memories, connect with people, or see what they are up to through their posts.

Meta didn’t give Ault a reason for shutting down her accounts and said only that her Facebook account “doesn’t follow our rules.”

Ault said she hadn’t posted on Facebook in years, though she did post frequently on Instagram.

She said she suspects someone tried to hack her account because she found a record of suspicious login attempts shortly before the account was deactivated. Meta also had her phone number associated with a person who lives in India.

Ault said she has only been able to talk to Meta’s AI chatbots, which have not been able to resolve the issue. After she requested a review, the chatbot told her it was unsuccessful and her Facebook account had been “permanently disabled.”

She said she hasn’t been able to contact a human being at the company despite signing up for and paying for a verified account, a service that Meta says includes direct help from human agents.

“If Facebook wants to be the main conglomerate for social media, they need to be accessible,” she said.

Media outlets have reported similar experiences among users of Meta’s platforms in the United States. In July, The New York Times profiled several users whose accounts were deleted by AI, and who then had to rely on AI to resolve the issue.

Meta restored some of the accounts after the newspaper flagged them to the company. Two of those accounts had been hacked before they were deactivated.

Markus Giesler, a professor of marketing at York University, said social media platforms have become very important to people’s personal lives and careers.

“We like to think of this as a customer service case when in actuality it’s a case of platform accountability,” he said.

“These platforms have been woven so much into our social fabric, into who we are as individuals and communities, that access to them is really important.”

Giesler said efforts to regulate social media platforms should also address issues like access and being able to talk to a human being at a company.

He said suspending an account can have personal financial consequences.

Ault, who is working full-time as a manager of marketing and communications, said she has used her social media in the past to find clients for her own consulting agency. Without her accounts, that’s not possible at the moment.

“They have nothing to look at. They can’t see my portfolio of work,” she said.

When contacted by The Canadian Press, a Meta spokesperson pointed to a blog post that provides information on how to access account support. It includes an update from March saying Meta was rolling out an AI support assistant.

The spokesperson did not provide any comment or respond to questions — such as how a person with a deactivated account can contact a human being at Meta.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: University of Guelph promises review, changes after chaotic homecoming party
stories.summary: The president of the University of Guelph says a large, unsanctioned homecoming party off campus last weekend risked the safety of students and neighbours and the school will work to prevent such incidents in the future.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
After an off-campus University of Guelph homecoming party descended into chaos last weekend, other Ontario universities say they are working to minimize the impacts of similar upcoming events.

Sept. 29, 2026

By Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press

The unsanctioned party in Guelph on Saturday risked the safety of students and neighbours, university president Rene Van Acker said in a statement.

Videos circulating online show massive crowds of young people filling the streets, and some of them throwing bottles and other items as police officers tried to control the situation. The videos also show police putting some people in handcuffs.

The president of the University of Guelph says a large, unsanctioned gathering near the campus last weekend risked the safety of students and neighbours. (Sept. 29, 2026)

The Canadian Press

“The University of Guelph is deeply disappointed by what occurred, and we are clear that this cannot happen again,” Van Acker said, adding that the school will review the incident.

He said the people who got involved in property damage and other disruptive behaviour also included those who do not attend the university.

Guelph police said the gathering was “significantly larger” than similar events in recent years and officers were dealing with objects being thrown, people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.

They said officers laid several criminal and provincial charges, including causing a disturbance and numerous alcohol-related offences.

“Homecoming is an opportunity for students, residents and visitors to celebrate together. Most people enjoyed the day responsibly, but behaviour that puts others at risk cannot be accepted,” said Guelph police Chief Gord Cobey.

Guelph is not the only university town that has at times struggled to contain rowdy off-campus parties in the fall.

In Ottawa, the annual Panda Game between Carleton University and the University of Ottawa football teams is taking place this weekend and Carleton said it recognizes the event can affect nearby communities.

Post-game misbehaviour in recent years included people flipping a car and stealing street signs, and has sent several people to the hospital.

Carleton University spokesperson Steven Reid said the school is working closely with the University of Ottawa, the city, Ottawa Police and others to ensure safety for everyone this year.

“We are taking steps before, during and after the game to minimize those impacts,” he said. “We are also continuing to communicate with students about their responsibilities, the importance of being good neighbours and the consequences of unlawful or disruptive behaviour.”

Another homecoming party is scheduled in Kingston, Ont., starting on Oct. 16 for Queen’s University students and alumni.

A spokesperson for the school said preparations for the event include planning and co-ordination with the city, police, student leaders and groups across the university.

Students are reminded of local bylaws and potential fines, as well as responsible behaviour, the university said.

“Those found in violation of nuisance party regulations, noise bylaws, or open liquor laws can face fines from $50 to $2,000 and sanctions under the Queen’s University Non-Academic Misconduct system,” it said.

stories.title: Trump’s Canadian booze ban will hurt American restaurants, U.S. body warns
stories.summary: Trump's previously announced bans — which affect some alcoholic drinks, dairy byproducts and motorcycles, among other goods — came into force at 12:01 a.m. ET Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war against Canada escalated on Tuesday with his outright ban on certain Canadian goods going into effect and a U.S. industry body is warning that his ban on Canadian alcohol will “ripple through” the U.S. restaurant industry.

“This new ban on Canadian alcohol products will ripple throughout the U.S. hospitality sector at a time when restaurants, bars and retailers are preparing for the busy holiday season,” Toasts Not Tariffs Coalition, an alliance of 59 U.S. alcohol industry groups, said in a statement.

Trump’s trade war against Canada has “has already taken a significant toll on U.S. wine and spirits producers,” the coalition added.

“The best outcome remains a negotiated solution that gets American spirits and wine products back on Canadian shelves, preserves consumer choice for consumers on both sides of the border and allows U.S. and Canadian hospitality businesses to focus on growth rather than becoming collateral damage in a trade dispute beyond their control,” the statement said.

Trump’s previously announced bans — which affect some alcoholic drinks, dairy byproducts and motorcycles, among other goods — came into force at 12:01 a.m. ET Tuesday.

0:45 New U.S. bans to take effect Tuesday: Here’s what’s affected

The bans mark the latest escalation of the trade war as the Trump administration seeks to pressure Canada into concessions in trade talks.

The trade restrictions could prove devastating for the affected industries, stakeholders say, though experts have cautioned the overall impact on Canada’s impact could be limited.

Trade talks collapsed between Canada and the United States last month after Ottawa walked away from the negotiating table in response to last-minute terms that Prime Minister Mark Carney says the U.S. demanded, including restrictions on Canada entering into new trade deals with other countries.

Since then, Trump has escalated his economic attacks against Canada, imposing multiple rounds of tariffs as well as import restrictions.

–with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: 16 charged in cocaine trafficking investigation in Quebec
stories.summary: The charges are the result of a years-long investigation called "Project Chrome" and led to people ranging in age from 24 to 73 being arrested.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
RCMP in Quebec say 16 people have been charged in connection with cocaine trafficking, with the search ongoing for one person who is believed to be abroad.

The arrests are the result of “Project Chrome,” an investigation that began in 2022 and included officers from the RCMP’s Combined Forces Special Enforcement Unit and Money Laundering Investigative Team. The Canada Revenue Agency assisted in the investigation.

Through the investigation, police determined six buildings were linked to members of an alleged criminal organization and are now subject to restraint orders.

The total value of property seized, according to RCMP, is more than $9 million. This includes 14 kilograms of cocaine and more than $145,000 in cash.

Of the 16 charged, 11 are from Montreal and range in age from 24 to 73.

Four of the accused are a 28-year-old and 55-year-old from Sainte-Julienne, a 44-year-old from Blainville, and a 30-year-old from Gatineau.

Several of the suspects are believed to be members of the Lopez-Oliverio family.

RCMP Cpl. Martina Pillarova says the arrested suspects include 61-year-old Franco Lopez, who allegedly led the group with assistance from his 53-year-old brother Pasquale and other family members.

Police say the group is alleged to have operated an illegal gaming house in Montreal as well as having sold drugs and used the proceeds to finance renovations to buildings linked to its members.

Police said one of the 16 suspects remains wanted abroad.

The suspects face multiple charges, including trafficking cocaine, possession of cocaine for the purpose of trafficking, laundering proceeds of crime, possession of and trafficking in property obtained by crime and conspiracy. They have also been charged with offences committed for the benefit of or at the direction of a criminal organization, and various offences under the Income Tax Act.

A court appearance is expected Tuesday with 15 set to appear.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Parti Québécois could win majority despite low support for sovereignty
stories.summary: With a fragmented electoral map, voters who want to avoid a referendum have failed to coalesce around any of the PQ’s opponents
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Quebec may be on the cusp of electing a Parti Québécois majority government that has promised to hold a referendum on independence in the next four years, despite the fact that most voters don’t want to separate from Canada.

Just under a week out from the Oct. 5 election , Quebec’s political landscape remains so divided that the PQ could nab a majority of the province’s 127 seats with scarcely 30 per cent of the vote. It would be an unprecedented ending to an unusual campaign, in which none of the PQ’s four opponents have been able to mount a compelling case against the sovereigntist party.

“Even though an overwhelming majority of Quebeckers, francophones included, do not want a PQ government, they are the least despised of all parties,” said David Heurtel, a political analyst and former provincial Liberal cabinet minister.

In an election that has failed to excite many voters, support for the PQ has barely moved. There is no groundswell of separatist sentiment in Quebec. But neither does there appear to be much concern about the prospect of a vote on secession in the not-too-distant future. After all, if there is a referendum, Quebeckers seem to be saying, they can just vote “no.”

The Parti Québécois has maintained a lead in the polls for the better part of three years, as the popularity of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec collapsed. But PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s promise to hold the province’s third referendum on independence has limited the party’s appeal beyond its sovereigntist base. For much of the campaign, which began in late August, his lead was narrow and his grasp on power seemed uncertain.

Still, the PQ has benefited from regional divisions that could see five parties win seats in the National Assembly next week. Three of the five oppose holding a vote on separation, but none has managed to rally the anti-referendum forces. Fewer than 30 per cent of Quebeckers say they would vote for independence.

Early in the campaign, the CAQ seemed to be making a comeback under the leadership of Premier Christine Fréchette, who positioned herself as a safe bet during an escalating trade war with the United States.

But weak debate performances and voters’ desire for change have taken the wind out of her sails. Three polls early this week showed support for the CAQ slipping below 20 per cent, and the party once again seems to be fighting for survival.

Meanwhile, the Quebec Liberals have not managed to connect with francophone voters outside Montreal, and the newcomer Conservatives, who have run a strong campaign, are not yet competitive across much of the province outside the Quebec City region. The left-leaning Québec solidaire is working to hold on to the handful of seats it holds in urban ridings.

The result is that the PQ could win the 64 seats it needs for a majority without ever having polled above 30 per cent during the campaign – the lowest vote share in Quebec history for a majority government, Mr. Heurtel said. “It just shows how broken the electoral system is,” he added. “The system was not built for five parties that are able to generate support between 12 and 30 per cent of the electorate.”

The PQ Leader has been consistent about his plan for a vote on secession since he took over the party in 2020, and he laid out his vision for an independent Quebec in a 524-page book published in June.

By being transparent, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon took the edge off people’s fears, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “He managed to normalize it,” she said. “I hear a lot of people say it doesn’t scare them that much. It doesn’t scare them that there could be a consultation on Quebec sovereignty and they will simply vote ‘no.’”

In August, the PQ Leader announced he would not hold a referendum until U.S. President Donald Trump exits the White House in 2029 – a move that ensured his rivals would struggle to capitalize on his Achilles’ heel. He has largely avoided speaking about independence ever since.

Sébastien Dallaire, chief insights officer at polling firm Leger, said younger voters who have no memory of the 1995 referendum may be less fearful about the implications of another divisive debate on sovereignty. “Throughout the campaign, we haven’t heard that much about what the consequences of another referendum would be,” he said.

According to a poll published Sunday by the firm Synopsis Recherche, only 14 per cent of Quebeckers believe the province would vote to separate from Canada in a referendum. Among those who said they would vote “yes,” only 40 per cent thought a referendum would be successful. (The poll surveyed 1,000 people recruited through online panels between Sept. 24 and 27.)

“For Quebeckers right now, in their minds, the referendum is kind of settled,” said Mr. Heurtel, who added that voters have much more prosaic concerns about the cost of living, health care and housing. “This is not today’s question.”

Still, he said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon would struggle to govern with just 30 per cent support, even with a majority. “Basically, you don’t have a mandate,” he said. “Most Quebeckers don’t feel he’s the guy.”
paragraphs: Quebec may be on the cusp of electing a Parti Québécois majority government that has promised to hold a referendum on independence in the next four years, despite the fact that most voters don’t want to separate from Canada.

Just under a week out from the Oct. 5 election , Quebec’s political landscape remains so divided that the PQ could nab a majority of the province’s 127 seats with scarcely 30 per cent of the vote. It would be an unprecedented ending to an unusual campaign, in which none of the PQ’s four opponents have been able to mount a compelling case against the sovereigntist party.

“Even though an overwhelming majority of Quebeckers, francophones included, do not want a PQ government, they are the least despised of all parties,” said David Heurtel, a political analyst and former provincial Liberal cabinet minister.

In an election that has failed to excite many voters, support for the PQ has barely moved. There is no groundswell of separatist sentiment in Quebec. But neither does there appear to be much concern about the prospect of a vote on secession in the not-too-distant future. After all, if there is a referendum, Quebeckers seem to be saying, they can just vote “no.”

The Parti Québécois has maintained a lead in the polls for the better part of three years, as the popularity of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec collapsed. But PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s promise to hold the province’s third referendum on independence has limited the party’s appeal beyond its sovereigntist base. For much of the campaign, which began in late August, his lead was narrow and his grasp on power seemed uncertain.

Still, the PQ has benefited from regional divisions that could see five parties win seats in the National Assembly next week. Three of the five oppose holding a vote on separation, but none has managed to rally the anti-referendum forces. Fewer than 30 per cent of Quebeckers say they would vote for independence.

Early in the campaign, the CAQ seemed to be making a comeback under the leadership of Premier Christine Fréchette, who positioned herself as a safe bet during an escalating trade war with the United States.

But weak debate performances and voters’ desire for change have taken the wind out of her sails. Three polls early this week showed support for the CAQ slipping below 20 per cent, and the party once again seems to be fighting for survival.

Meanwhile, the Quebec Liberals have not managed to connect with francophone voters outside Montreal, and the newcomer Conservatives, who have run a strong campaign, are not yet competitive across much of the province outside the Quebec City region. The left-leaning Québec solidaire is working to hold on to the handful of seats it holds in urban ridings.

The result is that the PQ could win the 64 seats it needs for a majority without ever having polled above 30 per cent during the campaign – the lowest vote share in Quebec history for a majority government, Mr. Heurtel said. “It just shows how broken the electoral system is,” he added. “The system was not built for five parties that are able to generate support between 12 and 30 per cent of the electorate.”

The PQ Leader has been consistent about his plan for a vote on secession since he took over the party in 2020, and he laid out his vision for an independent Quebec in a 524-page book published in June.

By being transparent, Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon took the edge off people’s fears, said political analyst Antonine Yaccarini. “He managed to normalize it,” she said. “I hear a lot of people say it doesn’t scare them that much. It doesn’t scare them that there could be a consultation on Quebec sovereignty and they will simply vote ‘no.’”

In August, the PQ Leader announced he would not hold a referendum until U.S. President Donald Trump exits the White House in 2029 – a move that ensured his rivals would struggle to capitalize on his Achilles’ heel. He has largely avoided speaking about independence ever since.

Sébastien Dallaire, chief insights officer at polling firm Leger, said younger voters who have no memory of the 1995 referendum may be less fearful about the implications of another divisive debate on sovereignty. “Throughout the campaign, we haven’t heard that much about what the consequences of another referendum would be,” he said.

According to a poll published Sunday by the firm Synopsis Recherche, only 14 per cent of Quebeckers believe the province would vote to separate from Canada in a referendum. Among those who said they would vote “yes,” only 40 per cent thought a referendum would be successful. (The poll surveyed 1,000 people recruited through online panels between Sept. 24 and 27.)

“For Quebeckers right now, in their minds, the referendum is kind of settled,” said Mr. Heurtel, who added that voters have much more prosaic concerns about the cost of living, health care and housing. “This is not today’s question.”

Still, he said Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon would struggle to govern with just 30 per cent support, even with a majority. “Basically, you don’t have a mandate,” he said. “Most Quebeckers don’t feel he’s the guy.”

stories.title: ‘A special opportunity’: Chayka explains Maple Leafs’ push for Marchenko-Knies blockbuster
stories.summary: Chayka thanked Knies, Steven Lorentz and Emil Andrae for their service and acknowledged that Columbus was getting a strong asset.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Luke Fox, Sportsnet

Posted September 29, 2026 12:12 pm.

The best player in the deal, regardless of cap hit or sweeteners or cost of doing business.

That is what John Chayka was gunning for in Monday’s blockbuster trade that sent cap-friendly power forward Matthew Knies to the Columbus Blue Jackets and brought top-line winger Kirill Marchenko to the Toronto Maple Leafs.

“There’s a lot of good players in the NHL, very few that can impact winning and can single-handedly dictate outcomes of games. We believe that Kirill is one of those players for us,” Toronto’s general manager said Tuesday morning, just hours after the trade and hours before the club’s home opener against the Montreal Canadiens (Sportsnet, Sportsnet+, 7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT).

Marchenko inked a six-year, $75-million extension, which required Mlse ownership’s stamp of approval, as part of the transaction.

“A big commitment from the club. That was a player that wasn’t willing to just go anywhere. Wants to win. He wants to be part of a world-class organization,” Chayka said.

“While it’s an expensive player, we think it’s a player that fits and we can build around.”

The GM described the deal as “complicated.” Discussions on sending Knies, who lacks trade protection, to Columbus began early in the off-season and grew serious over the past several weeks.

A fire was burning under all that smoke.

The Blue Jackets knew Marchenko had no interest in re-signing in Ohio and are adamant about changing their culture. They want players who want to be there.

Thing is, Knies wanted to stay in Toronto. That wasn’t enough, however, to prevent the aggressive Chayka from seeking an upgrade — a play driver with 40-goal potential who can complement centres Auston Matthews and John Tavares.

“You have to give up quality to get quality, and we gave up some quality people and some quality players,” Chayka said. “But ultimately, my job is to always make the team as best as possible. And not just collect talent but put together a team that fits and works.”

Simply put: The Leafs see more upside in Marchenko, a speedy right shot who can play both wings, transport the puck and snipe from distance.

“He skates very well with the puck,” coach Jim Hiller said. “A lot of times a player can skate really well, they get the puck and they slow down a little bit. He’s one of those guys that seems to accelerate with the puck. I know he loves having the puck.

“He’s a shot threat, and he distributes. So, there’s lots there for us. He’ll be a really strong addition.”

As for the subtraction, Chris Tanev says the room was “very surprised” by the deal, particularly with the timing of it landing one day before puck drop and a couple days after the club flew to Knies’s home state of Arizona to bond.

“It can be a s—– business, right?” Tanev said. “He’s a great guy and very good player, so Columbus is getting a horse with him. And just good person, good player. Obviously, he’ll be missed here. It’s a s—– part of the business, but we’re welcoming in an amazing player that I’ve heard nothing but great things about.

“(Marchenko) is a very dynamic player, and he’s tough to defend. So, we’re very excited to have him on our team as well.”

Chayka thanked Knies, Steven Lorentz and Emil Andrae for their service and acknowledged that Columbus was getting a strong asset.

“Matthew’s a great player. There’s no doubt about it,” Chayka said. “Look, I apologized to him for the noise over the last several months. I don’t think it was necessarily fair to him. This was the only (trade) we seriously considered as a management crew. These things happen. He understands. He’s a professional athlete, and he’s a smart kid. But he took the news well. I mean, it’s a good young team he’s going to. I think it’s a good fit for him. I think he’ll do well.”

Marchenko is in Toronto sorting out his immigration and work visa, but his availability for the home opener is unknown. If he plays, Chayka will dress eight(!) forwards making their Maple Leafs debuts.

That alone speaks to the GM’s overhaul of a roster he assures he’ll remain “patiently aggressive” to improve as the season unfolds.

The deal-maker ain’t done dealin’.

“We’re not going to do anything before tonight,” Chayka said, “but then we’ll react as the team plays.”

Miles Wood will have “a chance to earn his way back up” to the NHL, according to Chayka. The forechecker cleared waivers prior to the trade and will start the season with the Marlies.

Elvis Merzlikins (shoulder) will require four to six months of rehab and starts the season on long-term injured reserve. Chayka says he’s “hopeful” the goalie can return to action…. Rookie Gavin McKenna skipped Tuesday’s optional morning skate ahead of his pro debut. Power move.

By Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press

But it’s the British Columbia NDP leader’s election campaign that got a boost with the announcement of the $33-billion Phase 2 expansion of LNG Canada’s liquefied natural gas export terminal on the northern B.C. coast in Kitimat.

Eby smiled as he stepped onto a stage in Vancouver shortly after Carney welcomed LNG Canada’s final investment decision on Tuesday.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

“What a day for British Columbia, what a day for our country,” he said.

The NDP leader, who called a snap election last week, said LNG Canada’s decision is a “very big deal” that will create 4,000 new construction jobs and $28 billion in revenues for government to help fund public services.

Eby’s party took credit just minutes after the announcement was made.

“For years, the B.C. NDP worked closely with the federal government and the company to advance the project and build the confidence needed to secure this investment,” the party said in a statement.

Former B.C. Liberal premier Christy Clark first proposed a massive expansion of the liquefied natural gas industry, promising in the 2013 election campaign to use the revenue to wipe out provincial debt.

The LNG expansion would double LNG Canada’s capacity to 28 million tonnes a year and it is one of the first five developments referred to Ottawa’s major projects office last year.

Eby, who appeared at the event in his capacity as premier, thanked the prime minister for moving the project forward so quickly after Carney took office.

“I want to thank you for giving this project the attention it deserves, because it will change lives for the better here and around the world with stable, reliable, predictable, low-carbon Canadian energy,” he said.

Carney said at an unrelated news conference after he announced the expansion that the five companies that are part of LNG Canada determined the timing.

Stewart Prest, who teaches political science at the University of B.C., said the announcement will help Eby’s party blunt some of the attacks from the provincial Conservatives, who have accused government of standing in the way of resource projects.

“I think it is a really important proof point for the premier and the NDP to say that they are doing the kinds of the things that are necessary to get the province through this moment,” Prest said.

While the development might not convince Conservatives to switch their votes, it would allow New Democrats to neutralize the issue, he added.

Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson said at an unrelated news conference Tuesday that he is thrilled that the federal government has pushed the LNG expansion through.

“I know David Eby will certainly enjoy a moment here, but the reality is that we need to work with our federal government to promote this.”

The B.C. Conservatives announced on Monday that its government, if elected, would triple provincial LNG production by 2035, but the NDP noted that the promise already falls well below the current pace of development.

Doerkson was in Maple Ridge on Tuesday, where he announced that a future government of his would remove the Provincial Sales Tax on Canadian alcohol for the duration of the current trade war with the United States.

At the LNG announcement, Carney didn’t mention Eby past his opening address, but said that all levels of government were pulling in the same direction, along with dozens of First Nations, the private sector, workers and communities across northern B.C.

“This is team Canada at work,” Carney told a group of business leaders, First Nations and politicians at the event organized by LNG Canada.

Green Leader Emily Lowan says in a statement that she is deeply disappointed by the approval of the expansion, noting that LNG Canada is an entirely-foreign owned project.

“The profits from LNG development flow directly to shareholders and governments abroad, while the costs stay here,” she said.

“Families in Kitimat and Terrace are already living with the health effects: dirtier air, rising asthma rates, and rogue flares lighting up the sky.”

Eby has previously said that not all British Columbians support LNG, but Prest said he is not sure whether Lowan’s party could benefit from the announcement by attracting soft NDP voters concerned about resource development.

“Over the last 18 months or so, there is a greater willingness among the population to embrace the idea of resource development in the shorter term to meet the urgent need and to sort of place climate change on the back-burner, even though climate change has no interest in going on the back-burner itself,” Prest said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Heated Rivalry production company launches real-life Irina Foundation to support inclusivity in sports and arts
stories.summary: Created by Accent Aigu Entertainment co-founders Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady, new fund is based on Shane and Ilya’s fictional charity
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
The Toronto-based production company behind Heated Rivalry has announced the launch of Irina Foundation, a new fund dedicated to promoting mental well-being and inclusivity through organized sports and arts programs.

The foundation, launched by Accent Aigu Entertainment, will likely sound familiar to fans of Heated Rivalry or author Rachel Reid’s Game Changers series. In the books (and briefly teased in Heated Rivalry ’s first season), fictional hockey players Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov start a charity of the same name to raise money and awareness for mental illness.

Named after Ilya’s late mother Irina, the foundation ultimately serves as a symbol of Shane and Ilya’s love for one another – and, at least at first, as a means of concealing their deepening romantic relationship with each other.

The real-life Irina Foundation was created by Accent Aigu Entertainment co-founders Jacob Tierney and Brendan Brady, and announced on opening day of the 2026-27 NHL season . It will support organizations that create inclusive spaces for LGBTQ+ and other underserved communities.

“For many of us, some of life’s most meaningful moments happen on a team, in a studio or on a stage – places where we find our people, discover what lights us up and feel like we belong,” said Tierney and Brady in a media release. “We’ve been incredibly lucky to build something we love and along the way find a community that means so much to us. The Foundation is our way of giving back.”

The donor-advised fund has been established in Canada through TD Wealth’s Private Giving Foundation. In the U.S., the fund will be powered by Panorama Global, a 501(c)3 nonprofit organization that will provide the requisite philanthropic scaffolding for the foundation under U.S. charity law.

Kate Spade New York will be Irina Foundation’s inaugural donor. (Spade, the iconic fashion designer and entrepreneur, died by suicide in 2018.) U.S. men’s grooming brand Harry’s will also join as an early supporter of the fund.

“We hope to channel the love people have for the world Rachel has created, and for Shane and Ilya, into something that can make a meaningful difference in the real world,” said Jayme Alter Wilson, president of Accent Aigu Entertainment, in a statement.

Filming for Heated Rivalry ’s second season is under way. Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams will reprise their roles as Ilya and Shane. The show’s second season will also include newcomers Justice Smith, Charlie Gillespie, Emily Hampshire, Milla Jovovich, Paul Gross and Priyanka.

While a specific release date has not yet been confirmed for season two, it is expected to hit Canadian streaming service Crave in spring 2027.

stories.title: Only 12% of Canadians ‘very hopeful’ about democracy: StatCan
stories.summary: A new Statistics Canada study revealed that only 12 per cent of respondents were “very hopeful” about democracy, while 17 per cent were "not at all hopeful."
stories.author: Ted Ballantyne
stories.content:
A new Statistics Canada study revealed that only 12 per cent of respondents were “very hopeful” about democracy, while 17 per cent were “not at all hopeful.” The remaining 71 per cent of respondents were a little or somewhat hopeful about the future of democracy.

The survey also asked Canadians about their confidence in institutions and political engagement. More likely to be politically active Of the Canadians who reported being not at all hopeful about democracy, StatCan found those respondents were more likely to sign petitions and research political issues.

The survey also showed that 26 per cent of the least hopeful were likely to boycott or choose products based on ethical reasons, compared to 15 per cent of the most hopeful. One category that came out even across all levels of hopefulness was voting rates, according to the data.

Regardless of how much hope respondents had about democracy, voting rates for the 2021 federal election were similar across the board. However, the least hopeful Canadians were more likely to report participation in other political activities.

Less trust in information sources StatCan’s study showed that Canadians who had the least hope about the way democracy works were less likely to trust news outlets. The study said only 17 per cent of respondents who were not at all hopeful had a high feeling of trust.

Canadians who were more hopeful about democracy were more likely to trust information sources. Fifty-nine per cent of the most hopeful respondents reported high trust in news outlets, while 43 per cent who were a little or somewhat hopeful had a high feeling of trust.

The study noted similar patterns of trust in government communication and scientific sources. People who were more hopeful about democracy reported higher levels of trust in these sources than those were less hopeful. When it came to trust in close personal contacts and other Internet sources, levels of trust were similar across all groups.

More trust in institutions The data showed that respondents who were very hopeful about democracy were more likely to report high confidence in federal parliament, at 67 per cent. While only 11 per cent of the least hopeful respondents reported a feeling of high confidence.

The survey found similar trends for institutions such as the school system, justice system, courts, banks, major corporations and Canadian media. About the study The study titled, “Taking the pulse: Perceptions of democracy in Canada,” used data from a 2024 survey of people 15 and older.

The survey asked Canadians about their hopefulness in how democracy works in the country. The study also examined trust in information sources and institutions, as well as participation in political activities. According to StatCan, ‘hopefulness about the future’ was analyzed by asking this question: “Thinking about the future in Canada, how hopeful are you about the way democracy works in Canada?” Respondents could answer very hopeful, somewhat hopeful, a little hopeful and not at all hopeful.

People who were more hopeful about democracy reported higher levels of trust in these sources than those were less hopeful. stories.title: London officer suspended after video showing alcohol in police vehicle
stories.summary: Chief Thai Truong says a criminal investigation is also being launched as the video shows a service weapon being stored in "circumstances that raise concerns."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A police officer in London, Ont., has been suspended after a video that the force’s police chief says showed members entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside.

Chief Thai Truong says a criminal investigation is also being launched as the video shows a service weapon being stored in “circumstances that raise concerns.”

He says it happened June 24 in Toronto as officers left a restaurant after a police funeral.

That’s the day a funeral was held for Toronto police Const. Marc Pinizzotto, who was fatally shot during a raid while investigating multiple shootings, including one at the U.S. Consulate.

Truong says ToChief Thai Truong says a criminal investigation is also being launched as the video shows a service weapon being stored in “circumstances that raise concerns.”ronto police will investigate the handling and storage of the police firearm.

The chief says a senior officer has been suspended with pay, and the overall conduct of the members involved will be investigated after the criminal probe concludes.

stories.title: Calgary Chamber warns of economic fallout of Alberta split; CEOs join 'stay' camp
stories.summary: Calgary - A report commissioned by the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warns of dire economic consequences if Alberta were to separate from Canada.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press

CALGARY - Alberta business leaders have signed on to an open letter from the Calgary Chamber of Commerce warning of the dire economic consequences if the province were to separate from Canada.

Sept. 29, 2026

Updated at 6:38 p.m.

Jeff McIntosh / THE CANADIAN PRESS[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/alberta/calgary-chamber-warns-of-economic-fallout-of-alberta-split-ceos-join-stay-camp/article_ca625e61-10c3-5750-949b-e43a127d6c6e.html)

By Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press

“We must remain at the table and prioritize relationships, opportunities and stability that have helped make this province and this country prosperous,” reads the letter released Tuesday along with an analysis into the trade, labour and fiscal implications of separation.

“Alberta can be proud of Its identity while remaining confident in its future within Canada.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Among the signatories to the letter are the heads of AltaGas, ATCO, AltaLink, Capital Power, Keyera, BHE Transmission and Chirp Foods Inc., Canada’s largest McDonald’s franchise business. Tourism Calgary and Calgary Economic Development have also signed, as well as a former CEO of Trans Mountain Corp. The chamber said more are expected to join.

In three weeks, Albertans vote on 10 referendum questions, including one on whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the process of holding another referendum on separation.

The study by University of Calgary economist Trevor Tombe estimates trade costs would rise by five to eight per cent — the range the United Kingdom has seen since its withdrawal from the European Union.

It said Alberta is the most trade-exposed jurisdiction in the country, with nearly one in three workers having jobs in sectors significantly vulnerable to such disruptions.

The higher trade costs would translate into to job reductions of up to 175,000 in Alberta and an up to $62-billion annual hit to the economy, the report said.

Alberta would also find itself with a $9-billion fiscal shortfall if it were to separate, Tombe concluded. Closing the gap would require a 13 per cent sales tax, a 10 per cent corporate income tax hike or a 40 per cent cut in the transfers Alberta businesses and individuals now receive, like the Canada Child Benefit and old age security.

“When you hear something like GDP contracting, it seems like an abstract statistical notion, but this translates directly into real incomes and wages. How much goods and services can you afford to purchase with an hour of work?” Tombe told reporters.

Chamber president and CEO Deborah Yedlin said Alberta splitting from Canada would be like scoring on its own net, just to send a message.

The Canadian Press

“I grew up with this notion of the Alberta advantage — no sales tax, low taxes, good education, health care, social services. All of that would disappear and we would not be able to sustain that level of support for Albertans,” she told reporters.

“That, in turn, turns into a negative feedback loop, and you don’t get the investment, you don’t generate the tax revenue, you can’t provide the services unless you change how you operate, and that’s just not something anybody really wants to see.”

The vote also comes as “we stand on the doorstep of some significant opportunity,” Yedlin added. The world is clamouring for stable supplies of energy as wars rage in the Middle East and Russia. And the federal government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has made a raft of policy shifts embraced by businesses while demonstrating an eagerness to build new energy infrastructure.

Some people might be looking to send a message with a pro-separation-referendum vote after 10 years of former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s less oilpatch-friendly approach, Yedlin said.

“It’s easy to look in the rear-view mirror and it’s easy to be aggrieved and to focus on that. It’s much harder to be an optimist, but we’re at a point in time where we need to have that optimism ... This is a different set of circumstances, a different environment for Alberta, for the energy sector and we do need to look forward.”

Yedlin said some business leaders may have been reticent to wade into the debate so far because they don’t want to alienate workers in the field sympathetic to the separatist cause.

“The reality is, though, that as an entity, you can say this is what you stand for. And at the same time, you respect the right of your employees to vote according to what they feel is important to them,” she said.

“Ultimately, where you need to be is on the right side of history.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Anand to close Toronto summit on returning Ukraine kids from Russian captivity
stories.summary: Toronto - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will close a two-day conference on missing Ukrainian children today after multiple countries promised more action to bring home those abducted by Russia.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ukrainians Margaryta Shabanova (left), Matviy Chos and Dariia Tomashova (right) speak with Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand at the Pathways to Peace conference in Toronto on Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026.

Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press

TORONTO - More than 50 countries signed a pledge Tuesday at a conference in Toronto to boost their efforts to return Ukrainians from Russian captivity — including an estimated 20,000 children.

Sept. 29, 2026

Updated at 10:10 p.m.

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Sammy Kogan/The Canadian Press[](http://www.thestar.com/news/canada/anand-to-close-toronto-summit-on-returning-ukraine-kids-from-russian-captivity/article_3de90776-b7e2-5578-940a-8680ba33a2ef.html)

By Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press

“We have pledged to find Ukrainians who have been taken from their homes. We have pledged to bring them back, knowing that it can be dangerous, complex, difficult, but above all necessary,” Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said at the conference on Tuesday.

In 2024, Canada and Ukraine jointly launched an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia since it began its full-scale invasion in 2022.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

That work has since expanded to include efforts to return adult civilians and prisoners of war taken by Russia since its 2014 seizure of Crimea.

Anand co-hosted the conference in Toronto this week with Ukraine and Norway focused on marshalling efforts to return abducted Ukrainians. She said the conference included representatives from 83 countries and international organizations such as the Council of Europe.

More than 50 of those pledged to better co-ordinate the efforts of governments, civil society and international organizations to reunite Ukrainian families.

Officials in Ukraine say 2,650 of the 20,000 children deported to Russia have been returned. Anand said two-thirds of those returns have taken place since a Montreal conference two years ago.

Bring Kids Back, a coalition launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said many of those children have reported being subjected to physical and sexual violence while in captivity.

“Children are brainwashed. They are geared toward military service in the Russian armed forces,” coalition leader Maksym Maksymov said in a Tuesday interview.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says more than 50 countries and organizations have pledged to continue work on returning abducted children from Russia, along with civilians and prisoners of war. Advocates say those held in Russia and the occupied Ukrainian territories experience violence, and are returned to Ukraine amid frequent airstrikes. (Sept. 29, 2026)

The Canadian Press

“Ukrainian language, culture and history are removed from schools. Everything that is happening there is designed to sever the legal and emotional path back to Ukraine for these young people.”

Maksymov said a report published in July by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe offers independent confirmation of what Ukraine has been saying.

The OSCE — of which Russia and Canada are both members — reported Russian officials have compelled children to change their identities, physically tortured at least 10 kids and placed many in foster families where sexual violence has occurred.

“The practices of systemic indoctrination and militarization may also amount to a crime against humanity in the form of persecution, directed against Ukrainian children on discriminatory grounds, as part of a widespread and systematic attack,” the report reads.

“Canada has provided very significant practical support when it comes to tracing, when it comes to returns, when it comes to reintegration, all of the fronts,” Maksymov said.

Ukrainians attending the conference Monday shared first-hand accounts of life under Russian control. Teenagers from Crimea said they were being primed to fight against their fellow Ukrainians. One woman described her anguish after her husband vanished in Luhansk, only to show up in an online video three months later looking emaciated.

“These aren’t simply unfortunate consequences of war. They are documented violations of international law that demand attention,” Anand said Tuesday.

Ukrainian Social Policy Minister Denys Uliutin urged countries Tuesday to commit to concrete steps.

“Small things that are actually done are worth more to us than large things that were proclaimed on paper,” he told delegates at the close of the meeting.

He said the Montreal summit of two years ago was a success because countries took specific actions. They included the United Arab Emirates and the Vatican taking part in mediation efforts with Russia, and Qatar helping 80 children leave Ukraine. Lithuania also helped by setting up transportation routes.

Uliutin said more pressure needs to be put on Russia to identify the Ukrainians it’s still holding.

He noted 95 per cent of Ukrainian prisoners of war interviewed by United Nations monitors reported experiencing torture.

This week, the European Union announced a new round of sanctions on officials accused of helping to abduct Ukrainian children — something the International Criminal Court calls a war crime.

The European sanctions target a camp in North Korea where Brussels says Russia has sent abducted Ukrainian children. The Songdowon camp is not among the entities Canada has sanctioned.

On Monday, Anand told reporters Canada is using artificial intelligence to help identify Ukrainian children taken into Russia. She said Russian authorities have changed the names of some children, making them harder to track.

Alexandra Chyczij, head of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress, said Tuesday her understanding is that Canada is using data from cellphones owned by Ukrainian youth to establish their initial whereabouts, and using satellite imagery to identify detention centres.

Chyczij said this technology allows authorities to understand what is happening to children deported to Russia and those living in the occupied Ukrainian territories.

“The children who still remain living in occupation are absolutely as vulnerable,” she told reporters. “It really is important to keep raising awareness.”

stories.title: Anand closes Toronto summit on returning Ukrainian kids from Russian captivity
stories.summary: Toronto — Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will close a two-day conference on missing Ukrainian children Tuesday after multiple countries promised more action to bring home those abducted by Russia.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Posted September 29, 2026 11:21 am.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 2:30 pm.

Toronto — Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand will close a two-day conference on missing Ukrainian children Tuesday after multiple countries promised more action to bring home those abducted by Russia.

In 2024, Canada and Ukraine jointly launched an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia since it began its full-scale invasion in 2022.

That work has been expanded to include efforts to return adult civilians and prisoners of war taken by Russian officials since Russia’s 2014 seizure of Crimea.

The European Union has announced a new round of sanctions on officials accused of helping to abduct Ukrainian children — something the International Criminal Court calls a war crime.

The European sanctions target a camp in North Korea where Brussels says Russia has sent abducted Ukrainian children. The Songdowon camp is not among the entities Canada has sanctioned.

Norway, which is co-hosting this week’s conference in Toronto, has promised the equivalent of $35 million to support work by Unicef and the International Committee of the Red Cross to bring Ukrainian children home and help them reintegrate.

Officials in Ukraine say 2,600 of the 20,000 children deported to Russia have since returned.

Bring Kids Back, a coalition launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said many of those children have reported being subjected to physical and sexual violence.

“Children are brainwashed. They are geared toward military service in the Russian armed forces,” coalition leader Maksym Maksymov said in a Tuesday interview.

“Ukrainian language, culture and history are removed from schools. Everything that is happening there is designed to sever the legal and emotional path back to Ukraine for these young people.”

Maksymov said a report published in July by the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe offers independent confirmation of what Ukraine has been saying.

The Osce — of which Russia and Canada are both members — reported Russian officials have compelled children to change their identities, physically tortured at least 10 kids and placed many in foster families where sexual violence occurred.

“The practices of systemic indoctrination and militarization May also amount to a crime against humanity in the form of persecution, directed against Ukrainian children on discriminatory grounds, as part of a widespread and systematic attack,” the report reads.

This week’s Toronto summit builds on a similar one in May hosted in Brussels. Maksymov said 300 children have been returned to Ukraine in the four months since then.

“Canada has provided very significant practical support when it comes to tracing, when it comes to returns, when it comes to reintegration, all of the fronts,” he said.

On Monday, Anand told reporters Canada is using artificial intelligence to help identify Ukrainian children taken into Russia. She said Russian authorities have changed the names of some children, making them harder to track.

Alexandra Chyczij, head of the Ukrainian Canadian Congress, said Tuesday her understanding is that Canada is using data from cellphones owned by Ukrainian youth to establish their initial whereabouts, and using satellite imagery to identify detention centres.

Chyczij said this technology allows authorities to understand what is happening to children deported to Russia and those living in the occupied Ukrainian territories.

“The children who still remain living in occupation are absolutely as vulnerable,” she told reporters. “It really is important to keep raising awareness.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Man fighting for life, suspect still at large after OEV stabbing
stories.summary: Man fighting for life, suspect still at large after OEV stabbing CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London police say a man is in hospital with life-threatening injuries after a stabbing Monday evening in the city's Old East Village neighbourhood, as officers continue to search for the suspect.
· Posted: Sep 29, 2026 11:19 AM EDT | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago
London police say a man is in hospital with life-threatening injuries after a stabbing Monday evening in London's Old East Village neighbourhood.
Police were called to the north side of Dundas Street, just east of Adelaide Street, at around 6:15 p.m.
The injured man was found at the scene and taken to hospital by paramedics, where he remained Tuesday morning, police said.

"Police recognize that incidents involving violence in public spaces can be concerning for members of the community," the London Police Service said in a statement. "Officers are actively investigating this matter and will maintain a visible presence in the area as the investigation continues."
Police have not yet located the suspect.
Police describe the suspect as a man between 20 and 25 years old. He was last seen wearing a long-sleeved plaid button-up shirt and burgundy pants.
Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 6 and 6:20 p.m., or who May have information about the incident, to come forward.
Police are also asking anyone with dashcam footage or residential or business surveillance video that could assist with the investigation to contact the London Police Service or Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Trump’s import bans on Canadian liquor, whey, motorcycles take effect
stories.summary: Ottawa — U.S. President Donald Trump has escalated his trade war with Canada with outright bans on imports of certain Canadian goods.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 11:18 am.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 1:50 pm.

Washington — U.S. President Donald Trump has escalated his trade war with Canada with outright bans on imports of certain Canadian goods.

Trump’s previously announced bans — which affect some alcoholic drinks, dairy byproducts and motorcycles, among other goods — came into force at 12:01 a.m. ET Tuesday.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc’s office said Monday the government’s top priority remains “protecting and supporting Canadian workers, farmers, families and businesses from these unjustified actions.”

The bans mark the latest escalation of the trade war as the Trump administration seeks to pressure Canada into concessions in trade talks.

The trade restrictions could prove devastating for the affected industries but are unlikely to significantly undermine Canada’s overall economic growth in the near term.

Jacob Jensen, director of trade policy at the centre-right American Action Forum think tank, calculates that the ban will cover US$967 million worth of Canadian imports, based on 2025 numbers.

Of that, 87 per cent would be alcoholic beverages the U.S. targeted because some Canadian provinces responded to Trump’s provocations by banning U.S. booze from store shelves.

The U.S.-based group Toasts Not Tariffs, which represents farmers, distillers, retailers, restaurants and bars, said in a statement Tuesday it appreciates the Trump administration’s efforts to encourage Canada to reopen its markets to American spirits and wine.

“However, as this ban on Canadian spirits and wines takes effect today, America’s restaurants, bars, retailers and consumers are being pulled further into a trade dispute that has already taken a significant toll on U.S. wine and spirits producers,” the group said, calling for a negotiated resolution to the dispute that restores sales on both sides of the border.

The federal Conservatives on Tuesday accused the government of doing nothing to help the Canadian alcohol industry and urged the Liberals to pause the federal alcohol excise tax and suspend the escalator tax.

Conservative Canada-U.S. relations critic Shuvaloy Majumdar said in a media statement that this “is not the time for higher taxes on industries that are fighting to remain competitive.”

The ban also covers motorcycles. BRP Inc. in Quebec confirmed that its three-wheel Can-Am Spyder and Canyon motorcycles “will be excluded from importation into the U.S.” But BRP said the impact likely won’t be felt until next year because it has completed most production and shipments for the current season.

Official trade talks broke down down last month and both countries accused each other of adding eleventh-hour changes to the agreement.

Trump said Monday he expects Canada to return to the negotiating table in the coming weeks with an apology.

“I think what’s going to happen is over the next three or four weeks, they’re going to come to us and they’re gonna say, ‘We’re gonna get rid of all the tariffs,'” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office.

“We’re going to win everything.”

In the hours after negotiations broke down in August, the United States hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs. Ottawa responded with its own tariffs a few weeks later, targeting similar goods from the U.S. list.

Trump responded by signing an order directing some federal agencies to remove Canadian goods from procurement lists, and another to impose Tuesday’s import bans.

The president also signed an executive order to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America, a move that does not affect the lake’s name in Canada.

Canada is also being hit with 10 per cent tariffs, which the Trump administration claims are connected to forced labour in supply chains. Those duties do not apply to goods that comply with the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement on trade, known as Cusma.

And Canadian industries like steel, aluminum, automobiles and cabinetry are being slammed by Trump’s separate sectoral tariffs.

Ontario, which is particularly hard-hit, expanded eligibility on Tuesday for a $1-billion financing program to provide loans to businesses affected by tariffs, and for a $150-million fund that provides grants or loans to small- and medium-sized businesses looking to find new markets.

Ontario’s Economic Development and Trade Minister Vic Fedeli said in a media statement the government is working to ensure businesses “are not only equipped to navigate the challenges of present day but can take the necessary steps to reduce long-term reliance on a single market and diversify their international exports.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press.

Kelly Geraldine Malone, The Canadian Press
