stories.title: New Western chair honours heart rhythm research pioneer George Klein
stories.summary: Western University launches the Dr. George J. Klein Shah-Baylis Chair to advance heart rhythm research and patient care.
stories.author: Keri Ferguson
stories.content:
A combined gift from the Shah Family Foundation and the Gloria Baylis Foundation will help advance the diagnosis and treatment of heart rhythm disorders through a new Western chair. The chair will be named to honour Dr. George Klein, a pioneering electrophysiologist and professor at the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

The Dr. George J. Klein Shah-Baylis Chair recognizes Klein’s contributions to cardiac electrophysiology, a branch of cardiology that diagnoses and treats heart rhythm disorders, known as arrhythmias. It will also strengthen the London Heart Rhythm Program (LHRP). Founded by Klein in the 1970s, the LHRP is home to an acclaimed heart rhythm clinical and research fellowship training program at University Hospital in London, Ont.

Under Klein’s leadership, LHRP researchers have explored the cellular and electrical processes that cause arrhythmia and developed innovative treatments, including surgical and catheter ablation and implantable devices such as pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs). The impact these treatments make on patients’ lives is often profound, moving them from a state of constant fatigue and limited physical activity to a higher quality of life.

With about 25,000 pacemakers and 7,000 ICDs implanted in Canadians each year, and demand rising as the population ages and more patients survive to develop chronic heart failure, the need for devices promoting comfort and overall health grows.

The new endowed $8-million chair, funded by two gifts of $2 million each from the Shah Family Foundation and Gloria Baylis Foundation, and matched by a $4-million investment from Western, will help the LHRP respond to that demand.

John Yoo, dean of Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, thanked the donors on behalf of Western and the department of cardiology.

“We are grateful for the foresight and generosity of the Gloria Baylis Foundation and the Shah Family Foundation,” Yoo said. “Their transformational investment will advance cardiac electrophysiology research and have real-world impact, ensuring patients will continue to benefit from more effective, evidence-based care.”

For more than five decades, Dr. George Klein and the LHRP have helped transform the diagnosis and treatment of heart rhythm disorders.

From inventing the implantable loop recorder – a cardiac monitor that tracks, over the long term, the heart rhythm of patients with recurrent unexplained fainting – to holding 12 U.S. patents and training more than 65 research fellows, Klein has made countless lives better.

Frank Baylis

His achievements and breakthroughs align well with the values of the foundations supporting the Klein Shah-Baylis Chair, which share a commitment to expanding access to health care and education, and to supporting innovative, collaborative approaches that strengthen communities and create lasting benefits for future generations.

The foundation principals wished to name the chair in living tribute to Klein, recognizing his “extraordinary leadership, while ensuring his commitment to research, mentorship and innovation continues through future generations.”

“Dr. Klein is one of the giants in electrophysiology,” said Frank Baylis, chair of the Gloria Baylis Foundation. “We want to honour him and make sure people know his name, what he’s accomplished and how important he’s been – not just to the Canadian ecosystem, but globally.”

The foundations also wanted to acknowledge the collaborative approach that helped establish London as a centre for heart rhythm research and innovation.

“The greatest advances in health care begin with exceptional people working together,” said Kris Shah, president of the Shah Family Foundation. “Dr. Klein and his team have led the way to help patients with heart rhythm disorders. By investing in talented researchers and clinicians, we are helping to carry forward a legacy of meaningful research, innovation and collaboration that will improve patient care for generations to come.”

The London electrophysiology team played an important role in the growth of Baylis Medical, led by Baylis and Shah. The guidance and clinical insights from the LHRP over many years helped support the company’s research and development work in the field.

The new chair will help the LHRP increase its external research funding to design and run novel clinical trials that generate new scientific evidence to improve how arrhythmias are diagnosed and treated. A leading clinician-scientist will be recruited to help build research capacity and collaboration among researchers and trainees.

Baylis said it is gratifying knowing life-changing Canadian-based research and innovations will continue with support from the two foundations.

“The knowledge and changes we’ve seen in Dr. Klein’s career have been enormous, and the impact on people’s health, not just in London or Canada, but around the world, is tremendous,” he said. “We’re excited to see this impact continue through this chair.”

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.
paragraphs: A combined gift from the Shah Family Foundation and the Gloria Baylis Foundation will help advance the diagnosis and treatment of heart rhythm disorders through a new Western chair. The chair will be named to honour Dr. George Klein, a pioneering electrophysiologist and professor at the Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry.

The Dr. George J. Klein Shah-Baylis Chair recognizes Klein’s contributions to cardiac electrophysiology, a branch of cardiology that diagnoses and treats heart rhythm disorders, known as arrhythmias. It will also strengthen the London Heart Rhythm Program (LHRP). Founded by Klein in the 1970s, the LHRP is home to an acclaimed heart rhythm clinical and research fellowship training program at University Hospital in London, Ont.

Under Klein’s leadership, LHRP researchers have explored the cellular and electrical processes that cause arrhythmia and developed innovative treatments, including surgical and catheter ablation and implantable devices such as pacemakers and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs). The impact these treatments make on patients’ lives is often profound, moving them from a state of constant fatigue and limited physical activity to a higher quality of life.

With about 25,000 pacemakers and 7,000 ICDs implanted in Canadians each year, and demand rising as the population ages and more patients survive to develop chronic heart failure, the need for devices promoting comfort and overall health grows.

The new endowed $8-million chair, funded by two gifts of $2 million each from the Shah Family Foundation and Gloria Baylis Foundation, and matched by a $4-million investment from Western, will help the LHRP respond to that demand.
John Yoo, dean of Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, thanked the donors on behalf of Western and the department of cardiology.

“We are grateful for the foresight and generosity of the Gloria Baylis Foundation and the Shah Family Foundation,” Yoo said. “Their transformational investment will advance cardiac electrophysiology research and have real-world impact, ensuring patients will continue to benefit from more effective, evidence-based care.”
For more than five decades, Dr. George Klein and the LHRP have helped transform the diagnosis and treatment of heart rhythm disorders.

From inventing the implantable loop recorder – a cardiac monitor that tracks, over the long term, the heart rhythm of patients with recurrent unexplained fainting – to holding 12 U.S. patents and training more than 65 research fellows, Klein has made countless lives better.
Frank Baylis

His achievements and breakthroughs align well with the values of the foundations supporting the Klein Shah-Baylis Chair, which share a commitment to expanding access to health care and education, and to supporting innovative, collaborative approaches that strengthen communities and create lasting benefits for future generations.

The foundation principals wished to name the chair in living tribute to Klein, recognizing his “extraordinary leadership, while ensuring his commitment to research, mentorship and innovation continues through future generations.”

“Dr. Klein is one of the giants in electrophysiology,” said Frank Baylis, chair of the Gloria Baylis Foundation. “We want to honour him and make sure people know his name, what he’s accomplished and how important he’s been – not just to the Canadian ecosystem, but globally.”
The foundations also wanted to acknowledge the collaborative approach that helped establish London as a centre for heart rhythm research and innovation.

“The greatest advances in health care begin with exceptional people working together,” said Kris Shah, president of the Shah Family Foundation. “Dr. Klein and his team have led the way to help patients with heart rhythm disorders. By investing in talented researchers and clinicians, we are helping to carry forward a legacy of meaningful research, innovation and collaboration that will improve patient care for generations to come.”

The London electrophysiology team played an important role in the growth of Baylis Medical, led by Baylis and Shah. The guidance and clinical insights from the LHRP over many years helped support the company’s research and development work in the field.

The new chair will help the LHRP increase its external research funding to design and run novel clinical trials that generate new scientific evidence to improve how arrhythmias are diagnosed and treated. A leading clinician-scientist will be recruited to help build research capacity and collaboration among researchers and trainees.
Baylis said it is gratifying knowing life-changing Canadian-based research and innovations will continue with support from the two foundations.

“The knowledge and changes we’ve seen in Dr. Klein’s career have been enormous, and the impact on people’s health, not just in London or Canada, but around the world, is tremendous,” he said. “We’re excited to see this impact continue through this chair.”

stories.title: Toronto Maple Leafs, Montreal Canadiens to battle as new NHL season begins
stories.summary: Toronto is coming off completing a blockbuster trade that saw the front office acquire Kirill Marchenko from Columbus for Matthew Knies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A new NHL season kicks off tonight with some historic rivalries and the reigning Stanley Cup champions celebrating their title.

The Carolina Hurricanes will raise their championship banner before taking on a Florida Panthers side reinvigorated by the return of captain Aleksander Barkov.

Four Canadian teams are also in action, starting with No. 1 draft pick Gavin McKenna and the Toronto Maple Leafs hosting a Montreal Canadiens team that made it to the Eastern Conference final last season.

Toronto is coming off completing a blockbuster trade that saw the front office acquire Kirill Marchenko, Miles Wood and Elvis Merzlikins from the Columbus Blue Jackets for Matthew Knies, Steven Lorentz, Emil Andrae and a 2027 2nd-round pick.

The Edmonton Oilers also begin their first season under head coach Mike Babcock, hosting the rebuilding Vancouver Canucks.

Opening night play also includes an original six matchup between the Bruins and the New York Rangers in Boston, and a tilt between the Chicago Blackhawks and the Golden Knights in Vegas.

The Calgary Flames kick off their season Thursday at home against the Seattle Kraken, the Winnipeg Jets get started Friday when they host the Bruins, and the Ottawa Senators play their first game Saturday when they visit the Leafs in Toronto.

stories.title: Analysis: B.C. Conservatives get Caroline Elliott after all
stories.summary: “I don't know if I'm as ambitious as people think," she says. "I've never felt that it had to be, you know, me at the top of the totem pole.”
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
The tables have turned.

Four months ago, Caroline Elliott lost the B.C. Conservative leadership to Kerry-Lynne Findlay on a 51-49 fourth-ballot runoff. Findlay is gone. Elliott is now on the ballot in West Vancouver-Capilano, her North Shore turf, in the snap election Premier David Eby called for Oct. 24.

“If I was ready to jump in for leadership and lead the party — and ultimately, in an ideal world, the province,” she told me early Monday, “then I should be able to step up for my local riding.”

Eagle-eyed readers will note that I wrote about Elliott just last week , when she hadn’t yet confirmed she was running. She’s an important figure in this election, which is important for B.C., and I wanted to speak with her to follow up.

Lorne Doerkson, the interim leader the party board says will stay on if Conservatives win, gets her “full-hearted endorsement.” I asked, bluntly, about her own ambitions. She lost a knife-edge race to someone who did not last. There is not a whiff of woe-is-me.

“It’s funny,” she says. “I don’t know if I’m as ambitious as people think. I’m really driven on the issues, but if I can drive them in a different way, I’ve never felt that it had to be, you know, me at the top of the totem pole.”

Doerkson, she says, is the right person. “He’s such a good and decent man.” It is not only his legislative and business experience, “he brings an authenticity B.C. is ready for after years of David Eby, who does not present in the same way at all.”

“If he earns a mandate from the public of British Columbia, then I think it would be entirely reasonable for him to say that’s mandate enough to continue leading the party.”

She does not need the title; she wants the files. She is comfortable Doerkson cares about many of the same ones. “I feel pretty comfortable that I’ll be able to pursue those things under his leadership.”

She jumped into this race because commentary — she is a founder of Without Diminishment on Substack and a sometime contributor to National Post — is not the same as a vote in caucus. “I can write about [these issues] all day, I can post videos about them all day, I can speak at events about them all day, but the most effective way, I think, is to have a seat at the table where you’re really driving them.”

“That’s what I want to bring, is that voice at the table, explaining, all the time, the crucial importance of things like: what’s happening in our education system and how important it is when it comes to a whole generation of future citizens; the importance of bringing up things like the criminal justice system, which is more than just a catch-and-release program, there’s an underlying philosophy that’s I think cultural in nature.”

Then there are the Indigenous rights and land files she has been on for years. British Columbians, she says, are nervous about private property after the Cowichan title decision, and they understand the economic bite of Dripa.

The party wanted her, she says, because those ideas “have a place in the party” — and because she had a lot of support in the leadership race. They want members to see “this party is representative of what they’ve previously voted for or shown interest in.”

She knows voters also want the kitchen-table list. “There’s a crazy cost of living crisis in British Columbia, especially in the Vancouver area,” plus health care and schools. “We’re going to be needing to talk about a range of issues.”

Running where she can actually come home to was the other condition. Her daughter is nine, her son six. “I’m going to be away from home a lot, I’m going to be in Victoria a lot. If we’re fortunate enough to form government, there’s a lot of work to be done around the province for all of us. All I kept thinking was … when I come home to my riding, I really want to come home. I want to be able to involve my kids in local constituency issues, events, things like, you know, the Canada Day Parade or our pumpkin festival here in West Van.”

To make that possible, the party moved incumbent Lynne Block out of West Vancouver-Capilano — a Conservative gain in 2024 — and into neighbouring North Vancouver-Seymour, an NDP seat. Elliott is grateful Block took the harder assignment; the two have already talked about how to win both.

She pushed hard to lead the party; she sounds at peace running in the one riding she loves. The work is still hard but the toll on her family is smaller. “So I’m going to work hard, but I’m also going to enjoy it.”

“You have to find the wins where you see them, and I certainly feel fortunate.”

stories.title: Canada can do more to prosecute sophisticated money laundering cases: watchdog report
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada is making strides in the fight against criminal efforts to disguise illicit cash but can do more to investigate and prosecute complex money laundering cases, says a new international watchdog report.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Posted September 29, 2026 8:00 am.

Last Updated September 29, 2026 8:43 am.

Ottawa — Canada is making strides in the fight against criminal efforts to disguise illicit cash but can do more to investigate and prosecute complex money laundering cases, says a new international watchdog report.

The report, an independent, peer review assessment by the Financial Action Task Force and the Asia-Pacific Group on Money Laundering, says Canada has developed “a mature and nuanced understanding” of money laundering and terrorist financing threats and vulnerabilities.

It also applauds Canada’s strong co-ordination across government and ability to use financial intelligence to support criminal investigations and international efforts.

But the report calls on Canada to improve its supervision of non-financial sectors, including dealers in precious metals and stones and real estate.

Organized criminal groups involved in drug trafficking are known to invest in real estate to launder their proceeds of crime, meaning real estate brokers, sales representatives and developers can be exposed to high-risk clients, the report says.

It also notes while lawyers are subject to professional rules and oversight by law societies, they remain outside Canada’s proceeds of crime and terrorist financing legislative framework.

Law societies have taken positive steps to reinforce the implementation of anti-money laundering obligations but “uneven coverage, sectoral gaps and limited supervisory intensity” affect the level of effectiveness, the report says.

The evaluation is the result of a peer review assessment process which sees experts from different countries gauge the effectiveness of other countries’ measures against money laundering, terrorist financing and proliferation of weapons of mass destruction.

The report on Canada covered 14 months and included a three-week visit in November 2025. The reviewing organizations say the assessment team interacted with over 700 experts from the public and the private sectors, including the finance and justice departments, law enforcement agencies, supervisors, financial institutions and non-financial businesses.

“As a major global economy, Canada has a strong understanding of the illicit finance risks it is facing, and has taken significant steps to strengthen corporate transparency and the use of financial intelligence since its last mutual evaluation,” Financial Action Task Force president Giles Thomson said in a media statement.

“However, with the threats posed by fraudsters, organized crime networks and professional money launderers, Canada must step up efforts to investigate and prosecute complex money laundering cases, and strengthen oversight in the sectors most vulnerable to abuse.”

Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne welcomed the report, saying in a statement the government will review and act on the recommendations.

He said the report tracks an improvement since Canada’s last evaluation in 2016 and offers a “validation of the work the government is undertaking with agencies and provinces together to better protect Canadians against fraud and the financial system against nefarious activity.”

The report says money laundering in Canada is linked mainly to proceeds from drug trafficking, fraud, commercial trade fraud and tax crimes, often involving organized crime groups and professional money laundering intermediaries.

Key vulnerabilities are present in large banks, certain money service businesses, virtual asset service providers and private corporations, with “growing exposure” related to virtual assets, crowdfunding mechanisms and online gambling platforms, the report says.

Terrorist financing activity is “generally low in value and volume,” reflecting the risk associated with lone‑actor attacks with limited financing needs, the report says.

The federal Liberals have tabled legislation to create the Financial Crimes Agency, a specialized federal law enforcement agency that will investigate money-related offences and contribute to the recovery of proceeds of crime.

Canada should develop and implement a comprehensive strategy to help the new agency address sophisticated and complex financial crimes, the report says.

Champagne said in the media statement the new agency will bolster Canada’s capacity to combat serious and complex financial crime “and improve enforcement outcomes.”

stories.title: TC Energy’s Coastal GasLink to proceed after LNG Canada decision
stories.summary: Company says Coastal GasLink Phase 2 will nearly double the pipeline’s capacity through the addition of new compressor stations and upgrades
stories.author: Reuters
stories.content:
TC Energy TRP-T said on Tuesday its Coastal GasLink Phase 2 project will proceed after LNG Canada and its joint venture partners made a positive final investment decision on the LNG Canada expansion project.

The company said Coastal GasLink Phase 2 will nearly double the pipeline’s capacity through the addition of new compressor stations and upgrades along its existing 670-km route linking Dawson Creek and the LNG Canada export facility in Kitimat, British Columbia.

Tight global markets, outages among major producers and strong long-term demand growth from countries seeking to replace coal with cleaner-burning natural gas are driving interest in new LNG projects and more diversified sources of supply.

Earlier on Tuesday, LNG Canada partners led by Shell approved a multi-billion-dollar Phase 2 expansion of the Kitimat facility that will double its production capacity to 28 million metric tonnes a year from 14 million metric tonnes per annum (mtpa), strengthening Canada’s position in the global LNG export market.

LNG Canada, Canada’s first large-scale LNG export terminal, is a joint venture between Shell, Petronas, PetroChina, Mitsubishi Corp and Korea Gas Corp , and ranks among the country’s largest private-sector investments.

TC Energy operates a 58,100-mile network of pipelines, supplying more than 30 per cent of the clean-burning natural gas consumed daily across North America.

stories.title: London, Ont. police officers under investigation
stories.summary: London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.

In a statement, London Police Service Chief Thai Truong said the incident took place in Toronto on June 24, 2026, following a police funeral.

Truong said he personally reviewed the video and immediately directed that the matter be referred to Toronto police for a criminal investigation into the handling and storage of the firearm.

Once the criminal investigation is complete, the conduct of the officers involved will also be reviewed under the Community Safety and Policing Act, the statement said.

One senior officer has been suspended with pay pending the outcome of the investigations.

According to Truong, the decision on suspension should not be viewed as minimizing the seriousness of the allegations, noting that the legislative framework governing police discipline has not met the threshold required for a suspension without pay at this stage.

“Police officers are entrusted with significant authority and responsibilities,” said Truong. “With that comes an expectation that we will conduct ourselves in a manner that maintains the confidence of the community we serve.”

He added that those expectations apply to all members of the service and are particularly important for officers in leadership positions.

Truong said there will be no further comment on the evidence, citing the need to protect the integrity of the investigations, but said additional information would be released when appropriate.

No criminal charges have been announced and investigators have not released the identities of the officers involved.

stories.title: Woman sobs as she is acquitted in infant son’s death based on new medical evidence
stories.summary: An Ontario woman sobbed in court Tuesday as she was acquitted in the death of her infant son after more than two decades labelled as his killer.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario woman sobbed in court Tuesday as she was acquitted in the death of her infant son after more than two decades labelled as his killer.

Jennifer Gaskin pulled her mother into a long and tearful hug after Ontario’s top court found that she had been wrongfully convicted of manslaughter in the death of her 2 1/2-month-old son Joeseph based on now-discredited science.

On her other side stood her daughter, with whom Gaskin was reunited a day earlier for the first time since they were separated by child welfare services a day after Joeseph’s funeral.

Outside the downtown Toronto courthouse, Gaskin said she finally felt free after decades branded as a monster.

“Now that this is over, I’m hoping that I won’t feel like people still look at me that way, because I won’t look at myself that way,” she said. “Now I’m just going to live my best life.”

Though it took a long time, the court eventually “made it right,” she said.

Gaskin’s case is “another in the sad litany of cases of wrongful convictions based on the discredited ‘shaken baby syndrome’ as the cause of a child’s death brought about, in part, by unreliable expert evidence,” the Appeal Court said in its ruling.

“The fresh evidence shows that Ms. Gaskin’s conviction is unsustainable. She is the victim of a miscarriage of justice,” Justice Peter Lauwers said.

“As this court has stated in similar cases, it bears repeating that it is profoundly regrettable that, because of what has been shown to be flawed pathological evidence, Ms. Gaskin was wrongly convicted.”

One of Gaskin’s lawyers, James Lockyer, said the court referring to shaken baby syndrome as discredited science “was really a giant leap forward in the jurisprudence” and will make it easier to argue future cases on the issue.

“It was an important day. It May be the beginning of the end of shaken baby syndrome, at least in Ontario, potentially in Canada,” he said outside the courthouse.

Lockyer said he doesn’t know how many other shaken-baby cases there May be, but Innocence Canada, a national organization that aims to help clear people wrongfully convicted of crimes, is working on “more than one.”

“It was a hypothesis that was used frequently in courtrooms and it wasn’t properly refuted by the defence and people got convicted because of shaken baby syndrome when it never really had any validity,” he said, calling it “junk science.”

Gaskin was convicted in 2002 after two medical experts testified the child had died as a result of shaken baby syndrome.

Significant concerns about that medical evidence emerged years later after a coroner’s review found major flaws in the work of Dr. Charles Smith, who conducted more than 1,000 child autopsies during his tenure as the head forensic pathologist at the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto.

That led the Ontario government to launch an inquiry into pediatric forensic pathology, then a review of shaken-baby cases from the mid-1980s to the mid-2000s. Joeseph’s case was eventually examined by an international panel of medical experts.

The panel found there was uncertainty regarding the cause of Joeseph’s death and the timing of his injuries, court heard. His head injuries had been mischaracterized as bruising when they were in fact infarcts, or strokes, and it wasn’t clear whether they had caused the boy’s death, the panel found.

Court heard the three experts couldn’t rule out the possibility of an inflicted injury, but found Joeseph — a premature baby who spent the first two months of his life in hospital — could also have died from sudden unexpected infant death, previously known as sudden infant death syndrome.

The Crown agreed that the new findings should be admitted as fresh evidence and Gaskin should be acquitted, offering her its “deepest sympathies.”

“As of today, the original expert evidence supporting the conviction of the appellant at trial has been wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt,” the Crown said in its written submissions.

“The investigation of infant death is complex, involving forensic examination and external and internal dissections – none of which were available at the time of the appellant’s conviction.”

Gaskin, who served 18 months of her nearly two-year sentence in prison, laid out the impact of her conviction in an affidavit that was read out in court.

“As I have always said, I did nothing to cause Joeseph’s death, yet I have been branded as a killer for all these years,” she said.

“I could never grieve for Joeseph properly. I lost my other two children ... I did not see them grow up and that has hurt a lot. For 20 years, I missed them and wondered how they were.”

Gaskin had not yet been convicted when her children, a daughter roughly a year older than Joeseph and a son born while she was on bail, were taken by child welfare services, she said outside court Tuesday. She didn’t have the chance to hold her son after he was born, she said.

They got in touch recently through social media and Gaskin met her daughter Monday at the hotel where they were both staying, she said. Her son was set to attend court as well but fell ill and had to turn back, court heard.

While nothing can make up for the time she lost with her children, Gaskin said she looks forward to bonding with them from now on.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

“As of today, the original expert evidence supporting the conviction of the appellant at trial has been wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt,” the Crown said in its written submissions.
“The investigation of infant death is complex, involving forensic examination and external and internal dissections – none of which were available at the time of the appellant’s conviction.”
Gaskin, who served 18 months of her nearly two-year sentence in prison, laid out the impact of her conviction in an affidavit that was read out in court.
“As I have always said, I did nothing to cause Joeseph’s death, yet I have been branded as a killer for all these years,” she said.
“I could never grieve for Joeseph properly. I lost my other two children ... I did not see them grow up and that has hurt a lot. For 20 years, I missed them and wondered how they were.”

content_blocks.text: An Ontario woman sobbed in court Tuesday as she was acquitted in the death of her infant son after more than two decades labelled as his killer.

Jennifer Gaskin pulled her mother into a long and tearful hug after Ontario’s top court found that she had been wrongfully convicted of manslaughter in the death of her 2 1/2-month-old son Joeseph based on now-discredited science.
On her other side stood her daughter, with whom Gaskin was reunited a day earlier for the first time since they were separated by child welfare services a day after Joeseph’s funeral.
Outside the downtown Toronto courthouse, Gaskin said she finally felt free after decades branded as a monster.
“Now that this is over, I’m hoping that I won’t feel like people still look at me that way, because I won’t look at myself that way,” she said. “Now I’m just going to live my best life.”
Though it took a long time, the court eventually “made it right,” she said.

Gaskin’s case is “another in the sad litany of cases of wrongful convictions based on the discredited ‘shaken baby syndrome’ as the cause of a child’s death brought about, in part, by unreliable expert evidence,” the Appeal Court said in its ruling.
“The fresh evidence shows that Ms. Gaskin’s conviction is unsustainable. She is the victim of a miscarriage of justice,” Justice Peter Lauwers said.

“As this court has stated in similar cases, it bears repeating that it is profoundly regrettable that, because of what has been shown to be flawed pathological evidence, Ms. Gaskin was wrongly convicted.”

stories.title: LNG Canada to go ahead with Phase 2 expansion at Kitimat terminal
stories.summary: Project set to double capacity to 28 million tonnes a year
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Shell PLC SHEL-N and its partners in the LNG Canada project are banking on decades of rising demand for liquefied natural gas as they proceed with a more than $30-billion expansion of the facility on the B.C. coast.

Wars in Iran and Ukraine have disrupted global gas supplies and driven up prices, but the decision to double the capacity of the plant in Kitimat, B.C., is predicated on a longer-term transition away from more carbon-intensive fossil fuels, LNG Canada chief executive Chris Cooper said on Tuesday.

“You may argue that there’s some uncertainty right now, but if you look at that long-term demand profile and then the long-term outlook, we think we’ll invest through that cycle,” Mr. Cooper said in an interview. “So that element’s there – generating cash flow for decades. That’s the way we look at these projects.”

Shell said LNG Canada Phase 2, which got the green light from its partners on Tuesday, is one of many such plants that will be required in the coming decades. The company said it expects global LNG demand to increase 65 per cent to nearly 700 million tonnes a year by 2050. Mr. Cooper said some estimates are even higher.

A big risk is going over budget on construction, so LNG Canada’s decision to double up on equipment that has been in operation since last year helps lessen that, he said. The partners have already spent $100-million in preparation for Phase 2.

“So you have a really good risk profile on project execution – known location, known partners, known contracts, a known scope in terms of replication, and then a known market with five big institutional investors who fully support us,” he said.

The investment in the facility will increase production to 28 million tonnes of LNG per year, making it one of the largest such export facilities in the world, the partners said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has championed increasing energy shipments to diversified global markets to reduce the country’s reliance on the United States, which buys the lion’s share of Canada’s oil and gas exports. Projects such as LNG Canada Phase 2 and Alberta’s West Coast oil pipeline proposal are both aimed at bolstering the Canadian economy against U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war.

Meanwhile, with Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz , energy security has come into sharp focus for current and would-be buyers of Canadian oil and gas in Asia and Europe.

“Today’s investment is being made in a different environment. A more dangerous and divided world, a world where Canada fully values export diversification and the greater sovereignty it confers. A world where speed, reliability and predictability are major competitive advantages,” Mr. Carney said in Vancouver on Tuesday.

LNG Canada Phase 2 is among several West Coast projects moving forward, under construction or planned, including Cedar LNG, Woodfibre LNG and Ksi Lisims LNG.

The LNG Canada expansion was among the early projects referred to the Major Projects Office a year ago to be considered for fast-track approval. The project includes adding two processing trains at the facility in Kitimat, along with new storage and condensate tanks, a new loading berth and expanded utility and process systems.

In July, Gitga’at, Gitxaala, Haisla, Kitselas and Kitsumkalum nations in B.C. agreed to pay up to $1-billion for a majority equity stake in the massive new storage tank, providing the expansion went ahead.

The 670-kilometre Coastal GasLink pipeline, which ships gas to Kitimat from Dawson Creek in northeastern B.C. will be expanded by adding five new compressor stations. Capacity will nearly double from the current 2.1 billion cubic feet a day, TC Energy Corp., the line’s operator, said in a statement.

When construction hits its peak, the project is expected to employ as many as 4,000 workers in Kitimat, and create 2,100 jobs to build the new compressor stations along the pipeline.

Mr. Cooper said construction would be completed “in the early 2030s,” but did not specify which year.

Shell owns the largest stake in LNG Canada at 40 per cent, followed by Malaysia’s state-owned Petronas (25 per cent), Japan-based Mitsubishi (15 per cent), PetroChina (15 per cent) and South Korea’s Kogas (5 per cent).

Last September, U.S.-based MidOcean Energy acquired a 20-per-cent indirect interest in key Petronas assets in Canada, including natural gas operations in northeast B.C. and the Petronas stake in LNG Canada.

Some of the LNG Canada partners are also seeking to cash out of portions of their interests amid expressions of interest from global private-equity players and others . Mr. Cooper said any such deals would not change the trajectory of the expansion, and could, in fact, improve financial strength among the partners.

Environmental activists say the investment in LNG Canada runs counter to what they predict will be a worldwide transition to fossil-fuel-free energy. They have also criticized the impact on climate as a result of increasing emissions from the expanded facility and from increased drilling activity in northeast B.C. to supply the plant with gas.

“As the rest of the world rapidly scales up clean energy infrastructure, global gas demand destruction is under way. It’s happening regardless of the desires of the Carney government or foreign gas giants,” Richard Brooks, climate finance director of Stand.earth, said in a statement.

However, Energy Minister Tim Hodgson said energy companies from Japan, South Korea, Germany, Poland and elsewhere have expressed to him a strong desire to secure supplies of the fuel.

“When people say it’s not needed, you have to ask yourself: Are they talking to those who make those decisions, because the ones who make those decisions are committing to long-term contracts to buy our LNG,” he said in an interview.

stories.title: Mission Services of London receives $1.1M for addiction recovery aftercare
stories.summary: The funding will support men who have completed the four-month, live-in addiction treatment program at Mission Services of London’s Quintin Warner House as they transition to independent living.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
is receiving $1.1 million in philanthropic funding to expand aftercare services for men recovering from substance addiction.

The investment includes $500,000 from the RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation and a $600,000 contribution from an anonymous donor.

The funding will support men who have completed the four-month, live-in addiction treatment program at Mission Services of London’s Quintin Warner House as they transition to independent living.

The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation’s contribution will allow Mission Services to reopen all available transitional housing spaces, bringing the number of beds back to 17.

“This enables us to continue with our aftercare program, providing counseling, job education skills, continuation of building on the skills that individuals have learned through the Quinton Warner House Treatment program,” explained Tara Saunders, Director of Social Enterprise, Development & Communications.

The organization says continued access to housing, counselling and other supports can help graduates maintain their recovery as they move toward independent living.

As part of Monday’s announcement, the aftercare program was renamed the Wilfred Schlegel Aftercare Program, in honour of one of Mission Services of London’s founding community builders.

Wilfred Schlegel and his wife, Emma, were among the families involved in establishing Mission Services in 1951.

Rob Schlegel, Wilfred Schlegel’s grandson and a board member of the RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation, said the family wanted to continue his legacy.

“It was his way of giving back, helping community, and helping the most vulnerable. And it really resonates with us today, and what we’ve done through my parents and my brothers is going back and celebrating what Grandpa and Grandma had done,” Schlegel said.

Quintin Warner House provides a four-month, live-in addiction treatment program for up to 20 men aged 18 and older.

The program includes individual treatment plans, case management, life-skills support, diet and exercise programming, communications training and trauma-informed safety training.

was founded in 1951 and is marking its 75th anniversary this year.

The Christian faith-based organization provides emergency shelter, addiction treatment, mental health programs and other services for people experiencing homelessness, poverty, mental health challenges and addiction.

The Quintin Warner House program is funded in part by the Ontario Ministry of Health and through private donations.

Rob Schlegel, Wilfred Schlegel’s grandson and a board member of the RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation, said the family wanted to continue his legacy.

“It was his way of giving back, helping community, and helping the most vulnerable. And it really resonates with us today, and what we’ve done through my parents and my brothers is going back and celebrating what Grandpa and Grandma had done,” Schlegel said.
Quintin Warner House provides a four-month, live-in addiction treatment program for up to 20 men aged 18 and older.
The program includes individual treatment plans, case management, life-skills support, diet and exercise programming, communications training and trauma-informed safety training.
was founded in 1951 and is marking its 75th anniversary this year.

The Christian faith-based organization provides emergency shelter, addiction treatment, mental health programs and other services for people experiencing homelessness, poverty, mental health challenges and addiction.
The Quintin Warner House program is funded in part by the Ontario Ministry of Health and through private donations.

stories.title: How the CAQ losing ground in Quebec election could reshape campaign
stories.summary: If Quebec party leaders stick to their promise, the final stretch of the province’s election campaign will be a busy one.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Montreal - If Quebec party leaders stick to their promise, the final stretch of the province’s election campaign will be a busy one.

Parti Quebecois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has been leading in the polls for three years and is now eyeing a majority in the National Assembly.

“Put the pedal to the metal, isn’t that what they say in Nascar?” said Plamondon. “Yeah, we go all the way.”

With a majority, Plamondon would have the green light to go ahead with his promise of holding a referendum in his first mandate. He has been working to convince Quebecers not to fear the prospect of independence.

“I think they shouldn’t be afraid of that,” Plamondon told reporters at a stop in Ulverton, Que. “Hundreds of nations are governing themselves with their own government and their own institutions, and they’re doing it very well.”

But he also said that the decision before Quebecers now is not whether the province should be a country, but who should lead the province after the Oct. 5 election.

Nik Nanos, founder and chief data scientist at Nanos research, says while the PQ continues to lead when it comes to popular support, there seems to be a shift in the rest of the political landscape.

“The Liberals are up, and the Conservatives are starting to do a little better,” said Nanos. “The big news is that the CAQ, the incumbent party, is on the decline, and the question is where are those voters going to go?”

CAQ Leader Christine Frechette faced a barrage of questions on her handling of issues related to potential U.S. interference in the election. Frechette confirmed Monday that a staffer handed two essays from an American think tank to some journalists.

The blogs discussed supporting sovereigntist parties and efforts to destabilize the Canadian federation. Both essays had been online for months, and other parties and analysts questioned the Caq’s motives.

Analysts say a significant driver of voter support includes a desire for change after eight years of a CAQ government led by former premier Francois Legault.

Quebec’s Liberal party made a pitch that it can lead the province in a new direction.

“We are still seven days from the final decision of Quebecers,” said Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard. “If Quebecers are listening to us now and want change but do not want a referendum on the separation of Quebec, which is something that could be in the making in seven days from now, they need to hear me out. They need to join us and make sure that we can form the government.”

The Quebec Conservatives believes it could hold the balance of power after the election, and leader Eric Duhaime told CTV News in an interview that he is ready to collaborate with other parties on a wide range of issues, but not sovereignty.

“There is no way, form or shape that there’s going to be a referendum in Quebec if we have the balance of power,” said Duhaime. “We don’t want to have it, because 70 per cent of the population doesn’t want to have anything to do with a referendum. Right now, we have huge economic issues to deal with, and it is not time to split Quebecers between a ‘yes’ and a ‘no’ camp.”

All parties say with seven days to go, there is still plenty of time for Quebecers to make their final choice, and that they will continue to criss-cross the province.

stories.title: Surveillance video expected to play key role in McDermott murder trial
stories.summary: A jury has been selected for a second-degree murder trial at the London courthouse.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
A jury has been selected for a second-degree murder trial at the London courthouse.

After jury selection concluded Monday morning, the Crown delivered its opening address late in the afternoon.

Crown attorney Bianca DiBiase told jurors the case stems from a daylight shooting on Sept. 12, 2018.

According to the Crown, 22-year-old Christopher Clements-Card went to visit his girlfriend in the Bonaventure subdivision and encountered the accused, Zachary McDermott.

“There was a confrontation and Mr. Clements-Card punched Mr. McDermott,” DiBiase told the jury.

The Crown alleges Clements-Card then left and went to a nearby coffee shop.

Jurors were told surveillance video will show McDermott driving into the parking lot moments later.

“Mr. McDermott pulls into the parking lot ... seconds later Mr. McDermott shot Mr. Clements-Card twice,” DiBiase said.

The Crown alleges both bullets entered the victim’s body through his back before McDermott returned to his vehicle and drove away.

Clements-Card was taken to hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

McDermott, now 26, has pleaded not guilty to second-degree murder.

The court has heard more than 100 people are connected to the case. The trial is expected to last about four weeks.

stories.title: Internal Montreal police records describe ‘radicalized’ subculture among officers
stories.summary: Documents reveal details police chief never shared with the public about what May have led police management to disarm and dismantle a 16-member patrol unit
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
A “radicalized” subculture formed among the ranks of officers at a Montreal police station in a multicultural neighbourhood before it was rocked by allegations of racism and criminal misconduct, newly released internal briefing notes say.

The documents, obtained by The Canadian Press through access to information legislation, are part of a package prepared for the appearance of Fady Dagher, Montreal’s police chief, before a municipal public safety committee in August.

The newly released records reveal details Dagher never shared with the public about what may have led police management to disarm and dismantle a 16-member patrol unit at the station located in the city’s Montréal-Nord borough.

The documents include a copy of Dagher’s presentation to the municipal committee and draft speaking notes describing how police handled the incident at the Montréal-Nord station.

The speaking notes say the reaction inside the force – after some officers blew the whistle about alleged misconduct by their colleagues – reflects how the police force was seeing cracks in a “code of silence” as part of a cultural shift in the organization that left a few officers feeling isolated.

The internal records also confirm police had enough evidence to take action against members of the patrol unit a day before they dismantled the unit and informed the public late on a Friday night in mid-June.

The draft speaking notes say a subculture was developing within this patrol unit at the station, involving “a marginalized fringe [group] of our employees who were radicalized” and resisted efforts to eliminate misconduct and change the culture of the police force.

“These people reject all the work accomplished by Montreal police in recent years,” said one passage in the internal documents. “They rejected it and, in a way, made that known. They sought to recognize each other.”

The documents do not explain what the force meant by “radicalized,” how many employees it believed the term applied to, or what it meant when it said they had sought to recognize each other.

Dagher and other police officials have not shared details about alleged incidents that led police to dismantle the patrol unit; however, he has confirmed one of the allegations under review is about officers who allegedly cut the hair of racialized civilians to keep as trophies.

Montreal police said they were working on responses to questions from The Canadian Press about the newly released documents but did not immediately provide answers.

However, in a statement published Monday, police said they had sent the evidence to Quebec prosecutors, who will determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

Experts and anti-racism advocates have expressed alarm after being told about the language used in the internal documents.

The police force “is basically admitting that a process of change will create little cliques of marginalized people that become even more brutal,” said Ted Rutland, a professor of geography at Concordia University who researches policing in Canada. “And that is believable and scary, so it’s interesting that [Dagher] didn’t say that out loud.”

Martin Geoffroy, a sociology professor at Cégep Édouard-Montpetit, says it’s possible that officials were referring to far-right radicalization.

Geoffroy co-authored a federally funded study of far-right groups in Quebec and has studied far-right movements for over 20 years.

But he noted that he was speculating about what had happened within the patrol unit since the documents do not provide a detailed definition or explanation of its description of “radicalized” officers.

He said that his previous research found former police officers and military personnel were among members of far-right groups.

“What we can see in [the documents] is that there is resistance” to efforts to change the culture, he said.

The documents also reveal new details about how employees reacted to the scandal, suggesting that most of the force were upset about the alleged actions of officers at the Montréal-Nord station.

“You have no idea how many Montreal police officers wrote to me expressing shock about what they had learned,” said the speaking notes. “It was to the point where they were furious with their colleagues for dishonouring their uniform and destroying all the work they had tried to accomplish over the years.”

Dave Poitras, a sociologist at Université de Montréal who specializes in radicalization, said police forces are large organizations that can reflect the range of beliefs found in society.

But he cautioned that ideology alone cannot explain the alleged conduct at Station 39. He said the factors that lead someone to commit such acts “obviously go beyond adherence to any ideology.”

Poitras is scientific director of Villes sans violence, a non-profit group that focuses on preventing extremism and hate crimes. He said his organization defines radicalization as a process of adopting extreme beliefs and a willingness to use, encourage or facilitate violence to advance an ideology, political project or cause.

Such beliefs can involve placing certain groups above others, he said, citing racial hierarchies and white supremacy as examples.

He said some of the alleged conduct at Station 39 appears to have had a hateful character and that hateful incidents or crimes can result from radicalization. But not enough is known to determine whether individual officers were in fact radicalized, he said.

Radicalization is “not something that happens overnight,” Poitras said. “It really has to be understood as a process on a continuum that can take time.”

The records also appears to reveal more about what police knew before dismantling the Station 39 team.

An entry dated June 11 says: “We received confirmation of concrete investigative elements.” The next begins: “June 12: I decide to proceed immediately.”

Another document states that as of June 11: “A threshold for validating the information has been reached to justify decisive management actions.”

Dagher has rejected criticism about his decision to announce the news he was dismantling the unit late on a Friday evening, maintaining that he has been transparent about the investigation and acted as fast as possible

Police have said the intervening period between June 11 and June 12 was used to prepare the operation before the officers arrived for their next shift.

That evening, all 16 were disarmed, two were suspended, three were assigned administrative duties and the remaining 11 were relocated – measures the documents say were taken “to ensure the safety of the population.”

By mid-August, police said four officers had been suspended.

One part of the document also notes how Quebec’s Police Act requires a police chief to notify the minister responsible for public safety “without delay” of an allegation that an officer committed a criminal offence, unless, after consulting prosecutors, it is deemed frivolous or unfounded.

The notes say Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière was informed at 8:45 p.m. on June 12, shortly before police publicly announced they were taking action. Asked about the June 11 entry and whether the minister should have been notified earlier, a spokesperson for Lafrenière declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigations.

Poitras is scientific director of Villes sans violence, a non-profit group that focuses on preventing extremism and hate crimes. He said his organization defines radicalization as a process of adopting extreme beliefs and a willingness to use, encourage or facilitate violence to advance an ideology, political project or cause.
Such beliefs can involve placing certain groups above others, he said, citing racial hierarchies and white supremacy as examples.

He said some of the alleged conduct at Station 39 appears to have had a hateful character and that hateful incidents or crimes can result from radicalization. But not enough is known to determine whether individual officers were in fact radicalized, he said.
Radicalization is “not something that happens overnight,” Poitras said. “It really has to be understood as a process on a continuum that can take time.”
The records also appears to reveal more about what police knew before dismantling the Station 39 team.
An entry dated June 11 says: “We received confirmation of concrete investigative elements.” The next begins: “June 12: I decide to proceed immediately.”
Another document states that as of June 11: “A threshold for validating the information has been reached to justify decisive management actions.”

Dagher has rejected criticism about his decision to announce the news he was dismantling the unit late on a Friday evening, maintaining that he has been transparent about the investigation and acted as fast as possible
Police have said the intervening period between June 11 and June 12 was used to prepare the operation before the officers arrived for their next shift.

That evening, all 16 were disarmed, two were suspended, three were assigned administrative duties and the remaining 11 were relocated – measures the documents say were taken “to ensure the safety of the population.”
By mid-August, police said four officers had been suspended.

One part of the document also notes how Quebec’s Police Act requires a police chief to notify the minister responsible for public safety “without delay” of an allegation that an officer committed a criminal offence, unless, after consulting prosecutors, it is deemed frivolous or unfounded.

The notes say Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière was informed at 8:45 p.m. on June 12, shortly before police publicly announced they were taking action. Asked about the June 11 entry and whether the minister should have been notified earlier, a spokesperson for Lafrenière declined to comment, citing the ongoing investigations.

stories.title: TD executive sues after being fired for adding Christian symbol to her email signature
stories.summary: TD Insurance VP claims discrimination after losing $210,000 job; bank says she ignored warnings to bring her email signature into compliance
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
A Christian addition to her TD Insurance email signature has cost a senior manager her $210,000-per-year job.

In a statement of claim filed with the Ontario Superior Court of Justice in Toronto, Sonja Denobrega seeks more than $400,000 in damages from TD, alleging she was wrongfully dismissed after tagging “I am HIS ✝️” on to the end of her email signature in a stand against a company policy that she says “only allowed for gender/sex identification and allowed no room for other identities.”

Denobrega, the company’s former associate vice-president of underwriting operations, claims that her January 2026 firing was discriminatory, alleging that her termination was based partly on her creed and age.

For its part, TD says that 52-year-old Denobrega’s dismissal had nothing to do with her creed, age or any other protected characteristic under human rights legislation. Instead, the company’s statement of defence says that it had just cause to terminate Denobrega’s employment without notice, as a result of her wilful subordination after she repeatedly ignored warnings to bring her email signature into compliance.

“The Plaintiff’s employment was terminated solely due to her failure to comply with TD’s standards regarding email signatures, which were explained to her on several occasions,” the court document reads. “As a senior employee in a leadership position, the Plaintiff was expected to model compliance with TD’s policies, not to defy them. Her misconduct undermined TD’s ability to rely on her to follow TD procedures and guidelines and resulted in a loss of trust that irreparably damaged the employment relationship.”

According to Denobrega’s claim, she told a HR representative that she wanted TD to remove pronouns from its signature lines. However, the company’s response says that its policy of permitting – but not requiring – employees to identify their pronouns was non-negotiable.

“TD cannot reverse this policy as doing so would be a breach of its obligations under the Canadian Human Rights Act,” the company says in its statement of defence.

None of the allegations in either document have been proven in court. Denobrega did not respond to a request for comment, while a TD spokesperson said the company was unable to say anything further as the matter is before the courts.

Denobrega has more than 25 years of experience in the insurance business, but had only been at TD for a few months following a switch from a rival insurer, before the email-signature saga began in late October 2025.

According to TD’s account of events, that’s when its HR department received a complaint about one of Denobrega’s colleagues, who had modified her email signature to add “Pronouns: I am HIS ✝️,” which the complainant said could be taken as a micro-aggression against members of the Lgbtq+ community.

Denobrega’s claim says that the incident spurred her to offer support to the colleague and look into TD’s Christian-related resources, which ultimately left her unimpressed. Denobrega “felt that there were fewer resources for Christians at TD and more resources for the Lgbt community which she found unfair,” the statement of claim says.

When Denobrega found out that the colleague had been asked to remove the line from her email signature, she took her support a step further, adding the “I am HIS ✝️” line (without the reference to pronouns) to her own in solidarity.

In a meeting with her boss and two HR representatives, Denobrega called for a TD-wide review of email signature compliance, explaining that her problem with company’s policy was that she felt it “only allowed for gender/sex identification and allowed no room for other identities.”

Several more meetings followed, in which TD’s insistence that the email signature additions be removed and Denobrega’s push for a company-wide email signature check and escalation to the CEO were each rebuffed by the opposing sides. However, Denobrega did succeed in convincing TD to send an email blast reminding around 10,000 of its insurance division staff of the current email signature standards, according to her claim.

In court documents, Denobrega is seeking compensation for $235,000 in lost pay and bonuses during a 12-month notice period, as well as a further $210,000 for punitive damages and human rights violations, arguing that TD’s punishment was disproportionate to her alleged misconduct.

“Sonja had no intention of behaving in a manner that would jeopardize her employment” and was “completely unaware that her actions would result in her termination,” Denobrega’s claim reads.

TD’s defence says that the code of conduct it provides to every employee warns that any breach could result in discipline, including termination.

Meanwhile, its email signature standards prohibit personalization through “quotes, taglines, icons, images, slogans, or other personal statements.”

In addition, TD’s email signature rules permit “only limited, optional identifiers such as personal pronouns, consistent with its obligations” under the company’s code of conduct, respectful workplace policy and applicable law, the statement of defence continues.

Toronto employment lawyer Paulette Haynes, who has no involvement in the case, says each party will face its own challenge as the dispute progresses through the court system.

On the issue of alleged discrimination, Denobrega will have the burden of proving a link between her religious views and the reasons for her termination, Haynes explains.

“The bank’s defence says that she has not established that causal nexus,” she adds.

Meanwhile, the onus will shift to TD to back up its claim for “just cause” termination, which allows an employer to fire a worker without paying any severance.

“I always tell my employer clients that it’s an uphill battle when you terminate for just cause,” Haynes says.

“The misconduct has to be so egregious that it basically breaches the employment contract in a fundamental way,” she adds, explaining that proving a case depends heavily on the specific facts.

A judge who ultimately hears the matter will look closely at the context when assessing whether an employer was right to invoke just cause, including the worker’s employment history and disciplinary record, Haynes says.

“It’s a unique case and I’ll be watching closely,” she says.

stories.title: Bed Bath & Beyond Canada relaunches online, hopes to open first store next year
stories.summary: Bed Bath & Beyond Canada's new owner is hoping to use online shopping to wake up the dormant brand before it makes a brick-and-mortar comeback.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Bed Bath & Beyond Canada’s new owner is hoping to use online shopping to wake up the dormant brand before it makes a brick-and-mortar comeback.

Sleep Country Canada relaunched the home goods retailer Tuesday through an e-commerce website expected to precede stores opening next year.

The online revival comes about a year after Sleep Country purchased the Canadian and U.K. rights to the Bed Bath & Beyond name and logos from Overstock.com.

The online marketplace had picked up the trademarks in 2023, after Bed Bath & Beyond Canada filed for creditor protection and closed its stores amid “dramatic” declines in revenue. The U.S. arm of the company followed suit a few months later.

The retailer’s new Canadian iteration aims to revive the most cherished elements of the brand’s past but also take a more curated approach befitting an evolving market with the rise of e-commerce, new competitors such as H&M Home and Simons, the loss of Hudson’s Bay and sluggish home sales.

“We feel the timing is right and we feel like the market is ready for what we are doing,” Bed Bath & Beyond Canada president Carol Deacon said.

“There are endless options online … and there’s also a lot of other physical retail where there’s some very distinct styles and designs, but we think there’s an opportunity to make sure there’s a bit more choice.”

The new business will stock about 6,000 products in classic Bed Bath & Beyond categories like kitchen, decor, bedroom and bathroom, but also mix in trendier and domestic brands consumers are demanding.

That means shoppers will find KitchenAid, Umbra and Calvin Klein products alongside merchandise from Lacoste, Smeg and Sleep Country affiliates Endy, Bloom, Simba, and Silk and Snow.

While many parts of the Bed Bath & Beyond Canada business won’t dramatically change, two areas are being revamped significantly: furniture and baby.

The company is paring back on furniture, at least initially, because there’s a lot of competitors out there and it’s a category that is difficult for shipping, Deacon said.

With baby, it wants to focus more narrowly on products consumers could use to prepare their home for an infant rather than on everything tots would need.

“For us to come up with an offering across the home that we really were proud and comfortable with, we just went a bit narrower in some areas, but we know we will be expanding over time,” Deacon said.

That expansion will also eventually bring back the brick-and-mortar stores most customers remember Bed Bath & Beyond for.

The brand is still working out its store strategy but is on track to open a first location in late 2027, she said.

When it faltered in 2023, the company had 54 Bed Bath & Beyond stores and 11 BuyBuy Baby locations.

Deacon signalled that the brand is unlikely to have the same kind of store count or hulking properties it once did.

“It will likely be a lot more focused than it was historically for Bed Bath & Beyond in terms of footprint and store size,” she said.

Lisa Hutcheson, J.C. Williams Group retail strategist, thought it made sense for Bed Bath & Beyond Canada to test its revival online before opening small stores.

“There is infrastructure and whatnot required with e-commerce, but (this way) you’re not making those commitments to physical stores and you’re starting to learn more about how the customer is shopping your product,” she said.

What Bed Bath & Beyond will likely find is the retail environment it left is not the one it is returning to. Home sales are down and Canadians are making fewer home goods purchases, Hutcheson pointed out.

Statistics Canada data from July showed furniture, home furnishings, electronics and appliances sales dropped 4.9 per cent from a year prior.

“Mortgage rates aren’t coming down. They’re going up and there’s still that wave of people that have cheap mortgages that are coming up for renewal, so they’re being very, very cautious,” Hutcheson said. “And home furnishings typically are a bit more expensive.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 29, 2026.

Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Vancouver transit operator expands into real estate
stories.summary: TransLink hopes to improve transit network connections and create more housing
stories.author: Howard Chai
stories.content:
Vancouver’s major public transit operator is expanding to become a residential and commercial landlord.

As part of its 2022 investment plan, TransLink, which operates Vancouver’s SkyTrain, SeaBus and other public transportation services across the region, announced it will turn its real estate assets into a new non-fare, non-taxation revenue source.

Now known as its Real Estate Development Program, the initiative aims to enhance transit network connections and create more housing to the Metro Vancouver region as it grows.

The program speaks to the value of real estate in British Columbia and is the latest example of a non-real-estate business venturing into real estate development. Other recent examples in Canada include Vancouver-based telecom Telus and local bakery chain Breka Bakery , both of which submitted applications this year to redevelop properties they own into high-rise towers.

In late July, and in partnership with local developer PCI Developments, TransLink broke ground on its first real estate project: A 31-storey tower located at the southwest corner of West Broadway and Arbutus Street in Vancouver’s Kitsilano neighbourhood. Once complete, the property will include 256 at-market rental units, 47 below-market rental units, retail space and a public plaza.

TransLink, a publicly owned agency created by the Province of British Columbia, says it’s taking a long-term approach by developing on excess land that it owns instead of selling it. That approach allows TransLink to play a role in how the projects are built and ensures smoother integration with existing transit infrastructure.

In separate interviews, TransLink CEO Kevin Quinn and PCI Developments president Tim Grant said that the 50/50 partnership emerged because the two companies owned neighbouring properties that could better serve as a single site. The two organizations have had a long-standing relationship since PCI primarily develops large mixed-use hubs that are integrated with transit stations, such as the Marine Gateway in Vancouver and the King George Hub in Surrey.

The TransLink-PCI project comes as British Columbia nears completion on an extension of the SkyTrain’s Millennium Line – connecting Burnaby, Port Moody and Coquitlam to Vancouver’s Broadway corridor, where six new stations are being added. The project will be located across the street from the line’s final terminal, Arbutus Station. A ground-floor retail unit in the new building is also being built so it can be reconfigured into a secondary entrance for Arbutus Station if needed.

Mr. Quinn says the vision for the project was a “complete community” and transportation network, which is why a public plaza will connect the future Arbutus Station to the existing Arbutus Greenway – a nine-kilometre trail for pedestrians and cyclists that runs from near Granville Island to South Vancouver.

Throughout its history, TransLink has bought and sold pieces of real estate, usually in relation to its transit facilities and operations. It also manages retail space in some SkyTrain stations and often co-ordinates with developers that have projects near transit stations.

But developing housing is a completely new endeavour for the transit operator, which has already identified about eight sites that have the potential to be redeveloped, Mr. Quinn says. A few of those projects are already in the pipeline as part of the organization’s Real Estate Development Program, which first started to take shape in 2019.

One of those projects includes a new community development in Surrey, B.C. – a partnership between TransLink and the Surrey City Development Corporation (SCDC) that will see 35 city-owned acres and five TransLink-owned acres transformed into 2,200 news homes, 150,000 square feet of retail space and a new community centre. The property, part of TransLink’s and the SCDC’s Newton Master Development Plan , will be supported by a new rapid-transit bus route and station.

Elsewhere, TransLink is also planning a two-acre project with mixed-use towers rising 14 and 12 storeys near Moodyville Park in North Vancouver, as well as a redevelopment of a nine-acre site next to Coquitlam Central Station in Coquitlam that could accommodate as many as nine towers.

Mr. Quinn says TransLink has received feedback from both North Vancouver and Coquitlam and is now refining its designs, with the aim of returning to both councils with updated proposals in 2027. He says TransLink may also partner with private developers on those projects, recognizing that the company’s expertise is in transportation and not in development.

For TransLink, diversifying its revenue is important to the organization’s long-term growth.

“Certainly, a key part of this is looking at ways to diversify and generate long-term revenue, so we can continue to invest and upgrade our transit system,” says Mr. Quinn. “It allows us to rely a little less on fares and taxation. It’s a new innovative source for us that takes pressure off of other sources.”

Mr. Quinn says TransLink’s three major revenue streams are transit fares, the fuel taxes it collects from remitted gasoline sales and the property taxes it collects from homeowners.

Revenue generated from the organization’s Real Estate Development Program – an estimated $22-million over 10 years, according to Mr. Quinn – would be considered ancillary, along with revenue from other sources such as the development charges collected on new real estate developments in the region.

Asked whether TransLink will stick to rental housing and stay away from condo development, Mr. Quinn says the company is looking at projects on a case-by-case basis, including how they may support the goals of the local municipality.

TransLink is not the first transportation operator in the world to get into the real estate development business. The organization has looked toward Hong Kong’s MTR Corporation and MTR Properties as inspiration, but Mr. Quinn says he hopes to inspire others.

“Getting into the real estate development business is something we’ve wanted to do for quite some time. I’d like to think that we’re leaders in North America in this space – this new revenue stream – and we’re really proud of that,” he says.

stories.title: London, Ont. police officers under investigation
stories.summary: London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London’s police chief has ordered an investigation after a video surfaced appearing to show officers leaving a restaurant and entering an unmarked police vehicle with alcohol visible inside and a service-issued firearm stored in a manner that raised concerns.

In a statement, London Police Service Chief Thai Truong said the incident took place in Toronto on June 24, 2026, following a police funeral.

Truong said he personally reviewed the video and immediately directed that the matter be referred to Toronto police for a criminal investigation into the handling and storage of the firearm.

Once the criminal investigation is complete, the conduct of the officers involved will also be reviewed under the Community Safety and Policing Act, the statement said.

One senior officer has been suspended with pay pending the outcome of the investigations.

According to Truong, the decision on suspension should not be viewed as minimizing the seriousness of the allegations, noting that the legislative framework governing police discipline has not met the threshold required for a suspension without pay at this stage.

“Police officers are entrusted with significant authority and responsibilities,” said Truong. “With that comes an expectation that we will conduct ourselves in a manner that maintains the confidence of the community we serve.”

He added that those expectations apply to all members of the service and are particularly important for officers in leadership positions.

Truong said there will be no further comment on the evidence, citing the need to protect the integrity of the investigations, but said additional information would be released when appropriate.

No criminal charges have been announced and investigators have not released the identities of the officers involved.
