stories.title: Masked group seen on B.C. First Nation land are ‘cowards,’ officials say
stories.summary: Reaction is pouring in to what appears to be a group of white nationalists holding a demonstration on a B.C. First Nation on Sunday.
stories.author: Amy Judd, Kristen Robinson
stories.content:
Warning: This story contains details that May be disturbing to readers. Discretion is advised.

Reaction is pouring in to what appears to be a group of white nationalists holding a demonstration on a B.C. First Nation on Sunday.

Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc Kukpi7 Chief Rosanne Casimir told Global News on Sunday that several individuals wearing black clothing and hats with white material covering their faces showed up in the community on Sunday morning.

She said the photos she saw were believed to be individuals belonging to the Second Sons of Canada. Global News has not independently confirmed the identities of the individuals or if they are associated with any group.

Kamloops RCMP Supt. Jeff Pelley said in a release that the group of people seen on the First Nation also put up a sign.

“The posting of a banner bearing the words ‘got bones’, combined with the use of masks to conceal their identities while making such public statements is a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division,” he said.

“The RCMP is taking this matter seriously and will continue to engage the group as part of our response and current ongoing investigation.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on X that the group’s act was “cowardly” and “abhorrent.”

“It has no place in this country,” he said.

“My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate. This week, we will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It is a stark reminder of our shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system and the consequences still felt today. Courageous Survivors shared the truth, so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation.”

Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc was formally known as the Kamloops Indian Band.

In 2021, the First Nation shared findings that indicated the presence of more than 200 potential unmarked burials on the grounds of the former residential school there.

Wade Grant, Liberal MP and member of the Musqueam Nation, told Global News that this act is an example of why more education is needed.

“It’s about communicating with our next generations, but also those that are here today,” he said.

“And I, we’ve done a great job of that. We have so many people that are now wanting to learn more about Indigenous peoples, Indigenous cultures, and how that is an important fabric in this country we call Canada.”

Grant added that residential school denialism is opening up wounds that people have tried to heal for generations.

“I have two young children myself,” he added. “I don’t want them to grow up in a country where Indigenous and non-Indigenous are separated. We need to bring them together. And that’s all about coming together and having these conversations right now.”

BC NDP Leader David Eby called the group’s actions a “disgusting display” and “such an anti-British Columbia thing to do.”

He said they were cowards because they covered their faces.

“If you think you’ve got people on-side, you don’t hide your face, and they know that the repercussions would be swift and merciless, because British Columbians don’t stand for this,” Eby added.

“I call on every British Columbian and every politician who is running at every level to denounce this, to stand up to these cowards, to call them out and say not in our province.”

BC Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson echoed Eby’s words, saying these actions are “absolutely appalling.”

“I hope that our law enforcement does everything they can and everything that is available to them to make sure that events like that do not happen in our province. I thought it was absolutely disgusting.”

Anyone with information, photos or video footage of this incident, or knowledge of future gatherings is encouraged to contact the Tk’emlúps Rural RCMP Detachment at 250-314-1800 or the Kamloops RCMP Detachment at 250-828-3000 and cite file 2026-32566.

Anyone can also remain anonymous by calling Crime Stoppers at 1800-222-8477 (Tips).

The Indian Residential Schools Crisis Line (1-800-721-0066) is available 24 hours a day for anyone experiencing pain or distress as a result of their residential school experience.

The Hope for Wellness Help Line offers culturally competent counselling and crisis intervention to all Indigenous Peoples experiencing trauma, distress, strong emotions and painful memories. The line can be reached anytime toll-free at 1-855-242-3310.

stories.title: ‘I wouldn’t compare’ Alberta secession vote to Brexit, says Former British PM David Cameron
stories.summary: Echoes of 2016 referendum on EU membership, which prompted Cameron to resign, have loomed large over the province’s separation debate
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Former British prime minister David Cameron, who oversaw his country’s vote on Brexit as well as a referendum on Scottish independence, says he sees significant differences between those and Alberta’s coming vote on separation.

Speaking at an energy conference in Calgary on Monday, Mr. Cameron said he wishes he had spent more time at the negotiating table before allowing a vote that took the outcome out of his hands.

“I wouldn’t compare what you’re discussing here with the Brexit referendum,” he said.

“Brexit was about whether we wanted to stay in a trade association with an element of political union. I mean, Canada is not a trade association with an element of political union. Canada is an amazing country with an incredible history.”

Mr. Cameron, who resigned as prime minister in 2016 the day after Britain narrowly voted to leave the bloc, said he wishes he’d “pushed the pause button” and taken longer to negotiate with the European Union.

He added that he failed to convince people to vote in favour of remaining in the EU, suggesting he didn’t campaign forcefully enough for that side.

The former British prime minister made the comments exactly three weeks before Alberta voters will have their say on whether they want a second, binding secession referendum – a vote that frequently draws comparisons to Brexit.

Echoes of Britain’s 2016 referendum on its membership in the EU have loomed large over Alberta’s separation debate. Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was governor of the Bank of England at the time of the British vote, has called Alberta’s plan a “dangerous bluff” and pointed to parallels between the two referendums.

Mr. Cameron called the 2016 vote under pressure from segments of his party that were skeptical of the European Union. He campaigned to stay in the EU, but the loss led to more than four years of negotiations between Britain and the bloc.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, meanwhile, has pointed to discontent in her province over Ottawa’s direction on energy policy under former prime minister Justin Trudeau as the impetus for the Oct. 19 referendum. In March, 2025, Ms. Smith threatened an “unprecedented national unity crisis” if Ottawa did not scrap laws she viewed as hostile toward Alberta’s energy industry. Mr. Carney has since eliminated many of those laws.

While Ms. Smith has argued that she called the referendum because of public demand – notably in two competing petitions that garnered hundreds of thousands of signatures – her detractors have accused her of attempting to appease separatists who make up a substantial part of her political base, according to public opinion polling. The Premier has said she and her colleagues in the governing United Conservative Party favour remaining in Canada.

Polling shows that roughly a quarter of Albertans would vote to hold a binding referendum on abandoning Canada. Before the British referendum, the remain side also led in the polls but ultimately lost with 48 per cent of the vote.

Mr. Cameron has argued since Brexit that warnings about the consequences of leaving the EU were drowned out by an emotionally charged leave campaign.

“We wanted to remain a sovereign, independent United Kingdom, but part of this association. My regret is that I failed to convince people that that was the best answer,” he said Monday.

Mr. Cameron said Scotland’s 2014 independence referendum worried him more than Brexit because it threatened to break up the U.K. “If you have a referendum, you can’t guarantee what the result is going to be,” he said.

While polling suggests Alberta separatists will be defeated soundly next month, observers say voter turnout will play a major role in the result. Ms. Smith, who has spent the better part of her political career railing against what she views as an overstepping federal government, has also said she’s concerned voters may use the referendum to express their frustration with Ottawa. Indeed, some separatist groups are advertising the vote as a means to extract concessions from Mr. Carney and his Liberal government.

On Monday, Ms. Smith argued the conditions in Alberta’s referendum are different from Brexit, contending that the EU didn’t work to solve the problems that she believes motivated Britain’s referendum.

She contrasted that with Ottawa’s approach under Mr. Carney.

“I see a major reach-out on the part of Ottawa to not only acknowledge but also address in a very serious way the issues that caused the tension in the first place,” Ms. Smith said.

“I hope it has an impact on election day.”

Randall Hansen, a political science professor at the University of Toronto’s Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said Brexit and Alberta’s referendum have numerous parallels between them, but that doesn’t mean Alberta will immediately march down the same path as Britain.

What happens after the referendum will matter more, he said, pointing to Britain’s earliest rumblings of discontent in the 1980s over its relationship with Europe.

“The Alberta conservatives … cannot make the mistake the Tories made in the 80s, which is continually delegitimize the federation,” Prof. Hansen said.

“That two-thirds can become 50 per cent, and the next time around you might end up in a situation that everyone would regret on both sides, which is Alberta leaving the federation.”

stories.title: ‘We can’t live like this’: Residents demand garbage solution
stories.summary: An eyesore for residents at 234 Edgevalley Road, a massive pile of garbage they say has to go.
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
An eyesore for residents at 234 Edgevalley Road, a massive pile of garbage they say has to go.

“We need a permanent solution,” said resident Rana Nissan. “We can’t live like this.”

Nissan has lived in the complex since 2024 and said the mess has been an issue since she moved in.

“People from surrounding areas as well, they just come and dump their garbage and leave,” said Nissan. “I see it all the time.”

She said a private junk removal company comes during the week and picks up the trash but it piles up quickly.

“They don’t come during the weekend and it looks like this during the night time,” said Nissan. “They come in the morning and pick it up so basically we need someone 24 hours just to clean people’s garbage and it attracts a lot of animals during the night.”

Residents told CTV News there are often items like tables, chairs, and even mattresses being dumped.

“Sometimes the garbage is piled up so high we can’t get to my car,” said Nissan. “We have to go through the passenger side.”

London city councillor Peter Cuddy said he’s been in contact with the property management company, Reed Condominium Management Solutions, since last year.

“We came to a solution that they would do a better job managing it,” said Cuddy. “That didn’t happen.”

Nissan says she’d like to see the management company step in and do something.

The property management company said it’s looked into installing security cameras to help deter illegal dumping, but it’s not financially possible.

“We don’t have a pest issue, we don’t have a rodent issue, we don’t have an insect issue,” said Laurie Reed, CEO and President of Reed Condominium Management Solutions. “At the end of the day the board is doing its best to make sure the garbage is collected without having a serious financial impact on residents.”

Cuddy said more needs to be done

“I’m going to go back to speak to city staff about capping it permanently and then moving it,” he said. “This can’t go on.”

stories.title: Toronto Police constable pleads guilty after licence plate search uncovered by Project South
stories.summary: Information from Constable Elias Mouawad’s search was relayed to alleged organized crime figure at centre of the corruption probe, court heard Monday
stories.author: Molly Hayes
stories.content:
A Toronto Police constable charged as part of the large-scale Project South investigation pleaded guilty to unauthorized use of a computer Monday, in connection with a licence plate query he conducted for a former boss at a security company.

Constable Elias Mouawad was 24 years old and had only been with the police service for about a year and a half when he was swept up in February in what York Regional Police detectives have called the largest police corruption probe in Canadian history. It has led to charges against seven active Toronto Police officers, one recently retired constable and nearly 20 civilians.

Constable Mouawad was not a direct target of Project South and only came on to investigators’ radar because he ran a licence plate search for a suspect whose phone was being wiretapped by police, according to a statement of facts laid out in the courtroom. Information from the licence plate search was then relayed to an alleged organized crime figure at the centre of the corruption probe.

Defence lawyer Peter Brauti said despite the constable’s one-off involvement, a Google search of his client’s name yields pages’ worth of news articles about Project South.

“Some will always think he’s this corrupt cop from Project South,” Mr. Brauti said. “And that’s a very high price to pay for a single computer check.”

Mr. Brauti argued his client deserves a conditional discharge (meaning he would not have a criminal record provided he abides by agreed upon conditions) in order to give him a chance at keeping his policing job. The Crown, on the other hand, argued for a four-month conditional sentence, stressing the need for deterrence and denunciation.

“This is a case of an officer knowingly breaching his oath, and by that act, allowing criminals – even though he may not have subjectively intended it – by his carelessness, to co-opt and compromise the Toronto Police Service,” Crown attorney Sam Walker said.

The Project South probe, led by York Regional Police, began in June of last year, after the alleged attempted killing of a Toronto South Detention Centre correctional officer at his home. Investigators have said they worked backward after the attempted hit, and determined a Toronto Police constable, Timothy Barnhardt, had used confidential police databases to leak information about the guard to an alleged large-scale drug trafficker, Brian Da Costa.

As part of the investigation, police received judicial authorization to run wiretaps on a number of suspects in the project, including Constable Barnhardt, Mr. Da Costa and his alleged associate Daljit Singh, who runs private security companies that Constable Mouawad used to work for.

In mid-January, police listened in as Mr. Singh and Constable Mouawad spoke by phone about a licence plate query that Mr. Singh had asked him to do for “his boy.”

“Why does your boy need a photo of the thing?” Constable Mouawad asked Mr. Singh, who was at an industrial complex in Mississauga with Mr. Da Costa at the time, according to an agreed statement of facts submitted in the case Monday.

Mr. Singh told him they “just wanted to see if that was the right people.”

“Like he wants his ID photo?” Constable Mouawad asked, according to the facts.

Mr. Singh confirmed, assuring him “it’s nothing bad.”

Less than an hour after Constable Mouawad looked up the plate for a Black Chevy Tahoe rental car through confidential TPS databases, the agreed facts note Mr. Da Costa was observed climbing into the passenger seat of that very vehicle, parked in Vaughan.

The driver linked to the vehicle and nature of their association with Mr. Da Costa are unknown, the facts say. There’s no evidence that Constable Mouawad knew about any of it.

When Constable Mouawad was arrested on Feb. 4, he agreed to provide a statement, and handed over the passwords to his computer and phone.

He did not believe there was any nefarious reason for the request, the facts said, and he only ran the licence plate because Mr. Singh had been a “caring boss” while he’d worked for him.

Constable Mouawad, now 25, has been suspended from TPS without pay since his arrest, and has lost roughly $75,000 in wages as a result, Mr. Brauti said.

Court heard Monday that he has wanted to plead guilty since he was charged. But due to the massive amount of disclosure the Crown had to sift through, it was not prepared to accept a plea until recently.

Typically, these types of data breaches result in discipline proceedings and a few days’ docked pay, Mr. Brauti said in his submissions Monday. If this case wasn’t part of Project South, he argued, none of them would even be in that courtroom.

“We’d be in the police tribunal, and we’d be doing a joint submission for 10 days’ pay,” Mr. Brauti said.

Mr. Singh is charged under Project South with fraudulently obtaining a computer service. His lawyer Harval Bassi declined to comment Monday, as the matter is still before the courts.

Mr. Da Costa, who faces an array of charges, was released on bail of $1.5-million in March, only to have it revoked after a bail review in May. He too appeared briefly in court Monday, where his application for a bail review was dismissed.

Constable Barnhardt also remains in custody, after losing two bids at bail.

The charges against them have not yet been tested in court.

Justice Catherine Rhinelander reserved her decision on sentencing in Constable Mouawad’s case Monday. He is scheduled to return on Oct. 19. (A second charge he faced – breach of trust – was withdrawn as part of his plea.)

At the conclusion of court Monday, Constable Mouawad read out an eight-minute apology letter, accepting responsibility for his actions and vowing to learn from his mistakes.

“To this day, every time I see a police car rushing with their lights and sirens to a call, my heart would cry out, hoping that one day I could be back in that car again, and continue making a positive impact.”

content_blocks.text: A Toronto Police constable charged as part of the large-scale Project South investigation pleaded guilty to unauthorized use of a computer Monday, in connection with a licence plate query he conducted for a former boss at a security company.

Constable Elias Mouawad was 24 years old and had only been with the police service for about a year and a half when he was swept up in February in what York Regional Police detectives have called the largest police corruption probe in Canadian history. It has led to charges against seven active Toronto Police officers, one recently retired constable and nearly 20 civilians.

Constable Mouawad was not a direct target of Project South and only came on to investigators’ radar because he ran a licence plate search for a suspect whose phone was being wiretapped by police, according to a statement of facts laid out in the courtroom. Information from the licence plate search was then relayed to an alleged organized crime figure at the centre of the corruption probe.
Defence lawyer Peter Brauti said despite the constable’s one-off involvement, a Google search of his client’s name yields pages’ worth of news articles about Project South.
“Some will always think he’s this corrupt cop from Project South,” Mr. Brauti said. “And that’s a very high price to pay for a single computer check.”

Mr. Brauti argued his client deserves a conditional discharge (meaning he would not have a criminal record provided he abides by agreed upon conditions) in order to give him a chance at keeping his policing job. The Crown, on the other hand, argued for a four-month conditional sentence, stressing the need for deterrence and denunciation.

“This is a case of an officer knowingly breaching his oath, and by that act, allowing criminals – even though he may not have subjectively intended it – by his carelessness, to co-opt and compromise the Toronto Police Service,” Crown attorney Sam Walker said.

The Project South probe, led by York Regional Police, began in June of last year, after the alleged attempted killing of a Toronto South Detention Centre correctional officer at his home. Investigators have said they worked backward after the attempted hit, and determined a Toronto Police constable, Timothy Barnhardt, had used confidential police databases to leak information about the guard to an alleged large-scale drug trafficker, Brian Da Costa.

As part of the investigation, police received judicial authorization to run wiretaps on a number of suspects in the project, including Constable Barnhardt, Mr. Da Costa and his alleged associate Daljit Singh, who runs private security companies that Constable Mouawad used to work for.
In mid-January, police listened in as Mr. Singh and Constable Mouawad spoke by phone about a licence plate query that Mr. Singh had asked him to do for “his boy.”

“Why does your boy need a photo of the thing?” Constable Mouawad asked Mr. Singh, who was at an industrial complex in Mississauga with Mr. Da Costa at the time, according to an agreed statement of facts submitted in the case Monday.
Mr. Singh told him they “just wanted to see if that was the right people.”
“Like he wants his ID photo?” Constable Mouawad asked, according to the facts.
Mr. Singh confirmed, assuring him “it’s nothing bad.”

Less than an hour after Constable Mouawad looked up the plate for a Black Chevy Tahoe rental car through confidential TPS databases, the agreed facts note Mr. Da Costa was observed climbing into the passenger seat of that very vehicle, parked in Vaughan.
The driver linked to the vehicle and nature of their association with Mr. Da Costa are unknown, the facts say. There’s no evidence that Constable Mouawad knew about any of it.
When Constable Mouawad was arrested on Feb. 4, he agreed to provide a statement, and handed over the passwords to his computer and phone.
He did not believe there was any nefarious reason for the request, the facts said, and he only ran the licence plate because Mr. Singh had been a “caring boss” while he’d worked for him.
Constable Mouawad, now 25, has been suspended from TPS without pay since his arrest, and has lost roughly $75,000 in wages as a result, Mr. Brauti said.

Court heard Monday that he has wanted to plead guilty since he was charged. But due to the massive amount of disclosure the Crown had to sift through, it was not prepared to accept a plea until recently.

Typically, these types of data breaches result in discipline proceedings and a few days’ docked pay, Mr. Brauti said in his submissions Monday. If this case wasn’t part of Project South, he argued, none of them would even be in that courtroom.
“We’d be in the police tribunal, and we’d be doing a joint submission for 10 days’ pay,” Mr. Brauti said.
Mr. Singh is charged under Project South with fraudulently obtaining a computer service. His lawyer Harval Bassi declined to comment Monday, as the matter is still before the courts.

Mr. Da Costa, who faces an array of charges, was released on bail of $1.5-million in March, only to have it revoked after a bail review in May. He too appeared briefly in court Monday, where his application for a bail review was dismissed.
Constable Barnhardt also remains in custody, after losing two bids at bail.
The charges against them have not yet been tested in court.

stories.title: Flu and COVID vaccines are coming to London, but not yet. Seniors are looking forward to when they do
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/-JALIl20DKY With flu and COVID-19 season about to begin in London, members of the city's seni...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
With flu and COVID-19 season about to begin in London, members of the city’s senior community are looking forward to getting vaccinated, though they May have to wait a little longer.

As of Sept. 28, flu and COVID vaccines have begun being distributed in Ontario to elderly and high-risk individuals. The provincial Ministry of Health includes people aged 65 or above, patients and staff at hospitals, people with compromised immune systems and people living in long-term care homes and retirement homes as part of these groups of people.

Despite the beginning of this rollout, however, London May still have to wait. “The on-the-ground reality … is that the vaccine hasn’t arrived in London and Middlesex yet,” wrote Megan Cornwell, the manager of corporate communications and client relations at the Middlesex London Health Unit, in an email to XFM News.

Cornwell also said that even though the vaccines have begun to be available in Ontario, she doesn’t want to mislead the community by accident into thinking the vaccines are available in London just yet.

“The public conversation makes people in the community think they can get immunized now,” she wrote. “So they call and they are frustrated because there are no appointments yet (because there is no vaccine yet).”

The Health Unit said in an email to XFM News that people can follow them on social media or their website for updates on when the vaccines will arrive.

A pharmacy at Cherryhill Village Mall. When flu and COVID vaccines become available in London, seniors and high-risk people May go to places like this to receive them. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

Even though the vaccines are not yet available, members of London’s senior community are anticipating getting them. XFM News spoke to several seniors at Cherryhill Village Mall and found that many intend to get vaccinated.

“I’ve never missed one,” said Bob Smith. “I get my flu shot, COVID shot every year.”

Other seniors were just as adamant. Kathy Hamm also said she gets both vaccines every year, as did Muhammad Bhatti.

“My immune system is compromised, so I was told I should get it,” said Hamm.

Even so, not every person intended to get both vaccines. Elizabeth Lowe said that while she had only gotten the flu vaccine once, she gets the COVID vaccine every year. Conversely, Jon Mitsis said that while he gets the flu vaccine each year, he doesn’t want to get the COVID vaccine.

“I already took three shots quite a while ago,” said Mitsis. “I don’t think I’m going to take them anymore.”

Both Lowe and Mitsis both said they felt it was important to get their respective vaccines, citing personal experience and the advice of their doctors as to why.

“I did get COVID, but I only had it very slightly,” said Lowe. “I’d get [the vaccine] again, for sure.”

Others gave similar reasons for why getting both vaccines was important. “We’ve seen the results if you don’t get them,” said Smith. “Just protection, I guess.”

stories.title: University of Guelph pledges action after out-of-control homecoming parties
stories.summary: Off-campus street parties led to multiple arrests and sent around 60 people to hospital
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
The University of Guelph says it hopes to prevent future unsanctioned homecoming events after off-campus street parties spiralled out of control on the weekend, leading to multiple arrests and sending about 60 people to hospital.

Videos circulating on TikTok, Instagram and other social-media platforms showed thousands of people packed on to Chancellors Way, a street lined with off-campus student housing complexes in Guelph, a city of about 145,000 west of Toronto.

Some footage captured partygoers throwing bottles, scaling buildings and being subdued by police officers in riot gear.

Rowdy off-campus parties during the University of Guelph’s homecoming weekend are nothing new, but this year’s gathering was “significantly larger” than in the past and caused more public safety problems, the Guelph Police Service said in a statement Monday.

“Officers responded to incidents involving objects being thrown, people climbing buildings and other structures, as well as reports of shoplifting and vandalism affecting nearby businesses,” police said.

The pandemonium overwhelmed Guelph General Hospital, which treated approximately 60 patients for intoxication, lacerations and head injuries from thrown bottles.

“Homecoming-related visits place significant pressure on critical hospital resources,” Alex Folkl, the hospital’s chief of emergency medicine, said by e-mail.

“This weekend, our Emergency Department was stretched beyond capacity. Had we also experienced an influx of seriously ill patients or even a small multipatient trauma event, there was a real risk that we would not have been able to provide every patient with the timely level of care they required.”

Guelph is one of several Ontario cities that have struggled to contain drunken off-campus parties during homecoming, a university celebration that welcomes alumni and students to sanctioned events, and usually revolves around a football game.

In 2023, Queen’s University in Kingston announced it would move its homecoming events to mid-October for the next three years − timing that coincides with a fall break when many students leave campus. Queen’s went as far as cancelling homecoming for several years before that to curb wild unsanctioned keg parties.

Wilfrid Laurier University in Waterloo and Western University in London both held homecoming events on the weekend, but police and hospital officials in those cities didn’t report the same level of chaos that engulfed Guelph.

In London, where unsanctioned homecoming parties have raged in the past, police on Saturday afternoon declared the site of a traditional street party to be a “nuisance party” and directed people to leave.

“Those in attendance complied with directions from police without incident,” Sergeant Sandasha Bough of London Police Service said by e-mail.

Rene Van Acker, president and vice-chancellor of the University of Guelph, said the school was “deeply disappointed” by events on the weekend.

“We are clear that this cannot happen again,” he said in a statement released Monday.

Dr. Van Acker’s statement suggested some of the troublemakers had no connection to U of G.

“We are seeing a concerning trend in which individuals who are not U of G students, including students from other communities, travel to take part in unsanctioned gatherings and are among those involved in property damage and other disruptive behaviour,” he said.

However, Dr. Van Acker acknowledged that some U of G students engaged in “unacceptable behaviour.”

He said that the university would take unspecified action against students who violated university policy or broke the law.

Cam Guthrie, Guelph’s outgoing mayor, told CBC Radio on Monday that this year’s homecoming led to more problems than in the past.

“It’s been pretty clear that it was probably the worst amount of issues that we’ve ever experienced in the history of homecoming parties,” he said.

Mr. Guthrie later said in an e-mailed statement that he was encouraged to hear that police and the university have pledged to take action against individuals who broke the law or violated university policies.

The Guelph Police Service, meanwhile, said it is reviewing its response to the weekend’s events and expects to strengthen planning for future large gatherings.

Police already co-ordinate with the U of G, the municipal government, bylaw staff, the fire department, paramedic services and others to prepare for unsanctioned homecoming events in Guelph.

Editor’s note: This article has been corrected to state that Guelph is located west of Toronto, not northwest as previously published.

stories.title: Kelowna businesses raise safety concerns as mayoral candidates debate public safety
stories.summary: Business owner Gerald Goertsen says over the weekend security cameras captured someone ripping out lavender plants from the side of his commercial building.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Frustration is growing on Commerce Avenue in Kelowna.

Business owner Gerald Goertsen says over the weekend security cameras captured someone ripping out lavender plants from the side of his commercial building.

“Just complete destruction without, without any consequence,” Goertsen said.

He describes the latest incident as part of a pattern of crime and social disorder in the area.

Goertsen spoke to Global News two weeks ago about his concerns, including an incident in which the handles of his office doors were tied together with a plastic bag, temporarily locking him inside while his vehicle was broken into.

“It’s not safe to be here anymore, and something needs to change,” he said.

Incumbent Kelowna Mayor and mayoral candidate Tom Dyas is campaigning on a “safer streets” platform that includes pushing for more detox and treatment services.

Dyas also says he wants the city to add 75 new frontline public-safety positions over the next term, including RCMP, bylaw and firefighter positions.

“Bringing more RCMP to this community, continue to bring bylaw, continue to bring firefighters,” Dyas said.

In a recent social media post promoting his platform, Dyas said Cannan voted against measures he says are needed to address crime and social disorder.

“He voted against the RCMP officers. He voted against the bylaw. He voted against the firefighters,” Dyas said in a campaign video.

Cannan disputes that characterization.

“It’s disingenuous in my mind to make that comment,” Cannan said.

Cannan says his vote was against the overall budget spending, rather than against public-safety resources specifically.

He says he supports continued investment in public safety, but wants to first assess existing resources and how they are being deployed.

Cannan also says that, if elected, he would hold a town hall with the business community to discuss how public-safety resources could be used more efficiently.

“I’d love to have a town hall meeting with the business community and hear from the residents and how we can utilize those resources more efficiently,” Cannan said. “Just adding more officers maybe is not the best answer. It’s how they’re deployed, and looking strategically at where those resources are best allocated.”

For Goertsen, the political debate comes down to wanting the situation to improve.

“We care about those less fortunate,” Goertsen said. “We give a lot of money to charity and we do care. But when they’re vandalizing and smashing our windows and locking us in our building and tearing out our plants, that’s got to stop.”

content_blocks.text: Frustration is growing on Commerce Avenue in Kelowna.
Business owner Gerald Goertsen says over the weekend security cameras captured someone ripping out lavender plants from the side of his commercial building.
“Just complete destruction without, without any consequence,” Goertsen said.
He describes the latest incident as part of a pattern of crime and social disorder in the area.

Goertsen spoke to Global News two weeks ago about his concerns, including an incident in which the handles of his office doors were tied together with a plastic bag, temporarily locking him inside while his vehicle was broken into.
“It’s not safe to be here anymore, and something needs to change,” he said.
Incumbent Kelowna Mayor and mayoral candidate Tom Dyas is campaigning on a “safer streets” platform that includes pushing for more detox and treatment services.
Dyas also says he wants the city to add 75 new frontline public-safety positions over the next term, including RCMP, bylaw and firefighter positions.
“Bringing more RCMP to this community, continue to bring bylaw, continue to bring firefighters,” Dyas said.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Vancouver police chief on policies contributing to crime and disorder'

content_blocks.text: In a recent social media post promoting his platform, Dyas said Cannan voted against measures he says are needed to address crime and social disorder.
“He voted against the RCMP officers. He voted against the bylaw. He voted against the firefighters,” Dyas said in a campaign video.
Cannan disputes that characterization.
“It’s disingenuous in my mind to make that comment,” Cannan said.
Cannan says his vote was against the overall budget spending, rather than against public-safety resources specifically.
He says he supports continued investment in public safety, but wants to first assess existing resources and how they are being deployed.
Cannan also says that, if elected, he would hold a town hall with the business community to discuss how public-safety resources could be used more efficiently.

“I’d love to have a town hall meeting with the business community and hear from the residents and how we can utilize those resources more efficiently,” Cannan said. “Just adding more officers maybe is not the best answer. It’s how they’re deployed, and looking strategically at where those resources are best allocated.”
For Goertsen, the political debate comes down to wanting the situation to improve.

stories.title: Minimum wage not enough to live in Manitoba, report says
stories.summary: Many Winnipeggers struggle to make ends meet as the minimum wage is nearly $4 below what a resident needs to make per hour to live in the city, a new report finds.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Many Winnipeggers struggle to make ends meet as the minimum wage is nearly $4 below what a resident needs to make per hour to live in the city, a new report finds.

A Winnipeg worker needs to make at least $20.31 an hour in 2026 to get by, compared to $19.77 in 2025. The living wage in Brandon increased to $17.40 this year, compared to $16.22 last year.

For Thompson, the wage went up to $18.73 in 2026 from $17.89 in 2025, according to the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives Living Wage Update 2026 report.

Manitoba’s minimum wage is increasing 40 cents, from $16 to $16.40 on Oct. 1.

“With the way things are and how much expenses have increased, I just feel like it’s insufficient and kind of a token rise,” said Anika Atique, a Winnipegger.

The living wage doesn’t calculate savings for retirement or for a child’s education, and money for entertainment and recreation.

Food prices and higher transportation costs are some of the main reasons for the increased in living wages, according to the report.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: B.C. NDP, Conservatives both pledge to boost province’s resource development
stories.summary: Eby says his party would double critical mineral exports, Doerkson vows a Conservative government would double LNG production by 2032
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Leaders of the B.C. NDP and Conservatives on Monday laid out plans to accelerate development of the province’s natural resources, with David Eby pledging to double critical mineral exports within five years if re-elected and Lorne Doerkson vowing to double LNG production by 2032 if his party forms government.

The promises, made in the second week of campaigning ahead of the Oct. 24 provincial election , are the latest efforts by both leaders to put resource development at the centre of their economic pitches. The NDP’s Mr. Eby has made trade diversification and greater economic independence from the U.S. a throughline of his re-election bid, while interim Conservative Leader Mr. Doerkson has blamed NDP regulations for driving investment out of the province.

The pledges also come a week after the provincial and federal governments gave environmental approval to a major expansion of FortisBC’s Tilbury LNG facility in Delta, B.C.

Speaking from the Port of Prince Rupert, Mr. Eby said a re-elected NDP government would double critical mineral exports in part by running environmental assessments and permitting processes concurrently, which he said would cut timelines by more than 60 per cent. It would also set fixed permitting timelines for mineral exploration, a plan first announced in January.

As well, Mr. Eby pledged to fast-track construction of the multibillion-dollar North Coast Transmission Line, which his government committed to advancing in early 2025. It received legislative approval last November and broke ground earlier this month. One of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s designated nation-building projects, the transmission line is projected to contribute nearly $10-billion annually to B.C.’s economy.

“Doubling the critical metals and minerals exports from B.C. in the next five years means more jobs, more prosperity for British Columbians, more support for the cost of living and a clear response – and support – when we’re under direct attack” from U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war, Mr. Eby said.

Meanwhile, Mr. Doerkson said that a Conservative government would double the province’s LNG production by 2032 and triple it by 2035 with faster permitting and approvals, while upholding “the highest environmental standards in the world.”

“But we won’t let regulatory reviews become bureaucratic black holes that kill good projects through attrition,” he said from Vancouver. “If a project is good for B.C., it’s going to get a yes. In fact, it’s going to get a very quick yes.”

The NDP countered that Mr. Doerkson’s targets fall below the current pace of development, with five LNG projects moving toward final investment decisions “on track to more than triple production by 2035.”

Mr. Doerkson said a Conservative government would also host a global investment summit in Vancouver next year.

Werner Antweiler, an associate professor at the University of B.C.’s Sauder School of Business, said neither party pledge was outlandish but that the outlook for critical minerals was stronger. B.C. already has a substantial mining industry and a pipeline of proposed projects that could support the NDP’s target if global demand materializes.

“Depending on how narrow or broad you define ‘critical minerals,’ doubling that is entirely within reach because it is already well on its way,” Prof. Antweiler said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail.

The Conservatives’ goal of doubling LNG production also appears achievable through projects set in motion by predecessor governments, he said. He cited as an example the Ksi Lisims project, which would export liquefied natural gas to Asia from northwest B.C. and is expected to make a final investment decision later this year.

However, further expansion is much less certain because Canadian LNG products are “late additions to an increasingly crowded marketplace” with cheaper competitors, Prof. Antweiler said.

Andy Hira, a political science professor at Simon Fraser University who studies energy policy, questioned the economic assumptions underlying both plans. Doubling critical mineral exports is possible “because the exports hardly exist at this point.” But he would want the NDP to first demonstrate that sufficient demand exists to better understand B.C.’s competitiveness compared to other potential sources.

On LNG, Prof. Hira said a provincial government could encourage development but can not dictate how much gets built, with investment ultimately dependent on private-sector interest and global demand.

stories.title: Canada’s federal prisons to distribute paper straws to inmates for ‘safer snorting’
stories.summary: Canada’s federal prisons will begin issuing safe supplies for inmates to use while taking illegal narcotics.
stories.author: Joe Van Wonderen
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Canada’s federal prisons will begin issuing safe supplies for inmates to use while taking illegal narcotics.

An internal notice of the change issued to Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) employees was posted on social media on Sept. 22, detailing plans to issue paper straws and foil for “safer snorting.”

The notice said the straws will “reduce harm” by “lowering the risks of cuts or tears inside the nose,” reduce the risk of blood-borne infections spreading and “provide a safer option for snorting, recognizing that overdose and toxicity risk remain.”

Prisoners will be given access to drug testing strips for fentanyl, benzodiazepine and xylazine.

CSC confirmed the strategy in an email to CTVNews.CA on Monday.

“(CSC) maintains a zero-tolerance policy for the introduction of illicit drugs in its institutions,” spokesperson Laurence Cote told CTVNews.CA in an email on Monday. “We are aware that despite our best efforts, illicit drugs still enter facilities.”

“Harm reduction measures allow CSC to be better informed of offenders’ consumption reality, their needs and will help CSC direct offenders to the programs they need to address their addiction problems,” the email said.

According to a CSC report in May 2025 , a majority of men entering prisons reported an ongoing substance use problem. Between 20 and 22 per cent of men entering prisons reported “a lifetime history of injection drug use,” as did 27 to 29 percent of women, according to the same report.

CSC offers services for treating substance use beyond harm reduction tools, including treatment, psychoeducation and general support. They reported the number of inmates on an opioid treatment program at 3,431 in December 2024, a spike of more than 370 per cent from 920 inmates in December 2016.

They also run a needle exchange program to supply users with clean syringes. CSC reported 537 inmates using the program in late 2024.

Poilievre calls for ‘zero tolerance’

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took to social media to criticize Csc’s harm reduction efforts on Sunday.

“The Liberal government helps (drug users) do dangerous, addictive drugs in prison that make them even more violent when they come out,” he said.

He proposed returning to a “zero tolerance for drugs in prison” policy, saying “drug criminals must undergo regular drug tests to earn release, and isolation for prison drug kingpins.”

“Drug-free prisoners will focus on skill-building and rehabilitation so they can be good citizens on release,” he added.

stories.title: Mission Services welcomes $1.1M in donations, challenges London to match it
stories.summary: Mission Services welcomes $1.1M in donations, challenges London to match it CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: | CBC News | Posted: September 29, 2026 12:13 AM | Last Updated: 10 hours ago
The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation gave $500K, while another $600K came from an anonymous donor
Mission Services of London has received $1.1 million from two donors to strengthen its addiction recovery aftercare program and is challenging Londoners to match the contribution.
The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation donated $500,000, while an anonymous donor contributed another $600,000.

Rob Schlegel, whose grandfather Wilfred helped establish Mission Services 75 years ago, was at Quintin Warner House on Monday to unveil a sign for the newly renamed Wilfred Schlegel Aftercare Program.
Schlegel said the donation is a way to continue his grandfather's legacy of helping people in the community.

"It's something that we've been trying to do in terms of creating and strengthening community," he said. "This is a key part of that, and we've tried to continue my grandfather's legacy and this is just another way of celebrating that."
He said he hopes the second donation will inspire others to contribute.
"We hope the community will step forward with dollars and really get the whole program onto a roll to take it to the next level."

The aftercare program operates out of Quintin Warner House and other locations across London. It provides an abstinence-based environment for men who have completed addiction treatment and are transitioning back into the community.
Participants receive help with life skills such as budgeting, nutrition and job searching, along with case management, individual treatment plans and crisis and relapse supports.
Executive director Ericka Ayala Ronson said the program also gives participants a network of people supporting them through recovery.
"Because recovery is a choice that a person makes every moment of every day," she said. "It is not a process that is ever truly done."
Before the donations, Mission Services had closed some beds in the aftercare program because of funding gaps, Ayala Ronson said.
The new funding will allow the organization to reopen those beds, bringing the program back to its full complement of 17.
The money will also allow Mission Services to provide additional staff support outside regular business hours, she said.
While the program receives funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health, Mission Services also relies on donations to support its work.
Mission Services and the two donors are now asking Londoners to match the $1.1-million contribution.

| CBC News | Posted: September 29, 2026 12:13 AM | Last Updated: 10 hours ago

The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation gave $500K, while another $600K came from an anonymous donor

Mission Services of London has received $1.1 million from two donors to strengthen its addiction recovery aftercare program and is challenging Londoners to match the contribution.

The RBJ Schlegel Family Foundation donated $500,000, while an anonymous donor contributed another $600,000.

Rob Schlegel, whose grandfather Wilfred helped establish Mission Services 75 years ago, was at Quintin Warner House on Monday to unveil a sign for the newly renamed Wilfred Schlegel Aftercare Program.

Schlegel said the donation is a way to continue his grandfather's legacy of helping people in the community.

"It's something that we've been trying to do in terms of creating and strengthening community," he said. "This is a key part of that, and we've tried to continue my grandfather's legacy and this is just another way of celebrating that."

He said he hopes the second donation will inspire others to contribute.

"We hope the community will step forward with dollars and really get the whole program onto a roll to take it to the next level."

The aftercare program operates out of Quintin Warner House and other locations across London. It provides an abstinence-based environment for men who have completed addiction treatment and are transitioning back into the community.

Participants receive help with life skills such as budgeting, nutrition and job searching, along with case management, individual treatment plans and crisis and relapse supports.

Executive director Ericka Ayala Ronson said the program also gives participants a network of people supporting them through recovery.

"Because recovery is a choice that a person makes every moment of every day," she said. "It is not a process that is ever truly done."

Before the donations, Mission Services had closed some beds in the aftercare program because of funding gaps, Ayala Ronson said.

The new funding will allow the organization to reopen those beds, bringing the program back to its full complement of 17.

The money will also allow Mission Services to provide additional staff support outside regular business hours, she said.

While the program receives funding from Ontario's Ministry of Health, Mission Services also relies on donations to support its work.

Mission Services and the two donors are now asking Londoners to match the $1.1-million contribution.

Ayala Ronson said the goal is to build on the momentum created by the donations and ensure the program can continue supporting people through the often-challenging transition after treatment.

"That's what Londoners do," Ayala Ronson said. "This is a caring community and I have no doubt that once this becomes known, folks will want to help neighbours in need and men who are taking the courageous steps to to live in a different way and have a fresh start."

stories.title: Study challenges original theory about Canada’s first human case of bird flu
stories.summary: UBC researchers found avian flu doesn’t bind to cells like other similar viruses
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
University of British Columbia researchers say the unusual genetic mutations identified in Canada’s first human avian influenza case weakened the virus’ ability to bind to human cells, a critical first step in infection.

The findings were published in a study on Monday in Nature Communications . The authors said they conducted the research to explore whether the mutations signalled that avian flu was evolving to become better at infecting people, which was the prevailing assumption until this publication.

Senior author Sriram Subramaniam, a UBC professor of biochemistry and molecular biology, said he was surprised to learn the answer was no.

“We tested it exhaustively and, actually, it is really lousy at attaching to our human cells,” Dr. Subramaniam said in an interview. “The bottom line is that we should be looking at the functional effects of these mutations, and not just tracking the sequence changes alone.”

A B.C. teen from the Fraser Valley, who fell ill two years ago, was the first and remains the only person known to have contracted avian flu in Canada. The young girl was discharged from hospital in January, 2025, after spending roughly two months in critical condition. The source of the case may never be officially identified .

Scientists, at that time, identified three genetic mutations in the B.C. case that raised global concern. The new research focused on two of those mutations that were found in spike proteins, which act like a door for viruses to enter healthy human cells.

A similar mutation was detected in samples from a Louisiana patient whose death was announced in January last year. This was the first of two avian flu deaths that have been recorded in the United States.

Avian flu, also known as bird flu, is a contagious viral infection that most often turns up in wild and farmed birds. The virus is so contagious and severe in birds that more than 17.5 million, mostly chicken and turkeys, have died or been killed under orders from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency since 2022.

Human-to-human transmission of avian flu is exceedingly rare and there is no evidence of sustained spread among people. The version of this virus circulating in Canada is an H5N1 strain.

The UBC team used a series of tests to better understand the mutations, including by using cryo-electron microscopes to map their structures at near atomic detail. Dr. Subramaniam said the experiments showed that the mutations weakened receptor binding.

Viruses typically attach to cells within the upper respiratory tract but that did not happen with these mutations. However, he said that testing indicated that the virus could have infected cells lower down, which led to the severe illness in the B.C. patient.

“We don’t have proof that’s exactly what happened, but we think that the upper respiratory tract didn’t do the normal job of snagging the virus and letting it in,” he said. “There’s lots of complex factors, lots of interactions, and eventually we show that it had some capability to infect cells.”

The study found that the virus, after attaching to a cell, must fuse with the cell membrane. This allows its genetic material to enter the cell, where it can be replicated.

In human lung cells, the researchers found that the mutated protein could trigger this fusion despite its weak receptor binding, but it was far less efficient than with other H5N1 strains.

“Eventually, that let it gain some entry and that probably led to the effects that we saw in the individual,” Dr. Subramaniam explained.

The research underscores the need to learn more about how an animal virus is able to infect people, he said. A greater understanding will help scientists and public health officials better assess and respond to threats in the future.

“There’s a lot more to do,” Dr. Subramaniam said. “But the good news is that we’ve not seen evidence that the virus became better adapted to infecting human cells.”

stories.title: Doug Ford commits to footing part of the bill for proposed Alberta-Ontario pipeline
stories.summary: Ontario won’t seek to be majority partner in Northern Shield Energy Corridor, but its investment would be ‘substantial,’ Premier says in Calgary
stories.author: Emma Graney
stories.content:
The Ontario government is prepared to foot part of the bill for a proposed pipeline that would carry crude oil from Alberta to Sarnia, Ont., Premier Doug Ford said on Monday.

Mr. Ford and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the pipeline plan , called the Northern Shield Energy Corridor, in July. The 3,300-kilometre conduit would move roughly 500,000 barrels of oil per day across four provinces.

As for who’s going to pay for it, “We’re in,” Mr. Ford said at an energy services event in Calgary.

The provincial government is yet to determine its exact contribution. It wouldn’t seek to be a majority partner in the project, but the investment would be “substantial,” he told media after the event.

“I believe in getting the private sector to invest, but we’ll kick it off,” he said.

Mr. Ford said he believes investing public dollars in the Northern Shield project is the right decision, given the substantial economic gains the proposal presents Ontario and the rest of Canada.

“Like I said, any time I can clip a coupon and get a return on investment, I’m there,” he said.

Filling the line, however, would require significant investment from oil producers to pump more barrels into the market. And it would be a major financial undertaking for a private backer at a time when domestic energy companies have shown little appetite for such risk.

For example, the expansion of the Trans Mountain pipeline – which runs roughly 1,150 kilometres from Edmonton to the West Coast – came with a $34-billion price tag when it was finished in 2024. A new West Coast pipeline proposed by the Alberta government would cost between $35.2-billion and $43.7-billion, the province said in its Major Projects Office submission .

Mr. Ford made the comments just days before the federal government is due to announce whether the new pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast will be designated a project of national significance.

Both the Northern Shield and Western pipeline proposals are being positioned as projects that could be fast-tracked as part of Ottawa’s push to boost national infrastructure and increase global exports in response to the trade war with the United States.

But unlike the West Coast pipeline, the Alberta-Ontario proposal has no formal federal backing.

Ms. Smith said on Monday at the same Calgary event that she is “more and more confident every day” that the West Coast oil pipeline will not only receive a major project designation from Ottawa, but will be one of the first of those projects to go ahead.

With global oil markets in turmoil because of the Iran war, potential customers around the world are realizing that they lack secure supplies of energy.

“They’re looking to diversify,” Ms. Smith said, adding that Canada is one of the best countries to look to. That in turn has Ottawa pushing to get a pipeline built, she said.

Both the Northern Shield and West Coast pipelines are “absolutely critical” for Canada’s energy sovereignty, Mr. Ford said. Invoking Canada’s construction of a cross-country railroad in the 1900s, he said the two oil conduits should be built simultaneously.

Despite continuing trade tensions with the U.S., Mr. Ford said he still believes in “Fortress North America – in supporting each other, putting a ring around” the continent.

“We’re stronger together. Not just with Alberta, but everyone across the country, including our American friends,” he said.

“Make no mistake about it. The world is watching Canada and the U.S. right now. The world is watching to see what happens.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford says he agrees with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and hopes Alberta stays in Canada. Albertans are set to vote in a referendum on Oct. 19, and one of the 10 questions asks whether the province should stay in Confederation or if there should be a second, binding referendum on separation.

stories.title: Former top soldier weighs in on risk of U.S. military action against Canada
stories.summary: A former Canadian commander says he considers the risk of U.S. military action against Canada to be remote, but acknowledges the fact risk exists at all as a sign of the rapidly changing global security environment.
stories.author: Brennan MacDonald
stories.content:
Ottawa — A former commander of the Canadian Armed Forces says he considers the risk of U.S. military action against Canada to be remote, but he acknowledges the fact that risk exists at all as a sign of the rapidly changing global security environment.

Retired general Wayne Eyre, who served as chief of the defence staff between 2021 and 2024, made the comments in an interview on CTV Power Play with Vassy Kapelos while promoting his new memoir, “Into the Breach: A Soldier’s Journey.”

“As the prime minister said, it was extreme tail risk: so very, very small probability,” Eyre told Kapelos, when asked about Prime Minister Mark Carney telling The New York Times he had considered the possibility that U.S. President Donald Trump could order military action against Canada.

“One of the jobs of military planners is to imagine those possible scenarios, and you can only develop plans for so much in terms of putting the five Ws to something,” Eyre said. “And so you go from the imaginations (and) conceiving step to fleshing out a plan. Well, you have to decide: What is more probable? What is more likely? Where are you going to put your effort?”

“I would say this is a small probability. I’m not inside the tent anymore, so I don’t know what the current direction is,” Eyre added.

That said, the retired general said U.S. military action against Canada was never considered a probability when he was “inside the tent.”

“And the very fact that we are talking about it now shows how significantly the security environment has changed,” Eyre said.

Carney sat down for an hour-long interview with The New York Times last week, and his response to a reporter’s question asking if he was ever “seriously concerned” about a potential military threat to Canada made headlines around the world.

A transcript of the interview published by The New York Times notes the prime minister paused before answering.

“You have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told The New York Times. “So, and as the tail fattens when a leader of a country threatens your sovereignty, you adjust accordingly.”

“That’s just risk management,” he added. “That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to take certain things into consideration.”

When a reporter followed up and asked whether he had made certain preparations for potential military action, Carney responded: “I’ll leave my answer where it was.”

Carney has not spoken with Canadian media since sitting down for the interview with the U.S. news outlet.

Canada-U.S. relations have been strained since the very beginning of Trump’s second term, with the two countries locked in a worsening tit-for-tat trade war punctuated by the U.S. president’s consistent mocking approach to Canadian sovereignty.

After bilateral trade talks collapsed in August, Carney told reporters in Ottawa that Canada was “at war” with the United States over trade and accused the Trump administration of making demands that would infringe upon Canadian sovereignty.

Trump told reporters in the Oval Office Monday that Canada was treating the U.S. unfairly and said he believed Canada will fold on the trade dispute in the next “three to four weeks.”

stories.title: Alberta announces next step in high-speed rail plan to connect Edmonton, Calgary
stories.summary: Premier Danielle Smith says Ottawa has agreed to refer the project to its major projects office once a proponent has been selected.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Alberta’s government says it will launch this fall a formal request for private companies to submit a proposal for a high-speed rail system that would connect Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary.

Premier Danielle Smith says Ottawa has agreed to refer the project to its major projects office once a proponent has been selected.

Smith says the proponent would be selected by April 2027.

Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski, who represents an Edmonton riding, says Ottawa is prepared to work with Alberta on the project.

She says the work will include speaking to Indigenous communities, municipalities and the public to understand the costs, benefits and effects of a high-speed rail system.

Smith says the railway service would also include stops at Alberta’s two largest airports.

“Statistics Canada’s most recent population data shows that Alberta is growing faster than every other province in 2026 and the Calgary, Red Deer, Edmonton region is home to roughly 80 per cent of Alberta’s population,” Smith told a news conference in Calgary on Monday.

“That increasing demand is creating a greater need for modern transportation infrastructure to keep people as well as services moving efficiently.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government established the Calgary-based major projects office last year to speed along infrastructure deemed in the national interest.

stories.title: Masked white nationalists reportedly bring 'odious message' to Kamloops
stories.summary: "Screw off. Go home. Never come back. Reflect on your poor decisions," said Kamloops-Thompson-Cariboo MP Frank Caputo.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Mounties are investigating a masked white nationalist demonstration that took place Sunday near the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.

The Kamloops Castanet website is reporting that a “group of masked individuals appearing to be associated with Second Sons Canada” staged the event on the Tk’emlups te Secwepemc reserve, near the former residential school, and that RCMP are probing reports that members of the group held a banner reading “Got bones?” above the Trans-Canada Highway.

It was five years ago this past May when the Tk’emlups te Secwepemc First Nation announced that it had discovered hundreds of unmarked graves in Kamloops, B.C., using ground-penetrating radar. The announcement sent shockwaves throughout Canada and brought the residential school controversy to global attention. But in the years since the announcement, the Tk’emlups te Secwepemc has walked back its initial claims about graves at the former Kamloops residential school, and now refers to the findings as anomalies.

Second Sons Canada did not respond Monday to an interview request. On its website, the group, founded in 2024, describes itself as a “Canadian men’s nationalist club,” and “fraternal organization dedicated to health and fitness, camaraderie, activism and friendly support for those who share our values.”

Its members wear masks, according to the group’s site, to protect their identities and deny its “adversaries” information.

Kamloops-Thompson-Cariboo MP Frank Caputo condemned Sunday’s masked demonstration on social media.

“Screw off. Go home. Never come back. Reflect on your poor decisions,” Caputo wrote on X. “These cowards refuse to show their faces. Not surprising given their odious message. I will be in contact with Tk’emlúps leadership to offer my support.”

In a news release issued Sunday, Tk’emlups te Secwepemc Chief Rosanne Casimir said “that individuals associated with Second Sons Canada, a group linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology, have been seen and documented within our community.”

Neither Casimir nor the RCMP responded Monday to National Post interview requests.

The group’s presence and activity “in our community is deeply concerning and is being taken seriously by Chief and Council,” Casimir said in the release. “We recognize the fear, anger and concern this May create for our members, survivors, families and staff. We hear those concerns, and we are taking action.”

The “safety and well-being of our members is our priority,” said the chief. “Our people have the right to feel safe in their homes, in our community spaces and throughout our community.”

The band is “actively monitoring the situation, assessing additional security measures, and working with the RCMP,” she said in the release, noting a police file has been opened in the matter.

“With the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation approaching on September 30, we recognize that the presence of individuals associated with this group May heighten concern, particularly for survivors, intergenerational survivors, and their families,” the chief said.

“The presence of individuals associated with white supremacist ideology on Tk̓emlúps lands will not deter Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc, Indian Residential School survivors, intergenerational survivors, or their families from continuing to share the truth, honour the children and advance the work of truth, accountability and reconciliation.”

She advised band members to “remain vigilant and aware of your surroundings,” and not to “approach, confront, or engage with members of this group.”

The chief also urged band members to “please continue to look out for one another and check in with our elders, survivors, families, and neighbours who May be feeling concerned,” according to the news release.

“White supremacy, racism, and hate have no place in Tk̓emlúps.”

“The cowardly act that took place at Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc yesterday, is abhorrent. It has no place in this country. My thoughts are with everyone who are shaken and hurt by this disgusting display of hate.

“This week, we will mark the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. It is a stark reminder of our shared responsibility to confront the devastating legacy of the residential school system and the consequences still felt today. Courageous Survivors shared the truth, so that all Canadians could take up the work of reconciliation.”

The City of Kamloops also issued a statement about the matter.

“The City of Kamloops stands in unity with our neighbours at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc,” it said in an Instagram post. “There is no place for hate in Secwepemcúl’ecw. As we approach the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, we learn from those who have cared for this valley since time immemorial. We stand against those who deny our history and condemn all acts of racism, denialism and hate.”

stories.title: Hungary’s Deputy PM endorses deepening Canada’s economic, political ties with EU
stories.summary: In Toronto for a conference on repatriating Ukrainian children and POWs, Anita Orbán represents a sharp turn away from the policies of the previous government
stories.author: Janice Dickson
stories.content:
Hungarian Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán says making Canada an “associate member” of the European Union would be a great opportunity to increase trade and political co-operation and bolster their already strong ideological ties.

“We need to understand what it means. But for me, how I see it … this could be an umbrella framework bringing the EU and Canada closer together politically, because these two are already pretty close in terms of values, in terms of how they look at free trade, multilateralism, digital, critical raw materials, energy, security,” said Ms. Orbán, who is also the country’s Foreign Affairs Minister, in an interview in Toronto.

She was elected in April in a vote that overthrew Viktor Orbán (no relation), who had been in power for 16 years and was a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Earlier this month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member” − a status that does not officially exist and has yet to be defined − during her State of the Union address to the European Parliament.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has increasingly been courting European leaders as Canada’s relationship with the United States continues to sour. However, Mr. Carney has said that Ottawa is not seeking EU membership, concerned that it would compromise Canadian sovereignty and cause a permanent rupture in the country’s relationship with the U.S.

Steve Suarez: To resist American domination, Canada must fix its failing tax system

Ms. Orbán was in Toronto attending a conference that Canada is co-hosting with Ukraine and Norway on efforts to repatriate kidnapped Ukrainian children, detained civilians and prisoners of war from Russia and the occupied territories. She said she was also here to celebrate the coming 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution on Oct. 23, which resulted in tens of thousands of Hungarians moving to Canada.

“This is the very first time I am meeting and seeing a partner of mine officially in a non-EU country,” she said, referring to Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand. “It also shows how much we value the Canada-Hungary relationship, how much we value multilateralism, the rules-based order, the values-based realism which Canada is bringing to the multinational stage.”

In terms of forging deeper ties with Canada, energy could be one area, Ms. Orbán said, but more broadly she wants to see economic co-operation that benefits both countries. She said there is a solid Canadian business community in Hungary, for instance, and there’s room for it to grow.

Hungary is one of 10 EU countries that have not ratified the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta). Ms. Orbán said her office has reinitiated the process that had been halted by the previous government; it is currently under interinstitutional review, which, once completed, will go to a parliamentary vote.

Ms. Orbán said she also wants to talk with Ms. Anand about preserving multilateral institutions and adjusting them to the new realities.

“Middle-power countries, middle-sized countries, we need and work very much with multilateral organizations,” she said. “That’s one of the ways that we represent our interests, but of course we are not blind to the changing world, to the changing needs, and I really would like to propose that we work together and think together about how we can keep the rules-based order, international world order, multilateralism.”

Hungary has been undergoing a massive transformation since the electoral defeat of Mr. Orbán. The country is dependent on Russia for oil, gas and nuclear fuel and must strike a fine balance between maintaining a relationship with Moscow and deepening its ties with EU members and supporting Ukraine.

“We have also become clear when it comes to the Ukrainian conflict, as compared to the previous government, and we absolutely do recognize who is the aggressor,” Ms. Orbán said. “And we condemn the Russian activities going against Ukraine and we stand by, of course, the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine. And this May seem not new to you, but this is a very big step in the Hungarian context.

“So we are defending our national interests. We inherited an economy which is in really bad shape. We inherited existing energy supply contracts, but we are also trying to defend our sovereignty and national interest. Keeping the wider alliance, interest in mind, but we need to be also mindful of our own realities, which come from the dependency.”

In depth: How two Ukrainian children, taken to Russia, fought their way back home

Across Europe in recent weeks, leaders have warned that Russia could be preparing a strike on a Nato country. The Danish Defence Intelligence Service warned in a threat assessment last week that Moscow will likely escalate its hybrid war against the West and Nato “with greater consequences for the countries targeted than in the past.” It also said there is “a low but growing risk” that Russia would attack one or several Nato countries on its border.

Ms. Orbán called the increase in hybrid war and sabotage activity by Russia “really alarming.”

Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. A couple of weeks later, a drone was shot down in Lithuania. And around the same time, a Russian frigate fired two flares at a Danish military helicopter in international waters, just missing it.

Ms. Orbán pointed out that last week EU countries agreed to a deal worth €6.6-billion ($10.6-billion) in military aid for Ukraine. The European Peace Facility, an off-budget fund for defence initiatives, had been blocked by Mr. Orbán’s government, tying up crucial funds for Ukraine.

“The message is that all these [Russian] attacks will make European unity stronger,” she said. “We cannot be blind to it, it’s happening. We see it, again, it’s increased in terms of its frequency, in terms of its scale, and widened. And the only way to counter it is to stand united and try to deter it.”

With reports from Reuters
