stories.title: North Atlantic right whales feed closer to surface increasing collision risk: study
stories.summary: A portion of the North Atlantic right whale population, which is estimated to be approximately 384 whales, gathers to feed in the Shediac Valley each summer.
stories.author: Tori Fitzpatrick
stories.content:
A recent study has found that critically endangered North Atlantic right whales are feeding closer to the ocean’s surface at night, increasing their risk of being struck by boats.

The study, published earlier this month in the peer-reviewed journal Plos One, documented nighttime surface feeding in North Atlantic right whales, providing new evidence that could be used to prevent deadly collisions between the whales and vessels.

The paper’s lead author, Jay Kirkham, a PhD student at Dalhousie University in Halifax, said the research team worked with U.S.-based non-profit Ocean Alliance to tag 23 right whales in the Shediac Valley, an underwater valley in the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence.

A portion of the North Atlantic right whale population, which is estimated to be approximately 384 whales, gathers to feed in the Shediac Valley each summer.

Kirkham said the tags recorded video footage along with data on how the whales moved and in which direction they swam.

He said he used video footage to record right whale feeding behaviour during the day.

“When a right whale opens its mouth, it’s kind of like a big parachute opening on the front of their face … and that just slows them down an awful lot,” he said. “And so, they have to work harder, which they do by kicking their tail higher and faster.”

Kirkham said he used these observations to train a machine learning algorithm that could recognize a right whale feeding at night when he was unable to visually identify the behaviour.

This data revealed that whales are feeding within the same depth as large vessels at night, increasing the risk of collision, he said.

While right whales typically feed close to the seafloor during the day, Kirkham said the whales follow their food — zooplankton — higher up in the water column at night.

“These big ships that go through the gulf, they extend into the water maybe 10, maybe 15 metres,” he said. “The whales are in a sort of vertical overlap with that.”

He said collisions with vessels and entanglements in fishing gear are the leading causes of death in the population and this study May help inform conservation measures for the whales.

Transport Canada and Fisheries and Oceans Canada currently oversee protection measures for the population.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Fisheries and Oceans Canada said its measures focus on preventing whale entanglements in fishing gear and enforcing seasonal fishing closures.

The department said the study can help it develop “tailored management measures to protect North Atlantic right whales.”

Transport Canada implements speed restrictions and enforces a vessel exclusion zone in the Shediac Valley during the summer to reduce the risk of collisions between boats and right whales in the area.

However, Kirkham said that the whales he and his team tagged spent approximately 25 per cent of their feeding time outside of the vessel exclusion zone, exposing them to ship traffic.

In a statement to The Canadian Press, Transport Canada said it has a right whale surveillance program to help protect the whales from collisions by using both visual and audio detection tools.

“Acoustic monitoring systems and other complementary technologies can support whale detection regardless of daylight conditions and help inform protective measures when whales are present,” the statement said.

The department also said it uses the latest scientific research, monitoring data and feedback from stakeholders to inform its protection measures.

stories.title: Alberta’s response to COVID-19 outbreak at Cargill plant was ‘catastrophic failure,’ report says
stories.summary: More than 950 workers at High River plant were infected in 2020, leaving two workers dead and spreading to the community
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
Alberta’s response to Canada’s largest single outbreak of COVID-19 was a “catastrophic failure” that prioritized industry needs over workers’ lives, according to a new report.

Parkland Institute, a research centre at the University of Alberta, published a report on Monday examining how Alberta handled the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak at the Cargill beef-packing plant in High River, south of Calgary. The centre says it is the first public, independent review of what became North America’s largest single-site outbreak during the pandemic.

More than 950 workers at the plant, which was nearly half of the work force, were infected with the virus in the spring of 2020. Eighteen workers had to be hospitalized and two died – 67-year-old Bui Thi Hiep and 51-year-old Benito Quesada.

“Both lost their lives to COVID-19 and, ultimately, to Alberta’s catastrophic failure to place worker safety above industry interests,” the report says.

Secondary spread in the community led to hundreds more infections and four additional deaths. The Cargill cases were later linked to at least 22 other outbreaks, according to the report, which was authored by Jason Foster, director of the Parkland Institute, and Sean Tucker, a professor of occupational health and safety at the University of Regina,

Even though six years have passed, it is still important to provide an “accurate account” of the outbreak and push for accountability, Prof. Tucker said in an interview

“COVID will not be the last pandemic, and we can always learn from our mistakes,” he said. “It will probably open old wounds but maybe this will eventually lead to some closure.”

A 2020 Globe and Mail investigation into the outbreak found that Cargill was slow to implement measures to protect its workers from COVID-19. Some employees, many of whom were immigrants and temporary foreign workers, said they were pressed and even incentivized to continue working as infections grew at the facility.

How Cargill became the site of Canada’s largest single outbreak of COVID-19

Meat-processing plants were deemed an essential service during the pandemic, which exempted them from public-health restrictions, such as physical distancing and the sizes of gatherings. The second-largest outbreak in Canada was at another meat-packing plant – the JBS Foods Canada facility in Brooks, Alta. – and there were other outbreaks in similar sites elsewhere in Alberta and across Canada.

These facilities were ripe for outbreaks because of crowding, low temperatures that helped the virus survive longer, insufficient ventilation and socioeconomic vulnerabilities in the work force. Many workers lacked alternative sources of income and supported families in Canada or in their home countries.

Cargill implemented a one-time $500 “attendance bonus” and a $2 hourly wage top-up to workers during the early months of the pandemic.

The authors of the report said the Cargill outbreak is a story of “systemic regulatory failure” by the Alberta government and Alberta Health Services (AHS), the single provincial health authority at the time. They said Alberta was unprepared, overconfident and deliberately side-stepped available enforcement measures.

“The evidence shows that there was nothing inevitable about the scale of the outbreak. The tragedy occurred in a political environment that openly and enthusiastically prioritized economic growth over the health and safety of a largely invisible and vulnerable group of workers,” they concluded.

The Alberta government and Cargill did not respond to requests for comment from The Globe.

The report is based on the analysis of publicly available documents, such as media reports and legal decisions, documents obtained through freedom of information requests and select interviews, including with experts in public health. Cargill workers were not interviewed.

On April 3, 2020, AHS was made aware of the first Cargill worker testing positive for COVID-19. It then spread quickly among workers. About a week after the initial infection, the union representing workers demanded the site be closed immediately; it wasn’t.

Internal government e-mails referenced in the report show AHS managers expressed concern about rising case counts, worker complaints and symptomatic employees still at work. Sarah Nunn, an AHS manager who was the lead for Cargill, wrote on April 10, 2020, that “more drastic action” May need to be taken, but “there was no action,” according to the report.

Operations were eventually halted by Cargill on April 20, 2020, which lasted for two weeks, but the damage was already done.

Union blasts ‘shameful’ ruling on Cargill’s COVID response

The report said there were compounding issues at play, including an insufficient supply of masks and inconsistent masking guidance; a poor surveillance system by AHS to track the outbreak; disregard of workers’ rights; and no compliance orders by AHS or Alberta Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) to Cargill.

The authors say OHS abdicated its responsibilities to keep workers safe and that AHS and the government did not have the required expertise to properly handle the outbreak. Additionally, they stressed that AHS made incorrect assumptions on virus spread without epidemiological evidence.

“Workers were led to believe that the workplace was safe, that public health had based their assessment on evidence, and clearly that wasn’t the case,” said Prof. Tucker.

Thirty-six recommendations are included in the report to improve accountability in regulatory enforcement, enhance protection of vulnerable workers and strengthen the independence of operational health and safety and public health regulators in Alberta.

A public apology to Cargill workers is one of the main recommendations. Additionally, the authors urge Alberta to amend its legislation to make clear that OHS leads the workplace response during a public-health emergency, undertake a review of existing OHS policies and create a standing list of “essential services.”

Cargill implemented a one-time $500 “attendance bonus” and a $2 hourly wage top-up to workers during the early months of the pandemic.

The authors of the report said the Cargill outbreak is a story of “systemic regulatory failure” by the Alberta government and Alberta Health Services (AHS), the single provincial health authority at the time. They said Alberta was unprepared, overconfident and deliberately side-stepped available enforcement measures.

“The evidence shows that there was nothing inevitable about the scale of the outbreak. The tragedy occurred in a political environment that openly and enthusiastically prioritized economic growth over the health and safety of a largely invisible and vulnerable group of workers,” they concluded.
The Alberta government and Cargill did not respond to requests for comment from The Globe.

The report is based on the analysis of publicly available documents, such as media reports and legal decisions, documents obtained through freedom of information requests and select interviews, including with experts in public health. Cargill workers were not interviewed.

On April 3, 2020, AHS was made aware of the first Cargill worker testing positive for COVID-19. It then spread quickly among workers. About a week after the initial infection, the union representing workers demanded the site be closed immediately; it wasn’t.

Internal government e-mails referenced in the report show AHS managers expressed concern about rising case counts, worker complaints and symptomatic employees still at work. Sarah Nunn, an AHS manager who was the lead for Cargill, wrote on April 10, 2020, that “more drastic action” May need to be taken, but “there was no action,” according to the report.
Operations were eventually halted by Cargill on April 20, 2020, which lasted for two weeks, but the damage was already done.

The report said there were compounding issues at play, including an insufficient supply of masks and inconsistent masking guidance; a poor surveillance system by AHS to track the outbreak; disregard of workers’ rights; and no compliance orders by AHS or Alberta Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) to Cargill.

The authors say OHS abdicated its responsibilities to keep workers safe and that AHS and the government did not have the required expertise to properly handle the outbreak. Additionally, they stressed that AHS made incorrect assumptions on virus spread without epidemiological evidence.
“Workers were led to believe that the workplace was safe, that public health had based their assessment on evidence, and clearly that wasn’t the case,” said Prof. Tucker.

Thirty-six recommendations are included in the report to improve accountability in regulatory enforcement, enhance protection of vulnerable workers and strengthen the independence of operational health and safety and public health regulators in Alberta.

A public apology to Cargill workers is one of the main recommendations. Additionally, the authors urge Alberta to amend its legislation to make clear that OHS leads the workplace response during a public-health emergency, undertake a review of existing OHS policies and create a standing list of “essential services.”

“Both lost their lives to COVID-19 and, ultimately, to Alberta’s catastrophic failure to place worker safety above industry interests,” the report says.

stories.title: Goal to raise $1 million for heroic Belleville cop who stopped a Jewish slaughter
stories.summary: The organizer of a fundraiser for the police officer injured defending a Belleville synagogue wants more people to know about the cause.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
A fundraising campaign set up by the Canadian Jewish community for hero Belleville cop Const. Jeff Smith, severely injured while protecting a synagogue from a hate-motivated mass shooting, is aiming to raise $1 million in a show of gratitude to those who defend Canadians every day.

The GoFundMe started last week with an initial goal of $18,000 has raised more than $819,000 as of Monday morning.

“What began as an immediate expression of gratitude has become a national demonstration of what Canadians believe,” organizer Derek Kreindler wrote in a Sunday update. “When someone risks his life protecting others, the people he protected will remember him and stand behind his family.”

As of Monday morning, the campaign sits at roughly $817,000 and climbing.

Kreindler thanked the more than 7,200 who’ve already donated, and made clear he’s not asking them to do so again. Rather, he wants people to share Const. Smith’s story with people who May not have heard it in hopes of meeting the new fundraising goal.

“If you know a philanthropic family, foundation, business leader or other individual who might consider making a significant contribution, please consider forwarding the campaign privately or offering to make an introduction,” Kreindler continued.

“There is no expectation or pressure. We simply want those who May wish to participate to have the opportunity to do so.”

Smith’s story began around 7:10 p.m. last Sunday outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue, where he was parked as a small congregation gathered inside to mark the start of Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish faith.

According to officials, shooter Sean Ward opened fire on Smith, who suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his head and body before exiting his vehicle and engaging in a gunfight. Smith and another responding officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, were able to strike the 29-year-old shooter, who has since died in hospital.

Smith remains in the same hospital recovering from his injuries, with his wife Ashley Smith noting in an emotional Facebook post two days after the attack that he “has a very long, difficult road ahead.”

While GoFundMe’s top two donors ($14,128 and $10,000, respectively) are anonymous, the top public donor is criminal defence lawyer Solomon Friedman, who told National Post in an email last week that “words are insufficient to describe the debt that is owed” to the officers.

“They and their families are deserving of our endless gratitude and support,” he wrote.

“We have already accomplished something extraordinary,” Kreindler added Sunday.

“Together, let us carry this expression of gratitude to $1 million for Constable Smith and his family.”

In a campaign update on Saturday, Kreindler clarified that while the funds being raised are specifically for the benefit of Smith and his family, not McCurdy, he encouraged anyone interested in starting one to contact the Belleville Police Service to “ensure that whatever they propose is something that will be necessary and beneficial.”

He also reminded donors that the synagogue has its own GoFundMe to “rebuild and secure” the east end Belleville shul.

“Your donation will help fund essential security work, including repairing and reinforcing the windows damaged by gunfire, strengthening the building’s security, and putting critical measures in place to better protect everyone who walks through our doors,” organizer Hadas Brajtman posted.

As of Monday morning, it was less than $5,000 shy of its $90,000 goal.

“This is about more than repairing what was damaged,” Brajtman said. “It is about ensuring our children can grow up with a Jewish community they are proud of, families can gather for Shabbat and holidays, and our elders can walk through these doors feeling safe.”

stories.title: Here’s where couples are cutting corners to save money for their weddings during surging costs: experts
stories.summary: When Jessica Korchowiec and Kai Helsdon began planning their wedding roughly two years ago, it was a different world with different costs for vendors and services.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
Toronto - When Jessica Korchowiec and Kai Helsdon began planning their wedding roughly two years ago, it was a different world with different costs for vendors and services.

At the time, they had a painstakingly budgeted plan that would have them spending no more than $25,000 on their big day. But between then and their wedding date on Sept. 5, of this year, everything changed.

Over the next two years, couples and vendors faced higher food and service costs, trade tensions and more recently, higher fuel and transportation prices.

Their original budget was thrown out the window.

“The initial budget for me was around $25,000, but we ended up spending close to $40,000 and that was partially due to added costs and increase in some of the things that we weren’t expecting,” Korchowiec told CTV News

“I wasn’t expecting a house wedding to be so expensive,” she added.

“I think that’s what caught me off guard was that I thought that I had the power to do things cheaper.”

Wedding planners tell CTV News that wedding costs have soared this year. However, couples are finding different ways to mitigate the financial damage.

“There’s that ripple effect of everything. Fuel costs go up, which means delivery fees are going up, then wedding fees are going up,” said Toronto-based wedding planner Trevor Frankfort of Trevents Planning.

“Getting all of the product for the wedding has now become so much more expensive than it was last summer.”

Frankfort said that he’s having more conversations with his clients about their budget and what couples can trim from the event.

“Are they willing to go with a cheaper venue, even though it’s not all the glitz and glamor? Or do they need to scale back on food quality or guests? Where are they making those compromises?” he asked.

“Guest count is the biggest hurdle these days because everybody wants to invite everybody, but it’s the easiest way to reduce the cost of your wedding, but keeping it elevated still.”

Data shows higher costs for couples and guests

Statistics Canada data shows several costs tied to both hosting and attending a wedding have climbed over the past year.

Prices for food purchased from restaurants , which is a category indirectly tied to catering and food-service costs, saw an increase of roughly six per cent over two years.

Prices for alcoholic beverages served at licensed establishments rose 3.5 per cent year-over-year in June, following a 3.3 per cent increase the previous year. Those costs were about 6.9 per cent higher than in June 2024.

Fuel costs are also putting pressure on businesses that transport goods and supplies.

Statistics Canada’s Industrial Product Price Index shows producer prices for diesel fuel were 75 per cent higher in August 2026 than in August 2025. That figure measures prices received by Canadian producers rather than the retail price motorists pay at the pump, but it points to significantly higher fuel-related input costs for industries that rely on trucking and deliveries.

“The majority of flowers in Canada are shipped from South America, from Europe, from Asia,” said wedding planner Roxy Zapala who runs Art of Celebrations.

“There are some homegrown florals, but a lot of them are shipped, so when the gas prices go up, the price of flowers start to skyrocket. When we’re talking about things like a single bouquet, maybe the price goes up by $5 and $10.”

Wedding guests have also felt a financial hit this year. Travel prices have surged and accommodation costs have also risen.

Gasoline prices were 22.8 per cent higher in August than a year earlier, while air transportation prices rose 15 per cent over the same period. Travel-tour prices were up 26.1 per cent year-over-year in August, along with the introduction of fuel surcharges amid higher jet-fuel costs.

Accommodation also became more expensive. Traveller-accommodation prices were 10.1 per cent higher nationally in June 2026 than in June 2025.

The increase was even larger in Ontario, at 19.4 per cent although Statistics Canada said the provincial jump was driven in part by higher demand in Toronto during the Fifa World Cup.

“All of those things are affected. It’s like a ripple effect, and all of a sudden everything becomes so much more expensive,” added Zapala. “So maybe guests are declining coming to multiple weddings and only choosing to go to one or two for the year.”

Micro-weddings make a comeback as couples cut costs

Wedding planners have told CTV News their clients have been gravitating less towards destination weddings and more towards micro-weddings to save money.

“Micro-weddings have an average guest count of 20 to 50 (people) and that’s just their favorite people,” said Tracey Manailescu with the Wedding Planners Institute of Canada.

“They’re must-have people, like friends and family. So maybe you’re going to a restaurant, maybe you’re having a really particular winery or venue that you really want to have this beautiful, elegant setting. Or maybe it could be in your backyard and just downsizing it but upgrading on the florals or upgrading on the things that are really important to them,” she added.

Manailescu says micro-weddings were common during the COVID-19 pandemic and now they’re seeing it “creep back again” so that couples can allocate their funds to other expenses.

“Then that money that we’re saving, let’s put it towards our house, let’s put it towards our honeymoon, and let’s go to Europe for a month, as opposed to let’s go a week somewhere else and let it go.”

When it comes to wedding expenses, Frankfort believes the worst is yet to come. Many couple were able to lock in prices when they booked last year, but those who are booking vendors now might be in for a shock when they see the prices.

“What I’m seeing down the road is these trade wars just keep happening, and it’s getting worse and worse in every industry, not just the wedding industry,” said Frankfort.

“If I saw such a huge difference between last summer and this summer, I can’t even guess what next summer is going to look like for people. It’s scary.”

Frankfort adds that some vendors have been adding contract clauses to allow for price changes. Those clauses allow vendors to protect themselves in case prices for their supplies surge again.

“What I’m seeing is this wording changing, (vendors) anticipating costs to go up so that they aren’t affected by it as much. They can actually throw those costs off to the clients,” said Frankfort, who adds he hasn’t seen a clause of this nature in previous contracts.

“You’re feeling like vendors are protecting themselves against some of these astronomical costs.”

With files from CTV News’ Kristen Yu

That figure measures prices received by Canadian producers rather than the retail price motorists pay at the pump, but it points to significantly higher fuel-related input costs for industries that rely on trucking and deliveries.
“The majority of flowers in Canada are shipped from South America, from Europe, from Asia,” said wedding planner Roxy Zapala who runs Art of Celebrations.

“There are some homegrown florals, but a lot of them are shipped, so when the gas prices go up, the price of flowers start to skyrocket. When we’re talking about things like a single bouquet, maybe the price goes up by $5 and $10.”
Wedding guests have also felt a financial hit this year. Travel prices have surged and accommodation costs have also risen.

Gasoline prices were 22.8 per cent higher in August than a year earlier, while air transportation prices rose 15 per cent over the same period. Travel-tour prices were up 26.1 per cent year-over-year in August, along with the introduction of fuel surcharges amid higher jet-fuel costs.
Accommodation also became more expensive. Traveller-accommodation prices were 10.1 per cent higher nationally in June 2026 than in June 2025.
The increase was even larger in Ontario, at 19.4 per cent although Statistics Canada said the provincial jump was driven in part by higher demand in Toronto during the Fifa World Cup.

“All of those things are affected. It’s like a ripple effect, and all of a sudden everything becomes so much more expensive,” added Zapala. “So maybe guests are declining coming to multiple weddings and only choosing to go to one or two for the year.”
Micro-weddings make a comeback as couples cut costs
Wedding planners have told CTV News their clients have been gravitating less towards destination weddings and more towards micro-weddings to save money.
“Micro-weddings have an average guest count of 20 to 50 (people) and that’s just their favorite people,” said Tracey Manailescu with the Wedding Planners Institute of Canada.

“They’re must-have people, like friends and family. So maybe you’re going to a restaurant, maybe you’re having a really particular winery or venue that you really want to have this beautiful, elegant setting. Or maybe it could be in your backyard and just downsizing it but upgrading on the florals or upgrading on the things that are really important to them,” she added.
Manailescu says micro-weddings were common during the COVID-19 pandemic and now they’re seeing it “creep back again” so that couples can allocate their funds to other expenses.

“Then that money that we’re saving, let’s put it towards our house, let’s put it towards our honeymoon, and let’s go to Europe for a month, as opposed to let’s go a week somewhere else and let it go.”

When it comes to wedding expenses, Frankfort believes the worst is yet to come. Many couple were able to lock in prices when they booked last year, but those who are booking vendors now might be in for a shock when they see the prices.
“What I’m seeing down the road is these trade wars just keep happening, and it’s getting worse and worse in every industry, not just the wedding industry,” said Frankfort.
“If I saw such a huge difference between last summer and this summer, I can’t even guess what next summer is going to look like for people. It’s scary.”
Frankfort adds that some vendors have been adding contract clauses to allow for price changes. Those clauses allow vendors to protect themselves in case prices for their supplies surge again.

“What I’m seeing is this wording changing, (vendors) anticipating costs to go up so that they aren’t affected by it as much. They can actually throw those costs off to the clients,” said Frankfort, who adds he hasn’t seen a clause of this nature in previous contracts.
“You’re feeling like vendors are protecting themselves against some of these astronomical costs.”

stories.title: Another officer charged in Project South corruption probe pleads guilty
stories.summary: A Toronto police officer charged in the Project South corruption investigation has pleaded guilty, becoming the second to do so.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A Toronto police officer charged in the Project South corruption investigation has pleaded guilty, becoming the second to do so.

Const. Elias Mouawad, one of eight current and former Toronto police officers arrested in the probe, entered his plea at a downtown Toronto court Monday morning.

Mouawad, who was arrested in February, pleaded guilty to one count of unauthorized use of a computer. A charge of breach of public trust was withdrawn.

Court heard Mouawad was asked by a former employer, Daljit Singh, to run a search for a license plate.

Mouawad, 24, worked as a security guard at a company owned by Singh before becoming an officer. Singh was also arrested and charged with unauthorized use of a computer in Project South.

Mouawad had been a member of Toronto police for a year-and-a-half when Singh made the request, said Crown prosecutor Samuel Walker, citing the agreed statement of facts.

Singh had reported ties to Brian Da Costa, a major figure in the Project South probe, Walker told court.

Mouawad and Singh spoke on Jan. 17, and two days later, Singh reportedly asked Mouawad for the plate, saying it was for “his boy.”

Mouawad never learned who the inquiry was for but ran the search on Jan. 19. He provided the results to Singh because he had been a “caring boss” and believed the request wasn’t connected to any form of criminality, Walker said.

Mouawad is not alleged to have conducted other unlawful queries, and Walker said there is no evidence Mouawad intended to engage in future misconduct.

He added there wasn’t evidence to dispute Mouawad’s assertion in his police interview that he was remorseful for his conduct, vowing to never to engage in such a conduct again.

Mouawad had tried to plead guilty earlier

Project South began in June 2025 after a high-ranking employee at the Toronto South Detention Centre was identified as the target of an alleged attempted hit. The probe also has alleged links to Ryan Wedding’s apparent drug ring, an alleged gun-for-hire network and illegal dispensaries.

York Regional Police wrote in a recent, partially unsealed court document seeking to obtain a search warrant that the conduct by some officers “demonstrates a broader pattern of corruption, misuse of police authority, and facilitation of criminal activity.”

As part of the investigation, it’s alleged Const. Timothy Barnhardt and other Toronto police officers tapped into unauthorized information.

Mouawad’s lawyer, Peter Brauti, previously told Global News his client had asked to plead guilty immediately after he was charged.

He said Mouawad’s attempts were unsuccessful because the Crown wasn’t ready to take a plea. The Crown told the court the issue didn’t relate to their office or the initial delay in the plea, but that things were rapidly unfolding.

Brauti has said his client felt he had been wrongly swept up in Project South.

1:56 Toronto Police officer charged in Project South planned to plead guilty Tuesday

“When information was released to the press, it made our client appear as if he was part of very, very serious conduct that has been alleged in Project South, when that is not the case,” he said.

“This is an officer who did a single check, unauthorized, which is unrelated to all of these allegations of drug dealing, corruption, attempted murder, all that. It is a completely separate issue.”

He added Mouawad had been “under this cloud” after Project South and that the public had not been given a “true picture” about his “relatively minor” misconduct.

Walker told court Monday the Crown is asking for Mouawad to spend two months under house arrest and two months under curfew. That sentence would be a “clear message of denunciation and deterrence for leaking of confidential information by a police officer,” he said.

Meanwhile, Brauti is asking for a conditional discharge given Mouawad was “nothing short of an exemplary police officer” who had made the most arrests during his first year at his division.

A conditional discharge includes a finding of guilt, but no criminal record is registered as long as a set of conditions is followed.

Mouawad, who has been suspended without pay since his arrest, was emotional when he addressed court. He apologized for his actions and expressed remorse, saying he’s has taken complete accountability and responsibility since his arrest.

Mouawad’s sentencing hearing is scheduled for Oct. 19.

What other officers have plead guilty?

Mouawad is the second officer arrested to plead guilty.

In July, former police const. Derek McCormick pleaded guilty to two charges : theft under $5,000 for stealing a cellphone and breach of trust by stealing “found property.” He was initially charged with four counts of theft under $5,000, one count of breach of the trust by a public officer and another count of obstruction of justice.

At the time, York Regional Police alleged his involvement in Project South centred on his participation in the theft of personal property from a police facility. The personal property allegedly included driver’s licences, health cards and passports. A “substantial amount” of it was recovered.

McCormick resigned as a police officer earlier this year, a police spokesperson previously told Global News.

— with files from Catherine McDonald

stories.title: Canada needs more ‘urgency’ in rebuilding its military: ex-defence chief
stories.summary: The Carney government needs to move quickly to invest in armed forces before it loses 'social licence' to do so, former Chief of Defence Staff Wayne Eyre says.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Rapid change in both the political and physical world must be met with a greater sense of urgency in rebuilding the Canadian Armed Forces, says retired Gen. Wayne Eyre , former chief of the defence staff.

Speaking to The West Block host Jeff Semple in an interview that aired Sunday, Eyre said he’s been encouraged by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pledge to make generational investments in the CAF and bring Canada’s defence spending up to par with NATO allies.

But Eyre warned that the government needs to ensure Canadians understand the threats the country faces in order to maintain public support to foot the bill.

“The real danger, the critical vulnerability that the government is going to face, is if the berating from south of the border changes, and the very real threats to our country remain, the government will lose their social licence to continue,” Eyre said in the interview.

“And that’s why they need to lead through this moment, continue to educate Canadians on the very real threats to our sovereignty, our security and our way of life.”

After years of lagging behind NATO allies, the Carney government announced in 2025 that Canada expected to hit the alliance’s target of spending two per cent of GDP on defence that year.

The government’s 2025 budget committed the government to grow defence spending to four per cent of GDP by the end of the decade, but has yet to reveal a plan to reach that target.

The price tag will be substantial, and is not yet fully accounted for in the government’s fiscal framework. A Global News analysis of the government’s 2026 Spring Economic Statement suggests Canada will need to spend a total of $163 billion on an annual basis to meet the four per cent commitment by 2030 — $34.9 billion more annually on core defence spending compared to the government’s 2025 budget.

Asked about the lack of transparency around defence spending plans, Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said in January to stay tuned to the government’s 2026 budget, expected later this year.

“Obviously when we’re going to present Budget 2026 … we’ll be looking at measures to make the Canadian economy strong and make sure that, you know, the systems and procurement we’re doing meet the NATO requirement, but at the same time that the Canadian economy can finance these big investments,” Champagne said.

Eyre said time is of the essence, because defence investments take time to translate into actual new capabilities and “readiness” — which he defined as “our ability to respond fast enough with enough forces long enough” to a crisis.

The retired general said the CAF’s readiness has been suffering for a long time — from the end of the Cold War to the war in Afghanistan — and it can’t be changed overnight.

“We need a sense of urgency, much more of a sense of urgency in getting things done. The security environment is changing so rapidly, whether its geopolitical reordering, whether its technology, whether it’s climate change, all of those mean there’s multiple future scenarios that we could face and need to be prepared for,” Eyre told Semple.

“In the face of that uncertainty, the nation’s ultimate insurance policy is the military. And so getting things done as quickly as possible in terms of capability procurement? Essential.”

stories.title: Slate Grocery Reit to be acquired by Brixmor, Everview Partners in deal valued at $2.3-billion
stories.summary: Toronto-listed trust owns a portfolio of U.S. grocery store-anchored real estate properties
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Slate Grocery Reit SGR-UN-T has signed a deal to be acquired by Brixmor Property Group Inc. BRX-N and Everview Partners in an agreement that values the trust at US$2.3-billion.

The purchase comes after Slate launched a review of strategic alternatives in May.

The Toronto-listed trust, which owns a portfolio of U.S. grocery store-anchored real estate properties, says the buyers have agreed to pay US$13 per unit in cash to take it private.

Marc Rouleau, chair of Slate’s special committee, says the deal provides unitholders with immediate liquidity and certainty of value at an attractive all-cash price.

Brixmor owns and operates a portfolio of open-air shopping centres in the U.S., while Everview Partners is a private investment management firm.

The deal, which requires unitholder approval, is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.

stories.title: CBC’s ‘Hockey Night in Canada’ to return this season with Pwhl games
stories.summary: Toronto — The CBC says that "Hockey Night in Canada" will return this season in partnership with the Professional Women's Hockey League.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — The CBC says that “Hockey Night in Canada” will return this season in partnership with the Professional Women’s Hockey League.

The network says the first women’s game to be featured on the long-running program will be a Dec. 5 matchup between the Montreal Victoire and expansion club PWHL Hamilton.

National Hockey League games previously aired on Hockey Night.

Domestic rights-holder Rogers Communications and the CBC did not extend their sublicensing agreement for the upcoming NHL season.

The CBC first aired “Hockey Night in Canada” on television in 1952.

The program has been a Saturday-night mainstay for generations of hockey fans.

More to come

stories.title: Local conservation groups receive Great Lakes protection funding
stories.summary: Several organizations in southwestern Ontario are receiving a share of the funding through the Great Lakes Local Action Fund
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
Ontario is investing nearly $2 million in projects aimed at protecting water quality in the Great Lakes.

Several organizations in southwestern Ontario are receiving a share of the funding through the Great Lakes Local Action Fund, including the Ausable Bayfield Conservation Authority, the Lake Huron Coastal Centre, the Lower Thames Valley Conservation Authority and Lambton County.

Together, the local groups will receive nearly $300,000 for a range of environmental initiatives, including wetland restoration, increasing native plant species and supporting landowners undertaking projects designed to protect water quality.

The province says the funding is intended to help improve the health of the Great Lakes ecosystem and strengthen local conservation efforts.

Since 2021, the Great Lakes Local Action Fund has distributed more than $5.5 million to community-based projects across Ontario.

stories.title: Campbellton, N.B., mayor Michel Soucy dies suddenly in hospital
stories.summary: Michel Soucy previously served as the mayor of Atholville, N.B., before municipal changes made the village a part of Campbellton, N.B.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A New Brunswick community is mourning the loss of its mayor after he suddenly died on Saturday at the age of 75.

The Campbellton Regional Community in northern New Brunswick said in a Facebook post on Sept. 26 that Soucy died at the Campbellton Regional Hospital.

“Mr. Soucy had a deep love for our community and worked hard every day toward making it a better place to live, work and raise a family. His presence will be missed,” the community wrote in a post.

Soucy was elected mayor earlier this year in the May 11 municipal election and was sworn in May 27.

Being mayor of Campbellton was not his first stint in politics, having previously served as the mayor of Atholville, N.B., before it became part of Campbellton. He served that community as mayor from 2012 until 2016.

A post by Soucy’s family said Soucy died from cardiac arrest.

“In this moment, we want to express our deep admiration and gratitude for the man he was,” said Mario Soucy, one of the mayor’s children, in a Facebook post. “His actions were deeply rooted in his values and convictions.”

The Regional Community sent its sincere condolences to Soucy’s family and friends in their post.

It said further details would be announced when they are available.

stories.title: Toronto police ID second homicide victim found in burnt-out vehicle
stories.summary: Toronto police have identified a second homicide victim whose body was found in a burnt-out vehicle last week.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Toronto police have identified a second homicide victim who was found in a burnt-out vehicle last week.

Mohamud Kheyre’s body was found last Tuesday as police responded to two vehicle fires on opposite ends of the city.

The first incident was reported to police around 11:24 p.m. Sept. 21. Officers were called to a hydro field on Reesor Road, near Steeles Avenue East.

It was reported that there was a vehicle on fire. When crews arrived on scene, they found a body inside the vehicle. The victim in that case was identified Friday as 32-year-old Marcus Charles .

At 12:55 a.m. Sept. 22, police were called to James Garden Park in Etobicoke for another vehicle on fire. Police said smoke was seen coming from the park, and there were reports of what sounded like an explosion.

After crews arrived, Kheyre’s body was found inside the car. The 30-year-old’s identity was released Sunday afternoon.

Charles and Kheyre are Toronto’s 27th and 28th homicides of 2026.

Anyone with information is asked to call police.

stories.title: Bungalow near Sturgeon Lake hooks offers from two buyers
stories.summary: Three-bedroom home in Kawartha Lakes is close to shops, restaurants and the historic Flato Academy Theatre
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
7 Ranchers Rd., Kawartha Lakes, Ont.

Asking price: $699,000 (August, 2026)

Selling price: $686,500 (September, 2026)

Previous selling price: $227,000 (January, 2007)

Taxes: $4,306 (2026)

Days on the market: 18

Listing agents: Jason Challenger, John Ireland and Bryce Boyce, Affinity Group Pinnacle Realty Ltd.

This three-bedroom bungalow is on a roughly two-acre lot near Sturgeon Lake, about 140 kilometres northeast of downtown Toronto. Persuading buyers to travel to check it out was easier done with a list price under $700,000 this summer. Within the first week, two guests delivered competing purchase offers.

“That property is in a more rural environment, and it does take time for people to get there,” agent Jason Challenger said.

“But things that are priced appropriately still get multiple offers.”

Part of the appeal of this home was its proximity to shops, grocery stores and restaurants, as well as the historic Flato Academy Theatre in Lindsay, Ont.

“There were lots of properties available,” Mr. Challenger said.

“Ranchers Road is about five minutes outside of Fenelon Falls and about 10 minutes outside of Lindsay, kind of between two larger towns in the Kawarthas.”

This bungalow has an eat-in kitchen, three bathrooms and a laundry room, and is connected to well and septic systems.

stories.title: 10 Huron-Bruce women recognized for Rural Ontario Week
stories.summary: 10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.

The women recognized were Tara Terpstra, Emily Morrison, Carol Leeming, Miranda Klaver, Margaret Vincent, Becky Maus, Kristie Gilchrist, Barb Zettler, Amanda Hammell, and Christine MacIntyre.

“Women have always been an integral part of agriculture and rural life here in Huron-Bruce, and this year provides a special opportunity to recognize the women who continue to strengthen our farms, businesses, and communities,” Thompson said.

“I am proud to recognize these 10 women for their leadership, dedication, and hard work they bring to our rural communities. Their contributions are helping build a strong future for agriculture and rural Ontario.”

Rural Ontario Week runs Sept. 20 to Sept. 26.

stories.title: Exploring local democracy: Meet John, 56, your average municipal election candidate
stories.summary: Survey results suggest the average local candidate is likely quite different from the average local resident in their district.
stories.author: Jacquelyn Mitchell
stories.content:
Local government experts at Western University are studying the candidates who run for municipal office to learn more about their backgrounds as well as their experiences on the campaign trail.

With municipal voters in Ontario heading to the polls Oct. 26, Western researchers surveyed hundreds of candidates running in communities with populations over 2,000. It’s part of their larger Local Democracy Project, which explores who runs for municipal office in Canada, why they run and how they get their message out to voters.

Political science professor Zack Taylor spoke with Western News to share insights gleaned from almost 900 candidate responses.

Zack Taylor (ZT): The Local Democracy Project is a Sshrc-funded collaboration between Western researchers – I’m leading it alongside political science professor Martin Horak and our colleagues at Inrs-Urbanisation in Montréal and Dalhousie University. The project has several facets, including candidate surveys across Canada and in-depth case studies of local campaigns.

Since 2022, we have been fielding surveys across the country to learn about what drives candidates. We wanted to know how they campaign, how they raise and spend money, and what they think about local politics – what groups have influence and what role local government should play. We also ask them about their demographic characteristics. The survey is currently active in Ontario and has just been sent out in British Columbia (which has elections set for Oct. 17).

ZT: We only know about the people who have responded to our survey, and this group May not be completely representative. Among the almost 900 Ontario candidates who responded this year, the most common first name is John. About a quarter had run for municipal office before and most of those are incumbents. About 57 per cent identify as male and 37 per cent female. The average age is 56. Over half have a university degree and an annual household income of over $100,000. Over four in five are homeowners.

So, the average local candidate is likely quite different from the average local resident in their district.

ZT: Especially in larger and more urban municipalities, candidates need to raise money to buy signs, leaflets and conventional and social media advertising. In smaller places, running for office is more about showing up for events and word-of-mouth recommendations in the community – forms of influence that don’t cost money.

We won’t know how much money candidates raised or spent until months after the election, when they submit financial disclosures to the municipal clerk in their community. Almost 75 per cent of candidates told us they expect to pay for at least half of their campaign costs out of pocket. The median campaign cost, based on candidates’ estimates, is $2,600. It’s not necessarily a lot of money for the typical candidate we’ve described, but a sum of this size or larger May discourage low-income people from running for office.

A commonly raised issue around self-financing election campaigns is whether it gives wealthier people an advantage. The good news is research shows that spending doesn’t guarantee a win. In past municipal elections we’ve seen candidates spend a lot and lose, and other candidates spend very little and win. A lot hinges on how efficiently they use their resources and how well-known they are in the first place. Incumbency is a huge factor – mayors and councillors running for re-election have a lot of name recognition.

ZT: We found candidates overwhelmingly agree with placing restrictions on campaign spending, individual donations and self-financing, as well as prohibiting the building of “war chests” – where repeat candidates can use surplus funds raised in one election to cover expenses in future elections.

Candidates also broadly agreed with the principle of disclosure – that identities of donors and the amounts they gave should be made public. Interestingly, they are divided 50/50 on whether this information should be made public before or after election day. They broadly agreed with Ontario’s current rules, which require disclosure after the campaign is over.

ZT:Almost half identified as ideological centrists. Very few put themselves on the far left or far right.

Perhaps unsurprising given Ontario’s longstanding absence of political parties in local elections, fully 91 per cent of respondents disagreed with the statement that “municipal candidates should run as members of parties, because parties get things done better than independents” and 65 per cent disagreed with the statement that “municipal political parties would make it easier to know where candidates stand ideologically.”

Most have a utilitarian back-to-basics perspective on local government, with 57 per cent agreeing “the main purpose of local government is to provide services to property owners.” Only eight per cent disagreed with the notion that “municipal policymaking is about pragmatic decisions, not ideological disagreement.” Still, 44 per cent reported having been involved in a provincial or federal political party in the past five years.

ZT: This year we asked candidates a series of questions on policy issues that another project, the Canadian Municipal Barometer, asks of elected officials. We were surprised to find opinion was broadly in favour of what we might call progressive policy positions: for example, roads should be made accessible to walking and cycling, even if it means fewer driving lanes or parking. What we don’t know is whether progressive candidates were more likely to respond to our survey than conservative ones, though most identified as centrists when asked to place themselves on a left-right ideology scale and strongly supported non-partisan local politics.

Across all of our Local Democracy Project surveys, most candidates also believe term limits would make local government work better. This is perhaps surprising given there is no precedent for term limiting elected officials in Canada. But it May also represent a reaction to perceived incumbency advantage.

We don’t have results from Ontario in 2026 yet, as this question is part of our follow-up survey to be sent just before election day, but we also ask all candidates whether they experienced harassment or intimidation while campaigning. Our surveys from other provinces indicate about half of candidates experienced at least one incidence of belittling language or insults online and some type of interference with campaign materials such as lawn signs and posters. This confirms what we hear anecdotally from public officials, which is that social media is a very unfriendly place.

ZT: Democracy only works if people decide to run for office. This research tells us about how well our current candidates represent their communities at large, what candidates think the purpose of local government is and their impressions of local politics in general. We’ve only scratched the surface. We hope to understand how these factors vary according to the type of place a candidate seeks to represent and their personal characteristics.

More generally, we see opportunities for policy change. In an innovative approach, we are linking survey responses to election results and campaign finance disclosures, which is going to enable us to evaluate the effectiveness of provincial rules governing nomination, campaign fundraising and spending and advertising. Local campaigning has barely been studied in Canada up until now, so there’s lots more to explore and understand.

stories.title: At first, case stumped doctors who determined Ontario woman had fatal case of rat bite fever
stories.summary: Rat bite fever has an estimated death rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease destroyed large parts of the woman's heart.
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Rat bite fever has an estimated death rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease destroyed large parts of the woman's heart

For days and days on end, doctors didn’t know exactly what kind of organism they were up against. The infection spreading through the 48-year-old Ontario woman was so aggressive, large parts of her heart were destroyed. But all the usual blood work, all the cultures for typical bacterial infections came back negative. Doctors couldn’t fully understand what was feeding the infection. Until her sister wondered, could it be the rats? The woman’s death last year, published in a new case report , is being described as the first reported fatal case of rat bite fever that defeated even the most advanced “Hail Mary” form of out-of-body heart and lung bypass. The case “was a bit of a conundrum,” said cardiologist and intensivist Dr. Craig Ainsworth, chief of critical care at Hamilton Health Sciences, and co-author of the report in Jacc, the Journal of the American College of Cardiology. “Normally, when we have people with that degree of heart and heart valve infection, we usually get something in the blood work,” he said, typically one of the aggressive bugs “that do this sort of thing.” In this case, everything was negative until weeks later, when valve tissue taken during the woman’s emergency heart surgery was sent for specialized DNA testing, which ultimately identified streptobacillus moniliformis, a bacterium found in the oral, nasal and respiratory tract secretions of rats. The bug can be transmitted to people via broken skin, bites or scratches, but also from close contact, without a bite or scratch, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control. It can also be spread through exposure to contaminated food or water. Diagnosis can be challenging: the organism is “fastidious, difficult to grow and has limited diagnostic tests available for early detection,” Ainsworth and colleagues wrote in the Sept. 16 edition of Jacc Case Reports. The woman ultimately died, despite being treated with the proper antibiotics. “We just guessed and happened to guess properly,” Ainsworth said, however, the infection was too far gone by the time she was transferred to his ICU. “It wasn’t obvious to us for days and days what we were actually treating.” Rat bite fever is a rare infection with an estimated mortality rate of up to 13 per cent if left untreated. The disease often starts with vague symptoms such as fever, rash and generally just feeling unwell, which can delay people seeking medical attention. The woman was a bit of a “homebody” who kept to herself, Ainsworth said. She had some medical problems, including asthma and inflammatory bowel disease, and was a smoker. “She wasn’t a perfectly healthy 48-year-old, but she was totally functional and ambulatory.” After six to eight weeks of fatigue, lower back pain, facial flushing and peripheral numbness, the woman went to her local hospital’s emergency department, about 100 kilometres outside Hamilton. She described worsening diarrhea and fainting spells — spells owing to, in retrospect, “the infection eating into the electrical system of her heart,” Ainsworth said. Doctors suspected sepsis and started antibiotics, but while in emergency the woman suffered a cardiac arrest. The upper chambers of her heart were no longer communicating with the lower chambers, causing a dangerously slow heart rate. A temporary pacemaker was inserted. Three days later, a special echocardiogram that involves guiding a thin tube down the throat to examine the heart from inside the esophagus revealed extensive infection of various parts of the heart and valves. She was referred to a second hospital for urgent, complicated and prolonged heart surgery. Because of low oxygen levels, doctors couldn’t take the woman off the machine used to take over the function of her heart and lungs during surgery. She was placed on Ecmo, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, an advanced form of life support. Her heart muscle continued to deteriorate, and the woman was transferred to Hamilton General Hospital, “still without a specific diagnosis or a bug,” Ainsworth said. “By the time we received the call, she was at best a Hail Mary; she was very unwell,” he said. But because she was 48 and otherwise fairly healthy, they tried every measure they could. “She just didn’t get any better,” Ainsworth said. At one point her sister, from whom she was semi-estranged, remarked to Ainsworth, “You know, I just wonder if it’s related to the rats she has in her house.” “As a non-infectious disease doctor, I didn’t put two and two together,” he said. “I thought it was like a guinea pig or a hamster, just a little more unusual. “But when we ultimately got this bug back from the DNA testing, it became clear that almost certainly this was related to her pet rats.” After several weeks in hospital, the woman succumbed to the infection. Life support was withdrawn “given the unfortunate futility of what we were doing and her worsening, despite all the heroic interventions,” Ainsworth said. It’s not clear if the rats were purchased or had infested her home. The sister said the rats seemed more like pets. “I don’t think they were just innocent bystanders,” Ainsworth said. The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it. “It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans. Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said. “Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. The woman ultimately died, despite being treated with the proper antibiotics. “We just guessed and happened to guess properly,” Ainsworth said, however, the infection was too far gone by the time she was transferred to his ICU.

It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats.

The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said.

“Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said

“As far as I know, he did give away the rats.”

Doctors suspected sepsis and started antibiotics, but while in emergency the woman suffered a cardiac arrest. The upper chambers of her heart were no longer communicating with the lower chambers, causing a dangerously slow heart rate.

A temporary pacemaker was inserted. Three days later, a special echocardiogram that involves guiding a thin tube down the throat to examine the heart from inside the esophagus revealed extensive infection of various parts of the heart and valves.
She was referred to a second hospital for urgent, complicated and prolonged heart surgery.

Because of low oxygen levels, doctors couldn’t take the woman off the machine used to take over the function of her heart and lungs during surgery. She was placed on Ecmo, or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, an advanced form of life support.
Her heart muscle continued to deteriorate, and the woman was transferred to Hamilton General Hospital, “still without a specific diagnosis or a bug,” Ainsworth said.
“By the time we received the call, she was at best a Hail Mary; she was very unwell,” he said. But because she was 48 and otherwise fairly healthy, they tried every measure they could.
“She just didn’t get any better,” Ainsworth said.
At one point her sister, from whom she was semi-estranged, remarked to Ainsworth, “You know, I just wonder if it’s related to the rats she has in her house.”
“As a non-infectious disease doctor, I didn’t put two and two together,” he said. “I thought it was like a guinea pig or a hamster, just a little more unusual.
“But when we ultimately got this bug back from the DNA testing, it became clear that almost certainly this was related to her pet rats.”

After several weeks in hospital, the woman succumbed to the infection. Life support was withdrawn “given the unfortunate futility of what we were doing and her worsening, despite all the heroic interventions,” Ainsworth said.
It’s not clear if the rats were purchased or had infested her home. The sister said the rats seemed more like pets. “I don’t think they were just innocent bystanders,” Ainsworth said.

The bacterium S. moniliformis is ubiquitous in all rodents, said infectious disease specialist Dr. Omar Mourad, a co-author of the case report. “It lives in their mouth, in their oral flora. Any rodent — though certainly rats are the famous ones — will have it.
“It’s not harmful to the rats, similar to how we have a number of bacteria in our mouth and on our skin,” he said. But it can cause trouble when it gets into humans.
Despite its name, more often than not rat bite fever is transmitted merely by handling rats, Mourad said.
“Some people like to kiss the rat on the mouth, which I would not recommend,” he said. Or they don’t wash their hands properly after handling the rodents and get the bacteria into their mouth.
“Once it gets in, occasionally it will make its way into the bloodstream and cause more trouble,” Mourad said.
Classic symptoms of infection — rash, joint pain, vomiting and other GI symptoms — typically start three to 10 days after exposure.
Most people who get infected get better on their own after feeling flu-like for a couple of days.
“But you have to get it before it does anything like this,” Mourad said.
Left untreated, severe cases can cause not only endocarditis, as it did in the 48-year-old woman, but also meningitis — infection of the brain and spinal cord.
Although uncommon in Canada, rat bite fever is increasing because of “changing patterns of urban living (more dense urban housing) and pet-keeping practices,” other researchers have warned .

As of 2106, the-then-largest single episode in Canada found 11 cases of reported rat bite fever on Vancouver Island between 2010 and 2016. Seven cases required hospitalization, but there were no deaths “or significant morbidity.”

From the intensive care physician’s perspective, “It comes back to, if something is weird and a bit of a unicorn (exceptionally rare) case, I think it behooves us to dig deeper and start asking questions of loved ones and family members,” Ainsworth said.
“Just by having a conversation with the sister and asking about habits and unusual things, the rats came out, which was helpful information.”
It was the second case of a pet rat infection Mourad saw last year. The other involved a different bacteria called leptospirosis, spread through the urine of infected rats.
The man, who got infected from handling his pet rats, spent a few weeks in hospital “until we figured it out,” Mourad said.
“Fortunately, it ended much better, and the patient did very well,” he said
“As far as I know, he did give away the rats.”

stories.title: AI agents booking doctor’s appointments: Inside PocketHealth’s drive to improve patient care
stories.summary: PocketHealth’s second act is a response to health care organizations grappling with disconnected record systems and demanding administrative work that takes time away from patient care
stories.author: Leah Golob
stories.content:
It’s a critical time for Canada’s economy and its business community. The country needs innovation and growth more than ever, yet businesses across a wide range of industries are facing trade disruptions, rising costs and technological change, among other challenges. This series profiles forward-thinking Canadian companies that are growing their markets by re-examining their business practices and trying new things.

When Harsh Nayyar injured his ankle playing tennis while living in California’s Bay Area in 2014, he received his MRI images on a CD.

For Harsh and his brother Rishi, both technologists, the experience seemed shockingly outdated. Tech platforms such as YouTube and Netflix offered instant online streaming, yet medical images still needed to be burned onto physical discs.

The brothers decided to tackle the problem together, launching the Toronto-based software development company PocketHealth in early 2016 to help patients access, share and understand their medical imaging records and reports – all online, from any device. Rishi is chief executive officer and his brother Harsh is chief technology officer.

Ten years in, PocketHealth’s platform has reached more than three million patients across Canada and the United States and operates at more than 900 sites across more than 250 health care organizations, such as UHN, Sinai Health, Trillium Health Partners, Mackenzie Health, William Osler Health System and Niagara Health. Its annual revenue, the company says, is in the $10-million to $50-million range, growing more than 25 per cent year over year.

Rishi says PocketHealth’s medical image sharing services help patients discover the results of a biopsy or MRI quickly and efficiently, plus patients can more easily share findings from an emergency department visit with their family physicians.

The company also has examples of patients who spotted items missing in their report that they were then able to get corrected, he says. “It changed the path of their care.”

Now, the company is pursuing its second act, expanding beyond medical-image access into agentic artificial intelligence that can automate administrative tasks in hospitals and clinics, such as processing referrals and scheduling appointments.

This innovation is a response to health care organizations grappling with disconnected record systems and demanding administrative work that takes time away from patient care, Rishi says.

“We are in a heavily overburdened health care system.”

Dr. Andrew Pinto, a physician and director of Upstream Lab, a non-profit research lab based at MAP Centre for Urban Health Solutions, St. Michael’s Hospital in Toronto, says that one of the big problems with Canada’s health care system is that it is enormously fragmented. Individual hospitals, clinics, primary care organizations and public health have their own record systems, meaning there isn’t a single electronic health record for the country.

As a result, each of these systems has a different way of defining data, Dr. Pinto says, and data can’t flow easily from one system to another. While PocketHealth came up with a solution that solved this fragmentation, ideally the fragmentation wouldn’t exist, he adds.

“They are bringing a new perspective to a very old problem and they are showing us what technology can do,” Dr. Pinto says, adding that Canada needs legislation that would mandate interoperability.

PocketHealth’s agentic AI platform, PocketHealth Conductor, launched in late 2025. Rishi explains that Conductor has a coordinated network of AI agents that can complete non-clinical tasks autonomously.

For example, when a physician sends a referral, Conductor processes it, calls the patient and immediately books an appointment live over the phone. It’s also able to read faxed and uploaded documents.

The aim is to automate the health care industry’s time-consuming administrative workflows so providers can spend more time on patient care. And PocketHealth says Conductor is live in production today at “dozens” of hospitals and imaging providers in Canada and the U.S.

But adoption isn’t without its challenges, Rishi says.

“No matter how incredible [AI] is, every health care system, every clinic we deploy in has its own unique way of performing tasks,” he explains. In other words, a company can’t install an AI system without adapting it. Also, there’s a lot of ongoing effort to make agentic AI systems feel human and improve – rather than impede – the care journey.

“The obstacles are that it still requires a lot of configuration work, a lot of testing, which means you have to test very carefully, you have to roll out slowly, and I think we have very, very ambitious plans,” he says.

From Dr. Pinto’s perspective, AI has great potential. But he points out that the health care industry needs to address equity concerns around the technology, such as whether it’s lifting everybody up, whether it’s accurate and whether it works well for groups of people that May not have the digital literacy or devices to use it.

Investors are interested in what PocketHealth is doing. The company raised $45-million in Series B financing in March 2024, bringing their total equity funding to $75-million. The Series B financing was led by Round 13 Capital, with Deloitte Ventures and Samsung Next joining as new investors and additional investment from Questa Capital and Radical Ventures.

Rishi says that at least for now, PocketHealth plans to concentrate on Canada and the U.S. as it expands its AI offerings, rather than enter new international markets.

He hopes the technology will enable patients to reach out and schedule their own exams, and better understand the preparation needed for procedures instead of just receiving a phone call or a letter in the mail.

“I want it to be that they can call in and they’re never on hold and they get their questions answered,” he adds. As well, agentic AI can help new immigrants get the same quality and access of care in their first language as English speakers do.

“Agentic AI is still in its infancy,” Rishi says. “It needs more case studies, more deployment stories. We’re not even in inning one.”

stories.title: Mild weather expected before cooler air arrives Friday
stories.summary: Expect a stretch of mild fall weather this week as forecast calls for several days of above-average temperatures for late September before a cooler air mass arrives to end the work week.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Expect a stretch of mild fall weather this week as forecast calls for several days of above-average temperatures for late September before a cooler air mass arrives to end the work week.

According to Environment Canada, increasing cloudiness is expected Monday morning, while areas of fog will dissipate as the day progresses. Winds are forecast to shift to the north near noon at 20 km/h, with a daytime high of 22 C. The UV index is expected to reach five, considered moderate.

Partly cloudy conditions are forecast Monday night, with fog patches developing overnight and a low of 9 C.

Tuesday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud after morning fog patches clear. The high will climb to 23 C, while the UV index is forecast at six, or high. Cloudy periods are expected overnight Tuesday, with a low of 13 C.

Cloud cover is forecast to continue Wednesday, with a daytime high of 22 C. Wednesday night will remain cloudy, with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 14 C.

The chance of rain increases slightly Thursday, as Environment Canada is calling for cloudy skies and a 40 per cent chance of showers. The daytime high is expected to reach 23 C. Similar conditions are forecast Thursday night, with a low of 13 C.

Temperatures are expected to cool somewhat heading into Friday, when a mix of sun and cloud is forecast along with a high of 17 C.
