stories.title: Biossil raises $153-million in OpenAI-led funding to bring resuscitated drugs to market
stories.summary: Toronto startup uses AI to save once-promising drug candidates from pharmaceutical discard pile
stories.author: Sean Silcoff
stories.content:
OpenAI has led a US$153-million venture capital financing of Biossil Inc., a Toronto startup that uses artificial intelligence to give failed drug candidates a second chance at becoming approved therapies.

The AI giant, best known for ChatGPT, provided the majority of the round through its OpenAI Startup Fund.

This latest financing values Biossil at US$1-billion. OpenAI co-led Biossil’s last venture capital financing a year ago with Silicon Valley billionaire Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, when the Toronto company raised US$43-million.

Founders Fund, which led a previous US$22-million financing of Biossil in 2024, participated in the new deal, alongside existing investors Quiet Capital, Modern Capital, Golden Ventures and Panache Ventures, plus Duke University’s endowment fund and sovereign wealth fund Abu Dhabi Investment Council. Janet Bannister’s Staircase Ventures led Biossil’s $3.7-million seed financing in 2023.

Opinion: AI robots tempt the caregivers of loved ones with dementia to step aside

The latest deal was not announced, but details were shared by a source familiar with the matter. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source as they are not authorized to discuss the information.

Biossil plans to use the financing to expand its capacity for clinical development and selectively buy more drug candidates, the source said. It is an all-equity deal, with a small portion being paid to early employees.

The company also disclosed in an August filing with Corporations Canada that it had created a new class of 5.37 million preferred shares, each valued at US$28.69 – triple the value of shares issued in last year’s financing.

Anthony Mouchantaf, chief executive officer of Biossil, declined to comment.

The funding is happening as OpenAI and rival Anthropic expand beyond offering broadly used AI models to delivering sector-specific tools . One such sector is health care , where some believe AI purveyors could make the strongest case that their technology can benefit humanity by discovering life-saving therapies, countering mounting concerns their algorithms could threaten civilization.

Both AI giants have launched specialized models and programs to help speed up life-sciences research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it had set up a wet laboratory in the San Francisco Bay Area staffed by a life-sciences research group using its Claude AI assistant. It said Claude had already “discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of Crispr,” a genetic modification technology used by medical researchers.

Andrew Coyne: The question isn’t whether we should slow down AI development. It’s whether we still can

Mr. Mouchantaf, a lawyer turned tech entrepreneur who previously headed Royal Bank of Canada’s venture capital investment strategy, co-founded Biossil in 2023 with Alexander Mosa, who had trained to be an internal medicine specialist.

Several companies have designed drug candidates using AI and taken them into trials; none have yet made it to market.

Biossil has taken a different approach. It built a software platform using OpenAI’s large language models to uncover promising molecules from the pharmaceutical discard pile. The Toronto company’s algorithms scavenge through the expanse of drug candidates that failed trials at advanced stages, detecting ways to give them a second chance. For example, some drugs failed because they only worked in certain patients with particular attributes. In some cases, trials were poorly designed or pursued the wrong outcomes.

The founders figured that if they could bring the molecules back into trials in a modified fashion, they could forgo years of studies and hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and advance toward regulatory approval. Their approach quickly won over investors and researchers .

Biossil has bought or licensed 12 molecules, including a July deal where it paid US$500,000 up front for a precision antibiotic from Summit Therapeutics Inc., with more money to follow if the drug clears regulatory and commercial milestones and gets to market. The drug faltered in a late-stage efficacy trial five years ago as a treatment for patients suffering from C. difficile infections.

The Toronto company has partnered with universities and research hospitals in Canada, the United States and Europe, including Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Harvard University and the Mayo Clinic. It recently signed trial collaboration agreements with SickKids, Toronto’s University Health Network and Stanford University’s Skin Innovation and Interventional Research Group.

From doomsday warnings to economic upheaval, one AI expert tries to cut through the noise

Two Biossil molecules target sickle cell disease, a debilitating genetic condition that predominantly affects people of African or Indian descent. Johnson & Johnson JNJ-N and Pfizer Inc. PFE-N each attempted to develop the drugs with biotechnology startups but abandoned those programs after they failed late-stage efficacy trials.

In both cases, Biossil’s AI uncovered reasons to revisit the drug candidates. For example, the J&J drug, called senicapoc, failed to show significant improvement over placebos in relieving pain, the study’s main goal. But the data showed it was better at preventing the breakdown of red blood cells, which would cause anemia and other serious complications.

Biossil is now sponsoring a sickle cell disease trial with J&J’s abandoned molecule, with recruiting under way at SickKids, Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal and McGill University. It’s also launching a trial in Germany using the same molecule to treat glioblastoma, an aggressive cancerous brain tumour, in partnership with Heidelberg University Hospital and the German Cancer Research Center, and a separate trial for the same indication in Denmark with Aarhus University.

The company also disclosed in an August filing with Corporations Canada that it had created a new class of 5.37 million preferred shares, each valued at US$28.69 – triple the value of shares issued in last year’s financing.
Anthony Mouchantaf, chief executive officer of Biossil, declined to comment.

The funding is happening as OpenAI and rival Anthropic expand beyond offering broadly used AI models to delivering sector-specific tools . One such sector is health care , where some believe AI purveyors could make the strongest case that their technology can benefit humanity by discovering life-saving therapies, countering mounting concerns their algorithms could threaten civilization.

Both AI giants have launched specialized models and programs to help speed up life-sciences research. Earlier this month, Anthropic said it had set up a wet laboratory in the San Francisco Bay Area staffed by a life-sciences research group using its Claude AI assistant. It said Claude had already “discovered a novel enzyme system with properties reminiscent of Crispr,” a genetic modification technology used by medical researchers.
Andrew Coyne: The question isn’t whether we should slow down AI development. It’s whether we still can

Mr. Mouchantaf, a lawyer turned tech entrepreneur who previously headed Royal Bank of Canada’s venture capital investment strategy, co-founded Biossil in 2023 with Alexander Mosa, who had trained to be an internal medicine specialist.
Several companies have designed drug candidates using AI and taken them into trials; none have yet made it to market.

Biossil has taken a different approach. It built a software platform using OpenAI’s large language models to uncover promising molecules from the pharmaceutical discard pile. The Toronto company’s algorithms scavenge through the expanse of drug candidates that failed trials at advanced stages, detecting ways to give them a second chance. For example, some drugs failed because they only worked in certain patients with particular attributes. In some cases, trials were poorly designed or pursued the wrong outcomes.

The founders figured that if they could bring the molecules back into trials in a modified fashion, they could forgo years of studies and hundreds of millions of dollars in costs and advance toward regulatory approval. Their approach quickly won over investors and researchers .

Biossil has bought or licensed 12 molecules, including a July deal where it paid US$500,000 up front for a precision antibiotic from Summit Therapeutics Inc., with more money to follow if the drug clears regulatory and commercial milestones and gets to market. The drug faltered in a late-stage efficacy trial five years ago as a treatment for patients suffering from C. difficile infections.

The Toronto company has partnered with universities and research hospitals in Canada, the United States and Europe, including Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children (SickKids), Harvard University and the Mayo Clinic. It recently signed trial collaboration agreements with SickKids, Toronto’s University Health Network and Stanford University’s Skin Innovation and Interventional Research Group.
From doomsday warnings to economic upheaval, one AI expert tries to cut through the noise

Two Biossil molecules target sickle cell disease, a debilitating genetic condition that predominantly affects people of African or Indian descent. Johnson & Johnson JNJ-N and Pfizer Inc. PFE-N each attempted to develop the drugs with biotechnology startups but abandoned those programs after they failed late-stage efficacy trials.

In both cases, Biossil’s AI uncovered reasons to revisit the drug candidates. For example, the J&J drug, called senicapoc, failed to show significant improvement over placebos in relieving pain, the study’s main goal. But the data showed it was better at preventing the breakdown of red blood cells, which would cause anemia and other serious complications.

Biossil is now sponsoring a sickle cell disease trial with J&J’s abandoned molecule, with recruiting under way at SickKids, Centre hospitalier de l’Université de Montréal and McGill University. It’s also launching a trial in Germany using the same molecule to treat glioblastoma, an aggressive cancerous brain tumour, in partnership with Heidelberg University Hospital and the German Cancer Research Center, and a separate trial for the same indication in Denmark with Aarhus University.

stories.title: Popular Night Owls philosophy series builds new nest with first event at U of T
stories.summary: In a Stem-focused postsecondary landscape, evening with celebrity philosopher promotes talking about ideas purely for their own sake
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
In his brief remarks welcoming University of Toronto students to the first Canadian instalment of the after-dark philosophy series “Night Owls,” Randy Boyagoda commended the audience for coming to an event that wouldn’t juice their résumés or help them score a job.

“This is not going to get you into law school,” Prof. Boyagoda, the new director of U of T’s Jackman Humanities Institute, said with a wink. “No one’s going to write you a rec. letter for being here. I will sign no co-curricular transcripts because you are here.

“Why are you here? You are here because you have made the decision to live as if ideas matter.”

For the nearly three hours that followed last Thursday night, about 100 rapt students sat – or stood if they had trickled in late to the packed, fluorescent-lit lecture room – as celebrity philosopher Agnes Callard of the University of Chicago and Joe Heath, a political and economic philosopher at U of T, debated the ethics of capitalism.

The Night Owls event gave students a chance to hear ideas bandied about for their own sake, something that isn’t exactly in vogue in Canada’s job-obsessed postsecondary education sector, where funding is increasingly directed to Stem, trades and professional fields.

The freewheeling discussion roamed from a comparison of co-operative and competitive capitalism, to talk of whether modern dentistry could be seen as a triumph of pricing and markets, to the differences between true socialism and what Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders advocates for. (“That’s just Canada,” Prof. Heath said to laughs.)

“I thought it was great,” Tiara Maleki Yazdi, a first-year student who plans to major in philosophy and English, said over pizza and cans of Bubly sparkling water at the break.

She and her friends still weren’t sure how some of the philosophical concepts Prof. Callard and Prof. Heath tossed around would apply in real life, but said “it was a real privilege to listen to it and get exposed to a new perspective.”

Opinion: Capitalism has always been deeply political

The Ontario government is spending $1.7-billion over four years to fund 70,000 new seats at colleges and universities for programs in Stem, health care, teaching and skilled trades. Forty-thousand of those spaces were allocated only after schools consulted local businesses to make certain their program expansions met labour-market demands, the provincial government announced Sept. 10 .

The following day, Alberta unveiled the next phase of its expanded enrolment plan , adding 8,000 seats at colleges and universities by 2028-29 in nursing, teaching, paramedicine, engineering, technology and trades.

The humanities haven’t benefited from the same government largesse or student demand.

Liberal arts programs are mostly contracting, although the specifics differ by school and discipline. About 70,000 fewer students were enrolled in humanities programs at universities and colleges across Canada in 2023-24 compared with a decade earlier, according to the most recent data from Statistics Canada.

And that was before Ottawa’s curbing of international student visas, which deprived postsecondary institutions of a major funding source. The policy change led some schools to cut or freeze their offerings, notably in the humanities.

Prof. Boyagoda is a novelist, critic and longtime English professor, who in July became director of the Jackman Humanities Institute, which hosted the Night Owls event. He said he is sympathetic to students who want to major in the Stem or professional fields that seem likeliest to land them a job.

“I acknowledge fully the importance of providing students with the practical skills needed to succeed in the professions,” he said. “But at the same time, we shouldn’t mistake universities for technical institutes − for trade schools with better architecture.”

Many undergraduate students pursuing professional degrees are eager to study subjects such as history, art, literature, and – especially – philosophy as second majors, minors or electives at a time when artificial intelligence makes the human mind feel more valuable, he added.

Opinion: What’s university even for? Schools are broke, and degrees are worth less and less

The number of registrations in undergraduate philosophy courses has held steady or ticked up slightly since 2018-19 at U of T’s three campuses, the school’s data show.

“Philosophy is teaching you how to actually think,” said Julia Nefsky, chair of the philosophy department at U of T Scarborough. “So it’s like a power combo with a technical field.”

Prof. Nefsky and her colleagues Daniel Silver, a professor of sociology at U of T Scarborough, and Gurpreet Rattan, chair of philosophy at U of T Mississauga, proposed the Night Owls event to Prof. Boyagoda.

They were inspired by the late-night philosophy rap sessions of the same name that Prof. Callard has emceed at the University of Chicago for nearly a decade.

Topics have ranged from “How do we judge the dead?” and “The ethics of artificial intelligence,” to “Is love worth the pain?” and the “Philosophy of divorce.”

Prof. Callard hosted the latter event with her ex-husband, fellow University of Chicago philosopher Ben Callard. The former couple later philosophized to The New Yorker about living together with Agnes’s new husband.

The University of Chicago, historically a giant of humanities education, stunned postsecondary observers when its Arts and Humanities Division decided to pause admissions to most PhD programs for the 2026-27 academic year to help the indebted school get back on its financial feet.

Opinion: We mustn’t lose sight of Canada’s education reputation on the world stage

Only the philosophy department and one program in music escaped the freeze.

After the Toronto Night Owls event wrapped up around 10:45 p.m., Prof. Callard said in an interview that enrolment in philosophy courses at the University of Chicago has bucked the downward trend of the humanities overall, just like at U of T.

Philosophy endures as a popular second choice for students majoring in hard-edged subjects such as economics, physics and math, she added.

“A lot of the humanities might seem kind of inaccessible or you’re not really sure what their concerns are,” she said. “I think philosophy wears its heart on its sleeve.”

stories.title: Woman convicted of manslaughter in shaken-baby case hopes to clear her name
stories.summary: Jennifer Gaskin’s appeal is the latest in an effort to undo the damage caused by the now widely contested forensic theory of ‘shaken baby syndrome’
stories.author: Molly Hayes
stories.content:
More than 20 years after she was convicted in the death of her baby boy, and more than a decade after the science of “shaken baby syndrome” was called into question, Jennifer Gaskin is hoping to finally clear her name.

The 51-year-old, convicted of manslaughter in 2002, is preparing to appear before the Ontario Court of Appeal. In advance of the Sept. 29 hearing, Ms. Gaskin’s lawyers and the Crown have come together, jointly submitting to the court that her conviction be quashed.

“In light of the overwhelming weight of the current expert opinion, the appellant’s conviction cannot and should not stand,” Crown lawyer Elise Nakelsky said in written arguments, filed in court. “This Court ought to set aside her conviction for manslaughter and enter an acquittal.”

For Ms. Gaskin, who spent 18 months in prison, it is a chance to lift the stigma she has long carried and an opportunity to prove to her surviving children, who were taken from her after Joeseph’s death, that she is innocent.

“For 27 years, my other two children have thought I killed their brother Joeseph,” she said in a statement to The Globe and Mail. “If my appeal goes well, I pray they will realize I did not kill their brother, and accept me as their loving mother.”

The appeal is the latest in a decades-long effort to undo the damage caused by the now widely contested forensic theory of shaken baby syndrome (SBS).

The term was first coined in the early 1970s and became a go-to diagnosis for pathologists probing baby deaths in cases where infants had a combination of brain swelling, retinal bleeding and tissue damage to the brain lining.

But it came under scrutiny in the early 2000s, when some experts began to dispute the validity of the diagnosis and raise concerns that it had led to wrongful convictions.

From the archives: Experts divided over shaken baby syndrome

In Ontario, an inquiry into errors by Charles Smith, a former forensic pathologist at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, uncovered more than a dozen child-death cases that were tainted by flawed analyses, often involving marginalized families, including those involved with child welfare agencies.

A committee was established in 2008 to specifically probe so-called shaken-baby deaths in the province dating back to the 1980s. It reviewed 129 cases, ultimately narrowing in on 13 cases in which people were convicted.

Ms. Gaskin’s case was one of them.

The fresh evidence submitted by Ms. Gaskin’s legal team in her appeal includes the findings of that committee, along with new reports by a forensic neuropathologist, a biomechanical engineer and a forensic pathologist, who concluded that while it would be difficult to rule out an inflicted injury, natural causes could also have been to blame.

They pointed out that much more substantial testing and analysis would be done after a death like this today than was done (or even possible) at the time.

“As of today, the original expert evidence supporting the conviction of the appellant at trial has been wholly undermined and placed in grave doubt,” Ms. Nakelsky summarized in the Crown’s written arguments.

Baby Joeseph Gaskin was nine-and-a-half weeks premature when he was born via cesarean section on April 13, 1999.

He was intubated and ventilated for two days, according to the documents filed by Ms. Gaskin’s counsel, veteran wrongful convictions lawyer James Lockyer. He was kept on oxygen for five days, and was treated for moderate respiratory distress syndrome, hypoglycemia and an elevated white blood cell count usually associated with infection. He was given a 10-day drug regimen to fight bacterial infections.

As he gained weight, the monitoring was scaled back, and he was finally able to go home on June 11.

On June 30, Ms. Gaskin – who was 23 and also had a 13-month-old baby at the time – took Joeseph to the clinic, concerned that he’d been throwing up his formula feedings. According to the defence’s court filings, a nurse looked Joeseph over and said he was “fine as long as he kept peeing and pooping, and his skin didn’t get dried up.”

He’d gained half a pound from five days earlier. He was smiling and appeared healthy and hydrated. She took a swab of his right eye, which was crusty, but otherwise instructed not to overfeed him and to return if the vomiting continued.

The next day was Canada Day, so the clinic was closed. Ms. Gaskin remained concerned about Joeseph, who was still spitting up on and off, according to the defence’s court filings, but took solace in the nurse’s reassurances from the day before.

When a friend visited that evening, Ms. Gaskin told her she was having trouble coping, according to the defence’s court filings. She did not have a large support system in Ignace, Ont., where she was living with her boyfriend, Dale Jones, raising two kids under the age of 2.

After being diagnosed with severe pre-eclampsia during her pregnancy with Joeseph, she had asked the Children’s Aid Society to take care of her older baby on a temporary care arrangement.

A worker with CAS – who assisted the family after both babies came home – also visited on July 1. She said the baby seemed fine, according to the defence’s court filings, but noticed his eyes “had a type of glaze or a haze that wasn’t normal looking.”

Throughout the night and into the next morning, Joeseph continued to spit up, ON and off.

On the morning of July 2, Ms. Gaskin and Mr. Jones took the children to the health unit for their weekly weigh-in. A clerk recalled that the toddler seemed normal, but Joeseph was “cranky” and “pale looking,” according to her court filings.

Afterward, the couple ran into a friend and headed to a local restaurant for lunch.

When he got home and changed Joeseph’s diaper, Mr. Jones noticed the baby turning bright red, according to the defence’s court filings. He tried CPR and then sought help from neighbours before an ambulance was called. By then the baby was grayish-blue, unresponsive and not breathing.

Mr. Jones called her at the restaurant.

Mr. Doyle – who was convicted in 1997 and, like Ms. Gaskin, was represented on appeal by Mr. Lockyer – had maintained that he was dancing with the boy when he accidentally tripped and fell.

In the United States, too, the justice system continues to reckon with the fallout of the shaken-baby debate.

The 51-year-old, convicted of manslaughter in 2002, is preparing to appear before the Ontario Court of Appeal. In advance of the Sept. 29 hearing, Ms. Gaskin’s lawyers and the Crown have come together, jointly submitting to the court that her conviction be quashed.

“In light of the overwhelming weight of the current expert opinion, the appellant’s conviction cannot and should not stand,” Crown lawyer Elise Nakelsky said in written arguments, filed in court. “This Court ought to set aside her conviction for manslaughter and enter an acquittal.”

The term was first coined in the early 1970s and became a go-to diagnosis for pathologists probing baby deaths in cases where infants had a combination of brain swelling, retinal bleeding and tissue damage to the brain lining.

stories.title: City of London to remove non-compliant election signs after 'significant volume of complaints'
stories.summary: City of London to remove non-compliant election signs after 'significant volume of complaints' CBC
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The City of London is cracking down on election signs that violate the rules. As a result, some candidates May see their signs removed in the coming week.
· Posted: Sep 28, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: September 28
Bylaws outline where a candidate May place a sign, as well as size limits, when they can go up and when a candidate needs to remove it after the election.

In a communication sent to candidates, the city said it has received "a significant volume of complaints" about election sign violations, and that municipal compliance staff would conduct a sweep this week.
Some candidates welcomed the announcement.
"As someone who plays by the rules, it's hard to watch other people play without them," said Ward 14 candidate Sarah Lehman. "I'm kind of excited to see what this coming week is going to bring."

Lehman ran in 2022, so her team was familiar with the rules and has made sure to follow them, she said. Candidates are given a "pretty great booklet" at the start of the campaign that explains the rules clearly, she added.
Still, Lehman said she has seen a lot of signs outside the ward boundary that the candidate is running in, which is prohibited.

She has also seen other rules being ignored as well, including placing signs within 100 metres of each other, putting up signs on boulevards, city property, parks and buildings that will be used as polling stations.
"I've seen signs on fire hall properties, hospital property ... so it seems like people maybe have not opened that little booklet that we all received when we signed up to run," she said.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who is seeking re-election as the councillor for Ward 2, said he has seen many violations in his own ward, from signs littering the boulevards to signs posted on polling stations.
He said he's glad to see the city taking action against it, adding, "we all have a responsibility to follow the rules, and they're just not being followed."
Lewis pointed out that sometimes it's just an honest mistake.
His own volunteers had involuntarily broken the rules by placing signs in the wrong place, Lewis said. He clarified the rules to them and moved the signs so they complied with the bylaws, he added.
But when mistakes continue to happen "hundreds of times", it becomes an issue, he said.

"We have to follow all kinds of rules as members of council," he said. "If you're not gonna respect something as basic as where the signs are allowed to be, then I do think it kind of undermines your credibility as a legitimate candidate."

While he said the majority of sign violations he sees around London are from first-time candidates, he also sees experienced candidates with "a number of signs" that don't belong where they have been placed.

Any signs the city removes in its sweep will be taken to the A.J. Tyler Operations Centre on Bathurst Street, according to the memo sent to candidates, where they will be kept for 30 days should any candidates wish to retrieve them.

Lehman ran in 2022, so her team was familiar with the rules and has made sure to follow them, she said. Candidates are given a "pretty great booklet" at the start of the campaign that explains the rules clearly, she added.

Still, Lehman said she has seen a lot of signs outside the ward boundary that the candidate is running in, which is prohibited.

She has also seen other rules being ignored as well, including placing signs within 100 metres of each other, putting up signs on boulevards, city property, parks and buildings that will be used as polling stations.

"I've seen signs on fire hall properties, hospital property ... so it seems like people maybe have not opened that little booklet that we all received when we signed up to run," she said.

Deputy Mayor Shawn Lewis, who is seeking re-election as the councillor for Ward 2, said he has seen many violations in his own ward, from signs littering the boulevards to signs posted on polling stations.

He said he's glad to see the city taking action against it, adding, "we all have a responsibility to follow the rules, and they're just not being followed."

Lewis pointed out that sometimes it's just an honest mistake.

His own volunteers had involuntarily broken the rules by placing signs in the wrong place, Lewis said. He clarified the rules to them and moved the signs so they complied with the bylaws, he added.

But when mistakes continue to happen "hundreds of times", it becomes an issue, he said.

"We have to follow all kinds of rules as members of council," he said. "If you're not gonna respect something as basic as where the signs are allowed to be, then I do think it kind of undermines your credibility as a legitimate candidate."

While he said the majority of sign violations he sees around London are from first-time candidates, he also sees experienced candidates with "a number of signs" that don't belong where they have been placed.

Any signs the city removes in its sweep will be taken to the A.J. Tyler Operations Centre on Bathurst Street, according to the memo sent to candidates, where they will be kept for 30 days should any candidates wish to retrieve them.

stories.title: Anand hosting conference today on returning Ukrainian children from Russian abduction
stories.summary: Toronto — Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand is co-hosting a global meeting in Toronto today aimed at advancing work to return Ukrainian children abducted by Russian officials.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
TORONTO — Ukrainians who survived Russian captivity are thanking Canada for its advocacy and for funding programs to help children heal from trauma.

Dariia Tomashova, 18, told a Toronto conference Monday that she escaped Crimea four months ago, after a year of trying to flee the Ukrainian region Russia seized in 2014.

“Children were turned into Russians, into zombies,” she said through an interpreter.

Any mentions of Crimea being part of Ukraine were stripped from classroom instruction, as was any mention of the Soviet repression of the island’s Indigenous Peoples, Tomashova said. Children were made to write letters of support to Russian troops.

“We didn’t understand at that time that we were being prepared for a real war, that all of these events — when girls from being 10 years old, learning tactical medical support, boys being taught how to handle weapons — we were being trained to be Russian soldiers,” she said, pausing to hold back tears.

Tomashova was addressing a two-day conference aimed at advancing work to return Ukrainian children from captivity in Russia and the Ukrainian territories it occupies.

In 2024, the Trudeau government co-launched with Ukraine an international coalition of nations committed to finding and returning Ukrainian children abducted by Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine in 2014 and launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.

Ukrainian authorities cite what they say are more than 20,651 records of possible unlawful deportations or forcible transfers of Ukrainian children to Russia or Russian-occupied territories of eastern Ukraine.

Officials in Ukraine say 2,573 of those children have been returned.

Bring Kids Back, a coalition launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has reported that abducted children returned to Ukraine have reported being subjected to physical and sexual violence.

One of the coalition members, Save Ukraine, has used Canadian funds to support Ukrainians who have been sexually abused while held by the Russian state or in foster homes.

“Their rescue only begins when they’re coming back from (the) Russian trap, because with that trauma they have, we have to provide constant 24-7 support for months, sometimes for years,” Save Ukraine co-founder Mykola Kuleba said in an interview.

“We are so grateful for Canada leading and supporting our rescue missions,” he said.

Kuleba called for more pressure and sanctions on Russia, saying this would lead to more children being returned home.

On Monday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand announced $863,000 in new funding for civil society groups in Ukraine that help returned children and families. That sum brings Canada’s total funding for those efforts to $7 million.

Anand said Canada has used artificial intelligence technology to trace the whereabouts of Ukrainian children and prisoners of war. She noted that Russian officials have changed children’s names, making it harder to verify who is in an “indoctrination camp.”

“This is not an accident, this is not a side-effect of war. This is a systematic effort to separate Ukrainian children from Ukraine,” she said at a news conference.

“They must stop obstructing their return, provide information about where these children are (and) stop altering their identities.”

Ukraine’s allies have expanded their reunification efforts to include adult civilians and prisoners of war taken from parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.

Margaryta Shabanova described her husband being taken by Russian officials in 2022 during his work with an independent monitoring mission in the occupied region of Luhansk.

She said she only learned he was alive when video surfaced of her emaciated husband facing espionage charges for his work with the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe, a group of which both Canada and Russia are members.

“Thinking too much about this — where he is, and what he may be enduring there — is something you learn to manage. Not because the fear goes away, but because you cannot function, if you let it consume (you) entirely,” Shabanova said.

Tomashova and Shabanova were among four Ukrainians describing their experiences at this week’s conference. Dozens of countries sent representatives to the conference, including all G7 countries, most European states and other nations such as Qatar and Honduras.

But the flags of several major G20 countries were absent, including those of Brazil, China, India, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia. Global Affairs Canada did not immediately respond when asked for a list of conference attendees.

Anand said complex diplomacy has been required to get children out of Russia and the occupied Ukrainian territories. She said India’s direct talks with Russia have helped inform Canada’s work on understanding various Russian actions in the war.

“I have had numerous discussions with foreign ministers around the world about what more we can do to engage indirectly, and in some cases directly, with Russia,” she said.

“We’re very much relying on a full set of countries to assist with this process.”

This week’s talks are taking place in Toronto, where the CN Tower was set to project the blue and yellow colours of the Ukrainian flag Monday evening.

Since March 2023, Russian President Vladimir Putin and a senior Russian official have been subject to International Criminal Court arrest warrants on charges of unlawful deportation and transfer of children.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 28, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. election campaigns enter second week with candidate, policy announcements
stories.summary: Vancouver - The campaigns for the upcoming British Columbia election enter their second week, with major parties gearing up policy announcements and candidate nominations.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VICTORIA - Resource development and making British Columbia an “energy superpower” to grow the economy would allow for a new provincial government to pay down the record deficit, both the NDP and Conservative party leaders said on the campaign trail Monday.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson promised to double liquefied natural gas production by 2032, if elected, while NDP Leader David Eby announced his government would double the export of critical minerals within five years.

Doerkson said there’s a global energy crisis and “our allies in Asia and Europe desperately need Canadian LNG.”

While Eby picked up on the same theme, saying B.C. has an abundance of critical minerals that other countries need.

“Getting them to world markets means less dependence on the U.S., while creating family-supporting jobs and the prosperity needed to strengthen health care and public services,” said Eby, who was in Prince Rupert on Monday.

He also said an NDP government would expand the Prince Rupert port to be the second-largest facility of its kind in Canada by 2030.

Eby said that unlike the B.C. Liberals, Doerkson’s former party, the B.C. New Democrats delivered on LNG.

“There are five LNG facilities reaching final investment decision or under construction right now in the province of B.C.,” Eby said.

Doerkson said if the New Democrats would have been interested in LNG six or seven years ago, the province would be in a different situation.

“It’s shocking to me that (NDP) interest in LNG has shown up 20 days before an election,” Doerkson said. “We need to get going on this right now.”

When questioned about the $13.8-billion deficit that Eby’s NDP government accumulated while in power, both party leaders said their plans to grow the economy would help trim the shortfall.

British Columbians demand that the deficit be reduced, Doerkson said at an event in Vancouver.

“We can’t be dealing with a $14-billion deficit in British Columbia,” he said. “How do we manage anything, knowing that we are faced with these deficits year after year?”

Doerkson did not offer details about how a future Conservative government would balance the budget.

“The reality is that we’re not sure how bad the books are,” he said.

The interim leader, who replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay about a week ago following her resignation, pointed to an accounting error by the provincial government admitted to this year that overstated forecast revenues from natural gas by nearly $1.5 billion.

“It’s going to be almost impossible to commit to how quickly we will be able to arrive at balanced budgets,” he said. “But the reality is, we have to get back to that.”

Doerkson’s promised on Sunday that his government would not raise existing taxes or introduce new ones.

Eby said the promise of a tax freeze shows the Conservatives are not transparent about their plans.

“The math doesn’t work for the Conservatives,” he said. “It’s very clear that their agenda, when you do the math, is to dramatically cut health care and education.”

Eby pointed to comments from Conservative candidate Tony Luck, who is running for re-election in Fraser-Nicola.

Luck said in February 2024 that if education and health care are the two biggest budget items, then they will take “the brunt” of cuts.

Eby said there is no difference between the major parties when it comes fiscal sustainability.

The real question is how to get there, he said.

“We’ve got to end wasteful spending,” he said. “We’ve got to grow the economy with announcements like today’s.”

David Williams, vice-president of economics with the Business Council of B.C., said provincial spending has been out of control since 2021.

“Your fiscal situation is not the result of Donald Trump or external pressures or anything like that,” Williams said. “This is because of domestic policy choices around the rate of spending growth.”

Whoever forms government needs to get that spending under control, he said.

Bryan Yu, chief economist with Central 1 Credit Union, said there are many questions around how to boost the B.C. economy, which hasn’t grown much this year.

“It’s been a little bit troubling in terms … of business investment or business growth, like the number of business counts are very flat when it comes to Alberta and some of our other peer provinces,” he said.

B.C.’s public sector is quite large relative to the population and could be adjusted, Yu said.

“We really need to find a way to get more jobs, more private sector investment in the economy.”

Both leaders were also asked about a gathering of alleged white nationalists on a B.C. First Nation reserve on Sunday, just days away from National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk’emlups te Secwepemc nation, said a group of masked people dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops on Sunday questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.

Eby called the display “disgusting,” while Doerkson denounced the group.

In Victoria on Monday, Green Leader Emily Lowan said her party would lift the freeze on the NDP government’s $10-a-day childcare spaces, with a goal to achieve universal free children care space by 2031.

“Lack of access, lack of qualified educators, and unaffordable fees send a clear message to young people and families: the government is not investing in you,” Lowan said in a statement.

The current childcare model in B.C. is expensive and complicated, and it’s been exacerbated by the former NDP government’s funding pause in the last provincial budget, Lowan said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 28, 2026.

— With files from Nono Shen in Vancouver

When questioned about the $13.8-billion deficit that Eby’s NDP government accumulated while in power, both party leaders said their plans to grow the economy would help trim the shortfall.
British Columbians demand that the deficit be reduced, Doerkson said at an event in Vancouver.
“We can’t be dealing with a $14-billion deficit in British Columbia,” he said. “How do we manage anything, knowing that we are faced with these deficits year after year?”
Doerkson did not offer details about how a future Conservative government would balance the budget.
“The reality is that we’re not sure how bad the books are,” he said.

The interim leader, who replaced Kerry-Lynne Findlay about a week ago following her resignation, pointed to an accounting error by the provincial government admitted to this year that overstated forecast revenues from natural gas by nearly $1.5 billion.
“It’s going to be almost impossible to commit to how quickly we will be able to arrive at balanced budgets,” he said. “But the reality is, we have to get back to that.”
Doerkson’s promised on Sunday that his government would not raise existing taxes or introduce new ones.
Eby said the promise of a tax freeze shows the Conservatives are not transparent about their plans.
“The math doesn’t work for the Conservatives,” he said. “It’s very clear that their agenda, when you do the math, is to dramatically cut health care and education.”
Eby pointed to comments from Conservative candidate Tony Luck, who is running for re-election in Fraser-Nicola.
Luck said in February 2024 that if education and health care are the two biggest budget items, then they will take “the brunt” of cuts.
Eby said there is no difference between the major parties when it comes fiscal sustainability.
The real question is how to get there, he said.
“We’ve got to end wasteful spending,” he said. “We’ve got to grow the economy with announcements like today’s.”
David Williams, vice-president of economics with the Business Council of B.C., said provincial spending has been out of control since 2021.
“Your fiscal situation is not the result of Donald Trump or external pressures or anything like that,” Williams said. “This is because of domestic policy choices around the rate of spending growth.”
Whoever forms government needs to get that spending under control, he said.
Bryan Yu, chief economist with Central 1 Credit Union, said there are many questions around how to boost the B.C. economy, which hasn’t grown much this year.

“It’s been a little bit troubling in terms … of business investment or business growth, like the number of business counts are very flat when it comes to Alberta and some of our other peer provinces,” he said.
B.C.’s public sector is quite large relative to the population and could be adjusted, Yu said.
“We really need to find a way to get more jobs, more private sector investment in the economy.”
Both leaders were also asked about a gathering of alleged white nationalists on a B.C. First Nation reserve on Sunday, just days away from National Truth and Reconciliation Day.

Roseanne Casimir, chief of Tk’emlups te Secwepemc nation, said a group of masked people dropped a banner from an overpass in Kamloops on Sunday questioning reports of human burials at the former sites of residential schools.
Eby called the display “disgusting,” while Doerkson denounced the group.

In Victoria on Monday, Green Leader Emily Lowan said her party would lift the freeze on the NDP government’s $10-a-day childcare spaces, with a goal to achieve universal free children care space by 2031.
“Lack of access, lack of qualified educators, and unaffordable fees send a clear message to young people and families: the government is not investing in you,” Lowan said in a statement.
The current childcare model in B.C. is expensive and complicated, and it’s been exacerbated by the former NDP government’s funding pause in the last provincial budget, Lowan said.

stories.title: Alberta, Ontario premiers set to share stage in Calgary to talk energy policy
stories.summary: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are set to share the stage in Calgary today to talk energy.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
CALGARY — Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Ontario Premier Doug Ford are set to share the stage in Calgary today to talk energy.

The leaders will be in the city’s downtown to talk about how to best get Canada’s natural resources to market in a world of fluctuating politics and conflicts.

Smith has placed energy at the centre of her government’s agenda, particularly the need to get more oil to the British Columbia coast and from there to markets in Asia.

It also comes as Canada navigates an ongoing tariff war with the United States.

Smith has rejected using oil as leverage in the tariff battle with U.S. President Donald Trump.

Ford, however, has publicly stated he does not agree oil should be off the table, but says both he and Smith agree more oil needs to flow within Canada.

stories.title: Finding the right path: How the Grace Clinic helps older adults make informed decisions about surgery
stories.summary: September 28, 2026When Stuart Powers learned he would need to consider major surgery as part of his cancer treatment, he and his wife, Sharon, were faced with a difficult decision.
stories.content:
Dr. Rachel Kyle, Geriatrician at St. Joseph’s Health Care London and Dr. Brad Moffat, Surgeon at London Health Sciences Centre partnered to create the Geriatric Risk Assessment for Care Enhancement (Grace) Clinic to better support older adults as they make decisions about surgery Photo credit: St. Joseph’s Health Care London

September 28, 2026

When Stuart Powers learned he would need to consider major surgery as part of his cancer treatment, he and his wife, Sharon, were faced with a difficult decision.

The procedure could be life-changing, but so could the recovery.

Instead of navigating that decision alone, Stuart was referred to the Geriatric Risk Assessment for Care Enhancement (Grace) Clinic, a clinic partnership between London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) and St. Joseph's Health Care London (St. Joseph’s) that brings specialists together to optimize general health and function of patients prior to surgery and help patients make informed decisions to ensure the highest quality of life afterwards.

Older adults referred for surgery at LHSC are screened for frailty as part of their surgical assessment. For patients who May benefit from additional evaluation, surgeons can refer them to the Grace Clinic, where a collaborative team from the General Surgery and Geriatric Medicine divisions at LHSC and St. Joseph’s work with patients and care partners to consider the whole person, including factors that are often overlooked; such as functional status and personal priorities.

Together, the team discusses individualized surgical risks within the context of aging and frailty, helping patients decide whether surgery ultimately becomes part of their care plan.

During a single visit to the Grace clinic Stuart met with a team of specialists from both organizations to discuss every aspect of his health, treatment options and goals. Together, they explored if surgery is possible, and whether it was the right choice for him.

For Stuart, that collaborative approach made all the difference.

"I was treated extremely well by every doctor," says Stuart. "They really took their time with me, we chatted for three hours. They explained what surgery would involve, how long recovery would take, and all of my options."

For Sharon Powers, Stuart’s wife of 58 years, what stood out most wasn't just the expertise in the room but how the team approached one of the biggest decisions they had ever faced.

"They never told us what our decision should be," she says. "They just gave us all the information in a very kind and supportive way, then left it up to Stu."

The experience was unlike anything they had encountered before.

"The support was incredible," Sharon says. "They looked at everything from every angle. They even took me aside so I could share how I was feeling. We never felt rushed and we never felt pressured."

That patient-centred approach is at the heart of the Grace Clinic.

"We are focused on delivering whole person care,” says Dr. Rachel Kyle, Geriatrician at St. Joseph’s. “We help patients understand their surgical options and support them as they decide what approach best aligns with their personal health goals. In the cases where patients want to move forward with surgery, we create an individualized pre-surgical care plan to help optimize their overall health, which can include access to a range of services such as rehabilitation, nutrition support, medication review and discharge planning.”

After discussing the risks and benefits, Stuart decided that radiation, not surgery, was the best path forward.

Today, Stuart continues to enjoy spending summers up north at their cottage, where he can continue doing what he loves; fishing.

"It clears everything out of my mind, " he says,

For Sharon, that's why the experience at the Grace Clinic was so meaningful.

"He's still able to enjoy life," she says. "They helped us make the decision that was right for him."

For members of the Grace Clinic care team from St. Joseph’s and LHSC, the partnership has been deeply rewarding.

"We are truly wrapping care around some of our most vulnerable patients,” says Dr. Brad Moffat, Surgeon at LHSC. “We have a surgeon and a geriatrician from both organizations in the room when we meet with the patient, which allows us to deliver coordinated care that can address all questions and concerns within a single visit. It is incredibly unique to have a model that brings together expertise from across organizations in service to our patients, and we are proud of the support we’ve provided to date."

For Stuart, that collaborative approach made all the difference.

"I was treated extremely well by every doctor," says Stuart. "They really took their time with me, we chatted for three hours. They explained what surgery would involve, how long recovery would take, and all of my options."
For Sharon Powers, Stuart’s wife of 58 years, what stood out most wasn't just the expertise in the room but how the team approached one of the biggest decisions they had ever faced.
"They never told us what our decision should be," she says. "They just gave us all the information in a very kind and supportive way, then left it up to Stu."
The experience was unlike anything they had encountered before.
"The support was incredible," Sharon says. "They looked at everything from every angle. They even took me aside so I could share how I was feeling. We never felt rushed and we never felt pressured."
That patient-centred approach is at the heart of the Grace Clinic.

"We are focused on delivering whole person care,” says Dr. Rachel Kyle, Geriatrician at St. Joseph’s. “We help patients understand their surgical options and support them as they decide what approach best aligns with their personal health goals. In the cases where patients want to move forward with surgery, we create an individualized pre-surgical care plan to help optimize their overall health, which can include access to a range of services such as rehabilitation, nutrition support, medication review and discharge planning.”
After discussing the risks and benefits, Stuart decided that radiation, not surgery, was the best path forward.
Today, Stuart continues to enjoy spending summers up north at their cottage, where he can continue doing what he loves; fishing.
"It clears everything out of my mind, " he says,
For Sharon, that's why the experience at the Grace Clinic was so meaningful.
"He's still able to enjoy life," she says. "They helped us make the decision that was right for him."
For members of the Grace Clinic care team from St. Joseph’s and LHSC, the partnership has been deeply rewarding.

"We are truly wrapping care around some of our most vulnerable patients,” says Dr. Brad Moffat, Surgeon at LHSC. “We have a surgeon and a geriatrician from both organizations in the room when we meet with the patient, which allows us to deliver coordinated care that can address all questions and concerns within a single visit. It is incredibly unique to have a model that brings together expertise from across organizations in service to our patients, and we are proud of the support we’ve provided to date."

stories.title: Poilievre pushes for diesel plan as fuel prices soar
stories.summary: Conservative Leader called for removal of all taxes on the ‘vital fuel’ until at least Canada Day
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Canada faces a diesel-price emergency and must be energy independent, Pierre Poilievre said Sunday, while calling for a cut to federal taxes on the fuel in order to boost domestic production to a million barrels a day in the next five years.

Speaking at a gas station in suburban Ottawa, the Conservative Leader made a policy announcement calling for the removal of all taxes on the “vital fuel” until at least Canada Day. He proposed doing so by extending the excise-tax cut and removing the GST from the fuel purchase.

Currently, the federal government charges 5 per cent GST on diesel, which amounts to about 13 cents a litre. A federal excise tax, which usually amounts to about 4 cents per litre, is currently suspended by Ottawa until the end of next January.

Mr. Poilievre’s Sunday fuel proposal was made amid global turbulence that includes the wars in the Mideast and in Ukraine, has placed enormous pressure on the world’s energy supplies, spurring soaring diesel prices.

The Conservative Leader said that while there are global factors, it does not explain why Canada is paying about 32 cents more per litre than the U.S. for diesel.

Robyn Urback: Pierre Poilievre should oppose the government – but he can support it, too

Canada produces most of the diesel used in Canada, with refining capacity spread out across more than a dozen refineries.

In 2024, Statistics Canada reported a record production level of about 718,000 barrels per day. Industry experts say, depending on the year, that about 10 to 20 per cent of diesel is imported from outside the country.

Mr. Poilievre wants to see the price gap between Canada and the U.S. eliminated within a five-year period by increasing domestic production of diesel and other refined fuels.

“The goal is to immediately reduce prices through lower taxes, and within five years break our dependence on American diesel to ensure that every single Canadian has access to Canadian-made diesel,” he said.

South of the border, skyrocketing diesel prices are being debated ahead of the November U.S. midterms.

Republicans in key states such as Michigan and Iowa have urged an end to exporting diesel from refineries in America. U.S. President Donald Trump signalled that he supports the idea, but his energy secretary recently indicated a “blanket ban” will not happen.

Diesel prices hit record highs as wars squeeze global supplies

Diesel prices have hit a historic high in Canada. At the same time, the country uses more than 80 million litres of it per day, according to the Canadian Fuels Association.

Data show that the average cost of the fuel here is approximately $2.74 a litre, representing an 80-per-cent increase since last fall.

Diesel is typically used to power large transportation vehicles, buses, freight and passenger trains, cargo ships, as well as equipment for agriculture and construction.

Additionally, Natural Resources Canada says that nearly three quarters of the country’s 280 remote communities rely on diesel generators to produce their electricity. It also says that fossil fuels for heat and power contribute to local health and environmental issues.

The federal government previously set a goal of eliminating diesel-powered electricity generation in remote communities by 2030.

When asked Sunday if he sees Canada transitioning away from diesel in the future, Mr. Poilievre said he does not want to phase out Canadian oil and gas.

“I want to produce more of it and at a lower price,” he said.

Poilievre dismisses Bill C-39 as all talk, no action at outset of Commons debate

Mr. Poilievre said there is “no question that the use of Canadian energy, including Canadian oil and gas, has made the world a better place,” while he emphasized that the focus must be on its affordability.

His plan also calls for additional measures, such as granting pre-permits for areas that could be used as diesel refineries, transportation, as well as storage so companies can build as long as they follow safety and environmental rules.

As well, he sees the need to break down interprovincial trade barriers as central to helping to reduce diesel prices.

“Transportation regulations across the provinces and territories present a key obstacle to moving fuel across the country,” Mr. Poilievre said.

“I think that we should have national trucking regulations that are signed on to by all provinces to simplify the movement of those goods.”

In June, the Mark Carney government signed a memorandum of understanding on interprovincial trucking.

At the time, the Canadian Trucking Alliance said it was a “significant step toward reducing regulatory barriers and improving the efficient movement of goods across Canada.”

With a report from the Associated Press

stories.title: Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc chief says ‘white nationalist’ group protested on reserve
stories.summary: Chief Rosanne Casimir said they have had discussions with the RCMP, saying the Mounties have also provided them with recent updates.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The chief of the Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc First Nations says a group of masked individuals she believes are white nationalists held a demonstration on the reserve.

Video surfaced online Sunday showing several individuals wearing black clothing and hats with white material covering their entire face.

Kukpi7 Rosanne Casimir told Global News in an interview Sunday it was a “complete surprise” when the individuals showed up.

“Community members as well as our security had observed them, they documented and they got a hold of the police, they informed leadership,” she said. “Of course, many community members have seen them through social media at various locations and are very concerned.”

Casimir said with Sept. 30, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, approaching, it may have prompted this group’s appearance.

She said the photos she saw were believed to be individuals belonging to the Second Sons of Canada. Global News has not independently confirmed the identities of the individuals or if they are associated with any group.

“It is actually very disturbing,” she said. “Basically, potentially, this is like a hate crime, this is disturbing especially coming just before the National Day (for) Truth and Reconciliation, also known as Orange Shirt Day. For them, they have a lot of fear because this group, there was I don’t know, 20 to 30 of them, and they were wearing masks, they were wearing hats, they were carrying I think flags as well.”

She told Global News people are upset and had the right to be upset because it’s taking away from the meaning of the day.

The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation first began as Orange Shirt Day in 2013 in Williams Lake, B.C. It was established to honour residential school survivors, their families, and those who never returned home.

The group was asked to leave by security, with Casimir saying RCMP also arrived after being contacted to “back up” security.

Casimir said they have had discussions with the RCMP, saying the Mounties have also provided them with recent updates.

“The presence of individuals associated with hate, intimidation and extremist ideology on or near our ancestral lands is deeply concerning to our community and to our leadership,” she said.

Premier David Eby condemned the protest in a post on X, saying the province stands with Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc.

“White nationalists gathering on Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc land to intimidate people is disgusting, dangerous and cowardly – as they hide their faces,” Eby said.

Interim BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson also condemned the protest on X.

“The white nationalist gathering on Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc land this morning was hateful and meant to intimidate. It has no place in British Columbia,” Doerkson said.

Global News has contacted Kamloops RCMP for more information, but did not receive a response by publication.

The National Day for Truth and Reconciliation first began as Orange Shirt Day in 2013 in Williams Lake, B.C. It was established to honour residential school survivors, their families, and those who never returned home.
The group was asked to leave by security, with Casimir saying RCMP also arrived after being contacted to “back up” security.
Casimir said they have had discussions with the RCMP, saying the Mounties have also provided them with recent updates.
“The presence of individuals associated with hate, intimidation and extremist ideology on or near our ancestral lands is deeply concerning to our community and to our leadership,” she said.
Premier David Eby condemned the protest in a post on X, saying the province stands with Tkʼemlúps te Secwépemc.
“White nationalists gathering on Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc land to intimidate people is disgusting, dangerous and cowardly – as they hide their faces,” Eby said.
Interim BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson also condemned the protest on X.
“The white nationalist gathering on Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc land this morning was hateful and meant to intimidate. It has no place in British Columbia,” Doerkson said.
Global News has contacted Kamloops RCMP for more information, but did not receive a response by publication.

stories.title: Doerkson could lead party for years without leadership vote, B.C. Conservatives say
stories.summary: Province’s NDP says voters would have no guarantee who would serve as premier if Conservatives win coming election
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservatives say interim leader Lorne Doerkson could remain at the helm of the party for years without a leadership vote, pushing back against B.C. NDP warnings that voters would have no guarantee who would serve as premier if that party formed government after the Oct. 24 provincial election.

A legal opinion obtained by the Conservative Party of B.C. and provided to The Globe and Mail outlined a path by which Mr. Doerkson could remain interim leader for years without running afoul of party rules that prohibit an interim leader from stepping into the role permanently.

“In our opinion, in the event that the Conservative Party of B.C. wins the election, Lorne Doerkson would be invited by the Lieutenant-Governor to serve as Premier,” said Bruce Hallsor, lawyer for the party, in a Sept. 25 letter to party president Mauro Francis.

“He would also remain leader of the party until the board chooses to call a leadership election, which could be more than 18 months down the road or longer. During that time, there would be no mechanism for a membership review of his leadership, and the party constitution makes calling a leadership election a matter for the board’s discretion.”

Mr. Doerkson was appointed interim leader on Sept. 20 after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay . On Sept. 23, the Conservatives’ board of directors said it would make Mr. Doerkson permanent leader if the party forms government.

Lorne Doerkson takes the reins of B.C. Conservatives, with a party to rebuild and election ahead

However, the party’s constitution states that an interim leader cannot run for leadership once an election is called. The board said it would “pursue the appropriate means under the party’s constitution and bylaws and the Societies Act” to amend the rules, which would require a two-thirds vote from party members.

On Friday, NDP candidate Niki Sharma questioned the Conservatives’ ability to deliver on that promise.

“That’s the same membership that voted in Kerry-Lynn Findley,” said Ms. Sharma, the province’s attorney-general. “And what that means to me is that they can’t guarantee who their leader will be in the long run.”

In his legal opinion, Mr. Hallsor confirmed that the party’s constitution prohibits an interim leader from running for leadership, and that a special leadership election must be called within 12 months of a leader’s resignation. However, he said the latter provision is “open to some interpretation.”

“A plain reading would suggest that the party must ‘call’ the leadership election by Sept. 20, 2027, but the vote can be six months later, or extended past that date indefinitely,” Mr. Hallsor said. “By this interpretation, the ‘interim’ leader could remain the leader for another 18 months or ultimately, much longer.”

Such a move would leave plenty of time for the party to amend its constitution, Mr. Hallsor said.

Gary Mason: David Eby’s snap election call is cynical and self-serving

Elections BC said a political party is responsible for establishing its own processes to select a leader and that B.C.’s Election Act does not establish any rules that would prevent an interim party leader from running in a leadership contest or becoming premier.

“Since 1995, when the current Election Act was enacted, a political party must identify a leader to meet the legislated registration requirements; however, the selection process is at the discretion of the party,” Elections BC said in a statement to The Globe on Sunday.

“Since then, B.C. Conservative Party is the first major political party to run a provincial general election campaign under an interim leader.”

Asked by The Globe about Ms. Sharma’s comments, Mr. Doerkson said his leadership “is not up for conversation” and that Mr. Hallsor had outlined some options. He also cited an article in the Ndp’s own constitution that requires a secret ballot vote at every convention on whether to call a leadership election, turning the question back on NDP Leader David Eby.

“So I guess my question is: Is there any ability for Niki Sharma or David Eby to assure us that David Eby is going to get the support from the NDP at the next convention?” Mr. Doerkson said Sunday.

“The reality is, I think his members are concerned with everything that we’re seeing today.”

Andrew Coyne: The fix B.C. is in: An election without a reason, an opposition without a leader

Mr. Doerkson was speaking in Surrey at a campaign event during which he pledged that a Conservative government would freeze taxes across the board, and not introduce new taxes, as long as he is premier.

“There’s no exceptions to that,” he said. “There are no gimmicks to that. There’s no accounting tricks.”

He did not directly answer reporters’ questions about how the Conservatives would deal with B.C.’s $13.8-billion deficit , or respond to a sudden economic downturn, without new or increased taxes.

“Economic downturns are very serious,” he said. “Obviously, we work in a world market. But frankly, the thing that I’m worried about most in this current market is the damage that the NDP is doing to our industry.”

The NDP said in a statement that the Conservatives’ plan would require “either new revenues and/or deep cuts to services.”

Mr. Eby took his campaign to Prince Rupert on Sunday, while B.C. Green Leader Emily Lowan canvassed in Saanich North and the Islands, where she is seeking election.

stories.title: Authorities investigating Quebec helicopter crash that killed four Saturday
stories.summary: Three members of a Quebec family celebrating a birthday, as well as the pilot, lost their lives in the crash
stories.author: Jill Mahoney
stories.content:
Federal aviation safety experts are investigating a helicopter crash in a rural area southeast of Montreal on Saturday that killed all four people on board.

The fiery crash claimed the lives of three members of a Quebec family celebrating a birthday, and also killed the pilot, according to social-media posts.

“On September 26, part of my world flew away into the sky,” Océane Perreault wrote on Facebook. “A helicopter ride that was supposed to mark my wonderful mom’s birthday turned into a tragedy I could never have imagined.”

Ms. Perreault said the crash – which she witnessed – killed her mother, Chantal Raymond; her partner, Gabriel Jasmin; and her brother, Loucas Perreault. Mr. Jasmin was a host at radio station Énergie Sherbrooke. He and Ms. Perreault have a young daughter.

“I have no words to describe the pain, the shock and the emptiness I feel. Three people I love more than anything have left far too soon, right before my eyes,” Ms. Perreault wrote.

Martin Perreault, her father, wrote on Facebook that his wife, Chantal, was his “better half for almost 40 years.” He called his son Loucas “my pride, my successor,” and said Mr. Jasmin was a loving father who “had taken such a big place in our family.”

Four dead in helicopter crash near Montreal

Pilot Suzanne Jutras was also killed in the crash, according to a Facebook post by a local branch of an agricultural union that said her partner has a farm in the area. The helicopter went down in a field in Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, about 50 kilometres from Montreal.

“Our thoughts are with you in these moments of great sorrow,” said the post by the board of directors of the Haut-Richelieu region of L’Union des producteurs agricoles.

Ms. Jutras was also remembered on social media by the Félixeries, a festival that took place earlier this month in Saint-Félix-de-Kingsey, Que. The festival called Ms. Jutras, who provided helicopter tours for the event, its “favourite pilot.”

“We salute you. … Thank you for sending us soaring through the air with your kindness.”

Ms. Jutras became a helicopter pilot in 2020, according to her LinkedIn profile.

The helicopter crashed after experiencing unknown difficulty around 2:30 p.m. on Saturday, said Nancy Fournier, a spokesperson for the Sûreté du Québec, the provincial police force. The bodies of four people were found in the charred wreckage, she said.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada sent two investigators to the crash site to “assess the occurrence and gather information,” TSB spokesman Nic Defalco said in an e-mail.

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon offered condolences to those affected by the tragedy and said his department would appoint a minister’s observer to monitor the investigation.

“The safety of civil aviation operations is Transport Canada’s highest priority,” he said in a social-media post. “The department will continue to closely monitor the situation on the ground and stands ready to provide support and work with all relevant parties as the situation develops.”

stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
Les Lang knew building a custom house in today’s market would be more of a labour of love than an equity-building proposition.

Custom houses are a luxury that most people cannot afford, especially with high construction costs and a real estate market that’s in a downturn. The initial outlay May take years to recover, if ever.

Mr. Lang and wife, Sherri Acres, who moved from Calgary to build their home on 2.8 acres in Chilliwack, B.C., had to think hard about spending a premium to build over buying a spec house in a subdivision.

“If you’re buying a new build in a subdivision, then that’s a different story,” said Mr. Lang, a former consultant in the mining industry. “But if you’re going custom, you have to forget about that. And that was really where we kind of stalled in our planning process. Because we were looking at what it was projected to cost versus what we could get off the market for that same amount. But then when you got looking at it, you couldn’t have this and you couldn’t have that. And so, the lure of being able to build something custom exactly the way that we wanted drew us back in.

“But it was with eyes wide open that we knew this wasn’t all about the cheapest way to build.”

The couple moved into their home this past spring after waiting less than a year for completion, while living out of Mr. Lang’s parents’ Chilliwack basement suite. Their 2,100-square-foot home is a simple, linear Norwegian dogtrot design, two separate structures connected by the same roof and a covered outdoor breezeway at the midpoint.

The sustainable design is open concept and minimal, situated on Chilliwack Mountain with Hillkeep Regional Park to the rear.

They had purchased the vacant lot in 2016 and waited until 2023 to get started on the planning and design. It was the first house for the couple, who’d downsized from their homes in Calgary. While living in a basement suite, living out of suitcases, they realized that they didn’t need as much stuff as they originally thought, so their vision became more streamlined and considered. They focused less on square footage and more on design and finishings.

“We were looking at what thought we wanted to build, but it became clear that we couldn’t afford it,” said Mr. Lang. “We felt that we could live happier in a simpler home that was more jewel-box-like with nicer features rather than trying to invest the same dollars in square footage. Also, we were thinking forward about aging in place, with curbless showers, no stairs, things like that.”

The cost to build was around $1.9-million, said Mr. Lang, but including soft costs such as planning and design, the budget came in closer to $2.3-million. He paid an additional $300,000 for the lot.

“It’s not the biggest house or the most expensive house or any of that, but it’s one of the most unique homes I’ve ever built,” said builder Chris Klaassen, co-owner of Alair Homes.

Adding a green roof covered in six inches of soil and sedums meant beefing up the structural load by about 50 per cent, he said. Green roofs, which are becoming more common on residential buildings, offer insulation for heating and cooling, and works as a fire retardant. Mr. Klaassen said the design also added to the cost because it was three separate structures, including a 1,650-square-foot main living area, a 450-square-foot studio connected under the same roof, and a detached three-car garage. The design features natural wood inside and out, solid wood beams, extensive glazing, integrated lighting and a high-performance envelope. Finishings include copper wall panels, plaster walls and a steam shower.

“I would not call it an economical build by any stretch, and that’s because it has three distinct structures. There’s a high percentage of exterior wall surface, things like that relative to the square footage, including a fully detached garage,” Mr. Klaassen said. “So instead of everything being under one roof, it’s under three connected roofs. And the quality of finishing inside is very high end. So, there was lots of lots of detail in there that increase the cost.”

As for the market for custom homes, he said the market is healthy compared to the spec home industry, in which houses are prebuilt in subdivisions and designed for mass market tastes. As a result, he’s seeing more competition from spec builders who are moving into the custom house space.

“What I call market housing or spec housing is definitely really slow right now,” said Mr. Klaassen, whose company builds houses in the Fraser Valley and throughout Metro Vancouver.

“There are a combination of factors, but I would argue probably it’s largely affordability. The higher end renovation and even custom home space, which is not market housing, it’s a totally different demographic and the market is still relatively strong.”

He said his clients tend to be “high net worth individuals” who aren’t impacted by a sluggish economy.

“They’re a little more cautious for sure than they were, but some of them are still going ahead and spending money and getting that dream home they’ve always wanted.

“A lot of my clients have luxury cars, and I say, ‘Okay, so you go out and buy a car for $300,000. Is it three times better than the Honda? Probably not. But it’s pretty cool, and it puts a smile on your face every time you get into the driver’s seat. You buy it because you can, and it’s kind of the same thing with the houses we build.’ They’re bespoke, and it’s more of an emotional thing. There’s an investment component for sure – nobody wants to be foolish with their money. But it’s also like, ‘well if it takes me five to 10 years for this to be a really good investment, I’m okay with that trade-off.’”
