“Canada, including the Yukon, would be negatively affected if Alberta were to leave.”

While they May not be saying so now, one constitutional law expert said Smith’s office is correct in saying there could be enough support from other provincial governments to take two of the proposals beyond the ballot — having provinces pick provincial judges and opting out of federal programs without financial punishment.
“It’s extra provincial power. Why wouldn’t they want it?” said Gerard Kennedy, a constitutional law professor at the University of Alberta.
“To me, the big problem is going to be getting the federal Parliament to agree, because the federal government would have to be agreeing to reduce its own power for nothing in return.”

Smith, Moe, Ontario Premier Doug Ford and former Quebec premier François Legault penned a letter to Ottawa in March asking that all provincial Appeal Court and Superior Court judges be appointed from a pre-approved list submitted by the provinces.

Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser quickly shut the issue down, saying Ottawa wasn’t considering changes to the judicial appointment process. He pointed to the advisory committees set up across the country that review and advise on judicial applications to say that provinces already have input, since each government appoints some of the committee’s members.
Kennedy said the proposal about giving provincial laws paramountcy over federal laws probably won’t go anywhere, adding that there was no federation in the world with that setup.
He said regardless of the support that May exist, Alberta could be opening a can of worms if it makes serious efforts at working with other provinces.

“The problem if you open up constitutional negotiations is that some other provinces are going to have their pet projects and they’ll say, ‘well, we won’t agree to amend the Constitution on terms favorable to Alberta unless they’re also amended on terms that are favorable to New Brunswick or Quebec,'” he said.
“And then you end up having a package and too many provinces won’t like some part of the package and then it doesn’t get through.”
He said there’s a third way Alberta could try to amend the Constitution.

Some changes can be made with only the support of Parliament and the province that is being affected by the amendment. An example was in 2001, when the Constitution was amended to change the name of Newfoundland to Newfoundland and Labrador.

Alberta could try to go that route, Kennedy said, but the effort would likely end up in court, as granting the province special privileges others don’t have would go against the presumption that all provinces are treated equally.

Despite the premier and her office hinting that they’re committed to lobbying other provinces should the four proposals get majority approval on Oct. 19, some doubt Smith is willing to put in the effort.

Smith framed her referendum questions as presenting Albertans with a plan to better the province’s standing within Confederation so that voters don’t resort to separatism. She’s also blamed federal immigration policy for Alberta’s overburdened health and education systems.
Calgary-based political scientist Duane Bratt said the constitutional questions feel like an afterthought for the referendum.

Bratt said he’d feel differently if the questions were a bigger part of the premier’s messaging or the government’s $4-million ad campaign, which he said are far more focused on Smith’s five immigration proposals that are also on the ballot.
“She’s not really talking about the Constitutional questions,” Bratt said in an interview, pointing to recent speeches the premier has made.
“It’s immigrants who are the scapegoats and the villains here.”

Bratt, a professor at Mount Royal University, said the lack of attention Smith has given the constitutional proposals, combined with the amount of work needed to actually move the issues forward, means he doesn’t think she will act after Oct. 19.
“Where is their energy? Is their energy (on) building pipelines, restructuring the health-care system, or constitutional change? Because I don’t think they could do all of that.”
Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said this week that he thinks Smith is only trying to find new enemies to blame for Alberta getting a raw deal.
“She doesn’t want to get those things,” Nenshi told reporters Tuesday about the Constitution reforms.
“She wants to complain about not getting those things.
“She wants the other provinces to say no.”

content_blocks.text: Smith’s four proposals, three of which would likely require the support of seven legislatures representing over half of Canada’s population (known as the 7/50 rule) and Parliament to implement, are among 10 questions she’s putting to Albertans on Oct. 19.

Her ideas, in brief, are: to abolish the Senate; let Alberta, not Ottawa, pick provincial King’s Bench and Court of Appeal judges; allow Alberta to opt out of federal programs without losing the associated funding; and to give provincial laws standing over Ottawa’s when jurisdictional disputes occur.

Smith’s government concedes on its referendum website that abolishing the Senate, which would require unanimous cross-country support and the support of the Senate itself, is going to be a non-starter for other political leaders.

But the premier’s office says there’s support for the other proposals and that “targeted” amendments to Canada’s legal and administrative spine are more likely to become reality, which is why it wants a mandate from Albertans to proceed.
“Provinces across the country are tired of federal overreach and want more authority within Confederation, not less,” said Ryan Fournier, a communications adviser to Smith.
“We believe this conversation is a vital step towards a fairer Confederation.”
The Canadian Press reached out to premiers across the country to ask whether they supported Smith’s proposals, but many did not respond to repeated requests.
Some, such as Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe’s office, said they wouldn’t be commenting, and those who did respond didn’t answer directly.
“This is a matter for Albertans to consider through their referendum process,” said a spokesperson for Northwest Territories Premier R.J. Simpson.

stories.title: Corrections Canada to distribute items for 'safe snorting' in federal prisons
stories.summary: Corrections service says it also addresses the "introduction, trafficking, financing, and distribution of unauthorized substances."
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
The Correctional Service of Canada has confirmed that paper straws will soon be distributed in federal prisons to facilitate safe snorting of drugs.

This week a social media post included photos of a memo distributed to Corrections staff stating that paper straws were being newly “introduced” for “safer snorting” and “intended for inhaling substances in powdered form or inhaling vapour from heated substances.”

The explanation provided was that paper straws will “reduce harm” by lessening the risk of internal nose cuts that could occur from homemade or plastic straws and reduce infections from diseases such as hepatitis B and C, while “recognizing that overdose and toxicity risk remain.”

Meanwhile, according to the memo, foil strips are to be distributed “for safer smoking.” So were drug-testing strips for fentanyl, benzodiazepine and xylazine.

The memo states that these items are being introduced “in response to increased inhalation, smoking and snorting substances among federal inmates” adding that “harm reduction must adapt to reduce overdose risks, prevent the transmission of infectious diseases and align with current evidence-based practices.”

The new harm reduction items if found on their own, should not result in criminal charges, but the memo states that if they are “found alongside illicit substances or unauthorized paraphernalia, standard operational procedures … must be followed.”

In a statement emailed to National Post by Correctional Service Canada communications officer Laurence Côté, the CSC confirmed that the document shown in the social media post is genuine and “was developed … to provide information to all employees regarding the expansion of harm reduction products.”

The CSC stated that its health services include “harm reduction measures” designed to prevent and minimize “harms related to substance use.”

Judge sends Hamilton fentanyl dealer to prison despite 'immigration consequences'

The 'King' sent to U.S. prison for 20 years for running cocaine and meth smuggling into Canada

It says its National Drugs and Substances Strategy recognizes substance use as a health issue, and therefore approved harm reduction supplies are not considered contraband.

However, the counterbalance to provide these “safe snorting” items seems to be that the CSC says it “maintains robust measures” to address “introduction, trafficking, financing, and distribution of unauthorized substances … within its institutions, and holds those involved accountable.”

Finally, the CSC stated that harm reduction interventions “are widely recognized as cost-effective because they help prevent the transmission of infectious diseases such as HIV and Hepatitis C, reducing the need for significantly more expensive medical treatment and long-term health care costs associated with these conditions.”

Training for Health Services staff responsible for distributing the supplies to inmates is set to begin on Oct, 1, ahead of planned implementation on Oct. 13. At that time, says the CSC, “Health Services staff will provide education and guidance to support informed and appropriate use of these supplies.”

stories.title: One of Chile’s leading winemakers starts a new chapter in the Okanagan
stories.summary: Emily Faulconer embraces new role as technical director overseeing the Mark Anthony group’s Okanagan wineries
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Winemaker Emily Faulconer, who has produced some of Chile’s most iconic red wines, including Seña and Viñedo Chadwick, has embraced a new role as technical director overseeing the Mark Anthony group’s Okanagan wineries. Since starting in June, the 20-year veteran has worked with the winemaking and viticulturalist teams responsible for the company’s seven wineries, which include Mission Hill, Checkmate and Martin’s Lane, to map out plans.

Prior to her first visit to British Columbia’s largest wine region in February, Faulconer says she knew little about the Okanagan, but was quickly impressed by its potential. “The region is so beautiful,” she says. “It attracts a lot of tourists, and a lot of the wine is consumed here. That’s one of the reasons why the Okanagan isn’t well-known outside of this country. If you don’t come here, you won’t know about it.” Faulconer told The Globe and Mail what brought her to the Okanagan and how she is approaching her new role in Canada.

What is your approach to your first grape harvest in the Okanagan?

I think one has to be humble working as a winemaker. I am spending a lot of time in vineyards and with the winemakers to understand what can be done. I have a lot of ideas in my head that I am still validating. When it comes to viticulture and winemaking, I don’t believe in low intervention. Everything we do is intervention. The human factor, the decision making that leads to the final wine, is so important.

How has the recent wildfire in Summerland affected the harvest?

This is a challenging region. With the cold and the smoke, there isn’t much room for mistakes. Since the wildfire, it has rained and the smoke has cleared. Checkmate has picked most of its chardonnay grapes. We are optimistic about the white wines. We’re tasting the fermentations and don’t detect any smoke issues. This region has experienced smoke during harvest before. Few regions know better than this one how to manage that.

What attracted you to the Okanagan wine scene?

When I think of the types of wines that people are looking for today, there’s a huge opportunity here. I can see a balance between high acidity and good fruit ripeness that many consumers are looking for in wine. I am generally very, very interested in what the Okanagan can deliver. This should be a region that everyone is talking about. It’s very exciting. The Okanagan already has very nice wines, but I think there’s the opportunity now to put them on a global stage.

How can you help each in the Von Mandl Family Estates portfolio develop a distinct identity?

I always like to think that you’ve never made your best bottle of wine. There’s that challenge every year of how you fine-tune to get that precision, to achieve the best version of those vineyard sites in the glass. These winemakers are not aspiring to be Bordeaux, the Mosel or Burgundy, they aspire to be best version of the Okanagan. We might look to those historic regions for references, but this is a unique place. The wines, the grapes and the vineyards need to speak for themselves.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

I have a lot of ideas in my head that I am still validating. When it comes to viticulture and winemaking, I don’t believe in low intervention. Everything we do is intervention. The human factor, the decision making that leads to the final wine, is so important.
How has the recent wildfire in Summerland affected the harvest?

This is a challenging region. With the cold and the smoke, there isn’t much room for mistakes. Since the wildfire, it has rained and the smoke has cleared. content_blocks.text: What attracted you to the Okanagan wine scene?

When I think of the types of wines that people are looking for today, there’s a huge opportunity here. I can see a balance between high acidity and good fruit ripeness that many consumers are looking for in wine. I am generally very, very interested in what the Okanagan can deliver. This should be a region that everyone is talking about. It’s very exciting. The Okanagan already has very nice wines, but I think there’s the opportunity now to put them on a global stage.
How can you help each in the Von Mandl Family Estates portfolio develop a distinct identity?

I always like to think that you’ve never made your best bottle of wine. stories.title: 24 Sussex Drive is getting renovated. Some think the National Capital Commission should be overhauled too
stories.summary: As he makes his way north through Ottawa's Strathcona Park, Peter Meggs walks along a multi-use pathway run by a federal crown corporation.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — As he makes his way north through Ottawa’s Strathcona Park, Peter Meggs walks across the Adawe Crossing Bridge, veering away from the connecting path that leads to a parking lot.

Both the connecting path and the pedestrian bridge are municipal jurisdiction. The bridge overlooks the Rideau River, which is provincial responsibility, although the Rideau River Conservation Authority is the river’s watershed agency, which means it manages things such as environmental and flood monitoring.

After crossing the 125-metre bridge, Meggs then hangs a right and joins a smattering of cyclists, dog walkers and step counters for the home stretch along the multi-use pathway of his regular, 5-kilometre loop around his Overbrook neighbourhood. That means he’s now on property run by the National Capital Commission (NCC), the under-the-radar federal body whose mission, according to the organization’s web site, is to help the national capital region be “a dynamic and inspiring source of pride for all Canadians, and a legacy for generations to come.”

Before being turned into a park 119 years ago, Strathcona Park was a swampy floodplain overrun by mud and swarms of mosquitoes. But as Meggs’ brief trek across the bridge suggests, the 15-acre park May now be overrun by swarms of government.

The difference in this regard between the national capital region and other Canadian cities is the NCC. The commission’s critics have for years been asking why the national capital region needs – or perhaps deserves – an extra layer of government and extra source of taxpayer dollars than other Canadian communities.

Those questions have re-emerged in recent months because the Ncc’s profile has jumped over its management of the prime minister’s official residence, uninhabited for more than a decade but now on a path to repair. Some NCC critics are also asking if it’s not time that the commission undergo its own renovation.

The NCC, unlike municipalities, is run by unelected officials who are not directly accountable to the public – and, according to critics, seem fine with it that way.

“You have to accept the good and bad of democracy,” said Meggs, a former town councillor in Cornwall, P.E.I.

But Franco Terrazzano, federal director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, said the NCC needs greater scrutiny and accountability, in part because it spends and wastes a lot of taxpayers’ money. For example, he said, the crown corporation spent $140,000 to study and design – not build – a staircase, and $1 million for a barn at Rideau Hall, the governor general’s official residence.

“It must be the most incompetent agency in all of Canada — which is saying a lot.”

With the Carney government presumably looking for more cuts in the bureaucracy to help pay for big spending hikes in defence, infrastructure and other priorities, could the NCC be a target for this fall’s upcoming budget?

John Fragos, a spokesman for Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne, said it’s too early in the budget process to speak to any possible cutbacks.

Don Drummond, a former senior official at the Department of Finance and chief economist at TD Bank, said most of the discussions over the years about the NCC have been about democratic reform and transparency, not getting rid of it. For example, Drummond said, folding the NCC into a federal department that May have more experience writing cheques than running programs might be tempting but also might be a bad idea.

Supporters say the NCC, created through a House of Commons vote in 1959, is important because it helps make the National Capital Region – Ottawa and the city of Gatineau, Que. on the other side of the Ottawa River — a special region that all Canadians can be proud of. It brings a national perspective, they argue, to issues that would normally be local.

Results have included a protected Greenbelt on the outskirts of Ottawa, federal parklands and parkways including the popular Gatineau Park, and a wide range of recreational sites, such as cross-country ski trails, walkways, the Rideau Canal skating rink, and public swimming spots along local lakes and rivers — all considered attributes by local residents, and some visitors.

Supporters, such as former Ottawa city councillor Clive Doucet, say the NCC has made an excellent contribution towards presenting the national capital region as the country’s heart, not just another city, in a way that local governments likely wouldn’t.

“It’s been a great success in beautifying Ottawa.”

NCC defenders point out that Canada is by no means the only country that assigns a special government body to giving its capital extra care.

There’s no perfect comparison internationally, but India, France, Australia and Brazil are among those countries that have a federal body with a mandate similar to the NCC. In the U.S., the National Capital Planning Commission (Ncpc) serves as the federal government’s planning agency for Washington, D.C.

But in other ways, the District of Columbia is far from over-governed – or as governed as Canadians in the national capital area.

Unlike Ottawa-Gatineau, D.C. residents are less represented than those in any other part of the U.S. While the city of Washington has a mayor and council, the District is part of no state, which means that it has no governor or state legislature. It also means that D.C. also has just one non-voting representative in the U.S. House of Representatives and no representation in the influential U.S. Senate.

Doucet isn’t wrong that the Ncc’s job is to make the national capital region an enjoyable and attractive place to live or visit. In other words, the commission has goals that are often in line with most municipalities, even if the structures, and method of funding, are very different.

As a federal body, one key discrepancy is of course its source of money. The NCC, unlike municipalities, gets its funding from the federal government, which means taxpayers from across the country, not just those in Ottawa and Gatineau.

According to its annual report, the NCC received $164.3-million from Parliament in 2025, a 57 per cent increase from the previous year. While much of the Ncc’s annual budget is a function of the capital projects that it’s asked to manage during any given year, its operating budget has also been on the rise, a pace well above inflation.

By contrast, the crown corporation is now a larger organization by budget than the municipal governments in cities such as Maple Ridge, B.C., North Bay, Ont. and Moose Jaw, Sask.

Despite its low profile nationally, the NCC is a large organization by other metrics too.

According to its web site, the organization has 419 employees, although that figure doesn’t seem to have been updated since 2017.

And those pathways along the river at Strathcona Park are only a tiny fraction of the Ncc’s territory. It manages about 116,000 acres of land in the National Capital Region, about 11 per cent of the region’s land. That’s about eight times the size of Manhattan, more than double the size of Washington, D.C., and much larger than all of Vancouver.

The crown corporation, which reports directly to Parliament through Public Works Minister Joel Lightbound, is also responsible for management of 1,664 properties, including Rideau Hall (the governor general’s residence), Stornoway (the opposition leader’s residence), The Farm (the Speaker’s residence), 7 Rideau Gate (the government’s official guest house), and the prime minister’s two official residences: Harrington Lake, the prime minister’s cottage, and 24 Sussex, the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence.

With 24 Sussex Dr. uninhabited for more than a decade, there have also been fresh accusations that the NCC doesn’t do a good enough job of maintaining its properties.

The prime minister’s official residence has been vacant, in part, because of complaints about heating and cooling, asbestos, mould, and even rodents. The absence of a decision about what to do with the famous residence does not fall on the NCC, however, as the long-term pause can be traced back to the prime minister’s office.

Detractors have also pointed out that the organization makes important planning decisions about the national capital region, yet its board members are appointed, not elected. And related to that, the most frequent criticism of the NCC is likely that it lacks the transparency expected of other levels of government.

In 2023, when the Office of the Information Commissioner of Canada ruled that the NCC had improperly withheld information in response to an Atip request, it bolstered that case.

Neither NCC chief executive Tobi Nussbaum, nor a spokesperson, was available for interview.

Earlier this year, when asked for an interview about plans for the prime ministers’ official residence, an NCC spokesperson told National Post that that subject is one that the Crown corporation normally would only discuss after its board meetings. They’re held four times a year.

But are there not other models that would allow the capital region to get some extra care, without adding a layer of government that seems less transparent and accountable than our norm?

Jerald Sabin, a public policy specialist at Carleton University in Ottawa, called the NCC a “band-aid solution” designed to fix the fact that the Canadian constitution didn’t create a capital region structure.

In 1867, as the Canadian constitution was being drafted, Sabin said, there were more important issues that how to carve out special attention for the new country’s capital region. “They had bigger fish to fry.”

Beyond the cost to taxpayers, extra layers of government can also have other unintended consequences. During the 2022 truckers’ convoy protest in downtown Ottawa, for example, Ottawa police were tasked with enforcement, including on NCC property.

There have been no reports of a turf war at that time between the two organizations — the NCC has conservation officers, but no police force — but that doesn’t mean there wasn’t jurisdictional confusion, and more layers of communication required than otherwise would have been the case.

Andrew Sancton, a retired professor from Western University in London, Ont. who specializes in local government, said it’s “reasonable” to want a presentable national capital region for both foreign and domestic visitors.

He said he’s not sure why the NCC isn’t expected to be as open as municipal governments, but that getting rid of it would likely lead to a legal battle over which levels of government would inherit its land.

For the NCC, 24 Sussex represents perhaps its highest profile, and most politically sensitive, project in decades, even though the Carney government has limited the organization’s role in the process.

In April, the Auditor General of Canada reported that the Ncc’s systems and practices showed a “significant deficiency” in its handling of employee safety, and, among other things, that improvements were needed in its managing of assets and capital projects. While those findings likely didn’t help the Ncc’s case to play a bigger role in the 24 Sussex renovation project, Auditor General Karen Hogan also found there were “no significant deficiencies” elsewhere in the Ncc’s systems and operations.

Two months later, Carney announced a competition for the redesign and rebuild of the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence. That competition, which largely ends more than a decade of debate about where Canada’s prime ministers will live, will be led and largely judged by The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada — not the NCC. The institute, which has experience supporting architectural competitions, will review proposals and then make a recommendation to cabinet by July 1 of next year.

The residence, which sits on a 2.1-hectare property overlooking the Ottawa River, has been out of commission since the end of former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government years. The 35-room, 12,000-square-foot residence has suffered over the years from a range of problems. Both Carney and former prime minister Justin Trudeau have lived across the road at Rideau Cottage, ON the governor general’s grounds.

When he announced the competition in June, Carney also said the government will try to reduce the costs of the project by using a non-partisan charity, the Rideau Hall Foundation, to lead a national fundraising campaign to raise as much money as possible.

As of July 27, the fundraising effort, which has a $50-million cap, has received $735,000 in donations from 3,336 Canadians.

Despite being asked to play a limited role in the 24 Sussex reno, there’s little indication that the federal government is considering changing the Ncc’s role or reducing its budget.

Most Ottawa-Gatineau residents, living in a region where the federal government forms the economic base, are less concerned about jurisdictional divisions, and just happy to take advantage of the Ncc’s recreational sites, and other services.

Vino Bhindi, who grew up near Strathcona Park and crosses the pedestrian bridge to get to the Rideau Sports Club, also on NCC land, said the region seems to have a lot of government levels, but that never gets in the way of his tennis matches.

“I don’t feel the politics.”

content_blocks.text: Supporters say the NCC, created through a House of Commons vote in 1959, is important because it helps make the National Capital Region – Ottawa and the city of Gatineau, Que. on the other side of the Ottawa River — a special region that all Canadians can be proud of. It brings a national perspective, they argue, to issues that would normally be local.

Results have included a protected Greenbelt on the outskirts of Ottawa, federal parklands and parkways including the popular Gatineau Park, and a wide range of recreational sites, such as cross-country ski trails, walkways, the Rideau Canal skating rink, and public swimming spots along local lakes and rivers — all considered attributes by local residents, and some visitors.

Supporters, such as former Ottawa city councillor Clive Doucet, say the NCC has made an excellent contribution towards presenting the national capital region as the country’s heart, not just another city, in a way that local governments likely wouldn’t.
“It’s been a great success in beautifying Ottawa.”
NCC defenders point out that Canada is by no means the only country that assigns a special government body to giving its capital extra care.

content_blocks.alt: Park next to a river.
content_blocks.caption: Strathcona Park in Ottawa. Photo by Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia

content_blocks.alt: Park next to a river.
content_blocks.caption: Strathcona Park in Ottawa. Photo by Hyungcheol Park/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: There’s no perfect comparison internationally, but India, France, Australia and Brazil are among those countries that have a federal body with a mandate similar to the NCC. In the U.S., the National Capital Planning Commission (Ncpc) serves as the federal government’s planning agency for Washington, D.C.
But in other ways, the District of Columbia is far from over-governed – or as governed as Canadians in the national capital area.

Unlike Ottawa-Gatineau, D.C. residents are less represented than those in any other part of the U.S. While the city of Washington has a mayor and council, the District is part of no state, which means that it has no governor or state legislature. It also means that D.C. also has just one non-voting representative in the U.S. House of Representatives and no representation in the influential U.S. Senate.

Doucet isn’t wrong that the Ncc’s job is to make the national capital region an enjoyable and attractive place to live or visit. In other words, the commission has goals that are often in line with most municipalities, even if the structures, and method of funding, are very different.
content_blocks.html: Doucet isn’t wrong that the NCC’s job is to make the national capital region an enjoyable and attractive place to live or visit. In other words, the commission has goals that are often in line with most municipalities, even if the structures, and method of funding, are very different.

content_blocks.text: As a federal body, one key discrepancy is of course its source of money. The NCC, unlike municipalities, gets its funding from the federal government, which means taxpayers from across the country, not just those in Ottawa and Gatineau.

According to its annual report, the NCC received $164.3-million from Parliament in 2025, a 57 per cent increase from the previous year. While much of the Ncc’s annual budget is a function of the capital projects that it’s asked to manage during any given year, its operating budget has also been on the rise, a pace well above inflation.
content_blocks.html: According to its annual report, the NCC received $164.3-million from Parliament in 2025, a 57 per cent increase from the previous year. While much of the NCC’s annual budget is a function of the capital projects that it’s asked to manage during any given year, its operating budget has also been on the rise, a pace well above inflation.

content_blocks.text: By contrast, the crown corporation is now a larger organization by budget than the municipal governments in cities such as Maple Ridge, B.C., North Bay, Ont. and Moose Jaw, Sask.
Despite its low profile nationally, the NCC is a large organization by other metrics too.
According to its web site, the organization has 419 employees, although that figure doesn’t seem to have been updated since 2017.

And those pathways along the river at Strathcona Park are only a tiny fraction of the Ncc’s territory. It manages about 116,000 acres of land in the National Capital Region, about 11 per cent of the region’s land. That’s about eight times the size of Manhattan, more than double the size of Washington, D.C., and much larger than all of Vancouver.

The crown corporation, which reports directly to Parliament through Public Works Minister Joel Lightbound, is also responsible for management of 1,664 properties, including Rideau Hall (the governor general’s residence), Stornoway (the opposition leader’s residence), The Farm (the Speaker’s residence), 7 Rideau Gate (the government’s official guest house), and the prime minister’s two official residences: Harrington Lake, the prime minister’s cottage, and 24 Sussex, the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence.
With 24 Sussex Dr. uninhabited for more than a decade, there have also been fresh accusations that the NCC doesn’t do a good enough job of maintaining its properties.

The prime minister’s official residence has been vacant, in part, because of complaints about heating and cooling, asbestos, mould, and even rodents. The absence of a decision about what to do with the famous residence does not fall on the NCC, however, as the long-term pause can be traced back to the prime minister’s office.
content_blocks.html: The prime minister’s official residence has been vacant, in part, because of complaints about heating and cooling, asbestos, mould, and even rodents. The absence of a decision about what to do with the famous residence does not fall on the NCC, however, as the long-term pause can be traced back to the prime minister’s office.

content_blocks.text: Detractors have also pointed out that the organization makes important planning decisions about the national capital region, yet its board members are appointed, not elected. And related to that, the most frequent criticism of the NCC is likely that it lacks the transparency expected of other levels of government.

content_blocks.alt: Parliament Hill and Rideau Canal.
content_blocks.caption: A view of Parliament Hill and Rideau Canal. The National Capital Commission manages about 116,000 acres of land in the National Capital Region — about eight times the size of Manhattan. Photo by Ashley Fraser/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: In 2023, when the Office of the Information Commissioner of Canada ruled that the NCC had improperly withheld information in response to an Atip request, it bolstered that case.
Neither NCC chief executive Tobi Nussbaum, nor a spokesperson, was available for interview.

Earlier this year, when asked for an interview about plans for the prime ministers’ official residence, an NCC spokesperson told National Post that that subject is one that the Crown corporation normally would only discuss after its board meetings. They’re held four times a year.
But are there not other models that would allow the capital region to get some extra care, without adding a layer of government that seems less transparent and accountable than our norm?
content_blocks.html: But are there not other models that would allow the capital region to get some extra care, without adding a layer of government that seems less transparent and accountable than our norm?

content_blocks.text: Jerald Sabin, a public policy specialist at Carleton University in Ottawa, called the NCC a “band-aid solution” designed to fix the fact that the Canadian constitution didn’t create a capital region structure.

In 1867, as the Canadian constitution was being drafted, Sabin said, there were more important issues that how to carve out special attention for the new country’s capital region. “They had bigger fish to fry.”

Beyond the cost to taxpayers, extra layers of government can also have other unintended consequences. During the 2022 truckers’ convoy protest in downtown Ottawa, for example, Ottawa police were tasked with enforcement, including on NCC property.

There have been no reports of a turf war at that time between the two organizations — the NCC has conservation officers, but no police force — but that doesn’t mean there wasn’t jurisdictional confusion, and more layers of communication required than otherwise would have been the case.

Andrew Sancton, a retired professor from Western University in London, Ont. who specializes in local government, said it’s “reasonable” to want a presentable national capital region for both foreign and domestic visitors.

He said he’s not sure why the NCC isn’t expected to be as open as municipal governments, but that getting rid of it would likely lead to a legal battle over which levels of government would inherit its land.

For the NCC, 24 Sussex represents perhaps its highest profile, and most politically sensitive, project in decades, even though the Carney government has limited the organization’s role in the process.

In April, the Auditor General of Canada reported that the Ncc’s systems and practices showed a “significant deficiency” in its handling of employee safety, and, among other things, that improvements were needed in its managing of assets and capital projects. While those findings likely didn’t help the Ncc’s case to play a bigger role in the 24 Sussex renovation project, Auditor General Karen Hogan also found there were “no significant deficiencies” elsewhere in the Ncc’s systems and operations.

Two months later, Carney announced a competition for the redesign and rebuild of the prime minister’s dilapidated official residence. That competition, which largely ends more than a decade of debate about where Canada’s prime ministers will live, will be led and largely judged by The Royal Architectural Institute of Canada — not the NCC. The institute, which has experience supporting architectural competitions, will review proposals and then make a recommendation to cabinet by July 1 of next year.

content_blocks.alt: Mark Carney and Robert Prichard.
content_blocks.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney, with board chair of the Rideau Hall Foundation Robert Prichard, leaves a news conference at 24 Sussex Drive in Ottawa on June 25, 2026. Photo by Blair Gable/Postmedia

content_blocks.text: The residence, which sits on a 2.1-hectare property overlooking the Ottawa River, has been out of commission since the end of former prime minister Stephen Harper’s government years. The 35-room, 12,000-square-foot residence has suffered over the years from a range of problems. Both Carney and former prime minister Justin Trudeau have lived across the road at Rideau Cottage, ON the governor general’s grounds.

When he announced the competition in June, Carney also said the government will try to reduce the costs of the project by using a non-partisan charity, the Rideau Hall Foundation, to lead a national fundraising campaign to raise as much money as possible.
As of July 27, the fundraising effort, which has a $50-million cap, has received $735,000 in donations from 3,336 Canadians.
Despite being asked to play a limited role in the 24 Sussex reno, there’s little indication that the federal government is considering changing the Ncc’s role or reducing its budget.

Most Ottawa-Gatineau residents, living in a region where the federal government forms the economic base, are less concerned about jurisdictional divisions, and just happy to take advantage of the Ncc’s recreational sites, and other services.

Vino Bhindi, who grew up near Strathcona Park and crosses the pedestrian bridge to get to the Rideau Sports Club, also on NCC land, said the region seems to have a lot of government levels, but that never gets in the way of his tennis matches.

stories.title: Will the ferry between Nova Scotia and Maine be discontinued?
stories.summary: There is still no contract for 'The Cat' – the Yarmouth-based ferry that runs between Nova Scotia and Bar Harbor, Maine – to operate next year.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Yarmouth, N.S. – As the busy summer-fall tourism season winds down, there is still no contract for “The Cat” – the Yarmouth-based ferry that runs between Nova Scotia and Bar Harbor, Maine – to operate next year.

“I think it’s important that there are real signals to operators and the tourism industry at large, that the government, our province and the officials will have a deal in place,” said Yarmouth and Acadian Shores Tourism Association CEO Neil MacKenzie. “People who are booking travel need to know that the service will be here and they can plan their vacation ahead of time.”

The final crossing for the ferry will be Oct. 14. This year, through July, Mackenzie said ferry ridership is up nearly 30 per cent, compared to 2025.

The vessel is run by Bay Ferries Ltd., which is headquartered in Charlottetown and operates the ferry service through a contract with the U.S. Navy.

CTV News also reached out to the U.S. Navy, but they were unable to provide a response at this time.

Nova Scotia’s Public Works Minister Fred Tilley recently told reporters he is hopeful that a new long-term ferry contract could soon be signed, but did not offer any details related to the negotiations.

Sixteen years ago, Dalhousie University business professor Lorn Sheehan served on a panel that examined the Yarmouth ferry strategy.

“It was really a broad engagement of stakeholders around the economic realities of having that ferry,” said Sheehan, who speculated the trade tensions between Canada and the U.S. could be possibly slowing down contract negotiations.

“I think part of the reason that the delay is occurring, is because of the uncertainty in the trade environment,” said Sheehan. “Economically on balance, I think this ferry makes sense.”

According to the town’s mayor, the ferry is a job creator for Yarmouth.

“You’re talking about an entire season of folks going to the gas station, going to the restaurants, shopping in the shops,” said Yarmouth Mayor Pam Mood.

For those examining the overall financial viability of the ferry, Sheehan urged people to look at the economic impact for the entire province, not just Yarmouth and the surrounding area.

“It’s obviously important to Yarmouth, but it is also spread out throughout the whole province,” said Sheehan. “When Americans come across, it’s rare that they come to Yarmouth, and go back to Maine. They will go to the wine region in Nova Scotia, Halifax or visit Cape Breton and all these communities enjoy benefit from the ferry.”

MacKenzie said a new contract needs to be signed soon, or the province could lose a lot of tourism business in 2027.

“We know that visitors stay and travel around the province, we know that they are here on average seven or eight days, and we know they are spending more than $3,000 per party,” said MacKenzie.

There have been previous interruptions in the ferry crossings between Nova Scotia and Maine. The province cancelled its subsidy to Bay Ferries in 2009, which halted service until 2014. The ferry was also idle during the COVID-19 pandemic because of international travel restrictions.

stories.title: The Stunt Driver is the latest film from London-born filmmaker Michael Dowse
stories.summary: The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian" and his rivalry with Evel Knievel.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian" and his rivalry with Evel Knievel.
· Posted: Sep 27, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
The Toronto International Film Festival (Tiff) has wrapped up, and for those who missed out, some of those films are making their way to theatre screens across southwestern Ontario.
Among them is The Stunt Driver. It's the latest film from London, Ont.,-born filmmaker Michael Dowse, who is known for his work on Fubar and The F Word.

The Stunt Driver tells the true story of daredevil Ken Carter, also known as "The Mad Canadian," and his rivalry with Evel Knievel. In 1976, Carter set out to make a mile-long jump across the St. Lawrence River in a rocket-powered Lincoln Continental.

Afternoon Drive 6:59 The Stunt Drive: The Ken Carter Story

The Stunt Drive is a film telling the true story of The Mad Canadian, Ken Carter. Director Michael Dowse joins Afternoon Drive to share how he told the incredible daredevil story as it hits movie screens.
JL: What was it about Ken Carter's story that intrigued you so much?

MD: I think the first thing was just the physical scale of it. When you first even just look up the documentary, you see this massive ramp and this huge yellow car with wings, and you see something that looks impossible.

I was immediately intrigued by this crazy story that I'd never heard about that had happened in Canada — and this idea that when Evel Knievel was at the height of his fame, there was a Canadian guy that was sort of living in his shadow, trying to make his own mark. So that immediately spoke to me.

But then, when you watch the documentary that this film was based on, The Devil at Your Heels, and you get to know the real Ken Carter through that documentary. He's an incredible person. He's riddled with contradictions, like all of us. He's incredibly brave, optimistic, and just a real believer.

I think everybody has a bit of Ken Carter inside of them. Everybody has their own version of a 90-foot ramp and a two-tonne rocket car. I think people can get a lot out of this film and out of Ken's story.
JL: Through your research, what did you discover about Ken that drove him to this level of risk?
MD: I think he was a man who was obviously brave. He's a guy who comes from nothing and sort of fell into the mechanics' world. Then he joined the circus stunt team and travelled the world.

By the time this documentary captures him, he's around 37 years old. He's broken every bone in his body and still hasn't quite made his mark. So, he was a man who really wanted to prove to everybody what he could do — and for everybody to remember his name.

I think we can all understand that feeling, as you get older, that you wanna you wanna leave a legacy, and hopefully this film does a small part in terms of cementing his legacy and shining a spotlight on the story and who this man was.
JL: What does it mean to you to be able to bring these stories of lesser-known Canadians to the big screen?
MD: It's less about it being Canadian. It's just a great story.
Because it was Canadian, we knew we could raise some money to do it, so they sort of complemented each other beautifully. But for me, the story is universal.
I'm proud to tell a Canadian story, but it's never anything I try to lead with.
JL: This film is coming to the Forest City Film Festival in October. There will also be a theatrical release this Friday, is that right?
MD: Yes, it's coming out this Friday in Canada, and then in the United States. We're excited that it got a theatrical release. It's a rare thing these days and we think the film deserves it.
It's a really unique story driven by a fantastic performance by Jay Baruchel, who really puts the film on his back and and embodies the Ken Carter story.

I'm excited for everybody to see it and hopefully it gets some traction. Because of what's been happening right now, I think people are really hungry to support a Canadian-grown and Canadian-born story.

stories.title: Meet the London family who made libraries their must-see travel destination
stories.summary: A London, Ont., family has turned library visits into a travel tradition, visiting 50 libraries across Canada, the U.S. and India, and they aren't stopping there.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: A London, Ont., family has turned library visits into a travel tradition, visiting 50 libraries across Canada, the U.S. and India, and they aren't stopping there.
· Posted: Sep 27, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
The Nagpal family visit a library in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia on a road trip to Eastern Canada.(Submitted)
For some, the perfect vacation means hunting down the best local coffee shops, exploring a new trail or checking out the nightlife.
For one London, Ont., family, it's all about libraries.
The Nagpal family has made a tradition of visiting libraries wherever they travel — and this summer, they reached a milestone: their 50th library.
Guneet Kaur Nagpal and her husband, Robin, first started visiting libraries together about two decades ago while they were studying in India.
When they moved to the U.S. for school and eventually to Canada in 2013, they kept seeking out libraries along the way.
"We had less money, less to do, but still the library [was] a lot of fun," he said. "It just feels home to us, like a second home."
London, Ont., family Robin, Avraj, Guneet and Nehmat Nagpal pose outside the Grand Falls Public Library in New Brunswick. (Submitted)
That tradition only grew after their children were born, Guneet said. Now, whenever the family travels, they look for local libraries and make sure to spend some time there.
"Naturally we both liked it, and it has also played a huge part in our lives," Robin said.
It wasn't until Guneet decided to make a list of all the libraries they had visited that she realized the number was already more than 40.
"That's when it occurred to me: let's make it a deal as a family and try to reach 50 as a number," she said.
This summer, the family took a 5,000-kilometre road trip through Eastern Canada, stopping at libraries in Quebec, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.
They wanted their 50th stop to be something special.
They chose Maison de la littérature in Quebec City — or House of Literature — a library and cultural space housed in a renovated building filled with books and art installations.
The space is home to 25,000 works of Quebec literature and hosts cultural and creative programming, according to the library.
A crafted whale hangs from the ceiling of the children's section at the Bibliothèque de Montmagny in Montmagny, Que. (Submitted)
Back home in London, the family has visited almost every branch of the London Public Library.

One of Guneet's favourite spots is the reading garden at the Central Branch. The family has also visited libraries in St. Thomas and explored others across southern Ontario, from Paris to Wasaga Beach and Collingwood.
For eight-year-old Avraj, it's the books — especially graphic novels — that keep him coming back.
His six-year-old sister, Nehmat, also loves reading and spending time at libraries.
Robin said public libraries offer much more than books. He sees them as important community spaces for new parents, children, newcomers and anyone looking to learn something new.
"I think there are a lot of countries who could learn a lot about how Canada is using and maintaining its library infrastructure, which is providing benefits for so many people," he said.
And the Nagpals aren't stopping at 50.
They're already planning their next library visits, with stops around Parry Sound on the itinerary for an upcoming camping trip.
For this family, the library isn't just a place to visit, it's part of the journey.

stories.title: Can you turn left from a lane with a straight arrow?
stories.summary: Those arrows at intersections aren’t just helpful pointers – they’re usually showing you your only option
stories.author: Jason Tchir
stories.content:
An intersection near my condo has three lanes: a left-turning lane, a lane for going straight and a right-turning lane. Each lane has a sign with an arrow showing what you should do. I was in a line of cars waiting to turn left in the left-turning lane on the green light when a car bypassed us on the right and made the left turn from the lane with the straight arrow. A car in front of me in the left-turn lane made a wide turn and the two cars nearly hit each other – there was a lot of honking. Don’t you have to do what the arrows on the signs say? – Ted, Mississauga

Those arrows at intersections aren’t just helpful pointers – they’re usually showing you your only option.

“If a lane is designated [as] straight through, that’s the movement drivers are expected to make from that lane,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “If there is a dedicated left-turning lane and you make the left turn from the through lane beside it, that can absolutely result in a charge.”

In Ontario, the law states that when there are designated lanes, drivers “shall obey the instructions on the official signs.”

But even if there aren’t signs for a designated turning lane – or lanes – you’re supposed to turn from the leftmost lane.

If you turn left from the wrong lane, you could face charges including making an improper left turn, Shapiro said. That comes with an $85 fine – $120 in a community safety zone – and two demerit points . With fees, that comes to $110 or $150.

If the move is dangerous, you could also be charged with careless driving, which comes with a $400 fine – $490 with fees – and six demerits.

Typically, when there are signs with arrows, there are also painted arrows on the pavement. Sometimes, the arrows May show that you can make more than one move – for example, they May show that you can go straight or turn left.

Also, if the lane has a straight arrow, you shouldn’t be turning right from it either.

While the rules vary by province, they generally require you to obey signs and to turn from a designated left-turning lane – or if there isn’t one, the leftmost lane.

But the law aside, making a left turn from the straight lane is confusing to other drivers around you.

“Signs, signals and pavement markings allow us to anticipate what another driver is going to do,” Angelo DiCicco, chief executive officer of the Ontario Safety League, a non-profit which focuses on driver education, said in an email. “If I’m beside you in a lane designated for a left turn and you’re in a lane designated to proceed straight, I’m making decisions based partly on the reasonable expectation that you’re going straight.”

So, for example, that driver turning left next to the lane that goes straight has no reason to expect that a car will be turning there – so they likely won’t be looking out for you.

“It creates a conflict that other drivers aren’t expecting,” Shapiro said.

It doesn’t matter why you’re turning from the wrong lane, he said. Maybe you’re trying to “bypass the lineup” of cars waiting to turn. Or maybe you just ended up in the wrong lane by mistake.

“Traffic law doesn’t give you a free pass because you missed your lane,” Shapiro said. “[But] if someone realizes late that they’re in the wrong lane, signals, safely changes completely into the turning lane and then makes the turn, that’s different. They May have poor planning skills, but they haven’t necessarily committed an improper turn.”

Have a driving question? Send it to globedrive@globeandmail.com and put ‘Driving Concerns’ in your subject line. E-mails without the correct subject line May not be answered. Canada’s a big place, so let us know where you are so we can find the answer for your city and province.

content_blocks.text: An intersection near my condo has three lanes: a left-turning lane, a lane for going straight and a right-turning lane. Each lane has a sign with an arrow showing what you should do. I was in a line of cars waiting to turn left in the left-turning lane on the green light when a car bypassed us on the right and made the left turn from the lane with the straight arrow. A car in front of me in the left-turn lane made a wide turn and the two cars nearly hit each other – there was a lot of honking. Don’t you have to do what the arrows on the signs say? – Ted, Mississauga
Those arrows at intersections aren’t just helpful pointers – they’re usually showing you your only option.

“If a lane is designated [as] straight through, that’s the movement drivers are expected to make from that lane,” said Sean Shapiro, a road safety consultant and former Toronto traffic cop. “If there is a dedicated left-turning lane and you make the left turn from the through lane beside it, that can absolutely result in a charge.”
In Ontario, the law states that when there are designated lanes, drivers “shall obey the instructions on the official signs.”
But even if there aren’t signs for a designated turning lane – or lanes – you’re supposed to turn from the leftmost lane.

If you turn left from the wrong lane, you could face charges including making an improper left turn, Shapiro said. That comes with an $85 fine – $120 in a community safety zone – and two demerit points . With fees, that comes to $110 or $150.
If the move is dangerous, you could also be charged with careless driving, which comes with a $400 fine – $490 with fees – and six demerits.

Typically, when there are signs with arrows, there are also painted arrows on the pavement. Sometimes, the arrows May show that you can make more than one move – for example, they May show that you can go straight or turn left.
Also, if the lane has a straight arrow, you shouldn’t be turning right from it either.
While the rules vary by province, they generally require you to obey signs and to turn from a designated left-turning lane – or if there isn’t one, the leftmost lane.
But the law aside, making a left turn from the straight lane is confusing to other drivers around you.

“Signs, signals and pavement markings allow us to anticipate what another driver is going to do,” Angelo DiCicco, chief executive officer of the Ontario Safety League, a non-profit which focuses on driver education, said in an email. “If I’m beside you in a lane designated for a left turn and you’re in a lane designated to proceed straight, I’m making decisions based partly on the reasonable expectation that you’re going straight.”
So, for example, that driver turning left next to the lane that goes straight has no reason to expect that a car will be turning there – so they likely won’t be looking out for you.
“It creates a conflict that other drivers aren’t expecting,” Shapiro said.

stories.title: The Tragically Hip, Feist to be inducted into Canadian Songwriters Hall of fame
stories.summary: The artists will be celebrated at a star-studded Toronto gala featuring tributes from Jeff Tweedy, Finneas, Our Lady Peace and others
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Toronto’s indie music scene mainstay Feist and Kingston, Ont., alt-rock legends The Tragically Hip are among the musical acts who will be inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame during a star-studded gala on Saturday night.

Feist, whose first name is Leslie but is more commonly known by her last name alone, says it was surreal to have her songwriting honoured especially because writing songs begins as such a private act.

She says ahead of the show held at Toronto’s Massey Hall that she doesn’t know of any other event that celebrates the “quiet part” of songwriting, so it “does mean a lot.”

Feist talks Heated Rivalry, iPod ads and hit covers ahead of induction into Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame

Wilco lead singer Jeff Tweedy and Los Angeles songwriter-producer Finneas are set to perform some of Feist’s music. Finneas, who is Billie Eilish’s brother and collaborator, will also induct the singer, known for the hits 1234 and You and I , an acoustic duet with Tweedy.

Meanwhile, Our Lady Peace and City and Colour are among the artists performing songs by The Hip, while actor and filmmaker Jay Baruchel will induct the band into the Hall of Fame.

The Hip bassist Gord Sinclair says it’s special to be inducted as a band.

“That group dynamic and the way we wrote together was the most important thing that we did,” he says while standing alongside bandmates Rob Baker and Paul Langlois on the red carpet.

“We literally went around in a circle and bounced ideas off of each other. To be recognized for that, obviously we’re missing a huge part of our circle. But yeah, it really, really does mean a lot.”

Band frontman Gord Downie died in 2017.

Baruchel says the opportunity to induct The Hip into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame is a unique honour.

“As someone that was raised to believe that this is the best country in the world, it was always pretty special to me to have a band, a group of artists that were unconditionally Canadian and didn’t have aspirations to be anything but that,” Baruchel says. “And that told me that I could be that, too.”

Fellow inductees also include the songwriting partners behind Loverboy, Mike Reno and Paul Dean, as well as French-Canadian singer-songwriter Roch Voisine.

Other performers scheduled to take the stage include Allison Russell, Charlotte Cornfield and Amanda Marshall, who walked the red carpet wearing a T-shirt with “Loverboy” written across the front. The Canadian singer-songwriter is set to perform the rock band’s 1980 hit Turn Me Loose .

“It seemed only fitting that a woman sing this song because this genre, this kind of music, is very kind of hyper-masculine,” Marshall says. “It seemed fitting that a woman sing it and that I be that woman.”

Longtime Drake producer Boi-1da is slated to make a special appearance to pay tribute to The Hip. Also on hand as inductors are songwriter Jim Vallance and Olympic hockey gold medallists Marie-Philip Poulin and Laura Stacey.

The ceremony will be hosted by broadcaster George Stroumboulopoulos and singer Marie-Mai.

It will also be live-streamed globally via the Amazon Music Twitch channel and on Prime Video in Canada.

stories.title: ‘We’re in a rush’: Ottawa businesses want Canada-U.S. trade war resolved
stories.summary: Businesses on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border are feeling the effects of an ongoing trade dispute, even as the Trump administration signals it is comfortable with the status quo.
stories.author: Jeremie Charron
stories.content:
Ottawa — Businesses on both sides of the Canada-U.S. border are feeling the effects of an ongoing trade dispute, even as the Trump administration signals it is comfortable with the status quo.

At Infinity Flooring in Ottawa, tariffs have hit a large portion of the carpet products the family-owned business sells.

“It’s all tariffed,” said Heidi Gagne, co-owner and managing director of the store as she pointed to a large display of products.

Products from major American suppliers are now facing tariffs ranging from 25 to 50 per cent, depending on the materials used, Gagne said.

Some orders have increased by thousands of dollars, while Canadian alternatives are limited and in high demand.

“We could run into shortages as this progresses,” said Gagne.

The uncertainty is adding pressure to businesses that rely on cross-border supply chains.

“We’re in a rush, we want to see it resolved,” said Gloria Beaucaire, a sales representative who has worked at the store for more than two decades.

“We have employees, we have people who depend on people coming into our store.”

But while Canadian businesses are eager for a resolution, the Trump administration has indicated there is little urgency to reach a new trade agreement.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said this week that there is no rush to reach a deal and that U.S. President Donald Trump is comfortable with the current situation.

Kelly Anne Shaw, a former senior White House trade adviser under Trump, said Canada and the U.S. appear to have very different views of the current state of the relationship.

“The United States and Canada seem to be living in two different alternative realities about what the politics are, what the situation is,” Shaw said.

Shaw said the Trump administration believes Prime Minister Mark Carney was the one who walked away from a potential agreement and that Canada would need to make the request to return to the negotiating table.

Communication between Canadian and U.S. officials continues, but formal trade negotiations remain paused.

“The relationship is not in a great place, there are no formal negotiations,” said William Pelerin, an international trade lawyer with McMillan LLP in Ottawa.

Back at Infinity Flooring, the uncertainty is one of the biggest concerns for Gagne, who only recently took over the family business.

“We would like to see this resolved,” Gagne said. “I think it’s ridiculous that what’s going on is going on.”

Washington is also set to impose its latest round of trade measures Tuesday, including an import ban affecting a list of Canadian goods ranging from alcohol and dairy products to motorcycles.

For businesses like Infinity Flooring, the hope is that the uncertainty won’t last much longer.

stories.title: P.E.I. joins Alberta with fuel-tax break amid high gas and diesel prices
stories.summary: Filling the tank cost a little less for Islanders Saturday, with a pause on the provincial fuel tax taking effect for the next four months.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Borden-Carleton, P.E.I. - Filling the tank cost a little less for Islanders Saturday, with a pause on the provincial fuel tax taking effect for the next four months.

The break comes days after Alberta announced its own fuel-tax suspension, as high-energy costs add to affordability pressures. P.E.I.’s suspension takes 8.47 cents per litre off gasoline and 14.15 cents per litre off diesel. Premier Rob Lantz announced the changes Friday.

“It’s a little bit lower than it was yesterday,” said Peter Mullins at a gas station in Borden-Carleton. “It’s about five dollars a tank difference, so I can buy a coffee or two with the extra.”

But there was still pain at the pump.

“This is the worst price of gas we’ve witnessed in a very long time,” said another customer. “You cannot save any money.”

Ottawa has introduced legislation to continue its fuel excise tax holiday through Jan. 31, which could keep 10 cents per litre off gasoline and four cents off diesel.

P.E.I.’s reprieve will last until the same date, before it returns at 50 per cent of its regular rate on Feb. 1, and then is fully restored April 1.

“Fuel costs touch almost everything on our Island, from the commute to work to the price of goods delivered to store shelves,” Finance and Affordability Minister Jill Burridge said in a release. “Global markets are driving prices up, and Islanders shouldn’t have to face that alone.”

Straining industries reliant on gas

The gasoline reduction will be felt by many, said Ian Lee, associate professor at Carleton University’s Sprott School of Business.

“You see the prices going up, and you’re reminded every time you fill up your car,” he said. “That’s what I think makes it so toxic to us the citizens and to the ministers who realize they are becoming the target of the anger.”

The strain is particularly acute for industries that depend on diesel.

Hundreds of dump-truck drivers convoyed into Vancouver on Friday to protest record-high diesel prices.

The Vancouver area has the highest fuel-tax rates in the country. According to Natural Resources Canada the provincial comparison is 27 cents per litre on gasoline and 27.5 cents per litre on diesel.

While tax cuts could mean lower expenses for truckers and their companies, in P.E.I., the impact will be “trivial” on the cost of goods Lee said.

“It’s a little bit lower than it was yesterday,” said Peter Mullins at a gas station in Borden-Carleton. “It’s about five dollars a tank difference, so I can buy a coffee or two with the extra.”

“This is the worst price of gas we’ve witnessed in a very long time,” said another customer. “You cannot save any money.”
Ottawa has introduced legislation to continue its fuel excise tax holiday through Jan. 31, which could keep 10 cents per litre off gasoline and four cents off diesel.
P.E.I.’s reprieve will last until the same date, before it returns at 50 per cent of its regular rate on Feb. 1, and then is fully restored April 1.

“Fuel costs touch almost everything on our Island, from the commute to work to the price of goods delivered to store shelves,” Finance and Affordability Minister Jill Burridge said in a release. “Global markets are driving prices up, and Islanders shouldn’t have to face that alone.”

stories.title: 4 killed after helicopter crashes in field near Montreal
stories.summary: Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Montérégie, Que., in the Rang des Écossais area. It crashed into a field in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Montérégie, Que., in the Rang des Écossais area.

A spokesperson for the Sûreté du Québec (SQ) says the incident happened just after 2:30 p.m. Saturday.

The helicopter crashed into a field in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, southeast of Montreal.

The chopper caught fire, but police say it’s unclear if the fire began in the air or as a result of the crash.

Fire crews had the blaze under control within an hour.

The SQ says four occupants were declared dead at the scene.

The force’s major crime unit is investigating the incident, and the Transportation Safety Board of Canada has been notified.

stories.title: Four dead in helicopter crash near Montreal
stories.summary: Crash happened in Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, 50 kilometres southeast of Montreal
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Four people have died in a helicopter crash in Sainte-Brigide-d’Iberville, 50 kilometres southeast of Montreal, according to provincial police.

A spokesperson says police were called to the scene around 2:30 p.m. on Saturday.

They found the crashed aircraft on fire and later discovered the bodies of the four occupants, who were declared dead at the scene.

The provincial police have not yet identified the victims nor the cause of the crash.

The spokesperson says the helicopter seems to have been a private aircraft.

She says the investigation is ongoing and the Transportation Safety Board of Canada has sent investigators to the crash site.

stories.title: Thousands of students party under watchful eye of police; Western beats McMaster during homecoming weekend
stories.summary: Thousands of students packed Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street under the watchful eye of London Police during Homecoming weekend at Western University.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Thousands of students packed Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street under the watchful eye of London Police during Homecoming weekend at Western University.

‘It’s like Christmas,” said Hunter Ellis, a fourth-year student who has lived on Broughdale for three years.

“It’s the biggest party school in Canada.”

The street is the epicentre of the weekend party.

“It’s the best holiday ever,” said roommate Douglas Bond.

“We try to keep the house a little tame, but it gets a little messed up. It’s fun to see the whole school come together.”

Members of the London Police Service (LPS) along with paramedics and firefighters were all stationed along Audrey Street between Broughdale and Huron.

“We have additional officers from Windsor, from Hamilton, as well as the OPP assisting us on the ground here in relation to any of the unsanctioned gatherings that take place,” said Sgt. Sandasha Bough of the LPS.

This year the City of London put up barricades along Richmond Street and closed one of the southbound lanes to keep students away from traffic.

“We’ve closed at least one of the lanes on Richmond to ensure public safety,” said Bough.

“We’ve put some additional closures in and around Broughdale and Audrey to ensure that everybody who is out here gathering stays off of the roadway to ensure public safety as well.”

Across campus a much more subdued party was being held outside Alumni Stadium. Current and former cheerleaders were gathering for a tailgate party.

“It really is just a purple and proud moment,” said former National Champion cheerleader Michelle Brock.

On the way into the stadium, London Mayor Josh Morgan – a Western University graduate – stopped to tell CTV News what Homecoming means to him.

“I came here in 1998, and actually, it was my reason for coming to the city and I never left,” said Morgan, who came from outside the Sarnia-area to attend school.

“I ended up becoming the mayor, so Homecoming is a nice reminder to see old friends and where my story in London really began.”

More than 10,000 people witnessed London, Ont. wide receiver Emmett Charles haul in three touchdowns in the second quarter as the Mustangs won to improve to 4-0 this year.

Back at Broughdale Avenue, LPS were keeping a close eye on the activity. Bough told CTV News that information on incidents will be released in the coming days.

“We will collect information from our community partners throughout the weekend and hopefully at the beginning of next week at some point, we’ll be able to share those numbers with you,” said Bough.

Just after 4 p.m., the London police declared the festivities on Broughdale Avenue a nuisance party. Partygoers were asked to clear the area by police.

More photos of the weekend are available in CTV London’s photo galleries .

stories.title: $1 million donation to expand LHSC’s cardiac care
stories.summary: Andy and Helen Spriet have donated $1 million to London Health Sciences Centre to expand cardiac care.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Andy and Helen Spriet have donated $1 million to London Health Sciences Centre to expand cardiac care. The funds will go towards bringing a third Electrophysiology (EP) Lab to University Hospital. The third lab is part of a $6.5 million campaign to expand and modernize cardiac care.

“We’ve been fortunate to call London home for so many years, and we know how important it is to have the right care available when you need it,” said the Spriets. “When we learned more about the need for a third EP Lab, it was a project we felt strongly about supporting.

Most importantly, it will help improve timely access to life-changing cardiac procedures, reduce wait times, and enhance the overall patient experience.”

stories.title: Lawyer wins case against multinational firm behind day school settlement
stories.summary: A First Nations lawyer who started the quest for justice for day school survivors has won a lawsuit against a firm regarding compensation for her work.
stories.author: Melissa Ridgen
stories.content:
A First Nations lawyer who launched the legal fight for day school survivors before the file was turned over to a larger law firm as a class-action, has won a lawsuit against that firm.

Joan Jack filed the statement of claim for a group of day school survivors in 2009.

Gowling WLG took over the file in 2016 using work Jack and other lawyers had done, including a database of 12,500 potential class action members.

Gowling got a $1.5 billion settlement for day school survivors and were paid $55 million in legal fees.

Manitoba Judge Shauna McCarthy in a 46-page ruling found Gowling “had a contractual and fiduciary duty to present the plaintiffs’ fees to the Federal Court for approval with respect to work asserted to have been done by the plaintiffs in advancing the day school claims” and that “Gowling breached their obligations to do so.”

The six-year David versus Goliath battle “was hard” says Jack, and she feels “vindicated” by the ruling.

“Every human being wants to be recognized for their contribution in life and for us as Indigenous people, so often our contributions are erased, changed, ignored,” Jack said. “And so in that space, I feel very joyful.”

Gowling managing partner Lorraine Mastersmith said “we have significant concerns with elements of the judgment and are reviewing the decision to determine our next steps.”

How much Gowling will pay will be determined at a later date.

Nearly 200,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended more than 700 Indian day schools beginning in the 1920s. Many endured physical and sexual abuse at the federally-run schools. Under the settlement agreement, Canada compensated each eligible survivor between $10,000 and $200,000.

The six-year David versus Goliath battle “was hard” says Jack, and she feels “vindicated” by the ruling.

“Every human being wants to be recognized for their contribution in life and for us as Indigenous people, so often our contributions are erased, changed, ignored,” Jack said. “And so in that space, I feel very joyful.”
Gowling managing partner Lorraine Mastersmith said “we have significant concerns with elements of the judgment and are reviewing the decision to determine our next steps.”
How much Gowling will pay will be determined at a later date.

Nearly 200,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended more than 700 Indian day schools beginning in the 1920s. Many endured physical and sexual abuse at the federally-run schools. Under the settlement agreement, Canada compensated each eligible survivor between $10,000 and $200,000.

stories.title: Suspect wanted in hit-and-run involving a cyclist
stories.summary: A suspect is wanted by the Owen Sound police in connection with a hit-and-run involving a cyclist.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A suspect is wanted by the Owen Sound police in connection with a hit-and-run involving a cyclist.

On Saturday around 7 a.m., police were called to the incident at the intersection of 10th Street East and 1st Avenue East.

Officers believe the car is a dark-coloured Cadillac sedan with damage to the front, passenger-side corner. That includes a broken headlight, and it is believed to be missing the passenger side mirror.

After the crash, the Osps said the vehicle did not try to stop and drove westbound on 10th Street West.

The cyclist was taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

Police are asking anyone with information or dash cam footage of the incident to contact Const. Kinal at 215@owensoundpolice.com

stories.title: Kids starting a fire, taking a vehicle set off warning from Mounties in B.C.
stories.summary: Police say a seven-year-old boy found a small blow torch in his home on Sept. 18, managed to connect it to a propane cylinder and started a fire inside his home.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Mounties in Mission, B.C., are reminding parents just how “resourceful” children can be after separate situations last week.

Police say a seven-year-old boy found a small blow torch in his home on Sept. 18, managed to connect it to a propane cylinder and started a fire inside his home.

The local fire department attended and put out what police say was a small blaze.

The second incident, which happened the same day, involved a four-year-old boy who took the keys to his parents’ Cadillac Escalade and climbed inside.

The RCMP says Cctv footage confirmed the boy started the Cadillac and drove it into two parked cars that were nearby.

No one was hurt, but police say in a news release that parents should look around their homes and consider what they could do in order to reduce the risks.
