stories.title: 10 Huron-Bruce women recognized for Rural Ontario Week
stories.summary: 10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
10 women have been recognized by Huron-Bruce MPP Lisa Thompson for their contributions to agriculture in their communities, part of Rural Ontario Week.

The women recognized were Tara Terpstra, Emily Morrison, Carol Leeming, Miranda Klaver, Margaret Vincent, Becky Maus, Kristie Gilchrist, Barb Zettler, Amanda Hammell, and Christine MacIntyre.

“Women have always been an integral part of agriculture and rural life here in Huron-Bruce, and this year provides a special opportunity to recognize the women who continue to strengthen our farms, businesses, and communities,” Thompson said.

“I am proud to recognize these 10 women for their leadership, dedication, and hard work they bring to our rural communities. Their contributions are helping build a strong future for agriculture and rural Ontario.”

Rural Ontario Week runs Sept. 20 to Sept. 26.

stories.title: 2 teens charged with murder in connection to pedestrian collision that killed 16-year-old
stories.summary: Two teens from Guelph, Ont. are facing second-degree murder charges in connection to a fatal pedestrian collision last weekend that claimed the life of 16-year-old boy.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Two teens from Guelph, Ont. are facing second-degree murder charges in connection with a fatal pedestrian collision last weekend that claimed the life of a 16-year-old boy.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) and paramedics responded to the collision, which involved a minivan, on Wellington Road 29, south of Eramosa-Garafraxa Town Line just after midnight last Saturday.

The victim has been identified as a teen from Puslinch Township, OPP said.

According to police, officers arrested two 17-year-old boys on Friday. Both were held in custody and are scheduled to appear in Ontario Court of Justice in Guelph on Saturday.

Their identities are protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Anyone with information about this investigation is asked to contact the Wellington County OPP at 1-888-310-1122 or submit a tip anonymously through Crime Stoppers.

stories.title: Parts of Nova Scotia national park closed temporarily after coyote bite: Parks Canada
stories.summary: In a social media post, the parks agency says the MacIntosh Brook area where the incident happened has been temporarily closed.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Parts of a national park in northern Nova Scotia have been closed after a visitor was bitten by a coyote.

Parks Canada says the bite occurred in the Cape Breton Highlands National Park on Thursday evening.

In a social media post, the parks agency says the MacIntosh Brook area where the incident happened has been temporarily closed.

The post says the Lone Shieling trail and pull-offs in the surrounding area have also been closed as staff assess the situation.

Parks Canada says it will provide updates when more information is available.

Coyote attacks in the park are not uncommon but are rarely fatal.

stories.title: After Canada stopped using solitary confinement, it made an exception for these prisoners
stories.summary: Years after its segregation practices were supposedly halted, Canada still uses other forms of isolation on certain prisoners.
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
It is Nov. 5, 2024. Over the course of half an hour, a hand-held camera follows Joey Toutsaint as prison guards forcibly remove him from a cell, then lead him through a hall, across a yard and into another building. The camera captures him pleading.

“I’m not going to the observation cell. No. You guys are making a mistake. Put me back in my cell.”

At one point, he weeps. “I won’t self-harm … I give you my word. On my mother’s grave. On my daughter’s life…. I don’t want to live like this no more.”

“I recognize you have mental health issues,” an officer says at one point.

The prison guards lead Toutsaint, wrapped in a blanket after a strip search, into the observation cell.

“As you can see on camera,” one of the officers says to the person filming before the camera is turned off, “we had some challenges with Mr. Toutsaint and wanting to submit to going into the observation cell.”

Observation cells are bare rooms subject to 24/7 surveillance in which prisoners such as Toutsaint are placed, dressed in a sleeveless, untearable smock and sometimes without a blanket or mattress, when they have tried to harm themselves or are suspected of intending to do so.

Another variant on these isolation cells is the “dry cell,” which is similarly bare but lacks plumbing or running water. It’s used when prison staff want someone to excrete something they are suspected of having swallowed or hidden in their body, such as drugs.

Canada does not call these cells solitary confinement.

But their use meets a definition of solitary under international rules — to which Canada has agreed — that are meant to minimize the use of such isolation.

What are known as the “Mandela Rules” define solitary confinement as 22 hours a day or more without meaningful human contact, and define prolonged solitary confinement as a period exceeding 15 consecutive days. The rules say solitary confinement should only be used “in exceptional cases as a last resort” and should be “prohibited in the case of prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures.”

Yet the use of observation cells and dry cells has been rising, according to data obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau through access-to-information requests.

The number of times Canadian prisons used observation cells rose from 859 in 2018 to 1,316 in 2024 — a 53 per cent increase. In total, observation cells were used more than 8,000 times between 2018 and November 2025, CSC data show.

The number of times Canadian prisons used dry cells rose from 160 in 2022 to 291 in 2024 — an 82 per cent increase. Dry cells were used almost 700 times between 2022 and 2024.

Observation and dry cells can be used for indefinite periods in Canada. The prisoner has no immediate means of appeal.

“It doesn’t really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges,” former correctional investigator and current Canadian Civil Liberties Association head Howard Sapers said. “The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation, where people are locked down, locked in their cells, often for 24 hours a day, sometimes for 23 or 22….

“The fact that we don’t have the words ‘solitary confinement’ in our law does not mean that solitary confinement does not, in fact, take place.”

In observation cells, and in other special sections of prisons reserved for people deemed unsafe in the general population, Sapers says, Canadian federal prisoners are “being dealt (with) in a way that’s off the books, frankly.”

It doesn't really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges. The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation Howard Sapers, Canadian Civil Liberties Association head

Correctional Service Canada says placements like Toutsaint’s “must be used appropriately, humanely, and with strong oversight” and only “when less restrictive interventions cannot adequately manage an imminent risk of self-harm or suicide.” CSC spokesperson Laurence Côté said prisons conduct health team assessments and case reviews of these placements, but the head of the prison makes the final call.

Observation cells and dry cells are needed to keep prisons safe, says Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union.

“When an inmate is acting out and he’s trying to commit suicide, sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves.”

While dry cell use could be replaced by tools such as body scanners, he said, observation cells will continue to be necessary “to save lives.”

The IJB obtained 53 videos, about five hours’ worth of footage, shot in and around observation cells — videos legal aid organization Prisoners Legal Services obtained through federal Privacy Act requests.

The videos show how the cells are used and the force — tackling and handcuffing, pepper-spraying or tying down — employed to manage prisoners’ behaviour during transportation to and from these cells.

The IJB reviewed the Privacy Act request through which Prisoners Legal Services obtained the videos. Correctional Service Canada would not comment on their veracity.

Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s public safety minister, Gary Anandasangaree, did not respond to requests for an interview.

Sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union

The IJB found that Indigenous prisoners like Toutsaint are more likely than white people to be put in an observation cell.

The number of Indigenous men placed in observation cells annually more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, to 674 from 284, a period during which the number of white men placed in observation cells increased by about 5.6 per cent, to 397 from 376.

“CSC regularly reviews trends in the use of observation measures, including among Indigenous offenders, and continues to strengthen culturally responsive mental health services and Indigenous-specific interventions,” said Côté, the agency’s spokesperson.

There are also significant disparities by institution. The prison with the highest use of observation cells is one designed to meet the needs of mentally ill inmates: Saskatoon’s Regional Psychiatric Centre.

“Enhanced observation May be used more frequently at the Regional Psychiatric Centre because it serves offenders with complex mental health needs,” Csc’s Côté said.

A federal policy directive authorizes the use of “enhanced observation” in cases of suicidality, self-harm or severe mental illness with a serious impairment. It is only to be used as a last resort, according to the federal directive and instructions to officers the IJB reviewed.

It's easier just to lock people in Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society

In 2021, a Nova Scotia court deemed dry cells “a unique form of solitary confinement” after a woman spent more than 15 days in one, based on suspicions that she was smuggling contraband in her vagina. As a result of that ruling, the use of dry cells federally has been narrowed.

“(Dry cells) are only used as a last resort when there are reasonable grounds to believe that an inmate has ingested or is carrying contraband in either their digestive system or in their rectum, and not in an inmate’s vagina,” Côté said.

Since 2019-20, the CSC said, it has seized weapons or drugs more than 400 times following a dry cell placement.

The proliferation of unofficial forms of isolation, such as observation and dry cells, could be the result of a correctional mindset that seeks to deal with immediate security risks in the simplest way possible, Sapers said. Or, “it could very well be that it’s a system response to being overworked, overburdened, overcrowded, under-resourced.”

Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society, a non-profit focused on humane responses to crime, wants to prohibit these kinds of isolation for people with serious mental illness.

Dedicating sections of prison to vulnerable people could be an alternative to putting them in isolation, Latimer said. But this could take additional staff and reserved space.

“It’s easier just to lock people in, lock them down.”

It’s dehumanizing Kenny Allen, former inmate

Kenny Allen remembers his first time in an observation cell, in December 2007.

He was 18 and had just arrived in Saskatchewan Penitentiary on an armed robbery conviction. He’d spent the previous 14 years in and out of foster homes and juvenile institutions.

He didn’t feel safe — he had just left a gang — and said he was suicidal, hoping to be placed somewhere out of harm’s way.

Instead, he got a bare cell, people watching him pee, and no soap to wash his hands. He lost his clothes in exchange for a sleeveless smock.

“Degrading” is the word he uses, repeatedly, to describe the experience, which took place several times over the course of 15 years in federal prisons. The IJB has reviewed multiple videos of Allen’s placements, including one during which he is strapped to a stretcher before being rolled into a cell where he appears to sleep on and off, periodically struggling against his restraints and attempting to hurt himself. “It’s dehumanizing,” he said.

In late May 2018, Joey Toutsaint returned to prison following nine days in hospital after trying to sever his jugular vein.

Standing in the observation cell, he picked at a suture on his neck. The guards pepper-sprayed him. Fish-eye surveillance video shows the orange-red spray filling the cell; according to his lawyer, in a human rights complaint filed three years later, he “felt like he couldn’t breathe.”

Guards then led Toutsaint to a shower, put a spit hood over his head to stop him from spitting or biting and tied him down to a stretcher that was itself tied down in another observation cell.

Years after that event, Toutsaint spoke with the IJB from a video visit room at Kent Institution, about 60 kilometres northwest of Agassiz, B.C. His last observation cell placement was October of last year, after he swallowed razor blades.

On camera, he showed the self-inflicted white scars worming their way up his tattooed left arm. His memories of his times in observation cells are uncomfortably vivid: no clothes, no bedding, no sound, no communication with the outside world.

“There’s no help there,” he said.

Toutsaint doesn’t think anyone should be held in these forms of solitary.

“They should shut it down. Permanently.… It’s torture.”

The Investigative Journalism Bureau (IJB) at the University of Toronto’s Dalla Lana School of Public Health is a collaborative investigative newsroom supported by Postmedia that partners with academics, researchers and journalists while training the next generation of investigative reporters.

Another variant on these isolation cells is the “dry cell,” which is similarly bare but lacks plumbing or running water. It’s used when prison staff want someone to excrete something they are suspected of having swallowed or hidden in their body, such as drugs.
Canada does not call these cells solitary confinement.
But their use meets a definition of solitary under international rules — to which Canada has agreed — that are meant to minimize the use of such isolation.

What are known as the “Mandela Rules” define solitary confinement as 22 hours a day or more without meaningful human contact, and define prolonged solitary confinement as a period exceeding 15 consecutive days. The rules say solitary confinement should only be used “in exceptional cases as a last resort” and should be “prohibited in the case of prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures.”
Yet the use of observation cells and dry cells has been rising, according to data obtained by the Investigative Journalism Bureau through access-to-information requests.

The number of times Canadian prisons used observation cells rose from 859 in 2018 to 1,316 in 2024 — a 53 per cent increase. In total, observation cells were used more than 8,000 times between 2018 and November 2025, CSC data show.
The number of times Canadian prisons used dry cells rose from 160 in 2022 to 291 in 2024 — an 82 per cent increase. Dry cells were used almost 700 times between 2022 and 2024.
Observation and dry cells can be used for indefinite periods in Canada. The prisoner has no immediate means of appeal.

“It doesn’t really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges,” former correctional investigator and current Canadian Civil Liberties Association head Howard Sapers said. “The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation, where people are locked down, locked in their cells, often for 24 hours a day, sometimes for 23 or 22….
“The fact that we don’t have the words ‘solitary confinement’ in our law does not mean that solitary confinement does not, in fact, take place.”

In observation cells, and in other special sections of prisons reserved for people deemed unsafe in the general population, Sapers says, Canadian federal prisoners are “being dealt (with) in a way that’s off the books, frankly.”

It doesn't really matter what the correctional service calls these cells or units or ranges. The fact of the matter is they operate like segregation Howard Sapers, Canadian Civil Liberties Association head

Correctional Service Canada says placements like Toutsaint’s “must be used appropriately, humanely, and with strong oversight” and only “when less restrictive interventions cannot adequately manage an imminent risk of self-harm or suicide.” CSC spokesperson Laurence Côté said prisons conduct health team assessments and case reviews of these placements, but the head of the prison makes the final call.
Observation cells and dry cells are needed to keep prisons safe, says Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union.
“When an inmate is acting out and he’s trying to commit suicide, sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves.”
While dry cell use could be replaced by tools such as body scanners, he said, observation cells will continue to be necessary “to save lives.”

The IJB obtained 53 videos, about five hours’ worth of footage, shot in and around observation cells — videos legal aid organization Prisoners Legal Services obtained through federal Privacy Act requests.
The videos show how the cells are used and the force — tackling and handcuffing, pepper-spraying or tying down — employed to manage prisoners’ behaviour during transportation to and from these cells.
The IJB reviewed the Privacy Act request through which Prisoners Legal Services obtained the videos. Correctional Service Canada would not comment on their veracity.
Simon Lafortune, a spokesperson for Canada’s public safety minister, Gary Anandasangaree, did not respond to requests for an interview.
Sometimes we’ve got to protect them from themselves Frederick Lebeau, president of the federal correctional officers’ union
The IJB found that Indigenous prisoners like Toutsaint are more likely than white people to be put in an observation cell.

The number of Indigenous men placed in observation cells annually more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, to 674 from 284, a period during which the number of white men placed in observation cells increased by about 5.6 per cent, to 397 from 376.

“CSC regularly reviews trends in the use of observation measures, including among Indigenous offenders, and continues to strengthen culturally responsive mental health services and Indigenous-specific interventions,” said Côté, the agency’s spokesperson.

There are also significant disparities by institution. The prison with the highest use of observation cells is one designed to meet the needs of mentally ill inmates: Saskatoon’s Regional Psychiatric Centre.
“Enhanced observation May be used more frequently at the Regional Psychiatric Centre because it serves offenders with complex mental health needs,” Csc’s Côté said.

A federal policy directive authorizes the use of “enhanced observation” in cases of suicidality, self-harm or severe mental illness with a serious impairment. It is only to be used as a last resort, according to the federal directive and instructions to officers the IJB reviewed.
It's easier just to lock people in Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society

In 2021, a Nova Scotia court deemed dry cells “a unique form of solitary confinement” after a woman spent more than 15 days in one, based on suspicions that she was smuggling contraband in her vagina. As a result of that ruling, the use of dry cells federally has been narrowed.

“(Dry cells) are only used as a last resort when there are reasonable grounds to believe that an inmate has ingested or is carrying contraband in either their digestive system or in their rectum, and not in an inmate’s vagina,” Côté said.
Since 2019-20, the CSC said, it has seized weapons or drugs more than 400 times following a dry cell placement.

The proliferation of unofficial forms of isolation, such as observation and dry cells, could be the result of a correctional mindset that seeks to deal with immediate security risks in the simplest way possible, Sapers said. Or, “it could very well be that it’s a system response to being overworked, overburdened, overcrowded, under-resourced.”
Catherine Latimer, head of the John Howard Society, a non-profit focused on humane responses to crime, wants to prohibit these kinds of isolation for people with serious mental illness.
Dedicating sections of prison to vulnerable people could be an alternative to putting them in isolation, Latimer said. But this could take additional staff and reserved space.
“It’s easier just to lock people in, lock them down.”
It’s dehumanizing Kenny Allen, former inmate
Kenny Allen remembers his first time in an observation cell, in December 2007.
He was 18 and had just arrived in Saskatchewan Penitentiary on an armed robbery conviction. He’d spent the previous 14 years in and out of foster homes and juvenile institutions.
He didn’t feel safe — he had just left a gang — and said he was suicidal, hoping to be placed somewhere out of harm’s way.
Instead, he got a bare cell, people watching him pee, and no soap to wash his hands. He lost his clothes in exchange for a sleeveless smock.

“Degrading” is the word he uses, repeatedly, to describe the experience, which took place several times over the course of 15 years in federal prisons. The IJB has reviewed multiple videos of Allen’s placements, including one during which he is strapped to a stretcher before being rolled into a cell where he appears to sleep on and off, periodically struggling against his restraints and attempting to hurt himself. “It’s dehumanizing,” he said.
In late May 2018, Joey Toutsaint returned to prison following nine days in hospital after trying to sever his jugular vein.

Standing in the observation cell, he picked at a suture on his neck. The guards pepper-sprayed him. Fish-eye surveillance video shows the orange-red spray filling the cell; according to his lawyer, in a human rights complaint filed three years later, he “felt like he couldn’t breathe.”
Guards then led Toutsaint to a shower, put a spit hood over his head to stop him from spitting or biting and tied him down to a stretcher that was itself tied down in another observation cell.

Years after that event, Toutsaint spoke with the IJB from a video visit room at Kent Institution, about 60 kilometres northwest of Agassiz, B.C. His last observation cell placement was October of last year, after he swallowed razor blades.

On camera, he showed the self-inflicted white scars worming their way up his tattooed left arm. His memories of his times in observation cells are uncomfortably vivid: no clothes, no bedding, no sound, no communication with the outside world.
“There’s no help there,” he said.
Toutsaint doesn’t think anyone should be held in these forms of solitary.
“They should shut it down. Permanently.… It’s torture.”

stories.title: B.C. tribunal weighs in on who gets Walter the dog after women split
stories.summary: "When pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have 'custody'."
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
When couples split up, who gets the family pooch is more about money than love, according to a civil resolution tribunal out of British Columbia.

The tribunal heard the case of former romantic partners Misty Donovan and Makenzie Jade Murray who ended their two-year relationship in April 2024. The two women shared their dog, Walter, for another 10 months while living apart. Then in February 2025, Murray kept Walter and refused to bring him to Donovan’s home, where he’d been spending weekends.

Donovan asked the tribunal for an order requiring Murray to return Walter, who appears to be a Boston Terrier in their social media photos of him.

“While she claims $2,500, it is clear Ms. Donovan wants the dog, not monetary compensation,” said tribunal member Alissa Reynolds in the Sept. 23 decision that declares a dog, though loved like a child, is not in fact a child.

The tribunal’s task was not to award custody, Reynolds said, but to divide property, albeit nothing like a sofa or an espresso maker.

“The courts have recognized that animals are a unique form of personal property because they are living creatures and not inanimate objects,” she wrote in the decision.

“This means when pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have ‘custody’ of it.”

Relevant factors to consider, Reynolds said, include “who bought and selected the pet, who attended its veterinary appointments, who paid for the pet’s needs, who licensed it, and how the parties viewed ownership.”

Murray chose Walter, noted the adjudicator.

“She provided her messages to the breeder that show this. She says Ms. Donovan was not involved in selecting Walter, and Ms. Donovan did not deny that. So, I find this factor favours Ms. Murray.”

But Reynolds found that Donovan purchased the dog for $2,000, noting she “provided bank statements and e-transfer details that show she paid the breeder.”

That favours Donovan, said the adjudicator.

Text messages and veterinarian records show that before Murray refused Donovan access to Walter, both women “attended Walter’s vet appointments, together and individually,” said the decision.

“However, Ms. Donovan says she was the one who remembered to book Walter’s regular checkups and follow-ups and advised Ms. Murray when they were. Ms. Murray does not deny that.”

The evidence shows that Donovan attended more of Walter’s appointments without Murray, and that Murray only took Walter on one emergency vet visit this past February when she was caring for the dog.

“However, Ms. Donovan attended all the follow-up visits. For that reason, I find this factor favours Ms. Donovan slightly,” Reynolds said.

Both women “claimed that they paid for the majority of Walter’s needs,” said the decision.

“This is complicated by the fact that Ms. Murray had three other pets and often paid for their food and other supplies together.”

But after reviewing all the financial information both women provided, Reynolds said it shows that Donovan “paid nearly three times as much” as Murray for Walter’s vet bills, pet food and supplies. “I find this factor heavily favours Ms. Donovan.”

Murray testified that her “messages with the breeder show the parties always intended that she would own Walter,” said the decision.

“She relies on her first message that said, ‘I’m very interested in a puppy,’ and a later message when she said, ‘I have been hoping to find Pearl (another pet) a little friend.’ However, that same message thread shows she also referred to both parties adopting Walter, as follows: ‘We would like to proceed with adopting…,’ ‘A bit about us…,’ ‘We are going to be in Victoria…I was wondering if we could stop by quickly and meet Walter,’ and ‘Would we be able to come pick him up…we are so excited!’”

Reynolds found that the messages show that Murray “intended that the parties would own Walter jointly.”

That’s also supported by their “agreement to share Walter after they split up,” said the decision.

Reynolds found both women “care about Walter, spend a lot of time enriching his life, and both are capable of taking care of his needs and health. So, I find this factor does not favour either party.”

Reynolds concluded “that the balance of the factors favours Ms. Donovan.”

She ordered Murray to give Walter to Donovan within 30 days.

content_blocks.text: When couples split up, who gets the family pooch is more about money than love, according to a civil resolution tribunal out of British Columbia.

The tribunal heard the case of former romantic partners Misty Donovan and Makenzie Jade Murray who ended their two-year relationship in April 2024. The two women shared their dog, Walter, for another 10 months while living apart. Then in February 2025, Murray kept Walter and refused to bring him to Donovan’s home, where he’d been spending weekends.
Donovan asked the tribunal for an order requiring Murray to return Walter, who appears to be a Boston Terrier in their social media photos of him.

“While she claims $2,500, it is clear Ms. Donovan wants the dog, not monetary compensation,” said tribunal member Alissa Reynolds in the Sept. 23 decision that declares a dog, though loved like a child, is not in fact a child.
The tribunal’s task was not to award custody, Reynolds said, but to divide property, albeit nothing like a sofa or an espresso maker.
“The courts have recognized that animals are a unique form of personal property because they are living creatures and not inanimate objects,” she wrote in the decision.
“This means when pet-owners separate and there is a dispute about the pet, the question is who owns the pet rather than who should have ‘custody’ of it.”

Relevant factors to consider, Reynolds said, include “who bought and selected the pet, who attended its veterinary appointments, who paid for the pet’s needs, who licensed it, and how the parties viewed ownership.”
Murray chose Walter, noted the adjudicator.
“She provided her messages to the breeder that show this. She says Ms. Donovan was not involved in selecting Walter, and Ms. Donovan did not deny that. So, I find this factor favours Ms. Murray.”
But Reynolds found that Donovan purchased the dog for $2,000, noting she “provided bank statements and e-transfer details that show she paid the breeder.”
That favours Donovan, said the adjudicator.
Text messages and veterinarian records show that before Murray refused Donovan access to Walter, both women “attended Walter’s vet appointments, together and individually,” said the decision.
“However, Ms. Donovan says she was the one who remembered to book Walter’s regular checkups and follow-ups and advised Ms. Murray when they were. Ms. Murray does not deny that.”
The evidence shows that Donovan attended more of Walter’s appointments without Murray, and that Murray only took Walter on one emergency vet visit this past February when she was caring for the dog.
“However, Ms. Donovan attended all the follow-up visits. For that reason, I find this factor favours Ms. Donovan slightly,” Reynolds said.
Both women “claimed that they paid for the majority of Walter’s needs,” said the decision.
“This is complicated by the fact that Ms. Murray had three other pets and often paid for their food and other supplies together.”

But after reviewing all the financial information both women provided, Reynolds said it shows that Donovan “paid nearly three times as much” as Murray for Walter’s vet bills, pet food and supplies. “I find this factor heavily favours Ms. Donovan.”
Murray testified that her “messages with the breeder show the parties always intended that she would own Walter,” said the decision.

“She relies on her first message that said, ‘I’m very interested in a puppy,’ and a later message when she said, ‘I have been hoping to find Pearl (another pet) a little friend.’ However, that same message thread shows she also referred to both parties adopting Walter, as follows: ‘We would like to proceed with adopting…,’ ‘A bit about us…,’ ‘We are going to be in Victoria…I was wondering if we could stop by quickly and meet Walter,’ and ‘Would we be able to come pick him up…we are so excited!’”
Reynolds found that the messages show that Murray “intended that the parties would own Walter jointly.”
That’s also supported by their “agreement to share Walter after they split up,” said the decision.

Reynolds found both women “care about Walter, spend a lot of time enriching his life, and both are capable of taking care of his needs and health. So, I find this factor does not favour either party.”
Reynolds concluded “that the balance of the factors favours Ms. Donovan.”
She ordered Murray to give Walter to Donovan within 30 days.

stories.title: Say its name
stories.summary: Canada’s leaders need to denounce not just the crime but the ideology behind antisemitic attacks
stories.author: Marcus Gee
stories.content:
Authorities have reacted to last Sunday’s antisemitic attack in Belleville, Ont., in all the usual and necessary ways: with stern expressions of abhorrence and promises to protect Canada’s shaken Jewish community. What they have failed to do is to identify or challenge the ideology that is feeding the wave of hate sweeping this country.

That ideology is anti-Zionism.

Zionism is the idea that the Jewish people have the right to a national homeland: Israel. Anti-Zionism, as it has evolved, is the idea that Israel is an alien, illegitimate, colonial state imposed by violence on the Middle East.

We don’t know whether the ex-soldier who opened fire on the Belleville synagogue held such beliefs or what other dark motivations he May have had. And of course anti-Zionists themselves insist that they deplore antisemitism and any kind of violence directed at Jews. But it is obvious by now that the bitter, hateful rhetoric they use is fueling both. Painting Israel as a malevolent force pours gasoline on the ever-flickering flame on antisemitism.

Belleville’s tiny Jewish community vows to carry on after attack

Anti-Zionism has a long history, going back at least to the foundation of Israel. Like its older cousin, antisemitism, it is both stubborn and mutable, expressed in many different ways. Israel is an “apartheid” state. Israel is a racist “ethno-state.” Israel is not a state at all, but a “Zionist entity.”

It is not the same as antisemitism – you can be anti-Zionist without hating all Jews – but the two share the idea that their target is the cause of great evil in the world.

The Israeli statesman Abba Eban put it this way in 1975, when the United Nations General Assembly adopted a resolution calling Zionism a form of racism. “Classical antisemitism denies the equal rights of Jews as citizens within society. Anti-Zionism denies the equal rights of the Jewish people to its lawful sovereignty within the community of nations. The common principle in the two cases is discrimination.”

Half a century later, this species of discrimination is booming. “ Globalize the intifada ” is its war cry. Pop stars spout it. Famous actors embrace it. That Israel is the principal bad guy of the Middle East, if not the world, is conventional wisdom on university campuses.

Even the head of a major Canadian political party, the NDP, feels free to accuse Israel of the worst crime in the world as if it were an established fact. Avi Lewis, who is Jewish, marked Yom Kippur by lecturing fellow Jews that “we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name.”

Since the Oct. 7 terror attack on Israel and the start of the Gaza war nearly three years ago, Jews have come under threat in just about every corner of the world.

It often seems as if nowhere is safe. Not a synagogue in Manchester. Not a bus stop in Jerusalem. Not a beach party in Sydney. Not even a little synagogue in Belleville. Only the heroism of two police officers prevented that attack from ending in another massacre of innocents. “You are going to die for the Jews,” the gunman shouted at one of the officers before opening fire.

Opinion: The Belleville attack was a warning shot for the antisemitic attacks Canada has let fester

The bullet holes left in the synagogue’s stained-glass windows show what a near thing this was. A night of broken glass in a quiet corner of Southern Ontario. This is where we are.

“Last year, over two-thirds of all religion-motivated hate crimes were directed at Jewish Canadians, who make up only one per cent of the population,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said recently.

In a major address on the issue, he quoted the Jewish prophets, condemned “the scourge of antisemitism” and listed all the things his government is doing to combat it, but said nothing about Oct. 7, nothing about the anti-Zionists who March chanting through quiet Jewish neighbourhoods and wave their Palestinian flags in front of synagogues.

It was as if the haters came out of nowhere. In fact, they spring directly from the notion that Israel is to blame for all the horrors that are happening in its troubled corner of the world. In the guise of criticizing Israel, they demonize it.

It is one thing to call out Israel’s government for abusing Palestinian prisoners, tolerating violence by West Bank settlers or bombing Gaza into rubble; it’s quite another to call it a bloodthirsty imperial juggernaut bent on conquest.

It is time for Canada’s leaders to denounce such lies. It is time for them to name the twisted ideology behind the wave of hate that found expression in Belleville this week. Its name is anti-Zionism.

stories.title: Anand tells UN that Canada seeks ‘strategic autonomy,’ relies on civil debate
stories.summary: FForeign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Canada’s foreign policy is guided by establishing autonomy in strategic fields to limit superpower coercion, along with aspirations to lead middle powers.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa —Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Canada’s foreign policy is guided by establishing autonomy in strategic fields to limit superpower coercion, along with aspirations to lead middle powers.

“Great powers are walking away from global economic co-operation, dismantling economic integration,” Anand said Saturday in Canada’s annual address to the United Nations General Assembly.

“In the face of this rupture, Canada’s goal is to achieve greater strategic autonomy,” she said at the green marble dais.

Anand’s speech did not directly mention American tariffs nor last month’s collapse of trade talks between Canada and Washington, and she instead mentioned work to diversify trade beyond North America.

Her speech echoed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s rhetoric over the past year about middle powers forging deeper ties and working with countries on shared goals, including states that aren’t close partners.

She said that involves emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence production and energy — as well as the rule of law and respect for sovereignty.

“We are facing serious challenges in the global order,” Anand said.

“We will lead other middle powers to act collectively and decisively, because middle powers are playing a key role in building the framework for the new international order — which is being established as we speak.”

Anand used an analogy that she said comes from her roots in rural Nova Scotia. “The tide does not wait; you must move with it.”

She suggested countries form “long-term partnerships” with Canada for security and prosperity.

“Rather than yearn for days gone by, let us together take this opportunity to do right by our people, and build together,” she said.

Anand said state sovereignty “has been treated with disdain” but that Canada will defend that principle, and work toward stability and common rules.

She said that is why Canada is calling for a just peace in Ukraine, self-determination for Palestinians and Israelis, and an end to hate-based violence.

“We were tragically reminded of the scourge of antisemitism again, when a gunman carried out an attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont.,” she told the UN.

“Canada is an open, pluralistic society, with a public square full of robust and civil debate. Our success is underpinned by this civility, by our democratic institutions, and by respect for our differences,” she said.

Minister of Foreign Affairs Anita Anand of Canada speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Heather Khalifa)

For the second year in a row, Anand spoke instead of Carney, who was at the UN from Monday to Wednesday but whose officials said he could not deliver Canada’s address due to scheduling issues.

The UN schedules foreign ministers later in the rotation during the annual high-level week, with weekday, daytime speeches reserved for heads of state and government. Anand spoke late Saturday afternoon.

Anand also voiced support for the Nato alliance, amid an increase in warnings from European leaders about Russian hybrid attacks. She cited a recent defence agreement between Denmark, its autonomous territory Greenland and U.S. President Donald Trump.

“This agreement is yet another reminder that North America and Europe are stronger together. And as a founding member of Nato, our commitment to the transatlantic alliance is ironclad,” Anand said.

To that end, Anand reiterated work being done to better secure the Canadian Arctic, saying this is occurring in lockstep with Indigenous Peoples.

Anand said Canada supports the International Criminal Court amid Washington’s quest to dismantle the institution. Her comments come as Canadian critics argue Ottawa is not calling out American coercion, including the sanctioning of a Canadian judge for her work at the ICC.

She reiterated Canada’s bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council, through a vote expected in one year.

Anand said Ottawa is pursuing “values-based realism” while advocating for democracy in Iran, the return of Ukrainian children kidnapped by Russia and work to end Haiti’s gruesome gang crisis.

Rescue workers put out a fire on the roof of an office building damaged by a Russian drone strike, in Kyiv, Ukraine, Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka)

Her speech mentioned gender equality, Lgbtq+ rights, Sudan’s civil war, Hamas attacks on Israel, Israeli settler violence against Palestinians and safe approaches to artificial intelligence.

Anand also said Canada is ready to work with whoever UN members elect as their next secretary-general, referring in French to the role in the masculine and feminine titles.

That comment followed the Trudeau government calling for a woman to be the next secretary-general, in September 2024. The Carney government has not repeated that call.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 26, 2026.

content_blocks.text: Ottawa —Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Canada’s foreign policy is guided by establishing autonomy in strategic fields to limit superpower coercion, along with aspirations to lead middle powers.
“Great powers are walking away from global economic co-operation, dismantling economic integration,” Anand said Saturday in Canada’s annual address to the United Nations General Assembly.
“In the face of this rupture, Canada’s goal is to achieve greater strategic autonomy,” she said at the green marble dais.

Anand’s speech did not directly mention American tariffs nor last month’s collapse of trade talks between Canada and Washington, and she instead mentioned work to diversify trade beyond North America.

Her speech echoed Prime Minister Mark Carney’s rhetoric over the past year about middle powers forging deeper ties and working with countries on shared goals, including states that aren’t close partners.
She said that involves emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence production and energy — as well as the rule of law and respect for sovereignty.
“We are facing serious challenges in the global order,” Anand said.

“We will lead other middle powers to act collectively and decisively, because middle powers are playing a key role in building the framework for the new international order — which is being established as we speak.”
Anand used an analogy that she said comes from her roots in rural Nova Scotia. “The tide does not wait; you must move with it.”
She suggested countries form “long-term partnerships” with Canada for security and prosperity.
“Rather than yearn for days gone by, let us together take this opportunity to do right by our people, and build together,” she said.
Anand said state sovereignty “has been treated with disdain” but that Canada will defend that principle, and work toward stability and common rules.
She said that is why Canada is calling for a just peace in Ukraine, self-determination for Palestinians and Israelis, and an end to hate-based violence.
“We were tragically reminded of the scourge of antisemitism again, when a gunman carried out an attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont.,” she told the UN.

“Canada is an open, pluralistic society, with a public square full of robust and civil debate. Our success is underpinned by this civility, by our democratic institutions, and by respect for our differences,” she said.

For the second year in a row, Anand spoke instead of Carney, who was at the UN from Monday to Wednesday but whose officials said he could not deliver Canada’s address due to scheduling issues.

The UN schedules foreign ministers later in the rotation during the annual high-level week, with weekday, daytime speeches reserved for heads of state and government. Anand spoke late Saturday afternoon.

Anand also voiced support for the Nato alliance, amid an increase in warnings from European leaders about Russian hybrid attacks. She cited a recent defence agreement between Denmark, its autonomous territory Greenland and U.S. President Donald Trump.
“This agreement is yet another reminder that North America and Europe are stronger together. And as a founding member of Nato, our commitment to the transatlantic alliance is ironclad,” Anand said.

stories.title: Lorne Doerkson takes the reins of B.C. Conservatives, with a party to rebuild and election ahead
stories.summary: Doerkson has been handed two daunting tasks: to restore order to his party and persuade a skeptical electorate
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Mike Hager
stories.content:
Lorne Doerkson spent his birthday on Thursday doing media interviews as the new leader of the Conservative Party of B.C., a role he did not seek out but was suddenly appointed to last week, and that could see him elected premier by Halloween.

The two-term Cariboo-Chilcotin MLA was named interim leader of the beleaguered party last Sunday, after the sudden resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay amid a caucus revolt. Conservative MLAs selected Mr. Doerkson to replace her and the party’s board approved.

Mr. Doerkson, however, was in South Africa for a conference last weekend and learned of the developments during a layover in Amsterdam as he was travelling home.

“I had a call asking if I would accept the nomination,” Mr. Doerkson, 58, said in an interview between collecting signatures to get on the ballot and delivering items to the Clinton Food Bank.

“I knew the seriousness of the situation, of course, with rumours of a snap election being called, so at that point, I said yes.”

Opinion: Is David Eby about to gamble away his government?

His unplanned ascension caps a remarkable few weeks for a party battered by defections, controversy and internal warfare. On Friday, the provincial NDP seized on another complication, accusing the Conservatives of failing to make clear to voters that keeping Mr. Doerkson on as leader permanently would require a change to the party’s constitution backed by two-thirds of the same fractious membership that elected Ms. Findlay.

A spokesperson for the B.C. Conservatives did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Doerkson, a former newspaper publisher, small-business owner and bareback rodeo rider, has been handed two daunting tasks: to restore order to his party and persuade a skeptical electorate that Conservatives are not only ready to govern, but offer a better alternative to the incumbent NDP.

The Conservatives enter the race stronger than their recent turmoil might suggest. An Angus Reid Institute poll released on Thursday, two days after provincial NDP Leader David Eby called an early election for Oct. 24, put the Conservatives at 43 per cent support among decided and leaning voters – eight percentage points ahead of the NDP.

The results appear to reflect the frustration with Mr. Eby calling the election two years early, the institute said.

But the same poll captured the challenge confronting the new Conservative Leader: A majority (56 per cent) of respondents believe his party is “not ready to govern B.C.”

Mr. Doerkson himself remains an unknown entity to most – a factor that could be either hurtful or helpful, said Hamish Telford, a political scientist and professor at the University of the Fraser Valley.

“He’s a bit of a blank slate, and you can read into him whatever you want,” he said. “And he seems like a decent bloke.”

Mr. Doerkson’s appointment drew positive comments online, many from constituents who praised him for the daily video updates he provided during this summer’s wildfires. Others pointed to his votes to allow the introduction of bills to repeal B.C.’s Human Rights Code, and restrict gender-affirming care for minors and prevent students from changing pronouns at school. (Mr. Doerkson has said the votes allowed debate and did not signify support.)

British Columbia Premier David Eby has called an Oct. 24 election that he is framing as an urgent necessity to respond to the threat posed by U.S. President Donald Trump and his trade war, calling it an 'existential moment' for the province.

The Canadian Press

At an introductory press conference earlier this week, he said his No. 1 priority if the Conservatives formed government would be to repeal the province’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act . The legislation passed unanimously in 2019, with the help of three current Conservative candidates who were then MLAs: Peter Milobar, Teresa Wat and Ian Paton.

He added in an interview that the Conservatives would also prioritize the broader economy, health care and crime.

Mr. Doerkson also pushed back against Mr. Eby’s effort to make U.S. President Donald Trump a central theme of the campaign. The NDP Leader has spoken repeatedly of the existential threat posed by Mr. Trump’s trade war, casting the Conservatives as Maple Maga and his NDP as the only party able to stand up to him.

“He’s going to have to find some new material,” Mr. Doerkson said. “I’ll tell you right now: I think Donald Trump is an absolute bully, and the reality is that David Eby and his team have had an opportunity to strengthen this province and have chosen not to.”

Prof. Telford said the question of how the Conservatives will do extends beyond Mr. Doerkson himself to the ideological divisions and internal power struggles that have consumed the party and its two last leaders. Ms. Findlay lasted just 113 days – less than four months – before stepping down after an exodus of MLAs and a bitter revolt over her leadership. John Rustad, before her, resigned last December after an extended period of strife within the party, and to avoid a further “civil war.”

That conflict reflects a broader shift in B.C. conservatism, Prof. Telford said. Modern conservative populists are increasingly motivated by divisive social issues, whereas centre-right coalitions once bridged differences on social issues by focusing on shared fiscal and economic priorities.

The snap election and a new leader have, for now, brought those factions back under one roof. But the fault lines that so bitterly fractured the party remain, Prof. Telford said.

“They can probably hold it together for 30 days,” he said. “The question is: Could they hold it together if they form a government?”

The big B.C. reshuffle continues ahead of snap election

Mr. Doerkson also acknowledged the need to maintain order. Asked how he would handle a member who made inflammatory or otherwise unacceptable remarks, he drew a distinction between inadvertent mistakes and deliberate conduct.

“I think there has to be, obviously, some control around that for sure,” he said, adding that he would assess such incidents individually.

Mr. Doerkson began making phone calls the moment he arrived back in Canada from his conference. He contacted MLAs who had left the party, including the 13 who exited as a result of Ms. Findlay’s leadership, and invited them back.

“My pitch, really, was that we’ve got to be unified. Let’s get back together.”

Most took him up on his offer. Mr. Rustad, expelled from the caucus by Ms. Findlay the previous Friday, accepted the invitation to rejoin on Monday, but announced two days later he would not seek re-election.

Elenore Sturko, a former RCMP officer whom Mr. Rustad booted from caucus last September, said she would not return because too many members hold bigoted and conspiratorial views.

Ms. Sturko, who is now leader of the fledgling CentreBC party, said she likes Mr. Doerkson from their time serving in the caucus of the former BC Liberal party. But she said his rise to leadership is indicative of the instability typical of the Conservatives.

“I do have respect for Lorne Doerkson, but I can tell you that he’s been there the whole time, and yet the chaos within the party has existed during that time as well,” she said.

How Mr. Doerkson says he intends to keep the newly reunited caucus together starts with a philosophy more conciliatory than commanding: Listen and leave room for disagreement. He described himself as broad-minded, and says he subscribes to the maxim of “two ears and one mouth.”

“I can dig in on something that I might believe in, but I can certainly, through debate, have my mind changed,” he said. “I think nothing happens without a good conversation.”

Mr. Doerkson could also face another test of party unity over his own leadership. On Wednesday, he said he intended to remain leader if elected premier; however, because the party’s constitution bars an interim leader from seeking the permanent position, members would have to amend the rules by a two-thirds vote.

The announcement has already rankled some members, who argue that it is undemocratic to effectively install Mr. Doerkson just months after Ms. Findlay was elected.

NDP candidate Niki Sharma, who was attorney-general in the last cabinet, held a news conference on Friday to criticize the Conservatives for not explaining the internal votes needed to cement Mr. Doerkson.

“The bottom line is the B.C. Conservatives have no way of guaranteeing who would be the Premier if they won this election,” she said.

Prof. Telford said the move risks deepening the alienation of grassroots members who already believe party elites overturned their choice of leader. That poses a particular problem for a populist party whose appeal relies partly on the idea of ordinary people challenging elites, he said.

Mr. Doerkson acknowledged that the membership had elected Ms. Findlay.

“But the reality is, Kerry-Lynne resigned, and it left us in a position that we needed to address immediately,” he said. “With a looming rumour of a potential snap election, whatever were we to do?”

stories.title: How to clean up the messy human problem endangering bears
stories.summary: Human-bear encounters are rising across Canada, driven in part by bears being drawn to food and garbage left by people at campsites and parks
stories.author: Erin Anderssen
stories.content:
Trinity Nicholson was sitting by a fire at Ontario’s Cyprus Lake Campground in late July, with her father and two friends, listening to car alarms going off in the distance, when she heard rustling in the woods behind her. Turning around, she locked eyes with a massive black bear close enough that she could reach out and touch his nose.

“I froze,” says Ms. Nicholson, a 30-year-old nurse from Burlington, Ont. “I was staring at it, and it was staring back at me, and for a couple of seconds I was in shock, because I had no idea what to do.”

She leapt out of her chair and said, “There’s a bear,” to her dad, who thought she was joking until he pointed a flashlight into the trees. Instantly, everyone was yelling, leaping out of their chairs to get to the far side of the fire, the bear watching the commotion from the shadows. “I’m crying at this point,” says Ms. Nicholson. Wanting to run, knowing she shouldn’t, her mind raced through options. They decided to fast-walk to their car about three metres way.

Ms. Nicholson’s husband, sleeping inside the locked car with the keys, awoke to shouting and banging – “Let us in! There’s a bear! We’re not joking!” He opened the door, they scrambled inside, while the bear sniffed around their campsite.

This summer, it became clear that Ontario’s Bruce Peninsula National Park had a messy human problem. The park is perched on the cliffs of the Niagara Escarpment, flanked by cottage country about 300 kilometres from Toronto. Camping reservations at Cyprus Lake are snatched up each spring “in a mad rush like getting Taylor Swift tickets,” as Ms. Nicholson put it, and by summer, the area is filled with grilling, picnicking city-dwellers.

So it’s not surprising that somewhere in his travels, a particularly clever and single-minded bear had discovered a tasty meal – perhaps ketchup abandoned on a picnic table, scraps on the ground or a marshmallow by the fire – and determined that the two-legged visitors to its home offered easier and more mouth-watering food sources than grass and berry bushes.

Encounters between humans and bears have been steadily rising in Canada over the last 10 years, according to national Parks Canada data. In 2024, the most recent year available, Parks Canada staff managed 423 “co-existence incidents” involving black bears and “unnatural attractants,” more than twice as many as 2010. Human food and garbage are regular enticements. But as residential areas push farther into bear territory, encounters increasingly involve gardens, lawns and fruit trees.

At the Cyprus Lake Campground this summer, park staff repeatedly reminded campers to clean their sites bare, to pack away even toothpaste and scented soap in their cars. They supplied “bear resistant” bins to store food, and banned cooking after dark. They policed campsites and confiscated condiments and leftovers carelessly left on picnic tables.

Twice, they trapped and transported the same 300-pound male bear deeper into the park. But bears can smell grease on a grill from kilometres away. Each time, he returned.

The bear that Ms. Nicholson encountered never seemed aggressive, she says. “As scary as it was in the moment, he didn’t seem interested in us at all.” The experienced campers had cleaned up their steak dinner and stowed their food and garbage in the trunk of the car. Startled by a noise, the bear eventually lumbered off, seeking snacks at its next stop.

But as weeks passed, he grew bolder: pulling down the windows of cars and climbing inside, prying open the hardtops of pick-up trucks for treats and overturning the bear-resistant bins so the loosely latched lids flipped open and spilled gourmet treasure.

Finally, park staff made the rare decision to close the campsite to safeguard both bear and human life – a closing now extended to Oct. 31.

For the last few weeks, every time they see the “the individual” – as staff call the bear, avoiding a more sentimental name – they yell and clang pots, and shoot bean bags, trying to restore a fear of humans greater than its appetite for barbecue leftovers.

“We want to give the best possible chance of a good outcome for the bear,” says Camille Girard-Ruel, the park’s superintendent.

Sadly, these hazing efforts rarely work, says Martyn Obbard, a research scientist emeritus with the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, and an expert on the black bears of the Bruce Peninsula. “I certainly applaud the efforts to save the bear.”

But too often, the inevitable end is a dead bear. This month, a black bear habituated to approaching humans for food was euthanized in a Wyoming national park. “We need to be clear,” the park said in a Facebook post, “this bear was lethally removed because of poor decisions made by park visitors.”

And last year, in Yellowstone National Park, a black bear had to be put down after it repeatedly outsmarted food-storage measures – much like the one at Cyprus Lake.

“We underestimate the intelligence of these animals,” says Dr. Obbard. “When we give them easy access to high energy food and garbage, or even raiding coolers, they’re going to exploit that. And they’re damn good at it.”

A favourite example of bear ingenuity happened one summer, while Dr. Obbard was conducting research in Algonquin Provincial Park, in south-central Ontario. A black bear discovered that the tall white box on a cottage porch contained a delicious, chilled buffet. With the owners away at work, the bear leisurely visited one property after another, opening the outdoor refrigerators – until, Dr. Obbard says, it spotted the same white box through a kitchen window and smashed its way inside.

Ideally, the Bruce Peninsula bear in question wakes up next spring, discovers a bounty of berries and clover and beetles, and never thinks of peanut butter again. But hibernation doesn’t erase a bear’s memory, says Dr. Obbard. More likely, a whiff of burgers on the grill will have it haunting the Cypress Lake campground next year.

In a small B.C. town, a grizzly family stirs unease

Human-animal encounters like this raise a philosophical question, Dr. Obbard suggests: Having trespassed into its territory and caused the problem, what’s our responsibility to a single bear? “Some would say we do everything we can, and I would agree,” he says. “But everything we can May not be enough.”

In the end, the only bear-saving solution is prevention.

For decades, Dr. Obbard gave bear talks on best practices: finish cooking before dark, seal away toothpaste and soap, avoid sleeping in the same clothes you wore cooking, never feed human food to wildlife of any kind. And double-check bags and supplies. While backcountry camping with his family years ago, a nocturnal bear appeared at Dr. Obbard’s well-cleaned site, sniffing at his backpack. Jammed in the bottom, he found a forgotten, unused tea bag.

Bruce Peninsula park closely borders residences and tourist attractions that Ms. Girard-Ruel says also need to follow the same bear-safe practices around their houses and buildings – especially since the bear can’t be easily relocated.

He’s one of a few hundred genetically distinct bears living on the peninsula. Although not officially endangered, their low population and forced proximity to human development makes them vulnerable. It’s not clear how easily they’d adapt to a new location: Rather than using hollow logs and brush piles like other black bears, they mostly hibernate in limestone crevices along the Niagara Escarpment.

Kathleen Bowron and her husband slept at the Cyprus Lake Campground on Aug. 27 – the last evening before the park closed to overnight guests. Ms. Bowron says they listened for hours to screaming and car horns and the rumble of responding staff vehicles while a bear ravaged a site nearby – until, after midnight, she fell asleep wearing earplugs. She wasn’t worried: Their own campsite was bare of temptations.

“We’ve gotten used to be an apex predator,” she says. “And not many people understand that we still share space with wildlife. We need to protect it, as well as ourselves.”

At the end of the day, Ms. Nicholson says, “We’re invading their space, so we need to learn to be respectful. It’s their home, and we’re just guests.”

stories.title: Canadians more united despite separatist sentiment in Alberta, Quebec: Ipsos
stories.summary: Overwhelming majority of Canadians want Alberta to remain a part of a unified Canada, would vote for their province to remain as well.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
An overwhelming majority of Canadians want Alberta to remain part of a unified Canada and would vote for their own province to do the same, according to new data from Ipsos exclusively for Global News.

A full 81 per cent of respondents outside of Alberta said they want the Wild Rose province to remain part of Canada, with just nine per cent saying they want the province to leave.

The desire for Alberta to remain in Canada was weaker in Quebec, which is having their own conversation about independence. But 69 per cent of respondents in that province still wanted Alberta to reject separation.

Overall, Ipsos said their data suggests that Canadians are feeling more united despite separatist sentiment taking up the oxygen in Quebec and Alberta.

“The country’s more united right now, especially around the (trade) war with the United States … and dealing with Donald Trump and other issues, than they were in 2019,” said Gregory Jack, a senior vice president with Ipsos Global Affairs.

“(That’s) despite the fact that, you know, it feels like the country is really divided with a potential referendum in Quebec and a referendum here in Alberta.”

Just 16 per cent of respondents nationally — excluding Albertans — felt that their provinces would be better off if they separated from Canada, and just 22 per cent of Albertans agreed. Both numbers are down since Ipsos asked the same question in 2019, when 33 per cent of Albertans said they’d be better off alone.

Only 23 per cent of Canadians outside of Alberta said they felt less committed to Canada than a few years ago, with 28 per cent of Albertans saying they felt that way. Again, the percentage of Albertans who agreed with the sentiment was down sharply since 2019.

Canadians outside of Alberta were less likely than those in Alberta to feel their province was not getting its fair share from Ottawa, with just 26 per cent of respondents saying their province doesn’t get a fair shake. Nearly one in two Albertans (48 per cent) told the pollster their province didn’t get a fair deal from Confederation.

Among Albertans, that number is down from 51 per cent in January 2026 and 65 per cent in 2019.

“The major outlier is the measure on whether the province gets its fair share from Confederation, where Albertans remain more likely than other Canadians to believe this is the case,” Ipsos said in its polling results.

“The data suggest Albertans, while feeling closer to the national average on many measures, still want a discussion on benefits from Confederation, but that it doesn’t necessarily translate to desire to separate.”

Albertans will vote in a referendum next month that asks, among other questions, if they want to start the legally required process to hold a formal vote on separation. A victory for the separatists on Oct. 19 would kick off campaigning in earnest for both the separatists and those who want the province to remain within Canada.

Ipsos found that a strong majority (70 per cent) of Albertans want to remain part of Canada, while 20 per cent want to hold a referendum on separation. But Ipsos found that the separatist vote may be softer than believed.

If the province moves to holding a binding referendum on separation, the number of respondents who would vote to stay rises to 84 per cent, while just 16 per cent would vote for separation. That suggests more people want to hold a referendum than want to actually leave the country.

“Rural Albertans, older Albertans and male Albertans are more likely to say that they want to go and younger Allbertans, more urban Albertans here in Calgary or in Edmonton are more likely to see that they’re going to want to stay,” Jack said.

“We should see perhaps some more movement in the next couple of weeks as the referendum gets closer, but a lot people have a position on this. I think that they took it earlier in the campaign and they haven’t really changed their position whether they’re on the ‘yes’ side or the ‘no’ side.”

Both Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberals and Pierre Poilievre’s Conservative Party are committed to campaigning for Alberta to remain a province in Canada — although Ipsos’ had some surprising numbers about which politician might be better suited to arguing that position with Albertans.

In more bad news for Poilievre, Ipsos’ findings suggest Carney is more popular than he is in Alberta — traditionally the Conservatives’ heartland, and the province Poilievre now represents in the House of Commons.

Just over half (51 per cent) of Albertans said they had a favourable view of Carney, compared to 35 per cent who viewed the prime minister unfavourably. For Poilievre, support was more divided — with 44 per cent of Albertans viewing him favourably, compared to 40 per cent unfavourably.

“That’s something we don’t often see in Alberta,” Jack noted.

“(Carney) hasn’t played a key role so far in the referendum, but obviously these numbers suggest that he could in the future.”

The Ipsos poll was conducted for Global News between Sept. 18 and 22, and surveyed 1,500 voting-aged Canadians — 600 in Alberta, and 900 in the rest of Canada. A similar poll of 1,500 Canadians would be considered accurate within 3.1 percentage points. Regional and demographic breakdowns are less accurate than overall numbers.

stories.title: Belleville shooting a wake-up call for Canadians, survivor says in new statement
stories.summary: Sharlene Weitzman: "This is about Jew hatred rearing its ugly head .... We need leaders who incite safety, not hatred."
stories.author: Special to National Post
stories.content:
Sharlene Weitzman was among the small group of Jews who’d gathered Sunday evening at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., to worship on the faith’s holiest day, Yom Kippur, when a gunman arrived and opened fire.

She was there with her partner, Jennifer Aronson and her son, Finn Luke Weitzman.

The 59-year-old forensic social worker told her courageous story to National Post this week not to be a “spokesperson” for the tragedy that left the suspected shooter dead, a Belleville Police Service officer in hospital, and Canada’s Jewish population again questioning their safety.

She spoke candidly because she refused “to miss the opportunity to bear witness” to the crisis of Jew hatred in Canada and around the world.

“Stop telling us Jews that we’re overreacting. Stop telling us it’s not antisemitism, ‘It’s not all about you. Oh, where there’s smoke, there must be fire. If people hate you, there’s a reason,’” she said.

“But I’m not Benjamin Netanyahu. I’m not the leader of the government. I’m not Mark Carney. I’m just a Jewish mom trying to raise my family in the community that we’ve been in for 25, 30 years.”

Weitzman had more she wanted to say, with the following statement:

Thank you to Hashem and to both officers of the Belleville Police Service who saved my family’s lives this past Sunday, Yom Kippur 5787.

The BPS have been remarkable. Having experienced this traumatic event together, I believe they have a new understanding of the life-and-death challenges not only the police but Jews face daily. By Shekina’s hand and the officers’ heroics, there was only one casualty: the shooter. We pray for his family. They have suffered great loss.

We encourage you to support the GoFundMe for Constable Smith and his family as he faces the road to recovery. We pray for his full recovery.

I am speaking today to bear witness to Jew Hatred around the world. The Sons of Jacob shooting was not an isolated incident.

Your silence is harming us. Please take it upon yourselves to learn about the events of the massacre in Israel committed by Hamas and Gazan citizens on October 7. The massacre that began the current war.

There is a war in the Middle East. All wars are ugly and dangerous. Innocent people die. There is a war on Jews around the globe; it is dangerous and ugly, and innocent people are dying.

It is not, however, an accident.

Warren Kinsella’s recent award-winning book, The Hidden Hand, devastatingly traces the information war against Jews that has been waged across the world. The information war is working when Canadians are incited to kill Canadians because of their faith and connection to Israel.

Hatred grows in silence. Speaking out against it is an integral part of our Canadian social contract.

We can rebuild the Canada I grew up in better, bolder, more modern and safer.

A year ago, my son was in a safe room in Eilat, Israel, facing Houthi missile attacks. He was under attack for being a Jew. He was in the Jewish homeland, Israel.

This year he faced being shot at with a high-calibre shotgun. He was under attack for being a Jew. For being a Jew in Canada.

He is a third-generation Canadian Jew. Neither of his homelands is safe. Where can my son be safe? What mother wants to ask that question?

Jew hatred is not confined to a war over the land of Israel. What happened in Belleville is not about a centuries-old struggle in the Middle East.

This is about Jew hatred rearing its ugly head. This cycle has repeated throughout history each time humankind faced a major revolution. People become fearful, and the Jews become a target.

Fear promotes hatred.

We need leaders who incite safety, not hatred.

We need leaders who show up and who not only protect our economies from threats to our sovereignty but ensure we are alive to bear the fruits of that sovereignty.

Finally, my family, my little tribe, send our prayers to the congregation of the Sons of Jacob synagogue. We survived with you to live another day. After the shooting, our community joined hands and prayed. We prayed for life, peace, safety and the forgiveness of those we have harmed this past year. We sang and prayed for each of us to walk the path to become our G-d made best selves in the year ahead.

Shema Yisrael Adonai Elohaynu Adonai Ehud.

Sharlene Weitzman is a Canadian forensic social worker, educator, author, and children’s rights advocate with more than three decades of experience working at the intersection of family law, child development, mental health, and the justice system.

stories.title: Former federal public servant seeks better pensions for injured workers
stories.summary: A former public servant is calling for changes to pension rules for workers who have to retire early after getting injured on the job.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — A former public servant is calling for changes to pension rules for workers who have to retire early after getting injured on the job.

Paméla Marchand worked for Correctional Service Canada as a corrections officer for 15 years before her medical retirement at age 39.

Marchand said that after she experienced harassment by colleagues, a psychological injury forced her to leave her job.

Marchand said the situation deprived her of the opportunity to continue her career and reach 25 years of service, which is when front line workers can retire without penalty.

She said she lost salary increases and career progression and missed out on the pension she would have received after a longer career.

“A person who becomes disabled because of their work should not, in addition to losing their ability to work, suffer a permanent loss of the pension rights they would otherwise have continued to accumulate,” she said in French.

“Two correctional officers can suffer an occupational injury in Quebec but not receive the same protection for their pension rights, depending on whether one works for the provincial government and the other for the federal government.”

Marchand launched a petition calling for the pension rules to be changed so that any recognized occupational disability entitles an employee to an immediate pension without penalties, and with continued contributions.

It also calls for the continuation of employer contributions during a severe and prolonged disability, and for federal rules to be more consistent with provincial workers’ compensation systems.

“What I hope is that the government will genuinely examine the interaction between the different systems and establish clear protection for federal workers whose careers end prematurely because of an occupational disability,” Marchand said in French.

Marchand’s petition has received more than 1,140 signatures and will be presented in the House of Commons by NDP MP Don Davies on Oct. 7.

Davies said in an email that sponsoring petitions is an important way for MPs to facilitate citizen feedback to Parliament and does not necessarily imply endorsement of the contents.

“In this case, I wanted these workers to have the opportunity to express what they see as inequities in the way pensions are calculated for disabled workers, notably via occupational injury,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 26, 2026.

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press
