stories.title: Why do people return to Vancouver Island year after year to protect the forests?
stories.summary: What kind of relationship will we choose to have with forests that have witnessed multiple generations of history?
stories.author: Katherine KY Cheng
stories.content:
Katherine KY Cheng is an independent photographer and visual storyteller who, oscillating between traditional documentary photojournalism and experimental alternative processes, explores themes of climate change and social resistance.

It’s been five years since the height of the Fairy Creek blockades, the largest act of civil disobedience in Canadian history, and the future of the forest still remains uncertain.

Thousands of people joined protests against old-growth logging in and around the watershed on Vancouver Island, leading to more than 1,100 arrests. It was reminiscent of the War in the Woods in nearby Clayoquot Sound nearly three decades earlier.

Eventually, temporary logging deferrals were granted for roughly 1,200 hectares of the watershed, with the protections extended multiple times. They are set to expire at the end of the month.

Despite the movement taking a step back from the spotlight, some have chosen to remain among the giants.

In the years following, the movement has waxed and waned. Over the past five years, protesters have continued building trails, monitoring forests and organizing actions in the nearby Walbran Valley and cities alike.

Last year, a blockade known as “Cougar Camp” was established by many of the same protesters, although it was ultimately dismantled by the RCMP last November after an injunction order was granted .

Meanwhile, the British Columbia government had promised a broader transformation of old-growth management, with millions of hectares deferred . However, conservationists argue that meaningful action to limit logging in the rarest forests has fallen short, and independent analyses have raised concerns that at-risk ancient stands recommended for protection are logged at up to four times the rate of other old-growth areas.

The protesters’ dedication to standing for the forests despite the risk of arrests, long days and late nights and navigating remote logging roads, raises the question: Why do people return year after year to protect forests that are thousands of years old?

To better understand the continued commitment, my curiosity drew me to follow these pilgrimages to the forest for the past year, after the formation of Cougar Camp revived memories and dialogues of Fairy Creek – recollections that were wrapped in a language of mythology and lore.

The reasons that called each person to come were varied. Walking beneath old-growth canopies, they shared stories about commitments to the benefits of rare biodiversity, carbon storage, and vital watersheds. But underneath those arguments, there appeared to be a deeper and more personal layer that drew many to gather in what seemed to be a shared reverence for irreplaceable sacred spaces.

The ancient forests were depicted as teachers, sanctuaries and places of worship – spaces capable of transforming how a person understands their relationship with the living world, one another and themselves.

As the Fairy Creek temporary deferral is set to expire, decisions about old growth sit at an uneasy intersection of conservation, Indigenous sovereignty and a forest industry undergoing rapid change. With only 3 per cent of remaining old-growth forests in British Columbia being home to the largest ancient trees, the question is not necessarily about how many hectares will be logged or protected, but rather what the few surviving old-growth forests symbolize.

These photographs follow the faces of the forest defenders who have chosen to stay, seeking to unpack the meaning of Fairy Creek, why people devote themselves to protecting old growth, and where the fate of these ancient giants May lie.

This story was made possible with support from the Sitka Foundation and Science Media Centre of Canada’s ‘ Messengers of Biodiversity ’ grant.

stories.title: Ontario’s taxing problem with property owners
stories.summary: Lifting province’s property assessment freeze could cause municipal taxes to shoot up for some, while others May find they’ve been paying too much for years
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
It’s a kind of ticking tax bomb.

At the height of the COVID-19 emergency in 2020, Ontario ordered the non-profit corporation that reassesses property values across the province to take a pause, freezing the price estimates that municipalities use to calculate property-tax bills.

As taxpayers know full well, the freeze didn’t stop municipalities from raising their taxes: It just froze the valuations on which those property-tax bills are based, which are normally done in the province every four years.

Six years later, with other pandemic restrictions long gone, the government of Premier Doug Ford never turned its assessment system back on. Now, lifting this freeze, critics warn, could have explosive political consequences – but so could leaving it in place.

If assessments resumed, property owners with real estate that rose more in value than the average in their communities could face the sticker-shock of higher property-tax bills.

But the freeze has also created another problem, experts point out. It has meant that other taxpayers, whose homes and businesses didn’t appreciate as quickly, or sank in value, have long been paying more than they otherwise would have – in some cases, thousands of dollars a year more.

Almost half of Ontario condo units are worth less than $500,000 as prices plunge, Mpac reports

Paul Sullivan, a B.C. property-tax consultant, argues it is time to rip off the Band-Aid. The national tax and advocacy leader for his consulting firm, Ryan ULC, Mr. Sullivan has launched a campaign to lift Ontario’s freeze.

“I would say that the biggest problem with this issue is education and transparency,” Mr. Sullivan said in an interview. “People just don’t know. And if they did know, there would be outrage.”

Property assessments in Ontario for the municipal tax purposes are conducted by the non-profit Municipal Property Assessment Corp. Any increase in a property’s value is phased in gradually over four years, before the next assessment. Mpac was about to issue a reassessment for 2020, when COVID-19 struck.

This means Mpac’s last estimated values date from January, 2016. So Ontario property taxpayers have been paying bills based on that fully-phased-in 2016 value, now a decade out of date, for the past six years.

According to data Mpac provided to The Globe and Mail, residential properties across the province saw an estimated average price increase of 91 per cent from 2016 to 2025, with the figure for the GTA at 72 per cent – numbers that have slid back down a bit from large postpandemic spikes. Mpac estimates the median increase for commercial properties across the province at 103 per cent.

Other provinces (except for New Brunswick, which put in a one-year freeze this year as it reforms its property-tax system), have their regular reassessment systems running. B.C. and Alberta reassess properties every year. The Association of Municipalities of Ontario, which represents local governments across the province, has long called for a return to normal and suggested in a letter to the Premier in July that reassessments should be done every two years.

The Ontario government has said it is consulting on the issue. Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy told reporters in June he had no “time frame” on restarting reassessments. On Thursday he said the government was still reviewing the issue: “We have gone through a pandemic. We’re going through a tariff situation. We’ve had a lot of uncertainty and what people want is certainty.”

Mr. Ford’s critics note that the Premier regularly boasts of never raising a tax – and they suggest that a return to reassessments might prompt some taxpayers to blame him for their rising bills.

Unpacking the Carney government’s $2.7-billion housing pledge

Tax experts are quick to point out that a higher assessed value does not necessarily mean a higher property tax bill – that depends on whether your property rose more than the average in your municipality. A reassessment also has no bearing on the taxes you have already paid. And it does not mean your city gets a tax windfall. It just redistributes the basis for the tax burden differently, across the same taxpayers.

Those unknowingly paying too much because of the assessment freeze, Mr. Sullivan says, include many homeowners in the east Toronto inner suburb of Scarborough, where real estate prices in some neighbourhoods rose more slowly than elsewhere in the city.

His firm’s researchers reviewed the assessments and sales prices of 1,643 detached Scarborough homes that changed hands last year. They estimate that 40 per cent were paying more than $1,000 too much in property taxes.

The current condo crash has also produced more victims: Across the entire city of Toronto, Mr. Sullivan estimates that half of condo owners – based on 2025 sale prices – were also overpaying.

Among businesses, he says, the struggling regional shopping mall is among the worst hit. With the growth of online retail, malls have dramatically faded in value over the past 10 years – and yet are still paying property taxes as though it was 2016.

He also says it’s a similar story for many small retailers on main streets in Toronto, based on data he has pulled from 3,000 commercial sales between 2023 and 2025. Some retailers, Mr. Sullivan calculates, are being overcharged by tens of thousands of dollars. Meanwhile, businesses in the logistics and warehousing sector have been getting away with a break on their taxes and could end up paying more, Mr. Sullivan said.

Mr. Sullivan’s numbers are illustrative, but not exact tax-bill calculations. They assume taxpayers would owe taxes based on the full sale value of their properties, and therefore don’t reflect the four-year phase-in period that was part of Ontario’s system before it was shut off.

Previous changes to the assessment system have required governments to bring in measures to ease the transition.

Before Ontario’s current-value assessment system was adopted in 1998, residential properties in the former central city of Toronto were taxed on values set way back in 1940, while other municipalities used different dates. The new system, meant to fix the distortions this created, required a series of legislative moves to soften the impact on businesses.

After 1998, reassessments were initially done every year. But in 2007, the Liberal government of the day froze them after Ontario’s Ombudsman had condemned Mpac’s processes as secretive and unfair. In 2009, reassessments restarted with a new four-year phase-in period.

How are property tax rates calculated and what do they pay for?

John Kiru, the executive director of the Toronto Association of Business Improvement Areas (Tabia), says he is skeptical of Mr. Sullivan’s data and fears that a reassessment will harm already struggling storefronts in the city’s main-street shopping districts, such as those on pricey land near transit stations.

“Are we going to shut down a bunch of small businesses in Little Italy, in Greektown, in Cabbagetown, et cetera, if these tax shifts happen?” Mr. Kiru said in an interview.

Back in 1998, Mr. Kiru was among those advising then-finance-minister Ernie Eves on the tax caps and clawbacks brought in to ease the transition for small businesses. He says any change now needs to include similar measures.

Enid Slack, the director of the Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance at the University of Toronto, said the current government will need to carefully study how to mitigate the potentially harmful side effects before turning the system back on. But she says the province must eventually return to current-value assessment to solve the problems the freeze has created.

“People talk about the winners and losers from a reassessment,” she said. “But they fail to remember that there are winners and losers from keeping it where it is.”

Ontario Liberal MPP Stephen Blais, his party’s municipal affairs critic, said the government was right to freeze the system at the height of the pandemic, but wrong to have dragged its feet on restarting it – something he blames on the fear of political fallout.

“If the government acknowledges it, then they’ve got to start talking about taxes and at some point, taxes are going to go up on people,” Mr. Blais said. “And that would be counter to the Premier’s argument that he’s never raised taxes.”

Mr. Sullivan says the government could return to assessments but with a generous phase-in period, or even a 10-per-cent initial cap on any increases to smooth things over. But he warns that as his campaign reaches the many taxpayers he says are overpaying, pressure on the province will mount.

He says he met Mr. Ford at a PC fundraiser in April and that the Premier pledged to sit down with him and Mr. Bethlenfalvy to talk taxes. But that the meeting hasn’t happened yet.

“At some point, you have to unwind this,” Mr. Sullivan said. “So how long do we treat people unfairly before we get to that point? And you want to talk about political risk? Keep dragging this thing out. Some people will say there’s political risk in doing it. I want to say there’s political risk in not doing it.”

But the freeze has also created another problem, experts point out. It has meant that other taxpayers, whose homes and businesses didn’t appreciate as quickly, or sank in value, have long been paying more than they otherwise would have – in some cases, thousands of dollars a year more.
Almost half of Ontario condo units are worth less than $500,000 as prices plunge, Mpac reports

Paul Sullivan, a B.C. property-tax consultant, argues it is time to rip off the Band-Aid. The national tax and advocacy leader for his consulting firm, Ryan ULC, Mr. Sullivan has launched a campaign to lift Ontario’s freeze.
“I would say that the biggest problem with this issue is education and transparency,” Mr. Sullivan said in an interview. “People just don’t know. And if they did know, there would be outrage.”

Property assessments in Ontario for the municipal tax purposes are conducted by the non-profit Municipal Property Assessment Corp. Any increase in a property’s value is phased in gradually over four years, before the next assessment. Mpac was about to issue a reassessment for 2020, when COVID-19 struck.

This means Mpac’s last estimated values date from January, 2016. So Ontario property taxpayers have been paying bills based on that fully-phased-in 2016 value, now a decade out of date, for the past six years.

According to data Mpac provided to The Globe and Mail, residential properties across the province saw an estimated average price increase of 91 per cent from 2016 to 2025, with the figure for the GTA at 72 per cent – numbers that have slid back down a bit from large postpandemic spikes. Mpac estimates the median increase for commercial properties across the province at 103 per cent.

Other provinces (except for New Brunswick, which put in a one-year freeze this year as it reforms its property-tax system), have their regular reassessment systems running. B.C. and Alberta reassess properties every year. The Association of Municipalities of Ontario, which represents local governments across the province, has long called for a return to normal and suggested in a letter to the Premier in July that reassessments should be done every two years.

The Ontario government has said it is consulting on the issue. Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy told reporters in June he had no “time frame” on restarting reassessments. On Thursday he said the government was still reviewing the issue: “We have gone through a pandemic. We’re going through a tariff situation. We’ve had a lot of uncertainty and what people want is certainty.”
Mr. Ford’s critics note that the Premier regularly boasts of never raising a tax – and they suggest that a return to reassessments might prompt some taxpayers to blame him for their rising bills.
Unpacking the Carney government’s $2.7-billion housing pledge

Tax experts are quick to point out that a higher assessed value does not necessarily mean a higher property tax bill – that depends on whether your property rose more than the average in your municipality. A reassessment also has no bearing on the taxes you have already paid. And it does not mean your city gets a tax windfall. It just redistributes the basis for the tax burden differently, across the same taxpayers.

Those unknowingly paying too much because of the assessment freeze, Mr. Sullivan says, include many homeowners in the east Toronto inner suburb of Scarborough, where real estate prices in some neighbourhoods rose more slowly than elsewhere in the city.

His firm’s researchers reviewed the assessments and sales prices of 1,643 detached Scarborough homes that changed hands last year. They estimate that 40 per cent were paying more than $1,000 too much in property taxes.
The current condo crash has also produced more victims: Across the entire city of Toronto, Mr. Sullivan estimates that half of condo owners – based on 2025 sale prices – were also overpaying.

Among businesses, he says, the struggling regional shopping mall is among the worst hit. With the growth of online retail, malls have dramatically faded in value over the past 10 years – and yet are still paying property taxes as though it was 2016.

He also says it’s a similar story for many small retailers on main streets in Toronto, based on data he has pulled from 3,000 commercial sales between 2023 and 2025. Some retailers, Mr. Sullivan calculates, are being overcharged by tens of thousands of dollars. Meanwhile, businesses in the logistics and warehousing sector have been getting away with a break on their taxes and could end up paying more, Mr. Sullivan said.

Mr. Sullivan’s numbers are illustrative, but not exact tax-bill calculations. They assume taxpayers would owe taxes based on the full sale value of their properties, and therefore don’t reflect the four-year phase-in period that was part of Ontario’s system before it was shut off.
Previous changes to the assessment system have required governments to bring in measures to ease the transition.

Before Ontario’s current-value assessment system was adopted in 1998, residential properties in the former central city of Toronto were taxed on values set way back in 1940, while other municipalities used different dates. The new system, meant to fix the distortions this created, required a series of legislative moves to soften the impact on businesses.

After 1998, reassessments were initially done every year. But in 2007, the Liberal government of the day froze them after Ontario’s Ombudsman had condemned Mpac’s processes as secretive and unfair. In 2009, reassessments restarted with a new four-year phase-in period.
How are property tax rates calculated and what do they pay for?

John Kiru, the executive director of the Toronto Association of Business Improvement Areas (Tabia), says he is skeptical of Mr. Sullivan’s data and fears that a reassessment will harm already struggling storefronts in the city’s main-street shopping districts, such as those on pricey land near transit stations.
“Are we going to shut down a bunch of small businesses in Little Italy, in Greektown, in Cabbagetown, et cetera, if these tax shifts happen?” Mr. Kiru said in an interview.

Back in 1998, Mr. Kiru was among those advising then-finance-minister Ernie Eves on the tax caps and clawbacks brought in to ease the transition for small businesses. He says any change now needs to include similar measures.

Enid Slack, the director of the Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance at the University of Toronto, said the current government will need to carefully study how to mitigate the potentially harmful side effects before turning the system back on. But she says the province must eventually return to current-value assessment to solve the problems the freeze has created.
“People talk about the winners and losers from a reassessment,” she said. “But they fail to remember that there are winners and losers from keeping it where it is.”

Ontario Liberal MPP Stephen Blais, his party’s municipal affairs critic, said the government was right to freeze the system at the height of the pandemic, but wrong to have dragged its feet on restarting it – something he blames on the fear of political fallout.

“If the government acknowledges it, then they’ve got to start talking about taxes and at some point, taxes are going to go up on people,” Mr. Blais said. “And that would be counter to the Premier’s argument that he’s never raised taxes.”

Mr. Sullivan says the government could return to assessments but with a generous phase-in period, or even a 10-per-cent initial cap on any increases to smooth things over. But he warns that as his campaign reaches the many taxpayers he says are overpaying, pressure on the province will mount.
He says he met Mr. Ford at a PC fundraiser in April and that the Premier pledged to sit down with him and Mr. Bethlenfalvy to talk taxes. But that the meeting hasn’t happened yet.

“At some point, you have to unwind this,” Mr. Sullivan said. “So how long do we treat people unfairly before we get to that point? And you want to talk about political risk? Keep dragging this thing out. Some people will say there’s political risk in doing it. I want to say there’s political risk in not doing it.”

stories.title: 3 songs from London Morning to boost your weekend playlist
stories.summary: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role, picking tunes for the show. In any given week, that's about 25 songs. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from last week.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: London Morning associate producer Ryan Soulliere listens to a lot of music for his role, picking tunes for the show. In any given week, that's about 25 songs. Here are his top three local and Canadian picks from last week.
· Posted: Sep 05, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 34 minutes ago
S-Man Lib, Akintoye and Allison Russell are three artists featured on London Morning(Instagram/Facebook)
_WATCH | I Know It:_Video 8

I Know It by S-Man Lib is a nice, chill song to start this list. Mellow island beats and a smooth flow make I Know It a great song to enjoy the last weeks of summer, and it doubles as a relaxed day-starter. If you'd like to see S-Man Lib perform, you're in luck. Just head to Gibbons Park from 11 am to 9 pm today, September 5th. S-Man Lib is one of the performers on the African Caribbean Mosaic Cultural Festival.
_WATCH | The Farmer Freestyle:_Video 9

Have you ever looked down at your plate of food and wondered, how can I thank the farmer that made this possible? That's what rapper Akintoye just did with a new single: The Farmer Freestyle. This outstanding mid-tempo rap track with a luring beat, laced with sweet clarinet will work well on a variety of playlists.
_WATCH | My Love is a Golden Lion:_Video 10

Allison Russell's latest full-length album In the Hour of Chaos is a wonderful body of work with no two songs quite the same. In fact, the new album is a fantastic listening experience because of its diversity of sound. From the new one, London Morning played Love is a Golden Lion featuring Devon Gilfillian. This upbeat and happy-sounding track will work well on your next party playlist or when you want some motivation.

stories.title: Lions climb standings with win over Roughriders
stories.summary: Nathan Rourke passed for 375 yards and his B.C. Lions held off the Saskatchewan Roughriders for a crucial 31-24 victory on Friday.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
VANCOUVER – Six games into the CFL season, the B.C. Lions were floundering.

The team was 1-5 and seemed poised to linger at the bottom of the standings all year.

But the Lions have clawed their way out of the hole and, after beating the Saskatchewan Roughriders 31-24 on Friday, now sit second in the West Division with an 8-6 record.

“Ultimately, going into this stretch, we knew that we controlled our own destiny,” said Lions quarterback Nathan Rourke. “And so any type of win, especially against a West team, is huge for us, right? So, we just want to continue to focus one game at a time, and let the cards fall where they may.”

It was another stellar performance for the Canadian QB, who amassed 375 passing yards and 37 rushing yards with four touchdown passes.

Keon Hatcher Sr. chalked up a pair of majors for the Lions, while Jevon Cottoy and Jermaine Jackson also found the end zone, and Sean Whyte made a 14-yard field goal.

The result gives B.C. a 2-1 edge in a three-game season series between the two clubs and could be a crucial tiebreaker for home-field advantage in the playoffs.

“Obviously it’s big in the standings, with the West as tight as it’s been in recent years,” said Lions head coach Buck Pierce. “But we feel when we play at home, we should win. And that hasn’t changed.”

The Riders (8-6) got some key pieces back on Friday, including running back A.J. Ouellette, who tallied 77 rushing yards and a TD in his return from a knee injury that saw him sidelined for seven games.

Trevor Harris had 302 passing yards, throwing a touchdown to Dylan Djete in the second quarter. Kicker Dawson Hodge notched three field goals for Saskatchewan, including a 32-yard strike.

“We just weren’t executing what we were supposed to execute,” said Riders defensive back Marcus Sayles. “They’ve got a great team over there, they’ve got great players, and they just found a way to make some explosive plays. And that was pretty much the difference.”

The loss means Saskatchewan can no longer clinch a playoff spot this week.

“Every single game is frustrating when you lose. Because we’re all competitors, we all want to win,” Sayles said. “And when we don’t execute the way we expect ourselves to execute, it is frustrating at times.

“But at the same time, we’ve got more opportunities. We’ve got four more games to play, and however the dice roll, we’re just going to keep coming to practice, keep working, and it’s going to keep going until it’s all over.”

The visitors looked dangerous on their first possession of the game, with Harris working his way up the field.

Looking to connect with a teammate in the end zone, the QB sent a pass off of the upright, and Saskatchewan settled for a 27-yard field goal to open the scoring.

The Lions responded swiftly.

Rourke lobbed a massive pass up centre field to Stanley Berryhill III for a 56-yard gain, then followed up with a toss to Hatcher in the end zone. Whyte’s single-point convert gave the home side a 7-3 lead.

The two sides traded field goals before Saskatchewan put up a major.

With just over two minutes to go in the second quarter, Harris spotted Djete alone near the sideline and hit the unencumbered wide receiver with a 13-yard pass. Djete darted over the goal line, and Hodge made the single to put the Riders back on top by a score of 13-10.

The lead didn’t last until halftime.

Rourke made five passes up the field to put B.C. at Saskatchewan’s 19-yard line, then tossed a short ball to Hatcher, who avoided a tackle from Mike Rose en route to the end zone for his second major of the night. Whyte’s convert gave the Lions a 17-13 lead with 16 seconds to go in the first half.

Hatcher registered 66 receiving yards on the night and hit 1,015 for the season. It’s the fifth season in his CFL career that the 32-year-old American receiver has surpassed the 1,000-yard mark.

“I love Hatch. He’s one of my favourite teammates, just of all time in my career,” Rourke said. “He’s just such a hard worker, great leader. I love how he competes, his competitive nature. I trust him implicitly.”

“I think at this stage in his career, everyone’s looking for a reason not to have him around, and he continues to prove that he belongs here.”

The Lions boosted their advantage midway through the third after Rourke came up big with a giant pass to Justin McInnis that gave the home side a first down in the midfield.

Saskatchewan head coach Corey Mace challenged the play for offensive pass interference, but after video review, officials upheld the call on the field.

Rourke continued to push his team upfield and capped the drive with a pass to Cottoy just above the goal line for another TD. Another single-point conversion from Whyte gave B.C. a 24-13 lead.

The final play of the third quarter saw the Lions’ defence stymie Harris and his side deep in B.C. territory. The Riders’ short-yardage team tried to extend the drive but instead turned the ball over on downs.

The Lions’ defence has been making stops when it needs to, Pierce said.

“I think the biggest thing is they’re able to respond and analyze mistakes that were made and not hang on those mistakes and move on to the next play,” he said. “They’re playing with a lot of energy and a lot of confidence right now, and they’re playing good, clean football.”

Saskatchewan continued to push but struggled to break through the Lions’ back end. Another field goal from Hodge — this time a 32-yard kick — made it 24-16 for B.C. midway through the fourth quarter.

The crowd at BC Place jumped to their feet late in the final frame when Rourke scrambled out of the pocket under pressure, sprinted upfield and delivered a long bomb into the hands of McInnis.

The Canadian receiver was hauled down, but Rourke found Jermaine Jackson for yet another major on the next play to give the Lions a 31-16 lead.

With just over two minutes left on the game clock, Saskatchewan finally made its way back into the end zone with a two-yard plunge from Ouellette.

The Riders gave themselves hope when Tommy Stevens made it through the fray for a two-point conversion that left the score 31-24.

At least one provincial politician made room in his busy election campaign schedule to attend the game. Newly minted B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson was spotted at field level with former B.C. Premier Christy Clark before kickoff.

Riders: Host the Calgary Stampeders on Oct. 2.

Lions: Visit the Toronto Argonauts on Oct. 3.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

The Lions responded swiftly.

Rourke lobbed a massive pass up centre field to Stanley Berryhill III for a 56-yard gain, then followed up with a toss to Hatcher in the end zone. Whyte’s single-point convert gave the home side a 7-3 lead.
The two sides traded field goals before Saskatchewan put up a major.

With just over two minutes to go in the second quarter, Harris spotted Djete alone near the sideline and hit the unencumbered wide receiver with a 13-yard pass. Djete darted over the goal line, and Hodge made the single to put the Riders back on top by a score of 13-10.
The lead didn’t last until halftime.

Rourke made five passes up the field to put B.C. at Saskatchewan’s 19-yard line, then tossed a short ball to Hatcher, who avoided a tackle from Mike Rose en route to the end zone for his second major of the night. Whyte’s convert gave the Lions a 17-13 lead with 16 seconds to go in the first half.
Hatcher registered 66 receiving yards on the night and hit 1,015 for the season. It’s the fifth season in his CFL career that the 32-year-old American receiver has surpassed the 1,000-yard mark.

“I love Hatch. He’s one of my favourite teammates, just of all time in my career,” Rourke said. “He’s just such a hard worker, great leader. I love how he competes, his competitive nature. I trust him implicitly.”
“I think at this stage in his career, everyone’s looking for a reason not to have him around, and he continues to prove that he belongs here.”
The Lions boosted their advantage midway through the third after Rourke came up big with a giant pass to Justin McInnis that gave the home side a first down in the midfield.
Saskatchewan head coach Corey Mace challenged the play for offensive pass interference, but after video review, officials upheld the call on the field.
Rourke continued to push his team upfield and capped the drive with a pass to Cottoy just above the goal line for another TD. Another single-point conversion from Whyte gave B.C. a 24-13 lead.

The final play of the third quarter saw the Lions’ defence stymie Harris and his side deep in B.C. territory. The Riders’ short-yardage team tried to extend the drive but instead turned the ball over on downs.
The Lions’ defence has been making stops when it needs to, Pierce said.

“I think the biggest thing is they’re able to respond and analyze mistakes that were made and not hang on those mistakes and move on to the next play,” he said. “They’re playing with a lot of energy and a lot of confidence right now, and they’re playing good, clean football.”
Saskatchewan continued to push but struggled to break through the Lions’ back end. Another field goal from Hodge — this time a 32-yard kick — made it 24-16 for B.C. midway through the fourth quarter.
The crowd at BC Place jumped to their feet late in the final frame when Rourke scrambled out of the pocket under pressure, sprinted upfield and delivered a long bomb into the hands of McInnis.
The Canadian receiver was hauled down, but Rourke found Jermaine Jackson for yet another major on the next play to give the Lions a 31-16 lead.
With just over two minutes left on the game clock, Saskatchewan finally made its way back into the end zone with a two-yard plunge from Ouellette.
The Riders gave themselves hope when Tommy Stevens made it through the fray for a two-point conversion that left the score 31-24.

At least one provincial politician made room in his busy election campaign schedule to attend the game. Newly minted B.C. Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson was spotted at field level with former B.C. Premier Christy Clark before kickoff.
Riders: Host the Calgary Stampeders on Oct. 2.
Lions: Visit the Toronto Argonauts on Oct. 3.

stories.title: The Globe and Mail crosswords: Breaking down the Weekender's 'That's Such a Cliché,' cryptic clues and more
stories.summary: Don’t be a hoser
stories.author: Jess Shulman
stories.content:
Welcome back to Puzzle Pieces. Spoilers ahead! In this weekly column, I look at our Weekender crossword , highlighting some of my favourite clues, explaining how the puzzle’s theme works and sharing a note from the week’s constructor.

I also dive into the workings of a selected clue from our Weekender Cryptic crossword . My goal is to introduce more Globe readers to how our crossword puzzles work and to celebrate the people who make them.

Note that I use Caps for letters that end up in the grid and [square brackets] for clues.

Our Sept. 26 Weekender, That’s Such a Cliché , is our latest from Toronto constructor Carina da Rosa, whose cluing style never fails to delight.

Where do you stand in the great debate referenced at 27A, [Controversial butter tart additions]? I’m Team Raisins, all the way. Many sources trace the first butter tart recipe to the “Filling for Tarts” instructions on page 88 of the The Women’s Auxiliary of the Royal Victoria Hospital Cookbook printed in Barrie, Ont., in 1900. Among the four ingredients? Currants. Are dried currants pretty much just Raisins? Well, no, but the anti-Raisins people sure aren’t arguing for currants, either. If the earliest recipe calls for dried fruit, I’m all for it.

The word “PJS” often shows up in crosswords, as it does in 77A this week, often clued with reference to nighttime or sleepover apparel. I like Carina’s fresh angle, [Matching Xmas duds for the fam, maybe], and the fact that the abbreviations Xmas and fam are pointing the solver to an abbreviated answer.

Are you familiar with the [Numbers game that sounds like two Mattel dolls], at 18D? That’s Kenken, a game we feature in our daily print paper. Invented by a Japanese math teacher in 2004, it offers a different challenge from crosswords, sort of like Sudoku but with arithmetic operations. Give it a try!

Finally, at 58D, the clue might trip you up if you’re reading too quickly: [It helps when doing sift work?] That’s sift work, not shift work, a clever description of what you do with a Sieve.

Breaking down the theme

It was a bit of a journey to get to the puzzle theme you see before you. It started with Carina’s idea for some kind of “eh”-based puzzle, for a little Canadian flair.

First, we looked at a list of phrases whose endings were simply variations on the eh sound, like yogurt parf ait and anchors aw eigh . But we wanted a goofier transformation in the theme entries.

Next, we explored adding eh sounds to familiar phrases, making things like men are from mars eille . Then we hit on the idea of using Take OFF, EH as the revealer entry, and looked for ways to play with removing an eh sound. We couldn’t find enough examples with differently spelled eh sounds ... but then Carina had the great idea to just remove the letter that sounds like “eh,” i.e., the letter A. So simple, yet so full of funny possibilities.

She came back with the hilarious theme set you now see in the solved grid, each entry a familiar phrase with a letter A removed. The key is in the revealer clue for Take OFF EH at 115A: [Catchphrase for Sctv’s Bob and Doug McKenzie … or a phonetic hint to the starred clues].

31A: [*“Refrain from shaking R2-D2”?] - Don’t Rock THE BOT

46A: [*How an ancient Roman might turn down a request for a mid-month appointment?] - I’M ALL OUT OF Ides

82A: [*Totally amateurish triage centres?] - Mickey Mouse ERS

100A: [*“Please excuse my clever quips”?] - Sorry FOR THE WIT

A note from constructor Carina da Rosa

I come at this puzzle with only love, never judgment of anyone’s speech habits. I, too, have been known to utter the occasional “eh” at the end of a sentence, which my British husband enjoys pointing out.

The cutting room floor is littered with themers on this one, from back when we tried to make it a homophone/addition puzzle. I’ll leave you with these drafts:

Sleeping IN THE Buff ET : [Getting some zzz’s during an all-you-can-eat meal?]

Vitamin B AE : [Lover that makes sure you get your riboflavin?]

Sharp EI Dressers: [Wardrobe specialists for wrinkly dogs?]

Cryptic clue of the week

If you’re new to cryptics, a great place to start is Fraser Simpson’s article How to solve The Globe’s cryptic crossword . It won’t help you with this week’s clue, though. This clue uses a mechanism you don’t see in every cryptic, and rarely more than once in a puzzle. Not because it’s hard, but because it’s a bit of one-trick pony. But it’s a good trick.

From our Sept. 26 Weekender Cryptic , let’s look at 20A: [Vacant-looking Lassie guide mentioned by Spooner (6-4)].

Once you see “Spooner,” there’s no sense pursuing any other ideas. It’s a spoonerism .

William Archibald Spooner was a reverend known for verbal slips in which he swapped the first sounds or syllables of a phrase, to great comic effect. A cryptic spoonerism clue does exactly that.

Because “mentioned by Spooner” is part of the wordplay and appears at the end of the clue, the definition is very likely at the start: “vacant-looking.” We need to rack our brains for a phrase that means “vacant-looking” but, when it’s spoonerized , gives us “Lassie guide.”

This turns out to be straightforward, because we’re not looking for synonyms (collie leader? dog steer?) - we’re using the given words directly. Switch the first sounds of “Lassie” and “guide” and you get the answer: Glassy-Eyed.

Invented by a Japanese math teacher in 2004, it offers a different challenge from crosswords, sort of like Sudoku but with arithmetic operations. Give it a try!
Finally, at 58D, the clue might trip you up if you’re reading too quickly: [It helps when doing sift work?] That’s sift work, not shift work, a clever description of what you do with a Sieve.
Breaking down the theme
It was a bit of a journey to get to the puzzle theme you see before you. It started with Carina’s idea for some kind of “eh”-based puzzle, for a little Canadian flair.
First, we looked at a list of phrases whose endings were simply variations on the eh sound, like yogurt parf ait and anchors aw eigh . But we wanted a goofier transformation in the theme entries.

Next, we explored adding eh sounds to familiar phrases, making things like men are from mars eille . Then we hit on the idea of using Take OFF, EH as the revealer entry, and looked for ways to play with removing an eh sound. We couldn’t find enough examples with differently spelled eh sounds ... but then Carina had the great idea to just remove the letter that sounds like “eh,” i.e., the letter A. So simple, yet so full of funny possibilities.

She came back with the hilarious theme set you now see in the solved grid, each entry a familiar phrase with a letter A removed. The key is in the revealer clue for Take OFF EH at 115A: [Catchphrase for Sctv’s Bob and Doug McKenzie … or a phonetic hint to the starred clues].

46A: [*How an ancient Roman might turn down a request for a mid-month appointment?] - I’M ALL OUT OF Ides
82A: [*Totally amateurish triage centres?] - Mickey Mouse ERS
100A: [*“Please excuse my clever quips”?] - Sorry FOR THE WIT

I come at this puzzle with only love, never judgment of anyone’s speech habits. I, too, have been known to utter the occasional “eh” at the end of a sentence, which my British husband enjoys pointing out.
The cutting room floor is littered with themers on this one, from back when we tried to make it a homophone/addition puzzle. I’ll leave you with these drafts:

items: Sleeping IN THE Buff ET : [Getting some zzz’s during an all-you-can-eat meal?]
Vitamin B AE : [Lover that makes sure you get your riboflavin?]
Sharp EI Dressers: [Wardrobe specialists for wrinkly dogs?]

content_blocks.text: Cryptic clue of the week

If you’re new to cryptics, a great place to start is Fraser Simpson’s article How to solve The Globe’s cryptic crossword . It won’t help you with this week’s clue, though. This clue uses a mechanism you don’t see in every cryptic, and rarely more than once in a puzzle. Not because it’s hard, but because it’s a bit of one-trick pony. But it’s a good trick.
From our Sept. 26 Weekender Cryptic , let’s look at 20A: [Vacant-looking Lassie guide mentioned by Spooner (6-4)].
Once you see “Spooner,” there’s no sense pursuing any other ideas. It’s a spoonerism .
William Archibald Spooner was a reverend known for verbal slips in which he swapped the first sounds or syllables of a phrase, to great comic effect. A cryptic spoonerism clue does exactly that.

Because “mentioned by Spooner” is part of the wordplay and appears at the end of the clue, the definition is very likely at the start: “vacant-looking.” We need to rack our brains for a phrase that means “vacant-looking” but, when it’s spoonerized , gives us “Lassie guide.”

This turns out to be straightforward, because we’re not looking for synonyms (collie leader? dog steer?) - we’re using the given words directly. Switch the first sounds of “Lassie” and “guide” and you get the answer: Glassy-Eyed.

stories.title: What happened to Madi? In small-town Ontario, a family wrestles with a police investigation gone cold
stories.summary: Four years on, Madison Chard's family say they believe somebody in Port Hope, Ont., knows what happened, even if the police investigation has gone cold.
stories.author: Jim Rankin
stories.content:
PORT HOPE, Ont.—On a sticky summer day, there is relief in the shade of the foliage along the east bank of the Ganaraska River, though not from the mosquitoes. Mark Chard, a local firefighter, community theatre actor and musician, leads the way to a serene spot not far from the heart of a small town, where his daughter Madison was found dead four years ago.

The first time Mark visited this spot was days after the discovery of her body, accompanied by the lead Port Hope police detective probing Madison’s disappearance.

“He was afraid of what I might do to myself,” says Chard. “But I wasn’t thinking that.”

The grieving father says he was looking to connect with his daughter somehow, when along came “a stupid giant bumblebee. It kind of landed on me, and I thought it was her.”

A search party located Madison, 29, on May 19, 2022, a month after one of her last known messages — a late afternoon text exchange with her mother, Lori, who offered to arrange a ride home.

The Chard family filed a missing person report, and searches ensued, including around the very area where her body was ultimately found. The discovery finally came a day after Port Hope police floated the possibility in a news story that Madison had fallen prey to a human-trafficking operation.

Madison was lying flat on her back, clothed for cool spring weather. An autopsy and toxicology tests found she had died of hypothermia, with a lethal amount of fentanyl in her system, and some cocaine.

Four years on, a criminal investigation led by the Port Hope Police Service and directed by the Ontario Provincial Police is all but officially closed, leaving many questions unanswered and a family grappling with a grief that’s been compounded by the unknown. What happened to Madison? Did she die alone? Did police do enough to get to the bottom of it?

In a town where there is little local news coverage anymore, there remain plenty of rumours and speculation. One story the family has heard is that Madison overdosed and the people with her panicked and put her in a freezer, and later moved the body.

The Chard family believes people who use and sell illicit drugs know what happened.

“Somebody knows stuff,” says Lori, who still gets asked in the grocery store if there’s anything new in the case.

The OPP, in a statement to the Star on behalf of the OPP and the Port Hope Police Service, “acknowledge and sympathize with Madison Chard’s family as they continue to grieve their loss.” The statement said every avenue of inquiry was “thoroughly examined,” but ultimately no evidence was established to suggest foul play.

The Chards, who believe the police investigation was inadequate, filed a formal police complaint about the investigation, but it has since been informally resolved, with an agreement that police will consider any new leads passed their way by the family.

A story now, the family believes, may be among the Chards’ best chances to surface new information.

‘Stronger Than the Storm’

Madison had come back to live with her parents in the Chard family’s two-storey home on Ward Street with an ivy-covered front porch. Life had not been easy. She had a brief, bad marriage, and Madison had worked hard to overcome mental health and substance use problems.

Born and raised in Port Hope, along with her younger brother, Teigan, Madison’s ashes now rest on the mantel in the living room in an urn, behind a white butterfly light, overlooked by an angel statue.

As a kid, Madison — Madi to those who loved her, and there are many — adored dance and took ballet lessons, but also did karate and played soccer, with her father as coach in the Timbits league. She was “right from the get go very outgoing and chatty and headstrong,” says Mark, and when brother Teigan came along, “she became a little mother to him.”

Madison was a “Swiftie,” and grew to love theatre and musicals through her father, beginning with his role in a production of “Jesus Christ Superstar.” Madison went to every performance, sitting in the front row and learning the words to every song. There were more productions, and Madison would hang out and eventually started filling in when people were sick.

She also modelled from a very young age and was signed in her teens by an agent in New York. It was fun — father and daughter spent a month there — but it “never came of anything,” says Lori.

Madison had to overcome a lot. There was a diagnosis in her teens of bipolar disorder — there was Madi A for “awesome” and Mabi B who was not, says Lori — and later a brief, bad marriage with an abusive, controlling partner, which her parents believe led to post-traumatic stress disorder and a heroin addiction . Madison would use cocaine when she was slipping to manage the urge for heroin, Lori says. Madison sought treatment at Ontario Shores Centre for Mental Health Sciences, and obtained a diploma from Durham College, where she studied criminal psychology and behaviour. She had a job at Giant Tiger, but was out of work when she went missing.

One thing you would not get from looking at Madison was that inside she lacked confidence, says Mark.

Among the tattoos Madison had was a replica of a wire-art tree pendant Mark had made for her, a rendering of a family tree. She had it done on the back of her left hand.

“She used to say that the pain of getting a tattoo is better than, or masks, the pain that she felt in her heart, or in her existence,” Mark says.

After her death, the family held fundraising events for Ontario Shores, using the family tree as a symbol of Madison’s life, along with the slogan “Stronger Than the Storm.” It was a motto Madison lived by and wore on a necklace, a gift from her parents after one year of recovery.

Madison had been “85 per cent doing OK” for four years before she died, says Lori, but there were “slips.”

The trap house by the Ganaraska River

On April 15, 2022, Madison celebrated her 29th birthday with her family but was headed for one of those “slips.”

Madison had bought cocaine in early April from a woman operating out of what the Chard family discovered was a drug “trap house,” and had a seizure, the family says. The house was not far from where Madison’s body would be found, and backs onto the Ganaraska ravine. At the time of Madison’s disappearance, the woman owed Madison $150, Mark discovered. He believes Madison started buying elsewhere because she thought the supply was bad.

According to her family, she never deliberately used fentanyl, the opioid responsible for an epidemic of deaths and accidental drug poisonings across North America. In 2022 in Ontario, an average of seven people a day were dying from opioid toxicity. In the Haliburton Kawartha Northumberland Peterborough Health Unit, which includes Port Hope, there were 153 emergency department visits from April to June of that year, and 19 deaths, related to opioid toxicity.

On Tuesday, April 19, Madison left home early afternoon and would not come back.

For 30 agonizing days, there were false sightings of Madison, and Mark and Lori became de facto detectives.

They later compiled, organized and analyzed binders full of police records obtained in freedom-of-information requests, and had help from Don Sellar — an editor and journalist, and former Toronto Star public editor — who lives in Port Hope and occasionally writes on local stories involving the police. What emerged was a cast of characters involved in the local drug scene. Police seemed quite aware of who was who in that scene as the connections emerged, the family says.

Madison was texting with Lori and a close friend in the late afternoon of April 19. Madison had plans to get together with the friend the following weekend to celebrate their mutual birthdays. A text from Lori sent at 5:51 p.m. was delivered, but not read — none after that ever would be.

Madison was seen that afternoon at a rooming house on Walton Street, where she bought cocaine from known drug dealers, and later with a man who was headed to the trap house; he maintained the two then went in different directions.

When Madison did not come home, the Chards started to worry.

Today, they believe Madison made another stop that evening.

5:49 p.m., April 19, 2022 — Madison sends a text to her mom. After that, incoming texts to Madison’s phone are marked as “delivered,” but not “read.”

April 19, 2022 — Madison is last seen near a Pharmasave store in Port Hope. Earlier that afternoon, she is seen at a downtown rooming house, where she bought cocaine.

April 21, 2022 — Mark Chard reports his daughter missing. Police conduct “pings” on Madison’s phone and find it is moving. Police issue a “BOLO” for officers to be on the lookout for Madison.

April 22, 2022 — Mark Chard receives a phone call from a woman living at a Port Hope “trap house” backing onto the Ganaraska River. The woman has Madison’s phone, and the SIM card has been removed. Mark retrieves the phone and advises police. Police speak to a “friendly,” who provides Mark the password.

May 18, 2022 — The Toronto Sun publishes a story on Madison’s disappearance; police tell the Sun they are concerned she may have fallen prey to a human-trafficking operation.

May 19, 2022 — A search and rescue team resumes a search of the Ganaraska River ravine. Madison’s body is discovered on the east side of the river, not far from where she was last seen. Missing for 30 days, Madison’s body shows no sign of animal scavenging; the OPP steps in to assist in the investigation.

June 13, 2022 — Police identify a man who provided Madison with fentanyl and consult with a Crown attorney about a manslaughter charge.

August 2026 — After four years, no arrests have been made in the case; police tell the Star they found no evidence of foul play.

The mystery of Madison Chard’s cell phone

With a missing persons report filed, Mark, the police and others set out looking for Madison and clues. On Friday, three days after Madison’s last texts, Mark got a phone call from the woman at the trap house. She had Madison’s phone at the house and said a certain person had dropped it off, and that the SIM card was missing. When Mark went to retrieve it the next day, the woman was not there, but about eight other people were.

Mark got Madison’s Samsung Galaxy phone later the next day. The SIM card was indeed missing, along with the phone’s case.

Police would discover that on the Thursday, two days after Madison’s last texts, Madison’s phone “pinged” off cell towers in three places: on Phillips Road in Port Hope; on Division St. in Cobourg; and in Baltimore, north of Cobourg. In other words, Madison’s phone was moving, then it stopped.

Police told the family the woman at the trap house was questioned several times, as were others. Though the trap house has a security camera on the front door, it did not show Madison. However, the house had a back patio door, which the Chards say was commonly used. There was no camera there.

Mark set about investigating what he could on Madison’s phone, which was password-protected. Mark mentioned that to the lead Port Hope detective, and in short order, the detective got back with a four-digit code from a “friendly.” It was 5683, or L-O-V-E. And it worked. It raised obvious questions: How and why would someone know the code? And who?

When the family obtained police notes from the investigation, names and identifying information were mostly redacted, which is expected for privacy reasons in freedom-of-information requests. But the family determined who this “friendly” was.

Police did not ask Mark for the phone for 11 days before picking it up and sending it off to the OPP for a forensic analysis.

Police did not answer any of the Star’s questions about the phone, which has been returned to the family. Mark is trying to find someone who can independently examine the phone for any location data.

The day they found Madi

In April, along the banks of Ganaraska River, the foliage is sparse. The ravine was searched, and police used a drone at one point. Nothing was found.

On May 18, 2022, the Toronto Sun posted an online story about Madison being missing for nearly a month. In it, Port Hope police said new information suggested Madison may have been taken in by a human trafficker and, according to the story, “may be in their control somewhere between Montreal and Windsor.” A police inspector was quoted as saying that traffickers often take their victim’s phone away.

(The Chards believe the trafficking story was a red herring, cooked up and passed along by local “criminals.”)

The next morning, on May 19, the Sun story ran in print with a headline of “Where’s Madi?” Later that day, a search and rescue team returned to the ravine, and Madison’s body was located on the east side of the Ganaraska, where the river splits.

Paul Racine, 74, has lived nearby with his family for decades and knows the river well. Lately, he’s been keeping an eye on the beavers and their handiwork, bringing down aspen and ash trees. The river area is also frequented by turkey vultures and home to coyotes, foxes, raccoons, groundhogs, muskrats and “numerous dogs that are walked up and down there,” a lot off leash, says Racine.

“My contention,” says Racine, “is that there were Labs, there were setters, there were beagles, there were all kinds of dogs, and if (Madison) lay there for a month, there is absolutely no way that a dog wouldn’t have gone over and sniffed her out.”

Mark Chard believes there would have also been some wildlife interference if his daughter was there for so long.

According to weather records, Port Hope saw daytime high temperatures ranging from 10 to 21 C in the first seven days Madison was missing, and had climbed to highs of 26 to 27 C by the second week of May. Otherwise, temperatures were in the teens. Parts of Madison’s body showed “advanced” and moderate decompositional changes, according to a pathology report.

Police considered manslaughter charges

The police records obtained by the Chards indicate that police intended to consult with a Crown attorney about laying a manslaughter charge at one point.

One possible explanation is that police considered charging the person who sold or gave Madison tainted drugs.

A 2024 paper by York University graduate student Liam Michaud examined a “recent proliferation” of Canadian manslaughter charges and prosecutions of people involved in overdoses, who themselves use, share and sell drugs.

By looking at media reports and court decisions and through federal and provincial requests for information, Michaud found “the vast majority of those who face manslaughter charges are engaged in the lowest tiers of the drug trade, are themselves people who use drugs, and are often intimately known to the deceased.”

To date, no arrests have been made, and although police contemplated doing so, no search warrants were sought, according to police notes.

For years, the investigation remained open, and Mark passed along everything he discovered. Now, officers involved in the initial investigation are no longer on the case, and Port Hope has a new police chief.

The Star contacted the new chief, Tim Farquharson, to request an interview and shared a long list of questions about the investigation in writing in May. Following a couple of meetings Farquharson had with the OPP on the Star’s queries, the OPP responded by email with a statement on behalf of the two services.

“We are unable to comment on specific aspects of the investigation, including investigative processes, techniques, evidence-gathering methods or operational considerations,” Agata Czajkowski, Strategic Communications Advisor for the Ontario Provincial Police, said in the statement to the Star.

“Releasing such details could compromise investigative practices and operations.”

As for when to charge or not, Czajkowski said that in drug-related death cases “where investigators establish the necessary grounds, charges — including manslaughter, criminal negligence causing death or drug trafficking offences — will be pursued in accordance with the evidence.”

In police notes obtained by the Chards, a Port Hope officer references an unidentified male providing Madison with fentanyl and noted police will “need multiple witnesses to build manslaughter.”

The officer notes an OPP investigator on the case cautioning that if “witnesses are weak then we have nothing.”

Songs for Madi

Mark Chard holds a “Dad’s Walk” fundraising event for Ontario Shores annually in honour of his daughter. It takes place on the Port Hope Waterfront Trail along Lake Ontario, passing by a bench and tree with plaques bearing Madison’s name. He posts to Facebook on important anniversary dates, hoping they will get attention and maybe spark someone to speak up about what happened to a woman who is still very missed and loved.

Last August, more than 150 people turned out at the Port Hope United Church for “Songs for Madi” — a night of performances by friends and family, complete with drag performers — Mark was on drums with a band, including Mark’s older brother on guitar, playing “Day by Day” from the musical “Godspell.” Lori stood in a church pew, dancing. The event raised close to $5,000, again, for Ontario Shores, adding to $72,000 already raised.

“Madi is pissed that she’s not here,” said one of the emcee drag performers, prompting laughter.

Madison did make an appearance, however, when a video of her played on a large screen, made for her father’s 50th birthday. Accompanied by a guitar, Madison delivered a beautiful rendition of Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.

“Love you, daddy,” said Madison, blowing a kiss to the camera at the end.

During an evening of songs for Madi, one by her brought tears.

On Friday, three days after Madison’s last texts, Mark got a phone call from the woman at the trap house. She had Madison’s phone at the house and said a certain person had dropped it off, and that the SIM card was missing. When Mark went to retrieve it the next day, the woman was not there, but about eight other people were.
Mark got Madison’s Samsung Galaxy phone later the next day. The SIM card was indeed missing, along with the phone’s case.

Police would discover that on the Thursday, two days after Madison’s last texts, Madison’s phone “pinged” off cell towers in three places: on Phillips Road in Port Hope; on Division St. in Cobourg; and in Baltimore, north of Cobourg. In other words, Madison’s phone was moving, then it stopped.

Police told the family the woman at the trap house was questioned several times, as were others. Though the trap house has a security camera on the front door, it did not show Madison. However, the house had a back patio door, which the Chards say was commonly used. There was no camera there.

Mark set about investigating what he could on Madison’s phone, which was password-protected. Mark mentioned that to the lead Port Hope detective, and in short order, the detective got back with a four-digit code from a “friendly.” It was 5683, or L-O-V-E. And it worked. It raised obvious questions: How and why would someone know the code? And who?

When the family obtained police notes from the investigation, names and identifying information were mostly redacted, which is expected for privacy reasons in freedom-of-information requests. But the family determined who this “friendly” was.
Police did not ask Mark for the phone for 11 days before picking it up and sending it off to the OPP for a forensic analysis.
Police did not answer any of the Star’s questions about the phone, which has been returned to the family. Mark is trying to find someone who can independently examine the phone for any location data.
The day they found Madi
In April, along the banks of Ganaraska River, the foliage is sparse. The ravine was searched, and police used a drone at one point. Nothing was found.

On May 18, 2022, the Toronto Sun posted an online story about Madison being missing for nearly a month. In it, Port Hope police said new information suggested Madison may have been taken in by a human trafficker and, according to the story, “may be in their control somewhere between Montreal and Windsor.” A police inspector was quoted as saying that traffickers often take their victim’s phone away.
(The Chards believe the trafficking story was a red herring, cooked up and passed along by local “criminals.”)

The next morning, on May 19, the Sun story ran in print with a headline of “Where’s Madi?” Later that day, a search and rescue team returned to the ravine, and Madison’s body was located on the east side of the Ganaraska, where the river splits.

Paul Racine, 74, has lived nearby with his family for decades and knows the river well. Lately, he’s been keeping an eye on the beavers and their handiwork, bringing down aspen and ash trees. The river area is also frequented by turkey vultures and home to coyotes, foxes, raccoons, groundhogs, muskrats and “numerous dogs that are walked up and down there,” a lot off leash, says Racine.

“My contention,” says Racine, “is that there were Labs, there were setters, there were beagles, there were all kinds of dogs, and if (Madison) lay there for a month, there is absolutely no way that a dog wouldn’t have gone over and sniffed her out.”
Mark Chard believes there would have also been some wildlife interference if his daughter was there for so long.

According to weather records, Port Hope saw daytime high temperatures ranging from 10 to 21 C in the first seven days Madison was missing, and had climbed to highs of 26 to 27 C by the second week of May. Otherwise, temperatures were in the teens. Parts of Madison’s body showed “advanced” and moderate decompositional changes, according to a pathology report.
Police considered manslaughter charges
The police records obtained by the Chards indicate that police intended to consult with a Crown attorney about laying a manslaughter charge at one point.
One possible explanation is that police considered charging the person who sold or gave Madison tainted drugs.

A 2024 paper by York University graduate student Liam Michaud examined a “recent proliferation” of Canadian manslaughter charges and prosecutions of people involved in overdoses, who themselves use, share and sell drugs.

By looking at media reports and court decisions and through federal and provincial requests for information, Michaud found “the vast majority of those who face manslaughter charges are engaged in the lowest tiers of the drug trade, are themselves people who use drugs, and are often intimately known to the deceased.”
To date, no arrests have been made, and although police contemplated doing so, no search warrants were sought, according to police notes.

For years, the investigation remained open, and Mark passed along everything he discovered. Now, officers involved in the initial investigation are no longer on the case, and Port Hope has a new police chief.

The Star contacted the new chief, Tim Farquharson, to request an interview and shared a long list of questions about the investigation in writing in May. Following a couple of meetings Farquharson had with the OPP on the Star’s queries, the OPP responded by email with a statement on behalf of the two services.

“We are unable to comment on specific aspects of the investigation, including investigative processes, techniques, evidence-gathering methods or operational considerations,” Agata Czajkowski, Strategic Communications Advisor for the Ontario Provincial Police, said in the statement to the Star.
“Releasing such details could compromise investigative practices and operations.”

As for when to charge or not, Czajkowski said that in drug-related death cases “where investigators establish the necessary grounds, charges — including manslaughter, criminal negligence causing death or drug trafficking offences — will be pursued in accordance with the evidence.”
In police notes obtained by the Chards, a Port Hope officer references an unidentified male providing Madison with fentanyl and noted police will “need multiple witnesses to build manslaughter.”
The officer notes an OPP investigator on the case cautioning that if “witnesses are weak then we have nothing.”
Songs for Madi

Mark Chard holds a “Dad’s Walk” fundraising event for Ontario Shores annually in honour of his daughter. It takes place on the Port Hope Waterfront Trail along Lake Ontario, passing by a bench and tree with plaques bearing Madison’s name. He posts to Facebook on important anniversary dates, hoping they will get attention and maybe spark someone to speak up about what happened to a woman who is still very missed and loved.

Last August, more than 150 people turned out at the Port Hope United Church for “Songs for Madi” — a night of performances by friends and family, complete with drag performers — Mark was on drums with a band, including Mark’s older brother on guitar, playing “Day by Day” from the musical “Godspell.” Lori stood in a church pew, dancing. The event raised close to $5,000, again, for Ontario Shores, adding to $72,000 already raised.
“Madi is pissed that she’s not here,” said one of the emcee drag performers, prompting laughter.

Madison did make an appearance, however, when a video of her played on a large screen, made for her father’s 50th birthday. Accompanied by a guitar, Madison delivered a beautiful rendition of Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah.
“Love you, daddy,” said Madison, blowing a kiss to the camera at the end.
During an evening of songs for Madi, one by her brought tears.

content_blocks.text: In April, along the banks of Ganaraska River, the foliage is sparse. The ravine was searched, and police used a drone at one point. Nothing was found.

content_blocks.text: On May 18, 2022, the Toronto Sun posted an online story about Madison being missing for nearly a month. In it, Port Hope police said new information suggested Madison may have been taken in by a human trafficker and, according to the story, “may be in their control somewhere between Montreal and Windsor.” A police inspector was quoted as saying that traffickers often take their victim’s phone away.

content_blocks.text: The next morning, on May 19, the Sun story ran in print with a headline of “Where’s Madi?” Later that day, a search and rescue team returned to the ravine, and Madison’s body was located on the east side of the Ganaraska, where the river splits.

content_blocks.text: Paul Racine, 74, has lived nearby with his family for decades and knows the river well. Lately, he’s been keeping an eye on the beavers and their handiwork, bringing down aspen and ash trees. The river area is also frequented by turkey vultures and home to coyotes, foxes, raccoons, groundhogs, muskrats and “numerous dogs that are walked up and down there,” a lot off leash, says Racine.

content_blocks.text: According to weather records, Port Hope saw daytime high temperatures ranging from 10 to 21 C in the first seven days Madison was missing, and had climbed to highs of 26 to 27 C by the second week of May. Otherwise, temperatures were in the teens. Parts of Madison’s body showed “advanced” and moderate decompositional changes, according to a pathology report.

content_blocks.text: A 2024 paper by York University graduate student Liam Michaud examined a “recent proliferation” of Canadian manslaughter charges and prosecutions of people involved in overdoses, who themselves use, share and sell drugs.

content_blocks.text: By looking at media reports and court decisions and through federal and provincial requests for information, Michaud found “the vast majority of those who face manslaughter charges are engaged in the lowest tiers of the drug trade, are themselves people who use drugs, and are often intimately known to the deceased.”

content_blocks.text: Mark Chard holds a “Dad’s Walk” fundraising event for Ontario Shores annually in honour of his daughter. It takes place on the Port Hope Waterfront Trail along Lake Ontario, passing by a bench and tree with plaques bearing Madison’s name. He posts to Facebook on important anniversary dates, hoping they will get attention and maybe spark someone to speak up about what happened to a woman who is still very missed and loved.

content_blocks.text: Last August, more than 150 people turned out at the Port Hope United Church for “Songs for Madi” — a night of performances by friends and family, complete with drag performers — Mark was on drums with a band, including Mark’s older brother on guitar, playing “Day by Day” from the musical “Godspell.” Lori stood in a church pew, dancing. The event raised close to $5,000, again, for Ontario Shores, adding to $72,000 already raised.

stories.title: Knights continue winning streak to start season
stories.summary: The London Knights remain undefeated to start the 2026-27 season after defeating the Owen Sound Attack in a back-and-forth affair Friday night at Canada Life Place.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights remain undefeated to start the 2026-27 season after defeating the Owen Sound Attack 7-4 in a back-and-forth affair Friday night at Canada Life Place.

London fell down 2-1 halfway through the second period, before storming back with three goals in the span of four minutes off the backs of Cooper McAsian, Eloan Le Gallic, and Carson Hammer.

The Knights would extend their lead into the third period, before the Attacks would make things interesting, making it a one-goal game with five minutes to play.

Newly acquired Knight Thomas Zocco scored his first as a Knight to regain the two goal lead with under three minutes to go, while Evan Van Gorp would get the empty netter to secure the win for London.

The Knights will be back in action next Friday when they host the North Bay Battalion at Canada Life Place.

stories.title: Western Homecoming brings football, festivities and heightened safety measures for weekend
stories.summary: Western University’s campus is buzzing as students and alumni prepare for a weekend of football, festivities and Homecoming traditions.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Western University’s campus is buzzing as students and alumni prepare for a weekend of football, festivities and Homecoming traditions.

The annual event is expected to bring large crowds to campus and surrounding areas, prompting police, emergency services and university officials to prepare for the weekend.

“We’re excited for the weekend,” said Western University Provost (Students) John Doerksen. “It’s a great opportunity for alumni and students to come back to campus, reconnect with old friends and celebrate.”

Alongside the celebrations, authorities are mounting a major safety operation and warning people against large, unsanctioned street parties.

London police Inspector David Pratt said officers have been planning for the weekend for months with London Fire Services, paramedics, the City of London, Western University, Fanshawe College and other community partners.

“We’ll be well prepared and out in the community to show a presence,” Pratt said.

Police say additional officers will be deployed throughout the weekend, including support from neighbouring police services.

Hamilton police, Windsor police and the Ontario Provincial Police are expected to assist London police with enforcement and patrols.

Officials are urging people to avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, warning that violations can result in fines or criminal charges.

Western is encouraging students to take part in organized events on campus.

The football game remains a major draw, while the university is also hosting a Fan Festival featuring free food and activities for students.

“We have really good programming for students,” said Doerksen. “We have the football game, of course, that’s always a big draw, and we have something we call Fan Festival. So that’s an opportunity for students to come. There’s free food there. There’s all kinds of activities.”

London Health Sciences Centre is also preparing for a potentially busy weekend.

Dr. Vico Dagnone, head of emergency medicine at LHSC, said staff want people to enjoy Homecoming while making responsible decisions.

“We just want to make sure that everybody is safe and responsible,” said Dagnone. “We don’t want Homecoming remembered for the wrong reasons. We want it to be memorable for all the right reasons. But if you do need our medical care, we’ll be there for you.”

Officials say the goal is not to prevent people from celebrating, but to encourage people to do so safely and responsibly.

stories.title: RCMP remind drivers to stop for school buses after two Kelowna students are struck by a vehicle
stories.summary: Both students were taken to hospital with what police describe as serious injuries. Arbor View Drive was closed for hours while police investigated.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Two elementary school students were seriously injured after being struck by a vehicle in Kelowna’s Upper Mission Thursday.

“I thought it was my own kid because he gets off that bus as well,” said witness Kevin Dalman.

The incident happened on Arbor View Drive after the students got off the bus.

“The school bus had just dropped off the students,” said Kelowna RCMP Col. Steven Lang. “They were in the process of crossing the street and that’s when they were struck by the SUV, which was coming head-on towards the school bus in an opposite direction.”

Both students were taken to hospital with what police describe as serious injuries.

Arbor View Drive was closed for hours while police investigated.

One person was taken into custody but has since been released.

Police say no charges have been laid at this point.

“Alcohol is not considered to be a contributing factor. The other part of the criminality or related factors are under investigation,” Lang said.

Police are also investigating whether the school bus had activated its flashing red lights at the time of the incident.

The collision is prompting RCMP to remind drivers of the law when approaching a school bus.

“Drivers are required by law to stop on both sides of the school bus, remain stopped until those stop sign and lights are turned off, at which point they can proceed,” Lang said.

Several other students were still on the bus and witnessed the incident.

Central Okanagan Public Schools Superintendent Jon Rever issued the following statement:

“We are deeply saddened at this incident, and our thoughts are with the family and all those affected. Currently, our focus is supporting students and families. Our Post-Critical Incident Response Team is supporting students, staff, and conversations at home and school to ensure the safety and well-being of students.”
