stories.title: Feds grant New Brunswick $461 million for infrastructure projects
stories.summary: The federal government has announced it will transfer $461 million to New Brunswick for infrastructure projects as part of a new agreement.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
By Eli Ridder The Canadian Press

Posted September 25, 2026 4:10 pm

Updated September 25, 2026 6:16 pm

The federal government has announced it will transfer $461 million to New Brunswick for infrastructure projects as part of a new agreement.

A news release from the federal Department of Housing, Infrastructure and Communities says the funding includes $305 million for housing and post-secondary education projects and priorities.

The federal government says New Brunswick has agreed in the deal that it won’t increase any fees or taxes that hinder housing supply.

The province says $155 million of the funding is set aside for health infrastructure.

Officials say the Dr. Georges-L.-Dumont University Hospital in Moncton, N.B., will receive $25.7 million for endoscopy modernization and expansion, and $1 million for future planning.

The cash comes from Ottawa’s $51-billion Build Communities Strong Fund, which was announced as part of the 2025 federal budget.

“Canada and New Brunswick are making strategic investments that will help unlock new housing, strengthen post-secondary education and support modern, reliable health infrastructure,” federal Internal Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in a statement.

stories.title: Feist talks Heated Rivalry, iPod ads and hit covers ahead of induction into Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame
stories.summary: ‘It’s eclipsed anything that’s happened in my career so far,’ Mushaboom singer says of hit TV show
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
The first episode of the first season of the smash-hit Canadian gay hockey drama Heated Rivalry ends in a sexually charged locker-room encounter. “We can forget that happened in there, okay?” one player says to the other afterward. The second player, wearing nothing but a towel and a smile, isn’t buying it: Neither of them are forgetting anything.

The scene closes with the sounds of Leslie Feist’s song Sealion, from her 2007 album The Reminder. You can bet Feist isn’t forgetting that moment and another one just like it: Her My Moon My Man , co-written with Chilly Gonzales and from the same Grammy-nominated album, was used in a long, extended montage that opened Heated Rivalry ’s fourth episode. The song placements on the beyond buzzy television show have been a boon to her already highly successful career.

“It’s eclipsed anything that’s happened in my career so far,” she said on a recent video call. “I feel like the Beatles.”

Connecting the dots to explain Angine de Poitrine’s Polaris Music Prize win

Feist, 50, will be inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on Saturday at a gala concert held in Toronto’s Massey Hall. The 2026 class also includes the Tragically Hip, Roch Voisine and Loverboy’s Mike Reno and Paul Dean.

The induction ceremony will be livestreamed on Prime Video in Canada and globally through Amazon Music. Among the scheduled performers are Allison Russell, Amanda Marshall, Charlotte Cornfield, City and Colour, Finneas, Isabelle Boulay, Jeff Tweedy, Ludovick Bourgeois, Our Lady Peace and Ruby Waters.

Feist’s biggest moments of exposure didn’t come by any machinations of her own. Her breakout 2007 hit 1234 , a catchy, banjoed nursery rhyme co-written with Australian singer-songwriter Sally Seltmann, rocketed to chart success when the song’s video was used in an Apple iPod Nano commercial.

The song’s video was a simple and joyful dance production shot in an empty sound stage. At the time, MuchMusic and MTV were on the cultural decline, YouTube wasn’t the mainstream force it would become and TikTok was just a sound a clock made.

“I remember thinking, this is crazy,” Feist recalled. “There wasn’t really a place for it to go. The heart inside of it was so pure that when I was asked by Apple to use it, it felt like a no-brainer.”

As AI-generated music floods platforms, Canadian artists demand consent, transparency and pay

Though the Alberta-raised singer-songwriter wasn’t given money for the use of the video, the exposure was more than enough payment. The single made her internationally famous.

“Apple was saying, ‘We’re going to put your music video everywhere in the world.’ I thought, that sounds like a pretty fair deal. Let’s do it.”

On the morning of our interview, Feist received an e-mail from an Australian theatre company asking to use one of her songs. She doesn’t remember which one it was − “It May have been Mushaboom ” − and didn’t really give the matter a lot of thought before okaying its use.

“There’s no reason to stop the song’s expression from continuing to do its expressing.”

Bryan Adams gets patriotic with new album, plus more music coming up

In 2010, British singer-songwriter and producer James Blake covered Limit to Your Love , another song Feist co-written with Gonzalez. Blake’s minimalist version cracked the British Top 40 chart.

“I couldn’t be more grateful, because the song deserved to have a different set of wings,” Feist said. “It went different places than it could with me.”

The 12-time Juno winner feels the same way about covers by Blake and Bon Iver (who covered Feist’s The Park ) as she does about amateurs performing her compositions on Instagram.

“I see them from Argentina or Seoul or Saskatoon, and I love watching them. It’s my privacy travelling across wires, rays and beams that get songs from me to them and goes into someone else’s privacy. And if it can go all the way in to where they feel it’s their own, that’s the best outcome.”

Wilco’s Jeff Tweedy : “There’s an intimacy to Leslie’s songwriting. She’s letting you in. I believe she works really hard on not putting out anything that doesn’t feel great to her. The criteria she has is a very high bar.”

Quebec pop-classical pianist Jean-Michel Blais : “I recorded Mushaboom in 2018. Her songwriting has always fascinated me, especially here, in the way she makes the extraordinary emerge from the everyday. Mushaboom turns the mundane into a dream, bringing us with her. There is something I love about the way she imagines a future that already carries the flavour of a memory.”

Broken Social Scene’s Charles Spearin : “Leslie’s contribution to Broken Social Scene goes far beyond just the lyrics, melody and spirit of the songs she sings. She somehow changes the weather and the seasons, elevating all of us.”

The song placements on the beyond buzzy television show have been a boon to her already highly successful career.
“It’s eclipsed anything that’s happened in my career so far,” she said on a recent video call. “I feel like the Beatles.”
Connecting the dots to explain Angine de Poitrine’s Polaris Music Prize win

Feist, 50, will be inducted into the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame on Saturday at a gala concert held in Toronto’s Massey Hall. The 2026 class also includes the Tragically Hip, Roch Voisine and Loverboy’s Mike Reno and Paul Dean.

The induction ceremony will be livestreamed on Prime Video in Canada and globally through Amazon Music. Among the scheduled performers are Allison Russell, Amanda Marshall, Charlotte Cornfield, City and Colour, Finneas, Isabelle Boulay, Jeff Tweedy, Ludovick Bourgeois, Our Lady Peace and Ruby Waters.

Feist’s biggest moments of exposure didn’t come by any machinations of her own. Her breakout 2007 hit 1234 , a catchy, banjoed nursery rhyme co-written with Australian singer-songwriter Sally Seltmann, rocketed to chart success when the song’s video was used in an Apple iPod Nano commercial.

The song’s video was a simple and joyful dance production shot in an empty sound stage. At the time, MuchMusic and MTV were on the cultural decline, YouTube wasn’t the mainstream force it would become and TikTok was just a sound a clock made.

“I remember thinking, this is crazy,” Feist recalled. “There wasn’t really a place for it to go. The heart inside of it was so pure that when I was asked by Apple to use it, it felt like a no-brainer.”
As AI-generated music floods platforms, Canadian artists demand consent, transparency and pay
Though the Alberta-raised singer-songwriter wasn’t given money for the use of the video, the exposure was more than enough payment. The single made her internationally famous.
“Apple was saying, ‘We’re going to put your music video everywhere in the world.’ I thought, that sounds like a pretty fair deal. Let’s do it.”

On the morning of our interview, Feist received an e-mail from an Australian theatre company asking to use one of her songs. She doesn’t remember which one it was − “It May have been Mushaboom ” − and didn’t really give the matter a lot of thought before okaying its use.
“There’s no reason to stop the song’s expression from continuing to do its expressing.”
Bryan Adams gets patriotic with new album, plus more music coming up
In 2010, British singer-songwriter and producer James Blake covered Limit to Your Love , another song Feist co-written with Gonzalez. Blake’s minimalist version cracked the British Top 40 chart.
“I couldn’t be more grateful, because the song deserved to have a different set of wings,” Feist said. “It went different places than it could with me.”
The 12-time Juno winner feels the same way about covers by Blake and Bon Iver (who covered Feist’s The Park ) as she does about amateurs performing her compositions on Instagram.

“I see them from Argentina or Seoul or Saskatoon, and I love watching them. It’s my privacy travelling across wires, rays and beams that get songs from me to them and goes into someone else’s privacy. And if it can go all the way in to where they feel it’s their own, that’s the best outcome.”

content_blocks.text: 1,2,3 songwriters on Feist

Wilco’s Jeff Tweedy : “There’s an intimacy to Leslie’s songwriting. She’s letting you in. I believe she works really hard on not putting out anything that doesn’t feel great to her. The criteria she has is a very high bar.”

Quebec pop-classical pianist Jean-Michel Blais : “I recorded Mushaboom in 2018. Her songwriting has always fascinated me, especially here, in the way she makes the extraordinary emerge from the everyday. Mushaboom turns the mundane into a dream, bringing us with her. There is something I love about the way she imagines a future that already carries the flavour of a memory.”

Broken Social Scene’s Charles Spearin : “Leslie’s contribution to Broken Social Scene goes far beyond just the lyrics, melody and spirit of the songs she sings. She somehow changes the weather and the seasons, elevating all of us.”

stories.title: ROM to show McMichael collection while gallery undergoes renovation
stories.summary: The exhibition featuring paintings by Tom Thomson, the Group of Seven and leading Canadian women artists will run until 2028
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
For the next two years, visitors will be able to reach the McMichael Canadian Art Collection on the Bloor and University subway lines in Toronto.

The art gallery in bucolic Kleinburg, Ont., is currently closed for a three-year renovation and expansion, but is lending its classic Canadian paintings to the Royal Ontario Museum. The ROM announced on Friday that starting Nov. 22, it will host an exhibition adapted from Old Growth, the McMichael’s closing show that featured highlights of its collection.

Entitled This Land: The Group of Seven and their Contemporaries, the ROM show will include paintings by Tom Thomson and the Group of Seven, as well as their female peers – Emily Carr, Yvonne McKague Housser, Anne Savage and Bess Harris.

In recent years, the McMichael has made a point of showing the Canadian women who were painting alongside the all-male members of the Group.

“In an era when the world wants more Canada, the ROM is thrilled to host this landmark exhibition,” ROM director and chief executive Nicholas Bell said in a statement. Focusing on landscape, the exhibition will be organized in eight geographic sections, including Georgian Bay, Algonquin Park, Algoma, La Cloche Mountains, Lake Superior, Rocky Mountains, British Columbia, and the Arctic, as the members of the Ontario-based Group pushed west and north.

The ROM promises enhanced interpretation for the art show, drawing on its expertise in natural history to look at geography and plant life in the paintings. It will also investigate the Indigenous names and stories of the places depicted. The exhibition will run until Sept. 4, 2028.

The McMichael, the only major art museum in Canada devoted exclusively to Canadian art, is located on a forested site on the Humber River in Kleinburg, a village in Vaughan about 40 minutes north of downtown Toronto.

The McMichael renovation, expected to cost $150-million and last until 2029, will update the building’s systems and add new gallery spaces, more room for conservation and framing, and a revenue-generating event space.

The ROM-McMichael partnership is being funded by ROM board chair Jeff Willner and his wife Stacey Madge.

stories.title: MPs split on whether AI should be used in House of Commons
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canadian members of Parliament are split on whether — and how — artificial intelligence should be used by lawmakers.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Members of Parliament are split on whether — and how — artificial intelligence should be used by lawmakers following a report that said the technology is being used to write a significant amount of what MPs say in the House of Commons.

The Economist reported this week that as much as 20 per cent of what was said on the floor of the House of Commons in late 2025 was flagged as AI-generated.

The publication studied comments, speeches and questions from MPs of more than 100 words, as recorded in Hansard, and ran them through the AI detector tool Pangram.

It compared the results from different countries, including legislatures in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and the United States, and found Canada had the second-highest rate of AI use.

Some MPs in Ottawa flatly denied using AI tools to generate what they say in Parliament, while others said it can be useful for research.

“I think everybody’s using artificial intelligence,” said Conservative MP Sandra Cobena, who called it a great research tool but said it has to be used with care.

She said the Conservative party does not have specific rules on the use of AI to generate speeches or comments for MPs but “it is expected that everybody uses it responsibly.”

“Of course parliamentarians are using it,” she said.

Her caucus colleague Luc Berthold agreed its use is widespread and said he uses it for research.

“If the sentence is really good, I will probably put it in and use it,” he said.

But the technology usually can’t capture the way he wants to express himself, he added.

“Quebecers, we have a lot of emotion, and AI doesn’t have any,” he said.

Liberal MP Greg Fergus said he’s “an analog man” and he wouldn’t know how to use the technology.

“For actually creatively engaging, in a place where we’re supposed to be talking about our laws and representing our folks, no, I don’t think it’s useful,” he said.

Liberal MP Anthony Housefather said he would prefer it if MPs weren’t using AI-generated text but he doesn’t have an issue with it.

Fellow Liberal Ben Carr also said he’s not a user of AI because he wants to speak in his own voice.

He said that while he thinks using AI to generate an entire speech would be “somewhat problematic,” there’s nothing wrong with using it to collect your thoughts.

“We want people to be representing their communities as best as they can. And it doesn’t mean that you can’t represent your community by using the assistance of artificial intelligence to generate your thoughts and your views and your perspectives,” he said.

A spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office said neither the prime minister nor members of his office use AI to generate statements or responses delivered in the House of Commons.

Conservative MP Scott Reid said he used the tool on Friday to find information quickly in the middle of question period.

Reid said a Liberal member across the aisle was “heckling so loud that I could barely hear myself think” as he asked a question. Reid said he consulted AI to ask which Standing Order — the rules that govern the House of Commons — would be violated by the interruption so he could report that to the clerk.

The Green Party said its MPs are independent and party rules don’t allow the leader or anyone else in the party to dictate how a member carries out their duties.

“(Leader) Elizabeth (May) herself is very concerned about artificial intelligence and is deeply committed to avoiding AI in both her personal life and her role as an MP,” said party spokesperson Bianca Crêtes.

A spokesperson for the New Democrats said the party is developing a policy on AI usage for MP offices and is working with the union that represents its parliamentary staff.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie and David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Michigan CEO who posted 'Lake America' sweatshirt photo no longer with company
stories.summary: The Family First credit union did not state that if the public reaction to Smith's post was the reason for her departure.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Canada

Credit union says Jane Smith 'no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately'

Last updated 37 minutes ago[](http://nationalpost.com/news/Canada/michigan-CEO-who-posted-lake-america-sweatshirt-photo-no-longer-with-company#comments-area)

A map showing Lake Ontario as "Lake America" displayed as U.S. President Donald Trump speaks after signing an executive order on Aug. 27, 2026 to rename the lake.Photo by Andrew Harnik /Getty Images

The Michigan credit union CEO who recently shared a social media post with an AI-generated travel photo showing her and her family wearing “Lake America” sweatshirts is no longer with the company.

Her post stated she was “not sure” if Canada would like the sweatshirts, provoking an online backlash, as previously reported on by National Post.

This week, a statement posted on the credit union’s website said that Jane Smith was “no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately.” It was signed by Maurice Patterson, chairman of the Family First Credit Union board, as well as interim CEO and Chief Operations Officer Jason Acosta.

Family First did not state if the public reaction to Smith’s online post was the reason for her departure.

Smith had publicly explained that the photo in the post, shared on several social media platforms, was generated using ChatGPT. She apologized for it in a statement to ABC12, an ABC News affiliate in Michigan.

Taking further accountability for the stunt, she confessed, “I made a mistake. I own that mistake, and I am committed to learning from it.”

The credit union board issued its own statement last week saying that although “the post involved Ms. Smith in her personal capacity in connection with a family vacation, the post is unacceptable. Ms. Smith’s conduct does not reflect the values, mission, or culture of Family First Credit Union. We support and respect our Canadian neighbors, and we completely disavow Ms. Smith’s actions, which were undertaken without the authorization or knowledge of the Credit Union.”

Further, the board apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community” and told ABC12 it would be determining appropriate next steps for Smith.

The initial controversy followed U.S. President Donald Trump signing an executive order changing the name of the lake from Lake Ontario to Lake America on Aug. 27. As reported by National Post, he directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name, sparking negative reactions from politicians in Canada and the U.S.

The Michigan credit union CEO who recently shared a social media post with an AI-generated travel photo showing her and her family wearing “Lake America” sweatshirts is no longer with the company.
Her post stated she was “not sure” if Canada would like the sweatshirts, provoking an online backlash, as previously reported on by National Post.

This week, a statement posted on the credit union’s website said that Jane Smith was “no longer an employee of Family First Credit Union, effective immediately.” It was signed by Maurice Patterson, chairman of the Family First Credit Union board, as well as interim CEO and Chief Operations Officer Jason Acosta.
Family First did not state if the public reaction to Smith’s online post was the reason for her departure.

Smith had publicly explained that the photo in the post, shared on several social media platforms, was generated using ChatGPT. She apologized for it in a statement to ABC12, an ABC News affiliate in Michigan.
Taking further accountability for the stunt, she confessed, “I made a mistake. I own that mistake, and I am committed to learning from it.”

Ms. Smith’s conduct does not reflect the values, mission, or culture of Family First Credit Union. We support and respect our Canadian neighbors, and we completely disavow Ms. Smith’s actions, which were undertaken without the authorization or knowledge of the Credit Union.”
Further, the board apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community” and told ABC12 it would be determining appropriate next steps for Smith.

The initial controversy followed U.S. President Donald Trump signing an executive order changing the name of the lake from Lake Ontario to Lake America on Aug. 27. As reported by National Post, he directed the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases to reflect the new name, sparking negative reactions from politicians in Canada and the U.S.

stories.title: Showdown in the Downtown trying to punch out kidney disease
stories.summary: They will be kicking and punching it out for charity this Saturday night as Showdown in the Downtown returns for the 17th time in London, Ont.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
They will be kicking and punching it out for charity this Saturday night as Showdown in the Downtown returns for the 17 th time in London, Ont.

“This year on September 26 th , we’re at RBC Place and we are having a mixed martial arts tournament with 12 bouts,” said Dr. Faisal Rehman, a kidney specialist and one of the organizers of the event who also participates in the ring. “We have seven amazing charities that are benefitting from our event this year.”

The main beneficiary is kidney research. The money raised goes to help people like Cole Heessels, who lost an arm and a leg as a child linked to kidney failure.

“My disease causes blood clots all over the body and it caused my amputations and kidney failure,” said Heessels. “Events like Showdown in the Downtown helps with research money.”

Samantha Melnick suffers from a different ailment, but like Cole, she too is prone to blood clotting due to kidney problems. The mother of three started feeling ill about nine months ago, saying, “Every day my symptoms began to get a little bit worse.”

She added, “In a matter of days it went from celebrating with my family and friends on New Years Day to lying in a hospital bed fighting for my life. It was scary.”

“Both Cole and Samantha have rare conditions that cause blood clots everywhere and those blood clots can affect the brain and cause strokes and kidney failure along with nerve damage and amputations,” said Rehman.

Since 2009, Showdown in the Downtown has been successful in raising more than $3 million for local charities.

“The money benefits research that not only benefits people in London and across Canada but also everyone around the world,” said Rehman.

stories.title: Costco sees sales jump 11% and more customers eyeing ‘lower cost protein’
stories.summary: Costco's latest quarterly earnings report, released late Thursday, showed a jump in sales from a year earlier as the company describes consumers looking to stretch their dollars.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Costco ‘s latest quarterly earnings report, released late Thursday, showed a jump in sales from a year earlier as the company describes consumers looking to stretch their dollars as far as they can.

This comes as the heightened cost of living in Canada forces many households to cut back on some non-essential items and experiences, with a report released earlier this week showing even higher-income Canadians are dining out less than a year ago.

In the three months leading up to the end of August, Costco says net sales increased 11.2 percent to US$93.9 billion from $84.4 billion last year.

Meanwhile, membership fees totalled $1.85 billion, up about seven per cent from $1.724 billion in the same quarter of 2025. Costco’s membership fees have not changed since an increase in 2024.

Speaking during a conference call with analysts after the earnings release, chief financial officer Gary Millerchip said that Costco has 84.1 million paid members in total, up 3.8 per cent from a year earlier.

Costco said it believes its focus on value offerings is driving consumers to them for more of their shopping because they want to make sure that if they have to spend their money, they are getting the most they can in return.

Consumers are also grappling with high prices for many everyday items, including groceries, as consumer inflation in Canada and the U.S. was last measured in August at three per cent and 3.4 per cent, respectively.

4:40 More Canadian shoppers turning to second-hand shopping

The war in Iran and AI spending are putting pressure on prices for oil, gas, and related by products and well as electronics and components like memory chips . This, Costco said, has led to higher prices in some categories.

“Just to unpack inflation for you […] the area where we did see some increase in the current quarter was in non-foods. That was really, I wouldn’t say it was isolated, but the vast majority of it was in memory costs on consumer electronics and the items that you would expect to be related to oil,” said Millerchip.

“So gas prices, which we include in our inflation number, and petroleum-based items as well, So those would be the areas where we would’ve seen the increase in non-foods.”

Despite some areas where prices have increased, Costco said its members are still willing to open their wallets if they feel they are getting good value.

“We see members being very thoughtful about where they’re spending their dollars,” said Millerchip.

“They’re looking for value in everyday items. But they’re also, as I mentioned, willing to spend on items where they see it’s a great value, even if it is in some of those non-discretionary categories.”

1:54 Inflation drives Halifax discount retail boom

Millerchip continued and said there was more-than 50 per cent growth in sales of “non-foods,” and included examples ranging from tires to houseware and furniture, to health and beauty items, small appliances, and even massage chairs and saunas.

He also said that within the food section, there has been steady sales growth in “lower-cost proteins” as consumers look to fill the fridge while saving money.

At the same time, Millerchip said another example of consumers being willing to spend more if there is greater perceived value was more demand for premium or “indulgent” food products.

“Similarly, I would say in fresh, everyday items, it really shows up in ground beef and poultry, but then on premium items in USDA Prime and Wagyu beef,” he said.

“Also in bakery, we see tremendous strength in bakery, where we are offering really great quality, indulgent items for members to buy. I think it shows up in all the different categories.”

stories.title: Volkswagen subsidiary delays opening of EV battery plant
stories.summary: PowerCo Canada said the $7-billion project in St. Thomas will begin operations in 2029
stories.author: Eric Atkins, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
A subsidiary of Volkswagen Group has delayed by two years the opening of its electric-vehicle battery plant in Ontario, in another setback to Canada’s hopes of creating an EV manufacturing sector.

PowerCo Canada said in a press release on Thursday the battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., will begin operations in 2029 rather than the 2027 target set when the $7-billion project was announced in 2023. The company said at the time the project will be its largest battery plant and employ as many as 3,000 people.

“St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve,” PowerCo said in a statement on Thursday, describing the project as a “demand-aligned.”

Ontario EV battery plant to anchor new industrial megasite

PowerCo spokeswoman Tegan Versolatto said the company is taking a “phased approach” to ensure the plant is built to meet future market needs and advances in technology.

“The timeline reflects a disciplined approach to an evolving market, not a change in commitment,” Ms. Versolatto said in an e-mail Friday.

The delay underlines the headwinds faced by EV makers amid slowing demand in growth for zero-emissions cars after the U.S. government removed consumer purchase incentives.

The International Energy Agency estimates electric vehicles will account for almost one-third of global sales in 2026. But EVs were just 5.8 per cent of U.S. new cars sales in the second quarter, according to U.S. consultancy Cox Automotive. In Canada, zero-emissions cars accounted for almost 11 per cent of new sales in July, Statistics Canada says.

A handful of Canadian EV projects have been cancelled in the past two years, despite billions of dollars in taxpayer contributions federally and provincially.

Speaking to reporters at Queen’s Park, Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles on Friday said the delay was more evidence that the province’s EV strategy was in tatters, noting other auto companies that have pulled out of or delayed plans to build factories in the province.

The federal and Ontario governments have announced billions in incentives and subsidies in an effort to attract companies that will build an EV supply chain, from batteries to complete vehicles.

“I am going to remain optimistic that those jobs will be coming to the people of St. Thomas,” Ms. Stiles said. “We desperately need them. But I am very concerned.”

Ontario Premier Doug Ford said on Friday he is not worried by the delay.

Ottawa and the province agreed to provide $1.4-billion in funding to the project, but the money does not flow until certain benchmarks are reached.

“I know they said they’re going to delay it, but when you sign a $1.4-billion dollar agreement, a contract – that’s massive,” Mr. Ford said. “That says, ‘Okay, we’re in uncertain times around the world right now, but we have confidence in Ontario.’”

Opinion: Good EV plan, Canada. The risk now lies in execution

The province’s Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli said the two-year delay was actually good news, as PowerCo has signed a deal with a major contractor to go ahead with the massive plant.

“I think to me, the news yesterday was extremely exciting. I know there’s different takes on it, but for me, there are now shovels in the ground,” Mr. Fedeli told reporters Friday in Toronto. “The company has been hired, awarded a contract. There’s a $7-billion building and infrastructure being built there. To me, that’s nothing but good news.”

Mr. Fedeli called the news that Volkswagen intended to proceed with the plant a “massive relief,” noting it is one of three such battery sites it will have around the world, building not just for EVs but making other lithium-ion batteries for other uses as well.

He said provincial money given to the company– he did not say how much – along with spending by the local municipality in sewer and water pipes for the site would have been spent attracting other companies to the town’s industrial park. He said he expected other feeder companies to set up near the PowerCo project.

PowerCo mentioned the delayed start in the second-last paragraph of a press release announcing Canadian construction company EllisDon Corp. as the general contractor for the next phase of construction.

“Partnering with EllisDon allows us to keep construction moving while ensuring we retain the flexibility to scale the facility in line with market demand and long-term industry evolution,” said Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer of PowerCo Canada.

Much of the building’s structure is in place, with 60 EllisDon workers on site and a few hundred PowerCo employees working elsewhere. That’s according to St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who said in an interview he is confident the battery plant will open in 2029 but would have preferred to see it open sooner.

“I drive by the plant every day and there’s about a billion dollars’ worth of construction that’s already occurred,” Mr. Preston said by phone. “It will carry on being the largest of Volkswagen’s battery facilities and located in St. Thomas, Ontario. We’re still pretty excited about it.”

Recent reversals in Canada’s EV projects include Honda’s indefinite suspension of a $15-billion Ontario project this year and Northvolt of Sweden’s battery plant near Montreal, which collapsed in bankruptcy in 2025.

Stellantis in February walked away from its NextStar EV battery joint venture in Windsor, Ont., leaving it to LG Energy Solution. The factory has pivoted to energy storage as growth in demand for EVs slowed.

Additionally, General Motors last year cancelled the BrightDrop electric delivery van and laid off 1,150 people in Ingersoll, Ont. Ford, meanwhile, abandoned plans to make EVs in Oakville, Ont., in 2024 and switched to pickups powered by fossil fuels.

With a report from Laura Stone

He said provincial money given to the company– he did not say how much – along with spending by the local municipality in sewer and water pipes for the site would have been spent attracting other companies to the town’s industrial park. He said he expected other feeder companies to set up near the PowerCo project.

PowerCo mentioned the delayed start in the second-last paragraph of a press release announcing Canadian construction company EllisDon Corp. as the general contractor for the next phase of construction.

“Partnering with EllisDon allows us to keep construction moving while ensuring we retain the flexibility to scale the facility in line with market demand and long-term industry evolution,” said Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer of PowerCo Canada.

Much of the building’s structure is in place, with 60 EllisDon workers on site and a few hundred PowerCo employees working elsewhere. That’s according to St. Thomas Mayor Joe Preston, who said in an interview he is confident the battery plant will open in 2029 but would have preferred to see it open sooner.

“I drive by the plant every day and there’s about a billion dollars’ worth of construction that’s already occurred,” Mr. Preston said by phone. “It will carry on being the largest of Volkswagen’s battery facilities and located in St. Thomas, Ontario. We’re still pretty excited about it.”

Recent reversals in Canada’s EV projects include Honda’s indefinite suspension of a $15-billion Ontario project this year and Northvolt of Sweden’s battery plant near Montreal, which collapsed in bankruptcy in 2025.

Stellantis in February walked away from its NextStar EV battery joint venture in Windsor, Ont., leaving it to LG Energy Solution. The factory has pivoted to energy storage as growth in demand for EVs slowed.

Additionally, General Motors last year cancelled the BrightDrop electric delivery van and laid off 1,150 people in Ingersoll, Ont. Ford, meanwhile, abandoned plans to make EVs in Oakville, Ont., in 2024 and switched to pickups powered by fossil fuels.

PowerCo Canada said in a press release on Thursday the battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., will begin operations in 2029 rather than the 2027 target set when the $7-billion project was announced in 2023. The company said at the time the project will be its largest battery plant and employ as many as 3,000 people.

“St. Thomas is now expected to begin operations in 2029 to accommodate next-generation battery technology, while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve,” PowerCo said in a statement on Thursday, describing the project as a “demand-aligned.”
Ontario EV battery plant to anchor new industrial megasite
PowerCo spokeswoman Tegan Versolatto said the company is taking a “phased approach” to ensure the plant is built to meet future market needs and advances in technology.
“The timeline reflects a disciplined approach to an evolving market, not a change in commitment,” Ms. Versolatto said in an e-mail Friday.
The delay underlines the headwinds faced by EV makers amid slowing demand in growth for zero-emissions cars after the U.S. government removed consumer purchase incentives.

The International Energy Agency estimates electric vehicles will account for almost one-third of global sales in 2026. But EVs were just 5.8 per cent of U.S. new cars sales in the second quarter, according to U.S. consultancy Cox Automotive. In Canada, zero-emissions cars accounted for almost 11 per cent of new sales in July, Statistics Canada says.

stories.title: Swatting incident in Meaford draws large police presence
stories.summary: If you saw a big police presence in Meaford recently, police have confirmed it was a swatting incident. A swatting incident is the investigation of a fake emergency call.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
If you saw a big police presence in Meaford recently, police have confirmed it was a swatting incident. A swatting incident is the investigation of a fake emergency call.

On Thursday just before 6 p.m., Grey Bruce OPP received a call from a support service, saying an individual reported someone in their home was in crisis.

The helpline worker said they heard what sounded like gunshots in the background.

Police responded immediately to the home on Denmark Street between Edwin Street and Margaret Street.

Officers contained the area and more cops were sent to keep the surrounding community safe. A notification was issued to let residents know via social media.

The investigation was ruled unfounded. By 7 p.m., OPP confirmed it was a swatting call and cleared the area.

“These incidents are treated seriously, due to the risks they create for the public, emergency responders, and the individuals at the targeted location,” police said in a news release.

“Once a false emergency call is placed, emergency resources responding to that incident are unavailable to assist with legitimate emergencies elsewhere in the community.”

Police remind that making a false emergency call is a criminal offence.

stories.title: G7, G20 working on ‘pragmatic’ approach to AI regulation, minister says
stories.summary: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed on Wednesday that the government's Medicare website had been hacked by an OpenAI agent.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada is speaking to fellow member states of the G7 and G20 to work towards a “pragmatic way to regulate” AI globally, Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said on Friday.

Concerns around AI safety are “real concerns” that have “accelerated” in recent days with some major data breaches by AI agents, Solomon said.

“We need kind of like a red phone,” Solomon said, referencing the communication link set up for crisis contact between Washington and the Soviet Union during the Cold War: a time when diplomatic tensions were high and fears of existential dangers from nuclear war dominated geopolitics.

“We in the G7 and the G20 are talking,” he said at an event in Toronto.

Governments around the have been communicating on AI safety regulations, he said.

“We are all moving towards a pragmatic way to regulate this,” he added.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed on Wednesday that a government website had been hacked by an OpenAI agent.

The June hack targeted the website for Medicare, Australia’s publicly funded universal health insurance plan, he said.

Solomon did not specifically address the Australia hack. Global News reached out to his office to ask whether Canada had a response to the Australia hack and whether Ottawa plans to review its own safety regulations in light of the breach.

“I want to update Australians on an incident in which an artificial intelligence agent has infiltrated an Australian government website. This incident occurred in June this year and involved an open AI agent gaining unauthorized access into the public facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal,” Albanese told reporters in New York Wednesday, where he was attending a session of the United Nations General Assembly.

The AI agent accessed “both public and non-public files,” Albanese said.

OpenAI said in a statement it had reviewed activity involving several Australian government departments and discovered “our models took actions we did not intend.”

The company notified Australia of the breach in an email to a government department’s generic address on Sept. 10, Albanese said.

“I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” he said, adding that he was forming a task force to “to provide an urgent and immediate review into this incident to determine whether existing processes are appropriate to respond to AI-related cyber incidents.”

Generally, when AI companies are testing the capabilities of their agents, they are placed within a secure environment known as a “sandbox.”

Last month, OpenAI published a sweeping report of its rogue AI agents hacking Hugging Face, another AI firm.

Not only did the agents break out of their “isolated environment,” the company said they were communicating with each other to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

stories.title: Pitching in: Restaurateur tackles food insecurity from coast to coast
stories.summary: Mark Brand has built a network of social enterprises and charitable programs aimed at getting more meals to Canadians in need
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizer : Mark Brand

The pitch: Addressing food insecurity

Mark Brand has been cooking since he was a teenager and he opened his first restaurant in Vancouver in 2007, naming it after his mother Boneta.

He went on to open other eateries, a cocktail bar and entertainment venues but soon found that he wanted to have more of a social impact.

In 2010 he acquired Save on Meats a local institution in Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside. “I knew the owner and he was retiring, and it had been a place of food security for 57 years, where people could go and sit at the counter and have a burger for four bucks,” Mr. Brand, 50, recalled.

After extensive renovations, he kept its focus on social impact and sold tokens for $2.25 which donors could give to someone in need to redeem for a sandwich. There were also areas for people involved in urban agriculture. “We used it as a space for us all to learn together,” he said.

He incorporated Save on Meats as one of B.C.’s first benefit companies, a special designation for businesses that make a contribution to the community. “My entire mandate was: We can use business as a tool for good,” he said.

Pitching in: Friends retrace Toronto subway line on foot, raising money for unhoused people

To serve even more people in need, Mr. Brand launched a charity called The Better Life Foundation which provides regular meals to various groups such as women’s shelters and homeless organizations. The foundation also offers culinary training for at-risk people including ex-offenders.

Mr. Brand has expanded his social enterprise, called Upward Kitchens, and the foundation to his hometown of Halifax. Upward Kitchens runs a coffee shop called The Nook which is supported by sponsors and offers affordable meal and sells tokens. Upward also runs a farm in Dartmouth, a teaching kitchen for young people, and prepares meals for around 30 Halifax schools. Mr. Brand has also just launched a partnership with the Nova Scotia Community College and Saint Mary’s University to provide frozen meals for students.

Mr. Brand’s objective has always been to incorporate lessons from entrepreneurship into social impact. And he’s furious that food insecurity remains an issue in a country as rich as Canada. “It should be a national crisis,” he said. “Water and food and shelter should be guaranteed. As Canadians, we have no excuse.”

stories.title: Sunny weekend with intermittent clouds expected
stories.summary: A sunny weekend is expected, with some intermittent clouds, according to CTV Meteorologist Gary Archibald.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
A sunny weekend is expected, with some intermittent clouds, according to CTV Meteorologist Gary Archibald.

He says a ridge of high pressure is keeping the weather calm and quiet. No storms or rain is expected throughout the weekend.

“[Friday] was a cool start and below seasonal by 3 C, but mostly under cleat sky,” said Archibald.

“Might have seen some patchy fog and that dissipated over the last few hours of the morning. Now, we’re contending with a relatively weak front, at least across southern Ontario, that will bring some intermittent cloud, but of the fair-weather variety over the next several hours.”

Here’s a full look at your forecast:

Friday night: A few clouds. Low 7 C.

Saturday: Sunny. Wind northeast 20 km/h late in the morning. High 21 C.

Saturday night: Clear. Low 8 C.

Sunday: Sunny. High 22 C.

Monday: Sunny. High 22 C.

stories.title: 9 Islamic schools on high alert after email threatening ‘slaughter’ of Muslims
stories.summary: The Muslim Association of Canada says nine schools it operates across Canada are on high alert after the schools each received an email this week threatening violence against Muslims.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Multiple police forces are investigating threats made to Islamic schools across the country after the Muslim Association of Canada said nine of its schools received an email this week threatening violence.

Spokesperson Nabil Sultan said the same anonymous email was sent to schools in Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec over a 24-hour period.

The email, shared with The Canadian Press and signed by a “Citizen Vigilante,” threatens the “slaughter” of Muslims and vows Canada will be “Islam free.”

Sultan, whose own child attends a MAC school, said he was devastated to read the letter, and that MAC has hired paid security to keep students safe.

He said the organization is used to receiving threatening and Islamophobic emails, but this is the first time the non-profit’s schools have been targeted in such a direct way.

Police in Ontario’s Peel region said Friday they’re aware of a letter “containing hate-motivated threats” against Islamic institutions and have increased police patrols overnight near mosques and schools, which will continue into the weekend.

The force said its hate crime unit is investigating.

Police in London, Ont., and the province’s Waterloo region said they’re also investigating threatening emails sent to Islamic schools, and that they’re aware of similar threats made in other jurisdictions.

Officers visited a school and conducted safety planning with school officials, Waterloo police said.

Meanwhile, Ottawa police said they have increased police visibility at the locations that received the letters but there is no indication of a “specific or imminent threat.”

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree wrote in a statement that he is “deeply disturbed” by the threats.

“Every child deserves to learn in safety, and every family deserves to feel secure sending their child to school,” he wrote. “These threats are unacceptable and have no place in Canada.”

Sultan said the threats against Mac’s schools come amid a backdrop of rising Islamophobia in Canada.

He pointed to recent atrocities against Muslim communities, including the 2021 killings of four members of the Afzaal family in London, Ont., which was ruled an act of terrorism, as well as a 2017 shooting at a Quebec City mosque that left six worshippers dead.

“These threats are real, and we know that they are real,” Sultan said. “The targeting of children, the targeting of schools, in that kind of way is something that shook us to our core.”

The latest data from Statistics Canada shows the number of police-reported hate crimes against Muslims rose by more than 170 per cent between 2020 and 2024.

Sultan said students are feeling “scared and vulnerable” as they walk past security and police officers on their way to class, and that the threats have raised tough questions about who gets to be considered Canadian and who is labelled an outsider.

“All of the things that we try to teach our children in these schools is that they are equal to any other Canadian, that they have equal rights and responsibilities,” Sultan said. “Threats like this really make them question if they belong because of the way they pray and because of their faith.”

He argued Canada needs to address an “environment of Islamophobia and xenophobia” that breeds threats against Muslims and other visible minorities.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Fréchette warns of U.S. interference risk in Quebec election
stories.summary: CAQ Leader requests meeting with Carney after report said U.S. officials attempted direct negotiations with Quebec on tariffs
stories.author: Erika Morris
stories.content:
Quebec’s incumbent premier says she is “very concerned” about possible interference in the Oct. 5 provincial election by the United States.

Coalition Avenir Québec leader Christine Fréchette told journalists she reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney and requested a meeting with him to discuss the matter.

She was reacting to a news report published by Québecor media outlets that said American officials had attempted to negotiate directly with Quebec government officials regarding tariffs.

“I want to ensure that the full truth about this issue comes to light,” Fréchette said on the campaign trail. “[The election] must remain in the hands of and be decided by the people of Quebec.”

Canada’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.

“Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country,” she said.

She added that she will speak with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.

“Right now I have not seen the evidence,” Anand said.

stories.title: Two people found in burning cars at opposite ends of Toronto were murdered, police say
stories.summary: Police haven’t confirmed a connection between the two deaths but that remains under investigation
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi
stories.content:
Toronto police say two people who were found in burning vehicles overnight on opposite ends of the city earlier this week were targeted and killed before they were burned.

Police say the first body was found in a burning vehicle in the city’s northeast corner around Rouge National Urban Park just before 11:30 p.m. on Monday.

Det.-Sgt. Henri Marsman says the victim has been identified as 32-year-old Marcus Charles, who was living in Toronto.

He says Charles was identified using his fingerprints.

The second body was found about 90 minutes after the first, in James Gardens Park in the city’s west end.

Marsman says the second victim has not been identified yet as the body was badly burned.

He says officers are investigating both homicides.

Police say they haven’t confirmed a connection between the two deaths but that remains under investigation.

They say the first vehicle was a rental and the second one was stolen from the Greater Toronto Area.

stories.title: Mississauga woman faces upgraded murder charge after stabbing victim dies
stories.summary: A Mississauga woman has been charged with second-degree murder after the victim of a stabbing died in hospital days later.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A Mississauga woman has been charged with second-degree murder after the victim of a stabbing died in hospital days later.

Peel Regional Police said they responded to reports of a stabbing in the area of Dixie Road and Dundas Street East on Sept. 6 around 5:30 p.m.

When officers arrived on scene, they found a man with a “serious stab wound to the neck.”

The man was transported to hospital in critical condition.

Officers immediately arrested a man who was involved in an altercation with the victim but determined he was not responsible and was released.

The next day, officers located and arrested 42-year-old Lorena Sanchez and charged her with attempted murder.

On Sept. 10, police say the man died in hospital and Sanchez’s charges were upgraded to second-degree murder.

The investigation is ongoing.

stories.title: Muslim schools across Canada on high alert after receiving e-mails threatening violence
stories.summary: Same anonymous e-mail was sent to schools in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec this week, association spokesperson says
stories.author: Kathryn Mannie
stories.content:
The Muslim Association of Canada says nine schools it operates across Canada are on high alert after the schools each received an e-mail this week threatening violence against Muslims.

Spokesperson Nabil Sultan says the same anonymous e-mail was sent to schools in Ontario, B.C. and Quebec over a 24-hour period, and local police forces have been notified.

The email, shared with The Canadian Press and signed by a “Citizen Vigilante,” threatens the “slaughter” of Muslims and vows Canada will be “Islam free.”

Sultan, whose own child attends a MAC school, says he was devastated to read the letter, and that MAC has hired paid security to keep students safe.

He says the organization is used to receiving threatening and Islamophobic e-mails, but this is the first time the non-profit’s schools have been targeted in such a direct way.

Police in Ontario’s Peel region say they’re aware of a letter “containing hate-motivated threats” against Islamic institutions and increased police patrols overnight near mosques and schools, which will continue into the weekend.

The force says its hate crime unit is investigating.

Sultan says the threats against Mac’s schools come amid a backdrop of rising Islamophobia in Canada.

He pointed to recent atrocities against Muslim communities, including the 2021 killings of four members of the Afzaal family in London, Ont., which was ruled an act of terrorism, as well as a 2017 shooting at a Quebec City mosque that left six worshippers dead.

“These threats are real, and we know that they are real,” Sultan said. “The targeting of children, the targeting of schools, in that kind of way is something that shook us to our core.”

The latest data from Statistics Canada shows the number of police-reported hate crimes against Muslims rose by over 170 per cent between 2020 and 2024.

Sultan says students are feeling “scared and vulnerable” as they walk past security and police officers on their way to class, and that the threats have raised tough questions about who gets to be considered Canadian and who are labelled outsiders.

“All of the things that we try to teach our children in these schools is that they are equal to any other Canadian, that they have equal rights and responsibilities,” Sultan said. “Threats like this really make them question if they belong because of the way they pray and because of their faith.”

He argues Canada needs to address an “environment of Islamophobia and xenophobia” that breeds threats against Muslims and other visible minorities.

stories.title: ‘Zero chance’ U.S. attacks Canada, Alaska governor tells conference
stories.summary: Calgary — Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy says it would be shocking to the average American to see the United States invade Canada.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
BANFF — The governor of the U.S. state that shares the longest border with Canada expressed dismay at the notion that his country would ever invade its southern neighbour.

“I’d have a better chance of sprouting wings and flying around the audience here,” Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy said during an onstage discussion Friday at the Global Business Forum in Banff, Alta.

Dunleavy’s remarks come days after the New York Times quoted Prime Minister Mark Carney as saying his government has studied such a possibility as an “extreme tail risk.” Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty later told reporters in Ottawa that it’s “normal” for all militaries around the world to analyze risk scenarios.

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted he wants to make Canada the 51st state, but has said he would do so through economic, and not military, means.

Dunleavy, a Republican who called Trump “the best president for the state of Alaska in our entire history,” said there’s “zero chance” that the United States would contemplate a military incursion, and that “Pennsylvania has a better chance of being invaded by West Virginia.”

The average American would find the idea of attacking Canada “shocking” and even feel “hurt”, Dunleavy added.

“We see you as our brothers, siblings of the same mother.”

Jody Thomas, who was national security and intelligence adviser to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, is similarly unconvinced a military incursion is on the table, calling it “improbable, slightly impossible.”

She told the forum that in such an unlikely event, negotiations would kick into high gear right away.

“Immediately, there would be calls from the Prime Minister’s Office to the White House. There would be negotiations. The diplomats — State, Global Affairs, Canada, our ambassadors — would be talking. The chief of the defence staff would be talking to the chairman of the military committee to understand what’s going on and stop it,” Thomas said.

“The United States is 10 times larger than us … There’d be maybe a few days of mobilization and movement before I think it would stop because Canada would not want harm done to our citizens. We would not want to see loss of life.”

There are other potential threats that come to mind for Thomas that originate further afield.

“We have adversaries out there and it’s not something that ever has really entered the Canadian psyche,” she said.

“North Korea is an adversary. China can be an adversary. Russia can be an adversary, the threat of terrorist attacks emanating from the Middle East.”

Thomas said national security these days can’t be separated from a country’s economic health.

“You can’t have a weak economy and be a strong country from a perspective of national security. There are opportunities for organized crime. There’s opportunities for terrorism. You can be taken advantage of if you’re not strong economically,” she said.

“If you have not invested in your armed forces, you cannot defend your country. Environmental disasters can wipe out industries, and so we have to be strong environmentally.

“We have looked at things in silos in Canada for too long and it is time for systems thinking end-to-end about the implications of where we’re spending money and why.”

Dunleavy’s remarks come days after the New York Times quoted Prime Minister Mark Carney as saying his government has studied such a possibility as an “extreme tail risk.” Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty later told reporters in Ottawa that it’s “normal” for all militaries around the world to analyze risk scenarios.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood donates $1M to Western University for avian research chair
stories.summary: The legacy of celebrated Canadian author and bird conservation advocate Graeme Gibson will continue through a $1-million gift to Western University from his longtime partner, acclaimed author Margaret Atwood.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The legacy of celebrated Canadian author and bird conservation advocate Graeme Gibson will continue through a $1-million gift to Western University from his longtime partner, acclaimed author Margaret Atwood.

The donation will establish the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology, a new research position at the London, Ont., school focused on understanding how birds move, behave and adapt to changing environmental conditions.

Western president Alan Shepard said the gift will help advance the university’s internationally recognized bird and migration research programs.

“In addition to their extraordinary leadership in Canadian writing and the arts, Margaret Atwood and Graeme Gibson have been lifelong champions for birds and nature conservation efforts across Canada and around the world,” Shepard said. “Western is deeply honoured to receive this gift in Graeme’s memory to advance world-leading bird and migration research.”

Atwood said the donation honours Gibson’s lifelong passion for birds and conservation. Gibson, a Western arts graduate, died in 2019 at the age of 85.

The chairholder will join Western’s biology department and become part of the Centre for Animals on the Move, an interdisciplinary research hub that studies the movement of birds, bats, fish and insects. The successful candidate will also have access to the university’s Advanced Facility for Avian Research (Afar), which Atwood described as one of the country’s leading bird biology programs.

Atwood said the new chair builds on an existing connection between Western researchers and the Pelee Island Bird Observatory, which she and Gibson co-founded in 2003.

“Graeme would be very pleased. He was devoted to birds, evidenced by his best-selling The Bedside Book of Birds ,” Atwood said.

“Birds are the canaries in the coal mine. They indicate the health of an ecosystem. Also, imagine a world without birds or birdsong. Birds have long been a symbol of hope, and hope is what we need more of right now.”

Atwood said the gift also reflects Gibson’s ties to Western, where his experiences as a student inspired his first novel, Five Legs .

“Graeme would have gotten a kick out of a chair in his name at Western because he went there, with mixed and hilarious though ultimately beneficial results,” she said.

stories.title: Landlord withdraws rent increase after tenant strike at Toronto apartment: organizers
stories.summary: Tenant organizers say they have successfully beat back a landlord's attempt to retroactively raise rents by over five per cent at a west-end Toronto apartment building.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Tenant organizers say they have successfully beat back a landlord’s attempt to retroactively raise rents by over five per cent at a west-end Toronto apartment building.

In March, tenants at 75 Spencer Avenue began withholding rent payments after their building’s property manager applied for an above guideline rent increase, or AGI.

After six months of the rent strike, tenant organizers say Metcap Living has withdrawn the application.

The maximum allowable increase for rent-controlled buildings in Ontario was 2.5 per cent in 2025, but landlords can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for AGIs to fund renovations and building improvements.

The tenants told The Canadian Press in February that the landlord had renovated the lobby and turned an office into a rental unit.

They argued that those projects hadn’t directly improved their living conditions so they shouldn’t have to cover the costs by way of a rent increase, and that a 5.4 per cent increase in their housing costs would be unaffordable.

Organizers say the building in Toronto’s Parkdale neighbourhood was sold to a new owner in May, and tenants travelled to Montreal last weekend to confront them over the rent increase.

“The rent strike won because our neighbours did the thing that everyone talks about but almost no one does: they formed an independent organization, stepped outside of legal and political convention, and directly confronted their landlord,” said Bryan Doherty of Parkdale Organize, a group that advocates for tenants.

stories.title: Quebec author dropped from Goncourt amid AI, plagiarism allegations
stories.summary: The Académie Goncourt has removed Quebec author Thélyson Orélien’s novel from a list of finalists for the prestigious French literary prize.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
Quebec author Thélyson Orélien has lost his spot in the running for one of France’s most prestigious literary prizes over allegations that he used artificial intelligence to write his first book.

The Académie Goncourt announced Friday that it had removed Orélien’s novel, “C’était ça ou mourir,” which translates to “It was either that or dying” from the running for the Prix Goncourt amid allegations that the book was written using artificial intelligence, and separate plagiarism allegations involving his earlier work.

The decision marks the latest fallout from a controversy that has quickly spread through the French-language literary world, prompting Orélien’s Quebec publisher to suspend promotion of the novel, citing Orélien’s well-being, and a Quebec book fair to cancel his appearances.

1:27 ‘We need a red phone’: Governments collaborating on AI incident reporting, minister says

Orélien, who earlier this week vehemently denied using AI to write the novel, declined on Friday to respond to the new allegations or provide further comment.

“I can’t talk about it. I want to focus on my physical and mental health,” he said in a WhatsApp message to The Canadian Press.

The Académie Goncourt, which awards an annual prize recognizing the best French-language novel, said it was removing the novel from its long list of 16 titles to “preserve the integrity of the Prix Goncourt” and recognize “literature written by women and men.”

The academy said its decision was informed by several analyses conducted by researchers and journalists it considers credible who had reached similar conclusions and alleged that the novel may have been largely written using artificial intelligence. It also cited plagiarism allegations involving Orélien’s previous work.

The academy’s president, Philippe Claudel, did not immediately respond to a request for details about the evidence used to reach the decision. The short list for the prize comes out on Oct. 6.

1:18 Solomon announces $160M to create 10K paid AI internship placements

The academy’s decision comes days after allegations surfaced that Orélien used generative AI to write his novel.

The allegations were first raised by “Balance ton Claude,” a collective project that analyzed the book using AI-detection software Pangram.

In a post on X Friday, Samuel Fitoussi, a columnist for the French newspaper Le Figaro and one of the people behind the project, said the group had tested several other books and that “none reached such high AI scores.”

Fitoussi said the project grew out of broader concerns about the impact of artificial intelligence on writing and defended the decision to make its findings public.

“We obviously have compassion for the difficult days Orélien must be going through, and we hope he is being supported,” he wrote. “But we felt it was our duty to raise the alarm.”

He argued that readers should be able to know whether they are reading the work of a human or artificial intelligence so they can “choose with full knowledge of the facts.”

The controversy expanded Wednesday when La Presse reported separate allegations involving Orélien’s earlier work.

The newspaper said some articles attributed to him and published in Quebec and French media between 2012 and 2014 contained passages also found in previously published work by other authors.

1:56 New poll shows number of Canadians with negative views on AI increasing

La Presse said it used Pangram to identify a number of paragraphs that appeared to have been plagiarized.

The Canadian Press has not independently verified the AI or plagiarism allegations.

When CP put an excerpt of the novel through Pangram on Friday, a message on the platform alleged the text was “a mix of AI and human-written content.”

The British scientific journal Nature reported in August that Pangram has performed well in independent evaluations at differentiating AI-generated from human-written text, though researchers caution that its scores should not be treated as definitive proof of how much of a text was written by AI.

Les Éditions du Boréal, which published Orélien’s novel in Quebec, said Thursday it was concerned about the plagiarism allegations, saying they raise questions about copyright and editorial integrity.

“Plagiarism is an unacceptable practice,” the Montreal-based publisher said.

Boréal said it could neither confirm nor refute the allegations that artificial intelligence was used to write the novel. It said its editorial process began with a completed manuscript and included exchanges between the author and editor, language editing and proofreading, none of which involved the use of AI.

The book remains available for sale, the publisher said on Thursday.

The Salon du livre de l’Estrie, a book fair in Sherbrooke, Que., withdrew Orélien as a guest of honour Thursday and cancelled his participation in two activities.

The controversy follows a rapid rise for Orélien in the French literary world; the Goncourt recognition had marked a major literary breakthrough for him.

Michel Lacroix, a professor of literary studies at the Université du Québec à Montréal, told The Canadian Press earlier this month that it was extremely rare for a Quebec writer, particularly a debut novelist, to receive that level of recognition in France.

“C’était ça ou mourir” won France’s Prix du Roman Fnac earlier this week.

The novel remains in contention for several other major French literary prizes, including the Renaudot, Femina, Médicis and Prix Décembre.

The organizations behind the prizes did not immediately respond to questions about how they plan to respond to the controversy.

The Académie Goncourt awards its prize each fall to a work of French-language fiction. The winner receives a symbolic cheque for 10 euros, but the prestigious award typically brings significant attention and a major boost in book sales.

Orélien, who was born in Haiti and moved to Quebec after the 2010 earthquake, said he drew from his own experience as well as those of other migrants in writing the novel, which follows a Haitian man forced to flee his country and make a perilous journey through the Americas to Quebec.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 25, 2026.

stories.title: Flair Airlines ordered to pay B.C. passenger after jewelry goes missing from checked baggage: tribunal
stories.summary: A tribunal says Flair Airlines has been ordered to pay a woman more than $600 after she said jewelry disappeared from her checked baggage.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
The BC Civil Resolution Tribunal (CRT) says Flair Airlines has been ordered to pay a woman more than $600 after she said jewelry disappeared from her checked baggage on a flight from Mexico to Vancouver.

According to the decision, the woman had just flown home from a trip on Flair in February 2024. The next morning, when she opened her luggage, she says she noticed her bag appeared to have been repacked. She says she then noticed a pouch containing jewelry was missing.

She says she reported the loss to the airline via text on Feb. 7, 2024, tribunal member Amanda Binnie wrote in her ruling this week. After not receiving a reply, she says she then reported the loss, via the airline’s website, on April 10, 2024.

“On June 13, 2024, Flair acknowledged [the applicant’s] missing item claim, apologized for the missing items, and said it might contact her for additional information,” Binnie said. “Though neither party said when, they agree that Flair denied [her] claim because she did not provide an itemized list or receipts.”

The tribunal says the applicant provided a list of nine jewelry items, ranging in value from $15 to more than $535.24, for a total of $868.73. She didn’t provide receipts to support these amounts.

In the decision, the CRT says it found Flair was responsible for the loss.

However, the airline says jewelry should not be packed in checked baggage.

“Flair argues that under its international tariff, jewelry is unacceptable for transportation as checked baggage and can only be transported in a carry-on,” the ruling says.

Binnie says she acknowledges the airline’s argument that passengers shouldn’t put valuables in checked luggage.

“However … Flair did not provide any evidence, including its tariff,” she said.

“It also did not provide any evidence it told [the woman] she should only transport valuable items in carry-on luggage before her flight.”

Ultimately, the CRT found that under the Montreal Convention and the federal Carriage by Air Act (CAA), an airline can be liable for the loss of registered baggage while it is under the carrier’s care.

The tribunal didn’t award the woman the full amount claimed because she had no receipts, photos, or other evidence to show the condition or age of the jewelry.

Binnie ordered Flair to pay the applicant, within 30 days, $500 in damages, $38.68 in interest, and $67.50 toward her tribunal fees, for a total of $606.18.

stories.title: $680K raised for hero Belleville cop who prevented a Jewish massacre
stories.summary: The shooting described as hate-motivated by Police Chief Rodd occurred as a Yom Kippur service was being attended by roughly 25 congregants.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The GoFundMe campaign supported by the Canadian Jewish community for Belleville, Ont. police officer, Const. Jeff Smith has exceeded its initial goal of $18,000, raising more than $691,869 as of midday Friday.

The online campaign has garnered top donations from notable figures, including criminal defence lawyer Solomon Friedman.

Const. Smith prevented a mass shooting when he defended against multiple gunshots fired outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., by shooter Sean Ward , 29, ON Sunday night. Const. Smith sustained multiple gunshots wounds to his head and body. He was shot before he exited his vehicle, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said in a press conference on Thursday afternoon. Const. Michael McCurdy, a second police officer assisting Const. Smith, was not harmed.

“Cons. Jeff Smith put himself in mortal danger to defend innocent men, women and children whose only crime was to gather as Jews,” Friedman told National Post. “Words are insufficient to describe the debt that is owed to both Cst. Smith and his fellow officer, Cst. McCurdy. They and their families are deserving of our endless gratitude and support.”

The shooting described as a hate-motivated crime by Police Chief Rodd occurred as a Yom Kippur service was being attended by roughly 25 congregants and Const. Smith was stationed outside the synagogue for security reasons.

“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead,” Smith’s wife Ashley Smith said on Tuesday in a Facebook post as she shared a photo of her holding her husband’s hand. “But he is not walking it alone,” she added, expressing her gratitude for the outpouring of support.

The 29-year-old gunman opened fire after shouting “you are going to die for the Jews,” as seen during a video the police played during the Thursday conference. Police Chief Rodd added that the attack was an “exclusive threat to our Jewish community.”

As for the success of the GoFundMe campaign, campaign organizer Derek Kreindler said in an online post, “I am astounded at the donations that have poured in, and never imagined we would raise over $500,000. My hope is that we are able to reach $1,000,000 by the time Constable Smith has been discharged from hospital.”

“Think about that for a second. Running toward gunfire while everyone else is trying to get away,” Williams wrote on Facebook . “We’ve spent the last few days talking about tragedy, fear and hate. We should also take a moment to recognize extraordinary courage when we see it,” he wrote.

“Some donors have asked about the second officer that assisted Constable Smith before more backup arrived,” wrote GoFundMe organizer Kreindler. “Constable McCurdy faced the same danger as Constable Smith while protecting the synagogue and those gathered inside, and assisting his fellow officer. We are deeply relieved that he is safe, and grateful to learn that he was physically unharmed.”

Meanwhile, Sons of Jacob have also launched a fundraiser to help rebuild the damage sustained by gunfire and aims to raise $90,000.
