stories.title: Renovation needs force Canadian museums into a balancing act between closing and visitor access
stories.summary: Museums across the country are closing their doors now in a bid to open them to a wider audience later
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
On Toronto’s Bloor Street, the front doors of the Royal Ontario Museum have been closed for almost three years in a bid to give the community better access to the museum.

Nicholas Bell, the new chief executive and director who must complete the $130-million project, reopening the doors and giving the public free admission to part of the building, knows all about the ironies of museum renovations.

Until July, he was director of Calgary’s Glenbow Museum, which began a major overhaul in 2021 that promises free admission to its whole permanent collection once it reopens next year. Predictably, the renovation was slower than planned, running a year behind schedule, but the building is now complete; staff have moved back in to work on the new displays and exhibits.

The Glenbow, which ran a satellite gallery from 2022 to 2024, can hope the anticipation of reopening will win back both old friends and new visitors, after a long absence.

“Museums need buildings because they need a place for people to come to, but museums also need audiences … people to come and participate,” Bell said.

Fully closing a museum for renovations as the Glenbow did – so often over budget and behind schedule – means laying off staff and a loss of box office revenue. But worse, shutting the doors can break the museum habit for regulars just as institutions are recovering from the pandemic and trying to reach new audiences.

What follows can be trickier still: In an era that increasingly questions the social role of museum collections, those institutions must also consider how their displays will land with wider audiences when they reopen.

Overseeing OpenROM, as the project is called, May be the easier part of Bell’s new job. The museum, which covers both nature and culture, has remained open throughout using the old Queen’s Park doors, but currently has no Canadian or Japanese galleries, both lost to reconfiguring ground-floor space. Its South Asian gallery is closed for a redo and there are plans for a new gallery devoted to Sikh culture, although the ROM has few Sikh artifacts.

Meanwhile, staff acknowledge the First Peoples gallery is in immediate need of an update; less controversially, the European galleries are looking tired. On the science side, things have been updated more recently, including the Dawn of Life gallery, largely based on Canadian specimens, which opened in 2021.

On the Canadian file, the ROM and the McMichael Canadian Art Collection have hit on a mutually beneficial solution. The McMichael just shut its doors for a three-year renovation that will finally update its aging physical plant, and the ROM announced Friday it will host a two-year exhibition of the McMichael’s core collection, featuring work by Tom Thomson, the Group of Seven and their lesser-known female contemporaries.

At least that one looks like a win for access, giving visitors in downtown Toronto the McMichael experience, which normally requires a trip to the picturesque village of Kleinburg, Ont., about 40 minutes north in suburban Vaughan.

At the McMichael, executive director and chief curator Sarah Milroy also knows about those ironies. She made the tough decision to close for three years to finally bring the museum that began life in a log house up to contemporary building standards. The McMichael was last renovated in the 1980s; the Hvac systems are at the end of their life and a two-year closure was already under consideration when she decided to add a third year to fully renovate.

The plans will increase exhibition space by 30 per cent, improve back-of-house space for conservation and framing, and add a revenue-generating event venue, but the $150-million project has required the McMichael to lay off about two-thirds of its small staff, mostly the people working front of house.

Milroy said it was far more efficient to hand an empty site to the construction company, rather than renovate in stages and try to stay open. “The existing site is already too small for us to get done the things we need to do. So to be functioning with half of that, it’s just dragging out the misery,” she said. “We just want to rip off the bandage and get it done.”

“We are going to be making lots of noise while we are closed,” Milroy said.

In a much larger building, the ROM is able to stagger updates and only close a few areas, while rationalizing the 175,000-square-foot Crystal extension that added new galleries in 2007 but also some awkward transitions between the old and new wings, and a non-descript front door.

So far, the museum has only raised money for the first phase of OpenROM to be completed next spring. Future stages have yet to be finalized, but May include a restaurant and a large opening in the lobby ceiling, or oculus, that would provide views of the dinosaurs above. By closing off a multi-storey empty side lobby referred to as the Spirit House on the ground floor, it has already been able to enlarge the second-floor dinosaur gallery.

The rest of the current phase involves adding 6,000 more feet of gallery space, redoing the Bloor Street entrance to add a canopy and make the doors more visible, and adding a performance space in the lobby, where queues have become much shorter with online ticketing.

Perhaps the biggest goal of OpenROM, however, is to give the public access to a significant part of the museum without a ticket. Under its previous director Josh Basseches, who left last December, the museum began running pilot projects to test the logistics of moving the turnstile further into the building.

This fall, for the second year in a row, it is making the entire ground floor free for two months, giving the public easy access to a large installation tied to the Toronto Biennial of Art, as well as the Chinese and Korean galleries.

Bell, headhunted from Calgary, is a strong advocate for free admission and initiated the plan at the Glenbow for free entry when it reopens (with the exception of special exhibitions).

Admission prices are continual source of discussion in the museum community, where most believe the public deserves easy access to public collections, and that expensive tickets stand in the way of diversifying audiences.

The ROM has found that its experiments with free admission to the ground floor encourage brief drop-in visits at lunch or at the end of the workday from people who wouldn’t bother if they had to pay about $30. The problem is how to fund open entry: Provincial and federal grants in Canada are not sufficient to allow museums to forgo box-office revenue.

At the Glenbow, the Shaw Family Foundation will underwrite admission with a $35-million donation; at the ROM, the Temerty Foundation has established a $30-million endowment to cover the free portion of the site. Both are notable departures from traditional bricks-and-mortar, name-on-the-building philanthropy, although OpenROM is being funded entirely by private donations.

Free admission is perhaps the simplest way of ensuring accessibility; at the ROM, it means making sure people from all walks of life see those doors on Bloor Street and know they are welcome. (Indigenous visitors are already granted free admission to the entire museum.) But what stories and objects people encounter inside is another important test for access.

Traditionally, museums saw their role as reaching the public with scholarship based on their collections. But the current drive to decolonize institutions that are often warehouses of colonial plunder involves fashioning new stories, directly addressing historical wrongs such as residential schools and slavery.

In the U.S., the Trump administration, with a view that museums should be exclusively celebratory, has pushed back against the Smithsonian Institution’s willingness to confront the darker side of American history, accusing the Washington museums of being “woke.”

The politics in Canada are gentler, although leadership at the National Gallery of Canada did get caught in several controversies surrounding its decolonizing policies in 2022, including the departure of an Indigenous curator. Bell treads carefully, positioning himself at the intersection of tradition and activism.

“We’re just looking for versions of truth that can help communities understand themselves and each other,” he said. “I don’t necessarily think of that as activism, but truths are sometimes difficult to confront.”

Bell pointed to the Rom’s 2025 show Auschwitz. Not long ago. Not far away as an example of the museum’s willingness to discuss difficult topics. He also praised curatorial staff for managing the sensitive task of installing galleries dedicated to the ancient Middle East, where contemporary politics might come into play.

Bell identified an immediate need to update the First Peoples gallery, which was abruptly “paused” in 2022, while Cree artist Kent Monkman was in residence at the museum. At the time, ROM management recognized that dioramas of Indigenous life had become an embarrassment, and the gallery was tweaked before it reopened with Indigenous interpreters on-site. A complete overhaul is being planned with no firm timeline.

“The Canadian audience is growing more sophisticated in terms of what it would consider to be a standard for intercultural dialogue around Indigenous spaces, and ROM should be at the front of that conversation,” Bell said.

Reopening the Rom’s Canadiana gallery is another priority. It was closed in 2022 and controversially, its space was filled with temporary exhibitions, including one devoted to the Harry Potter spinoff Fantastic Beasts . That leaves the ROM without a display of national icons at a time when Canadian sovereignty is in the headlines.

If closing the building risks breaking the museum habit, Bell points out that the excitement of reopening should bring in new audiences. Yet, the artifacts on display in the Canadiana gallery May seem fusty – or worse – to new museum-goers.

The old gallery included early examples of Canadian decorative arts, but also such sensitive historical material as Benjamin West’s The Death of General Wolfe. The giant colonial painting of the 1759 battlefield on the Plains of Abraham depicts the British general who defeated New France as a beatific martyr, while a kneeling Indigenous warrior looks on. There were also several early 20th-century nationalistic illustrations of mighty moose, pristine forests and proud Indigenous people – stereotypes that might offend if not carefully placed in their historical context.

ROM promises enhanced interpretation as it welcomes the McMichael’s early 20th-century collection, remounting that gallery’s summertime show devoted to Thomson, the Group and their contemporaries. It will draw on the museum’s geological and botanical expertise to look at the landscape painting from new angles.

It will also make connections to Indigenous place names and stories that were originally omitted by the artists, perhaps reactivating a curatorial debate as to whether the Group was guilty of propagating the myth of the empty land, or painting a land from which Indigenous people had already been driven away.

Bell said the museum’s nature-and-culture mandate gives it a strong advantage in the global conversation about how we make sense of a changing planet.

“What are we doing here? Where do we go? What does it mean be Canadian? What does it mean to be on this land? In living through a complex world, there’s no better place to have those conversations than a place like the ROM.”

Friday, 25 September 2026 09:39

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

The Braves, the Merchants, and the Trojans each two games on the schedule for this weekend.

Pjhl - All of Oxford County's Junior C hockey teams have home games tonight.

The Tavistock Braves will battle the Paris Mounties, while the Thamesford Trojans take on the North Middlesex Stars, and the Norwich Merchants welcome the Dorchester Dolphins to Nor-Del Arena. The puck will drop at 7:45 p.m. in Thamesford and Tavistock, and at 8:00 p.m. in Norwich.

Thamesford and Norwich will also be in action tomorrow with the Trojans facing the Spitfires in Aylmer at 7:15 p.m. and the Merchants visiting the Applejacks in Wellesley at 7:30 p.m.. The Braves will be in Hespeler on Sunday for matinee matchup against the Shamrocks. That game should get underway at 3:30 p.m..

The Braves are currently tied with the Applejacks for first place in the Doherty Division with six points each. They're followed by the Mounties with five points, and the Merchants and New Hamburg Firebirds with four points each. The Dolphins are in fourth place with two points, just one ahead of the last place Shamrocks.

The Trojans are currently tied with the Aylmer Spitfires for fourth place in the Yeck Division with two points each. They're behind the Petrolia Flyers and Exeter Hawks with four points each, and the Mount Brydges Bulldogs with six points. The North Middlesex Stars sit on top of the standings with eight points, while the Port Stanley Sailors sit at the bottom with the Lucan Irish with zero points each.

stories.title: Police are cracking down on public drug use, London Mayor says it was always the plan
stories.summary: As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something that was always part of the original plan.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something that was always part of the original plan.
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:00 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago

As Windsor's police chief promises a more enforcement-focused response to drug use in public spaces, London Mayor Josh Morgan said a similar approach is happening in London, something he said was always part of the original plan.
London police report hundreds of drug seizures as open drug use crackdown enters new phase
"We've now entered Phase 2," said Morgan, "which has a greater enforcement focus: More seizures of drugs, more charges laid, but absolutely still we will have referrals to service."
With public concern growing about blatant drug use on sidewalks, in storefronts and even on transit buses, London Police Service launched a plan to deal with public drug use in spring 2025.

The plan was to initially follow an education-first approach, using foot patrols that teamed police officers with health-care workers to speak with people using drugs. At the time, arrests and charges were not the primary focus. Instead, the foot patrol teams worked to connect people suffering from addiction with services.
Morgan said enforcement actions are now stepping up in part because it's been made clear that public drug use isn't allowed. However, referrals to services will still be offered.
London police report hundreds of drug seizures as open drug use crackdown enters new phase
London police chief launches new strategy to curb blatant drug use in public

"We've had a 3,000 per cent increase with charges laid," said Morgan. "Referrals to service are still an important part of this. Even if someone gets charged or arrested, that doesn't break someone's addiction. We need to refer them to services as well."
Morgan said Windsor consulted with London Police Service before deciding to follow a similar approach.

Statistics presented to London's Police Service Board last month show recorded opioid-possession occurrences increased from 49 in 2024 to 1,430 in 2025. In the same period, other controlled-drug possession occurrences increased from 54 to 474.

Kevin Morrison heads London's Old East Village BIA, a part of downtown where open drug use is a persistent problem. He said while the response is often not always perfect, he believes police are doing their best to address a complicated problem.

"It seems to go in cycles," said Morrison. "We'll have a week where it's great and a week where it's not. Everyone seems to be doing what they can with what they are able to do. For the police, it's almost like moving water. [Drug users] hide for a while and then they're back at it. The police can't be everywhere."

Morrison recently attended the Association of Municipalities of Ontario conference as a representative of local business associations. One of the speakers was Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, who said the province is looking into ways take steps to help businesses.
"They're looking at making some changes as to how we're going to deal with the street crisis," said Morrison. However, he said the province didn't release any firm details.
Morgan said Londoners regularly send him photos of open-air drug-use, including a recent and widely shared image of a man using drugs outside London Police headquarters on Dundas Street.

"Every once in a while I see a photo on the internet, I send it to the police chief and I say: 'What's going on?' In some cases he gets back to me and says: 'Yeah, that's an individual who's been charged.'"
Both Morrison and Morgan said there needs to be more services available to people in need.

stories.title: Ex-RCMP official convicted of breaching secrets law granted day parole
stories.summary: A former RCMP intelligence official convicted of breaching Canada's secrets law has been granted day parole to help him prepare for his full return to society.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
A former RCMP intelligence official convicted of breaching Canada’s secrets law has been granted day parole to help him prepare for his full return to society, including possible employment as an electrical worker.

Records show the Parole Board of Canada approved day parole, with specific conditions, for Cameron Jay Ortis , who was found guilty in November 2023 of violating the Security of Information Act.

Ortis was sentenced to 14 years in prison in early 2024 but he had only seven years and 155 days left to serve due to time already spent in custody.

In February this year, the parole board approved day parole at a separate location — likely a private residence — for six months with a nightly curfew.

Late last month, the board granted a six-month extension of the arrangement.

Day parole allows offenders to participate in community-based activities during the day, but they must return to a designated location in the evening.

Ortis, 54, led an RCMP group that assembled secret information on cybercriminals, terror cells and transnational criminal networks.

He pleaded not guilty in court to all charges — including breaking the secrets law by revealing classified information to three individuals of interest to police in 2015 and trying to do so in a fourth instance.

Ortis, who was born and raised in British Columbia, obtained a PhD in political science and international relations and completed a post-doctoral fellowship. His sensitive work at the RCMP involved access to top secret documents.

At Ortis’s trial, a picture emerged of a driven, quick-minded individual — an avid runner who kept his personal life to himself.

Ortis testified he did not betray the RCMP. Rather, he said, he offered secret material to targets in a bid to get them to use an online encryption service set up by an allied intelligence agency to spy on adversaries.

The Crown argued Ortis had no authority to disclose classified material and that he was not doing so as part of a legitimate undercover operation, though it could not pinpoint a motive.

Jurors declared Ortis guilty of three counts of violating the Security of Information Act and one count of attempting to do so, as well as breach of trust and fraudulent use of a computer system.

In sentencing Ortis, Ontario Superior Court Justice Robert Maranger said the former Mountie was in a position of “extreme trust” at the RCMP and that his actions could have put lives at risk.

Maranger said these actions undermined Canada’s international reputation in the intelligence community.

Ortis is appealing his conviction and sentence and the Crown is appealing the length of his sentence.

He was granted bail in 2024 but opted to remain in custody during the appeal process.

In approving Ortis’s application for day parole, the parole board concluded his “risk to reoffend can be safely managed.”

“The board notes that your offending took place within a very specific set of circumstances related to your past employment and that these circumstances are unlikely ever to reoccur,” the board’s February record of decision reads. “There is no information indicating your involvement in any other form of criminal behaviour.”

The board imposed conditions on Ortis, including a ban on communicating with known criminals, restrictions on the use of internet-connected devices and regular reporting of financial transactions.

The record of decision says that at the start of his sentence, Ortis maintained he believed he had the authority to share the information. He noted that his job required him to make these kinds of decisions approximately five to six times a year, while occasionally walking a fine line.

“You now acknowledge and understand you did not have the authority to share the information you did and that you should have consulted with others and gathered more information about the decisions you were making,” the record says. “You have expressed regret for your actions and are aware of the negative impact your actions have had on others.”

The parole board said Ortis provided letters of support from family members and others willing to support him in the community.

“The board has also directly received support letters from friends, associates and family members,” the record of decision reads. “These letters consistently attest to your good character and specifically address the kind of support they are willing to provide to you.”

The board noted that Ortis planned to take part in an online technology program in preparation for a specialized position in the electrical field.

While in custody, Ortis completed an apprenticeship program for electricians and an environmental operators certification program that allowed him to obtain work at the institution’s wastewater treatment plant.

The Canadian Press has reached out to lawyers for Ortis requesting comment but has not yet received a response.

A record of the August parole decision in Ortis’s case says the board received a letter in March from one of his former colleagues who opposed his community release.

The record says the former colleague, with whom Ortis worked directly, “feels that you have never taken accountability for your offences and have failed to truly represent your intentions” concerning the offences.

stories.title: Volkswagen delays production at St. Thomas, Ont., EV plant
stories.summary: Opening pushed back two years to 2029
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The opening of a massive Volkswagen electric vehicle battery plant in southwestern Ontario has been pushed back two years until 2029.

PowerCo Canada, a subsidiary of the German automaker, says it is delaying production at the $7-billion factory in St. Thomas, Ont., in order to align the project’s timeline and product strategy with evolving market demand, technological advancements and the Volkswagen Group’s long-term strategy.

It says the later opening date will allow for next-generation battery technology while retaining the flexibility to scale over time as market conditions evolve.

Joel Karlsberg, chief procurement officer for the battery company, says the move is “about getting the pacing right ... to protect our long-term investment (and) support regional jobs.”

PowerCo also announced Thursday it has selected Canadian construction firm EllisDon Corp. as general contractor for construction of the factory as it moves into its next phase, which will focus on core infrastructure and structural work.

The plant was announced in 2023, with the federal government committing $700-million in upfront capital costs to build the factory and Ontario kicking in $500-million.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood donates $1-million to establish research chair for bird science
stories.summary: Donation will allow Western University to add a new hire to its biology faculty with the goal of advancing scientific knowledge about birds and bird migration
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Margaret Atwood has long been a hero to book lovers but they May soon be overtaken by a second, feathered fan club.

On Friday, Western University in London, Ont., announced a $1-million gift from Ms. Atwood to set up a research chair in bird science.

The donation will allow the university to add a new hire to its biology faculty with the goal of advancing scientific knowledge about birds and bird migration.

Within the field, Western is known for its Advanced Facility for Avian Research , with resources that include a wind tunnel for studying birds in flight under different conditions.

The university said the newly created position will be named the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology, after Ms. Atwood’s late partner.

Mr. Gibson, who died in 2019, was a novelist and a former president of PEN Canada. He was also an alumnus of Western and his experiences there served as an inspiration for his first novel, Five Legs , published in 1969. Its story unfolds as a university lecturer and a student travel to a funeral.

How Margaret Atwood and her family helped turn Pelee Island into a migratory bird research hub

In the middle of his life, Mr. Gibson became an avid bird enthusiast, particularly once he and Ms. Atwood began spending time on Pelee Island, a major stopping point for migrating birds. In 2005 he published The Bedside Book of Birds , a bestselling compendium of writings about birds and their relationship to people.

Ms. Atwood said that her recent donations are intended to enable such work, which Mr. Gibson also actively supported during his life.

stories.title: Margaret Atwood honours Graeme Gibson with new bird research chair at Western
stories.summary: A $1-million gift from Margaret Atwood in honour of her longtime partner will create the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology at Western.
stories.author: Megan Stacey
stories.content:
Graeme Gibson’s legacy as a celebrated author and champion of bird conservation will live on through a $1-million gift to Western University from his partner, literary icon Margaret Atwood.

The donation will create the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology, with the goal of better understanding the fundamental processes that shape how birds move, behave and adapt in a changing environment.

“In addition to their extraordinary leadership in Canadian writing and the arts, Margaret Atwood and Graeme Gibson have been lifelong champions for birds and nature conservation efforts across Canada and around the world,” said Western President Alan Shepard. “Western is deeply honoured to receive this gift in Graeme’s memory to advance world-leading bird and migration research.”

Atwood, one of Canada’s most acclaimed and internationally renowned authors, made the gift to recognize Gibson’s legacy and passion for conservation. A Western arts alum (BA’58), he passed away in 2019 at the age of 85.

Once appointed, the Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology will join the Faculty of Science’s biology department and become a member of Western’s Centre for Animals on the Move. The chairholder will have the opportunity to conduct research in the university’s world-class Advanced Facility for Avian Research (Afar), which Atwood called “one of the pre-eminent bird biology programs in the country.”

Western is a global leader in the study of avian migration, with Afar housing the world’s only hypobaric climatic wind tunnel designed for bird flight. Afar supports cutting-edge research on how birds navigate and respond to the challenging conditions they encounter in flight, while serving as a core facility for the Centre for Animals on the Move, an interdisciplinary research hub investigating the movement of birds, bats, fish and insects.

The new chair is a natural fit to advance research at Western, Atwood said, given the existing connection between Afar and the Pelee Island Bird Observatory (Pibo), which she co-founded with Gibson in 2003.

“Graeme would be very pleased. He was devoted to birds, evidenced by his best-selling The Bedside Book of Birds,” Atwood said.

“Birds are the canaries in the coal mine. They indicate the health of an ecosystem. Also, imagine a world without birds or birdsong, as author Rachel Carson did in her book Silent Spring. Birds have long been a symbol of hope, and hope is what we need more of right now.”

Atwood said the gift also reflects Gibson’s connection to Western, where his experiences as a student inspired his debut novel,Five Legs, which follows a professor and student on a winter journey to a fellow student’s funeral.

“Graeme would have gotten a kick out of a chair in his name at Western because he went there, with mixed and hilarious though ultimately beneficial results,” Atwood said.

A writer and lifelong naturalist who became a champion of birds, Gibson was named to the Order of Canada in 1992 and awarded the 2015 Gold Medal from the Royal Canadian Geographical Society, alongside Atwood.

In addition to his popular The Bedside Book of Birds and its follow up, The Bedside Book of Beasts, he wrote four novels and published Eleven Canadian Novelists, a collection of interviews with the country’s great fiction writers.

Graeme Gibson (Penguin Random House)

On top of his own success as an author, Gibson also co-founded the Writers’ Trust of Canada, Writer’s Union of Canada and advocated for generations of writers during his tenure as president of PEN Canada, the writers’ human rights organization.

He was deeply invested in birding and conservation work, holding leadership roles with the World Wildlife Fund Canada and serving as president of BirdLife International’s Rare Bird Club with Atwood.

The couple helped establish Pibo, which is focused on the study and protection of birds that use the island as a key migration stop, and the Gibson family remains closely involved. The Atwood-Gibson Bird Centre, a new facility for research, education and conservation on Pelee Island, opened earlier this month.

Atwood said Gibson’s commitment to birds was defined by perseverance.

“When he first offered The Bedside Book of Birds to publishers, none of them ‘got’ it. He stuck to it, and 10 years later, in 2005, it was published to great success,” Atwood said. “Graeme was always ahead of the curve, sometimes a lonely place to be.”

She said he would be pleased to know birding is now immensely popular among young people today.

“But many birds are under threat, which is what makes the work of Western and Pelee so important,” Atwood said.

Western researchers have long collaborated with Birds Canada and other research programs across the country, including Pibo and the Long Point Bird Observatory. Both are important regional conservation and research hubs situated along major migration routes travelled by roughly 10 million birds each year, making them perfect training sites for Western students.

“The Graeme Gibson Chair in Avian Biology will bring new ideas, vitality and student researchers to ensure Western remains a leader in bird research, from basic biology to ecology to advanced tracking and conservation. It offers an important opportunity to continue our critical research into the future,” said Chris Guglielmo, biology professor and director of Western’s Centre for Animals on the Move.

For Guglielmo and his colleagues, bird research is more than a job – it’s a calling.

### “We are scientists, so we work to push the limits of knowledge and train the next generation to do the same. This gift from Margaret Atwood is an investment in the fundamental importance of science.” – Chris Guglielmo, biology professor and director of Western’s Centre for Animals on the Move

Using field studies and advanced tracking technology, researchers at Western’s Centre for Animals on the Move investigate how small animals, including birds, bats and insects, find warmer or cooler weather, more food and safe places to breed – everything they need to survive. Motus, a global network of more than 2,400 automated radio-telemetry towers spanning 34 countries, is one of the key tools supporting this work.

Migration research is increasingly important as habitat destruction and a changing climate create significant challenges for many species of Canadian wildlife, Guglielmo said.

“Our birds, whales, salmon, caribou and insects are migratory, they have to be able to move to perform their ecosystem functions. Sometimes even small habitat improvements – changes you can make around your home – can have a positive impact on birds that are flying and refuelling.”

The centre’s research is helping scientists identify emerging patterns in animal movement, understand the challenges species face, and develop solutions to protect wildlife in a changing environment.

“Because these animals are so mobile, they can often adapt to changing conditions by altering when and where they migrate. Studying those changes helps us understand how species are responding to habitat loss and climate change, and provides insights to help us with protection efforts,” Guglielmo said.

He and his Western colleagues are looking beyond the next generation of research, working to ensure the Centre for Animals on the Move has the people, technology and resources to remain at the forefront of animal migration science for decades to come.

For Guglielmo, the gift from Atwood is about building that lasting legacy – strengthening the ability to answer vital questions about migration while encouraging others to invest in the research and conservation of migratory species.

“We have a wonderful, vast country with a lot of amazing places,” he added. “Collectively, we have a special responsibility to protect those areas and our migrating species.

Baseball is full of long days and short years, which is how it can simultaneously feel like George Springer’s been with the Toronto Blue Jays forever and that the six seasons in his then-club-record $150-million free-agent contract have flown by.

So much has happened since he signed that fateful agreement Jan. 23, 2021, while the federal government’s pandemic restrictions that locked the club out of its home for a season-and-a-half were still in place.

Despite 91 wins, the Blue Jays missed the playoffs by one measly game in that vagabond three-home-sites ’21 season, before jarring wild-card exits followed in each of the next two years.

As a three-stage renovation completely transformed the Rogers Centre, a train-wreck 2024 was chased by the exhilarating run to — and subsequent heartbreak of — the 2025 World Series, the slugger delivering a franchise-pantheon Game 7 ALCS homer along the way.

He earned an all-star selection and a Silver Slugger, poured into his teammates, set a standard in the clubhouse, became a symbol of the club’s re-emergence as a legitimate player in the free-agent market and is so ingrained within the organization’s fabric that his seven preceding seasons with the Houston Astros feel more like fever dream than reality.

Yet suddenly, the end is nigh, with three games versus the visiting Cincinnati Reds beginning Friday night (7 p.m. ET / 4 p.m. PT, Sportsnet, Sportsnet+) all that remains of those six years, and perhaps in his career, too.

“It’s emotional to think about it,” Springer said Wednesday in a quiet corner of the visitors’ clubhouse at Camden Yards, after an Orioles doubleheader sweep eliminated the Blue Jays from the wild-card chase.

“Very, very grateful to our fans, this team, this organization. Obviously this is not the way that we all wanted it to end. But if it is, I’m going to do my best to embrace being back home for one last time and making sure that I do anything I can to reciprocate to the fans.”

Springer is coy about the future beyond that, although some close to him expect that he will retire once all is said and done. At 37, having willed his way through far more ailments than he will acknowledge, having won one World Series, tainted as it may be by the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal, and come within inches of another, with 308 homers and a career OPS of .823 over 13 seasons, his resume is substantial.

His final season — .251/.323/.407 with 15 homers and 54 RBIs — would surely look different if a foul tip hadn’t fractured his left big toe May 11 and forced him to play compromised for weeks once he returned.

In 58 games since the all-star break, though, he’s posted an .800 OPS with six homers and 32 RBIs, demonstrating that even through subsequent shoulder issues, he can still do damage. Combined with his veteran leadership and experience, there is sure to be a market for him during the off-season, if he wants to continue playing.

“I don’t know,” he replied. “I love this organization. I loved being a Blue Jay. I’ve loved every single bit of being here. I haven’t really gotten that far yet. I’ve kind of taken every day with these guys in stride.”

As he usually does, Springer shrugged off the toll his aggressive style has taken on him physically and insisted that won’t tip the scales in his decision-making.

“If my mind can say it, then my body can do it – my body can do whatever I tell it to do, hopefully,” he said. “But I’ll cross that road once I get to it. We’ve still got to get through these next three and then we’ll go into the off-season and I’ll see what happens.”

More of a factor will be the needs of his family as Springer and wife Charlise have three sons aged five, three and three-months-old. The two older boys have been clubhouse staples this season, often walking around with either a bat or a glove in hand, following their dad through each stage of his pre-game. During a recent homestand, they each took a round of batting practice on the field once the Blue Jays were done and ran the bases after.

“It’s hard to be away from them and to miss things,” said Springer. “I want to be able to give them hugs and say, I love you in person. It’s been a long year for me off the field. But those are my kids and I love them. I’ll sit down with my wife at the end of this year and we’ll discuss whatever’s going to happen. But I love my family and if that requires me to be with them, I’ll be with them.”

In some ways that would be a natural transition, given the way Springer’s grown into a father-figure type during his time with the Blue Jays.

During one down stretch in May, Vladimir Guerrero Jr. pointed out that “George is my advice guy,” and praised Springer for telling him to “go out there and be yourself, laughing, joking” because “sometimes you put too much pressure and then sometimes you change your body language, so he always tells us to go out there and have fun.”

Myles Straw, who also played with Springer in Houston, recently praised the way he brought calmness and energy through games of increasing leverage, saying, “I’ve seen George do it for years now … Even in the playoffs, it’s like Game 1 of the season for George.”

Manager John Schneider, who’s praised Springer in so many ways over the years, pointed out last month how important his guidance was through this summer’s trade deadline, when the Blue Jays traded away Kevin Gausman, Daulton Varsho and Jeff Hoffman but still crawled back into contention.

“That’s part of the reason we signed him when we did, he’s remarkably aware of how things can change and he doesn’t panic,” said Schneider. “That rubs off on everyone and his will to say like, ‘Hey, I’m going to do whatever it takes to win today,’ has rubbed off on some guys. He’s been great. He’s still having fun and he’s still affecting people around him.”

During his 3.5 seasons with the Blue Jays, Varsho grew especially close to Springer, who’d regularly walk through the clubhouse calling, “Daulton,” when he couldn’t find the centre-fielder.

“I’m going to cherish every moment that we’ve had together because he’s taught me a lot about myself, just what it means to be a leader and how to do it in the right way,” Varsho said Aug. 1.

“He’s a lead-by-example guy and he’ll use his voice every once in a while when he needs to. It’s a pretty spectacular career he’s had. Obviously I keep talking to him, I want him to keep playing, but obviously for him it’s his choice and his family’s choice. But he’s had a hell of a career and it’s always been enjoyable for me to play alongside him.”

All combined, it’s a sizable legacy Springer has carved out with the Blue Jays, who signed him to push the franchise to the next level and saw him do precisely that. At the time of his 2021 signing, president and CEO Mark Shapiro said, “there’s no limit to what this market can be, it’s a behemoth and we’re going to continue to get better and continue to add the players and keep the players that we have necessary to be a championship team year-in, year-out.”

In that way, the Blue Jays achieved what they envisioned — save for the championship — when they invested in Springer six years ago.

Asked if he’s accomplished all he wanted with Toronto, minus the title, Springer replied, “I don’t know. I hope so.”

“I’d hope that over the last six years, I’ve been able to show the fans and this organization that I love them and I’ll play as hard as I can every single day with whatever I’ve got,” he continued. “At the end of the day, the goal was to win the World Series and we came an eyelash shy. But to see all the progress that we made as organization and a team, just to be standing on that field in Game 7 was a dream come true for me. So yeah, I’d love to be the last team standing, but this has been a hell of a six years.”

One series left. Time sure does fly.

stories.title: Transport truck, SUV collide in Zorra
stories.summary: Two people were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries following a collision involving a transport truck and an SUV
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries following a collision involving a transport truck and an SUV in Zorra Township early Friday morning.

Ontario Provincial Police, along with Oxford County fire and paramedic services, responded to reports of the two-vehicle crash on 19th Line, north of Road 96, at about 5:30 a.m.

Police said the lone occupants of both vehicles were transported to hospital with injuries that were not considered life-threatening.

The collision prompted the closure of 19th Line between Elginfield Road and Road 96 for several hours. The roadway has since reopened.

The cause of the crash remains under investigation. No charges had been laid at this time.

stories.title: Report on Tumbler Ridge shooter’s ChatGPT conversations shocks B.C. attorney general
stories.summary: The report also says ChatGPT advised the shooter how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia’s attorney general says she’s shocked by an article describing alleged interactions between the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter and ChatGPT, in which the AI chatbot vividly describes the effectiveness of a shotgun in a classroom.

The report, in U.S.-based magazine Mother Jones, also says ChatGPT advised shooter 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar how to get around its own safeguards to obtain information about violent scenarios by framing the content as fictional.

Attorney General Niki Sharma says the details in the article, which does not describe its sources, are “shocking and, as a parent, they are worse” than she ever imagined.

She says on social media platform Bluesky that corporations urgently need mandatory and strict regulation to protect children.

OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company behind ChatGPT, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the article about the chatbot’s interactions with Van Rootselaar, who killed eight people in Tumbler Ridge in February, including five students, before killing herself.

The B.C. government, survivors and witnesses of the shootings at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School are suing OpenAI, alleging negligence.

The article published on Thursday says Van Rootselaar’s ChatGPT account was banned for discussing committing an attack with a “famous real-world mall as the target.”

But it says she then used a second account, which advised her about how to “never get flagged again” by describing situations as fictional or hypothetical.

“Don’t use real-world locations,” the article quotes ChatGPT as saying, before adding: “You can still be twisted. Just be clever about it.”

It says that Van Rootselaar asked ChatGPT for a scenario about attacking a college campus with a shotgun for maximum effect.

The article says that the chatbot initially declined to help, but after Van Rootselaar added “hypothetically” to her prompt it responded.

“In a hallway, indoors, or a crowded classroom, the 870 (Remington shotgun) is brutal,” it quotes ChatGPT as saying. “Close quarters is its playground.”

The article says ChatGPT went on to say: “Assuming each shell results in one hit, you might down 10 to 20 people max, depending on spacing, density, reaction times, and chaos.”

OpenAI did not immediately respond to an email sent to their general press address and to an individual spokesperson. General counsel for the company, Che Chang, did not immediately respond to a message sent to his LinkedIn profile.

RCMP Staff Sgt. Kris Clark said the investigation into the shootings had “utilized all available legal processes to obtain all information available from various social media and digital platforms” relevant to the attack.

“To date, all companies that have received requests have complied,” Clark said.

stories.title: Application period for mail-in Alberta referendum ballots ending, 673K requested
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says it will stop accepting applications as of midnight and that mail-in ballots must be returned by Oct. 16 at 5 p.m.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Friday is the last day to apply for a mail-in ballot for Alberta’s referendum.

Elections Alberta says it will stop accepting applications as of midnight and that mail-in ballots must be returned by Oct. 16 at 5 p.m.

The agency says that as of Thursday afternoon it’s received 673,000 requests for mail-in ballots.

The total marks a staggering increase from the nearly 60,000 requested for the province’s 2023 general election, though the rules for who could vote by mail have relaxed since then.

Albertans are to vote Oct. 19 on 10 questions put forward by Premier Danielle Smith’s government, including whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting Confederation.

Albertans can start voting in person at advance polling stations on Oct. 13, which will be open until Oct. 17.

stories.title: Law & Order Toronto returns with familiar scene partners playing new cop partners
stories.summary: Emmy-winning actor Luke Kirby joins Kathleen Munroe after Aden Young exits the show
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
It’s new cop partners, new scene partners on Law & Order Toronto: Criminal Intent this season.

After three years on the beat with Detective Sergeant Henry Graff, Detective Sergeant Frankie Bateman is returning to fight Toronto’s war on crime with a different case-solving consort: Detective Sergeant John Darcy.

That means that Kathleen Munroe, who plays Bateman, is working with a new co-star: Emmy-winning actor Luke Kirby, who plays the new detective who’s got her six in the Six. The switcheroo was precipitated by Australian-Canadian actor Aden Young, who played Graff, moving back down under at the end of a three-season contract.

“It’s totally bittersweet,” Munroe says in a video call interview from Toronto. “I miss my buddy Aden – and I also could not imagine a better partner than Luke in this scenario.”

Law & Order Toronto was originally built around Young as Graff. He was cast first, and then four actors came in to do chemistry reads with him. Munroe landed the part of Bateman after her fourth audition, she says.

Nestruck: Canadian TV is going to the (literal) dogs, and other lessons

Matchmaking Monroe with Young’s replacement was a less involved affair: one and dun dun . The producers floated the idea of Kirby to the actor and she was immediately enthusiastic.

Kirby felt similarly about joining Munroe.

“Her intelligence and curiosity and complexity was something I was very drawn to,” he says, in a video interview from New York. “Knowing that she was going to be leading the charge on this show, I thought that I would be in safe hands.”

The actors, both Canadian, were not strangers to one another, having played a couple in a suicide pact who take a wedding party hostage in a particularly intense 2009 episode of the CTV cop show Flashpoint .

“We cried in each other’s mouths for weeks,” Munroe recalls.

In other words, no chemistry read was required. “I don’t know what he would need to prove ever, in anything,” she says. “He’s such a deft performer.”

Speaking to one actor right after the other, the complementary contrasts between Kirby and Munroe are apparent.

Kirby does his interview vertically on his phone, walking and talking his way through Prospect Park like he’s auditioning for an Aaron Sorkin TikTok series.

Munroe, ON the other hand, stays stationary and horizontal, curled up on a chair at her home, occasionally chomping on an Ontario peach in between interview answers like a low-key Marlon Brando.

Even the main thing the actors have in common – being born in Hamilton – is a point of playful divergence.

“He will say, ‘I’m from Guelph’,” Munroe says. “That man was born in Hamilton, Ontario.”

“She’ll claim that I’m from Hamilton,” Kirby says. “I feel like it’s incumbent upon me to inform people that I was only there for 48 hours before going up Highway 6 to Guelph for the next, you know, 19 years.”

The onscreen dynamic between them as Bateman and Darcy is more subtly distinguished.

Law & Order Toronto ’s original cop partnership of Graff and Bateman was a variation on the classic detective double act of Sherlock and Watson. Graff was always pulling out some esoteric fact to help solve a case, while Bateman was the one who excelled in the empathy department.

Both Munroe and Kirby say the new dynamic cannot be so easily defined.

“There was a real fluidity to it,” Munroe says. “There is a little bit of like a pull and a curiosity and a growing reliance on each other.”

Munroe, who knows the American Law & Order franchises well, says Bateman and Darcy are not like either of her favourite former pairings: Jerry Orbach’s Lennie Briscoe and Benjamin Bratt’s Rey Curtis from seasons 6 through 9 of the original series, or Mariska Hargitay’s Olivia Benson and Christopher Meloni’s Elliot Stabler’s 12-year partnership – known to fans as “Bensler” – on Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.

The demanding shooting schedule of the police procedural, Kirby says, was such that he and Munroe developed their characters’ relationship and its progression as the season was shot, rather than planning it out much in advance. “It was just about sort of circling each other in the space and finding it inside the scenes.”

In this season’s opening episode (Oct. 1 on City-TV), Bateman and Darcy’s cop-partner meet-cute takes place in a coffee shop – when she interviews him as a witness to the shooting of a mob boss not knowing he’s an undercover police officer.

His cover blown, Darcy joins the Specialized Criminal Investigations Unit to help Bateman on this one case with his knowledge about the dead mobster. (Of course, it ends up being more than one case.)

Darcy’s ability to blend in and shape-shift after years in covert operations is a big part of how producer Tassie Cameron pitched Kirby on the character, the actor says.

“Darcy has maybe developed this kind of knack for switching his language depending on who he’s with,” he says. “He can adjust his behaviour and carriage to the level of whoever the suspect, to figure out a way to pin them down long enough to get them in handcuffs.”

In other words, Darcy is a performer – and performing as a performer is one of Kirby’s strong suits.

The actor first grabbed attention on the small screen in Canada in the cult classic Slings & Arrows playing a young Hollywood star recruited to play Hamlet at the fictional New Burbage Festival on the Stratford Festival-inspired TV series .

Years later, in 2019, Kirby won his Emmy playing the comedian Lenny Bruce on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel.

Canadian Luke Kirby ‘stunned’ to nab Emmy nomination for playing Lenny Bruce

Most recently, he starred as Jack McMillan, the artistic director of the New York Metropolitan Ballet, in Étoile, a short-lived Amazon Prime Video series created by Mrs. Maisel’ s Amy Sherman-Palladino and Daniel Palladino.

Playing Darcy in Law & Order Toronto marks a switch from streaming serialized fare to procedural fare – one that Kirby embraced. “You’re not really meant to know too much about the character’s backstory, and it sort of affords the actor some flexibility from week to week of who they are,” he says. “I found that to be an invigorating exercise.”

Working out a new onscreen relationship was far from the hardest part of the fourth season shoot for Munroe. She suffered through a concussion (from a fall while hiking), a collapsed lung (asthma related), a broken foot (from dropping a cast-iron skillet on it, an injury written into the show) and then got mononucleosis (from sharing a water bottle at a line-dancing event).

Kirby showed up for her on set, she says, always present and generous amid her health challenges. “I give him his flowers in a huge way,” she says. “I never would have imagined needing anybody the way that I needed him in that role.”

content_blocks.text: Speaking to one actor right after the other, the complementary contrasts between Kirby and Munroe are apparent.
Kirby does his interview vertically on his phone, walking and talking his way through Prospect Park like he’s auditioning for an Aaron Sorkin TikTok series.
Munroe, ON the other hand, stays stationary and horizontal, curled up on a chair at her home, occasionally chomping on an Ontario peach in between interview answers like a low-key Marlon Brando.
Even the main thing the actors have in common – being born in Hamilton – is a point of playful divergence.
“He will say, ‘I’m from Guelph’,” Munroe says. “That man was born in Hamilton, Ontario.”

“She’ll claim that I’m from Hamilton,” Kirby says. “I feel like it’s incumbent upon me to inform people that I was only there for 48 hours before going up Highway 6 to Guelph for the next, you know, 19 years.”
The onscreen dynamic between them as Bateman and Darcy is more subtly distinguished.

Law & Order Toronto ’s original cop partnership of Graff and Bateman was a variation on the classic detective double act of Sherlock and Watson. Graff was always pulling out some esoteric fact to help solve a case, while Bateman was the one who excelled in the empathy department.
Both Munroe and Kirby say the new dynamic cannot be so easily defined.
“There was a real fluidity to it,” Munroe says. “There is a little bit of like a pull and a curiosity and a growing reliance on each other.”

Munroe, who knows the American Law & Order franchises well, says Bateman and Darcy are not like either of her favourite former pairings: Jerry Orbach’s Lennie Briscoe and Benjamin Bratt’s Rey Curtis from seasons 6 through 9 of the original series, or Mariska Hargitay’s Olivia Benson and Christopher Meloni’s Elliot Stabler’s 12-year partnership – known to fans as “Bensler” – on Law & Order: Special Victims Unit.

The demanding shooting schedule of the police procedural, Kirby says, was such that he and Munroe developed their characters’ relationship and its progression as the season was shot, rather than planning it out much in advance. “It was just about sort of circling each other in the space and finding it inside the scenes.”

content_blocks.caption: Both Munroe and Kirby say the new partners’ dynamic can’t be as easily defined as the show’s old duo. Steve Wilkie/Supplied

content_blocks.text: In this season’s opening episode (Oct. 1 on City-TV), Bateman and Darcy’s cop-partner meet-cute takes place in a coffee shop – when she interviews him as a witness to the shooting of a mob boss not knowing he’s an undercover police officer.
His cover blown, Darcy joins the Specialized Criminal Investigations Unit to help Bateman on this one case with his knowledge about the dead mobster. (Of course, it ends up being more than one case.)
Darcy’s ability to blend in and shape-shift after years in covert operations is a big part of how producer Tassie Cameron pitched Kirby on the character, the actor says.

“Darcy has maybe developed this kind of knack for switching his language depending on who he’s with,” he says. “He can adjust his behaviour and carriage to the level of whoever the suspect, to figure out a way to pin them down long enough to get them in handcuffs.”
In other words, Darcy is a performer – and performing as a performer is one of Kirby’s strong suits.

The actor first grabbed attention on the small screen in Canada in the cult classic Slings & Arrows playing a young Hollywood star recruited to play Hamlet at the fictional New Burbage Festival on the Stratford Festival-inspired TV series .
Years later, in 2019, Kirby won his Emmy playing the comedian Lenny Bruce on The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel.
Canadian Luke Kirby ‘stunned’ to nab Emmy nomination for playing Lenny Bruce

Most recently, he starred as Jack McMillan, the artistic director of the New York Metropolitan Ballet, in Étoile, a short-lived Amazon Prime Video series created by Mrs. Maisel’ s Amy Sherman-Palladino and Daniel Palladino.

Playing Darcy in Law & Order Toronto marks a switch from streaming serialized fare to procedural fare – one that Kirby embraced. “You’re not really meant to know too much about the character’s backstory, and it sort of affords the actor some flexibility from week to week of who they are,” he says. “I found that to be an invigorating exercise.”

Working out a new onscreen relationship was far from the hardest part of the fourth season shoot for Munroe. She suffered through a concussion (from a fall while hiking), a collapsed lung (asthma related), a broken foot (from dropping a cast-iron skillet on it, an injury written into the show) and then got mononucleosis (from sharing a water bottle at a line-dancing event).

Kirby showed up for her on set, she says, always present and generous amid her health challenges. “I give him his flowers in a huge way,” she says. “I never would have imagined needing anybody the way that I needed him in that role.”

stories.title: New Westminster condo owners sell low, but can buy low as well
stories.summary: Patience pays off for sellers making a move to Vancouver
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
608 Belmont St., Unit 201, New Westminster, B.C.

Asking price: $549,000 (May 19)

Selling price: $515,000 (July 2)

Previous selling price: $485,000 (2020)

Monthly maintenance fee: $544.62

Taxes: $2,723.13 (2025)

Days on market: 31

Sellers’ agent: Dennis Sepulveda, Stilhavn Real Estate Services

The listing agent had helped the sellers purchase the property in 2020, for $485,000. They wanted to move to a comparable home in Vancouver.

“We knew that the market was trending downward, which meant we wouldn’t be able to get 2024 pricing on their condo,” said Dennis Sepulveda. “But I assured them that the market drop had affected all neighbourhoods, so they would be able to recover any discounts on the buying side.”

Their worries had been confirmed. The first weekend they had zero groups through two open houses, he said.

“We didn’t panic or do any price adjustments. We stuck to our guns.”

After two weeks of inactivity, they started to get private showings. Because it was a unique corner unit in a well-maintained concrete building, they soon got an offer.

This one-bedroom, one-bathroom, 793-square-foot condo is in the Uptown neighbourhood of New Westminster, with retail on the main level, and within walking distance of shops and parks.

The bright corner unit overlooks a treed courtyard. Built in 2011, the concrete building has large windows, balconies, EV chargers, bike rooms, a gym and parking.

The unit has wood floors, an updated open-concept kitchen with an island and wood-panelled cabinets, a flex room and an updated bathroom.

“My clients were very happy with a quick sale at a good price in such a tough market.”

He said they ended up purchasing a Vancouver condo for $37,000 below the asking price.

The sale completed on Sept. 24.

CBC News · Posted: Sep 25, 2026 7:32 AM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) say roads are closed northeast of London Friday morning as they investigate a serious crash in Oxford County.(Ontario Provincial Police)

Drivers are being asked to use alternate routes Friday morning as police investigate a serious collision involving a passenger vehicle and a transport truck in Zorra Township.
19th Line is closed between Elginfield Road and Road 96, according to Ontario Provincial Police.
Police say injuries are being assessed and the road is expected to remain closed for an extended period during the investigation and cleanup.
The OPP is asking drivers to avoid the area and use alternate routes.

stories.title: How a medical drone pilot program aims to help residents in rural Ontario with medical emergencies
stories.summary: The drone "is another tool that May help a bystander begin care while paramedics are on the way," says Brian Gibson.
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Residents of Bolton, Ont., who call 911 could receive critical life-saving equipment delivered from a drone, with the launch of a Medical Drone Pilot Program this week by Peel Regional Paramedic Services.

The program has been designed to support residents of the small town of approximately 27,000 residents northwest of Toronto, when they are facing time-sensitive emergencies, during the crucial moments before paramedics arrive. That includes cardiac arrests, overdoses, severe bleeding and allergic reactions.

Paramedics will be providing real-time guidance for use of the equipment through a video connection, says Brian Gibson, chief and director of Peel Regional Paramedic Services. The drone will not replace paramedics or change the 9-1-1 response.

“It is another tool that May help a bystander begin care while paramedics are on the way,” he says.

Ultimately, the pilot project will feed into research done in collaboration with the Sunnybrook Centre for Prehospital Medicine in Toronto about drone-enabled delivery of automated external defibrillators (AEDs), with the aim of expanding access to life-saving defibrillation.

When a 911 call is received, a paramedic crew is dispatched as usual and the drone is launched at the same time. “It follows a planned route while a trained pilot and safety team monitor the flight in real time,” says Gibson. “The route can be changed or the flight can be stopped if weather, people, pets, wildlife or another hazard creates a safety concern.”

If a drone cannot complete a delivery safely, the response is cancelled while the regular 911 response continues.

Gibson says t he drone can operate on five different radio frequency bands to ensure optimal connectivity during a flight, enabling remote control and audio-video.

If the drone arrives first before the paramedics, it lowers the medical package into a safe, open area. A 911 dispatcher or paramedic guides the caller or bystander by phone or video on how to retrieve and use the equipment. For an AED, no special training is needed because the device provides clear instructions and will only deliver a shock when appropriate.

“When paramedics arrive, they take over patient care,” says Gibson.

The pilot project involves just one drone. “ The drone itself is not unique,” says Gibson. “To date other drone programs have used drones primarily for search and rescue, and have tested the concept of delivery. We are actually doing it.”

The drone weighs approximately 15 kilograms and can carry a 5.5 kilograms payload. It’s 98 centimetres long and 76 centimetres wide.

There is no cost to the taxpayers for the pilot project, says Gibson. Instead, the costs to launch and maintain the program were covered by grants and funding from organizations such as the Cardiovascular Network of Canada and Zoll Medical , a Mississauga, Ont., company that develops medical care devices for cardiopulmonary and respiratory conditions.

The pilot was not launched in response to a specific community request, says Gibson. Instead, it has been designed to build evidence about whether drones can safely and reliably improve access to life-saving equipment throughout communities where paramedic responses can take longer.

“The lessons and data from this work May help inform future research and decisions about drone-enabled emergency care in rural, remote and Indigenous communities across Ontario. Any future expansion would depend on the results of the pilot, safety analysis, community need and regulatory approval.”

Gibson says Bolton was chosen because it provides the right setting to test the piloting safely and learn how the service could work in different conditions.

“The area includes urban and rural neighbourhoods, longer travel distances, varied road networks, protected and conservation lands, and local airspace considerations. These conditions allow Peel Regional Paramedic Services to test how the drone performs while managing the types of operational and safety challenges that May exist in other communities.”

Gibson notes that there were 417 9-1-1 calls to the Bolton area in 2025, which might have been responded to by a medical drone as well as paramedics.

“It really depends on the emergency,” says Gibson. Paramedics transport “to the hospital that can provide the appropriate care for the condition. In most cases this will be Brampton Civic Hospital and Cortellucci Vaughan Hospital.”

The project started with a simple question about how can Peel Regional Paramedic Services get life-saving equipment to people sooner, says Gibson. “The first focus was delivering automated external defibrillators, or AEDs, during cardiac arrest.” The pilot was expanded to test delivery of other emergency supplies, he explains, including naloxone, bleeding-control supplies and epinephrine auto-injectors.

The Peel project journey began in 2017 by looking at how to optimize drone delivery of AEDs in Ontario. It got further inspiration from Sweden , he says, where in 2022, a cardiac arrest victim received a defibrillator delivered by drone three minutes before emergency responders.

“That was the first time a drone-delivered AED was used in a real emergency response,” says Gibson. “We have been in collaboration with the Swedish team since 2020. Regulatory approvals for us in Canada took longer.”

content_blocks.text: Residents of Bolton, Ont., who call 911 could receive critical life-saving equipment delivered from a drone, with the launch of a Medical Drone Pilot Program this week by Peel Regional Paramedic Services.
content_blocks.html: Residents of Bolton, Ont., who call 911 could receive critical life-saving equipment delivered from a drone, with the launch of a Medical Drone Pilot Program this week by Peel Regional Paramedic Services.

content_blocks.text: The program has been designed to support residents of the small town of approximately 27,000 residents northwest of Toronto, when they are facing time-sensitive emergencies, during the crucial moments before paramedics arrive. That includes cardiac arrests, overdoses, severe bleeding and allergic reactions.

That includes cardiac arrests, overdoses, severe bleeding and allergic reactions.

content_blocks.text: Paramedics will be providing real-time guidance for use of the equipment through a video connection, says Brian Gibson, chief and director of Peel Regional Paramedic Services. The drone will not replace paramedics or change the 9-1-1 response.
“It is another tool that May help a bystander begin care while paramedics are on the way,” he says.

Ultimately, the pilot project will feed into research done in collaboration with the Sunnybrook Centre for Prehospital Medicine in Toronto about drone-enabled delivery of automated external defibrillators (AEDs), with the aim of expanding access to life-saving defibrillation.
How is the drone piloted to the recipient?

When a 911 call is received, a paramedic crew is dispatched as usual and the drone is launched at the same time. “It follows a planned route while a trained pilot and safety team monitor the flight in real time,” says Gibson. “The route can be changed or the flight can be stopped if weather, people, pets, wildlife or another hazard creates a safety concern.”

content_blocks.text: If a drone cannot complete a delivery safely, the response is cancelled while the regular 911 response continues.
Gibson says t he drone can operate on five different radio frequency bands to ensure optimal connectivity during a flight, enabling remote control and audio-video.

content_blocks.text: What would a typical drone interaction between the paramedic service and recipient look like?

If the drone arrives first before the paramedics, it lowers the medical package into a safe, open area. A 911 dispatcher or paramedic guides the caller or bystander by phone or video on how to retrieve and use the equipment. For an AED, no special training is needed because the device provides clear instructions and will only deliver a shock when appropriate.
“When paramedics arrive, they take over patient care,” says Gibson.
What equipment is used?

The pilot project involves just one drone. “ The drone itself is not unique,” says Gibson. “To date other drone programs have used drones primarily for search and rescue, and have tested the concept of delivery. We are actually doing it.”

There is no cost to the taxpayers for the pilot project, says Gibson. Instead, the costs to launch and maintain the program were covered by grants and funding from organizations such as the Cardiovascular Network of Canada and Zoll Medical , a Mississauga, Ont., company that develops medical care devices for cardiopulmonary and respiratory conditions.

content_blocks.text: Is the pilot project a response to calls for faster medical responses from Ontario communities?

The pilot was not launched in response to a specific community request, says Gibson. Instead, it has been designed to build evidence about whether drones can safely and reliably improve access to life-saving equipment throughout communities where paramedic responses can take longer.

“The lessons and data from this work May help inform future research and decisions about drone-enabled emergency care in rural, remote and Indigenous communities across Ontario. Any future expansion would depend on the results of the pilot, safety analysis, community need and regulatory approval.”
Why Bolton, Ont.?
Gibson says Bolton was chosen because it provides the right setting to test the piloting safely and learn how the service could work in different conditions.

“The area includes urban and rural neighbourhoods, longer travel distances, varied road networks, protected and conservation lands, and local airspace considerations. These conditions allow Peel Regional Paramedic Services to test how the drone performs while managing the types of operational and safety challenges that May exist in other communities.”
Gibson notes that there were 417 9-1-1 calls to the Bolton area in 2025, which might have been responded to by a medical drone as well as paramedics.
Where are Bolton patients eventually transported?

“It really depends on the emergency,” says Gibson. Paramedics transport “to the hospital that can provide the appropriate care for the condition. In most cases this will be Brampton Civic Hospital and Cortellucci Vaughan Hospital.”
