stories.title: Is genius a gift, serendipity or something else?
stories.summary: Childhood giftedness May provide the raw material, but it does not predict what an adult will ultimately do with their talents
stories.author: Thomas Verny
stories.content:
Thomas R. Verny is a clinical psychiatrist, academic, award-winning author, poet and public speaker. He is the author of eight books, including the global bestseller The Secret Life of the Unborn Child and The Embodied Mind: Understanding the Mysteries of Cellular Memory, Consciousness and Our Bodies .

I recently saw Early Genius, a play by much-loved veteran Stratford Festival actor, Steve Ross. The comedy centres on four children under eight, each with a genius-level IQ.

Seeing the show and talking to Steve about what attracted him to write it made me question the idea that a high IQ was really enough to constitute genius.

In surveying the landscape of current scientific knowledge about giftedness I discovered the work of Rena F. Subotnik, an American psychologist and a prominent scholar in giftedness, talent development and gifted education. She argues that giftedness should not be thought of simply as possessing an unusually high IQ or an exceptional ability in childhood. Early potential must be transformed through education, practice, opportunity, motivation, persistence, and other psychosocial factors into increasingly sophisticated expertise and, in rare cases, eminence (her term for genius). [1]

While people like Marie Curie, Mozart, or Picasso were conspicuously gifted as children, most gifted children do not rise to the level of geniuses. Some May become very successful but not geniuses.

The converse is also true. Many children who later in life reach genius status show little promise in their youth. Thomas Edison struggled with conventional schooling, while Albert Einstein, despite his early mathematical ability, failed the general portion of the entrance examination to the Swiss Federal Polytechnic at age 16.

In search of the eureka factor

William Shakespeare received only the standard grammar-school education until his mid-teens, when he had to quit to help the family financially. He never attended university. Importantly, there is no historical evidence of extraordinary literary precocity in his childhood. Yet he became arguably the greatest playwright who ever lived.

Leonardo da Vinci received even less formal education. Born illegitimate, he was instructed mainly in ordinary spoken and written Italian rather than in Latin, and received no teaching in Greek, philosophy and mathematics available to boys destined for higher education. Still, da Vinci became one of the greatest painters and most diverse scientific minds in history.

Giftedness and genius are not synonymous. Historically, both became enmeshed with IQ testing, but scientists now realize that this was a mistake. [2] Childhood giftedness May provide the raw material for genius, but it does not predict what the adult will ultimately do with it. Giftedness is better understood in terms of potential for exceptional achievement within a field whereas genius implies that exceptional potential has actually been converted into consequential accomplishment, genuine breakthroughs. [3]

A child with an IQ of 160 is extraordinarily gifted, but we don’t automatically call that child a genius. Einstein is considered a genius not because someone measured his IQ but because he changed our understanding of space and time.

When Albert Einstein died in 1955, the pathologist who performed his autopsy removed his brain. What followed was perhaps the most extraordinary foraging for genius in three pounds of greyish, gelatinous tissue ever undertaken.

The original and most famous study was performed by neuroscientist Marian Diamond. She and her team were the first to publish evidence that the brain can change with experience and improve with enrichment, what is now called neuroplasticity.

She was a professor of anatomy at the University of California, Berkeley. Dr. Diamond and colleagues compared samples of Einstein’s brain with those of 11 men. They reported that in the left Brodmann area 39, better known as the angular gyrus, Einstein had significantly more glial cells per neuron. Neuroscientists regard it as a hub where different kinds of information are integrated to create meaning. The authors cautiously stated that the difference might relate to increased metabolic activity associated with unusually complex neuronal activity. [4]

Others found that Einstein’s prefrontal cortex had greater neuronal density, although neuron size and the number of neurons beneath a given cortical surface area did not differ. [5]

Dean Falk, distinguished research professor at Florida State University, and her team, analyzed 14 previously unpublished photographs of Einstein’s entire cerebral cortex. They compared his cortical anatomy with descriptions of 85 other human brains. They reported that Einstein’s brain had a complex prefrontal cortex and distinctive parietal anatomy, a brain area involved in mathematical, visuospatial and other forms of higher cognition. [6] A few years later, this finding was supported by the research of Sandra F. Witelson, a neuroscientist at McMaster University in Hamilton. [7]

In a later study Prof. Falk, collaborating with Weiwei Men at the Shanghai Key Laboratory of Magnetic Resonance, found that Einstein’s corpus callosum, the brain’s main communication highway bridging the two cerebral hemispheres, was thicker than those of comparison groups. They interpreted this as suggesting unusually extensive interhemispheric connectivity. [8]

These studies examine one extraordinary individual after his death, often using small and imperfectly matched control samples. They cannot establish that Einstein’s anatomical peculiarities accounted for his genius.

Apart from the studies on Einstein’s brain, there is surprisingly little neuroscience that studies “genius” itself, for the obvious reason that the designation “genius” is generally retrospective. Hardly anyone is considered a genius in their lifetime. The strongest academic literature therefore comes from two overlapping areas: exceptional creativity and high intelligence.

I think the most relevant of these is a recent paper by scientists from Drexel University, Philadelphia. Twenty eminent creators, people with remarkable accomplishments in their fields, and 16 smart, well-educated individuals were asked to think of unusual uses for familiar objects. As they did so their brains were scanned with fMRI.

The authors concluded that exceptional creativity May depend on how effectively brain systems responsible for generating ideas and judging them work together. Highly creative people do not necessarily possess different brain machinery. They May be unusually good at co-ordinating two normally competing mental processes: letting the mind roam freely enough to produce unexpected ideas, while maintaining enough control to recognize which ideas are worth pursuing. [9]

However, this was a very small study, only 36 people, so it suggests a neurological difference associated with creative eminence; it does not establish that this brain pattern causes genius or exceptional creativity. This study and studies on Einstein’s brain are intriguing clues. At best, they point the way to future research into the neurobiology of genius.

In my pursuit of unlocking the mystery of what makes a genius I stumbled across The Geography of Genius, a book by Eric Weiner. The author demonstrates how creative genius flourished in specific places at specific times like Athens in 450 BC, Renaissance Florence, Vienna of 1900 and Silicon Valley in the present, to name a few. We learn of the importance for the growth of creativity by having the opportunity to engage in stimulating intellectual frisson with other like-minded friends, in a society that values the achievements especially in the arts and science. And that includes financial rewards. You cannot succeed and you certainly cannot become a genius on your own.

Even a solitary genius depends upon other people: teachers, patrons, publishers, institutions, audiences, rivals, and a culture prepared to recognize and value their contributions.

The Latin genius originally referred not to exceptional intelligence but to a guiding or generative spirit associated with a person. Only much later did the word migrate from a person having a genius to a person being a genius.

Popular culture has long cherished the image of the “mad genius,” brilliant but eccentric, emotionally unstable, socially unconventional, and hovering somewhere near the border between inspiration and lunacy. Science supports a small kernel of truth behind the stereotype, while proving that creativity and mental illness are not synonymous.

Many authorities report that highly creative scientists and artists tend to be open to experience, unconventional, self-confident, driven, ambitious and independent, while often being somewhat less conscientious in the conventional sense. [10, 3] Others associate artistic creativity with openness, imagination, perceptual sensitivity, fantasy, emotion and aesthetic engagement while high intellectual versatility is more strongly connected with scientific creativity. [11, 12]

It seems that some unconventional traits associated with creativity May help, but any serious mental disorder itself would interfere rather than further the creative process. [13]

“What allows genius to flower is not neurosis, but its opposite, ‘ego strength,’ meaning among other things ordinary, Sunday-school virtues such as tenacity and above all the ability to survive disappointment” wrote cultural critic and author Joan Acocella. [14].

AI friends and lovers: promise and peril

Consider the career of Sir Alexander Fleming, the discoverer of penicillin. He chose to attend St Mary’s Hospital Medical School in London, partly because, as a teenager, he had played water polo against its team and made some friends there. While there, Fleming became an excellent shot, so his supervisor wanted to keep him at St Mary’s on its rifle team. Thus encouraged, Fleming stayed at St. Mary’s to study bacteriology.

Then came the famous accident. A mould contaminated one of his bacterial cultures. Plenty of scientists might simply have thrown the spoiled dish away. Fleming noticed something peculiar: Bacteria were not growing around the mould. He pursued the observation, and penicillin was born.

Observe that Fleming was talented, certainly, but people also liked him, admired him and wanted to keep him around. Doors opened. He was invited to enter. He entered.

Not all geniuses are like Fleming. Geniuses May not always be “nice” people or easy to get along with. They have their faults like the rest of us. But they have something that induces other people to take an interest in them. That “something” might be charm, confidence, usefulness, persuasiveness, excitement, or the extraordinary quality of the work itself.

For neuroscience and psychology, genius is an unusually difficult subject to quantify because the designation is subjective and often retrospective.

What we know for certain is that genius is not about psychometric tests, or brain architecture or creativity, though all these are contributing factors.

In the scientific field it is a sudden flash, sometimes referred to as a lightbulb moment. A connection is made that no one else ever made. Like Newton watching the apple fall.

Or it is the gradual development in a person with talent and personality, who patiently and often single-mindedly keeps perfecting their craft over time. A good example is Toni Morrison whose linguistic originality, psychological depth and treatment of history transformed American literature. She won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.

Life throws you a pass. Catching it shows you are gifted. Convert it to a touchdown and you enter the pantheon of geniuses. Giftedness is potential; genius is what you do with it.

A good example is Toni Morrison whose linguistic originality, psychological depth and treatment of history transformed American literature. She won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.
Life throws you a pass. Catching it shows you are gifted. Convert it to a touchdown and you enter the pantheon of geniuses. Giftedness is potential; genius is what you do with it.

content_blocks.text: Thomas R. Verny is a clinical psychiatrist, academic, award-winning author, poet and public speaker. He is the author of eight books, including the global bestseller The Secret Life of the Unborn Child and The Embodied Mind: Understanding the Mysteries of Cellular Memory, Consciousness and Our Bodies .
I recently saw Early Genius, a play by much-loved veteran Stratford Festival actor, Steve Ross. The comedy centres on four children under eight, each with a genius-level IQ.
Seeing the show and talking to Steve about what attracted him to write it made me question the idea that a high IQ was really enough to constitute genius.

In surveying the landscape of current scientific knowledge about giftedness I discovered the work of Rena F. Subotnik, an American psychologist and a prominent scholar in giftedness, talent development and gifted education. She argues that giftedness should not be thought of simply as possessing an unusually high IQ or an exceptional ability in childhood. Early potential must be transformed through education, practice, opportunity, motivation, persistence, and other psychosocial factors into increasingly sophisticated expertise and, in rare cases, eminence (her term for genius). [1]
While people like Marie Curie, Mozart, or Picasso were conspicuously gifted as children, most gifted children do not rise to the level of geniuses. Some May become very successful but not geniuses.

The converse is also true. Many children who later in life reach genius status show little promise in their youth. Thomas Edison struggled with conventional schooling, while Albert Einstein, despite his early mathematical ability, failed the general portion of the entrance examination to the Swiss Federal Polytechnic at age 16.
In search of the eureka factor

William Shakespeare received only the standard grammar-school education until his mid-teens, when he had to quit to help the family financially. He never attended university. Importantly, there is no historical evidence of extraordinary literary precocity in his childhood. Yet he became arguably the greatest playwright who ever lived.

Leonardo da Vinci received even less formal education. Born illegitimate, he was instructed mainly in ordinary spoken and written Italian rather than in Latin, and received no teaching in Greek, philosophy and mathematics available to boys destined for higher education. Still, da Vinci became one of the greatest painters and most diverse scientific minds in history.

Giftedness and genius are not synonymous. Historically, both became enmeshed with IQ testing, but scientists now realize that this was a mistake. [2] Childhood giftedness May provide the raw material for genius, but it does not predict what the adult will ultimately do with it. Giftedness is better understood in terms of potential for exceptional achievement within a field whereas genius implies that exceptional potential has actually been converted into consequential accomplishment, genuine breakthroughs. [3]

A child with an IQ of 160 is extraordinarily gifted, but we don’t automatically call that child a genius. Einstein is considered a genius not because someone measured his IQ but because he changed our understanding of space and time.

When Albert Einstein died in 1955, the pathologist who performed his autopsy removed his brain. What followed was perhaps the most extraordinary foraging for genius in three pounds of greyish, gelatinous tissue ever undertaken.

The original and most famous study was performed by neuroscientist Marian Diamond. She and her team were the first to publish evidence that the brain can change with experience and improve with enrichment, what is now called neuroplasticity.

She was a professor of anatomy at the University of California, Berkeley. Dr. Diamond and colleagues compared samples of Einstein’s brain with those of 11 men. They reported that in the left Brodmann area 39, better known as the angular gyrus, Einstein had significantly more glial cells per neuron. Neuroscientists regard it as a hub where different kinds of information are integrated to create meaning. The authors cautiously stated that the difference might relate to increased metabolic activity associated with unusually complex neuronal activity. [4]
Others found that Einstein’s prefrontal cortex had greater neuronal density, although neuron size and the number of neurons beneath a given cortical surface area did not differ. [5]

Dean Falk, distinguished research professor at Florida State University, and her team, analyzed 14 previously unpublished photographs of Einstein’s entire cerebral cortex. They compared his cortical anatomy with descriptions of 85 other human brains. They reported that Einstein’s brain had a complex prefrontal cortex and distinctive parietal anatomy, a brain area involved in mathematical, visuospatial and other forms of higher cognition. [6] A few years later, this finding was supported by the research of Sandra F. Witelson, a neuroscientist at McMaster University in Hamilton. [7]

In a later study Prof. Falk, collaborating with Weiwei Men at the Shanghai Key Laboratory of Magnetic Resonance, found that Einstein’s corpus callosum, the brain’s main communication highway bridging the two cerebral hemispheres, was thicker than those of comparison groups. They interpreted this as suggesting unusually extensive interhemispheric connectivity. [8]

These studies examine one extraordinary individual after his death, often using small and imperfectly matched control samples. They cannot establish that Einstein’s anatomical peculiarities accounted for his genius.

Apart from the studies on Einstein’s brain, there is surprisingly little neuroscience that studies “genius” itself, for the obvious reason that the designation “genius” is generally retrospective. Hardly anyone is considered a genius in their lifetime. The strongest academic literature therefore comes from two overlapping areas: exceptional creativity and high intelligence.

I think the most relevant of these is a recent paper by scientists from Drexel University, Philadelphia. Twenty eminent creators, people with remarkable accomplishments in their fields, and 16 smart, well-educated individuals were asked to think of unusual uses for familiar objects. As they did so their brains were scanned with fMRI.

The authors concluded that exceptional creativity May depend on how effectively brain systems responsible for generating ideas and judging them work together. Highly creative people do not necessarily possess different brain machinery. They May be unusually good at co-ordinating two normally competing mental processes: letting the mind roam freely enough to produce unexpected ideas, while maintaining enough control to recognize which ideas are worth pursuing. [9]

However, this was a very small study, only 36 people, so it suggests a neurological difference associated with creative eminence; it does not establish that this brain pattern causes genius or exceptional creativity. This study and studies on Einstein’s brain are intriguing clues. At best, they point the way to future research into the neurobiology of genius.

In my pursuit of unlocking the mystery of what makes a genius I stumbled across The Geography of Genius, a book by Eric Weiner. The author demonstrates how creative genius flourished in specific places at specific times like Athens in 450 BC, Renaissance Florence, Vienna of 1900 and Silicon Valley in the present, to name a few. We learn of the importance for the growth of creativity by having the opportunity to engage in stimulating intellectual frisson with other like-minded friends, in a society that values the achievements especially in the arts and science. And that includes financial rewards. You cannot succeed and you certainly cannot become a genius on your own.
Even a solitary genius depends upon other people: teachers, patrons, publishers, institutions, audiences, rivals, and a culture prepared to recognize and value their contributions.

The Latin genius originally referred not to exceptional intelligence but to a guiding or generative spirit associated with a person. Only much later did the word migrate from a person having a genius to a person being a genius.

Popular culture has long cherished the image of the “mad genius,” brilliant but eccentric, emotionally unstable, socially unconventional, and hovering somewhere near the border between inspiration and lunacy. Science supports a small kernel of truth behind the stereotype, while proving that creativity and mental illness are not synonymous.

Many authorities report that highly creative scientists and artists tend to be open to experience, unconventional, self-confident, driven, ambitious and independent, while often being somewhat less conscientious in the conventional sense. [10, 3] Others associate artistic creativity with openness, imagination, perceptual sensitivity, fantasy, emotion and aesthetic engagement while high intellectual versatility is more strongly connected with scientific creativity. [11, 12]
It seems that some unconventional traits associated with creativity May help, but any serious mental disorder itself would interfere rather than further the creative process. [13]

“What allows genius to flower is not neurosis, but its opposite, ‘ego strength,’ meaning among other things ordinary, Sunday-school virtues such as tenacity and above all the ability to survive disappointment” wrote cultural critic and author Joan Acocella. [14].
AI friends and lovers: promise and peril

Consider the career of Sir Alexander Fleming, the discoverer of penicillin. He chose to attend St Mary’s Hospital Medical School in London, partly because, as a teenager, he had played water polo against its team and made some friends there. While there, Fleming became an excellent shot, so his supervisor wanted to keep him at St Mary’s on its rifle team. Thus encouraged, Fleming stayed at St. Mary’s to study bacteriology.

Then came the famous accident. A mould contaminated one of his bacterial cultures. Plenty of scientists might simply have thrown the spoiled dish away. Fleming noticed something peculiar: Bacteria were not growing around the mould. He pursued the observation, and penicillin was born.
Observe that Fleming was talented, certainly, but people also liked him, admired him and wanted to keep him around. Doors opened. He was invited to enter. He entered.

Not all geniuses are like Fleming. Geniuses May not always be “nice” people or easy to get along with. They have their faults like the rest of us. But they have something that induces other people to take an interest in them. That “something” might be charm, confidence, usefulness, persuasiveness, excitement, or the extraordinary quality of the work itself.
For neuroscience and psychology, genius is an unusually difficult subject to quantify because the designation is subjective and often retrospective.
What we know for certain is that genius is not about psychometric tests, or brain architecture or creativity, though all these are contributing factors.
In the scientific field it is a sudden flash, sometimes referred to as a lightbulb moment. A connection is made that no one else ever made. Like Newton watching the apple fall.

Or it is the gradual development in a person with talent and personality, who patiently and often single-mindedly keeps perfecting their craft over time. A good example is Toni Morrison whose linguistic originality, psychological depth and treatment of history transformed American literature. She won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Literature.
Life throws you a pass. Catching it shows you are gifted. Convert it to a touchdown and you enter the pantheon of geniuses. Giftedness is potential; genius is what you do with it.

stories.title: Breaking the spell of drone advertising
stories.summary: An ad-free night sky is a natural treasure worth protecting
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
More than 1,000 aerial drones will soar above Toronto for two nights this weekend, conjuring up a mesmerizing spectacle of wizard hats and magic wands. The show will be at once a dazzling triumph of choreography and also a visual blight and pollution of a night sky enjoyed by all of us.

The show is timed to coincide with a promotional campaign related to the 25 th anniversary of the first Harry Potter movie. It was staged last week in North Edmonton and in the Old Port of Montreal and is scheduled for Friday and Saturday nights in north Toronto. Although the shows are ticketed-entry, the display cannot help but intrude on people in the area.

The display is also the latest in a growing trend of drone marketing. Only a few weeks ago, Loblaw used drones in Toronto to write huge messages in the night sky promoting its AI-powered health chatbot.

Harry Potter drone show will bring a magical open-air spectacle to Canadian cities starting this week

There’s a certain tragedy of the commons at play here. The sky doesn’t belong to any specific person. It belongs to all of us. So it can’t be used for just any purpose at all. An ad-free sky is a natural treasure worth protecting.

Lest you accuse of us being muggles – characters who cannot perform magic or even, in this case, recognize it – this is not a criticism of Harry Potter, per se . Millions of fans love the franchise and will welcome the revival now under way. The movies are being re-released, merchandise and memorabilia pop-ups have been staged and a new television show is set to launch.

Fan enthusiasm does not give licence for a commercial takeover of the sky.

The commercial aspect of the drone show is one thing that sets it apart from purely celebratory events such as fireworks displays. The Harry Potter show is a collaboration between the studio behind the movies and others. It May be entertaining but is, ultimately, advertising.

Meanwhile, our phones push us ads and sports broadcasts are saturated with advertising. Even sidewalks are placarded with ads for people who look down as they walk.

It can be comforting for any one individual to believe that they are immune to these ads. That they are able either to tune out the ads as they wash by, or not fall prey to their message. That’s an appealing thought. But the advertising community, which spent $20-billion last year in Canada alone, obviously feels that we are susceptible.

That’s business, and this space would not advocate for a ban on marketing. Still, the onslaught of ads can be too much. There is a need to protect the beauty of public space, which is more than a backdrop for brand logos, ad slogans and promotional campaigns. The value of a garden or a sky cannot be reduced to how much advertisers would be willing to pay to splash their message on it.

Until recently, there were practical limitations on advertising in the sky. In previous decades there might have been a skywriting pilot, forming words that dissipated within minutes. Or perhaps there was a plane towing a message or a blimp painted with one. But these were expensive undertakings, which reduced their use. Drones are relatively cheap and can be deployed in large numbers. They can be accompanied by music and also used to light up the night, heightening their impact both on willing viewers and those irritated by the intrusion.

Cities are, undoubtedly, crowded and busy places. They can be kaleidoscopic in their intensity, with lights and noise forming a backdrop to daily life.

However, cities also have their peaceful side. Because of the hubbub, residents value moments of escape from what author Robert Caro called “the abrasions of city life.” Even though urban lights reduce the darkness of the night sky, people in even the densest neighbourhood can look up and dream, lost in wonder at the vastness of the heavens.

Selling off that sky is more than a tragedy of the commons. It dispels the magic of life.

stories.title: Rejecting Trump’s Lake Ontario order was ‘pretty easy decision,’ MapQuest GM says
stories.summary: Refusing to rename the body of water has led to millions of app downloads, and fresh support from Canadians
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
When MapQuest’s general manager woke up in Toronto on Thursday morning, the Texan visiting for a conference knew he couldn’t leave without visiting one place.

Doug Berger made a beeline south from his hotel, wandering past the dock where the ill-fated Captain John’s restaurant used to moor and heading deeper toward the city’s shoreline.

The vast body of water he arrived at – Lake Ontario – was an essential stop for Berger because it made his company the talk of the tech world and beyond last month. Unlike many of its rivals, MapQuest had rejected U.S. President Donald Trump’s name change to Lake America.

“It’s what gave MapQuest this moment,” Berger said of the lake as he walked toward the waterfront for a second time Thursday. “I just wanted to get over there and mark the moment.”

That moment began in the dying days of August, when the MapQuest team started monitoring Trump after he said he was “giving serious consideration” to swapping the lake’s name.

Explainer: Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario. What does it actually change?

MapQuest had been through this before. Last January, Trump ditched the Gulf of Mexico moniker in favour of Gulf of America. MapQuest stuck with the original name because it wanted to give users familiarity and its navigation products “integrity,” Berger said.

MapQuest makes name changes all the time as roads get built, buildings are demolished and new tracts of land are settled, but the political nature of Trump’s Lake Ontario edict felt different, he reasoned.

When the team discussed how to handle a change, if one ever came to fruition, they made the “pretty easy decision” to ignore it.

“It’s one of the Great Lakes. There are acronyms like Homes, and this is the ‘O,’” Berger explained, almost exasperated.

“Because of the location and because Canada’s our friendly neighbour to the north … renaming it didn’t make a whole lot of sense to us and we saw it as another moment for MapQuest to kind of take a stand.”

Two days later, when Trump signed his executive order christening the body of water Lake America, it took the company mere minutes to post a map of Lake Ontario with the caption, “we’re not changing it.”

Meanwhile, Google and Apple adopted “Lake America” for users in the United States while retaining Lake Ontario for those in Canada.

Berger said he knew MapQuest was going to be the outlier, using Lake Ontario everywhere in the world.

With roughly 50 staff, he said his company has a nimbler team and more independence in general than the tech giants, which Berger estimates have thousands of staff working on mapping alone and under more pressure.

MapQuest’s decision paid off.

Three million new users, including many Canadians, have downloaded the app since the executive order. Many told Berger they respected that the company kept the Lake Ontario name.

Their support became like “lightning in a bottle” for the MapQuest team, who soon started selling “We’re not changing it” mugs, sweaters and T-shirts.

But the team was also anxious not to let this moment pass.

Shannon Proudfoot: Welcome to the map resistance

Opinion: Google Maps has become a tool of digital imperialism

Thirty years ago, MapQuest was spun out of R.R. Donnelley & Sons, a commercial printing business dating back to the 19th century. It is now owned by System1 SST-N , a California-based advertising company.

While decades ago, MapQuest was a dominant name in the world of navigation services, the evolution of smartphones and GPS products for cars, as well as the rise of rivals, has diminished much of the business’s lustre.

Some young people had never heard of the app when the Lake Ontario moment happened, but if you are over 30, Berger said, there’s a good chance you remember being in the family car “being yelled at to turn right in 0.1 miles and you still have the printouts.”

MapQuest still delivers directions to users but now there’s no need for a printout. Customers can generate the company’s maps on a phone or its app.

And thanks to all those new users, the maps are getting even better than before, Berger said.

Very recent feedback from consumers, particularly those in Toronto, encouraged the company to add local transit options to its maps and offer support for Android Auto, a mobile app that mirrors a car’s dashboard.

While MapQuest is revelling in all the feedback and attention the Lake Ontario renaming has brought, Berger thinks one of the best parts has been how interested people are in the discussions MapQuest staff have every day.

“Isn’t it fun we are talking about geography?” he said.

When the team discussed how to handle a change, if one ever came to fruition, they made the “pretty easy decision” to ignore it.
“It’s one of the Great Lakes. There are acronyms like Homes, and this is the ‘O,’” Berger explained, almost exasperated.

“Because of the location and because Canada’s our friendly neighbour to the north … renaming it didn’t make a whole lot of sense to us and we saw it as another moment for MapQuest to kind of take a stand.”

Two days later, when Trump signed his executive order christening the body of water Lake America, it took the company mere minutes to post a map of Lake Ontario with the caption, “we’re not changing it.”
Meanwhile, Google and Apple adopted “Lake America” for users in the United States while retaining Lake Ontario for those in Canada.
Berger said he knew MapQuest was going to be the outlier, using Lake Ontario everywhere in the world.

With roughly 50 staff, he said his company has a nimbler team and more independence in general than the tech giants, which Berger estimates have thousands of staff working on mapping alone and under more pressure.
MapQuest’s decision paid off.
Three million new users, including many Canadians, have downloaded the app since the executive order. Many told Berger they respected that the company kept the Lake Ontario name.
Their support became like “lightning in a bottle” for the MapQuest team, who soon started selling “We’re not changing it” mugs, sweaters and T-shirts.
But the team was also anxious not to let this moment pass.
Shannon Proudfoot: Welcome to the map resistance
Opinion: Google Maps has become a tool of digital imperialism

Thirty years ago, MapQuest was spun out of R.R. Donnelley & Sons, a commercial printing business dating back to the 19th century. It is now owned by System1 SST-N , a California-based advertising company.

While decades ago, MapQuest was a dominant name in the world of navigation services, the evolution of smartphones and GPS products for cars, as well as the rise of rivals, has diminished much of the business’s lustre.

Some young people had never heard of the app when the Lake Ontario moment happened, but if you are over 30, Berger said, there’s a good chance you remember being in the family car “being yelled at to turn right in 0.1 miles and you still have the printouts.”
MapQuest still delivers directions to users but now there’s no need for a printout. Customers can generate the company’s maps on a phone or its app.
And thanks to all those new users, the maps are getting even better than before, Berger said.

Very recent feedback from consumers, particularly those in Toronto, encouraged the company to add local transit options to its maps and offer support for Android Auto, a mobile app that mirrors a car’s dashboard.

While MapQuest is revelling in all the feedback and attention the Lake Ontario renaming has brought, Berger thinks one of the best parts has been how interested people are in the discussions MapQuest staff have every day.
“Isn’t it fun we are talking about geography?” he said.

stories.title: Farmers turn their antique tractors into ‘square dancing’ tractors at IPM
stories.summary: To the delight of crowds at this year’s International Plowing Match, Bruce County’s Square Dancing Tractors have come out of retirement, to swing, swivel, and square dance their way around a square dirt track near Walkerton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Who knew tractors could dance?

To the delight of crowds at this year’s International Plowing Match, Bruce County’s Square Dancing Tractors have come out of retirement, to swing, swivel, and square dance their way around a square dirt track near Walkerton.

The squad of square dancers have had their tractors in storage since 2019.

The 12 drivers, and one square dance caller have been practicing since March perfecting their tight turns, and spinning wheels into a spectacle for all to see.

“Oh, it is a lot of fun. Hundred percent, both on the square and off the square it’s a lot of fun with the group. So that’s why we do it,” said one of the drivers/dancers, Jamie Gowland.

“Never say never, but if you want to see us, get here,” said Scott.

stories.title: As referendum looms, 70% of Albertans want province to remain in Canada
stories.summary: Ipsos found a strong majority (76 per cent) of Albertans are aware there are several questions in the upcoming referendum, and 62 per cent plan to vote on all 10 questions.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
In three and a half weeks, the Alberta referendum will ask residents if they want to hold a formal vote on whether to stay or leave Canada — and most have their minds made up.

An Ipsos poll exclusively for Global News conducted online interviews with 1,500 Canadian adults between Sept. 18 and 22, including 600 Alberta residents.

Seven in 10 Albertans said they plan to vote for Alberta to remain a province of Canada in the upcoming referendum on Oct. 19 — a statistically insignificant drop of two per cent from similar polling conducted between May 28 to June 1 .

Among the 20 per cent who said they would vote for Alberta to commence the process of holding a binding independence referendum, support was highest among men (25 per cent), the Gen Z demographic born between 1997 and 2012 (28 per cent) and Albertans outside of Calgary and Edmonton (28 per cent).

“It’s not really surprising that rural Albertans, older Albertans and male Albertans are more likely to say that they want to go,” said Ipsos Public Affairs senior vice-president Gregory Jack. “Younger Albertans, more urban Albertans in Calgary or in Edmonton are more likely to say that they’re going to want to stay.

“The numbers on who wants to go or who wants to stay haven’t really changed throughout the campaign.”

Voter turnout will be key, however.

“I think in this particular referendum, it’s going to be more important than usual because the ‘no’ side — the side that wants to stay — is not as motivated as the ‘yes’ side is,” Jack said.

“The ‘yes’ side are the ones that want to ask the question, they’re the ones who want to be having this conversation. So if they have a high voter turnout and the ‘no’ side stays home or doesn’t vote, you might see a higher level of ‘yes’ than you would see if the entire population had voted.”

10:21 Road to the Referendum: Mitch Sylvestre, head of the Stay Free Alberta | FULL

Ipsos found a strong majority (76 per cent) of Albertans are aware there are several questions in the upcoming referendum, and 62 per cent plan to vote on all 10 referendum questions.

The ballot contains 10 government-initiated questions dealing largely with immigration and constitutional reform.

The referendum, announced Feb. 19, initially contained nine questions pertaining to immigration and the Constitution.

Then on May 21, Premier Danielle Smith announced a 10th question was being added , putting the issue of Alberta separatism in the hands of voters.

Since then, public and political attention has largely focused on that final question asking Albertans whether they want to remain in Canada or proceed to a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

“For the ‘yes’ side, they’re going to want to suggest that this is not a final referendum — there’s going to be another referendum, and it’s an opportunity to send a message to Ottawa,” Ja

1:39 7 in 10 Albertans say they plan to vote for Alberta to remain in Canada

“For the ‘no’ side, they’re gonna suggest that this the time to put this issue to rest.”

In January, an Ipsos poll found about three in 10 residents supported independence , but a deeper dive revealed that when faced with the costs and consequences of doing so, only half of those interested in separatism are truly committed to following through.

7:28 Road to the Referendum: Former UCP finance minister speaks on behalf of Lead, Not Leave group

While the polling data continues to suggests the separatist momentum isn’t powerful enough to move past the initial referendum in October, Ipsos asked Albertans what their intentions would be if that binding referendum were to somehow still happen.

In that hypothetical situation, the “stay” crowd remained firmly entrenched in their position: 74 per cent would opt to stay — with 90 per cent of those people saying definitely. That’s an increase from when Ipsos asked the same question in June , when 72 per cent said they would vote to stay.

Those most likely to say they would vote to stay include Boomers (80 per cent), university grads (80 per cent), women (79 per cent) residents of Edmonton (79 per cent) and Millennials born roughly between 1981 and 1996 ( 75 per cent.)

2:01 Foreign interference intensifies ahead of Alberta separation vote

Meanwhile just 14 per cent of the 600 people polled would vote to still leave and 69 per cent of them felt strongly about their position. That’s down from June, when 18 per cent of Albertans would vote to leave Canada.

Those who felt strongest about their view included men (20 per cent), Gen Z (18 per cent) and Gen Xers born roughly between 1965 and 1980 (18 per cent).

Those outside of the major city centres were more likely to be undecided: 12 per cent, compared to seven per cent in Alberta as a whole.

Jack believes many Albertans picked a side months ago and have stuck with it.

“We should see perhaps some more movement in the next couple of weeks as the referendum gets closer, but a lot of people have a position on this,” Jack said.

“I think both campaigns are going to want to get their supporters out as much as possible, because people have made up their minds, to a large extent, on issues like this.”

The overall poll of 1,500 Canadians is accurate to within +/- 3.1 percentage points, 19 times out of 20, had all adult Canadian residents been polled. Questions asked of Albertans only (n=600) have a credibility interval of +/- 4.9 percentage points. Questions asked of Canadians outside Alberta (n=900) have a credibility interval of +/- 4.0 percentage points.

The credibility interval will be wider among subsets of the population. All sample surveys and polls may be subject to other sources of error, including, but not limited to coverage error, and measurement error.

stories.title: Winnipeg judge grants Iranian voyeur a conditional discharge to avoid deportation
stories.summary: The Iranian-born chemist had surreptitiously and repeatedly filmed the backsides of two women at the lab where they all worked.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Winnipeg judge has granted a conditional discharge to an Iranian-born chemist so he can avoid deportation for surreptitiously and repeatedly filming the backsides of two women at the lab where they all worked.

Seyed Reza Mir Heidari, who pleaded guilty in Manitoba provincial court to two counts of voyeurism, is living in Canada on a work permit that was recently extended until April 2027. He has applied for permanent residency, but that application is on hold because of the voyeurism charges.

His lawyer argued a conviction would make him liable for deportation.

“Given Mr. Mir Heidari’s lack of record, rehabilitative work done, his remorse and insight, the significant collateral consequences that could result from a conviction, and the fact he is well educated and has held a full time job long term, I am persuaded that it is in the public interest that he be able to move forward without a criminal record, so that he can continue being a contributing member to Canadian society,” Judge Catherine Carlson wrote in a recent decision.

The judge also handed Mir Heidari three years of probation.

She pointed out that a criminal record would hurt his ability to get a new job after the lab fired him and it would have significant consequences on his immigration status.

If Mir Heidari “is deported, he would be deported to Iran,” Carlson said in her Sept. 17 decision.

“Iran is at war with the United States. Mr. Mir Heidari’s wife is an American citizen. It is unlikely Mr. Mir Heidari would be able to go to the United States or that his wife would be able to go to Iran. The practical result is likely that Mr. Mir Heidari would not be able to be in the same country as his wife. That of course could be expected to have a detrimental impact on their marriage.”

The judge found that a conditional discharge was in Mir Heidari’s interest.

“But for this offence, he is a person of good character with no prior convictions. Specific deterrence is not required by a sentence, as in my view his arrest, being charged and navigating through the criminal proceedings is sufficient to address specific deterrence,” Carlson said.

“A criminal conviction May indeed have significant adverse repercussions in terms of job opportunities, immigration consequences, and as an adjunct of those, ON his marriage. A sentence that would result in a conviction, given the significant professional and personal collateral consequences for Mr. Mir Heidari, would be crushing.”

Mir Heidari, 29, admitted that between Nov. 1, 2024, and Jan. 9, 2025, “he took photos and videos of two female co-workers in their mutual workplace,” said the decision.

“The photos and videos depicted the victims’ faces, backsides and buttocks. The victims were fully clothed.”

The Crown recommended Mir Heidari get a suspended sentence, with three years of probation. “The Crown says a criminal conviction in this case is needed to recognize the seriousness of the offences.”

The two women were both in their 20s at the time of the offences.

After they noticed he was filming them “from behind,” the women filed a formal complaint with their employer on Jan. 9, 2025, and “Mir Heidari was immediately suspended.”

The women contacted police two days later, who searched Mir Heidari’s apartment, seizing documents and his cell phone.

A forensic analysis of his cell phone located 55 images of the victims. Investigators also found 82 images and short videos in a folder on the phone dubbed “project session.”

While there were some duplicates, the images and videos “depict the victims’ faces, buttocks and backsides, all taken without their knowledge or consent.”

One of his victims “stated that this incident has changed her life forever, affecting her mental and physical health, her career and her sense of safety,” said the decision.

“Mr. Mir Heidari’s actions made her feel objectified and sexualized in a place where she was just doing her job. She is still scared about what was being done with the images, since they were beyond her control.”

His other victim “said that she felt violated by Mr. Mir Heidari’s actions. Watching him take photos on the video footage made her physically sick. His actions took away her sense of safety, dignity and ability to trust. She is now hyper vigilant.”

Mir Heidari, who was born in Tehran, relocated to Dubai with his family “when he was young, and he spent most of his formative years there,” said the decision.

His parents now live in Iran. His father sent him to Canada at the age of 17 to complete high school at the International College of Manitoba.

Mir Heidari later obtained a Bachelor of Science degree from the University of Manitoba, where he met his wife — a banker who lives in Minneapolis, Minn. — in 2017.

She is unable to work in Canada because her application for a work visa was denied. She returned to the United States in January 2026, after a removal order was issued.

Mir Heidari “says he is unable to work in the United States or even enter that country, as Iran is one of seven banned Muslim countries.”

“They are committed to their marriage, but … the future of their relationship is unknown given the uncertainties surrounding their residencies,” said the decision.

Mir Heidari “was experiencing a professional and a personal crisis” around the time of the offences, said the decision, which notes he was working long hours in a “toxic” environment.

“During this time, his wife’s inability to work in Canada meant they were apart geographically, which fractured their intimacy and communication,” it said.

“He also felt culturally isolated and lacked supports. Mr. Mir Heidari says he relied on pornography as a mechanism to cope with these challenges. He says his use of pornography is now more limited.”

stories.title: Perfect games are nearly impossible in five-pin bowling. Here’s how a Winnipeg teen beat the odds
stories.summary: Logan Newton, 17, finds his groove in a proudly Canadian sport
stories.author: Jana G. Pruden, Illustrations by Jonathan Dyck
stories.content:
The manager was busy and distracted when one of his employees tapped him on the shoulder. It was the second day of the national youth five-pin bowling championships at Dakota Lanes in Winnipeg, and the place was alive with the thud of balls and clatter of pins.

“Hey,” the kid said. Something in his voice caught his boss’s attention. “We’re going for perfection over here.”

Justin Keen looked over to where 17-year-old Logan Newton stood surrounded by a gathering crowd.

Five, six, seven strikes in a row – that happened at Dakota Lanes with some frequency. Impressive, but not uncommon for competitive bowlers.

Eight strikes was different.

And at nine strikes, word was burning through the alley: Logan Newton is going for a perfect game.

Other lanes grew quiet as people left their games to watch. Even as a spectator, Justin was trembling and nervous. He’d been bowling his whole life, and he knew how rare and difficult it was to bowl 12 strikes in a row – how overwhelming the mounting pressure could be.

“I’m sitting back here thinking, ‘Is he okay? Is he going to break down?’” Justin says. “Some people, the emotions can overrun you. You never know what’s going to happen.”

Logan Newton had thrown nine strikes in a row.

Just three more strikes to a perfect game.

If you aren’t a bowler, what you May be picturing right now – dense pyramid of pins, finger holes drilled into a big black ball – isn’t what we’re talking about. That’s 10-pin, and it’s American.

Five-pin bowling is our sport. Invented, played and loved almost exclusively in Canada.

Five-pin bowling uses smaller balls and pins, broader spacing and a different score structure. It was invented by flamboyant Toronto sportsman (and pageant judge) Tommy Ryan, who introduced it at his swank Toronto Bowling Club in 1909 after deciding 10-pin bowling was “too slow and uninteresting.”

Perfect games are common in 10-pin. The ball is so big, there are so many pins clustered so closely together. The United States Bowling Congress estimates tens of thousands of perfect 10-pin games rolled every year, with the odds of an average bowler throwing a perfect game in league play about one in 11,500.

Meanwhile, a champion five-pin bowler could go their whole lives without a perfect game. The Canadian 5 Pin Bowlers’ Association records about a dozen a year.

“I’ve won everything. I’ve won TSN. I’ve won CBC. I won over $100,000, but I’ve never thrown a perfect game,” says Cameron Boon, with a rueful chuckle. He’s a veteran Manitoba bowler who also owns and runs Polo Park Bowling Centre in Winnipeg with his brother.

“It’s got to be 99 per cent will never throw a perfect game in their life.”

In 62 years and a quarter-million matches, there had only ever been one perfect game in Youth Bowl Canada’s national competition, thrown by 16-year-old Jenna Lamoureux in Calgary a decade ago.

But on this spring afternoon in Winnipeg, Erin Newton saw clearly how it could happen. Logan was throwing every ball in the same spot with the same momentum and the same pace and the same movement. Everything was just there.

It was around Logan’s ninth strike of the game that Erin realized he had a real chance.

“Oh my goodness,” she thought. “This could happen.”

It was, perhaps, inevitable that Logan Newton would end up at that place, ON that day, with all those strikes. In a way, you could say his whole life had been leading to such a moment.

His grandparents met bowling, and his family has been bowling ever since. His grandfather was a national level bowler, his grandmother and mother have both competed and won at national competitions, and he and his brothers grew up at Rossmere Lanes, the Winnipeg bowling centre owned by their father, Jamie Newton, who is also an accomplished bowler and Logan’s coach.

“When dad’s at work, what do you do?” Logan says. “Chuck balls.”

The popularity of five-pin bowling has ebbed and flowed through the years. It’s been threatened both by changing social habits and by the pervasive influence of 10-pin, an easier and in some ways more dramatic game (all those pins flying!), which is the dominant form of bowling around the world.

But competitive five-pin bowling has a dedicated and tight-knit community around Canada. New players are drawn by a game that’s accessible to almost anyone of any age and ability, but also challenging enough to keep the attention of competitive players for decades.

Part of the challenge of five-pin bowling is that, ON paper, it should be easy. The external variables are relatively minor, with only slight variations to account for in the slickness of the lane, the ball, the shoes. In theory, all you have to do to get a strike is roll the ball straight down the lane and hit the headpin slightly off-centre.

And yet, as anyone who has attempted to do that, and instead seen their ball careen into the gutter, knows, it isn’t even close to that simple.

And that’s just one strike.

Throwing 12 strikes in a row is a matter of skill and luck combined: The skill to hit the side of the headpin 12 times. The luck to have all the pins fall every time and not leave a pin wobbling in the corner.

“The first time I had nine strikes in a row I was 20 years old, and I got the perfect game,” says Geoff Born, another national champion five-pin bowler in Winnipeg. He’s thrown the first nine strikes nearly a dozen times since then, but never had a second perfect game.

“I’m still trying,” he says. “I’m 63 now, so that’s 43 years.”

Logan has been particularly inspired by the women bowlers in his life, especially his mother and grandmother. He’d also spent the year bowling with a woman named Sandi Anderson, who he’d invited to join his Monday night league team, because he admired how she seemed to be able to handle the pressure and throw a strike whenever she needed one.

“A perfect game doesn’t sound that crazy because it’s just right down the middle every time,” Logan says. “But of course, it’s mental as well.”

Sandi had taught him the value of the routine, the discipline of doing the exact same thing. The same shot over and over again.

“It goes into your head, so just being cool and collected,” he says. “Especially as a teenager, it can be hard to do sometimes, but just learning from how she did it and my mom did it, just trying to go back to a routine.”

Going into his 11th ball, Logan wasn’t paying much attention to what was happening around him.

He didn’t fully notice how many people were crowded in, couldn’t hear the shouting and clapping, didn’t see the phones recording. He was paying attention only to his teammate and his dad, trying to stay calm and keep the moment light. They had a running joke about a perfect game, and here it was, within reach.

The 10th strike put Logan over 400 points for the first time in his life, and secured him a pot of money for a scholarship. After that, he told himself he’d be happy, no matter what. His grandfather had rolled two perfect games, but his parents and grandmother never had, despite being excellent national-level bowlers.

His mother always told him, “You can’t get frustrated or get super upset, as long as you do what you can to the top of your abilities. That’s all you can hope for, right? You can get a bad break. You can’t control where a pin is going to fly. And of course, there’s going to be some days where you get a little lucky.”

And some days when you don’t.

Last year, after a competition in Calgary, Logan spent months thinking about whether he wanted to continue competitive bowling at all, or whether he should focus on his baseball. But he started practising again.

He sent the 11th ball hurtling down the lane. Another strike.

He just needed one more.

But where was his ball? It wasn’t sliding out of the ball return. Logan and his dad gestured to Dakota Lanes’ staff that the ball was caught. People in the crowd anxiously called “Ball!” to get the game moving again.

Logan wondered if he should use another ball. He didn’t want to change the rhythm of the game. His dad stopped him.

“No, no, no. You’ve been using that ball. Wait until the ball’s back,” he said. “The ball isn’t ready to be bowled yet.”

When it was ready to be bowled, Logan’s ball came rolling back to where he waited on Lane 15. Now it was time. Rinse and repeat, his father told him. Just keep doing the same thing. Don’t get in your head about it. It’s just one more strike.

People clapped and called out.

“Your time buddy, your time.”

Walk up, grab the ball. Keep everything the same. Logan’s hands were getting sweaty. He picked up his ball and wiped it with a towel. Don’t chuck it in the gutter. Don’t faceplant on the lane.

Logan found his spot on the approach and slid one foot back and forth, feeling its slip beneath his shoe. He wore a bright yellow and black shirt, with his name in sprawling script across the back.

Then three steps, left, right, left, slide. Quick and smooth. Arm straight back, reaching straight through to release the ball. Exactly how his grandma told him to do it when he was a kid, exactly how he’d been trying to do it ever since.

It felt good the moment it left his hand.

Logan dropped down to one knee and watched as his ball rolled down the lane, straight and true. Everyone was screaming before it even hit the pins.

paragraphs: The manager was busy and distracted when one of his employees tapped him on the shoulder. It was the second day of the national youth five-pin bowling championships at Dakota Lanes in Winnipeg, and the place was alive with the thud of balls and clatter of pins.
“Hey,” the kid said. Something in his voice caught his boss’s attention. “We’re going for perfection over here.”
Justin Keen looked over to where 17-year-old Logan Newton stood surrounded by a gathering crowd.
Five, six, seven strikes in a row – that happened at Dakota Lanes with some frequency. Impressive, but not uncommon for competitive bowlers.
Eight strikes was different.
And at nine strikes, word was burning through the alley: Logan Newton is going for a perfect game.

Other lanes grew quiet as people left their games to watch. Even as a spectator, Justin was trembling and nervous. He’d been bowling his whole life, and he knew how rare and difficult it was to bowl 12 strikes in a row – how overwhelming the mounting pressure could be.
“I’m sitting back here thinking, ‘Is he okay? Is he going to break down?’” Justin says. “Some people, the emotions can overrun you. You never know what’s going to happen.”
Logan Newton had thrown nine strikes in a row.
Just three more strikes to a perfect game.
If you aren’t a bowler, what you May be picturing right now – dense pyramid of pins, finger holes drilled into a big black ball – isn’t what we’re talking about. That’s 10-pin, and it’s American.
Five-pin bowling is our sport. Invented, played and loved almost exclusively in Canada.

Five-pin bowling uses smaller balls and pins, broader spacing and a different score structure. It was invented by flamboyant Toronto sportsman (and pageant judge) Tommy Ryan, who introduced it at his swank Toronto Bowling Club in 1909 after deciding 10-pin bowling was “too slow and uninteresting.”

Perfect games are common in 10-pin. The ball is so big, there are so many pins clustered so closely together. The United States Bowling Congress estimates tens of thousands of perfect 10-pin games rolled every year, with the odds of an average bowler throwing a perfect game in league play about one in 11,500.
Meanwhile, a champion five-pin bowler could go their whole lives without a perfect game. The Canadian 5 Pin Bowlers’ Association records about a dozen a year.

“I’ve won everything. I’ve won TSN. I’ve won CBC. I won over $100,000, but I’ve never thrown a perfect game,” says Cameron Boon, with a rueful chuckle. He’s a veteran Manitoba bowler who also owns and runs Polo Park Bowling Centre in Winnipeg with his brother.
“It’s got to be 99 per cent will never throw a perfect game in their life.”
In 62 years and a quarter-million matches, there had only ever been one perfect game in Youth Bowl Canada’s national competition, thrown by 16-year-old Jenna Lamoureux in Calgary a decade ago.

But on this spring afternoon in Winnipeg, Erin Newton saw clearly how it could happen. Logan was throwing every ball in the same spot with the same momentum and the same pace and the same movement. Everything was just there.
It was around Logan’s ninth strike of the game that Erin realized he had a real chance.
“Oh my goodness,” she thought. “This could happen.”
It was, perhaps, inevitable that Logan Newton would end up at that place, ON that day, with all those strikes. In a way, you could say his whole life had been leading to such a moment.

His grandparents met bowling, and his family has been bowling ever since. His grandfather was a national level bowler, his grandmother and mother have both competed and won at national competitions, and he and his brothers grew up at Rossmere Lanes, the Winnipeg bowling centre owned by their father, Jamie Newton, who is also an accomplished bowler and Logan’s coach.
“When dad’s at work, what do you do?” Logan says. “Chuck balls.”

The popularity of five-pin bowling has ebbed and flowed through the years. It’s been threatened both by changing social habits and by the pervasive influence of 10-pin, an easier and in some ways more dramatic game (all those pins flying!), which is the dominant form of bowling around the world.

But competitive five-pin bowling has a dedicated and tight-knit community around Canada. New players are drawn by a game that’s accessible to almost anyone of any age and ability, but also challenging enough to keep the attention of competitive players for decades.

Part of the challenge of five-pin bowling is that, ON paper, it should be easy. The external variables are relatively minor, with only slight variations to account for in the slickness of the lane, the ball, the shoes. In theory, all you have to do to get a strike is roll the ball straight down the lane and hit the headpin slightly off-centre.
And yet, as anyone who has attempted to do that, and instead seen their ball careen into the gutter, knows, it isn’t even close to that simple.
And that’s just one strike.

Throwing 12 strikes in a row is a matter of skill and luck combined: The skill to hit the side of the headpin 12 times. The luck to have all the pins fall every time and not leave a pin wobbling in the corner.

“The first time I had nine strikes in a row I was 20 years old, and I got the perfect game,” says Geoff Born, another national champion five-pin bowler in Winnipeg. He’s thrown the first nine strikes nearly a dozen times since then, but never had a second perfect game.
“I’m still trying,” he says. “I’m 63 now, so that’s 43 years.”

Logan has been particularly inspired by the women bowlers in his life, especially his mother and grandmother. He’d also spent the year bowling with a woman named Sandi Anderson, who he’d invited to join his Monday night league team, because he admired how she seemed to be able to handle the pressure and throw a strike whenever she needed one.
“A perfect game doesn’t sound that crazy because it’s just right down the middle every time,” Logan says. “But of course, it’s mental as well.”
Sandi had taught him the value of the routine, the discipline of doing the exact same thing. The same shot over and over again.

“It goes into your head, so just being cool and collected,” he says. “Especially as a teenager, it can be hard to do sometimes, but just learning from how she did it and my mom did it, just trying to go back to a routine.”
Going into his 11th ball, Logan wasn’t paying much attention to what was happening around him.

He didn’t fully notice how many people were crowded in, couldn’t hear the shouting and clapping, didn’t see the phones recording. He was paying attention only to his teammate and his dad, trying to stay calm and keep the moment light. They had a running joke about a perfect game, and here it was, within reach.

The 10th strike put Logan over 400 points for the first time in his life, and secured him a pot of money for a scholarship. After that, he told himself he’d be happy, no matter what. His grandfather had rolled two perfect games, but his parents and grandmother never had, despite being excellent national-level bowlers.

His mother always told him, “You can’t get frustrated or get super upset, as long as you do what you can to the top of your abilities. That’s all you can hope for, right? You can get a bad break. You can’t control where a pin is going to fly. And of course, there’s going to be some days where you get a little lucky.”
And some days when you don’t.

Last year, after a competition in Calgary, Logan spent months thinking about whether he wanted to continue competitive bowling at all, or whether he should focus on his baseball. But he started practising again.
He sent the 11th ball hurtling down the lane. Another strike.
He just needed one more.

But where was his ball? It wasn’t sliding out of the ball return. Logan and his dad gestured to Dakota Lanes’ staff that the ball was caught. People in the crowd anxiously called “Ball!” to get the game moving again.
Logan wondered if he should use another ball. He didn’t want to change the rhythm of the game. His dad stopped him.
“No, no, no. You’ve been using that ball. Wait until the ball’s back,” he said. “The ball isn’t ready to be bowled yet.”

When it was ready to be bowled, Logan’s ball came rolling back to where he waited on Lane 15. Now it was time. Rinse and repeat, his father told him. Just keep doing the same thing. Don’t get in your head about it. It’s just one more strike.
People clapped and called out.
“Your time buddy, your time.”

Logan found his spot on the approach and slid one foot back and forth, feeling its slip beneath his shoe. He wore a bright yellow and black shirt, with his name in sprawling script across the back.

Then three steps, left, right, left, slide. Quick and smooth. Arm straight back, reaching straight through to release the ball. Exactly how his grandma told him to do it when he was a kid, exactly how he’d been trying to do it ever since.
It felt good the moment it left his hand.
Logan dropped down to one knee and watched as his ball rolled down the lane, straight and true. Everyone was screaming before it even hit the pins.

stories.title: A beginner’s guide to reading Ben Macintyre
stories.summary: Here are eight routes into the author’s world of spies, swindlers, escapes and betrayals
stories.author: Emily Donaldson
stories.content:
Join The Globe and Mail for an evening with author Ben Macintyre as he discusses his latest book, Redwood, with former Ottawa Bureau Chief Bob Fife, and books editor Judith Pereira, ON Oct. 5 in Toronto. Visit tgam.CA/macintyre for more.

Ben Macintyre belongs to a generation of narrative non-fiction writers, among them Patrick Radden Keefe, David Grann and John Vaillant, who’ve made a specialty of harnessing the machinery of thrillers and novels to exhaustively researched true stories. They take the raw materials of non-fiction – archives, interviews, historical records – and alchemize them into compulsive reading.

Macintyre’s subjects of choice are spies, double agents, con men and other masters-of-deception types, most often operating in the shadow worlds of the Second World War and the Cold War. People who put their lives on the line for country, profit or, in the case of his newest book, Redwood , a cure for erectile dysfunction. The stories have proved remarkably adaptable: Three of his books have been turned into films or television dramas, while several others have inspired documentaries.

My own portal into Macintyre’s work was The Spy and the Traitor , his riveting account of Oleg Gordievsky, the KGB officer who became one of Britain’s most valuable Cold War agents. First love being the most indelible, it’s still the book I’d recommend first.

Espionage May not run in Macintyre’s family (though he likely wouldn’t tell us if it did) but the British establishment certainly does. Born in Oxford in 1963 into a well-connected academic family, Macintyre, a long-time columnist and associate editor at the London Times, is the son of an Oxford historian and descended on both sides from minor British aristocracy. (For his own history degree, he ventured to Cambridge.) In person, however, he is strikingly free of any establishment hauteur: open, affable and unguarded.

For readers coming to Macintyre for the first time – or wondering where to venture next – here are eight routes into his world of spies, swindlers, escapes and betrayals.

For one Soviet spy, the Cold War proved a little too cold: In Macintyre’s timely, page-turning latest, the fate of nations turns, improbably, ON a man’s sex life – or lack thereof. In 1981, KGB major Vladimir Kuzichkin, stationed in Iran in the turbulent aftermath of the 1979 revolution, approached British intelligence with a proposition: He would trade his country’s secrets for help with one of his own.

Kuzichkin was suffering from erectile dysfunction, which he was convinced Western medicine could cure (it couldn’t, the golden age of Viagra having not yet dawned). MI6 gave the 6-foot-4 Russian the codename Redwood, after the tree. (It took some time before anyone twigged to the unintentional joke: RED for communist, Wood for what eluded Kuzichkin.)

MI6 officer Ian McCredie became his handler, and the bond between the two is at the heart of the book. Kuzichkin supplied intelligence about Soviet activities and Iran’s communist Tudeh Party. When the KGB, which had begun to suspect Kuzichkin, summoned him back to Moscow, MI6 was forced to engineer an escape from Iran.

The intel Kuzichkin provided was ultimately handed to the Iranian regime, contributing to a brutal purge of communists and helping strengthen a government the West would come to regard as an enemy. Macintyre is particularly good on that bitter irony: an intelligence triumph whose unintended consequences are still being felt.

Operation Mincemeat

Had Ocean’s Eleven been set in wartime Whitehall, it might have looked something like Operation Mincemeat.

In 1943, with the Allies preparing to invade Sicily, British intelligence devised an audacious plan to convince Hitler that the Allies’ real targets were Greece and Sardinia. The scheme required a corpse, dressed as a fictitious Royal Marine named William Martin and equipped with an entire invented life, including a briefcase containing false military documents. The body was then deposited off the coast of Spain in the hope that the papers would find their way into German hands.

Revelling, as do we, in both the ingenuity and absurdity of the operation, Macintyre introduces an eccentric cast of intelligence officers, scientists, secretaries and others who helped make the imaginary major Martin convincing. Mincemeat has all the pleasures of a great caper: watching an outlandish ruse assembled piece by piece, knowing that thousands of lives May depend on whether the mark takes the bait.

Macintyre gravitates to real-life characters who seem too improbable for fiction, and few are more improbable than Ursula Kuczynski.

Born into a well-to-do Jewish family in Berlin in 1907, Kuczynski was a committed Communist by her teens. Her espionage career began in Shanghai – where she was recruited by legendary Soviet spy Richard Sorge – and would take her through China, Japanese-occupied Manchuria, Poland and Switzerland before she finally landed in Britain in 1941. Code-named Sonya, she became a colonel in Soviet military intelligence while raising three children. (Who says women can’t have it all?)

Her greatest coup took place in an Oxfordshire village, where, under cover as an unassuming housewife and mother, she handled Klaus Fuchs, the German-born British physicist who passed atomic secrets to Moscow. MI5 came close to outing her but was hampered, Macintyre suggests, by an inability to imagine – and really who would? – that a mum baking cakes in the English countryside might also be a formidable Soviet spy.

Colditz: Prisoners of the Castle

In 1940, the Nazis began using Colditz Castle – a forbidding, supposedly escape-proof gothic fortress perched above the eastern German town of the same name – to hold Allied officers who’d proved particularly troublesome, or particularly adept at escaping from other prisoner-of-war camps.

The castle immediately became a hothouse of ingenuity and sheer bloody-mindedness. Prisoners tunnelled, scaled walls, impersonated German officers and dreamed up increasingly elaborate routes to freedom. One group of British inmates secretly built a two-man glider in the castle attic.

The thrills are in the escapes themselves, of course, but the richer story is arguably what happened when hundreds of men from different nations and classes were locked up together for years. Macintyre presents Colditz as a society in miniature, with its own hierarchies, rivalries, prejudices, alliances and divisions among prisoners and captors alike – complicating the familiar Great Escape image of plucky officers united against their Nazi captors.

The Spy and the Traitor

Perhaps no Macintyre book makes the case for non-fiction as thriller quite as forcefully as this one.

Oleg Gordievsky was a rising KGB officer who, increasingly disillusioned with the Soviet system, began secretly working for MI6 in the 1970s. Over the next decade he supplied the British with a stream of intelligence from inside the KGB, eventually becoming acting head of the Kgb’s London station.

In 1985, however, Gordievsky was abruptly summoned back to Moscow, where he realized he had been betrayed and was under surveillance. What follows is the book’s nail-biting set piece: an elaborate MI6 operation to smuggle him across the Soviet border in the trunk of a car. Macintyre reconstructs the escape almost minute by minute, turning border guards, a bag of cheese-and-onion potato chips and a soiled diaper into instruments of almost unbearable suspense.

The Napoleon of Crime

Published in 1997, Macintyre’s second book predates his focus on espionage but shows that many of his other preoccupations were already in place.

Adam Worth was a German-born American bank robber, art thief and criminal mastermind who made his name in late 19th-century London, moving fluidly between respectable society and the underworld and becoming a prototype of the gentleman thief.

He amassed a fortune, travelled the Mediterranean on his own yacht and orchestrated crimes across Europe and America, all while cultivating a strict personal code: He abhorred violence, was fiercely loyal to his accomplices and kept his criminal life secret from his family.

His most famous exploit was the 1876 theft of Gainsborough’s portrait of Georgiana, Duchess of Devonshire, originally intended as leverage to free his imprisoned brother. When his brother was released without it, Worth kept the now virtually unsaleable painting hidden for the next quarter-century, apparently developing a deep attachment to it.

Macintyre tells Worth’s story as both a Victorian criminal adventure and a character study, finding in his double life the kind of divided loyalties and carefully constructed identities that would later animate his spy books. An inspiration for Arthur Conan Doyle’s professor Moriarty, Worth made and lost fortunes over a spectacular criminal career, only to die penniless.

A Spy Among Friends

Kim Philby wasn’t merely one of the most damaging Soviet spies ever to penetrate British intelligence, he was also exceptionally good at inspiring trust. A member of the Cambridge spy ring, Philby spent decades passing British and American secrets to Moscow while rising through the ranks of MI6.

Macintyre brings a fresh eye to one of the best-known tales of espionage and betrayal by telling it largely through Philby’s friendship with fellow intelligence officer Nicholas Elliott, a product of the same privileged world of public schools, clubs and old-boy networks.

That intimacy gave Philby’s deception its particular sting, while exposing a vulnerability of the British establishment: a system in which class, charm and the connections could make a certain sort of chap seem inherently trustworthy.

When suspicion finally hardened around him, Philby fled to Moscow in 1963. Part of Macintyre’s achievement is making the reader understand not just how he got away with it for so long, but why his friends found it so difficult to believe the truth.

A perfect entry point to Macintyre’s fascination with morally slippery characters, Agent Zigzag tells the story of Eddie Chapman, an English safecracker, conman and inveterate charmer with a taste for fast cars, gambling and other people’s money.

Imprisoned on Jersey when the Germans invaded and occupied the Channel Islands in 1940, Chapman, who knew an opportunity when he saw one, volunteered his services to German intelligence. The Nazis trained him in espionage and parachuted him into Britain with orders to blow up an aircraft factory. Upon landing, he promptly turned himself over to MI5, becoming a double agent codenamed Zigzag.

Chapman was brave, reckless, chronically unfaithful and noticeably unburdened by principle, leaving those around him wondering precisely what his motivations were. That moral elasticity is the engine of Macintyre’s book, and the result is part spy thriller, part picaresque: a story of fake sabotage, imminent danger, a rotating cast of girlfriends and an incorrigible crook who discovered in wartime espionage the one career for which his specific array of talents amounted to a qualification.
