stories.title: 'You are going to die for the Jews,' said Belleville shooting suspect: police
stories.summary: The 29-year-old suspect had the "means, the mechanism and the motive" to launch a larger attack.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The attack was an 'exclusive threat to our Jewish community,' said Belleville police chief

The suspect in the synagogue attack in Belleville, Ont., shouted “You are going to die for the Jews” before an exchange of gunfire with police, according to a video played at a police press conference Thursday.

Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said it was a hate-motivated crime and that 29-year-old Sean Ward had the “means, the motive and the mechanisms” to launch a larger attack.

“The loss of life and the irreversible damage that could have been rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated,” he said.

This is the Disturbing antisemitic terror attack and hate crime outside the Sons of Jacob in Belleville on Yom Kippur. pic.twitter.com/Mr8MA2finK — Joe Warmington (@joe_warmington) September 24, 2026

Although he said he could not go into more detail, the evidence collected shows Ward’s intent was to specifically target the Jewish community.

The attack was an “exclusive threat to our Jewish community,” said Rodd.

He shared the seconds-long video in which a man can be heard yelling, followed by the sound of two loud shots outside of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue just after 7 p.m. on Sunday. Inside the synagogue about 25 people were gathered for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. None were injured.

Rodd said Ward used a shotgun and had other resources available, including gasoline, and a “significant amount” of ammunition on him. Earlier that day, Ward was doing reconnaissance near the synagogue, according to the chief. Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed there for the evening service, saw the suspect but did not see him do anything suspicious.

“He was then ambushed on a second pass. That’s when the shooting started,” Rodd said.

He said Ward was only stopped by Smith and a second officer, identified as Const. Mike McCurdy, who arrived at the scene a little more than two minutes after the gunman opened fire.

Smith was shot in his vehicle but managed to get out and pursue the gunman.

Ward was shot and fatally injured. He died in hospital on Monday.

Smith was taken to hospital in critical condition. He sustained “multiple gunshot wounds to his head and his body, and continues to receive treatment for significant injuries,” said Rodd.

“He is expected to undergo multiple surgeries related to serious head trauma. While his recovery will be lengthy and challenging, he is making progress every day.”

McCurdy was not injured.

The police chief called both officers heroes.

Insp. Christine Belair of the RCMP’s Integrated National Enforcement Team could not confirm if Ward had been radicalized while serving in the military. The Department of National Defence told National Post that a man with the same name as Ward served in the Canadian Armed Forces for five years, starting in 2017.

There have also been reports that Ward was released from service due to his refusal to get a COVID-19 vaccine, according to Global News and The Globe and Mail. Belair could not confirm.

Ward was from Quinte West, a small city 18 kilometres west of Belleville.

Ontario Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, who was also at Thursday’s press conference, said as a proud Jewish person he takes the events of the last few days to heart.

“It’s one thing to say hate has no place here in our province and in our country, but we already know that. We have to go further and faster,” he said.

According to the Belleville police chief, the force has a lengthy relationship with the local Jewish community and has provided security “whenever they considered it necessary.”

“I guess one of the messages to my colleagues around the province and the country is it is clearly time that we all be proactive,” Rodd said.

stories.title: Carney prepared for risk that Trump might order U.S. to invade Canada. Expert says it's a valid concern
stories.summary: The prime minister had several talking points in his interview with the New York Times. But invasion was the one that stood out.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney touched on a wide range of topics during an hour-long interview with the New York Times yesterday — F-35 jets, Starlink satellites, trade in potash and automobiles and more — but the biggest takeaway was that he had prepared over the past year for the “extreme tail risk” that U.S. President Donald Trump might order military action against Canada.

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” said Carney, using a term from the financial world that was his metier as a former central banker for Britain and Canada. “That’s just risk management … it would be irresponsible not to.”

The expression refers to a scenario that is considered unlikely but not impossible — the “tail” of a probability curve where the centre represents the most likely outcomes.

Carney told the Times that, based on Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state, he had carefully examined the possibility of U.S.-led military action, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

Timothy Sayle, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s comments indicate a valid concern.

“It makes sense to me that it’s at the real extreme end of possibilities, but I don’t think it’s a zero per cent chance,” he told National Post.

The U.S. incursion into Venezuela this year and its threats against Greenland made its allies, including Canada and Europe, take notice, Sayle said.

“It can seem outlandish, but … the United States has made these decisions to enter Venezuela and then to attack Iran that were pretty low-probability events, and yet they did happen. So that’s why I can understand the prime minister’s point that it’s maybe very very very low risk but, as he said, can’t be totally ignored.”

As to what form a potential invasion might take, Sayle said the “wild unpredictability of the current American administration” made it difficult to predict, but he imagined several small-scale scenarios. They included “some sort of hot pursuit of a suspected criminal, or somebody that ICE was seeking, across the Canadian border.”

He added: “You could imagine an increase of U.S. forces, like the strengthening of U.S. forces in Canada in some way.” (According to the U.S. Department of Defense , as of March there were 159 active duty military personnel serving in Canada, plus 33 civilian DoD staff.)

Sayle also suggested “the presence of naval ships, the presence of or overflights by aircraft and … what could be described as something in the shared interest, but in which Canada was not consulted in the usual means. Americans could either publicly or invisibly flex their might and indicate that Canada’s sovereignty wasn’t quite as secure as we’d like to think.”

The notion has been ridiculed at high levels. This month, when a Canadian reporter asked Admiral Samuel J. Paparo, commander of the U.S. Pacific Command, about the possibility of military action against Canada, he was met with incredulity. Paparo called it “preposterous” and added: “Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?”

The expression refers to a scenario that is considered unlikely but not impossible — the “tail” of a probability curve where the centre represents the most likely outcomes.

Carney told the Times that, based on Trump’s threats to make Canada a 51st state, he had carefully examined the possibility of U.S.-led military action, but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.
Timothy Sayle, a professor at the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto, said Carney’s comments indicate a valid concern.
“It makes sense to me that it’s at the real extreme end of possibilities, but I don’t think it’s a zero per cent chance,” he told National Post.
The U.S. incursion into Venezuela this year and its threats against Greenland made its allies, including Canada and Europe, take notice, Sayle said.

stories.title: Going to the movies does more than entertain me – it helps shape who I am
stories.summary: Movies have always been an essential part of my life. It’s how I learned English when my family immigrated from Lithuania
stories.author: Ema Brazdeikyte
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

I cling to my jacket tighter, somehow believing the tighter I hold onto it, the less cold I’ll feel. With my head down, I push forward, imagining I’m dodging the wind, as I make my way toward the theatre on a cold night.

Entering the building, I’m relieved. It’s warm and it smells like hot, buttered popcorn. Still, even with some modern updates, I feel as though I’m transported back to the early 2000s every time I go to the movie theatre and that also makes me relieved. My phone is immediately put on “do not disturb” and then it doesn’t exist.

I get there early. I always get there early so I can watch the trailers, even though I’ve seen more than half of them before.

There’s chatter and laughter as people make their way to their seats. I’m by myself, which means I eavesdrop. Has anyone struck a conversation with a random moviegoer before?

The lights dim and the premovie chatter dies down until silence envelops the room. It feels for a moment in time like we can be somewhere different, someone different, and that, to me, is the magic of cinema. I never liked a crowded theatre but over time I began to appreciate the camaraderie that comes with being in a room full of strangers. The jumps or gasps or laughs in unison. We’ve never met and yet, here we are, sharing a moment of joy or sadness or fear.

Contemplating my autumn garden offers moments of self-reflection

I often go to the movies with family and friends but recently I’ve also started going by myself. And although I miss the postmovie discussions where we eagerly share what we’ve been thinking the entire time and what we liked or didn’t, I also don’t mind a silent reflection from time to time.

Movies have always been, and remain, an essential part of my life. It’s how I learned English when my family immigrated from Lithuania to the United States and then eventually to Canada. And although I do believe my ESL classes helped, I give most of the credit to watching movies. Once or twice a week, my dad would take my brother and me to Blockbuster. I remember how excited we’d be to go and explore the endless aisles of VHS tapes. Everywhere we looked was another adventure, another lesson. It quickly wove itself into a family night tradition in our home. Watching a movie for us went beyond simply evoking a deep sense of emotion. It also served as a gateway into exploring a different language and culture altogether. In many ways, it helped us navigate the new countries we found ourselves trying to call home.

And wherever we moved, friends changed, neighbourhoods changed, communities changed – but movies stayed constant. It was always important to find a video rental store nearby and a movie theatre.

My love for movies has only grown over the years. When I find one that’s painfully relatable or I see myself in one of the characters or I leave questioning my entire life and the world around me, it feels like striking gold. Finally, something I can think about for the rest of my life! Of course, I’m no expert, and some of my favourites are comedies dismally rated by critics on Rotten Tomatoes (but who really judges a movie based on what critics think?).

Our lives keep expanding, but my pen pal and I still make room for each other

I believe whether or not we connect with a movie is an entirely subjective and personal experience – shaped by mood, interests and stages of life. That’s why there are always wildly different opinions and reviews.

And maybe this all sounds excessive but it’s how I learned a language, it’s what constantly leaves me inspired and, ultimately, it has helped shape who I am and what I like.

The screen fades to black and the credits start rolling. The chatter begins again as people sling on their jackets and make their way out. I listen to their first impressions and find myself smiling along. It was a work of art. And I leave the theatre floating on air, as I always do.

Ema Brazdeikyte lives in Toronto.

Ema Brazdeikyte lives in Toronto.

stories.title: First-time buyers should still prepare for the ‘Wild, Wild West’ entering today’s housing market
stories.summary: Buyer expectations and seller memories of boom days have created a disconnect
stories.author: Mariya Postelnyak
stories.content:
I’ve recently embarked on a rite of passage for millennials in Toronto. For the first time, my partner and I cautiously dipped our toes into the housing market to check the temperature.

Like many before us, we quickly pulled them right back out.

We encountered AI-generated listing photos covering up surprise gut jobs, a lineup of properties with tenants and listing prices far below what the owner was actually likely to accept.

What made the experience more frustrating was that we went into our search amid signals of a more welcoming climate for buyers. Home prices have plummeted by an average of $176,600 across Canada since the 2022 peak, with drops averaging $353,900 for Toronto (and as high as $529,100 for Oakville).

“We are seeing condos selling for, or below, 2017 values at this point,” Toronto realtor Anya Ettinger told me.

But in large swaths of the market, “there’s still a big disconnect between a buyer’s willingness to pay versus the seller’s expectation of value.”

Much like the ghosts in The Five People You Meet in Heaven who teach Mitch Albom’s protagonist lessons about life, Ms. Ettinger has identified three scenarios that offer lessons to first-time buyers in the housing market this fall.

The first involves owners who list properties well below what they actually expect to get. It’s a phenomenon well known to Toronto buyers scouring the heated market in the past, but more surprising given the rumours of a chill in prices.

Buyers still regularly pay not just tens of thousands but $100,000 or more above asking for properties in high-demand areas such as Riverdale and the Beaches in Toronto’s east end and Little Portugal in the West, especially as workers return to their downtown offices.

The second type of listing involves properties with tenants and fixer-uppers where prices can still be negotiated, Ms. Ettinger said. For those uninterested in becoming landlords, homes with an existing renter present the risk of dealing with a tenant who doesn’t want to move out despite being served legal notice.

The third, and most noticeable category as of late, is what Ms. Ettinger dubs “the Wild, Wild West.”

This is when a pricing strategy shows “absolutely no rhyme or reason,” she said.

Brokerage notes on one recent listing simply said “seller unmotivated, price not flexible” Ms. Ettinger recalled. In another case, a house had been sitting for 180 days, in “terrible condition,“ with the seller expecting well above asking.

Ms. Ettinger attributes some of the disconnect to memories of the boom days. “A lot of people maybe saw that really high number back in 2022 and have held on to that,” she said.

She blames a narrative that has been ingrained in peoples’ minds: “You buy real estate in Toronto, you will make money,” Ms. Ettinger said.

Now, some are confronting the possibility of not recouping even what they paid.

The lesson for first-time buyers is the need to challenge their idea of a starter home, and accept that a house is no longer automatically a short, or even medium-term, financial bet.

“We got used to an era for upwards of a decade where there was consistent appreciation,” Ms. Ettinger said. “That’s not a guarantee any more.”

Do you have lessons of your own from a recent home search, or a first-home search? Drop me a line at mpostelnyak@globeandmail.com

stories.title: A list of the whales and dolphin that died after being moved out of Marineland
stories.summary: Another beluga, Beethoven, lived at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, but died after the move.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Four beluga whales and one dolphin that were shipped out of Marineland this summer have since died at their new homes. Another beluga, Beethoven, lived at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago, but died after the move.

Here is the list of the animals who died:

– Female beluga, age 23

– Caught in Russian waters and sent to Marineland in 2003

– Moved to Shedd Aquarium on Aug. 12, 2026

– Died on Aug. 25, 2026

– Female beluga, age 20

– Caught in Russian waters and sent to Marineland in 2006

– Died on Sept. 2, 2026.

– Female beluga, age 19

– Born at Marineland in 2007

– Moved to Oceanografic Valencia, in Spain, on Aug. 26, 2026

– Died on Sept. 18, 2026

– Female beluga, age 26

– Caught in Russian waters and sent to Marineland in 2001

– Moved to Shedd Aquarium on July 20, 2026

– Died on Sept. 21, 2026

– Female dolphin, believed to be 30 years old

– Caught in the Black Sea and sent to Marineland around 2000

– Moved to Oceanografic Valencia on Aug. 26, 2026

– Died on Sept. 23, 2026

stories.title: Child murders report says Canada's courts are prioritizing 'parental contact' over safety
stories.summary: A proposed change to the Divorce Act would prohibit courts from considering 'parental alienation' when one parent accuses the other of abuse
stories.author: Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
One April morning in 2019, paramedics called to a Granby, Que., house found a malnourished seven-year-old girl without vital signs wrapped in layers of adhesive tape, including over her head, obstructing her airways. Her father had helped restrain her before leaving her with her stepmother, who bound her with packing tape, a Quebec corner would later conclude in the case that became known as the “Granby Girl.”

Ten months later, in February 2020, four-year-old Keira Kagan’s body was discovered, alongside that of her 35-year-old father’s, at the base of a 30-metre cliff in a conservation park outside Toronto. It had been the father’s scheduled weekend visit. The child and father were found after he failed to respond to his ex-wife’s calls and text messages.

The horrific and heartbreaking deaths, as well as those of six other victims of “fillicide,” the deliberate killing of a child by a parent, are reconstructed in a new paper linking a “pro-contact culture” and accusations of “parental alienation” to the murders of the eight children in five families in Ontario and Quebec.

The authors say their findings back a controversial private member’s bill now before Parliament.

Introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, the bill proposes to amend the Divorce Act to prohibit courts from considering evidence that one parent in a high-conflict custody case is actively trying to “alienate” the other parent and manipulating and coaching the child to resist contact.

It would also prevent judges from restricting a child’s time with one parent “to whom the child has a close connection” to improve the relationship with the other parent, and it would prevent courts from forcing children to attend so-called “reunification therapy.”

The proposed legislation has passed second reading, and is now before the justice and human rights committee.

Proponents say that in cases involving allegations of domestic violence, alienation claims are being weaponized and used as a legal tactic by parents — mostly fathers accused of abuse — to discredit the other parent.

If a parent — most often mothers — insist a child is in danger, “they run the risk of being perceived as an uncooperative, alienating parent,” the authors said.

The court’s attention shifts away from potential violence “towards preserving the parental bond.”<

Alienation claims “are systematically used as a litigation strategy to deflect attention from abuse, undermine the child’s disclosure of fear and portray a protective mother as hostile, irrational or manipulative,” Suzanne Zaccour, director of legal affairs at the National Association of Women and the Law, or Nawl, and a co-author of the research paper, said at a press conference on Parliament Hill Thursday.

“Rather than asking why a child is frightened or resistant to contact, the system can wrongly assume the child has been influenced or brainwashed.”

Even when there is documented family violence or other concerns, in a pro-contact culture “a father-child relationship can be treated as the overriding goal,” Zaccour said.

The proposed bill — Keeping Children Safe — says that a court “shall not take into consideration” any allegation that one parent has deliberately encouraged a child to become estranged from the other. Judges would not be permitted to order “reunification therapy” or, in extreme cases, reverse custody.

Opponents say ignoring all claims of alienation will harm children. “The legislation reflects a profound distrust of the Canadian family justice system,” said Queen’s University law professor Nicholas Bala, an internationally recognized expert on family and children’s law.

“As tragic and concerning as child homicides are, and they have to be dealt with more effectively, the legislation does not address that issue in a meaningful way” and risks exploiting child murders that aren’t related to alienation, Bala said.

While fathers kill disproportionately more children than mothers, most child homicides involve cases where child protection services failed children, he said, “which is tragic.”

And the bill, Bala said, “doesn’t deal with the child protection system at all.”

In Canada, parents have a presumptive right to have a relationship with their children. “There are cases where children are being abused or treated poorly by parents on their visits, and there are good reasons for the child not to see the other parent,” he said.

He supports amendments that would require lawyers to screen for the risk of family violence, and allow courts to interview children . But the bill would also prevent lawyers from presenting evidence that one, or both parents, are acting to undermine the child’s relationship with the other, which Bala said is occurring in an increasing number of cases.

His research shows that judges reject more than half of alienation claims. In more than one-third of cases where the court finds alienation, it’s the mother who has been alienated from her children by an abusive husband.

“It’s very unfair, and very contra in the interests of the children, to decide cases on an absolute rule that says, ‘We can never hear this evidence,'” Bala said. Each case should be decided based on the best interests of the particular child, he said.

“There are some people, a very small number who, in the midst of a custody battle, are so unbalanced they decide to kill their children. That’s a terrible tragedy,” Bala said.

“The issue of parents killing their children is a huge concern” but the proposed bill is not the appropriate response, he said.<

Nawl, which pushed for the proposed legislation, teamed up with professors from University of Sherbrooke’s faculty of law as part of a broader project supported by the federal Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.

In all five cases, the deaths were foreshadowed by warnings that were downplayed or dismissed by family courts or child protection services, according to the authors.

“Their fathers were known to systems in charge of protecting children” and women (in one case, a paternal grandmother) who raised concerns were disbelieved “and even framed as the problem, in part through institutions adopting the controversial framework of ‘parental alienation.'”

The paper isn’t a random sample of child homicides. Rather, the cases were selected based on three criteria: the murders occurred during custody disputes, institutions such as police, child protection services and family courts had intervened before the child’s death and enough public information (coroner’s reports, published court decisions, media sources) was available to reconstruct what happened.

It’s not an attempt to be representative, but the findings are consistent with child murders in other countries, the authors said. The details were edited to be less graphic. “But the level of violence and betrayal on the children” is evident, Zaccour said.

Several cases are anonymized to protect the identity of the children. In three of five cases, children were killed within days of a scheduled court hearing, according to the report — in one case, two days after a mother asked her lawyer about seeking sole custody, fearing for the safety of her two boys, aged two and five. Their father killed them both.

“We can’t speculate, but perhaps the father knew he might lose custody,” said Zaccour, co-author of the report.

“If you think, nothing can be done and there are these crazy individuals who will just lash out and kill their children, what can we do? There were years of documentation of the risk in some cases before death.”

While the five deaths date back to 2011, new cases occurred as they were finalizing their report: In Calgary, a 38-year-old father is facing two charges of first-degree murder for the deaths of his three-year-old daughter and five-year-old son in April this year. The man and his estranged wife shared custody. Police were called to the family home four times during the couple’s six-year common-law relationship. No charges were laid, CBC reported.

In June, a double murder-suicide in Ottawa left two boys, ages seven and 12, and their father dead. Police said 40-year-old Mohammed Al-Lami killed his sons after picking them up for a scheduled parenting time. It’s believed the boys were killed inside Al-Lami’s house before he set fire to his dental practice, about an hour’s drive from Ottawa, and then killed himself inside his vehicle.

A police investigation revealed a history of intimate partner violence. Al-Lami was on probation at the time of the deaths after being charged with threatening his wife and her new partner, CBC reported.

The new report, “Institutional Failures and Child Murder in Canada,” describes the case of the “Granby Girl,” who had been under the supervision of child protection services since she was a newborn and taken from her mother due to parental instability and physical neglect.

The girl was placed with her paternal grandparents, who raised her for the first three years of her life.

“By 2014, the father’s circumstances were considered more stable, in part because of his new partner, and youth protection services began considering placing the child back in his care,” according to the report.

The grandmother raised concerns over unsanitary living conditions and the father’s immaturity. She warned of a risk of sexual abuse, “which youth protections services deemed unfounded.” A case worker concluded the grandmother was no longer able to “control her emotions” and that she was undermining the father-child relationship, according to the report.

Custody was awarded to the father.

The authors say their findings back a controversial private member’s bill now before Parliament.

Introduced by Liberal MP Lisa Hepfner, the bill proposes to amend the Divorce Act to prohibit courts from considering evidence that one parent in a high-conflict custody case is actively trying to “alienate” the other parent and manipulating and coaching the child to resist contact.

It would also prevent judges from restricting a child’s time with one parent “to whom the child has a close connection” to improve the relationship with the other parent, and it would prevent courts from forcing children to attend so-called “reunification therapy.”
The proposed legislation has passed second reading, and is now before the justice and human rights committee.

Proponents say that in cases involving allegations of domestic violence, alienation claims are being weaponized and used as a legal tactic by parents — mostly fathers accused of abuse — to discredit the other parent.
If a parent — most often mothers — insist a child is in danger, “they run the risk of being perceived as an uncooperative, alienating parent,” the authors said.
The court’s attention shifts away from potential violence “towards preserving the parental bond.”<

“Rather than asking why a child is frightened or resistant to contact, the system can wrongly assume the child has been influenced or brainwashed.”
Even when there is documented family violence or other concerns, in a pro-contact culture “a father-child relationship can be treated as the overriding goal,” Zaccour said.

The proposed bill — Keeping Children Safe — says that a court “shall not take into consideration” any allegation that one parent has deliberately encouraged a child to become estranged from the other. Judges would not be permitted to order “reunification therapy” or, in extreme cases, reverse custody.

Opponents say ignoring all claims of alienation will harm children. “The legislation reflects a profound distrust of the Canadian family justice system,” said Queen’s University law professor Nicholas Bala, an internationally recognized expert on family and children’s law.

While fathers kill disproportionately more children than mothers, most child homicides involve cases where child protection services failed children, he said, “which is tragic.”

Nawl, which pushed for the proposed legislation, teamed up with professors from University of Sherbrooke’s faculty of law as part of a broader project supported by the federal Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.

Her father pleaded guilty to forcible confinement and was sentenced to three years and six months In January 2022. The girl’s stepmother was convicted of second-degree murder and forcible confinement and sentenced to life in prison without possibility of parole for 13 years.

Police had been called to the house two dozen times before the girl’s death in a case that shocked Quebec. Youth protection services had conducted follow-up calls for months, but never a surprise home visit, “making it impossible to detect physical signs of abuse,” according to Institutional Failures. The paternal grandmother lost custody “after being perceived as hostile for reporting the dangers the girl was exposed to while in her son’s care.”

content_blocks.text: In July 2012, in Warwick, Que., Jocelyn Marcoux killed son Lindsey, 13, and daughter Karen, 11. Their bodies, along with their father’s, were found in a burning garage at his home.
Marcoux and his ex-partner, Nadine Brilliant, separated in 2002 and had been engaged in custody disputes for years.
“Nadine Brillant shared that her life with Marcoux was heavily marked by domestic violence,” including a guilty plea to charges of intimidation and uttering threats against Brillant in 2006.
At the time of the children’s deaths, Marcoux had sole custody. Brillant was seeking a court order to modify the arrangement after the children expressed a wish to return to live with their mother.
“As part of these proceedings, the children were expected to appear before the Court to express their wish to return to live with their mother,” according to the report.
“The father killed them on the very day the hearing was scheduled to take place.”

Keira Kagan’s parents, Robin Brown and Jennifer Kagan, separated when she was still an infant. Ontario’s Domestic Violence Death Review Committee concluded that the circumstances of Keira’s death were “highly consistent” with previous cases of murder-suicide involving a father and a child.

Her parents had been embroiled in lengthy legal disputes spanning four years and involving 10 judges and 53 court orders. Brown had subjected Jennifer Kagan to years of domestic violence, including physical and sexual assault. On Jan. 28, 2020, she filed an urgent motion seeking to suspend or restrict his visitations to supervised visits “due to his increasingly erratic behavior,” according to the child murders report.

Brown had subjected Jennifer Kagan to years of domestic violence, including physical and sexual assault. On Jan.  28, 2020, she filed an urgent motion seeking to suspend or restrict his visitations to supervised visits “due to his increasingly erratic behavior,” according to the child murders report.

content_blocks.text: “The judge ruled the matter non-urgent and scheduled a hearing for two weeks later.” Twelve days later, Keira was found dead at the bottom of a cliff in the Rattlesnake Point Conservation Area in Milton, Ont., a 45-minute drive from Brown’s home.
“Every time (Jennifer Kagan) tried to raise the issue of abuse, there was a counter claim of alienation,” Zaccour said.

“There were 53 court decisions in this case, and many of those court decisions raised serious red flags, but no judge took the added step of restricting his parenting rights,” said Keira’s stepfather, Philip Viater, who has been practising family law for 17 years.

At Thursday’s press conference, Viater said the “mere suggestion” of alienation shifts the focus from allegations of safety concerns “to whether the protective parent is actually doing enough to preserve the relationship.”

Two days before the murder, a child protection agency called to say Brown was displaying behaviour consistent with fathers who harm or kill their children, Viater said. “Yet they did not act. We were forced and directed to permit Keira to be in her biological father’s care unsupervised.”

“At a minimum, this bill will provide a safeguard that children will not be ripped away in favour of ‘reunification therapy’ or other ideological purposes consistent with parental alienation,” Viater added in an interview.

The report includes two other cases in Quebec: The killing of two-year-old Alex, and five-year-old Olivier by their father, Michael Chicoine, in a home in Wendake, a Huron-Wendat First Nations territory near Quebec City, in 2020; in 2011, the deaths of two-year-old Florence and her eight-year-old brother, Zackary, in a fire their father, Martin Houle, set in his pickup truck.

Chicoine turned himself in to police and is currently serving a life sentence for the double murder. At his sentencing hearing, a Quebec Superior Court judge suggested Chicoine killed his boys “to quench your thirst for revenge” against his ex-wife, who reported her fear to youth protection services that Chicoine might harm their children.
Houle’s body was found by hikers in a wooded area near Drummondville, Que., the day after his children died by asphyxiation.
A third child, a six-year-old, escaped the truck fire. The parents had been separated for more than a year and were engaged in a custody dispute.
Custody was granted to Houle after he alleged his former wife, who publicly reported experiencing intimate partner violence, was suicidal and a threat to their children.
One month later, Florence and Zackary were dead.
In 2023, federal legislation known as “Keira’s Law” requiring judges to be educated in domestic violence and coercive control passed the Senate.
The same year, Ontario’s chief coroner announced an inquest would be held in Keira’s death.
A date has not yet been set.

In 2025, 12 children under 17 in Canada were killed by a biological, adopted, step or foster parent — seven by a father, five by a mother — down from 27 the previous year, according to Statistics Canada.

stories.title: Jewish students say they have come across 'Heil Hitler' salutes, antisemitic graffiti on Canadian university campuses
stories.summary: Jewish students in Canada shared experiences of antisemitic graffiti, Heil Hitler salutes, and dismissals of their concerns about safety.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Jewish university students in Canada have spoken about experiencing antisemitic graffiti, “Heil Hitler” salutes, and dismissals of their concerns about safety on campus at a news conference at Parliament Hill, in Ottawa, ON Thursday.

Kate Blumberg, an undergraduate at McMaster University, said she found herself as a representative of the Student Representative Assembly (SRA) “consistently fielding concerns” from her fellow Jewish students about “being singled out in their tutorials, about being excluded from groups, and about not knowing where to turn when campus spaces no longer felt welcoming.”

Livia Mamane, a student at Université du Québec à Montréal, said she has seen stall doors in washrooms with “Death to Zionists” and “Israel should burn” graffitied on them. “How would you feel if you had to submissively sit in classes while being surrounded by students who wanted to burn your own homeland?” she asked.

The students were joined by Jay Solomon, CEO at Jewish student organization Hillel Ontario, Liberal MP Anthony Housefather, Conservative MP Adam Chambers and Noah Shack, CEO at the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija), at the conference, where they shared their firsthand experiences of antisemitism on campus and called for action to ensure the safety of Jewish students at Canadian universities.

Blumberg also described how she and a fellow Jewish student wrote a motion addressing the antisemitism students had been experiencing on campus. “When brought to the (SRA) agenda, there were more votes of abstention and decline than of willingness for the motion to be discussed,” she said. “While the eventual passing of the motion was a monumental step for the Jewish community on campus, the sheer pushback and minimization of experience in chambers was baffling.”

She added: “When our highest student governing body treats the safety and inclusion of Jewish students as an open political question rather than an enforceable right, it signals to the entire university that our safety and inclusion are negotiable.”

Last month, the Campus Antisemitism and Student Experiences (Case) report found that more than nine in 10 Jewish students have experienced or seen antisemitism on campus over the past year.

Elsewhere, the report found that 71 per cent of Jewish students had seen antisemitic graffiti on campus, more than one in five had witnessed physical violence targeting Jews, and students also reported targeted incidents like mezuzahs being torn from the doors of Jewish dorm rooms in residence halls.

Another of the report’s key insights was that Jewish students also face antisemitism from professors and other university employees, with faculty cited in 18 per cent of antisemitic incidents reported in the survey. A further 14 per cent of incidents involved either teaching assistants or non-teaching staff.

This finding was echoed in Mamane’s testimony. “I have walked through the cafeteria and seen professors I truly respected associate themselves with causes that made me question whether I was welcome in class, or even whether my grades could be jeopardized,” she said.

She also shared an incident experienced by a friend at McGill University, who was walking across campus wearing their Star of David when a person approached them and performed a “Heil Hitler” salute.

The Case report found that more than three in 10 said they’d considered dropping a course or leaving their program because of antisemitism from professors or other students.

Blumberg said she had heard from other students who felt that they didn’t belong in a classroom because of political discussions, despite the subject of study being unrelated.

“Students are avoiding certain professors, avoiding certain classrooms where they know there’s going to be an intense debate that they will feel alone in,” she said.

National Post has reached out to McMaster University, Université du Québec à Montréal and McGill University for comment.

The news conference comes in the wake of a shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville , Ont., ON Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, which left one policeman injured.

The officer, Const. Jeff Smith , is in stable condition but “continues to face a significant road to recovery,” according to Belleville police’s Deputy Chief Sheri Meeks. GoFundMe pages have been set up both for Smith and to raise money for repairs and security at the synagogue .

The suspect in the Sept. 20 shooting, identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward from Quinte West, died in hospital on Monday and is reported to have “spouted” antisemitic conspiracy theories , including one that blamed the Jewish community for COVID.

Speaking at Parliament Hill on Thursday, Noah Shack said the Jewish community is “profoundly grateful” to Smith, adding that the “extreme violence” in Belleville should be a wake-up call.

“ This could have happened anywhere. We’ve seen hate targeting schools, seniors’ homes, workplaces, and universities across this country…universities are supposed to be institutions that advance higher learning and cutting-edge research. But on too many campuses, these extremists have been permitted to undermine this fundamental function in a free and democratic society.”

Shack added that Cija is meeting with cabinet members this week to urge concrete action on providing safety and security for Canadians, and to hold universities accountable for keeping students safe.

The shooting comes two months after Statistics Canada data showed that Jews were targeted in 71 per cent of religious hate crimes in Canada last year . While this represented a 16 per cent decline from the previous year, it remained 50 per cent higher than in 2022.

Meanwhile, advocacy group B’nai Brith Canada said in a statement that advance data for the group’s Annual Audit of Antisemitic Incidents indicates violent antisemitic incidents have already more than tripled during 2026 when compared to the total recorded during 2025.

“A mass-casualty event during this past weekend seems to have been avoided only because of the actions of trained and armed law enforcement,” the statement continued. “This reinforces the need for Canadian leaders to ensure members of law enforcement are present at every Jewish institution moving forward.”

Simon Wolle, CEO at B’nai Brith Canada, added: “In the wake of these harrowing events, Canada’s Jewish community cannot wait any longer for the Government to act. B’nai Brith has warned about the dangers of inaction for too long. The only acceptable response to this violent attack is for all levels of Government to take the decisive, urgent action needed to safeguard Jewish life in Canada.”

stories.title: Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting was a ‘hate-motivated’ crime, police say
stories.summary: Shooting during Yom Kippur was ‘a targeted attack against the Jewish community,’ police chief says
stories.author: Molly Hayes, Greg Mercer
stories.content:
The shooting at a synagogue in the Ontario city of Belleville during Yom Kippur Sunday evening was a deliberate and hate-motivated attack on the Jewish community, police confirmed Thursday, sharpening calls to combat antisemitism.

The assailant, a former member of the Canadian military, had arrived prepared to carry out a mass-casualty attack, armed with multiple firearms, ammunition and gasoline, police said.

“Make no mistake, this was a targeted attack against the Jewish community,” Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said at a press conference.

Chief Rodd played a short video clip captured by a witness at the scene of the attack, which unfolded just after 7 p.m. He said the shooter’s motives – targeting “specifically and only the Jewish community” – have been “corroborated in documentary and video evidence to date.”

The video shows the shooter standing behind a parked car a few metres from a police officer, Constable Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue in an unmarked vehicle. The shooter can be heard yelling “you are going to die for the Jews” before opening fire on the officer.

The video left Norman Weddum with chills. As president of the synagogue, he was among the roughly 25 worshippers gathered for prayers inside when the gunfire began, just as service was starting for Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

“There’s no question we’d all be dead. It really gets to you when you think about what could have happened,” he said.

“I hope this is a wake-up call to the government and the whole country.”

Constable Smith was stationed at the synagogue as part of long-established police department efforts to protect Jewish worshipers, said Chief Rodd. Similar measures have been implemented in cities across the country in response to an increasing number of gunfire, arson, window-breaking and other types of vandalism at Canadian synagogues.

Once the attack began, Constable Smith called for backup, and a gunfight ensued, said Chief Rodd. A second officer, identified Thursday as Constable Mike McCurdy, arrived and fired on the shooter.

Dozens of shots were discharged, with about 20 coming through the synagogue’s front stained-glass window. None of the worshippers were injured.

These officers are the only thing that prevented a greater attack, Chief Rodd said.

The Chief said the shooter came equipped with the “means to carry on a gun battle for a long period of time.”

Constable Smith was shot multiple times, including in the head, and remains in hospital with multiple surgeries ahead of him, Chief Rodd said Thursday. Constable McCurdy was not injured.

“They are both heroes,” Chief Rodd said. “Their actions represent the very definition of courageous policing.”

He said investigators are still downloading evidence from relevant devices and computers, but that they are “in the early stages of making sense of the rest of all of that.”

The Chief said the shooter had other firearms and ammunition, as well as extra gasoline in his vehicle.

“We are trying to understand what the magnitude of potential damage would have been with that,” he said.

Chief Rodd said the shooter had conducted reconnaissance earlier in the day, but nothing that triggered the officer’s alarm.

Mr. Weddum, the synagogue president, praised police leadership for calling Sunday’s shooting what it was.

“I was really pleased they designated this a hate crime directed against the Jewish community, because this wasn’t targeted against anyone else,” he told The Globe and Mail after the news conference. “It’s about time someone official finally said that.”

Shima Viggoda, vice-president at Sons of Jacob, stood with tears in his eyes at the press conference. He said the local Jewish community was doing its best to support one another during this difficult week.

“We find strength in each other, and I also think that we find great strength in our traditions,” he said.

Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, urged federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser to convene his provincial and territorial counterparts to establish a co-ordinated plan.

“Canada is at a precipice – one step closer to the tragedies witnessed in Bondi Beach, Manchester and Boulder – and our leaders must take urgent and concrete actions before it is too late,” Mr. Shack said in a statement, alluding to previous attacks against Jews in Australia, Britain and the United States.

“Constable Smith and Constable McCurdy stepped forward when it mattered most. Our political leaders must do the same,” he said.

Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Thursday that the issue of antisemitism in Canada doesn’t stem from a single source.

“There are a number of different actors right now, lone wolf in some cases, radicalization in all forms, that has no particular ideology,” he said on his way into a cabinet meeting on Parliament Hill.

Mr. Anandasangaree said the federal government will ensure that security support is available to Sons of Jacob, and said the government stands with the Jewish community – and the family of Constable Smith.

The shooting outside a Belleville, Ont., synagogue was a hate-motivated attack targeting the Jewish community, Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said.

The Canadian Press

The shooter, who has been identified as 29-year-old Sean Ward, of Quinte West, Ont., died in hospital Monday night.

The province’s Special Investigations Unit, which handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury, is also investigating the case. A postmortem examination on Mr. Ward’s body took place in Kingston on Wednesday, SIU spokesperson Kristy Denette said previously.

The RCMP’s Integrated National Security Enforcement Team in Ottawa is there “supporting and assisting” Belleville Police, RCMP Inspector Christine Belair said Thursday.

Mr. Ward served in the military from July, 2017, until June, 2022, when he was released with the rank of corporal, according to the Canadian Armed Forces. He was a member of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry regiment and did not deploy overseas during his service.

The Canadian military has not said where precisely Mr. Ward was posted. However, a private named Sean Ward was previously listed as a member of the Edmonton-based 3rd Battalion of the PPCLI, according to the regiment’s annual publication.

Mr. Ward was deemed unsuitable for further military service and released under a category called 5F , an involuntary discharge, because he refused to take the COVID-19 vaccine, The Globe reported on Wednesday.

Further details about Mr. Ward’s stand against the COVID-19 shot are detailed in a lawsuit filed in Federal Court by 128 current and former members of the military who didn’t want to be vaccinated.

Mr. Ward invoked religious grounds to resist receiving the vaccine and claimed that he suffered financial losses of $140,000 after he was released under the 5F classification, according to the lawsuit.

In a statement of defence that described the lawsuit as “scandalous, frivolous, and vexatious,” the federal government said vaccination was a key component in protecting the health of soldiers during the pandemic.

In an e-mailed statement ahead of the press conference Thursday, General Jennie Carignan, Chief of the Defence Staff, said she was “deeply troubled to learn of the shooting in Belleville. My thoughts are with Constable Jeff Smith, his family and colleagues, as well as the Jewish community in Belleville and all those affected by this incident.”

“We condemn in the strongest terms any form of antisemitism, extremism or violent behaviour in our society. They will not be tolerated in the Canadian Armed Forces, full stop,” she said.

“As this matter remains under police investigation, it would not be appropriate to comment further.”

At an event in Toronto, Premier Doug Ford said he reached out to the doctor at the Kingston hospital to thank him for saving Constable Smith’s life.

“Our prayers are with Jeff and his family,” he said.

Ontario Solicitor-General Michael Kerzner, who also spoke at the press conference Thursday, expressed the personal impact the attack has had on him, as “a proud kippah-wearing Jew, the first ever elected to any Parliament in Canada.”

“We will go forward after the events. … We will consider ourselves lucky that there were no lives lost in the synagogue on the holiest day of the year,” Mr. Kerzner said. “But we will never normalize antisemitism or hate of any kind, and let me be clear … I will not ever see my country surrender to hate and to antisemitism.”

With reports from Mercedes Stephenson and Stephanie Levitz in Ottawa and Laura Stone in Toronto

stories.title: Belleville attack should be ‘wake up call’ on rising antisemitism, Jewish group says
stories.summary: Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, made the comment just days after the Yom Kippur gun attack.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The head of a major Jewish advocacy group says the recent violent attack at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., should serve as a “wake-up call” to the “much broader problem” of rising antisemitism and racist conspiracies in Canada.

Noah Shack, CEO of the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, made the comment just days after the Yom Kippur gun attack that left a police officer critically injured and the shooter dead.

Shack told a press conference on Parliament Hill today that Sunday’s attack could have happened anywhere in the country.

Shack was speaking alongside Jewish university students who told reporters they’re experiencing more frequent instances of antisemitism both on and off campus.

Parliament passed the Combatting Hate Act in June this year, which creates new Criminal Code offences for hate-motivated intimidation of identifiable groups, including through the intentional display of certain Nazi symbols.

Liberal MP Anthony Housefather says he wants to see specialized prosecutors responsible for all hate cases and the federal justice and public safety ministers seem receptive to the idea.

On Thursday, police said the shooting outside the synagogue was a hate-motivated attack targeting the Jewish community.

Police Chief Murray Rodd says the shooter shouted, “You’re going to die for the Jews” before he opened fire on an officer outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue.

The suspect, 29-year-old Sean Ward, was fatally injured in the police shootout and Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue as those inside marked the start of Yom Kippur, was taken to a hospital in critical but stable condition.

Ward died on Monday night .

None of the roughly two dozen people inside the synagogue were injured. At a news conference on Thursday, Rodd also shared video of the attack.

stories.title: Boys found ‘healthy and happy’ following alleged July abduction
stories.summary: The Globe and Mail offers the most authoritative news in Canada, featuring national and international news
stories.author: Chris Zwick, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter, Town & Country News
stories.content:
Two young brothers who were the subjects of an Amber Alert in July were found safely in BC Sept. 17 after a 10-week investigation.

The Alberta RCMP Major Crimes Unit announced on Sept. 18 that the boys, 4 and 6, were found in West Kelowna, accompanied by their mother Krista Morrison and Daniel Ludwig, the father of the youngest. They were arrested on outstanding warrants and taken into custody without incident.

“From the outset, our primary focus was (the children’s) safety and well-being. After approximately two-and-a-half months of sustained investigative efforts, we are grateful to report that both children have been found safe as a result of the investigation,” said Inspector Breanne Brown, Acting Officer in Charge of the Alberta RCMP Serious Crimes Branch.

She credited the co-operation of several departments and detachments including RCMP Southeast BC District Emergency Response Team, RCMP Federal Policing, RCMP Air Services, and investigative services from both West Kelowna and Kelowna RCMP detachments.

“This outcome reflects not only the strength and collaboration across the RCMP, but also the dedication of approximately 70 investigators, in addition to civilian support staff in Alberta, who spent countless hours pursuing leads, coordinating resources, and conducting searches across multiple jurisdictions across Canada,” said Brown. “This was an exhaustive and a complex investigation, and the determination to locate these children safely never diminished.”

Beaverlodge RCMP notified the public of the Amber Alert on July 9, saying the eldest had been “taken” by his mother from Valhalla Centre. The Amber Alert was cancelled July 10 as there was “no reasonable expectation the public, in Alberta, will be able to action the instructions in the alert,” said the media release.

There are four criteria that must all be met for an Amber Alert to be activated — a child or adult with a proven mental or physical disability has been abducted; the child or adult is in danger of serious harm or death; there is enough descriptive information on the abducted, the abductee, or the mode of transportation involved; and there is a reasonable expectation the abductee could be returned, or the abductor apprehended.

While the initial alert was for only the eldest child, S/Sgt. Derrick Gladdish of the Major Crimes Unit with the Serious Crimes Branch, said by the time they were ready to add the youngest child to the alert, the criteria were no longer met.

Gladdish added the children seemed healthy and happy when the parents were taken into custody.

“I won’t get into specific locations or where that was exactly, but they were in good health. My investigators did send me a picture, and they seemed to be happy young children. They did not seem to be in any sort of distress at the time that they were apprehended,” he said.

Brown added the file is still under investigation and will be before the courts where more details will be heard.

Morrison and Ludwig, both 35, are each charged with contravening a custody order.

Their bail hearing took place in a Kelowna court Sept. 18, with the pair appearing via video link from jail. The judge ordered a six-day remand period to allow them to be transferred back to Alberta where they face criminal charges, according to Kelowna-based online news site, Castanet.

At the time of the announcement the children were in the custody of Ministry of Children’s and Family Services in British Columbia, and arrangements were being made to turn them over to Children and Family Services in Alberta.

stories.title: Nova Scotia government spent nearly $2-billion outside of budget
stories.summary: Province closed 2025-26 fiscal year with record-high deficit of $1.4-billion, Finance Minister says
stories.author: Lyndsay Armstrong
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government says it spent a record $1.9-billion beyond its budget in the 2025-26 fiscal year.

Finance Minister John Lohr says there are plenty of reasons why the Progressive Conservative government needed the flexibility to spend that amount on what the government describes as additional appropriations.

The financial phrase refers to extra spending that is not included in the budget, but is approved by cabinet without a vote in the legislature.

In the most recent fiscal year, the government used some of that additional funding to cover the $40.4-million cost of public works projects and another $13.8-million on emergency management for the 2025 wildfire season.

A well, Lohr told a news conference that the province closed the 2025-26 fiscal year with a record-high deficit of $1.4-billion.

While revenue was slightly higher than expected, at just under $18-billion, it was outpaced by $19.4-billion in spending.

Welcome to the inaugural CEO Speaker Series, a series of Report on Business magazine events bringing together some of Canada’s largest corporate leaders for a monthly in-depth conversation with ROB magazine editor Dawn Calleja in Toronto.

On Friday, Calleja will have a fire-side chat with Éric Martel, President and CEO, Bombardier, as they explore lessons from the company’s reinvention, how renewed ambitions are reshaping the future of Canadian aerospace industry and what it will take for the country to compete in the world’s most high-value technology sectors.

For those who can’t attend in person, we’re livestreaming the event starting at 8:00 A.M. EST .

You can view the full schedule for the talk here .

stories.title: Ottawa orders Appeal Court to review Saskatchewan sisters’ murder convictions
stories.summary: Canada's federal justice minister ordered the courts to reopen the sisters' case, after they spent almost three decades in prison for what May be wrongful murder convictions.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Federal Justice Minister Sean Fraser has ordered the courts to reopen the case of two Saskatchewan sisters who spent almost three decades in prison for what may be wrongful murder convictions.

Fraser says he is sending the case of Odelia and Neressa Quewezance back to an Appeal Court for a review.

Fraser, in a statement Thursday, cited reasonable grounds to conclude that a miscarriage of justice occurred in the 1994 convictions.

“My decision does not decide guilt or innocence, as that will rest with the courts,” Fraser said.

“Our responsibility is to make sure Canadians can trust their justice system, and that means, in rare cases, returning cases to the courts.”

Fraser noted there is new information that was not before the courts during the trial or during the appeal.

James Lockyer, the sisters’ lawyer, said the information that led to their new appeal pertains to their time in custody after their arrest.

Lockyer said the women were held in an RCMP detachment in Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Saskatoon. They were questioned by white male police officers for days, he said, which was in violation of a court order to send them to the local jail.

“We’ve discovered some more information in that regard that I don’t feel free to talk about at the moment, but will certainly be presented to the Court of Appeal,” he said in a phone interview Thursday.

He said the women were more vulnerable to pressures from police because of their time spent in residential schools. He said their alleged incriminating statements were never recorded and their in-custody environment increases the likelihood their confessions were false.

Lockyer applied for a ministerial review in December 2021, which was granted in June 2022. The two Saulteaux sisters were granted bail in 2023, but have since been returned to custody for breaching bail conditions.

“It’s very difficult for them, when they’ve spent all this time in prison, to be able to readjust in the community,” said Lockyer.

He added they both struggle with substance abuse.

Court documents show both sisters attended St. Philips Indian Residential School and Qu’Appelle Indian Residential School. Their mother and stepmother both died from drug overdoses.

Lockyer said he will be bringing further bail applications for them in the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal.

The sisters said in a statement Thursday that they’re encouraged by the decision, but added that the battle continues.

“We have never stopped fighting,” Odelia said in the statement on behalf of her and her sibling.

“Thank you to all those who have kept the faith in us.”

The statement was issued through Innocence Canada, an organization that fights for those it believes were wrongfully convicted. It assisted the sisters in this case.

Lockyer, also a lawyer with Innocence Canada, said the Quewezance sisters’ case was flagged to the organization by David Milgaard, who spent 23 years in prison for the 1969 murder of a Saskatoon nursing student before his conviction was overturned. He died in 2022.

The two sisters were found guilty of second-degree murder in the 1993 stabbing death of 70-year-old farmer Anthony Joseph Dolff near Kamsack, Sask., about 270 kilometres northeast of Regina.

The women from the Keeseekoose First Nation have always maintained their innocence. Another person, who was a youth at the time, confessed to the killing and was sentenced to five years in prison.

Court has heard the sisters and the youth were drinking with Dolff at his farmhouse that fateful night when he was killed.

Court documents show Dolff was found dead in the bedroom of his home located near Keeseekoose First Nation. It says he had been stabbed 17 times and had a phone cord wrapped around his neck.

The sisters’ bid for an appeal was dismissed by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1996.

The federal Justice Department said after launching its review in June 2022 that there may be a reasonable basis to conclude there was a miscarriage of justice.

stories.title: Feds’ tariff response requires a ‘Team Canada’ approach, expert says
stories.summary: Municipalities are on the ground connecting with businesses and residents, which one economist said gives them valuable intel integral to Canada’s economic response.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Canada’s tariff response must ensure that no community is left behind, a new report says.

The report, released by the Federation of Canadian Municipalities , in partnership with the City of London and Ivey Business School found that the consequences of the U.S.-Canada trade war are felt all across Canada, but the severity of those impacts are unevenly distributed.

The industrial composition of a community is more closely tied to how it feels the pressure of tariffs than its size alone, the report said.

“There is an opportunity … to strengthen the Team Canada approach in terms of responding and creating resilience in the economy. I think we should take that seriously,” Romel Mostafa, an economist and assistant professor of international business at the Ivey Business School, told Global News.

Municipal governments are on the ground connecting with businesses and residents, which Mostafa said gives them valuable intel that is integral to the federal government’s economic response.

Whether it is Mackenzie, B.C., a town of 3,700 residents that relies on forestry and mining; Windsor, Ont., with deep roots in the auto industry; or a larger city that has multiple tariff-impacted industries, all of these communities have had to respond to the consequences of the trade war.

“Understanding these nuances means that there are different policy implications for it,” Mostafa said.

One of the biggest challenges for municipalities has been working through the uncertainty brought forth by a constantly evolving economic relationship with the U.S., London, Ont., Mayor Josh Morgan told Global News.

“The uncertainty has created a real pause in investment and job creation. In some cases there are job losses, in some cases, there are job gains,” he said. “For the most part, many businesses have just paused their decision-making, waiting to see a more stabilized environment because the unpredictability of the state we’re in is really not conducive to business investment.”

London recorded the highest unemployment rate among Canada’s 20 largest municipalities, sitting at 9.1 per cent in March, compared to six per cent a year earlier. But Morgan said the statistics don’t tell the whole story.

“We have seen actual net job creation. But we’ve seen a migration of the labour force from smaller communities that May be more impacted by the trade situation, migrating to larger cities like London for job opportunities,” he said. “And so the labour force has actually expanded at a pace faster than job creation we’ve had in the city.”

This context behind the statistics is the intel that Morgan said municipalities can bring to the table in discussions with upper levels of government as well as with cities on the other side of the border.

“Municipalities in Canada and municipalities in the U.S. are facing the same sort of impacts. We have that common ground and we are actively talking to each other,” he said. “We’re not against them, we’re on their side, we’re on the same team here.”

Mostafa said it is important to bring all of these voices into the conversation.

“I think there’s a real opportunity to think about, given the lanes that we have, how can we make the process of getting municipal intelligence to reach the policymakers at the higher order of the government?” he said.

stories.title: Lions eager for crucial clash with Roughriders
stories.summary: Mathieu Betts knows exactly what will be on the line when his B.C. Lions line up against the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Friday.
stories.author: Gemma Karstens-Smith
stories.content:
VANCOUVER – Mathieu Betts knows exactly what will be on the line when his B.C. Lions line up against the Saskatchewan Roughriders on Friday.

If everything goes Saskatchewan’s way, the Riders could punch their playoff ticket this week — and the Lions are looking to stop that from happening.

“It feels like the most important game of the year, and I’m pretty sure it’s not the last time I would tell you that this year,” Betts said.

“At the end of the day, to get where we want to go, we need to play good football. So no matter what’s at stake, we need to play good football.”

The Lions (7-6) come in with wins in six of their last seven contests, including a 48-29 victory over the Montreal Alouettes on Sept. 12 before the team headed into a bye week.

The Roughriders (8-5), meanwhile, sit second in the West Division and are coming off a 19-6 loss to the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sept. 12.

Saskatchewan could clinch a post-season berth this week, but will need help on the out-of-town scoreboard. The Riders need the Toronto Argonauts to beat the Bombers and the winless Ottawa Redblacks to upset the Calgary Stampeders.

Most importantly, the Riders need a victory over the Lions.

A Lions win would give B.C. a tiebreaker between the two sides in an ultracompetitive West Division where the second- and fifth-place teams are currently separated by just four points.

“We all understand where the standings are right now,” said Lions head coach Buck Pierce. “And both teams have put themselves in position to have everything they want in front of them, right? So, two competitive teams that are playing good football … getting healthy, hopefully at the right time. So it should be a good game.”

Friday will mark the final regular-season matchup between the two sides, and each team comes in with a win.

The Riders took first blood with a 31-27 home victory on June 13 before the Lions earned a 30-16 decision in Vancouver on Aug 23.

B.C.’s defence has grown stronger over the course of the season, said Saskatchewan head coach Corey Mace.

“I think just having a little bit more understanding of what they want to accomplish,” he said. “I think they play very well to the pieces that they have. They do a really good job, they can get after the passer, they do a bunch of stuff on the back end that makes it tough on quarterbacks, their linebackers run and hit.

“They’ve been doing a really good job making it tough on offences across the league.”

The Riders have been stingy all year, giving up a league-low 340 points.

Getting the right combination of players on defence has been an evolution, Mace said.

“We’re doing a good job,” he said. “We’ve just got to continue pushing the envelope and creating some turnovers. We’ve been a little bit more consistent with that. And giving ourselves an opportunity to, obviously, not only stay in the game but take it over.”

The Lions will see changes to their secondary this week after defensive backs Josh Hagerty and Ronald Kent Jr. were each suspended for following a melee in B.C.’s win over Montreal. Hagerty received a two-game ban while Kent was suspended one game. Alouettes defensive back Don Callis was also banned for one game and three other Alouettes players received fines.

If everything goes Saskatchewan’s way, the Riders could punch their playoff ticket this week — and the Lions are looking to stop that from happening.
“It feels like the most important game of the year, and I’m pretty sure it’s not the last time I would tell you that this year,” Betts said.
“At the end of the day, to get where we want to go, we need to play good football. So no matter what’s at stake, we need to play good football.”
The Lions (7-6) come in with wins in six of their last seven contests, including a 48-29 victory over the Montreal Alouettes on Sept. 12 before the team headed into a bye week.
The Roughriders (8-5), meanwhile, sit second in the West Division and are coming off a 19-6 loss to the Winnipeg Blue Bombers on Sept. 12.

Saskatchewan could clinch a post-season berth this week, but will need help on the out-of-town scoreboard. The Riders need the Toronto Argonauts to beat the Bombers and the winless Ottawa Redblacks to upset the Calgary Stampeders.
Most importantly, the Riders need a victory over the Lions.

“We all understand where the standings are right now,” said Lions head coach Buck Pierce. “And both teams have put themselves in position to have everything they want in front of them, right? So, two competitive teams that are playing good football … getting healthy, hopefully at the right time. So it should be a good game.”
Friday will mark the final regular-season matchup between the two sides, and each team comes in with a win.
The Riders took first blood with a 31-27 home victory on June 13 before the Lions earned a 30-16 decision in Vancouver on Aug 23.
B.C.’s defence has grown stronger over the course of the season, said Saskatchewan head coach Corey Mace.

“I think just having a little bit more understanding of what they want to accomplish,” he said. “I think they play very well to the pieces that they have. They do a really good job, they can get after the passer, they do a bunch of stuff on the back end that makes it tough on quarterbacks, their linebackers run and hit.
“They’ve been doing a really good job making it tough on offences across the league.”
The Riders have been stingy all year, giving up a league-low 340 points.
Getting the right combination of players on defence has been an evolution, Mace said.

“We’re doing a good job,” he said. “We’ve just got to continue pushing the envelope and creating some turnovers. We’ve been a little bit more consistent with that. And giving ourselves an opportunity to, obviously, not only stay in the game but take it over.”

The Lions signed American defensive backs Jordan Oladokun and Thomas Graham to the practice roster on Monday, then re-signed Robert Carter Jr. on Tuesday.
The American defensive back returns to B.C. after attending NFL training camp with the Indianapolis Colts.

stories.title: Stevenson promises review of BRT spending, road construction if elected mayor
stories.summary: Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says she would push for a public accounting of London’s Bus Rapid Transit project and proposed North Link if elected.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson says she would push for a public accounting of London’s Bus Rapid Transit project and proposed North Link if elected.

Stevenson made the announcement Thursday morning in front of the BRT shelters at King and Burwell streets.

She outlined three commitments: A full public accounting of BRT and the proposed North Link, an annual road construction plan approved by council, and practical improvements to everyday travel.

Stevenson said she would take a closer look at how the city is spending money on major transportation projects, including BRT and the proposed North Link.

“People have a lot of questions. We spent almost half a billion dollars on this investment, and they would like to see it laid out in plain English in one spot where they can really see and get the answers as to what was spent,” Stevenson said.

“What was the reason for the $174 million overruns? Were there construction delays? Like, how well did we do in managing this project, and what is it that we’ve committed to going forward?”

Stevenson is also proposing an annual road construction plan aimed at better coordinating roadwork, utility projects and development, while keeping businesses and emergency routes accessible.

She said residents and businesses should receive more advance notice when construction is expected to affect them.

Her platform also calls for a review of traffic signals, turning restrictions and cycling lanes, along with a greater focus on road and sidewalk maintenance.

Stevenson said she would work with London Transit and local employers to explore transit options for industrial areas, including service timed around shift work.

“Getting around London should be something we can count on,” Stevenson said.

The current Ward 4 councillor said she would begin the BRT review and construction-coordination work within her first 100 days in office.

stories.title: Canada’s first F-35 takes flight in Texas
stories.summary: Canada’s first F-35 has taken to the skies. It’s the first new model of fighter jet with Canadian markings in 44 years.
stories.author: John Vennavally-Rao
stories.content:
Toronto - Canada’s first F-35 has taken to the skies. It’s the first new model of fighter jet with Canadian markings in 44 years.

The historic first flight took place Wednesday in Fort Worth, Texas, home to Lockheed Martin’s final assembly plant.

The F-35 will replace at least some of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s (Rcaf) aging CF-18 Hornets, which Canada first took delivery of in 1982.

Canada signed on in 2023 to buy 88 of the jets, but Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered a review in March 2025 amid tensions with the United States. The first 16 aircraft are committed, while the government weighs whether to buy the remaining 72 or turn to alternatives such as Sweden’s Saab Gripen.

The CF-35A Lightning II with “Canada” painted behind the cockpit and a maple leaf on the tail, took off just before noon for what witnesses say was a roughly 90-minute flight.

View this post on Instagram

“There were quite a few people!” Victoria Fontana told CTV News in a message when asked if there was a crowd. She said the Dallas-Fort Worth area has a sizable plane-spotting community that are interested in both military and commercial aircraft.

The only apparent official acknowledgement came from Lockheed Martin Canada’s X account, which posted: “The first CF-35A took to the skies for the first time today.”

The first CF-35A took to the skies for the first time today. pic.twitter.com/SAHsXdKwas — Lockheed Martin Canada (@LMCanadaNews) September 23, 2026

Asked for more details, a spokesperson for Lockheed Martin said, “questions would be best addressed by the Department of National Defence (DND).” CTV News has reached out to the DND for comment but has not yet received a response.

“I think the silence is ordered,” says Scott Clancy, a retired Rcaf major-general, an adviser at Henley Strategies and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.

“So, this is now just a political decision and that’s why the Canadian Armed Forces has been specifically told you will not comment on that,” said Clancy.

Clancy said pilots in the Canadian Armed Forces including future F-35 pilots are excited for the new plane.

“They’re very excited about this generational advancement that they’re going to make in terms of technology and they are preparing hard for that.”

Despite the controversy around the purchase of the jet, Clancy said Canadians should take notice of the first flight.

“I think we should be proud because a significant portion of that jet, although we call it an American jet, is Canadian,” he said.

Lockheed Martin says each F-35 contains more than $3 million in Canadian-made components from suppliers in six provinces, including the F-35A’s horizontal tail assemblies built by Magellan Aerospace in Winnipeg.
