stories.title: Scientist Jim Bruce was a globally renowned voice on the dangers of climate change
stories.summary: A founding member of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, he was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore
stories.author: James Cullingham
stories.content:
Jim Bruce was one of Canada’s foremost scientists and international representatives concerning environmental and climate issues. He provided extraordinary leadership that helped to rehabilitate the Great Lakes and through proposing the UN’s Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (Ipcc) was among the first to show how the world could address the damaging climate change caused by the burning of fossil fuels. He became a globally renowned and trusted voice who raised awareness about the risks of climate change, especially flooding and drought.

“If climate change is a shark, water is its teeth,” Mr. Bruce said, according to MP Francis Scarpaleggia, who quoted the scientist when addressing the House of Commons in 2022. “Like a fish that doesn’t notice the shark until it feels its sharp bite, humans will first feel the effects of climate change through water.”

Mr. Bruce, a leading member of the Ipcc, was the only Canadian representative in the delegation that accepted the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize jointly with former U.S. vice-president Al Gore, who was honoured for his work on climate change, including the Oscar-winning film An Inconvenient Truth .

Jim Bruce died at the age of 97 in Ottawa on Aug. 23. He had suffered for many years from inclusion body myositis (IBM).

“[Mr. Bruce] was one of the first to raise and develop to prominence so many issues like floodplain mapping, hydrometeorology, the imperative to control climate change. There’s both a scientific and organizational legacy,” said John Pomeroy, distinguished professor at the University of Saskatchewan. “He showed us that Canada could be leaders in such matters. He was a great Canadian.”

Rower Archie MacKinnon helped usher in a golden age for his sport on Canada’s West Coast

James Philip Bruce was born in Toronto on Sept. 29, 1928. His father, Peter Bruce, worked in the shoe department at Eaton’s department store. His mother, Winnifred Bruce, was an elementary school teacher who left her job when she had children. She later continued her vocation as an English as second language instructor. As a young person, Jim accompanied his father, a tenor vocalist, ON piano and organ at church services.

Mr. Bruce received a bachelor’s degree from the University of Toronto in 1948. That year he began a career at the Meteorological Service of Canada working mostly at air force bases. In 1949 he married Ruth (née Richardson), to whom he was married for 77 years. In 1952, Mr. Bruce went back to the University of Toronto and earned a master’s degree in physics.

The devastation of Hurricane Hazel in 1954 was a pivotal moment in his understanding of climate. He did floodplain mapping which led to the mitigation of future risk in the immediate area of the Humber River in Toronto’s west end, where loss of life and extensive property damage had occurred, and elsewhere.

Mr. Bruce and others developed systems to prepare for and avoid risks of flooding in several parts of Canada. That work also led to the creation of park space around urban rivers. His son, Peter Bruce, a former senior civil servant and now a learning and leadership associate at the Institute on Governance, a think tank, posed the query: “Do you know why it’s green around the Don Valley Parkway [in Toronto]? It’s because of my father.”

He was head of hydrometeorology for the Meteorological Service of Canada, based in Toronto, from 1959 to 1967. Mr. Bruce then moved to Burlington, Ont., where he led the Centre for Inland Waters and became co-chair of the International Joint Commission (IJC), dedicated to protection of water quality of the Great Lakes. That was the beginning of a series of international roles that saw Mr. Bruce involved with Ipcc and the World Meteorological Organization in Geneva.

In 1988, he helped organize a landmark conference in Toronto titled “The Changing Atmosphere: Implications for Global Security.” That gathering marked the first time a global conference called for a reduction – 20 per cent – in greenhouse gas emissions. Mr. Bruce helped write the conference statement, which began: “Humanity is conducting an unintended, uncontrolled, globally pervasive experiment whose ultimate consequences could be second only to a global nuclear war.”

Following that Toronto conference, Mr. Bruce was among an international team that formed the Ipcc. This body provides scientific assessments that inform decision-makers at United Nations climate conferences, known as Conferences of the Parties (COPs), and has helped shape international agreements including the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Mr. Bruce reflected on his Ipcc experience in his 2016 book A Canadian Environmental Chronicle (1954-2015) . “While many climate activists have rightly considered Ipcc Reports to be cautious in tone, this characteristic is inevitable in reports that represent a consensus of a large, diverse, international group of scientists,” he wrote.

In a 2022 interview with John Woodside for Canada’s National Observer, Mr. Bruce signalled his growing dissatisfaction on the climate-change mitigation front: “Now it [the Ipcc] hasn’t been very successful in getting real action, in my view, but that’s a political problem.”

Public awareness, however, has grown. Mr. Bruce wrote about the moment he and his colleagues returned to their hotel after the Nobel Peace Prize gala: “We were astonished to find a large crowd waiting for our return from the ceremony. They began shouting ‘I-P-C-C, I-P-C-C’ and continued for some time. In my experience, this only happened to winning sports teams.”

Filmmaker Georgina Lightning set out to change how Indigenous people were seen and heard

His daughter Cathy Bruce, president and vice-chancellor of Trent University, laughingly recalled chatting with her father before he headed to Oslo: “He asked, ‘Do you think I should rent a suit?’ I said, ‘Dad, maybe this is a time you should buy a new suit.’” Dr. Bruce said she tries to implement her father’s style in valuing mentoring and in striving to make complex ideas understandable both in speech and writing.

Dr. Pomeroy first met Mr. Bruce in 1981 at the University of Saskatchewan. “I was a 20-year-old undergraduate asked to drive to the airport to pick up this leading figure. I was terrified. It turns out he was a nice, humble person who immediately put me at ease.”

Earlier this month, Dr. Pomeroy was among the scientists who honoured Mr. Bruce at the World Climate Research Programme’s International Network for Alpine Research Catchment Hydrology meeting in Kananaskis, Alta.

Mr. Bruce’s scientific output alone is a significant legacy, Dr. Pomeroy said, pointing to a breakthrough 1965 text on hydrometeorology and the instrumentation embedded by Mr. Bruce’s team in the Canadian Rockies headwaters of the Bow River in the early 1960s that helped scientists later understand the causes of the massive floods of 2013 and how better to predict such events.

Elizabeth Dowdeswell, former lieutenant-governor of Ontario, met Mr. Bruce in the 1980s when they both worked for the federal government. She came from behavioural sciences rather than a meteorological or hydrological background.

“He was always there for you, teaching in the most gentle way. He was a mentor,” Ms. Dowdeswell said, adding that she felt welcomed by Mr. Bruce. She would assume senior roles at Canada’s Atmospheric Environmental Service and as head of the United Nations Environment Programme in Nairobi, Kenya. She fondly recalled an interaction early in her Ottawa stint when she was “flabbergasted” by the number of acronyms used in the governmental scientific reports. “I told Jim I was determined to write a report without acronyms. Jim said, ‘good luck with that!’”

Green Party Leader Elizabeth May, formerly an activist and environmental lawyer, first encountered Mr. Bruce after she became an adviser to Thomas McMillan, then federal minister of the environment, and through the intense period of the 1988 Toronto conference, after which Ms. May resigned from the minister’s office. Their relationship deepened from 1999 to 2005 when they both served on the board of the International Institute for Sustainable Development (Iisd).

Ms. May admired Mr. Bruce’s ability to engage with diverse colleagues and to make complex scientific issues understandable. Mr. Bruce “was a kind of polymath,” she said. “He had moral courage, mental clarity and depth of scientific expertise. I relied on him and loved him enormously.”

Jim and Ruth Bruce led an active, engaged family life. As long as his health permitted, Mr. Bruce played both jazz and European classical on the piano. He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the Ipcc delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.

Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

He particularly admired Oscar Peterson, Diana Krall and J.S. Bach. Both Cathy Bruce and her brother, Peter, remember music and travel as indelible parts of family life.

“My father took us on lots of adventures,” Peter recalled. “He was very interested in archaeology and history.” Skiing also figured at a family chalet at Mont Sainte-Marie in the Gatineau region and in the Alps when members of the extended family visited Jim and Ruth while they were stationed in Geneva.

Ms. May made a point of regularly dropping by Jim and Ruth Bruce’s condo overlooking the Ottawa River. Her most recent visit took place last winter. “Jim never lost hold of moral certainty based on clear evidence and science.” She recalled that even with his deteriorating medical condition, “I never heard a syllable that could amount to self-pity. He grabbed every moment to get all the joy from life that he could.”

Both Ms. May and Ms. Dowdeswell said their final conversations with Mr. Bruce included discussion of climate change. Mr. Bruce was particularly alarmed about Canadian backsliding, Ms. May said. “We were both angry to the point of tears.”

After leaving the federal civil service and WMO, Mr. Bruce remained engaged with writing, speaking at conferences and advising on domestic and international panels. He expressed mounting concern over what he saw as insufficient action on the environment.

“One of the long-standing requirements of government,” he wrote in his 2016 book, “is to ensure stewardship of our inherited land, air, water and wild creatures – to pass them largely unharmed to the next generation. This role has recently been abysmally short-changed.”

Before that book was published, Peter had expressed concern that the conclusion his father drafted might be too dire, so he advised his father to tone it down a bit, which he did. But more recently, upon reflection, Peter thought, “Well, Dad, I guess you were right again.”

Among his many honours, Jim Bruce was named an officer of the Order of Canada and Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada in 1997, was awarded honorary doctorates from McMaster and Waterloo universities as well as being a member of the Ipcc delegation for the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize.
Mr. Bruce leaves his wife, Ruth; children, Peggy Marcoux, Peter Bruce, Connie Bruce and Cathy Bruce; eight grandchildren and seven great-grandchildren.

stories.title: Back split in Grimsby, Ont., sells $35,000 below its 2021 sale price
stories.summary: Home was in move-in condition and in a prime location close to the marina and beach
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
45 Sandra Cres., Grimsby, Ont.

Asking price: $829,900 (June, 2026)

Selling price: $820,000 (July, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $855,000 (September, 2021); $512,000 (November, 2017); $305,000 (August, 2015); $183,000 (September, 2004); $147,500 (October, 1990)

Taxes: $4,484 (2026)

Days on the market: 10

Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and Graydon Moyer, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

Buyer’s agent: Michael St. Jean, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

The sellers of this three-bedroom house were well aware that prices had declined since they bought the home in 2021. They took that into account when choosing to list the home for sale at $25,100 below what they had paid. Within 10 days, a deal was struck with the buyer trimming a further $9,900 from the asking price.

“The market had gone up and come down,” said agent Michael St. Jean.

“[The owner] is selling it in a different environment unfortunately, but the offer came in close to what they had paid a number of years earlier.”

Building tenant wins contest for large lakefront condo

The buyers, also clients of Mr. St. Jean, had seen enough properties to appreciate that this more than 30-year-old house had two major assets: it’s in move-in condition, complete with a new roof and laundry room, and it’s in a prime setting, backing onto a park and less than two kilometres from the QEW, GO train station, beach and marina.

“Everything in this house was completely done, and it’s turnkey,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“It’s in a nice neighbourhood, close to the highway, and not far from the lake and beach.”

This detached backsplit house has four floors, including a finished basement, and an attached garage.

The living and dining areas are on the main floor along with a kitchen that has a side exit to the 37- by 100-foot lot.

Seller of Swansea penthouse sets baked-in price buffer

Across the rear, the upper level has two bedrooms and an updated, semi-private bathroom.

The level directly below has a third bedroom, a bathroom and a recreation area with a new fireplace and sliding doors to a south-facing patio.

“It’s a four-level back split, and they’re not really building these any more,” Mr. St. Jean said.

stories.title: 'Right now, he is fighting': Wife of injured Belleville police officer is grateful for outpouring of support
stories.summary: 'Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead. But he is not walking it alone.'
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
The wife of the police officer who was shot while stopping a gunman outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. , has released an emotional thank you to supporters and “every scared soul” who was inside the building that night.

In a message on Facebook Tuesday night, Ashley Smith posted a photo of herself holding the hand of Const. Jeff Smith, who is in critical but stable condition in hospital.

“Today, I held Jeff’s hand. And I thought about all of those hands. All of the people who have carried him, cared for him, prayed for him, fought for him and held us up when we didn’t know how we were going to stand,” she wrote. “I will never forget any of it.”

A GoFundMe for the family, organized by the Canadian Jewish community , raised $518,231 as of Thursday, surpassing its initial goal of $450,000.

Below, Ashley Smith’s statement:

Hello, world. I don’t know where to begin. My words aren’t strong or steady yet, but I knew I needed to find them. I needed to use my voice for my dear Jeff, until he is able to use his.

From the deepest part of my heart and soul, thank you.

Thank you to this good and kind world that has surrounded Jeff and our family with more love, compassion, generosity and selflessness than I could ever put into words.

I cannot begin to express what the outpouring of love and support has meant to us. I know there are things happening every day that I don’t even know about yet. Messages being sent. Prayers being said. People checking in. Hands reaching out. And I know that my gratitude will never be enough.

I am witnessing real-life miracles. And so many of them have happened through human hands.

The life-saving hands of paramedics and police. The hands of an angel neurosurgeon. The steady, capable hands of trauma teams, doctors, nurses, RTs, PSWs and so many others whose names we May never know, but whose kindness and skill we will carry with us forever. The helping hands of neighbours, friends, community members and volunteers. And then there are the hands that held me and my sweet girls when we were living through the scariest and darkest day of our lives.

Today, I held Jeff’s hand. And I thought about all of those hands.

All of the people who have carried him, cared for him, prayed for him, fought for him and held us up when we didn’t know how we were going to stand.

I will never forget any of it.

I also want to send my love and prayers to the Jewish community, and to every scared soul who was there on Sunday night. Please know that your love, your prayers and your support have reached us. We are deeply grateful. We love you, we see you, we pray for you.

So I am asking for one thing. Keep it coming. Prayer. Hope. Faith. Love. Whatever you have to give, please keep giving it. We will take every bit of it we can get. Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead. But he is not walking it alone. He has an army of love behind him. And I know Jeff. He is the best man I know. He loves his family with his whole heart. He cares deeply. He gives freely. He shows up. He is a man of integrity. He is my safest place. And right now, he is fighting. So we will fight with him. Thank you for loving him. Thank you for believing in him. Thank you for honouring him. Thank you for holding our family up. Our hero. Your hero.

With heartfelt gratitude, Ashley

stories.title: Starbucks to close 250 more stores in Canada and the U.S.
stories.summary: Starbucks plans to close 250 North American stores later this week in the second big round of store closures under Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol, who joined the company in 2024.
stories.author: Dee-ann Durbin
stories.content:
Starbucks plans to close 250 North American stores later this week.

It is the second big round of store closures under Starbucks Chairman and CEO Brian Niccol, who joined the company in 2024. Last September, Starbucks closed 627 stores in North America and Europe and laid off 900 non-retail employees.

In a letter to employees, Starbucks Chief Operating Officer Mike Grams said the locations targeted either aren’t delivering acceptable financial results or can’t provide the kind of experience that Starbucks wants for customers and employees.

The company didn’t say Thursday which coffeehouses will close or how many are located in the U.S. It also didn’t say how many of the affected coffeehouses are unionized. More than 700 U.S.

Starbucks stores have voted to unionize since late 2021, but Starbucks doesn’t support the unionization effort and the union and the company have yet to reach a labor agreement.

Grams said Starbucks is continuing to retrofit its North American coffeehouses to make them cozier and more inviting. The company expects 1,500 stores will be retrofitted by Sept. 30, which is the end of Starbucks’ fiscal year.

“This progress has given us a clearer view of the performance of every coffeehouse,” Grams said in his letter. “While most are benefiting from this overall momentum, some coffeehouses continue to underperform despite the hard work and commitment of all of you.”

Grams said Starbucks is still committed to growing its store count in North America.

Starbucks said it will transfer employees to other stores if possible or provide severance support if it’s not able to place an employee in another location.

In May, Starbucks laid off an additional 300 corporate employees and closed some underused U.S. offices.

Global News sent a request to Starbucks asking how many stores would be closed in Canada and how many Canadian workers could be impacted. A spokesperson did not disclose exact numbers for Canada.

Starbucks shares fell 0.3 per cent Thursday morning as trading opened.

– with a file from Global News’ Ariel Rabinovitch

“This progress has given us a clearer view of the performance of every coffeehouse,” Grams said in his letter. “While most are benefiting from this overall momentum, some coffeehouses continue to underperform despite the hard work and commitment of all of you.”
Grams said Starbucks is still committed to growing its store count in North America.
Starbucks said it will transfer employees to other stores if possible or provide severance support if it’s not able to place an employee in another location.
In May, Starbucks laid off an additional 300 corporate employees and closed some underused U.S. offices.
Global News sent a request to Starbucks asking how many stores would be closed in Canada and how many Canadian workers could be impacted. A spokesperson did not disclose exact numbers for Canada.
Starbucks shares fell 0.3 per cent Thursday morning as trading opened.

stories.title: This dairy-free dessert is being recalled. Here’s why.
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”

The notice from Sept. 22 affects 500-ml products of So Delicious Dairy Free salted caramel with a cashew base.

The products have a best-before date of Sept. 8 2027, Oct. 15 and 16 in 2027, Feb. 3 and 25 in 2028, and March 30 and 31 in 2028.

Consumers are advised to not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product.

Caitlin Gray, external communications adviser for Sobeys, confirmed on Thursday that the recalled products have been removed from all banner stores in all regions.

The banner stores include FreshCo, Safeway, IGA and Foodland. The products have also been removed from Voilà by Sobeys, an online grocery delivery service owned by Sobeys’ parent company, Empire Company Ltd.

Danone Inc., the company that produces the products, issued its own recall notice in the U.S. on Sept. 15.

The notice affects all pints with best-by dates on and before April 3, 2028, due to the presence of “foreign materials,” such as small stones and other hard objects within the cashew inclusions.

The U.S. notice stated that the issue had been identified via consumer complaints and that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has been informed of the recall. It added that unaffected product is still on shelves in retail stores and product shipped going forward is not affected by the recall.

A similar food recall notice was posted by the Cfia on Jan. 2, 2026, which applied to all pints with best-before dates from Feb. 13 of this year to July 10, 2027.

stories.title: ‘God cleaned the slate’: Ashes pave the road to recovery after B.C. wildfires
stories.summary: Joel Patan says his "life is ashes" now, as he sifts the ruins of his home that was incinerated last month, along with most structures in the small community of Faulder.
stories.author: Darryl Greer
stories.content:
Joel Patan says his “life is ashes” now, as he sifts the ruins of his home that was incinerated last month, along with most structures in the small community of Faulder outside Summerland, B.C.

“It’s just gut-wrenching,” he said.

Patan, who runs an Hvac company, said his family moved onto their “dream property” in December 2024, buying it after flipping two other homes.

He said there were once more than 80 homes in Faulder but most were destroyed by the Bald Range wildfire that roared eastward on the evening of Aug. 7, setting off an evacuation of thousands from the Okanagan communities. An 80-year-old woman who lived in Meadow Valley nearby died suddenly during the evacuation, and Penticton RCMP said it was believed her death was “a result of the wildfire.”

“Running from a fire, grabbing everything you have, like I don’t think people understand. When we talk about ‘we ran from a fire,’ we ran,” Patan said.

“I had RCMP yelling at me, ‘get out of your house’ after I found the cat finally, (they were) basically saying, ‘the flames are right there.'”

The Bald Range fire is still burning but is listed as under control by the B.C. Wildfire Service. Wildfire activity is dying down as summer weather gives way to fall.

And families like Patan’s now face the prospect of rebuilding and recovering from the devastation of losing the roof over their heads.

The wildfire season in B.C. has burned far less area than usual, just 1,350 square kilometres, only about a quarter of the 20-year average.

But it has been one of the most devastating seasons on record for property destruction, with more than 500 homes or other structures destroyed or damaged.

About 150 of those were lost to the Bald Range fire, including 110 in Faulder and Meadow Valley, and 40 in the nearby Okanagan lakeside community of Summerland.

On the northern shores of Okanagan Lake, the Bradley Complex of fires near Vernon brought ruin right to the waterline, some residents watching from boats as their homes burned in early August. Some 230 homes on the lands of the Okanagan Indian Band were lost.

About 240 kilometres to the northwest, the Big Bar Complex of fires destroyed structures on around 120 properties outside Clinton, B.C., while the Brunswick Complex of fires outside Boston Bar in the Fraser Canyon, 200 kilometres northeast of Vancouver, damaged seven structures, four of them homes or cabins.

There is no singular path to recovery, either on an individual or community level.

The Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness said in a statement that “recovery looks different for each community and is led by local governments and First Nations with support from the province, federal partners, non-government organizations, businesses and community members.”

It said it has assigned “community recovery officers” to work with impacted areas and will “continue supporting local governments and First Nations as they lead recovery efforts in their communities, including through recovery planning, governance, co-ordination and available supports.”

Access to Faulder is still restricted, with a checkpoint allowing people in only if they have a permit. Private security guards roam the community to protect against looting.

Blackened trees line Princeton-Summerland Road to Faulder, where homes have been reduced to their foundations, with burnt shells of vehicles a common sight along the winding road into the hills above the valley.

Patan said he’s now dealing with his insurer, considering himself lucky since many Faulder residents were either uninsured or underinsured and are now focused on survival.

The cleanup of damaged properties, he said, also has to factor in other potential hazards, including silica dust, asbestos and other potential contaminants like lead and mercury.

“People are trying to bring their trailers in with no water and that’s another scary thing. They’re bringing in trailers. Some people don’t have electrical. We don’t an adequate source of water right now … but people need somewhere to live.”

The smell of the fire still hangs in the air around the charred foundation of Patan’s home. Broken glass and other debris crunches and cracks under his feet as he surveys the ruin.

Patan descends the stairs into what used to be his basement, pointing out one of his daughter’s porcelain doll’s head in the rubble.

“You’re standing in what above me was my master bedroom,” he said, his arms outstretched to the sky.

Exactly how far his insurance will go is an open question, but he laments all that was lost in the evacuation, including one of his daughter’s first pair of shoes.

Soft-spoken Patan said even though there have been tears and grief, he’s optimistic, a childhood trait.

“My Mom and Dad would tell you, when I had a bad day, I would wake up the next day like it never happened,” he said.

“We’ll build a house that is good for wildfire interface, good for our family, still the same four bedrooms, three baths, things that we May have not liked about our house, we’ll repair, we May fix, but again, we have to see within the confines of our insurance, but whatever we can do to get back what we had, and then it’s just a new beginning, and we just move forward.”

“I will buy my daughters every toy they want,” he added.

Trying to ease burden of recovery

Erick Thompson, senior manager of communications and engagement with the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, said the focus is both on recovery and “providing support to those people who have lost property, lost a home, lost outbuildings.”

“Recovery is a long phase and there’s a lot that goes along with that,” he said. “Remediation of properties, removal of debris, so the Rdos is helping with other agencies to co-ordinate a lot of that.”

“But in the aftermath of this wildfire, recovery is always a challenge and when people have lost a home, especially if they’re not insured, the local government’s role is to advocate for them.”

He said the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention in Vancouver last week saw regional district staff advocating for things like waiving provincial sales tax for people trying to rebuild and help with debris removal.

The regional district said in a statement on Monday that officials at the convention “emphasized the need for measures that help reduce the financial burden on residents rebuilding homes, properties, and livelihoods.”

Relief from provincial sales tax, it said, is “a critical area for provincial consideration.”

“Many residents are facing substantial rebuilding costs, including debris removal, site preparation, construction materials, utility reconnections, and code compliance requirements.”

Police, meanwhile, are still looking into the cause of the Bald Range wildfire.

Penticton RCMP said in a statement this week that its investigators are part of a multi-agency effort to find out the fire’s cause believed to have started in the afternoon hours of Friday, Aug. 7.

“The investigation remains ongoing,” the statement said. “Investigators are seeking to speak with anyone who May have witnessed suspicious activity or observed individuals, vehicles, or other actions in the vicinity of Princeton-Summerland Road and Bathville Road, including the Crump Recreation Site and Trout Creek Recreation Site.”

Brian Callow’s Summerland mushroom farm, What the Fungus, was also a casualty of the fire. The property that housed its operations is now strewn with twisted metal, burned vehicles and equipment and the skeletons of greenhouses.

The property, owned by his business partner whose tree-service business supplied the wood chips to grow the mushrooms, is still strewn with debris and they have yet to obtain a demolition permit, which requires a hazard assessment.

Callow said the District of Summerland has voted to reduce the cost of demolition permits, but the town’s dump remains closed and “getting rid of all the waste seems to be a big issue right now.”

He said the farm wasn’t insured, but they’ve raised money in an online fundraiser and had offers of help from people in the community to replace lost tools and for materials to rebuild.

“But replacing all the specialized mushroom equipment, especially with the tariff war that’s going on with the U.S. and Canada, all of our equipment comes from the U.S.,” he said. “So, I don’t even have a price of replacing that yet. It’ll be quite expensive.”

The fire’s behaviour, he said, was puzzling but it ended up on multiple sides of the property, burning up vehicles and buildings.

An orange Kubota tractor stands out among the rubble, looking like it had been mostly spared by the flames, and Callow said it had been started and moved by firefighters.

“But by the time he got there it had already been half-melted and believe it or not that’s about $20,000 worth of damage on it,” he said.

He said he’d been sent a video of the property engulfed in flames. He didn’t even recognize it as he watched it burn.

‘everybody’s forgotten us’

The destruction of Faulder and evacuation of thousands of people from Summerland were defining moments of B.C.’s wildfire season, playing out on videos and images that flooded social media and went around the world.

But earlier in the season, residents in and around Clinton in the Cariboo region also fled fires that merged into the Big Bar Complex of wildfires.

Steve and Kathy Naseth had lived in their modular home outside Clinton for 25 years, and after the evacuation order was lifted and Steve returned to begin the clean up, “it was devastation.”

“The problem I’m finding is I think everybody’s forgotten about us,” he said.

The couple has insurance, but they said they felt failed by the provincial and regional governments.

While the spotlight was on the evacuation of Summerland, they said those on the outskirts of Clinton haven’t received attention despite being displaced after their homes were destroyed.

The couple, both in their early 60s, is staying in a trailer on their property, but they’ll be staying in Cache Creek during the winter, and face years of rebuilding that has delayed their retirement plans.

Their son-in-law has been helping with cleanup, but they also have hectares of range lands that need to be refenced.

“We don’t have the mobility or the machinery to do that and that’s going to come out of our insurance, which is costly. It takes away from what we can put back into our home,” Kathy said. “We had a four-bedroom modular home. It was beautiful. Now we have to shrink it down to three, possibly even two, just to make sure we’ve got a roof over our head because we don’t know where else to go.”

“This was our retirement home and we were going to sell it and of course then go travelling.”

She said they’ll likely have to work for a few more years because of the loss, even with their insurance because it’s not “going to be enough.”

“We were here for 25 years,” she said. “We don’t have 25 years again to build that all up again, and we’ve lost photos, we’ve lost heirlooms, we’ve lost everything. And we’re not the only ones, like the rest of this valley, they lost everything. Most of them don’t have insurance. ”

Louis and Shorty Fred’s home on the Okanagan Indian Band reserve near Vernon, B.C., was destroyed in the Bradley Creek blaze in early August, and they’re expecting a “long haul” as a phased recovery gets underway.

They said they got a chance to attend their property soon after the fire.

“There’s not much to go through, it’s just all ash and rubble right now,” Shorty Fred said.

Louis Fred said there’s still dangerous trees to be dealt with, and while the road is open and power lines are back up, the cleanup and environmental assessment will be “quite the process.”

They said they don’t plan to rebuild on the same part of their property, moving to a part that wasn’t hit by the fire.

“It’s going to be a while, but we’re really fortunate,” he said.

Louis Fred said he was diagnosed with cancer a few years ago, and a tumour the size a golf ball was found on his spine. He was on crutches for a while.

“I went through one heck of a time,” he said.

They said their Christian faith helped them through the health scare, and they’re relying on it to get them through the aftermath of the fire.

“You don’t realize these things. It’s the little things that we all take for granted nowadays. Until you lose it, then you realize like, hey, you’ve got to take a better look at your life and thank God,” Shorty Fred said.

Louis Fred recalled not being able to eat during his cancer treatment and being grateful after a trip to A&W where he had “the best doggone Mama Burger I ever ate in my life. It tasted so good I was laughing and crying at the same time.”

He said he turned 78 a week after the fire and believes “God cleaned the slate.”

“We have a new opportunity to start over again and do it right this time. Do everything right,” he said. “We feel bad about the things that we did lose that you can’t replace, like all our pictures and stuff back from my grandma. But life goes on.”

content_blocks.text: Joel Patan says his “life is ashes” now, as he sifts the ruins of his home that was incinerated last month, along with most structures in the small community of Faulder outside Summerland, B.C.
“It’s just gut-wrenching,” he said.
Patan, who runs an Hvac company, said his family moved onto their “dream property” in December 2024, buying it after flipping two other homes.

He said there were once more than 80 homes in Faulder but most were destroyed by the Bald Range wildfire that roared eastward on the evening of Aug. 7, setting off an evacuation of thousands from the Okanagan communities. An 80-year-old woman who lived in Meadow Valley nearby died suddenly during the evacuation, and Penticton RCMP said it was believed her death was “a result of the wildfire.”
“Running from a fire, grabbing everything you have, like I don’t think people understand. When we talk about ‘we ran from a fire,’ we ran,” Patan said.
“I had RCMP yelling at me, ‘get out of your house’ after I found the cat finally, (they were) basically saying, ‘the flames are right there.'”
content_blocks.html: “I had RCMP yelling at me, ‘get out of your house’ after I found the cat finally, (they were) basically saying, ‘the flames are right there.'”

content_blocks.text: The Bald Range fire is still burning but is listed as under control by the B.C. Wildfire Service. Wildfire activity is dying down as summer weather gives way to fall.
And families like Patan’s now face the prospect of rebuilding and recovering from the devastation of losing the roof over their heads.
The wildfire season in B.C. has burned far less area than usual, just 1,350 square kilometres, only about a quarter of the 20-year average.
But it has been one of the most devastating seasons on record for property destruction, with more than 500 homes or other structures destroyed or damaged.
About 150 of those were lost to the Bald Range fire, including 110 in Faulder and Meadow Valley, and 40 in the nearby Okanagan lakeside community of Summerland.

On the northern shores of Okanagan Lake, the Bradley Complex of fires near Vernon brought ruin right to the waterline, some residents watching from boats as their homes burned in early August. Some 230 homes on the lands of the Okanagan Indian Band were lost.

About 240 kilometres to the northwest, the Big Bar Complex of fires destroyed structures on around 120 properties outside Clinton, B.C., while the Brunswick Complex of fires outside Boston Bar in the Fraser Canyon, 200 kilometres northeast of Vancouver, damaged seven structures, four of them homes or cabins.
There is no singular path to recovery, either on an individual or community level.

The Ministry of Emergency Management and Climate Readiness said in a statement that “recovery looks different for each community and is led by local governments and First Nations with support from the province, federal partners, non-government organizations, businesses and community members.”

It said it has assigned “community recovery officers” to work with impacted areas and will “continue supporting local governments and First Nations as they lead recovery efforts in their communities, including through recovery planning, governance, co-ordination and available supports.”
Access to Faulder is still restricted, with a checkpoint allowing people in only if they have a permit. Private security guards roam the community to protect against looting.

Blackened trees line Princeton-Summerland Road to Faulder, where homes have been reduced to their foundations, with burnt shells of vehicles a common sight along the winding road into the hills above the valley.
Patan said he’s now dealing with his insurer, considering himself lucky since many Faulder residents were either uninsured or underinsured and are now focused on survival.
The cleanup of damaged properties, he said, also has to factor in other potential hazards, including silica dust, asbestos and other potential contaminants like lead and mercury.

“People are trying to bring their trailers in with no water and that’s another scary thing. They’re bringing in trailers. Some people don’t have electrical. We don’t an adequate source of water right now … but people need somewhere to live.”
The smell of the fire still hangs in the air around the charred foundation of Patan’s home. Broken glass and other debris crunches and cracks under his feet as he surveys the ruin.
Patan descends the stairs into what used to be his basement, pointing out one of his daughter’s porcelain doll’s head in the rubble.
“You’re standing in what above me was my master bedroom,” he said, his arms outstretched to the sky.
Exactly how far his insurance will go is an open question, but he laments all that was lost in the evacuation, including one of his daughter’s first pair of shoes.
Soft-spoken Patan said even though there have been tears and grief, he’s optimistic, a childhood trait.
“My Mom and Dad would tell you, when I had a bad day, I would wake up the next day like it never happened,” he said.

“We’ll build a house that is good for wildfire interface, good for our family, still the same four bedrooms, three baths, things that we May have not liked about our house, we’ll repair, we May fix, but again, we have to see within the confines of our insurance, but whatever we can do to get back what we had, and then it’s just a new beginning, and we just move forward.”
“I will buy my daughters every toy they want,” he added.
Trying to ease burden of recovery
content_blocks.html: TRYING TO EASE BURDEN OF RECOVERY

content_blocks.text: Erick Thompson, senior manager of communications and engagement with the Regional District of Okanagan Similkameen, said the focus is both on recovery and “providing support to those people who have lost property, lost a home, lost outbuildings.”

“Recovery is a long phase and there’s a lot that goes along with that,” he said. “Remediation of properties, removal of debris, so the Rdos is helping with other agencies to co-ordinate a lot of that.”
“But in the aftermath of this wildfire, recovery is always a challenge and when people have lost a home, especially if they’re not insured, the local government’s role is to advocate for them.”

He said the Union of British Columbia Municipalities convention in Vancouver last week saw regional district staff advocating for things like waiving provincial sales tax for people trying to rebuild and help with debris removal.

The regional district said in a statement on Monday that officials at the convention “emphasized the need for measures that help reduce the financial burden on residents rebuilding homes, properties, and livelihoods.”
Relief from provincial sales tax, it said, is “a critical area for provincial consideration.”
“Many residents are facing substantial rebuilding costs, including debris removal, site preparation, construction materials, utility reconnections, and code compliance requirements.”
Police, meanwhile, are still looking into the cause of the Bald Range wildfire.
Penticton RCMP said in a statement this week that its investigators are part of a multi-agency effort to find out the fire’s cause believed to have started in the afternoon hours of Friday, Aug. 7.

“The investigation remains ongoing,” the statement said. “Investigators are seeking to speak with anyone who May have witnessed suspicious activity or observed individuals, vehicles, or other actions in the vicinity of Princeton-Summerland Road and Bathville Road, including the Crump Recreation Site and Trout Creek Recreation Site.”

Brian Callow’s Summerland mushroom farm, What the Fungus, was also a casualty of the fire. The property that housed its operations is now strewn with twisted metal, burned vehicles and equipment and the skeletons of greenhouses.

The property, owned by his business partner whose tree-service business supplied the wood chips to grow the mushrooms, is still strewn with debris and they have yet to obtain a demolition permit, which requires a hazard assessment.

He said he’d been sent a video of the property engulfed in flames. He didn’t even recognize it as he watched it burn.
‘everybody’s forgotten us’

stories.title: Global Business Forum kicks off in Banff, Alta. under theme ‘thriving in chaos’
stories.summary: Lois Mitchell, the former Alberta lieutenant-governor who co-chairs the forum, says rarely have participants seen such turmoil and rupture in the international order.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
The serene alpine setting will stand in stark contrast to the theme of this year’s Global Business Forum conference: “thriving in chaos.”

It’s the 27th year for the conference, held annually at the stately Banff Springs Hotel nestled in the Rocky Mountains west of Calgary.

Lois Mitchell, the former Alberta lieutenant-governor who co-chairs the forum, says rarely have participants seen such turmoil and rupture in the international order.

Sessions are to cover global security, strained Canada-U.S. relations, space travel, artificial intelligence and more.

Among the speakers are Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen, former Canadian ambassador to the United States Kirsten Hillman and Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy.

Executives with Shell Canada, Canadian National Railway Co. and Telus Corp. are also on tap to share their perspectives.

stories.title: Suzuki says Carney driving Canada ‘into a ditch’ on climate
stories.summary: Suzuki said he now feels he was ‘wilfully blind’ to Carney’s promises of action on climate
stories.author: Nick Murray
stories.content:
David Suzuki said that when Prime Minister Mark Carney was first elected last year, he celebrated. Having met and interviewed the prime minister before, the national environmentalist icon said he knew Carney understood the challenges of climate change.

But in an interview with The Canadian Press, Suzuki said he now feels he was “wilfully blind” to Carney’s promises of action on climate, despite warnings from his longtime friend the late Stephen Lewis, who predicted the agenda of a banker – and now politician – would supersede Carney’s views on addressing climate change.

“I don’t see that there’s going to be any deviation from the driving of our country into the ditch,” Suzuki said.

He acknowledges that Carney’s actions come as Canadians’ views on climate have shifted to other priorities.

“I think that’s because of that disconnect of what are the really basic things are that keep us alive,” he said.

For decades, Suzuki brought millions of Canadians into the world of science and nature. From their living rooms, viewers of The Nature of Things could learn about the intersection of humanity and nature and its impact on the planet.

Suzuki, 90, retired from hosting the show four years ago, but still wants to talk to Canadians about the environment. This time though, the educational message is tinged with exasperation.

Canadians and people around the world have their priorities wrong, he said.

“Brazil’s Amazon, the greatest terrestrial ecosystem on the planet, has no economic value until it is logged, mined, dammed, or grows soy, cattle, or houses,” Suzuki said.

“So if that doesn’t tell you right there what kind of a f--ked-up system we have, that is exploiting the very things that keep us alive. And we don’t put any value on it.”

Canada’s record on battling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change has been spotty. The federal government has committed to multiple different targets since 1990 and despite implementing dozens of new policies to cut emissions, it has never met any of its targets.

Since taking office in March, 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney has pushed many of those policies aside in the name of economic prosperity – particularly as Canadians grapple with the cost of living on a planet that is facing increasingly destructive weather events every year.

He cancelled the consumer carbon tax on his first day in office, repealed a mandate to phase out gas-powered cars in favour of electric models, and scrapped an emissions cap on oil and gas production.

Carney said most of those policies were too divisive and costly and he is looking to introduce cuts over a longer term, with investments in clean technology. He also has backed the idea of another oil pipeline to the West Coast and has adjusted some policies to make it more likely.

Which one of those actions made Suzuki raise his eyebrows the most?

“I haven’t read any of it,” Suzuki said.

“The problem is, it doesn’t really matter to me. Fundamentally, the problem is that the underlying systems that we’ve developed to guide, shape, manage human behaviour have left out the most fundamental thing, which is that our very survival and well-being depends on Mother Earth.

“If you look at our legal, our political and our economic systems, the planet has been left out. The economy is the system that is driving us on the destructive path.”

He doesn’t even give much credit to the government of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose government enacted some of the most climate friendly policies Canada has ever had. Even Trudeau, Suzuki argues, didn’t aim high enough.

Suzuki said Carney “understands very clearly what the challenges of climate change represent.”

But he said Carney is advocating for climate action as a banker, with an agenda that suits that title.

“He still believes the economy must be kept going the way it is and that it can be used to keep emissions down and keep the economy going,” he said. “I think it’s impossible.”

Carney was in Strasbourg, France last week to address the European Parliament, ON a mission to deepen ties with the EU – particularly on trade, as Canada tried to lessen its dependence on the United States. Canada’s offer to the EU is largely based on its access to resources, including natural gas and critical minerals, but Suzuki said it’s a catch-22.

“(Carney) is standing up to (Trump). Thank God for Mr. Carney for doing that. But our arrangements with Europe, they’re all based on economics,” Suzuki said.

“What does Canada have to sell to these other countries to take our dependence away from the United States? It’s going to be minerals, forests, water, and it’s not based on the fundamental protection of those things. It’s all going to what economic value can we extract. So I think we’re kind of hooped.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

Suzuki said there are two things the government can do right now to get the country’s climate action back on track: set hard targets and declare an emergency.

“When you declare a state of emergency, all these economic and political arguments disappear,” he said. “You’ve got to deal with that crisis now, and that’s what we need. And Mr. Carney could go a long way if he would take his party now and declare state of emergency and get it going now.”

Suzuki also said the media has failed to fact-check messages from world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump.

Suzuki said he is still saying the same things he always has, but he’s not sure it’s being received the way it used to be, and figuring out how to fix that has left him at a loss.

“There was a time when, believe it or not, Canadians knew who the hell I was and they listened to me. They took me seriously. But you know, the world is so different now, that I think that kind of celebrity is just not possible.”

Carney said most of those policies were too divisive and costly and he is looking to introduce cuts over a longer term, with investments in clean technology. He also has backed the idea of another oil pipeline to the West Coast and has adjusted some policies to make it more likely.
Which one of those actions made Suzuki raise his eyebrows the most?
“I haven’t read any of it,” Suzuki said.

“The problem is, it doesn’t really matter to me. Fundamentally, the problem is that the underlying systems that we’ve developed to guide, shape, manage human behaviour have left out the most fundamental thing, which is that our very survival and well-being depends on Mother Earth.
“If you look at our legal, our political and our economic systems, the planet has been left out. The economy is the system that is driving us on the destructive path.”

He doesn’t even give much credit to the government of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose government enacted some of the most climate friendly policies Canada has ever had. Even Trudeau, Suzuki argues, didn’t aim high enough.
Suzuki said Carney “understands very clearly what the challenges of climate change represent.”
But he said Carney is advocating for climate action as a banker, with an agenda that suits that title.
“He still believes the economy must be kept going the way it is and that it can be used to keep emissions down and keep the economy going,” he said. “I think it’s impossible.”

Carney was in Strasbourg, France last week to address the European Parliament, ON a mission to deepen ties with the EU – particularly on trade, as Canada tried to lessen its dependence on the United States. Canada’s offer to the EU is largely based on its access to resources, including natural gas and critical minerals, but Suzuki said it’s a catch-22.
“(Carney) is standing up to (Trump). Thank God for Mr. Carney for doing that. But our arrangements with Europe, they’re all based on economics,” Suzuki said.

“What does Canada have to sell to these other countries to take our dependence away from the United States? It’s going to be minerals, forests, water, and it’s not based on the fundamental protection of those things. It’s all going to what economic value can we extract. So I think we’re kind of hooped.”
In a statement, a spokesperson for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
Suzuki said there are two things the government can do right now to get the country’s climate action back on track: set hard targets and declare an emergency.

“When you declare a state of emergency, all these economic and political arguments disappear,” he said. “You’ve got to deal with that crisis now, and that’s what we need. And Mr. Carney could go a long way if he would take his party now and declare state of emergency and get it going now.”
Suzuki also said the media has failed to fact-check messages from world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump.
Suzuki said he is still saying the same things he always has, but he’s not sure it’s being received the way it used to be, and figuring out how to fix that has left him at a loss.

“There was a time when, believe it or not, Canadians knew who the hell I was and they listened to me. They took me seriously. But you know, the world is so different now, that I think that kind of celebrity is just not possible.”

stories.title: Live updates: Kenneth Law sentencing hearing enters second day with more grieving family members set to speak
stories.summary: Ontario man who sold lethal substances online pleaded guilty to aiding 14 suicides in Canada and admitted to role in dozens more in U.K.
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
A Toronto man whose son died by suicide after purchasing poison from Kenneth Law called for a public inquiry while speaking at a Wednesday sentencing hearing .

Stephen Mitchell called on the Ontario government to take action, as he and other relatives of Mr. Law’s victims delivered harrowing public victim-impact statements on the first day of the hearing. Mr. Mitchell’s son, Stephen Jr., died just weeks before Mr. Law’s arrest in 2023. Mr. Mitchell criticized Canadian law enforcement for not recognizing the threat that Mr. Law posed before a British newspaper exposed his business in the spring of 2023.

He said grieving families want to know why the 61-year-old Mississauga engineer was able to operate an online business selling toxic salts and other deadly paraphernalia for years before his arrest. By the time Mr. Law was stopped, he had shipped more than 1,200 deadly parcels, including 330 to Britain and 157 within Canada, mostly to young people at risk of suicide.

Mr. Mitchell said that earlier intervention could have saved lives, including his son’s. “Premier Ford, I respectfully ask you to authorize an independent third-party inquiry into what occurred,” he said outside the court.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the idea of a public inquiry earlier this year. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Crown attorney Peter Westgate said the court will hear victim-impact statements from a total of 74 people this week.

In court documents filed ahead of his sentencing hearings earlier this month , Kenneth Law had told a psychiatrist that he considers himself a “pathfinder” and not a psychopath.

“I was just trying to serve a need that I thought was humane,” Mr. Law said during interviews with psychiatrist Jonathan Rootenberg conducted in a Lindsay, Ont., jail this July.

“I’m not a diabolical madman.”

In the post-conviction medical interviews, Mr. Law describes his upbringing and his crimes in his own words, while arguing that much of what he did was morally defensible even if it violated the law.

“Now I can look back and say that what I was doing was legally wrong ... that’s why I pled guilty. It’s about taking ownership and responsibility for your actions,” Mr. Law told the psychiatrist. “We all learn from our mistakes.”

Read the full story here.

- Colin Freeze, Mike Hager

The sentencing hearing is scheduled to run for several more days as the families of victims from Canada and the U.K. provide victim-impact statements.

Kenneth Law’s victims in Ontario included two 16-year-olds, a 21-year-old found dead by his brother and a 19-year-old honour-roll student, as well as dozens more in the U.K. whose deaths he has admitted a role in.

Here are five of their stories .

In May, Kenneth Law pleaded guilty in an Ontario court to aiding in the suicides of 14 people in Ontario, and also admitted to assisting in 79 other deaths in Britain by shipping toxic substances and suffocation equipment to people seeking to die.

Prior to pleading guilty to the 14 counts of aiding suicide, Mr. Law signed a lengthy agreed statement of facts, which was read aloud in court by prosecutors.

In the agreed facts, Law admits to shipping hundreds of packages of his products from a Canada Post office near his Mississauga home. Prosecutors named dozens of countries that received shipments but said most went to the United States (431 packages), Britain (330) and Canada (157).

- The Canadian Press

Nearly four years since a coroner’s report on woman’s death in the U.K. listed details police later linked to Kenneth Law in Ontario, the marathon criminal proceedings in Canada are nearing a close.

But the path to Law’s guilty pleas for aiding 14 suicides in Canada – and his admission of involvement in dozens more abroad – has not been a straight line.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case .

stories.title: What to watch this weekend: Binge this rich-people thriller The Perfect Lie
stories.summary: Or try a comedy about (rumoured) brothers Woody Harrelson and Matthew McConaughey
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
The Perfect Lie, Netflix

Netflix knows exactly what it’s doing. The streamer has retitled its Dutch miniseries De Eetclub – which directly translates to “The Dinner Club” – as The Perfect Lie in English, and it’s become a hit with subtitles.

The seven-part thriller, based on a novel popular in the Netherlands, does indeed feel like a cross between the narratives and tones of popular American beautiful-rich-people shows The Perfect Couple and Big Little Lies . (Singalongs during car rides to school? Check. A big choreographed number with the whole cast? Check.)

The Perfect Lie follows four wealthy, irresponsible couples living seaside in Bergen, whose kids go to the same Waldorf school. The show opens with a police interrogation of the main mom character Karen (Loes Haverkort) – and flashes back to the events leading up to and after a fire that left the group’s most handsome husband, Evert (Edwin Jonker), dead and that nearly consumed his wife Babette (Noortje Herlaar) and their two kids as well.

Drinking, drugs and games of truth or dare are all involved. This is bingeable pulp, elevated by a few excellent grounded performances by the European ensemble – especially Rifka Lodeizen as a wounded woman whose husband stops sleeping with her.

Brothers, Apple TV

This new stoner comedy, co-created by Canuck writer for screen and stage David West Read ( Schitt’s Creek , & Juliet ), is “based on a true rumour,” as the opening disclaimer proclaims.

Woody Harrelson, playing a fictionalized version of himself, shows up one day at his old True Detective co-star Matthew McConaughey’s Texas ranch with his wife and daughters in tow. There, he stumbles upon the possibility that his father may have been his friend’s father, too.

Woody keeps this a secret for no clear reason beyond needing a narrative arc for a season of TV. He settles in for a long visit to help manage Matthew’s run for Texas governor, and get on the nerves of his friend’s wife (played by Natalie Martinez).

The first episode is a little rough in writing and execution, but the second settles into an Odd Couple rhythm. The gentle friction between Woody and Matthew over veganism versus hunting is easily resolved by getting blazed together. Harrelson is better at playing himself in an amusing manner, and at hitting comic beats; McConaughey does the Lincoln ad version of himself over and over.

Blue Heron, Crave

Director Sophy Romvari’s deeply affecting feature debut (streaming Sept. 25) follows a large Hungarian-Canadian family as they figure out how to deal with the difficult behaviour of their teenage son Jeremy (Edik Beddoes, in a haunting performance).

The parents quickly hit the limits of social services and understanding of mental health in 1990s B.C.; the young kids try to ignore or observe from a distance. The moving third act of the movie shifts time frames – and, in another way, doesn’t – to follow sister Sasha (Amy Zimmer) still trying to understand and process what happened with her brother.

“Ultimately, Blue Heron is an epic exploring the power and fissures of memory,” The Globe and Mail’s Barry Hertz wrote in his Critic’s Pick review . “But there is no chance that audiences will ever forget what Romvari has accomplished here.”

I Used to Be Funny, CBC Gem

Another Globe Critic’s Pick film lands on another Canadian streamer on Sept. 25. Written and directed by Ally Pankiw, this dark dramedy follows stand-up comedian Sam ( I Love LA ’s Rachel Sennott) as she struggles with PTSD after a sexual assault.

“I love how Pankiw drops important pieces of information in almost casual ways, because she knows that’s how people, especially funny people, talk,” Johanna Schneller wrote in her review . “Listen for the line that Sam’s ex, Noah (Ennis Esmer), said in the immediate aftermath of Sam’s assault – the one he wishes he could take back, the one she can’t get over. Huge traumas crash your life, but the smallest betrayals can break your heart.”

Perfect Storm, Disney+

Empathie , Florence Longpré’s wonderful drama about a prison psychologist, won 14 awards at the Prix Gémeaux last week, a record haul for a single season of a show at Canada’s awards for French-language television. This was something the whole country could celebrate: The Crave drama has a strong fan base among English-speaking Canadians because it has been distributed on the bilingual streaming service with subtitles right from its debut.

Readers of this column are less likely to have watched L’oeil du cyclone , the long-running, lighthearted Radio-Canada show about a single mother of three (Christine Beaulieu) that finally eked out Best Comedy at the Gémaux for its sixth season. That’s because CBC/Radio-Canada is a linguistically divided public broadcaster that thinks like a prestreaming private broadcaster, and rarely makes the content it commissions with your tax dollars available in both official languages.

But the first four seasons of L’oeil du cyclone are now available with English subtitles for the first time on Disney+ in Canada, under the title Perfect Storm . I sampled a few episodes and found it an enjoyably modern family sitcom, kind of a Quebec corollary to CTV’s Children Ruin Everything .

Editor’s note: A previous version of this article stated that Matthew McConaughey’s wife in Brothers was played by his real wife. While the character in question is inspired by his real wife, the role is played by actor Natalie Martinez.

stories.title: This dairy-free dessert is being recalled. Here’s why.
stories.summary: The Canadian Food Inspection Agency has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (Cfia) has published a recall for a brand of dairy-free frozen desserts due to “plastic-like” and “gravel-like fragments.”

The notice from Sept. 22 affects 500-ml products of So Delicious Dairy Free salted caramel with a cashew base.

The products have a best-before date of Sept. 8 2027, Oct. 15 and 16 in 2027, Feb. 3 and 25 in 2028, and March 30 and 31 in 2028.

Consumers are advised to not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected product.

Caitlin Gray, external communications adviser for Sobeys, confirmed on Thursday that the recalled products have been removed from all banner stores in all regions.

The banner stores include FreshCo, Safeway, IGA and Foodland. The products have also been removed from Voilà by Sobeys, an online grocery delivery service owned by Sobeys’ parent company, Empire Company Ltd.

Danone Inc., the company that produces the products, issued its own recall notice in the U.S. on Sept. 15.

The notice affects all pints with best-by dates on and before April 3, 2028, due to the presence of “foreign materials,” such as small stones and other hard objects within the cashew inclusions.

The U.S. notice stated that the issue had been identified via consumer complaints and that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has been informed of the recall. It added that unaffected product is still on shelves in retail stores and product shipped going forward is not affected by the recall.

A similar food recall notice was posted by the Cfia on Jan. 2, 2026, which applied to all pints with best-before dates from Feb. 13 of this year to July 10, 2027.

stories.title: $11.5M from Sturgeon Lake trust helped fund Rath firm’s Tallcree payment: receiver
stories.summary: Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath’s firm took $11.5 million from one First Nation trust to help him make a court-ordered refund to another First Nation, court documents show.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
A court-appointed receiver says Alberta separatist leader Jeffrey Rath’s firm moved $11.5 million from a First Nation trust it controlled to help cover a court-ordered payment it owed to another First Nation client, Global News has learned.

The receiver’s latest filings show that on Jan. 23, 2024, the Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation Trust’s bank accounts issued two cheques totalling $11.5 million to RathPC. The next day, the firm moved the money into another RathPC account and commingled it with other funds.

Within a week, RathPC paid $8.5 million into the Alberta Court of King’s Bench, which was deciding whether the money belonged to Tallcree First Nation or its trust, filings show.

“Without the transfers from the Scotiabank Accounts, the Rath Parties would not have had sufficient funds in [the Rath PC account] to cover the court-ordered payment of $8,518,075 into Court in the Tallcree dispute,” the receiver’s report states.

Both First Nations retained the Foothills lawyer and his firm, RathPC, to pursue claims against the federal government, resulting in settlements worth tens of millions of dollars. The firm then became trustee of the funds held for beneficiaries, including minors.

In 2017, Rath’s professional corporation, RathPC, collected $11.5 million under a contingency fee agreement with Tallcree after the band settled a $ 57.6 million claim with the federal government. A judge later ruled the payment unreasonable and ordered the firm to repay $8.5 million.

“At each step of this proceeding, our worst fears come true,” says Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake. saying the repayment was made by taking money from “the children of our Nation.”

“It is enraging that he is still being given a platform in this province, and this is hardly being mentioned,” Sunshine said. “This will have a generational impact.”

Rath did not respond to questions from Global News.

1:51 Alberta separatism proponent shares transition plan for independence

The revelation comes as Rath finds himself at the centre of a legal maelstrom. Sturgeon Lake and Tallcree First Nations are each suing Rath and his firm, alleging that RathPC improperly withdrew tens of millions of dollars from its trusts and withheld financial statements that would have revealed the withdrawals.

In July, Tallcree obtained an interim Mareva injunction, which is a court order that freezes a person’s or company’s assets and prohibits a defendant from hiding or moving funds that could otherwise satisfy a future judgment. A final determination of the order is pending.

That same month, the Alberta court also appointed a receiver, financial advisory firm AlixPartners, to trace the funds the First Nations claim are missing.

Global News reported that, around the same time, financial auditor Doane Grant Thornton raised concerns about several withdrawals from the Sturgeon Lake trust in 2024, including two in January, for $9.8 million and $1.7 million.

Rath said the payments were retroactive administrative fees covering 2017 to 2024, according to court documents.

Those two withdrawals, the receiver says, went towards Tallcree’s multi-million-dollar, court-ordered repayment.

Rath has filed four appeals challenging the trustee removal, the asset freeze, the receivership and the receiver’s access to the firm’s records.

Tallcree and Sturgeon Lake’s allegations remain contested and have not been finally adjudicated.

Rath lost $3M trading bullion: receiver

The $8.5-million refund involved a complicated path through RathPC’s accounts.

RathPC first paid the money into court, allegedly using the proceeds of millions transferred from Sturgeon Lake, while Tallcree and the firm disputed whether the refund belonged to the Nation or its settlement trust.

Eventually, on Nov. 5, 2025, the court ordered RathPC to return the money to the Tallcree trust. Instead, 12 days later, court-filed banking records show that the money was quickly converted into $8 million in bullion, plus a $500,000 draft payable to Rath.

From there, the money trail widens. RathPC’s account at Bow Valley Credit Union became the hub for millions of dollars in precious-metals trading, according to the receiver.

Between November 2025 and March 2026, $11.4 million was transferred from the account to purchase bullion in a series of trades, according to the receiver’s court documents.

The sales yielded almost $8 million, resulting in an estimated net trading loss of about $3.25 million due to market fluctuations, the receiver states.

The receiver also identified another $200,971 in physical gold and silver purchases, but says it does not know where those coins are.

It says Rath’s lack of cooperation has hampered its investigation and that it has been unable to interview him about the disputed transactions.

When asked for comment, Rath said he would not respond.

Meanwhile, as the legal battles continue, Rath has remained active in Alberta separatist politics on social media and in interviews, calling for Premier Danielle Smith’s resignation and promoting separatism ahead of the province’s Oct. 19 referendum.

stories.title: David Eby’s BC election gamble
stories.summary: British Columbians will be heading to the polls two years ahead of schedule this fall.
stories.author: Joseph Ryan
stories.content:
British Columbians will be heading to the polls two years ahead of schedule this fall.

The snap call by Premier David Eby comes amid turmoil within the B.C. Conservative Party, his chief opponents, and at a sensitive time for the province, as the government has attempted to deal with controversy around Indigenous rights legislation.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks with Shannon Waters, a B.C. political and environmental reporter for The Narwhal, about the gamble Eby took by dropping the writ, the drama surrounding the B.C. Conservative Party, and how much of an election issue Indigenous rights and DRIPA might be.

stories.title: Dolphin shipped out of Marineland dies in Spain after move
stories.summary: Echo is the fifth animal from the closed Niagara Falls tourist attraction to die after a massive movement of whales and dolphins over the summer
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
A dolphin shipped out of Marineland has died in Spain, making it the fifth animal from the closed Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction to die after a massive movement of whales and dolphins over the summer.

Oceanografic Valencia said Echo, a blind Black Sea bottlenose dolphin believed to be 30 years old, died Wednesday.

“In recent hours, Echo began experiencing difficulties swallowing and respiratory problems and was transferred to the medical pool,” Oceanografic said in a statement.

“Her condition deteriorated rapidly throughout yesterday and, despite the care provided by Oceanografic’s animal care and veterinary teams, she passed away overnight.”

Echo, along with three other dolphins and two belugas, was sent to the Spanish aquarium on Aug. 26 in an epic 19-hour voyage from the shuttered Niagara Falls, Ont., tourist attraction.

One of those belugas, Jelly Bean, died last week .

Oceanografic is conducting necropsies on both animals along with an examination by pathology experts at CEU Cardenal Herrera University to try to understand the cause of death.

“The other four animals rescued from Canada are doing well and remain under the care and monitoring of Oceanografic’s professional teams,” Oceanografic said.

“Echo’s loss is an especially difficult moment for the Oceanografic team, who had been particularly dedicated to her care and well-being since her arrival due to her specific needs.”

Fourth Marineland whale dies after relocation from Niagara Falls park

Four belugas and one dolphin have now died since Marineland shipped out 30 belugas and four dolphins to five different parks over the summer.

Three of those belugas died at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago along with one of the park’s resident belugas.

Marineland closed in 2024 and had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for its whales. If they were not moved, the park was set to euthanize them.

Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson nixed a deal Marineland had with Chimelong Ocean Kingdom in China, saying it was not in the whales’ best interest to send them there.

She said China did not have the same laws as Canada, which banned whale and dolphin captivity in 2019 but grandfathered in Marineland’s animals.

In response, Marineland said it would euthanize the whales if it did not get emergency funding, a threat that made international headlines.

Marineland pivoted to a consortium of American and Spanish aquariums for help. The move of its whales and dolphins began in mid-July and wrapped up by the end of August.

Both Shedd and Oceanografic are investigating to better understand what caused the animals’ deaths.

Veterinarians from all parks were at Marineland in the months leading up to the move and cleared the animals for transport, as did Thompson, who signed off on the moves after receiving updated health information.
