stories.title: Trump and Xi May extend their truce, but Canada still faces a rare earth squeeze
stories.summary: A U.S.-China deal could ensure Chinese rare-earth supply for Canadian manufacturers, but that comes at a cost.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Trade tensions are becoming a familiar problem for Washington and this week President Donald Trump is putting his deal-making skills to the test as he hosts China’s president at the White House.

Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, D.C., ON Wednesday, and he and Trump will hold talks on Thursday. They are expected to discuss Iran, Taiwan, and AI safety standards , but the main focus will be on trade — and particularly U.S. access to Chinese rare-earth magnets and processed materials that also feed Canadian supply chains.

The summit comes nearly a year after Xi and Trump forged a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, suspending selected retaliatory measures — including some Chinese export controls on rare-earth magnets and critical materials — and reducing some U.S. tariffs.

Now, that truce is set to expire on Nov. 10, and Trump is seeking an economic victory ahead of November’s midterms. He also must ensure the continued flow of Chinese rare-earth exports to U.S. manufacturers.

Canadian leaders will be watching for any sign of a deal, but trade analysts say Ottawa is likely to lose either way, whether Xi and Trump fail or succeed in coming to an agreement. A collapsed truce could disrupt Canadian manufacturers that rely on Chinese magnets and processed rare earths, while an extension could bring short-term stability but leave Canada dependent on Chinese supply. An extended truce would also leave Canada exposed to a wider U.S.-China trade deal that diverts sales and investment to the U.S.

“No matter what happens, the Canadians are going to be in a position [where] they’re worried about how much of the piece of the pie they’re going to lose,” said Stephen Nagy, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute.

China, pushing for greater stability, wants to extend the truce until the end of the Trump presidency, while the White House is pushing for just a six-month extension.

U.S. and China extend trade truce by two months as Xi met by Trump for start of visit

How China leveraged its critical minerals dominance over the U.S.

The rationale for the shorter extension, explained Dominic Chiu, a senior China and Northeast Asia analyst at Eurasia Group, is that the U.S. believes “it gives them more leverage to extract concessions and to continue the momentum to negotiate with the Chinese … in exchange for additional extensions along the way.”

The report on Washington’s Section 301 structural excess capacity investigation against China has reportedly been punted until after the summit, but that probe May be factoring into Trump’s timeline demands.

“Giving more than six months would effectively be indicating that the 301 investigation is null,” said China scholar Anna Ashton, of Ashton Intelligence.

“The U.S. side will want to have those 301 investigation findings as future leverage for the next round of talks,” she added, noting she expects a six-month extension of the truce to result.

Few expect major breakthroughs this week, but most of the trade watchers said a six-month to year-long truce extension is likely. Chiu said he’s mostly anticipating pomp and circumstance rather than tangible deliverables on Thursday. He expects a truce agreement to come closer to the November deadline. Neither Ashton nor Chiu, however, anticipate any concrete Chinese commitments on rare-earth licensing volumes, turnaround times, minimum supply levels, or enforcement.

If the truce lapses, Canadian manufacturers could face more costly and less reliable access to Chinese magnets and processed rare-earth materials. That could increase pressure for Ottawa to de-risk more quickly by building the infrastructure and industry Canada needs to mine and process rare earths domestically.

But there will be no quick Canadian replacement. Building rare-earth capacity takes years of sustained financing, permitting, infrastructure, and technical expertise. The Carney government has already signalled support for expanding the sector, but it will take several years.

“You don’t just open up supply chains in these rare earths quickly,” said Mark A. Smith, CEO of Colorado-based critical-minerals developer NioCorp Developments.

But Reza Hasmath, a politics professor at the University of Alberta, argues that a longer period of stability could be more useful to Canada’s industrial strategy than a supply crisis. A longer truce, he said, would give Canada more time to build the processing capacity and infrastructure it needs.

“From a strictly rare earth perspective, though, I would suggest that the greater the extension, the better it is for (Canada) because it gives manufacturers much more stability, but it also buys us time to develop that industry a bit more,” he said.

More broadly, however, he sees better U.S.-China relations as bad news for Ottawa.

“When Chinese-U.S. relations are terrible, that gives (Canada) the most leverage, and when they are less tense and when there is a greater truce, generally speaking, it’s not to (Canada’s) advantage,” he said.

Hasmath said a truce is still preferable for Canadian manufacturers, but he explained that Washington has more incentive to seek Canadian alternatives when its relationship with Beijing deteriorates.

According to Ashton, no truce or a shorter truce extension could give Beijing more incentive to preserve commercial options with Canada. That could boost Ottawa’s bargaining leverage as it seeks to extend Chinese tariff relief on Canadian canola meal, lobster, and crab, which is set to expire in December.

Nagy cautions, however, that if the U.S. administration takes a harder line on Beijing, Trump May demand Ottawa’s alignment under threat of more tariffs.

But the same stability that protects manufacturers could weaken the political case for building Canadian alternatives, some warned. More predictable Chinese supply could ease the political urgency — and public-financing momentum — to build Canadian processing capacity.

“On the whole, it’s beneficial to industry at large, but it could slow down the momentum for the critical minerals industry in Canada specifically,” said Chiu.

Smith said the underlying case for diversification should survive either way.

“We cannot sit here and be dependent on any single country for any single item. We have to have alternatives,” he said.

But Hasmath and Nagy agree an extended truce could pose another downside: a wider U.S.-China trade deal could undercut Canadian exporters.

The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese

Most trade watchers believe Beijing will agree — whether it’s this week or in the weeks to come — to buy more U.S. agricultural goods and Boeing aircraft and that the two sides will announce an intention to begin AI-related security talks. Washington May offer China limited relief on access to lower-grade semiconductors, and it May reduce tariffs on some Chinese imports.

Those possible U.S. commercial wins could hurt Canada, because if Beijing buys more U.S. products, Canadian exporters May lose share in those markets.

“The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese,” Hasmath said, pointing to three sectors that could be hit hard: agriculture, aircraft, and LNG.

The tradeoff is a catch-22, he said. Canada benefits when a truce keeps Chinese rare-earth materials flowing to manufacturers, but it has more geopolitical leverage when Washington needs non-Chinese alternatives.

So this week’s summit will not provide Canada with a win or a simple choice. An extended truce would help manufacturers with rare-earth supplies, but it would also prolong their reliance on China — and possibly weaken Ottawa’s push to build domestic processing capacity.

The test will be how Canada uses any period of stability a truce might bring. Will it use the time to build the infrastructure and domestic processing capability it needs to supply rare-earth materials itself? How it responds will determine whether the next U.S.-China trade spat leaves Canada with more leverage — or bigger supply problems.

“When Chinese-U.S. relations are terrible, that gives (Canada) the most leverage, and when they are less tense and when there is a greater truce, generally speaking, it’s not to (Canada’s) advantage,” he said.
Hasmath said a truce is still preferable for Canadian manufacturers, but he explained that Washington has more incentive to seek Canadian alternatives when its relationship with Beijing deteriorates.

According to Ashton, no truce or a shorter truce extension could give Beijing more incentive to preserve commercial options with Canada. That could boost Ottawa’s bargaining leverage as it seeks to extend Chinese tariff relief on Canadian canola meal, lobster, and crab, which is set to expire in December.
Nagy cautions, however, that if the U.S. administration takes a harder line on Beijing, Trump May demand Ottawa’s alignment under threat of more tariffs.

But the same stability that protects manufacturers could weaken the political case for building Canadian alternatives, some warned. More predictable Chinese supply could ease the political urgency — and public-financing momentum — to build Canadian processing capacity.
“On the whole, it’s beneficial to industry at large, but it could slow down the momentum for the critical minerals industry in Canada specifically,” said Chiu.
Smith said the underlying case for diversification should survive either way.
“We cannot sit here and be dependent on any single country for any single item. We have to have alternatives,” he said.
But Hasmath and Nagy agree an extended truce could pose another downside: a wider U.S.-China trade deal could undercut Canadian exporters.
The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese

Most trade watchers believe Beijing will agree — whether it’s this week or in the weeks to come — to buy more U.S. agricultural goods and Boeing aircraft and that the two sides will announce an intention to begin AI-related security talks. Washington May offer China limited relief on access to lower-grade semiconductors, and it May reduce tariffs on some Chinese imports.
Those possible U.S. commercial wins could hurt Canada, because if Beijing buys more U.S. products, Canadian exporters May lose share in those markets.
“The more the Chinese buy from the Americans, that’s less of our exports going to the Chinese,” Hasmath said, pointing to three sectors that could be hit hard: agriculture, aircraft, and LNG.

The tradeoff is a catch-22, he said. Canada benefits when a truce keeps Chinese rare-earth materials flowing to manufacturers, but it has more geopolitical leverage when Washington needs non-Chinese alternatives.

So this week’s summit will not provide Canada with a win or a simple choice. An extended truce would help manufacturers with rare-earth supplies, but it would also prolong their reliance on China — and possibly weaken Ottawa’s push to build domestic processing capacity.

The test will be how Canada uses any period of stability a truce might bring. Will it use the time to build the infrastructure and domestic processing capability it needs to supply rare-earth materials itself? How it responds will determine whether the next U.S.-China trade spat leaves Canada with more leverage — or bigger supply problems.

content_blocks.text: Washington, D.C. — Trade tensions are becoming a familiar problem for Washington and this week President Donald Trump is putting his deal-making skills to the test as he hosts China’s president at the White House.

Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, D.C., ON Wednesday, and he and Trump will hold talks on Thursday. They are expected to discuss Iran, Taiwan, and AI safety standards , but the main focus will be on trade — and particularly U.S. access to Chinese rare-earth magnets and processed materials that also feed Canadian supply chains.

They are expected to discuss Iran, Taiwan, and AI safety standards, but the main focus will be on trade — and particularly U.S. access to Chinese rare-earth magnets and processed materials that also feed Canadian supply chains.

content_blocks.text: The summit comes nearly a year after Xi and Trump forged a trade truce in Busan, South Korea, suspending selected retaliatory measures — including some Chinese export controls on rare-earth magnets and critical materials — and reducing some U.S. tariffs.

Now, that truce is set to expire on Nov. 10, and Trump is seeking an economic victory ahead of November’s midterms. He also must ensure the continued flow of Chinese rare-earth exports to U.S. manufacturers.

Canadian leaders will be watching for any sign of a deal, but trade analysts say Ottawa is likely to lose either way, whether Xi and Trump fail or succeed in coming to an agreement. A collapsed truce could disrupt Canadian manufacturers that rely on Chinese magnets and processed rare earths, while an extension could bring short-term stability but leave Canada dependent on Chinese supply. An extended truce would also leave Canada exposed to a wider U.S.-China trade deal that diverts sales and investment to the U.S.

“No matter what happens, the Canadians are going to be in a position [where] they’re worried about how much of the piece of the pie they’re going to lose,” said Stephen Nagy, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute.
China, pushing for greater stability, wants to extend the truce until the end of the Trump presidency, while the White House is pushing for just a six-month extension.

stories.title: Five takeaways from final debate of Quebec election campaign
stories.summary: Montreal - After being greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters, the leaders of Quebec's five major political parties dove into their third and final debate of the election campaign, hosted by Radio-Canada on Wednesday evening.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - After being greeted by a raucous crowd of supporters and protesters, the leaders of Quebec’s five major political parties dove into their third and final debate of the election campaign, hosted by Radio-Canada on Wednesday evening.

Here are five takeaways from a debate featuring Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette, Quebec Liberal Leader Charles Milliard, Québec solidaire co-spokesperson Ruba Ghazal, Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon and Quebec Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime.

1. There was a one-hour wait for sparring on sovereignty and a referendum.

The leaders discussed five major themes during Wednesday’s debate. But voters watching at home had to wait until the second hour to hear one of the evening’s most animated exchanges — during a segment about the future of Quebec.

The PQ leader and Québec solidaire’s co-spokesperson are both in favour of sovereignty, with slightly different approaches. Ruba Ghazal promoted her plan to get Indigenous people and English-speaking Quebecers to buy into a campaign to make the province a country. This was the only mention of Quebec’s English-speaking population in the entire debate.

St-Pierre Plamondon quickly found himself on the defensive over his recent pledge to wait until after U.S. President Donald Trump leaves the White House before triggering a referendum.

Milliard pressed St-Pierre Plamondon on whether this delay was an admission a referendum would weaken Quebec — a theory, the PQ leader dismissed.

“It’s proof that we are living a very unusual moment with the Americans that is unacceptable on the part of the Trump administration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in French. “It’s not a serene climate (while Trump is president) to reflect on our future.”

The PQ leader has pledged to spend $130 million in government to organize a referendum. This would include money for a roving commission to hold consultations on the issue in the years leading up to a vote after January 2029.

Milliard said his rivals all support sovereignty or would have supported it in the past and argued his party was the only federalist option.

Fréchette and Duhaime have said Quebecers are not interested in a referendum.

2. Waiting times in hospitals are still a problem.

Fréchette found herself on the defensive early in the debate after being challenged by her rivals from the Liberals and Parti Québécois about broken health-care promises and long wait times in hospitals after her party’s eight years in government.

Milliard said Quebecers had been betrayed by the Coalition Avenir Québec’s promises to reduce emergency room wait times and ensure every Quebecer had a doctor. St-Pierre Plamondon agreed, saying the latter promise was “disrespectful of people’s intelligence.”

Fréchette acknowledged there was still work to do, but said her party had made improvements, including in increasing the number of surgeries performed and signing up hundreds of thousands of Quebecers for groups of family doctors.

3. St-Pierre Plamondon talked a lot.

Radio-Canada tracked how long each leader spoke during the debate.

By the end of the evening, the moderator, Radio-Canada journalist Patrice Roy, allowed the PQ leader to speak for nearly 24 minutes, while the Liberal and Conservative leaders got less than 18 minutes of airtime to talk about their policies and ideas.

Québec solidaire’s Ghazal spoke for a little more than 20 minutes, while Fréchette spoke for close to 21 minutes.

4. The baby that shook the campaign landed in debate.

A baby found at a homeless encampment in east Montreal in mid-September became the topic of one of the opening segments of the debate. Police say the discovery triggered an investigation and the intervention of social services and youth protection workers.

The story has brought the plight of unhoused people and affordability issues to the forefront of the Quebec campaign, with the leaders expressing shock and pledging to address them.

Each leader was asked about the incident and had a few seconds to respond before moving on to the next topic.

5. There were five leaders on stage.

Political analysts have said Quebec voters are fragmented in a tight race that could lead to a minority government when ballots are cast Oct. 5.

That dynamic was evident on stage as each leader tried to make their points, with multiple voices in the background.

There was limited opportunity for anyone to take specific aim at a rival before others interrupted or tried to change the topic.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026

stories.title: AFN regional chiefs to represent First Nations at meeting with Carney, premiers
stories.summary: Ottawa — Assembly of First Nations regional chiefs will join premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney for a rare meeting in late October — the first such meeting between chiefs and first ministers in decades.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

Posted September 24, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated September 24, 2026 5:19 am.

Ottawa — Assembly of First Nations regional chiefs will join premiers and Prime Minister Mark Carney for a rare meeting in late October — the first such meeting between chiefs and first ministers in decades.

A source shared details of a Wednesday planning meeting held by the Assembly of First Nations on the condition they not be named because they were not authorized to discuss it.

The premiers, Carney and First Nations representatives are set to meet in Ottawa on Oct. 26, just as tensions are rising over the federal and provincial governments’ major projects agenda.

National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak has invited premiers and Carney to a daylong ceremony ahead of the October meeting. She told The Canadian Press last week that First Nations leaders want to bring their own cultural practices to that meeting and she hopes all premiers accept the invitation.

The meeting was promised by Carney earlier this year.

Woodhouse Nepinak and her predecessors have for years been calling for First Nations representation at meetings between the prime minister and the premiers. Those calls got louder last year when the federal and provincial governments started discussing among themselves ways to fast-track major infrastructure projects.

Woodhouse Nepinak has said the meeting will be a “big test” of Canada’s ability to reconcile economic growth with First Nations rights.

Topics up for discussion at the meeting include long-term political governance — including rights and treaties, jurisdiction, health care, policing and land — economic partnerships and prosperity, the source told The Canadian Press.

There will be 28 seats in the main meeting room — one for the prime minister, one for the national chief, 13 for provincial and territorial leaders and 13 for First Nations representatives. The First Nations representatives in the main meeting room will mostly be regional chiefs from the Assembly of First Nations.

An additional 44 First Nations leaders are invited to attend, including one youth representative and representatives from Treaties 6, 7 and 8. The Assembly of First Nations is calling for those 44 entry passes to be interchangeable so they can accommodate a larger number of leaders.

While the meeting will be livestreamed, it’s not clear if that livestream will be available for public viewing, as the AFN has requested.

The location of the meeting has not yet been made public. The AFN and the federal government will only say it will be somewhere in Ottawa.

The AFN is a national advocacy body that takes its direction from some 630 First Nations chiefs through special and annual general assemblies. It is not a rights-holding institution but it represents rights-holding chiefs.

Carney and his cabinet met with First Nations chiefs last July in Gatineau, Que. It was a tightly controlled meeting and chiefs were asked to send their questions about the major project agenda in advance.

Media were barred from the meeting site and First Nations leaders, including Woodhouse Nepinak, had to engage with reporters outside in the summer heat.

The AFN called for the entire meeting to be made public and Woodhouse Nepinak later apologized for having to hold a press conference outside the meeting location.

In early August, the Privy Council Office told The Canadian Press it was working with the Assembly of First Nations, modern treaty groups and self-governing First Nations on planning the meeting with first ministers.

“The meeting aims to advance nation-to-nation and government-to-government relations and will provide an opportunity to work together to address priorities of shared interest,” spokesperson Pierre Cuguen wrote in an emailed statement.

Cuguen said at the time discussions about representation at the meeting were ongoing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 24, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: London Health Sciences Centre completes Canadian first using "heart in a box" technology for cardiac transplantation
stories.summary: September 24, 2026
stories.content:
September 24, 2026

In a transplant first for a Canadian recipient, the provincially shared Transmedics Organ Care System kept a donor heart beating outside of the body, helping to expand transplant possibilities for London Health Sciences Centre patient, Raj Mittal.

The heart transplant team from London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) completed a cardiac transplant using the Transmedics Organ Care System (OCS) organ care system, often referred to as a "heart in a box", to implant a donor heart that May otherwise May not have been available for transplant.

Taking place in February 2026, the milestone procedure was made possible through access to the provincially acquired TransMedics Organ Care System Heart technology, specialized team training, and years of collaboration with Ontario Health and Trillium Gift of Life Network.

Unlike traditional cold storage that preserves an organ using ice in a standard cooler during transport from one hospital to another, heart in a box systems are used to revive a donor heart that has stopped beating after circulatory death. It keeps the heart warm, beating, and perfused with oxygenated blood, while also providing the transplant team with real-time insight into heart function and suitability for transplantation.

With better preservation of organ quality, the technology also extends potential transport time to 12 hours, making it possible for a donor heart to reach a recipient that is much farther away from where it was retrieved than previously possible.

"This is a great example of the profound impact advancements and investments in technology can have on patients and their families," says Dr. Dave Nagpal, Medical Co-Director, Multi-Organ Transplant Program and Director of Cardiac Transplantation at LHSC. "With this technology we can now transplant organs that might not have been medically suitable otherwise. This gives patients on the organ donor waiting list a greater chance of receiving a lifesaving transplant and better allows teams to honour the wishes of donors and their families to generously give the gift of life."

For first patient Raj Mittal, the transplant followed a year of serious illness and uncertainty. In June 2025, Mittal was working in his backyard when he began feeling chest pain. His wife called 911 and he was taken to LHSC, where he later went into cardiac arrest and underwent a triple bypass surgery. Complications followed including pneumonia and kidney issues, and Mittal spent weeks between the intensive care and inpatient units, before being well enough to be discharged in September. At that time, his care team presented the possibility that one day he May need a heart transplant.

After another hospital admission in January of this year, Mittal was presented with two options; a left ventricular assistive device (Lvad) or a heart transplant. Following research to better understand the options, conversation and careful consideration, Mittal and his wife made the decision to move forward with a transplant, and he was placed on the provincial organ donation wait list. The call that a donor heart was available followed two weeks later.

Once the donor offer was accepted, a recovery team, led by Dr. Rashmi Nedadur, Cardiac Surgeon at LHSC traveled to the donor site, where the heart had been recovered and placed on the OCS machine. While beating in the system, the heart was assessed and deemed viable for transplant before being transported back to LHSC.

"The quality and function of the heart looked great when we arrived," says Dr. Nedadur. "When we implanted the heart, it took off immediately."

Heart transplantation is a highly coordinated and time-sensitive procedure. While one team recovers and assesses the donor heart, the recipient team prepares the patient for surgery.

During implantation, the surgical team examines the donor heart, trims the major vessels so they fit the recipient’s anatomy and carefully sews the new heart into place. The heart is protected throughout the process using specialized solutions and temperature control. Once the heart is in place, the team warms the patient, restores normal blood chemistry, and gradually transfers the work of circulation from the heart-lung machine to the new heart.

For Mittal, the impact of his transplant has been life changing. The day after surgery he was up and moving in the ICU. Within days, he was transferred to the transplant unit. Although his recovery included additional monitoring and a brief return to intensive care to manage blood pressure and fluid levels, he was discharged later that month and continues to improve.

"I am improving every day," says Mittal. "Before, I could not move much. I was sitting or lying down, and I could not spend time with my family. Now my energy is much better. I can walk, spend time with my family, and after the heart transplant there is hope I can get my normal life back."

For Dr. Nagpal and the teams at LHSC, the case reflects the combination of surgical expertise, innovation, and teamwork required to advance both complex cardiac care and the future of transplantation.

"There are a lot of details and nuances with transplantation, but the goal is always to make sure the donor heart is protected and that the recipient has the best possible chance at a successful outcome," says Dr. Nagpal. "Having this technology available marks an important step forward in what is possible in the field of organ donation and transplantation."

This cardiac transplant first builds on the rich legacy of excellence in donation and transplantation within LHSC’s Multi-Organ Transplant Program, home to the longest continuously running heart transplant program in Canada, offering new hope to patients who May benefit from expanded donor heart options in the future.

Members of the cardiac transplant team are pictured alongside heart transplant recipient, Raj Mittal.

Complications followed including pneumonia and kidney issues, and Mittal spent weeks between the intensive care and inpatient units, before being well enough to be discharged in September. At that time, his care team presented the possibility that one day he May need a heart transplant.

After another hospital admission in January of this year, Mittal was presented with two options; a left ventricular assistive device (Lvad) or a heart transplant. Following research to better understand the options, conversation and careful consideration, Mittal and his wife made the decision to move forward with a transplant, and he was placed on the provincial organ donation wait list. The call that a donor heart was available followed two weeks later.

Once the donor offer was accepted, a recovery team, led by Dr. Rashmi Nedadur, Cardiac Surgeon at LHSC traveled to the donor site, where the heart had been recovered and placed on the OCS machine. While beating in the system, the heart was assessed and deemed viable for transplant before being transported back to LHSC.
"The quality and function of the heart looked great when we arrived," says Dr. Nedadur. "When we implanted the heart, it took off immediately."
Heart transplantation is a highly coordinated and time-sensitive procedure. While one team recovers and assesses the donor heart, the recipient team prepares the patient for surgery.

During implantation, the surgical team examines the donor heart, trims the major vessels so they fit the recipient’s anatomy and carefully sews the new heart into place. The heart is protected throughout the process using specialized solutions and temperature control. Once the heart is in place, the team warms the patient, restores normal blood chemistry, and gradually transfers the work of circulation from the heart-lung machine to the new heart.

For Mittal, the impact of his transplant has been life changing. The day after surgery he was up and moving in the ICU. Within days, he was transferred to the transplant unit. Although his recovery included additional monitoring and a brief return to intensive care to manage blood pressure and fluid levels, he was discharged later that month and continues to improve.

"I am improving every day," says Mittal. "Before, I could not move much. I was sitting or lying down, and I could not spend time with my family. Now my energy is much better. I can walk, spend time with my family, and after the heart transplant there is hope I can get my normal life back."

For Dr. Nagpal and the teams at LHSC, the case reflects the combination of surgical expertise, innovation, and teamwork required to advance both complex cardiac care and the future of transplantation.

"There are a lot of details and nuances with transplantation, but the goal is always to make sure the donor heart is protected and that the recipient has the best possible chance at a successful outcome," says Dr. Nagpal. "Having this technology available marks an important step forward in what is possible in the field of organ donation and transplantation."

This cardiac transplant first builds on the rich legacy of excellence in donation and transplantation within LHSC’s Multi-Organ Transplant Program, home to the longest continuously running heart transplant program in Canada, offering new hope to patients who May benefit from expanded donor heart options in the future.

stories.title: Quebec doctors call for inquest after five physician suicides in five months
stories.summary: The signatories write that doctors face death and suffering every day and take on a lot of responsibility, sometimes without adequate support.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

Over 1,500 Quebec doctors are calling for a coroner’s inquest after five doctors in the province reportedly died by suicide over a five-month period this year.

The doctors sent a letter to Quebec’s chief coroner Sept. 18 asking for an inquest into suicides in their profession.

The signatories write that doctors face death and suffering every day and take on a lot of responsibility, sometimes without adequate support.

They also say some doctors avoid getting help for mental health issues because they fear professional repercussions.

Every suicide in Quebec is investigated by a coroner, regardless of the deceased person’s profession, to establish the causes and circumstances of the death.

Quebec’s coroner’s office told The Canadian Press it has begun an in-depth analysis of the doctors’ request.

“For now, it is too early to comment on whether such a public inquiry will be held,” it says.

Jean-Paul Brutus, a plastic surgeon who signed the letter, says growing workloads and the public denigration of doctors — sometimes referred to in Quebec as “doctor-bashing” — contribute to psychological distress.

He says successive governments have pointed fingers at doctors for years and blamed them “for all the failings of the public system.”

“There is more and more medical-administrative pressure, more and more patients, fewer and fewer resources to help us do the work we have to do,” Brutus says.

Brutus says the well-being of health-care workers can also affect the quality of care patients receive.

“This isn’t a doctors’ problem. This isn’t a health-care workers’ problem. It’s a public health problem,” he says.

The signatories argue the available information is not detailed enough to determine whether doctor suicides are increasing.

— With files from Katrine Desautels

stories.title: Carney says he studied risk of U.S.-led military action in NYT interview
stories.summary: Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called "extreme tail risk."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

In a lengthy New York Times interview published Wednesday, Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called “extreme tail risk.”

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to (prepare).”

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and while he ruled out using military force to annex Canada in January 2025, he has said he would consider using “economic force” to get Canada to become part of the United States.

Carney also spoke in the interview about Canada’s plans to reduce its reliance on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service.

He also discussed Canada considering alternatives to buying American F-35 fighter jets.

1:58 Carney says he studied risk of U.S. military invasion

Canada’s plan to procure a full fleet of F-35 stealth fighters remains under a political review by Carney’s government. The review was launched more than a year ago in response to the trade war started by Trump.

The trade war between Canada and the United States has been escalating after efforts to reach a trade deal failed in mid-August.

The day after talks broke down, Trump imposed 50 per cent duties on $28 billion in Canadian goods, while Canada implemented retaliatory tariffs in early September.

The president also signed an order to identify and remove products of Canadian origin from U.S. government procurement systems.

The New York Times report said Carney disclosed that he and Trump speak “frequently” even after trade talks collapsed, something the prime minister has said multiple times in recent weeks.

At a news conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier this month, Carney said he speaks to Trump regularly and that they can “compartmentalize.” He added that part of their responsibility is to work together to resolve global issues like the war in Ukraine.

Earlier Wednesday, the president claimed on social media that Canada is “destroying itself” by allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Trump provided no evidence for these claims but called it a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly.”

Carney and Trump did not meet when they both attended the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly this week. It was Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

stories.title: Veteran’s alleged role in Belleville synagogue attack could tarnish military, former top soldier fears
stories.summary: Suspect Sean Ward served in the Canadian Armed Forces for five years before being deemed unsuitable for further service
stories.author: Mercedes Stephenson, Jill Mahoney, Greg Mercer, Stephanie Levitz
stories.content:
Canada’s former top soldier said he is appalled by the attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., saying the alleged involvement of a veteran could risk tarring the reputation of the military.

Retired general Wayne Eyre led the military when suspect Sean Ward was released in 2022 from the Canadian Armed Forces after serving five years.

“I was horrified to hear of the events,” he said in an interview. “I was disappointed to learn of the perpetrator’s military affiliation.”

Mr. Ward was deemed unsuitable for further military service and released under a category called 5F, an involuntary discharge, The Globe and Mail reported on Wednesday according to two Department of National Defence sources. One source said Mr. Ward was removed because he refused to take the COVID-19 vaccine. The Globe is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss the matter.

Mr. Eyre said that regardless of the fact the Mr. Ward was out of the military for several years, the Forces can still be tarred with the same brush and the same dishonour.

Belleville residents searching for answers after shooting outside synagogue, MP says

Chief of the defence staff from 2021 to 2024, Mr. Eyre enacted a vaccine mandate in October, 2021. At the time, he said it was a lawful order necessary for force protection and to maintain operational readiness.

The DND website says a 5F release refers to people who are removed from the military because they are considered “unsuitable for further service,” for multiple reasons. The military has used this administrative mechanism to oust troops accused of racism and sexual misconduct, among other behavioural issues. Mr. Eyre approved the 5F designation being used during the COVID mandate for those who refused an order to get vaccinated.

General Jennie Carignan, the current Chief of the Defence Staff, did not immediately provide comment for this story.

The 29-year-old Mr. Ward, of Quinte West, Ont., died in hospital on Monday night. He was injured in a gunfight with police outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville on Sunday.

Mr. Ward allegedly opened fire on an officer stationed outside the small synagogue as worshippers gathered to mark Yom Kippur, the holiest day on the Jewish calendar.

Officials have not commented on a specific motive for the attack.

Liberal MP Chris Malette, whose riding includes Belleville, said he met with police, the mayor and the province’s Solicitor-General in the eastern Ontario city on Tuesday. He also went to the site of the shooting.

“What we found out about him just from seeing the scene – this individual clearly came with some intent to do some serious harm to these people, and we saw that graphic detail yesterday,” he told The Globe. He declined to discuss what police told him or what he saw at the crime scene, citing the continuing investigation.

Opinion: The Belleville attack was a warning shot for the antisemitic attacks Canada has let fester

On Wednesday, outside the Belleville home where a neighbour said Mr. Ward lived with his mother, there were seven police vehicles, including a black forensic investigation van, parked around the property. Two officers stood in the driveway.

Neighbour Sheri Skanes said Mr. Ward had lived at the house for several years. She said the situation, and the constant police presence, has rattled the neighbourhood.

“It’s shocking,” she said. “They were quiet people. They kept to themselves and didn’t cause a lot of noise.”

Her son, Jordan Skanes, said police had been at the address since Sunday night. He said apart from occasionally playing host to some visitors from Alberta, who stood out in the neighbourhood with their cowboy hats and out-of-province licence plates, there was nothing remarkable about the people who lived there. Mr. Ward could occasionally be seen using the backyard pool or playing with his dog, he said.

Mr. Ward served in the military from July, 2017, until June, 2022, when he was released with the rank of corporal, according to the Armed Forces. He was a member of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry regiment and did not deploy overseas during his service.

The Canadian military has not said where precisely Mr. Ward was posted. However, a private named Sean Ward was previously listed as a member of the Edmonton-based 3rd Battalion of the Ppcli, according to the regiment’s annual publication.

Mr. Ward attended Quinte Secondary School in Belleville, which closed in 2018 as part of a consolidation. He was an athlete and played on the rugby team, said former principal Liane Woodley.

Ms. Woodley said she has been in touch with past colleagues and students this week about the “very tragic” shooting.

“People are surprised, they’re shocked that someone that we’ve known could be involved in something like that,” she said.

The Special Investigations Unit, which handles cases involving Ontario police that result in death or serious injury, has wrapped up its investigation at the scene of the shooting.

A postmortem examination on Mr. Ward’s body took place in Kingston on Wednesday, said Kristy Denette, an SIU spokesperson.

Constable Jeff Smith, the Belleville Police Service officer who was wounded in the shootout with the suspect, remains in hospital in Kingston.

His wife, Ashley, thanked paramedics, police, “an angel neurosurgeon,” doctors, nurses, friends, neighbours, the Jewish community and other well-wishers in a Facebook post on Tuesday evening.

“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead. But he is not walking it alone. He has an army of love behind him,” she wrote in the post, which was shared by Belleville Police.

Early on Sunday evening, about 25 worshippers were about to begin evening prayers inside the Sons of Jacob synagogue, while Constable Smith kept watch in the parking lot in an unmarked vehicle.

According to the SIU, around 7 p.m., the suspect fired on Constable Smith with a shotgun and a gunfight began. A second officer arrived and fired at the suspect, who was injured in the exchange.

Retired general Wayne Eyre led the military when suspect Sean Ward was released in 2022 from the Canadian Armed Forces after serving five years.
“I was horrified to hear of the events,” he said in an interview. “I was disappointed to learn of the perpetrator’s military affiliation.”

Mr. Ward was deemed unsuitable for further military service and released under a category called 5F, an involuntary discharge, The Globe and Mail reported on Wednesday according to two Department of National Defence sources. One source said Mr. Ward was removed because he refused to take the COVID-19 vaccine. The Globe is not identifying the sources, who were not authorized to publicly discuss the matter.
Mr. Eyre said that regardless of the fact the Mr. Ward was out of the military for several years, the Forces can still be tarred with the same brush and the same dishonour.

Chief of the defence staff from 2021 to 2024, Mr. Eyre enacted a vaccine mandate in October, 2021. At the time, he said it was a lawful order necessary for force protection and to maintain operational readiness.

The DND website says a 5F release refers to people who are removed from the military because they are considered “unsuitable for further service,” for multiple reasons. The military has used this administrative mechanism to oust troops accused of racism and sexual misconduct, among other behavioural issues. “What we found out about him just from seeing the scene – this individual clearly came with some intent to do some serious harm to these people, and we saw that graphic detail yesterday,” he told The Globe. He declined to discuss what police told him or what he saw at the crime scene, citing the continuing investigation.
Opinion: The Belleville attack was a warning shot for the antisemitic attacks Canada has let fester

On Wednesday, outside the Belleville home where a neighbour said Mr. Ward lived with his mother, there were seven police vehicles, including a black forensic investigation van, parked around the property. Two officers stood in the driveway.

“It’s shocking,” she said. “They were quiet people. They kept to themselves and didn’t cause a lot of noise.”

Her son, Jordan Skanes, said police had been at the address since Sunday night. He said apart from occasionally playing host to some visitors from Alberta, who stood out in the neighbourhood with their cowboy hats and out-of-province licence plates, there was nothing remarkable about the people who lived there. A postmortem examination on Mr. Ward’s body took place in Kingston on Wednesday, said Kristy Denette, an SIU spokesperson.
Constable Jeff Smith, the Belleville Police Service officer who was wounded in the shootout with the suspect, remains in hospital in Kingston.
His wife, Ashley, thanked paramedics, police, “an angel neurosurgeon,” doctors, nurses, friends, neighbours, the Jewish community and other well-wishers in a Facebook post on Tuesday evening.
“Jeff has a very long, difficult road ahead. But he is not walking it alone. He has an army of love behind him,” she wrote in the post, which was shared by Belleville Police.

stories.title: Families detail lasting grief as judge weighs Kenneth Law’s sentence
stories.summary: Father of victim calls for public inquiry into how Ontario man operated for so long, aiding scores of suicides
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
A Toronto man whose son died by suicide after purchasing poison from Kenneth Law called for a public inquiry while speaking at a Wednesday sentencing hearing for Mr. Law, who has admitted he helped end the lives of at least 93 people.

Stephen Mitchell called on the Ontario government to take action, as he and other relatives of Mr. Law’s victims delivered harrowing public victim-impact statements on the first day of the hearing. Mr. Mitchell’s son, Stephen Jr., died just weeks before Mr. Law’s arrest in 2023. Mr. Mitchell criticized Canadian law enforcement for not recognizing the threat that Mr. Law posed before a British newspaper exposed his business in the spring of 2023.

He said grieving families want to know why the 61-year-old Mississauga engineer was able to operate an online business selling toxic salts and other deadly paraphernalia for years before his arrest. By the time Mr. Law was stopped, he had shipped more than 1,200 deadly parcels, including 330 to Britain and 157 within Canada, mostly to young people at risk of suicide.

“For more than two years, Mr. Law openly and knowingly sold deadly products to young vulnerable people around the world – including Canadians, including my son” Mr. Mitchell said.

Mr. Mitchell said that earlier intervention could have saved lives, including his son’s. “Premier Ford, I respectfully ask you to authorize an independent third-party inquiry into what occurred,” he said outside the court.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the idea of a public inquiry earlier this year. His office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

Last May, Mr. Law pleaded guilty to multiple counts of aiding 14 suicides in Ontario, while also admitting to playing a role in 79 suicides in Britain. A court heard earlier this year that he made $300,000 after selling suicide kits for as little as $80 apiece.

Justice Michelle Fuerst is now hearing evidence that will help her mete out a penitentiary sentence against Mr. Law.

Crown attorney Peter Westgate said the court will hear victim-impact statements from a total of 74 people this week.

Grieving families detail immense loss at Kenneth Law sentencing hearing

Prosecutors have read several written statements into the record, including one from British parents of a 14-year-old boy.

The child died in 2021 and his parents said they will always remember him as a “beautiful young man.” The parents wrote they will forever wonder what their son would have grown up to look like, had he lived to be 16, 18 or 21 years old.

Prosecutors also read a statement from Leonardo Bedoya Forero, an asylum seeker from Colombia. He found his daughter Jeshennia dead in his family’s home in Aurora, Ont., four years ago.

Now, he says, the indelible image of finding his daughter on that day has overtaken almost all his memories of happier times. “How was I supposed to protect my daughter?” Mr. Bedoya Forero wrote. “There are the dangers that you look out for, and the dangers that you don’t know exist.”

He described Mr. Law as a sinister presence in his dealings with young people he met online – a man who did not “guide them toward hope,” he said, but who instead “paved a path toward death.”

Kenneth Law, who admitted to aiding suicides, told psychiatrist he saw his actions as humane

Some parents tearfully appeared in the witness box to speak of heart-wrenching loss. Some said that pain that began with the immediate mourning of their children has never stopped, and has since snowballed into fractured relationships and lost livelihoods.

Sarabjit Rana, a Toronto-area mother, told the court she desperately wishes she could still say three words to her 21-year-old son: “Amrit, it’s ready.”

The mom told the court she misses constantly cooking in her kitchen to feed her young son. “Mom, is the chicken and rice ready?” Ms. Rana remembered her son always asking her. “Such an ordinary question. Such an ordinary moment.”

Amritraj Rana consumed a chemical he bought from Mr. Law on Oct. 29, 2022. He was overheard vomiting in the bathroom of his family home, and asked his mother to call an ambulance before he was pronounced dead.

Kenneth Law, man accused of selling toxic substances, pleads guilty to aiding suicides

Mr. Law, wearing a black jacket and khaki pants, listened impassively to these accounts of loss.

When Mr. Mitchell took the witness stand, the Toronto father looked at Mr. Law and challenged him. He told him that he had wrongly chosen to truncate the lives of innumerable young people who May have been on the cusp of recovering from depression and other mental-health conditions.

“You May one day regain your freedom, Mr. Law, but you will never erase the consequences of what you have done,” he said.

Ultimately, he said, Canada needs better systems and law enforcement.

“He’s just a narcissistic psychopath – that’s all,” Mr. Mitchell told reporters outside court. “What I really wanted to focus on is how society deals with people like that.”

stories.title: Carney says he studied risk of U.S.-led military action in New York Times interview
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called "extreme tail risk."
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he studied the possibility of U.S.-led military action in Canada.

In a lengthy New York Times interview published Wednesday, Carney declined to discuss in detail what that examination involved, but he suggested it would be irresponsible not to prepare for what he called “extreme tail risk.”

“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to (prepare).”

U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about turning Canada into the 51st state and while he ruled out using military force to annex Canada in January 2025, he has said he would consider using “economic force” to get Canada to become part of the United States.

Carney also spoke in the interview about Canada’s plans to reduce its reliance on Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite internet service.

He also discussed Canada considering alternatives to buying American F-35 fighter jets.

Canada’s plan to procure a full fleet of F-35 stealth fighters remains under a political review by Carney’s government. The review was launched more than a year ago in response to the trade war started by Trump.

The trade war between Canada and the United States has been escalating after efforts to reach a trade deal failed in mid-August.

The day after talks broke down, Trump imposed 50 per cent duties on $28 billion in Canadian goods, while Canada implemented retaliatory tariffs in early September.

The president also signed an order to identify and remove products of Canadian origin from U.S. government procurement systems.

The New York Times report said Carney disclosed that he and Trump speak “frequently” even after trade talks collapsed, something the prime minister has said multiple times in recent weeks.

At a news conference with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy earlier this month, Carney said he speaks to Trump regularly and that they can “compartmentalize.” He added that part of their responsibility is to work together to resolve global issues like the war in Ukraine.

Earlier Wednesday, the president claimed on social media that Canada is “destroying itself” by allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Trump provided no evidence for these claims but called it a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly.”

Carney and Trump did not meet when they both attended the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly this week. It was Carney’s first trip to the United States since trade negotiations fell apart last month.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: The big B.C. reshuffle continues ahead of snap election
stories.summary: Parties have until Oct. 3 to file candidate applications
stories.author: Andrea Woo, Mike Hager
stories.content:
John Rustad, who resurrected the Conservative Party of B.C. and brought it within three seats of forming government two years ago, is not seeking re-election in next month’s early vote, while former Green leader Andrew Weaver will return under the banner of the fledgling CentreBC party.

The announcements Wednesday add to a frenetic reshuffling of the province’s political landscape that has seen candidates change allegiances, leaders come and go and parties scramble to assemble slates for an election arriving two years early. On Tuesday, NDP Leader David Eby announced a snap election to be held on Oct. 24.

Mr. Rustad has represented the riding of Nechako Lakes since 2009 and served as party leader from 2023 to 2025, resigning amid a party revolt. He was ousted from caucus last Friday by former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay and rejoined on Monday.

“Under his leadership, our party grew from less than 2 per cent of the vote to Official Opposition,” the party said in a statement. “The Conservative Party of B.C. would never have reached where it is today without his conviction, hard work and willingness to stand up when few others would.”

Every other Conservative MLA will run again, the party said. As well, its board will “pursue the appropriate means” under its constitution and bylaws to ensure interim leader Lorne Doerkson “will remain leader if elected.”

Opinion: Is David Eby about to gamble away his government?

Meanwhile, CentreBC announced its recruitment of climate scientist and University of Victoria professor Andrew Weaver to run in his old riding of Oak Bay-Gordon Head.

Mr. Weaver joined the Conservative Party of B.C. earlier this year to vote for Kamloops Centre MLA Peter Milobar in the party’s leadership race, cancelling his membership when the polarizing Ms. Findlay won. He then supported CentreBC from the sidelines and was dismayed when seven of the eight Conservative MLAs who had joined the more centrist party, including Mr. Milobar, returned to the Tories on Tuesday.

Even with Mr. Doerkson replacing Ms. Findlay, who resigned Sunday, Mr. Weaver said he could not back a party whose membership had chosen her as leader just months earlier.

He agreed to run moments after learning that Elenore Sturko would remain and become CentreBC’s new leader.

“I thought, ‘Oh, for heaven’s sake. Does anyone have any principles left?’” he said in an interview Wednesday. “So I thought, you know what, Elenore needs help. She’s sticking her neck out there. Good for her. I’ve always respected her. So I let them know.”

Ms. Sturko, an independent MLA and former RCMP officer who was booted from the Conservatives a year ago after a falling out with Mr. Rustad, said CentreBC is now vetting applicants who want to run in all of the province’s 93 ridings.

Mr. Weaver said he hopes CentreBC can win enough seats to deny the NDP a majority government, noting the province’s $13.8-billion deficit under Mr. Eby.

“My wish is that there’s a minority government and that nobody trusts anyone with the keys to the House by themselves, because they have not demonstrated their ability to act like adults in the legislature,” he said.

The Editorial Board: The crosswinds of Canadian conservatism

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer at the University of British Columbia, said the upstart CentreBC faces a massive uphill battle for relevance compared to the Conservatives. But, he said, Mr. Weaver qualifies as a star candidate capable of breaking through in the tony region that houses his alma mater, the University of Victoria.

“He’s the kind of person who can create his own weather in that particular riding,” Prof. Prest said.

Mr. Weaver was elected to the riding in 2013, becoming the province’s first Green MLA, and re-elected in 2017, when he and his two fellow Green MLAs signed a cooperation agreement with the New Democrats that swung a hung Parliament and ended 16 years of successive BC Liberal governments.

As CentreBC announced Mr. Weaver’s candidacy, NDP Leader Mr. Eby held a campaign event at a B.C.-Washington State border crossing in Surrey, where he pledged a tripling of a government advertising campaign to lure U.S. health care workers to the province if re-elected.

A $5-million blitz that started in June, 2025 and targeted workers in Washington State, Oregon and California has resulted in about 800 doctors, nurses and other health care professionals accepting job offers in B.C., Mr. Eby said. A re-elected NDP government would commit an additional $10-million and expand the campaign to Republican-controlled states where such workers face restrictions on their ability to provide life-saving reproductive care, he said.

Opinion: David Eby’s snap election call is cynical and self-serving

Mr. Eby’s remarks repeated the messaging of his election address one day earlier, when he sought to link B.C.’s political right to U.S. President Donald Trump and position the NDP as the party to stand up to Maga-style policies.

He cited a February, 2025, social media post by Conservative MLA Heather Maahs, who said that “Eby needs to comply” with the Trump administration’s demand to stop the flow of illicit fentanyl into the U.S. from Canada in order to avoid tariffs. He argued that a B.C. Conservative government would create the same repressive conditions from which U.S. health care workers are fleeing.

“If we turn our province into America Jr., we put all of that at risk,” Mr. Eby said.

(The Globe and Mail has debunked Mr. Trump’s claim that the synthetic opioid was pouring south across the border.)

The NDP also announced Wednesday that former Global News and CBC legislative reporter Richard Zussman will be its candidate in Saanich South.

Meanwhile, Brenda Bailey became the fourth NDP cabinet minister to announce that she would not be seeking re-election, after Ravi Kahlon, Lana Popham and Kelly Greene.

B.C. Green Leader Emily Lowan, who does not have a seat in the legislature, announced Wednesday that she will run in the riding of Saanich North and the Islands, after Green MLA Rob Botterell announced his retirement.

stories.title: From meat to the saddle: B.C. rancher trains yaks to carry riders
stories.summary: “Our hope is that as we raise them from calves to be well handled that you can continue training them and then they would have a purpose aside from just being butchered,”
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For Jamie Kamps, yaks have traditionally been raised for one main purpose: meat.

Kamps, who operates Black Yak Cattle Co., has about 30 Tibetan yaks on her farm close to Salmon Arm. The herd is primarily raised for grass-finished meat, while cows and calves can also be raised for their wool and fibre.

Kamps estimates there are only about 1,000 yaks in Canada, making them a relatively uncommon livestock animal.

But one of her younger yaks, Toro, could have a different future. To one day carry a rider.

Yaks have traditionally been used in parts of Central Asia to carry people and heavy loads. Their thick coats also help them withstand cold conditions, with their winter coats growing longer and providing insulation in low temperatures.

Kamps describes the roughly one-and-a-half-year-old Toro as a “chill dude” who is calm, tolerant and easy to handle. She says that temperament has her looking beyond the traditional meat market and toward training some of her animals to become riding or pack yaks.

“So our hope is that as we raise them from calves to be well handled, that you can continue training them and then they would have a purpose aside from just being butchered,” Kamps said.

Toro is already being trained, and Kamps says he could potentially carry a rider at around two years old. She says yaks can also be trained to pull a sleigh or carry loads.

The animals’ build makes them suited to riding, according to Kamps. She says their hump works well with a western saddle and that they can be less “flighty” than horses.

For Kamps, the idea is about giving some of her animals another purpose.

“Well, we found that the stock we’re producing have such a nice temperament and such great trainability that if they can be utilised for something outside the meat market, people enjoy them, they’ll have a good life as a pleasure animal, not just a meat animal.”

Kamps says the long-term goal is to build up a group of mature, well-trained animals that could be sold for packing and other recreational uses.

She also hopes to eventually use some of the mature animals for petting zoos and similar experiences, but only once they are old enough, trained and ready to safely interact with the public.

For now, that means waiting for the animals to grow and continuing their training. Toro is just one of the first yaks Kamps hopes can help demonstrate what these animals can do beyond the meat market.

stories.title: How President Trump’s White House bans have left Fanshawe journalists feeling unsettled
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/7EffmiqaJsQ Journalists at Fanshawe College are concerned and unsure about the future of jour...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
Journalists at Fanshawe College are concerned and unsure about the future of journalism in politics because of the recent spat between U.S. President Donald Trump and American news media.

The uncertainty comes in the aftermath of President Trump banning CNN, Msnbc, and Politico from the White House, accusing them of being “fake news”. In retaliation, several news outlets have either boycotted the White House’s press releases or have declined to collect audio from Trump as he speaks.

“This has been taken to a whole different level,” said Steve Young, the former news and information director at CTV News London and current program coordinator of Fanshawe’s multimedia journalism program. He also said he was unsurprised that the journalistic community was acting in support of the banned publications.

A collection of logos for London-based news outlets. Journalists in the city believe their profession’s community would support each other if they and politicians became at odds like in the U.S. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

“It is very important from a journalistic standpoint that we all stand up and say ‘we have a right to be able to hold politicians accountable,'” said Young. “You don’t know if their media organization might be the next one to be banned from the White House.”

The concerns extend to those entering the journalistic community as well. When asked, several students in the multimedia journalism program shared many of the same feelings on the situation between President Trump and U.S. news media.

“I feel like he’s forcing other companies to have one opinion and one opinion only,” said Owen Schuller. “The whole point of a journalist is be [unopinionated] and to have just the facts right.”

Fellow student Georgia Chambers echoed Schuller’s concerns about President Trump’s relationship with news media, saying she feels he is “a little bit scared of the media” and that she believes it to be the reason for his actions.

Another concern raised was how the situation might change the relationship between politicians and journalists, who are traditionally referred to in politics as the “fourth estate”.

“I do think it’s going to create a big rift in the media and political landscape going forward,” said Ryan Baynton, another student in the journalism program.

The impact of the situation May not be limited to the U.S. Schuller, Chambers, and Baynton each expressed concern that a shift in how journalists deal with politics could affect their careers.

Young also commented on the possibility of politician/journalist relationships in Canada changing because of the situation, saying he hopes they will not. Him and Baynton both believe if it did happen though, the journalistic community would respond the same way it has to President Trump.

“We have to have that ability to be able to [hold politicians accountable] on this side of the border,” said Young.

As for what will happen next, Young believes that journalists will continue to be a part of politics, and that the banned outlets will get access to President Trump by going to other locations or by taking the bans to court to try to have them lifted.

“It will be very interesting to see how this ends,” said Young. “How that will happen is anybody’s guess.”

stories.title: Western university unveils indigenous themed mural
stories.summary: Western University unveiled a new mural depicting the creation story of the Anishinabek tribe. The mural, depi...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
Western University unveiled a new mural depicting the creation story of the Anishinabek tribe. The mural, depicting how the Earth was created on the back of a turtle shell according to the Anishinabek myth, was revealed on Sept 21 at the Thames Hall Jeff and Shelley Parr Family Atrium.

“T here are different versions of the creation story .” Said Jeanette Ladd, the painter of the mural. “O ther people that you know share the same story, b ut there might be a little bit of a tweak of something added. O ur language is spoken not written so things, May have changed along the way.”

Radd was able to create this mural for Western through a special program Western was hosting. “I t was an open proposal for any artist to apply,” Radd said. “ I love the creation story and so I wanted t o paint it. Yo u could have chosen like any of the walls within the atrium space you could do anything in the atrium space. I had to d o like a timeline of how long it would take, materials that I wanted to use, even the maintenance of the piece if I was the accepted artist.”

Radd hopes that her art brings comfort to Western students, both indigenous and otherwise. “F or the indigenous students I want them to see a little little piece of home like. F or the other students, I’m hoping that they feel a piece of calm when they look at the piece .”

Western’s students seem to really appreciate the new mural, and what it represents. “I think it’s a beutiful piece to add to Western,” said Jacklyn Bagley, a student at Western University. “I’ve honestly never seen anything that represents Indigenous identity and culture at Western, so I think it’s a great staple.”

stories.title: Politics Insider: Ottawa City Council votes to rename Trump Avenue
stories.summary: Residents of the street no longer want to be associated with the U.S. President
stories.author: Laura Stone
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Ottawa City Council today voted unanimously to rename Trump Avenue, a residential street named more than 20 years ago.

The street is a part of an Ottawa neighbourhood called Central Park, which is filled with New York-themed names such as Staten Way, Bloomingdale Street and Grammercy Park. The U.S. President was basically a Manhattan novelty act when the streets were first set out in the subdivision.

“I’m embarrassed that in the nation’s capital we have Donald Trump honoured in this respect,” Riley Brockington, the city councillor whose ward contains the street, told council when he initially brought up the rebranding idea in the heat of the trade war between Canada and the U.S.

Now that the motion has passed, the councillor said he’ll form a working group with a handful of residents to come up with new potential names to put to a vote.

Mr. Brockington said no other street in his ward generates anything near the “constant” volume of complaints that Trump Avenue does. This is the second attempt to change the street’s name, after a 2021 effort that was strategic in its timing, the councillor said.

“I said, I don’t want to do anything while he’s in office because I feared retribution – honest to goodness” he said. “So he came out of office January ’21, and that’s when I did the outreach.”

That process failed to get two-thirds of the residents of the street to vote in favour of the change. Mr. Brockington suspects that those who voted no at the time didn’t necessarily like the original name – they just didn’t want to be bothered changing their addresses.

Trump says Canada is ‘destroying itself’ with ‘unchecked’ immigration: Trump took aim at Canada again today, this time to claim that it is allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

Amid shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on the UN’s stage: Since a watershed speech to the World Economic Forum in January, Prime Minister Mark Carney has become a leading voice of what he and some others call “middle powers.”

Canada ratifies landmark High Seas Treaty and commits funding to ocean protection: Carney pledged $82-million over five years to a global ocean-monitoring alliance, highlighting Canada’s responsibilities as a country with the world’s longest coastline.

Prime Minister’s Day: Carney was in New York this morning, where he spoke at a United Nations event to support the OceanEye International Alliance before heading back to Ottawa. Party Leaders: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attended his party’s caucus meeting on Parliament Hill. NDP Leader Avi Lewis hit the picket lines with striking Bank of Canada security guards. Green Party Leader Elizabeth May spoke to reporters about the government’s new economic legislation, Bill C-39, which she called “a monster, in every sense of the word.” Belleville synagogue shooting makes it into Parliament: Belleville residents are angry and looking for answers after a shooting on Sunday outside a synagogue in the Ontario city, said Liberal MP Chris Malette, who represents the area. Stephanie Levitz reports.

“Canada’s special envoy is here. Diana – make sure I get the last name right – Fox Carney, who’s working tirelessly on this.” – Prime Minister Mark Carney , at the United Nations OceanEye International Alliance event, speaking about his wife, who has been named Canada’s first Ocean Envoy.

With B.C. Premier David Eby officially calling a snap election, the province’s Conservative Party is scrambling to present a united front in the hopes of winning power from the NDP. How many leaders (or interim leaders) has the party had since becoming Official Opposition in March, 2023? (Bonus points for their names!)

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Mark Carney gets to work on the plumbing

In its first year, Mr. Carney’s government built a lot of workarounds and special powers that were supposed to cut through the thicket of bureaucracy. Now, it’s trying to clear away some of that underbrush. stories.title: Students hit the stage for ‘School of Rock’ musical at London’s The Grand theatre
stories.summary: The Grand Theatre High School Project is blasting, bringing the tunes to downtown London this fall. Local students are hitting the stage with their own version of the 2003 blockbuster film, ‘School of Rock’.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The Grand Theatre High School Project is blasting, bringing the tunes to downtown London this fall. Local students are hitting the stage with their own version of the 2003 blockbuster film, ‘School of Rock’.

Professional theatre director Lezlie Wade says the students are putting on quite a show and highlighting their many talents.

“This performance is such a great chance for them to explore the rock and roll side of their personalities and slightly rebellious side as well,” said Wade.

“However, it’s very inspirational.”

H.B Beal Secondary School student Isaac De Melo plays the role of Dewey Finn in the musical, a fake substitute teacher who helps the kids get out of their shell.

“I would say it’s a group full of kids who just want to be heard and I’m trying to let them find their voice,” said De Melo.

Isabelle Parent is another Beal student who plays the part of the principal in the play, Rosalie Mullins.

“She kind of has this hardened exterior but she grew up loving rock music and that’s discovered later in the show,” said Parent.

“With Dewey’s help, she rediscovers her younger self.”

Wade says the group on stage performs like pros.

“It doesn’t look like they are students and that great and the greatest compliment you can pay them,” Wade said.

If you would like to catch the first production of the brand-new season at the Grand Theatre, School of Rock is on now until Oct. 3.
