stories.title: Canada’s Derek Cornelius to hospital after non-contact injury
stories.summary: The 28-year-old from Ajax, Ont., has played 48 matches for Canada's national team, including four at this summer's World Cup.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
A key member of Canada’s national soccer team could be out for a while.

Derek Cornelius sustained a non-contact lower-body injury at practice on Wednesday in Toronto, Canada Soccer confirmed in a statement .

Cornelius was transported to a local hospital and is undergoing evaluation, per Canada Soccer.

The 28-year-old from Ajax, Ont., has played 48 matches for Canada’s national team, including four at this summer’s World Cup.

Cornelius, a defender, has just one goal for country. He also plays professionally for Marseille, where he is in the midst of his third season.

Canada is preparing for friendlies against Chile, Peru and the U.S. over the next couple weeks — its first matches since being eliminated in the World Cup in the second round of the knockout stage after a 3-0 loss to Morocco.

stories.title: Anand to see if Netanyahu is crossing Canadian airspace with arrest warrant in effect
stories.summary: Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says she is checking on whether Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an international arrest warrant, will be travelling through Canadian airspace on Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says she is checking to see if Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu — who faces an international arrest warrant — will be travelling through Canadian airspace on Thursday.

“I actually have asked my department to provide me with information relating to this particular flyover, which I did not have before coming to the United Nations,” Anand told reporters Wednesday outside UN headquarters in New York.

In November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes in the Gaza Strip.

Netanyahu is set to visit New York on Thursday. Prime Minister Mark Carney said in October that the Israeli leader will be arrested if he enters Canada.

Foreign dignitaries need to request permission from Ottawa three working days before flying through Canadian airspace. Canadian authorities decide whether to give permission for flyovers, in consultation with air traffic officials.

Permission generally includes the duty to assist aircraft that require an emergency landing.

Legal experts have criticized Canada for allowing Netanyahu’s plane to traverse Canadian airspace on previous occasions since the arrest warrant was issued. The U.S. does not recognize that warrant.

Mark Kersten, a University of the Fraser Valley professor who specializes in the International Criminal Court, noted in July that the ICC requires member states to arrest people facing ICC warrants when they are in their territories. He noted that the court in unrelated cases has interpreted “territory” as including airspace and territorial seas.

“Respect for the ICC — and the dignity of the victims of atrocity perpetrators — as well as self-respect for state sovereignty, surely demands that states act to prevent suspects from flying over their territory,” Kersten wrote.

Anand would not say Wednesday whether Canada sees Netanyahu as a war criminal.

“Our position is … to respect decisions of international courts and … to support, at all times, people who are suffering, including in Gaza and Palestine and the West Bank, and to ensure that crimes against humanity are addressed as such,” she said.

“We have strong views relating to suffering that has occurred and invasions.”

While Ottawa has supported Israel’s fight against Hezbollah, which it considers a terrorist group, it has expressed alarm over Israel’s invasion of Lebanon.

Netanyahu is expected to make a short visit to New York to address the UN. New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he wanted the Israeli leader arrested for his treatment of Palestinians in Gaza but he has no such authority.

The Trump administration has for the second year in a row denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas a visa. Abbas is instead is addressing the UN through a video link.

The hosting agreement the United States has with the UN requires Washington to allow diplomats from all member nations to attend UN meetings.

Carney has accused Netanyahu’s government of failing to prevent a humanitarian crisis in the Gaza Strip by repeatedly restricting the delivery of essential aid to Palestinians, and through attacks on civilians. Israel has insisted those attacks targeted Hamas operatives.

The Israeli government has said Canada is undermining peace in the region through its growing criticism of the country, its withdrawal of support in United Nations votes and its formal recognition of a Palestinian state.

Israeli officials have called on Ottawa to instead focus on tackling a rise in antisemitic acts in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026

With files from The Associated Press

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Health Canada suspends licence of Grifols site in Winnipeg
stories.summary: A 22-year-old donor experienced heart problems at the site and later died
stories.author: Chris Hannay
stories.content:
Health Canada says it has suspended the licence of the Grifols plasma collection site in Winnipeg where a young donor experienced heart problems that led to her death.

Grifols is the only major commercial collector in Canada of plasma, a component of blood used to make some types of medicine. It operates under a partnership with Canadian Blood Services.

Grifols has been the subject of public scrutiny in recent months following the deaths of two donors and a number of critical inspections conducted by Health Canada.

Explainer: What we know so far about Grifols’s plasma pause and Health Canada’s safety concerns

Plasma machine at Grifols collection centre issued five alerts before Winnipeg donor’s death

The company voluntarily stopped collecting plasma in Canada on Aug. 14 , saying the pause would be temporary as it worked through improvements to address Health Canada’s concerns.

Rodiyat Alabede, a 22-year-old university student, began experiencing cardiac problems during a donation at a Grifols site on Taylor Avenue last October and was pronounced dead at hospital about an hour later.

Health Canada told media there was “no linkage” between Ms. Alabede’s death and the donation activity. Her family disputes this and has asked for an investigation.

Health Canada said Wednesday it had suspended the licence of the Taylor Avenue location, further complicating Grifols’ plans to reopen it.

stories.title: Canada’s population growth continues its decline, StatCan says
stories.summary: This marked the lowest July-to-July growth in total population size since 1944/1945 and the lowest July-to-July percentage increase since 1915/1916, the agency added.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canada’s population growth rate continues to decline, largely owing to declining migration trends, Statistics Canada said on Wednesday.

The population of Canada reached an estimated 41,798,407 people on July 1, 2026, an increase of 189,425 people or 0.5 per cent from July 1, 2025.

This marked the lowest July-to-July growth in total population size since 1944/1945 and the lowest July-to-July percentage increase since 1915/1916, the agency added.

Canada’s population growth rate for July peaked at 2.8 per cent in 2023/2024, but has been steadily slowing on an annual basis since then.

The growth rate has more than halved compared to July 2024/2025, when it was 1.1 per cent.

In the second quarter of the year, from April 1 to July 1, Canada saw its population increase by 80,343 people or 0.2 per cent. This was the lowest growth in a second quarter since the second quarter of 2020, when the COVID-19 pandemic had all but halted immigration levels.

Statistics Canada credited “changing international migration trends” with not only the slowdown in the population growth rate, but also with the average age in Canada increasing over the past two years.

As of July 1, 2026, the average Canadian was 42.1 years old.

The number of non-permanent residents in Canada dropped by 154,614 people from July 2025 to reach 2,779,774 on July 1, 2026, or 6.7 per cent of the total population.

On Oct. 1, 2025, non-permanent residents were 7.2 per cent of the total population.

This was mostly led by a massive decline in the number of study permit holders (declined by 140,827) and work-and-study permit holders (81,163 drop).

The two segments that saw the largest declines in population were people between 20 and 24 years (2.4 per cent) and people between 25 and 29 (3.1 per cent).

Canada welcomed 99,148 immigrants in the second quarter of 2026, according to Statistics Canada. This number is 4.2 per cent lower than in the second quarter of 2025 (103,527).

Canadians over 65 now form 20 per cent of the population, an increase of 0.6 per cent, while Canadians aged 0 to 14 form 15 per cent of the population, a decline of 0.1 per cent.

Alberta had the fastest growing population (1.5 per cent), while British Columbia had the slowest rate of growth (0.1 per cent). The only province or territory to register a decline in population was the Northwest Territories, where the population declined by 0.3 per cent.

1:59 World fertility rates slide into ‘unprecedented decline’: UN

In 2025, Canada’s fertility rate was unchanged at 1.26 children per woman.

The fertility rate has been steadily declining in Canada since 2009. The drops got sharper between 2017 and 2023, except for 2021 when an increase was recorded.

There was a smaller 0.8 per cent decline in 2024, before plateauing in 2025.

There were 372,521 babies born in Canada in 2025, a 1.6 per cent increase compared with 2024. There were more boys (51.3 per cent) born in Canada than girls (48.7 per cent).

In 2025, 43.8 per cent of mothers who gave birth in Canada were born in other countries, up from 32.7 per cent in 2021.

stories.title: Charges laid months after cyclist killed on Melbourne Road
stories.summary: Two drivers have now been charged after a collision that claimed the life of a cyclist in Southwest Middlesex earlier this year.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two drivers have now been charged after a collision that claimed the life of a cyclist in Southwest Middlesex earlier this year.

Middlesex OPP say emergency crews were called to Melbourne Road between Ina Dale Drive and Olde Drive on May 4 at about 12:17 p.m. following reports of a collision involving a vehicle and a cyclist.

Police, along with members of Oneida Nation Police, Strathroy-Caradoc police, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service and local firefighters, responded to the scene.

The cyclist, a 25-year-old resident of Southwest Middlesex, was taken to hospital, where they were pronounced dead. The driver of the vehicle was also taken to hospital as a precaution.

Following a months-long investigation, police have charged a 19 year old of Middlesex Centre with careless driving causing death. He is also charged with driving with an open container of liquor and being a person under 19 years old in possession of liquor under the Liquor Licence Control Act.

Investigators said a second collision occurred at the scene when another vehicle struck the rear of the vehicle involved in the fatal crash.

As a result, a 72-year-old Appin resident has been charged with careless driving.

Both accused were released and are scheduled to appear in Ontario Provincial Offences Court in London at a later date.

stories.title: Immigration Department looking into termination of refugee sponsor policy: Diab
stories.summary: The Immigration Department will monitor for any negative effects from a recent decision not to extend a policy that gave permanent residency sponsorship exemptions to some refugees.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The Immigration Department will monitor for any negative effects from a recent decision not to extend a policy that gave permanent residency sponsorship exemptions to some refugees, Immigration Minister Lena Diab said Wednesday.

The policy was introduced in 2019 to allow some refugees to sponsor some undeclared family members for permanent residency but it expired earlier this month and was not renewed.

“It predated my election as well as ministry. And when it ended, it simply ended,” Diab said on her way into the weekly Liberal caucus meeting Wednesday.

“The department is looking at it right now, and we’ll do briefings and see if there’s any consequences that have arisen out of it ending that we need to fix, we will.”

The Immigration Department previously said the policy was dropped because of “potential integrity concerns” but refused to explain what those were, or to state whether some applicants had misused the policy.

“I respect the department’s findings that there are integrity concerns, and they are looking to ensure that we did not and we will not affect or people that we should be helping the wrong way. So we will be looking at it,” Diab said.

Advocates and academics say the policy was used primarily to sponsor children and LGBTQ+ partners and a previous department review said some refugees have legitimate reasons for not declaring a family member.

Lawyers and advocates say a refugee might not have declared a dependent child because the child was born in a refugee camp after the initial paperwork had been filed. In other cases, they said, a family might learn afterward that a child believed dead was actually alive.

All permanent residency applicants are required to list all family members and are permanently barred from later sponsoring any undeclared family.

The department has said it will consider applications for exemptions on a case-by-case basis through humanitarian and compassionate applications.

But refugee lawyers and advocates point out the department’s own website shows the current wait time for humanitarian and compassionate applications runs to more than 10 years.

The Canadian Council for Refugees has called on Diab to reverse the decision not to extend the policy. In a letter sent earlier this month, the council said the decision to revert to “the cruelty of the previous situation” was “inexplicable.”

A department memo issued ahead of the 2023 extension of the policy described its program integrity risk as “minimal.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Belleville synagogue shooting suspect 'spouted' theory that blamed Jews for COVID: reports
stories.summary: The suspect of the shooting outside of a Belleville, Ont. synagogue previously served in the Canadian military.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Sean Ward, the 29-year-old suspect of a shooting that took place outside a synagogue in Belleville, Ont. served in the Canadian military and was discharged after refusing a COVID-19 vaccine, according to reporting by Global News and The Globe and Mail .

One source told Global News that he “spouted” antisemitic conspiracy theories, including one that blamed the Jewish community for COVID. According to the World Jewish Congress , myths about Jews being responsible for the pandemic spread online and at demonstrations around the world. “While some of these bigoted messages appeared new, they were repackaged antisemitic tropes,” the congress said.

Two sources from the Department of National Defence told the Globe and Mail that after five years, Ward was released because he was unsuitable for service.

His release, the sources said, was categorized as 5F. According to the National Defence website , 5F is when a person is deemed “unsuitable for further service.”

One source told the Globe and Mail and Global News that his release was due to his refusal to get a COVID vaccine.

It is believed that Ward arrived near the synagogue in a truck and was armed with a shotgun on Sept 20. There were roughly 25 congregants inside the building for evening prayers on Yom Kippur, the holiest day for the Jewish community.

Ward allegedly opened fire on Belleville police Const. Jeff Smith, who was stationed there due to safety concerns from the community. According to Global News, Belleville police were only assigned to the synagogue because congregants had reported a suspicious vehicle parked outside a week earlier. Smith and other officers who were called to the scene fired back at Ward, Special Investigations Unit spokesperson Kristy Denette said at a news conference.

Ward was taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries. He died on Tuesday. An autopsy is set for Wednesday.

Smith is in critical but stable condition. A GoFundMe set up on behalf of Toronto’s Jewish community for the officer has reached more than $350,000.

The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed to National Post on Tuesday that a man named Sean Ward joined the forces in July 2017 and was “released in June 2022 at the rank of corporal.”

He was part of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton, and was never deployed.

In the 2018 issue of The Patrician , a publication by the Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, a member named Sean Ward was listed as being part of the regiment’s 3rd battalion, based in Edmonton.

The Ppcli Regimental Headquarters and the Department of National Defence did not immediately respond to National Post’s request for comment about Ward.

stories.title: Doctors urge women to remove fallopian tubes to reduce ovarian cancer risk
stories.summary: The procedure is quick and done on patients already undergoing surgery in the abdominal area and who don't want children or have finished having children.
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
Doctors are urging women to consider removing their fallopian tubes as growing evidence suggests it could reduce the risk of developing ovarian cancer by roughly 80 per cent.

About 3,000 women in Canada are diagnosed with ovarian cancer every year, and 2,000 of them will die, Dr. Elyse Lackie, an OB/GYN, told Global News.

But a highly effective procedure to remove the fallopian tubes, where most ovarian cancers are believed to develop — known as an opportunistic salpingectomy — is proving to be an effective preventative measure, she explained.

2:03 Call for greater access to ovarian cancer treatments in Canada

The procedure takes less than five minutes and is done on patients already undergoing surgery in the abdominal area and who don’t want children or have finished having children.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

Ovarian cancer is particularly deadly because it is often caught in its later stages due to a lack of observable symptoms or accurate tests that help to catch it early, resulting in low survival rates and limited treatment options.

“Essentially you’re not gonna see it at all, you’re not going to feel it at all, until it’s really advanced and that’s often too late,” Lackie said.

According to a study at the University of British Columbia (UBC) earlier this year, removing the fallopian tubes leaves the ovaries intact, preserving important hormone production and leading to minimal side effects from the added procedure.

“This study clearly demonstrates that removing the fallopian tubes as an add-on during routine surgery can help prevent the most lethal type of ovarian cancer,” said co-senior author Dr. Gillian Hanley, an associate professor of obstetrics and gynaecology at UBC.

“It shows how this relatively simple change in surgical practice can have a profound and life-saving impact.”

Shaheen Mawani, who received the operation last year, told Global News it was an “opportune thing” that she went ahead with during a procedure to remove her uterus.

“This seemed like a brainer for me,” she said.

Dr. Peter Stotland, North York General Hospital Chief of Surgery, said the surgery will see “lives saved” alongside the avoidance of intensive chemotherapy, radiation, and surgical treatments.

“We’ve really put a concerted effort into getting this out there,” he said, so people are aware of the option, which adds very little time to abdominal area procedures that are already underway.

Lackie also called on the Canadian government to invest in the procedure through education and implementation of what she described as a “really simple” operation, with small financial costs that will save the system “so much money” in the long run if ovarian cancer can be prevented.

The opportunistic salpingectomy approach was developed and named by Dr. Dianne Miller, a gynaecologic oncologist with BC Cancer and Vancouver Coastal Health, and associate professor emerita at UBC.

“If there is one thing better than curing cancer, it’s never getting the cancer in the first place,” Miller said.

Symptoms of ovarian cancer can include constipation, bloating, early satiety after eating and back pain. It tends to occur in post menopausal women; though anyone can be at risk, according to the Mayo Clinic .

About 20 per cent of all ovarian cancers are caused by a genetic mutation that also affects a woman’s risk of breast cancer.

The cancer tends to respond well to chemotherapy and radiation but also has a high recurrence rate.

stories.title: StatCan says fertility rate remains at the all-time low seen the previous year
stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the country’s fertility rate in 2025 remained at an all-time low recorded the previous year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — Statistics Canada says the country’s fertility rate in 2025 remained at an all-time low recorded the previous year.

The agency says the rate of 1.26 children per woman was virtually unchanged from 2024.

Fertility rates have been falling around the world since 2009, with Canada ranking in the bottom seven among 20 high-income countries.

The average age of mothers giving birth has meanwhile increased to a new high of 31.9 years. StatCan notes it’s been rising for decades – in 1976, the average age was 26.7.

The data also shows the number of women giving birth at home is back to pre-pandemic levels seen in 2019.

Home births peaked in 2021, with more than 9,000 babies born outside of hospitals that year, the agency says, as some families chose home births to reduce the risk of COVID-19 transmission.

The number of non-hospital births returned to around 7,000 last year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Woman charged after suspected fatal impaired-driving crash in Ottawa
stories.summary: A 30-year-old man was critically injured and died on the way to the hospital. A 32-year-old man was also taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A 30-year-old man is dead after a vehicle crashed into a Ottawa barber shop Tuesday in a suspected impaired-driving incident.

Ottawa police said its crews were called to CuTzz Barber Salon, located in the 100 block of McArthur Avenue, around 5:40 p.m. Sept. 22 for the crash. Two men inside the business were hurt after the vehicle crashed into it.

The 30-year-old man was critically injured and died on the way to the hospital, police said. A 32-year-old man was also taken to hospital with serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

A 57-year-old woman was arrested at the scene and charged with impaired driving-related offences. She was scheduled to appear in court Wednesday.

The identities of those involved were not released.

Police are asking anyone with information regarding the collision, or who may have cameras on their property or at home, or a dash cam that may have captured the incident, to contact them.

stories.title: David Suzuki says Mark Carney is driving Canada ‘into a ditch’ with shift on climate
stories.summary: Suzuki said there are two things the government can do to get Canada's climate action on track: set hard targets and declare an emergency.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

Posted September 23, 2026 1:23 pm.

David Suzuki said that when Prime Minister Mark Carney was first elected last year, he celebrated. Having met and interviewed the prime minister before, the national environmentalist icon said he knew Carney understood the challenges of climate change.

But in an interview with The Canadian Press, Suzuki said he now feels he was “wilfully blind” to Carney’s promises of action on climate, despite warnings from his longtime friend the late Stephen Lewis, who predicted the agenda of a banker — and now politician — would supersede Carney’s views on addressing climate change.

He acknowledges that Carney’s actions come as Canadians’ views on climate have shifted to other priorities.

“I think that’s because of that disconnect of what are the really basic things are that keep us alive,” he said.

For decades, Suzuki brought millions of Canadians into the world of science and nature. From their living rooms, viewers of The Nature of Things could learn about the intersection of humanity and nature and its impact on the planet.

Suzuki, 90, retired from hosting the show four years ago, but still wants to talk to Canadians about the environment. This time though, the educational message is tinged with exasperation.

Canadians and people around the world have their priorities wrong, he said.

“Brazil’s Amazon, the greatest terrestrial ecosystem on the planet, has no economic value until it is logged, mined, dammed, or grows soy, cattle, or houses,” Suzuki said.

“So if that doesn’t tell you right there what kind of a f–ked-up system we have, that is exploiting the very things that keep us alive. And we don’t put any value on it.”

Canada’s record on battling the greenhouse gas emissions driving climate change has been spotty. The federal government has committed to multiple different targets since 1990 and despite implementing dozens of new policies to cut emissions, it has never met any of its targets.

Since taking office in March 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney has pushed many of those policies aside in the name of economic prosperity — particularly as Canadians grapple with the cost of living on a planet that is facing increasingly destructive weather events every year.

He cancelled the consumer carbon tax on his first day in office, repealed a mandate to phase out gas-powered cars in favour of electric models, and scrapped an emissions cap on oil and gas production.

Carney said most of those policies were too divisive and costly and he is looking to introduce cuts over a longer term, with investments in clean technology. He also has backed the idea of another oil pipeline to the West Coast and has adjusted some policies to make it more likely.

Which one of those actions made Suzuki raise his eyebrows the most?

“I haven’t read any of it,” Suzuki said.

“The problem is, it doesn’t really matter to me. Fundamentally, the problem is that the underlying systems that we’ve developed to guide, shape, manage human behaviour have left out the most fundamental thing, which is that our very survival and well-being depends on Mother Earth.

“If you look at our legal, our political and our economic systems, the planet has been left out. The economy is the system that is driving us on the destructive path.”

He doesn’t even give much credit to the government of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose government enacted some of the most climate friendly policies Canada has ever had. Even Trudeau, Suzuki argues, didn’t aim high enough.

Suzuki said Carney “understands very clearly what the challenges of climate change represent.”

But he said Carney is advocating for climate action as a banker, with an agenda that suits that title.

“He still believes the economy must be kept going the way it is and that it can be used to keep emissions down and keep the economy going,” he said. “I think it’s impossible.”

Carney was in Strasbourg, France last week to address the European Parliament, ON a mission to deepen ties with the EU — particularly on trade, as Canada tried to lessen its dependence on the United States. Canada’s offer to the EU is largely based on its access to resources, including natural gas and critical minerals, but Suzuki said it’s a catch-22.

“(Carney) is standing up to (Trump). Thank God for Mr. Carney for doing that. But our arrangements with Europe, they’re all based on economics,” Suzuki said.

“What does Canada have to sell to these other countries to take our dependence away from the United States? It’s going to be minerals, forests, water, and it’s not based on the fundamental protection of those things. It’s all going to what economic value can we extract. So I think we’re kind of hooped.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.

Suzuki said there are two things the government can do right now to get the country’s climate action back on track: set hard targets and declare an emergency.

“When you declare a state of emergency, all these economic and political arguments disappear,” he said. “You’ve got to deal with that crisis now, and that’s what we need. And Mr. Carney could go a long way if he would take his party now and declare state of emergency and get it going now.”

Suzuki also said the media has failed to fact-check messages from world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump.

Suzuki said he is still saying the same things he always has, but he’s not sure it’s being received the way it used to be, and figuring out how to fix that has left him at a loss.

“There was a time when, believe it or not, Canadians knew who the hell I was and they listened to me. They took me seriously. But you know, the world is so different now, that I think that kind of celebrity is just not possible.”

“He still believes the economy must be kept going the way it is and that it can be used to keep emissions down and keep the economy going,” he said. “I think it’s impossible.”

Carney was in Strasbourg, France last week to address the European Parliament, ON a mission to deepen ties with the EU — particularly on trade, as Canada tried to lessen its dependence on the United States. Canada’s offer to the EU is largely based on its access to resources, including natural gas and critical minerals, but Suzuki said it’s a catch-22.
“(Carney) is standing up to (Trump). Thank God for Mr. Carney for doing that. But our arrangements with Europe, they’re all based on economics,” Suzuki said.

“What does Canada have to sell to these other countries to take our dependence away from the United States? It’s going to be minerals, forests, water, and it’s not based on the fundamental protection of those things. It’s all going to what economic value can we extract. So I think we’re kind of hooped.”
In a statement, a spokesperson for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is committed to fighting climate change and reaching net-zero emissions by 2050.
Suzuki said there are two things the government can do right now to get the country’s climate action back on track: set hard targets and declare an emergency.

“When you declare a state of emergency, all these economic and political arguments disappear,” he said. “You’ve got to deal with that crisis now, and that’s what we need. And Mr. Carney could go a long way if he would take his party now and declare state of emergency and get it going now.”
Suzuki also said the media has failed to fact-check messages from world leaders, including U.S. President Donald Trump.
Suzuki said he is still saying the same things he always has, but he’s not sure it’s being received the way it used to be, and figuring out how to fix that has left him at a loss.

“There was a time when, believe it or not, Canadians knew who the hell I was and they listened to me. They took me seriously. But you know, the world is so different now, that I think that kind of celebrity is just not possible.”

stories.title: Opioid use disorder among older adults has doubled in Ontario since 2017, new study finds
stories.summary: The number of older adults in Ontario living with opioid-use disorder (OUD) has more than doubled since 2017, a new study out of Toronto’s St. Michael’s Hospital has found.
stories.author: Joanna Lavoie
stories.content:
The number of older adults in Ontario living with opioid use disorder (OUD) has more than doubled since 2017, a new study out of Toronto’s St. Michael’s Hospital has found.

In a 43-page report released Wednesday, the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network (Odprn) said the quarterly number of Ontarians age 55 and up with OUD that have interacted with the healthcare system has jumped from 7,116 in mid-2017 to 15,231 by the end of 2025.

This represents roughly one in 350 older adults in the province.

The study also showed that opioid toxicity death rates have increased substantially over the last decade.

Data cited by the researchers showed that there were 1,087 opioid toxicity deaths among older adults in Ontario in 2023 and 2024, which equates to roughly one a day.

A staggering 75 per cent of those deaths occurred in people between the ages of 55 and 64.

It also found that only one-third of opioid toxicity deaths in Ontario involved prescribed opioids, although that statistic increases with age.

Co-author Bisola Hamzat, a senior epidemiologist with the Odprn, which is part of St. Michael’s Hospital, said researchers didn’t expect to see such a high number of Ontarians struggling with opioid addiction.

“I think what we’re seeing is that many people who developed opioid-use disorder during the opioid boom of the past decade are now ageing into that 55-plus age group,” she told CP24 earlier this week.

“I think that also begs the question around system readiness for an ageing population that has more complex care needs, especially when substance-use services have perhaps been more catered to or designed for a younger population.”

Study calls for systemic change

Hamzat said the reason why researchers launched the study was because they were observing a “rise in public health or publicly reported indicators of opioid toxic harms and treatment use among older adults in the province.”

“Community members were worried because we’re seeing an ageing population in Canada as a whole, which also means an aging population of people with an opioid-use disorder,” she said.

“So we really wanted to just do an analysis to understand gaps in care and support for this population. And really, the broader question is: if there’s an ageing population of people who use drugs, people with an opioid-use disorder, is the system ready and capable to handle this shift?”

In the end, Hamzat said the goal of the study is to help reduce and prevent opioid-related harms and deaths among older adults in the province, which are primarily due to fentanyl.

She said researchers will now share their findings with the community, individuals, and agencies most directly impacted, and then with policy makers and government leaders.

The epidemiologist says it’s imperative that substance-use harm reduction services are prioritized in the province as people age.

“So when someone with a substance use disorder does come in, as we’re seeing population age, (staff are) better equipped and prepared to care for that population,” said Hamzat.

“Also just building the clinical infrastructure and pharmacy relations to dispense some treatments within those settings and just making sure people can stay connected to their community supports and addiction specialists, or having people that can help transition or navigate people with substance use histories into long-term care, and make sure their substance use and pain needs are prioritized.”

For this study, researchers analyzed trends over time in healthcare interactions related to OUD, Opioid Agonist Treatment use, non-fatal hospital-treated opioid toxicities, and opioid toxicity deaths among older adults in Ontario between Jan. 1, 2013 and Dec. 31, 2025.

Based on data availability, they also looked at demographic characteristics, circumstances surrounding death, substances contributing to death, prior health history, and healthcare interactions for older adults who were confirmed to have died of an opioid toxicity between January 1, 2023 and December 31, 2024. Coroner’s records were also linked to their research for opioid toxicity fatalities during that period.

All data in the study came from the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences, which is an independent, non-profit research institute that legally collects and analyzes health care and demographic data in Ontario, without consent, for health system evaluation and improvement.

stories.title: All the new Michelin-approved restaurants in and around Toronto for 2026
stories.summary: No new restaurants were awarded Michelin stars this year, while five new restaurants received the Bib Gourmand recognition
stories.author: Abigale Subdhan
stories.content:
The Michelin Guide Toronto & Region unveiled its 2026 selections at a gala in Toronto on Tuesday night. No new restaurants were awarded Michelin stars this year, while five new restaurants received the Bib Gourmand recognition. Eleven new spots were also added to its recommended list.

Restaurant Pearl Morissette , a restaurant in the Niagara Region that offers contemporary cuisine, kept its two stars from last year. Fourteen other restaurants maintained their one-star designation.

There are currently 15 Michelin-starred restaurants in the Toronto region, down from 17 last year. Toronto restaurant Aburi Hana lost its only star and wasn’t featured on this year’s list, while Hexagon in Oakville, Ont., has since closed down.

Toronto became the first Canadian city to be featured by the French tire company’s gastronomic guide in 2022. It has since awarded restaurants outside the city limits in surrounding regions up to two hours away.

Here’s a look at the newest additions to this year’s guide.

This year’s Michelin Guide inspectors gave five new restaurants its Bib Gourmand designation, which recognizes eateries for “great food at a great value.” There are currently 31 Toronto eateries with the Bib Gourmand recognition .

View this post on Instagram A post shared by @antyliatoronto

Type of cuisine: Latin American

Chefs: Aldo Camarena and Ashley McKay

Neighbourhood: Dufferin Grove (1059 Bloor St. W)

According to Michelin: “How do you honor Ontario’s seasons and ingredients but give them a unique boost? Just ask Antylia, a talented kitchen that takes diners on a trip through Mexico and Latin America. Chef/owners Aldo Camarena and Ashley McKay take the details seriously, nixtamalizing and grinding all of their heirloom corn masa in house using a volcanic stone mill imported from Puebla, Mexico.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Golden Horseshoe Barbecue (@goldenhorseshoebbq)

Type of cuisine: Barbecue

Chefs: Andrew Golden (who won this year’s Michelin Young Chef award)

Neighbourhood: Annex (657 Dupont St.)

According to Michelin: “This is true Texas-style barbecue, specializing in the holy trinity of brisket, ribs and sausage (if you happen to swing by on a Thursday, you’ll be rewarded with pastrami, though). While all eyes are trained on the meat, sides like charro beans with jalapeños and cotija cheese, and cornbread slathered in cinnamon butter, are far from a second thought.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Les Incompetents (@barlesincompetents)

Type of cuisine: Modern and French cuisine

Neighbourhood: St. Catharines, Ont. (386 St. Paul St.)

According to Michelin: “The thoughtful, endlessly tempting menu is loosely French in inspiration and delivers knockout flavors in style. Who knew that egg mayonnaise with celeriac remoulade could be this good or that mackerel tastes best skewered and grilled? Cocktails, meanwhile, are sophisticated, refined efforts that should be explored with abandon.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by RPM Bakehouse (@rpm_bakehouse)

Type of cuisine: Bakery

Neighbourhood: Jordan Station in Niagara (3839 Main St.)

According to Michelin: “The daytime relative of Pearl Morissette offers a casual, evolving menu that never fails to delight. To complement a vibrant salad, sourdough grilled cheese with golden beets and aged cheddar is the move to make. If still available, swing for the quiche, a custardy indulgence that has few equals. A cup of hot coffee, a buttery danish, a seat on the sunny patio – is there a better way to start the day?”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Lunch Lady Toronto (@thelunchladytoronto)

Type of cuisine: Vietnamese

Chefs: Benedict Lim and Allan Lu

Neighbourhood: Trinity-Bellwoods (93 Ossington Ave.)

According to Michelin: “This Toronto outpost serves elevated Vietnamese cuisine rooted in the recipes of Nguyen Thi Thanh, the original Lunch Lady of Saigon. The restaurant channels those original flavors into a lively, neighborhood-driven dining room that’s been busy ever since it opened.”

Restaurant Pearl Morissette , a restaurant in the Niagara Region that offers contemporary cuisine, kept its two stars from last year. Fourteen other restaurants maintained their one-star designation.

There are currently 15 Michelin-starred restaurants in the Toronto region, down from 17 last year. Toronto restaurant Aburi Hana lost its only star and wasn’t featured on this year’s list, while Hexagon in Oakville, Ont., has since closed down.

Toronto became the first Canadian city to be featured by the French tire company’s gastronomic guide in 2022. It has since awarded restaurants outside the city limits in surrounding regions up to two hours away.
Here’s a look at the newest additions to this year’s guide.

This year’s Michelin Guide inspectors gave five new restaurants its Bib Gourmand designation, which recognizes eateries for “great food at a great value.” There are currently 31 Toronto eateries with the Bib Gourmand recognition .
View this post on Instagram A post shared by @antyliatoronto
Type of cuisine: Latin American
Chefs: Aldo Camarena and Ashley McKay
Neighbourhood: Dufferin Grove (1059 Bloor St. W)

According to Michelin: “How do you honor Ontario’s seasons and ingredients but give them a unique boost? Just ask Antylia, a talented kitchen that takes diners on a trip through Mexico and Latin America. Chef/owners Aldo Camarena and Ashley McKay take the details seriously, nixtamalizing and grinding all of their heirloom corn masa in house using a volcanic stone mill imported from Puebla, Mexico.”
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Golden Horseshoe Barbecue (@goldenhorseshoebbq)
Type of cuisine: Barbecue
Chefs: Andrew Golden (who won this year’s Michelin Young Chef award)
Neighbourhood: Annex (657 Dupont St.)

According to Michelin: “This is true Texas-style barbecue, specializing in the holy trinity of brisket, ribs and sausage (if you happen to swing by on a Thursday, you’ll be rewarded with pastrami, though). While all eyes are trained on the meat, sides like charro beans with jalapeños and cotija cheese, and cornbread slathered in cinnamon butter, are far from a second thought.”
View this post on Instagram A post shared by Les Incompetents (@barlesincompetents)
Type of cuisine: Modern and French cuisine
Neighbourhood: St. Catharines, Ont. (386 St. Paul St.)

According to Michelin: “The thoughtful, endlessly tempting menu is loosely French in inspiration and delivers knockout flavors in style. Who knew that egg mayonnaise with celeriac remoulade could be this good or that mackerel tastes best skewered and grilled? Cocktails, meanwhile, are sophisticated, refined efforts that should be explored with abandon.”
View this post on Instagram A post shared by RPM Bakehouse (@rpm_bakehouse)
Type of cuisine: Bakery
Neighbourhood: Jordan Station in Niagara (3839 Main St.)

According to Michelin: “The daytime relative of Pearl Morissette offers a casual, evolving menu that never fails to delight. To complement a vibrant salad, sourdough grilled cheese with golden beets and aged cheddar is the move to make. If still available, swing for the quiche, a custardy indulgence that has few equals. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Lunch Lady Toronto (@thelunchladytoronto)
Type of cuisine: Vietnamese
Chefs: Benedict Lim and Allan Lu
Neighbourhood: Trinity-Bellwoods (93 Ossington Ave.)

According to Michelin: “This Toronto outpost serves elevated Vietnamese cuisine rooted in the recipes of Nguyen Thi Thanh, the original Lunch Lady of Saigon. The restaurant channels those original flavors into a lively, neighborhood-driven dining room that’s been busy ever since it opened.”

stories.title: Ottawa city council approves Trump Avenue name change
stories.summary: Council passed the motion to rename the street hours after the U.S. president renewed hostilities toward Canada in a social media post.
stories.author: Aedan Helmer
stories.content:
Council passed the motion to rename the street hours after the U.S. president renewed hostilities toward Canada in a social media post

Ottawa city councillors moved unanimously to remove Trump Avenue signs in the city’s Central Park neighbourhood and will form a working group with residents to rename the street.

River Coun. Riley Brockington said he was “embarrassed” to have a street named after U.S. President Donald Trump in the nation’s capital and in his ward and said he would lead the effort to come up with a new name.

The city-led effort to rename the street was first introduced in August amid an escalating trade war, punitive tariffs and an effort by the White House to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.

Ottawa city council passed the motion to rename the street on Sept. 23, hours after the U.S. president renewed hostilities toward Canada in a social media post criticizing the country’s immigration policies.

“I could speak at great length why I believe strongly it is time to rename Trump Avenue, but I don’t want to give a platform any more to the person who’s on the current street sign blades,” Brockington told his fellow councillors on Wednesday. “I do believe this is about a new beginning, and I want this to be a community-led process where the community ultimately will select and recommend to city council what that new name will be.”

Brockington said he will form a community group with three to five residents of Trump Avenue to draft a list of alternatives.

The Central Park neighbourhood was constructed in the 1990s with many of the streets named around a New York City theme.

Trump Avenue “was never intended to be commemorative,” City of Ottawa staff said in a statement.

“The city aims to ensure street names reflect current naming standards and community values. Under today’s commemorative naming criteria, the name would not meet the requirements for a commemorative street name.”

An attempt to rename the street failed in 2021 after Trump’s first term in office, when 42 votes were received from the 62 homes on Trump Avenue, with 21 in favour of changing the name and 21 opposed.

Brockington said he’s received overwhelming support for renaming the street since the idea resurfaced in recent weeks.

“I’m embarrassed about a street in our city, let alone my ward named in his honour,” Brockington said after introducing the notice of motion earlier in September. “We’re at the point where it’s just completely unacceptable to have the street named after this individual.”

I’m embarrassed about a street in our city, let alone my ward named in his honour River Councillor Riley Brockington

Brockington said he’s received “overwhelming” support from the community and the city, along with a flood of support from across Canada, the U.S. and countries around the world.

Mayor Mark Sutcliffe said he supported the motion as long as residents on the street are willing to go through the administrative process of changing their documents with an updated street address.

“I don’t like the idea of anything that’s named for Donald Trump, who’s demonstrated hostility towards Canada, in our city,” Sutcliffe said.

stories.title: Forest City grows greener as annual tree giveaway sees huge turnout
stories.summary: Residents of the Forest City embraced National Tree Day with overwhelming enthusiasm Wednesday morning, flocking to a massive city-sponsored giveaway event
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Residents of the Forest City embraced National Tree Day with overwhelming enthusiasm Wednesday morning, flocking to a massive city-sponsored giveaway event that saw thousands of trees distributed to eager gardeners and environmental stewards.

The annual giveaway, a cornerstone of London’s commitment to expanding its urban canopy, drew long queues of vehicles eager to collect their share of saplings.

The event, held at a dedicated lot on Westminster Drive, transformed the area into a hub of green activity. By mid-morning, cars were lined up for over a kilometer.

City staff managed the flow, funneling vehicles into four lanes where they were greeted with a selection of over a dozen tree species. Each car was permitted up to two free trees, with more than 2,000 saplings made available.

This year’s giveaway carries particular significance with London named the 2026 Forest Capital of Canada by the Canadian Institute of Forestry.

“It helps with climate resiliency and urban habitat for wildlife and shade, carbon sequestration and all those good things,” explained Jaclyn Ellah, forestry supervisor, highlighting the multifaceted benefits of the initiative.

Shawna Chambers, director of climate change, environment & waste management, echoed the sentiment. “We are excited to once again celebrate National Tree Day with a tree giveaway for Londoners,” Chambers stated. “Each year, we give out more than 5,000 trees to Londoners – and our crews plant about 5,000 across the city. This helps us grow, maintain and protect our thriving urban forest.”

The city’s ambitious Urban Forest Strategy aims to achieve 34 per cent tree canopy cover by 2065, a goal London is reportedly on track to meet. With over seven million trees currently in the city, including approximately 1.8 million owned and maintained by the municipality, initiatives like the giveaway are crucial for continued growth.

Residents had their pick from a diverse range of species, including popular choices like Sugar Maple, Red Maple, Tulip Tree, and White Pine, alongside fruit-bearing options such as Honeycrisp Apple, Bartlett Pear, and Romeo & Juliet Cherry.

City officials reminded residents that newly planted trees require protection and care during their first year.

As an added bonus, each car participating in the giveaway also received a free bag of Green Bin compost, further supporting residents’ gardening efforts.

The Council Highlights are not an official record of County Council proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Council Meetings and Minutes.

Council supports advocacy efforts calling for permanent increase to Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF)

Middlesex County Council endorsed advocacy efforts calling on the Province of Ontario to permanently maintain the Ontario Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF) at $400 million annually. The resolution supports a request from the Municipal Finance Officers' Association of Ontario, calling for stable, predictable funding for municipalities to renew aging infrastructure and investments that support growth and housing.

The OCIF is a critical source of formula-based funding that helps municipalities plan and prioritize long-term infrastructure projects. Middlesex County maintains more than 1,700 lane kilometres of roads and 254 bridges and culverts, many of which are approaching the end of their expected service lives. Predictable funding is considered essential to support asset management planning and avoid costly infrastructure deterioration.

The County received $1.37 million in OCIF funding in 2026, more than double its 2021 allocation. Any reduction in future OCIF funding could increase pressure on property taxes, reserves, or debt financing, and may require planned capital projects to be delayed.

To learn more, read theOntario Community Infrastructure Fund (OCIF) Advocacy report").

Public Health in Middlesex County – Middlesex-London Health Unit Delegation

The Middlesex-London Health Unit provided County Council with an update highlighting current health trends, public health services, and emerging community health challenges across the region. The Health Unit serves approximately 600,000 residents across the City of London and Middlesex County and delivers a wide range of services, including disease prevention, immunization programs, health inspections, public education, and outbreak management.

The presentation highlighted several initiatives aimed at improving access to public health services across Middlesex County. In recent years, the health unit has expanded county immunization clinic opportunities from approximately 12 to 36 annually, and began offering nurse-led sexual health clinics in communities including Strathroy, Dorchester, and Lucan. School-based immunization programs, oral health programs, breastfeeding supports, and environmental health inspections continue to play a key role in serving residents throughout the County.

For more information, see the Public Health in Middlesex County presentation").

Intersection Control Policy Motion

County Council directed staff to develop an Intersection Control Policy that will establish a consistent, data-driven approach for evaluating and implementing traffic control measures across the County road network.

This aims to standardize criteria and processes for assessing, selecting, and installing intersection controls helping ensure decisions are based on engineering principles, safety considerations, traffic volumes, and operational needs. Once completed, the policy will be presented to Council for consideration and is expected to serve as a framework for future transportation planning and traffic management decisions throughout Middlesex County.

Recommendations made by the Committee of the Whole at the September 22, 2026, meeting will be considered by County Council at its next regular meeting on October 13, 2026. The Legislative Services Department maintains the official record for all County government proceedings.

stories.title: Ottawa votes to rename ‘Trump Avenue’ as city distances itself from U.S. president
stories.summary: The move comes amid heightened tensions between Trump and Canadian leaders, including recent disputes over tariffs.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
Ottawa city council has voted to rename Trump Avenue, ending ongoing debate over the street’s politically charged name and formally severing its symbolic link to U.S. President Donald Trump.

The decision follows a staff report recommending the change and comes at a time when Canada–U.S. relations have been strained by trade disputes.

The street, located in Ottawa’s Central Park neighbourhood, was created in the late 1990s and early 2000s as part of a development built on former Experimental Farm land.

The entire neighbourhood was designed with an explicit New York City theme, featuring streets and parks named after Manhattan landmarks, including Manhattan Crescent, Staten Way, Bloomingdale Street, and Madison Park. At the time, Trump was known primarily as a high‑profile New York developer.

Council’s vote means the city will begin the process of selecting a new name, notifying residents, and updating municipal records. The change will also require coordination with emergency services, utilities, and Canada Post to ensure a seamless transition.

The move comes amid heightened tensions between Trump and Canadian leaders, including recent disputes over tariffs , trade negotiations, and public remarks that have spilled into municipal politics. Ottawa councillors noted that while the street was never intended to reference the U.S. president, its continued presence had become a point of discomfort for residents.

City staff say the renaming process will include consultation with affected homeowners before a final name is approved.

stories.title: Belleville was not a bolt out of a clear sky
stories.summary: Antizionism is driving the violence against Jews that we’ve seen already for years, and we need a whole-of-government approach to stop it
stories.author: Steven Wernick
stories.content:
Steven Wernick is senior rabbi of Beth Tzedec Congregation in Toronto.

On Kol Nidre night, as the community of Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., gathered for the opening of Yom Kippur – when the congregation asks, together, to be forgiven and spared – a man outside with a shotgun opened fire. Stained glass shattered; shots meant for people at prayer struck nearby cars and houses.

Constable Jeff Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville Police Service, stood between that gunfire and the door. He was hit and critically wounded. Premier Doug Ford called him a hero who stopped a tragedy. In my own tradition, the Torah commands, in Leviticus, to “not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour.” Constable Smith followed that command without ever hearing it in the language of the Hebrew Bible, and a member of my congregation has already raised more than $100,000 for his family on GoFundMe. The Canadian Jewish community, through the UJA Federation of Greater Toronto, has established a fund as well.

That is what a community can do in a day. The state has done less. Belleville was not a bolt out of a clear sky. It capped three years of the same: bullet holes at a Montreal yeshiva; a synagogue and a Federation CJA office firebombed in a Montreal suburb; the synagogue firebombed again a year later; an arson at a Vancouver synagogue; a Toronto Jewish school shot at repeatedly in a single year; three more synagogues hit by gunfire in Vaughan and Toronto this past March; a Molotov cocktail thrown at a Montreal temple in June. Each time, concern was expressed and seriousness promised. Each time, the target moved closer to the sanctuary door, and this week it reached the officer standing in front of it.

Shooting at Belleville synagogue an escalation of antisemitic violence, advocates say

Within hours, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said what needed saying: “Jewish Canadians should not need armed police outside their synagogues simply to pray safely. Canadians cannot accept a future, as now exists in Europe, in which synagogues and Jewish schools can only operate safely behind permanent armed police and soldiers with machine guns.”

The Cija called on leaders to say clearly that antizionism is driving this violence.

That is not a new accusation. It has a name: the “three Ds,” coined by the Soviet refusenik turned Israeli statesman Natan Sharansky – demonizing Israel in language reserved for absolute evil, holding it to double standards applied to no other country and delegitimizing its right to exist as a Jewish state. None of that invalidates honest criticism of a government; Israeli ministers themselves have pursued policies that betray their country’s founding values. But what we saw in Belleville is different: the conviction that Jewish self-determination is itself worthy of punishment, turning every Jew, everywhere, into a stand-in for a state a gunman has never set foot in.

Canada adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism in 2019 and published a handbook on applying it in 2024. In June, after his own address on antisemitism, I asked Prime Minister Mark Carney in an op-ed to commit to implementing that handbook across every federal institution. He did not.

Editorial: The courage needed to face down hatred

Ontario adopted the same definition in 2020, by order-in-council – but the bill that would have written it into actual law, binding every ministry to what its own preamble called a “whole-of-government approach,” passed second reading that February and has sat in committee ever since. Mr. Ford says he expects those responsible for the Belleville shooting to be prosecuted to the full extent of the law. Good – but also, his government should pass the bill it let die. We are not short on laws that make this a hate crime. We are short on the will to enforce them, consistently, at every level.

Law by itself is only words on a page; it earns the right to be defended only when it delivers justice to the people it was written to protect. Jewish Canadians in Belleville, Vaughan, Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver need federal funding for paid-duty police at threatened synagogues and schools, delivered in days, not months. They need the regimes bankrolling this violence, starting with Iran, confronted by name. And they need “do not stand idly by the blood of your neighbour” to bind a government too. Mr. Carney, Mr. Ford: As Cija put it, “No more thoughts and prayers. The clock is ticking and our leaders must act before lives are lost.”

Yom Kippur asks a question: who shall live, and who shall die? This year in Belleville, a police officer answered that question with his own body before God. He should not have had to. That is what I am asking Canadians, our Prime Minister and our premiers to hear.

The Canadian Jewish community, through the UJA Federation of Greater Toronto, has established a fund as well.

That is what a community can do in a day. The state has done less. Belleville was not a bolt out of a clear sky. It capped three years of the same: bullet holes at a Montreal yeshiva; a synagogue and a Federation CJA office firebombed in a Montreal suburb; the synagogue firebombed again a year later; an arson at a Vancouver synagogue; a Toronto Jewish school shot at repeatedly in a single year; three more synagogues hit by gunfire in Vaughan and Toronto this past March; a Molotov cocktail thrown at a Montreal temple in June. Each time, concern was expressed and seriousness promised. Each time, the target moved closer to the sanctuary door, and this week it reached the officer standing in front of it.

Within hours, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs said what needed saying: “Jewish Canadians should not need armed police outside their synagogues simply to pray safely. Canadians cannot accept a future, as now exists in Europe, in which synagogues and Jewish schools can only operate safely behind permanent armed police and soldiers with machine guns.”
The Cija called on leaders to say clearly that antizionism is driving this violence.

That is not a new accusation. It has a name: the “three Ds,” coined by the Soviet refusenik turned Israeli statesman Natan Sharansky – demonizing Israel in language reserved for absolute evil, holding it to double standards applied to no other country and delegitimizing its right to exist as a Jewish state. None of that invalidates honest criticism of a government; Israeli ministers themselves have pursued policies that betray their country’s founding values. Canada adopted the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism in 2019 and published a handbook on applying it in 2024. stories.title: Toronto Zoo seeking names for ‘little potato’ baby wombat
stories.summary: In a social media post, the tourist attraction said its southern hairy-nosed wombat had given birth to a baby girl who needs a new name.
stories.author: Isaac Callan
stories.content:
The Toronto Zoo has another new arrival, and it is turning to the public to decide how to name the “little potato.”

In a social media post, the tourist attraction said its southern hairy-nosed wombat had given birth to a baby girl who needs a new name.

“She May still be cozy in mom’s pouch, but this little potato is getting braver every day and starting to peek out and explore her world,” Toronto Zoo wrote online.

The public will have until next week to vote on the best name for the new arrival.

The southern hairy-nosed wombat hails from Australia and can live for decades. In 2016, Toronto Zoo had a 34-year-old hairy-nosed wombat, claimed at the time to be the world’s oldest wombat.

Voting to name the zoo’s youngest wombat will close on Sept. 30.

stories.title: Royal Ontario Museum provides crucial genetic samples for revising bat family tree
stories.summary: Global research project suggests bats first arose in Europe some 65 million years ago, coinciding with the abrupt disappearance of dinosaurs
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
If someone threw a party for every type of mammal on Earth, a large portion of the guest list would be taken up by bats.

Bats account for about 20 per cent of total mammal diversity, with more than 1,500 documented species worldwide.

Now, a multiyear, international effort to explore the underlying genetics behind that diversity has yielded a new family tree and a better understanding of where and when bats arose.

The results, published online Wednesday by the journal Nature, suggest that bats, with their distinctive mode of powered flight, first arose in Europe some 65 million years ago.

That’s about 10 million years earlier than the oldest known bat fossils and coincides with the abrupt disappearance of dinosaurs along with three quarters of Earth’s plant and animal species in a mass extinction event.

If bats first appeared at that time, it implies they were able to exploit an ecological niche that was available after the mass extinction but not filled by birds. The genetic analysis suggests that bats evolved their powers of echolocation at a similarly early date. This method of using soundwaves to identify both obstacles and prey made bats ideal nocturnal hunters.

More than 100 researchers from 64 countries were involved in the effort, called Bat1K . It included sequencing and comparing the genomes of 103 species, which cover each of the 21 known families of bats.

About one-third of the species sampled in the study came from just one source: a freezer at the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto that contains tissue gathered over decades from a wide range of bat species.

Canadian among researchers to discover dinosaurs nested farther south than previously known

In a small B.C. town, a grizzly family stirs unease

Burton Lim, assistant curator of mammals at the museum and a co-author of the study, said the Rom’s collection proved invaluable because researchers opted to store the bat tissue in liquid nitrogen, which they brought with them into the field.

“The colder the better, to keep the DNA intact,” Dr. Lim said.

The preservation enabled researchers to assemble whole bat genomes from longer strands of DNA than would have been available through other methods. In addition to comparing different species more easily, it meant researchers could determine that the ancestral bat genome was likely organized into 26 chromosomes.

“This is a landmark study for bat biology, and for comparative genomics more generally,” said Josefin Stiller, a biologist at the University of Copenhagen, in an accompanying commentary in Nature.

Dr. Lim added that in addition to illuminating bat evolution, results from the Bat1K project can inform both conservation and health. In a 2025 study , the project revealed the genetic information it gleaned about how bats tolerate viruses, including those that can be passed to humans, such as the coronaviruses responsible for Sars and COVID-19.

stories.title: Canada working ‘alongside’ partners on AI safety, minister says
stories.summary: AI Minister Evan Solomon said Canada is taking a "very leading" role by investing $150 million in Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio’s efforts to build a safer AI.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says Canada is “advocating alongside our partners” on AI safety.

Solomon says he met with his international counterparts after Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke recently to other leaders about setting up a “technology stability” board to regulate AI.

But when he was asked whether Canada is taking a leadership role in those efforts, Solomon pointed to domestic legislation, including proposed regulations on AI chatbots.

He also said Canada is taking a “very leading” role by investing $150 million in Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio’s efforts to build a safer AI.

Bengio is set to address the UN Security Council today, which will also hear from major AI companies.

Warnings about the risks AI poses to humans, and documented cases of AI bots disregarding human instructions, have prompted global alarm in recent weeks.

stories.title: Trump says Canada is ‘destroying itself’ because of ‘unchecked’ immigrants
stories.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump claims Canada is "destroying itself" by allowing millions of people into the country "essentially unchecked and unvetted."
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump claims Canada is “destroying itself” by allowing millions of people into the country “essentially unchecked and unvetted.”

In a social media post Wednesday, Trump said this is causing unspecified problems that “will soon be too big to handle” and described it as a “Liberal takeover that will end very badly.”

He said the immigration policy is already resulting in high unemployment numbers.

Trump provided no evidence for these claims.

Canada’s unemployment rate in August was 6.4 per cent. The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.1 per cent last month.

Ottawa has reduced its immigration intake over the last two years after abandoning plans to work toward admitting 500,000 permanent residents annually. It also introduced targets for admissions of international students and temporary workers following sharp increases in both those populations.

Immigration Department data shows the number of temporary residents coming to Canada between January and July this year is 66 per cent lower than the number of arrivals over the same period in 2024, when reduction measures began.

Statistics Canada population estimates show Canada’s population growth has been flat recently due to reduced immigration, and the parliamentary budget officer expects zero population growth this year.

The Immigration Department’s website says all visitors, temporary foreign workers, students, immigrants and refugees undergo comprehensive security screening protocols and can be deemed inadmissible on grounds of security, human or international rights violations, or organized criminality.

stories.title: How volunteers fill the gaps in Canada’s health system, according to our experts
stories.summary: Readers asked what they can do for their own communities and how the clinics and hospitals can better care for their patients
stories.author: Globe Staff
stories.content:
On Sept. 17, health editor Caroline Alphonso and national health reporter Alanna Smith answered reader questions on what health care volunteers are doing across the country , and how the Canadian system can better care for its patients.

Over the summer, we featured the stories of volunteers in Canadian health care in our Care Between the Lines series. From a non-profit organization in Saskatchewan that drives locals to their medical appointments , stylists giving free haircuts in a Charlottetown hospital , cyclists taking seniors out for outdoor excursions and many more stories, the series celebrated these volunteers while highlighting the gaps in a system that can feel isolating for patients.

Readers asked how these volunteers got involved, what they can do for their own communities and how the clinics and hospitals can better care for their patients. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

How did this series come to be? What has stuck out to you about these stories?

Caroline Alphonso: Kristy Kirkup had written a lovely piece around the Christmas holidays on a woman who volunteered her time in an infant cuddling program at St. Michael’s Hospital .

That sparked the series idea. We wanted to tell stories of volunteers who showed kindness during what can be a scary and isolating time, while also showcasing some of the gaps in the health care system.

I have loved assigning and editing this series. The news cycle can feel bleak at times. But these stories have been some of the bright spots throughout the summer. The stories are heartfelt; the pictures and videos are beautiful.

I was moved by the story featuring Nanette Godbout and the work she did sitting beside dying patients who didn’t have family and friends nearby. What prompted you to look for a volunteer in the area of end-of-life care?

Alanna Smith: This volunteer role was first brought to my attention by someone working in Alberta’s health care system and it immediately sparked my interest. Death is still very much a taboo topic and I thought that bringing this important work to light would encourage difficult but important conversations.

It looks like most of the volunteers in these stories are retirees. Why is that?

Alphonso: It’s true that many of the volunteers we featured were retirees. Many of them have more free time after leaving their careers and perhaps want to maintain a sense of purpose and connection. I loved reading about the woman who made finger puppets at Stevenson Memorial Hospital in Alliston, Ontario.

However, there are many younger people who also spend time volunteering in the health care sector, and I know they are warmly welcomed by patients and health care staff.

At this Ontario hospital, a volunteer corps preserves small-town warmth

In one story, you wrote that the number of volunteers in the hospital sector has dropped in recent years. What’s the reason for the decline and what can we do about it?

Alphonso: I asked health science reporter Jennifer Yang about this, as she touched on it in her piece . This was her response:

I posed this exact question to Michelle Nelson, a professor with the University of Ottawa who studies volunteers in health care.

Dr. Nelson said that this trend is something researchers are still trying to better understand, but the COVID-19 pandemic definitely had an impact. Many volunteer programs shut down in the early months and years of COVID-19 – and many volunteers just didn’t return in the aftermath. Hospital volunteers tend to be older adults and many didn’t feel safe returning to a hospital environment. Volunteer programs that were shuttered also had to be rebuilt, with new volunteers recruited and retrained.

Women’s Auxiliary Volunteers at SickKids bring warmth to patients and their families

But Dr. Nelson pointed out that there could be something happening specifically around women, who make up the bulk of volunteers within hospitals. The impacts of COVID-19 were gendered, and women disproportionately shouldered a lot of the unpaid caregiving work that was needed during peak-pandemic years. This made it a lot harder for women to shift back to their volunteer commitments even after the pandemic eased up.

There are likely many other structural issues at play. The current economic environment and job market is perhaps making it more difficult for people to volunteer their time. Caregiving demands and pressures remain high, especially for women. There are also differences in how younger people volunteer; they tend to give their time more episodically, whereas hospital volunteer programs often require volunteers who can commit to regular hours.

The series has made me wonder how I can get involved in my own community. But how can I find where my efforts will be most needed?

Smith: People who spoke to me for this series came to volunteering in different ways. In Saskatchewan, locals in the community of Gravelbourg created their own volunteer-led transportation network to help residents get to medical appointments after a provincial bus service shut down. Another volunteer we profiled in Alberta contacted a nearby hospital directly to offer her artistic talents to decorate radiation masks.

But I recommend starting your search by visiting the websites of local health organizations, regional health bodies and/or provincial authorities. Volunteer positions and applications are typically listed on these sites. In Alberta, for example, you can search for volunteer opportunities here .

Are volunteers just patching up the gaps in Canadian health care that should be handled by more funding and government attention?

Smith: You’ve hit at the heart of a debate across Canada. There are definitely some areas (long-term care comes to mind) where volunteers are filling gaps that arguably should be handled by funded health care workers. Part of the issue is that there is a significant staffing problem in this field, which leads to a greater reliance on volunteers.

That being said, there are many volunteer positions that don’t fit into that box. From a non-profit organization in Saskatchewan that drives locals to their medical appointments , stylists giving free haircuts in a Charlottetown hospital , cyclists taking seniors out for outdoor excursions and many more stories, the series celebrated these volunteers while highlighting the gaps in a system that can feel isolating for patients.

Readers asked how these volunteers got involved, what they can do for their own communities and how the clinics and hospitals can better care for their patients. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.
How did this series come to be? What has stuck out to you about these stories?
Caroline Alphonso: Kristy Kirkup had written a lovely piece around the Christmas holidays on a woman who volunteered her time in an infant cuddling program at St. Michael’s Hospital .

That sparked the series idea. We wanted to tell stories of volunteers who showed kindness during what can be a scary and isolating time, while also showcasing some of the gaps in the health care system.

I have loved assigning and editing this series. The news cycle can feel bleak at times. But these stories have been some of the bright spots throughout the summer. The stories are heartfelt; the pictures and videos are beautiful.

I was moved by the story featuring Nanette Godbout and the work she did sitting beside dying patients who didn’t have family and friends nearby. What prompted you to look for a volunteer in the area of end-of-life care?

Alanna Smith: This volunteer role was first brought to my attention by someone working in Alberta’s health care system and it immediately sparked my interest. Death is still very much a taboo topic and I thought that bringing this important work to light would encourage difficult but important conversations.

Alphonso: It’s true that many of the volunteers we featured were retirees. Many of them have more free time after leaving their careers and perhaps want to maintain a sense of purpose and connection. I loved reading about the woman who made finger puppets at Stevenson Memorial Hospital in Alliston, Ontario.
However, there are many younger people who also spend time volunteering in the health care sector, and I know they are warmly welcomed by patients and health care staff.
