In one story, you wrote that the number of volunteers in the hospital sector has dropped in recent years. What’s the reason for the decline and what can we do about it?
Alphonso: I asked health science reporter Jennifer Yang about this, as she touched on it in her piece . This was her response:
I posed this exact question to Michelle Nelson, a professor with the University of Ottawa who studies volunteers in health care.

Many volunteer programs shut down in the early months and years of COVID-19 – and many volunteers just didn’t return in the aftermath. Hospital volunteers tend to be older adults and many didn’t feel safe returning to a hospital environment. Volunteer programs that were shuttered also had to be rebuilt, with new volunteers recruited and retrained.

But Dr. Nelson pointed out that there could be something happening specifically around women, who make up the bulk of volunteers within hospitals. The impacts of COVID-19 were gendered, and women disproportionately shouldered a lot of the unpaid caregiving work that was needed during peak-pandemic years. This made it a lot harder for women to shift back to their volunteer commitments even after the pandemic eased up.

There are likely many other structural issues at play. The current economic environment and job market is perhaps making it more difficult for people to volunteer their time. Caregiving demands and pressures remain high, especially for women. There are also differences in how younger people volunteer; they tend to give their time more episodically, whereas hospital volunteer programs often require volunteers who can commit to regular hours.

But I recommend starting your search by visiting the websites of local health organizations, regional health bodies and/or provincial authorities. Volunteer positions and applications are typically listed on these sites. In Alberta, for example, you can search for volunteer opportunities here .

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.

2027 Library Budget Discussion

Middlesex County Library Board discussed opportunities to align the 2027 budget with strategic priorities. The upcoming budget will focus on how the library can create exceptional experiences, expand its reach, and support lifelong learning. The library aims to strengthen both traditional and digital services, reduce barriers to access, support staff development, and create engaging spaces that foster creativity and curiosity. Plans also include expanding partnerships with schools, Indigenous communities, and local organizations while continuing to develop libraries as community hubs.

Opportunities identified for the 2027 budget include vehicle reserve contributions, replacement of the Ilderton Service Desk, implementation of the Facility Master Plan, Indigenous-led programming, and a library accreditation project. Board members also noted economic pressures and branch operations as ongoing challenges. Draft budgets will be submitted this fall before review by the Library Board and County Budget Committee. See the2027 Library Budget Discussion presentation") for more information.

EarlyON Program Reaches More Than 2,800 Participants in Second Quarter

Middlesex County Library Board received an overview of EarlyON programming in the second quarter of 2026. More than 1,600 children and 1,200 caregivers were uniquely served representing 2,846 unique participants and nearly 6,800 visits across in-person programs.Expanded evening and weekend programming also helped working families access services at more convenient times.

EarlyON delivered 309 programs and 590 hours of programming at 10 locations, while introducing new initiatives such as specialized programming to support children with autism and their families and the popular Little Sensory Seekers program. Child development remained a key focus through Kinder Connect, Ready Set Learn, and Check & Connect clinics, which completed 73 developmental screenings and connected families to specialized support services when needed.

Middlesex EarlyON strengthened partnerships with community agencies, expanded Indigenous cultural programming with Chippewa of the Thames First Nation, and offered virtual learning opportunities on topics including CPR, choking prevention, and kindergarten readiness. Looking ahead, EarlyON will continue enhancing kindergarten transition supports, exploring new themed programming, and expanding Indigenous resources and community partnerships.

For more information, read theEarlyON Program Update, Quarter 2 report").

Library Activity Report highlights major projects, community partnerships and upcoming fall events

The Middlesex County Library Board received updates on several strategic initiatives, technology improvements, and upcoming community programs across the library system.

Progress continues on the Library’s Facility Master Plan, with research, facility assessments, and community engagement activities now complete. Consultants are expected to present recommendations in October, helping guide future investments in library facilities, accessibility improvements, and service delivery across Middlesex County.

The Library also successfully completed a major software migration in June, transitioning collections, patron records, and circulation services to a new platform with minimal disruption. Staff are now preparing to launch a new mobile app to enhance access for patrons.

Looking ahead, branches will celebrate Ontario Public Library Week with themed activities from October 18 to 24, a costume swap is planned at the Lucan branch on September 28, and expanded Indigenous books and literacy resources will be available in recognition of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Read theLibrary Activity Report")for more information.

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.
2027 Library Budget Discussion

Middlesex County Library Board discussed opportunities to align the 2027 budget with strategic priorities. The upcoming budget will focus on how the library can create exceptional experiences, expand its reach, and support lifelong learning. The library aims to strengthen both traditional and digital services, reduce barriers to access, support staff development, and create engaging spaces that foster creativity and curiosity. Plans also include expanding partnerships with schools, Indigenous communities, and local organizations while continuing to develop libraries as community hubs.

Opportunities identified for the 2027 budget include vehicle reserve contributions, replacement of the Ilderton Service Desk, implementation of the Facility Master Plan, Indigenous-led programming, and a library accreditation project. Board members also noted economic pressures and branch operations as ongoing challenges. Draft budgets will be submitted this fall before review by the Library Board and County Budget Committee. See the2027 Library Budget Discussion presentation") for more information.
EarlyON Program Reaches More Than 2,800 Participants in Second Quarter

Middlesex County Library Board received an overview of EarlyON programming in the second quarter of 2026. More than 1,600 children and 1,200 caregivers were uniquely served representing 2,846 unique participants and nearly 6,800 visits across in-person programs.Expanded evening and weekend programming also helped working families access services at more convenient times.

EarlyON delivered 309 programs and 590 hours of programming at 10 locations, while introducing new initiatives such as specialized programming to support children with autism and their families and the popular Little Sensory Seekers program. Child development remained a key focus through Kinder Connect, Ready Set Learn, and Check & Connect clinics, which completed 73 developmental screenings and connected families to specialized support services when needed.

Middlesex EarlyON strengthened partnerships with community agencies, expanded Indigenous cultural programming with Chippewa of the Thames First Nation, and offered virtual learning opportunities on topics including CPR, choking prevention, and kindergarten readiness. Looking ahead, EarlyON will continue enhancing kindergarten transition supports, exploring new themed programming, and expanding Indigenous resources and community partnerships.
For more information, read theEarlyON Program Update, Quarter 2 report").
Library Activity Report highlights major projects, community partnerships and upcoming fall events
The Middlesex County Library Board received updates on several strategic initiatives, technology improvements, and upcoming community programs across the library system.

Progress continues on the Library’s Facility Master Plan, with research, facility assessments, and community engagement activities now complete. Consultants are expected to present recommendations in October, helping guide future investments in library facilities, accessibility improvements, and service delivery across Middlesex County.

The Library also successfully completed a major software migration in June, transitioning collections, patron records, and circulation services to a new platform with minimal disruption. Staff are now preparing to launch a new mobile app to enhance access for patrons.

Looking ahead, branches will celebrate Ontario Public Library Week with themed activities from October 18 to 24, a costume swap is planned at the Lucan branch on September 28, and expanded Indigenous books and literacy resources will be available in recognition of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Read theLibrary Activity Report")for more information.

stories.title: Canada working with partners on AI safety, minister says
stories.summary: Evan Solomon says he met with his international counterparts
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says Canada is “advocating alongside our partners” on AI safety.

Solomon says he met with his international counterparts after Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke recently to other leaders about setting up a “technology stability” board to regulate AI.

But when he was asked whether Canada is taking a leadership role in those efforts, Solomon pointed to domestic legislation, including proposed regulations on AI chatbots.

He also said Canada is taking a “very leading” role by investing $150 million in Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio’s efforts to build a safer AI.

Bengio is set to address the UN Security Council today, which will also hear from major AI companies.

Warnings about the risks AI poses to humans, and documented cases of AI bots disregarding human instructions, have prompted global alarm in recent weeks.

stories.title: Former U of M law dean arrested in Europe as part of extradition request: police
stories.summary: The former law dean has been disbarred in Manitoba and the U.K. after being found to have misappropriated hundreds of thousands of dollars from the university.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A former law dean at the University of Manitoba has been arrested in France, Winnipeg police confirmed on Wednesday.

The police service confirmed to Global News that Jonathan Black-Branch had been arrested “as a result of an extradition request” and that the matter was currently before the French court system.

“We are not in a position to provide further information regarding the extradition proceeding while the matter remains before the courts,” said Const. Stephen Spencer in an email. “Further information will be provided should the extradition application be successful and Black-Branch be returned to Winnipeg.

Spencer added that there is a Canada-wide arrest warrant in place for Black-Branch on a charge of fraud over $5,000, which will remain in effect until he is returned to Winnipeg and arrested by police.

Black-Branch was the dean of law at the University of Manitoba from 2016 to 2020.

The Discipline Committee of the Law Society of Manitoba reported in December 2023 that he misappropriated approximately $600,000 from the university and/or the Marcel A. Desautels Centre for Private Enterprise and the Law. It allegedly occurred between April 20, 2017, and February 2020.

An affidavit presented to the committee indicated the former dean spent $518,000 on activities listed as professional development, with $472,282 charged to the Desautels Endowment, and $46,441 to operating funds. Among the activities were attending non-degree programs at Harvard and Yale Universities while he was under contract at the university.

It noted professional development expenses charged to the university by all other Faculty of Law personnel in the same period was $18,928.

Black-Branch was also found to have expensed about $75,000 to the International Society of Law and Nuclear Disarmament, of which he served as president of its board of trustees at the time.

The University of Manitoba sued Black-Branch in August 2024. The university obtained a default judgement from the Court of King’s Bench against him in May 2025.

The judgement requires the former dean to pay approximately $682,000 to the school.

Months after the hearing, in February 2024, the Law Society of Manitoba disbarred Black-Branch in the province. He was also ordered to pay $36,000 in costs to the society.

The Bar Tribunals and Adjudication Service, the board for England and Wales, also disbarred Black Branch in February 2025 after finding all five charges against him had been proven. Those charges included not disclosing the proceedings in Manitoba to the United Kingdom regulator. He did not appear nor was he represented at the hearing, the written decision said.

stories.title: Quebec doctors call for inquest into suicides among profession
stories.summary: Five doctors in the province reportedly died by suicide over a five-month period this year
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Over 1,500 Quebec doctors are calling for a coroner’s inquest after five doctors in the province reportedly died by suicide over a five-month period this year.

The doctors sent a letter to Quebec’s chief coroner Sept. 18 asking for an inquest into suicides in their profession.

The signatories write that doctors face death and suffering every day and take on a lot of responsibility, sometimes without adequate support.

They also say some doctors avoid getting help for mental health issues because they fear professional repercussions.

Every suicide in Quebec is investigated by a coroner, regardless of the deceased person’s profession, to establish the causes and circumstances of the death.

Quebec’s coroner’s office told The Canadian Press it has begun an in-depth analysis of the doctors’ request.

“For now, it is too early to comment on whether such a public inquiry will be held,” it says.

Jean-Paul Brutus, a plastic surgeon who signed the letter, says growing workloads and the public denigration of doctors – sometimes referred to in Quebec as “doctor-bashing” – contribute to psychological distress.

He says successive governments have pointed fingers at doctors for years and blamed them “for all the failings of the public system.”

“There is more and more medical-administrative pressure, more and more patients, fewer and fewer resources to help us do the work we have to do,” Brutus says.

Brutus says the well-being of health-care workers can also affect the quality of care patients receive.

“This isn’t a doctors’ problem. This isn’t a health-care workers’ problem. It’s a public health problem,” he says.

The signatories argue the available information is not detailed enough to determine whether doctor suicides are increasing.

stories.title: Outfitters warn any N.B. ban on American hunters and anglers would devastate industry
stories.summary: Pressure is mounting on the premier to scrap a proposal to retaliate against American tariffs by preventing U.S. citizens from obtaining provincial hunting and fishing licences.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
Pressure is mounting on New Brunswick Premier Susan Holt to scrap a proposal to retaliate against American tariffs by preventing U.S. citizens from obtaining provincial hunting and fishing licences.

Clay Harrison, head of the United Guides and Outfitters of New Brunswick, says any move to block foreigners from hunting and fishing would be devastating for local outfitters.

Harrison says about 85 per cent of the industry’s clients are from the United States, with some local businesses relying solely on American customers.

A study from the Canadian Federation of Outfitter Associations says that of the $8.9 million spent in New Brunswick by clients of outfitters who came to hunt and fish in 2017, $7.3 million came from foreign clients.

Scott Ellis, the federation’s vice chair, says the industry has continued to thrive despite the trade war.

He says a licence ban would only harm Canadians.

“It’ll be a devastating impact to tourism businesses across the country if this crazy idea got traction,” Ellis said in an interview.

stories.title: AI minister says Canada working ‘alongside’ partners on AI safety
stories.summary: Ottawa — Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon says Canada is "advocating alongside our partners" on AI safety.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Canadian AI pioneer Yoshua Bengio and the heads of two major American AI companies pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to set controls on the burgeoning technology.

Bengio told the UN Security Council Wednesday that AI poses an “unprecedented threat.”

“One that none of its members would choose, that none can contain alone, and that does not respect the borders we defend,” Bengio said, in a copy of his prepared remarks.

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, also made presentations to the Security Council, warning the council must set actual controls to prevent the technology from becoming too powerful to rein in.

“If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole,” said Amodei.

“We could lose control of the future to AI,” Altman warned.

The dire warnings come as alarm has grown in recent weeks about the risks AI poses to humans amid documented cases of AI bots disregarding human instructions.

That included a claim from an AI researcher who worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic that those building the technology “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

OpenAI disclosed over the summer that its AI agents hacked AI startup Hugging Face without being instructed by any human to do so.

On Wednesday, Bengio urged the Security Council not to dismiss the warnings as a marketing stunt.

“I understand the distrust, but let me be clear. These AI behaviours are well documented and validated by many independent experts,” he said. “The dangers are real and imminent.”

He said that although “the future remains uncertain and debated, the severity of these risks is extraordinary.”

But Bengio said there are also solutions, including international agreements on technical solutions that would make AI safe by design.

His remarks came a day after Canada joined 19 other countries in issuing a joint statement during the UN General Assembly calling for stronger oversight of AI, even as the United States continued to reject any effort to regulate the technology.

Prime Minister Mark Carney signed the statement, which says “the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.”

“Recently, we have seen capable AI systems circumventing testing safeguards, exploiting vulnerabilities and gaining unauthorized access to real-world systems,” the statement says.

It says UN member states should “explore creating an international institution, able to set standards, enable verification, and convene states when capability thresholds are crossed.”

Other countries that signed the statement include Finland, Norway, Germany, Ireland, South Africa and Turkey.

The statement came out on the same day U.S. President Donald Trump told the UN General Assembly that the United States rejects any attempt to “construct a globalist scheme” to regulate artificial intelligence.

Experts cautioned Wednesday that Canada and other countries are limited in what they can do without the United States and China on board. Both countries are among the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

Florian Martin-Bariteau, research chair in technology and society at the University of Ottawa, said a “middle power collaboration network” would be great.

“But if we want to be really impactful on the global stage, you need to ensure that especially China and the U.S. are part of this conversation,” he said, adding: “I do not think that they’re very keen on such oversight and cooperation.”

Duncan Cass-Beggs, executive director of the global AI risks initiative at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said what’s needed “first and foremost” is a deal between the U.S. and China on AI safety.

“It may not be an elaborate treaty, it might be just a handshake or an agreement…but ultimately what it requires is both of those countries recognizing that the potential risks are close and real, that they both have an interest in not allowing the development of autonomous superintelligence systems until they can be controlled.”

He said Canada and other countries should be “figuring out how they can support and facilitate” that kind of agreement.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said Wednesday Canada is working with other countries on AI safety, but suggested the government isn’t taking a leading role internationally.

Solomon told reporters in Ottawa he met with his international counterparts after Carney spoke recently to other leaders about setting up a “technology stability” board to regulate AI.

“We are absolutely advocating alongside our partners to work together to set up … regulation on AI safety and reliability,” Solomon said.

But when he was asked whether Canada is taking a leadership role in those efforts, Solomon pointed to domestic legislation, including proposed regulations on AI chatbots.

He also said Canada is taking a “very leading” role by investing $150 million in Bengio’s efforts to build a safer AI.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 23, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Publishers stand by Haitian-Canadian author accused of using AI to write award-winning novel
stories.summary: Origins of Thelyson Orelien’s C’était ça ou mourir have sparked a debate about race, literary merit and originality in the French literary world
stories.author: Gabriel Stargardter and Maria Cheng
stories.content:
The publishers of an award-winning novel by Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien have defended the writer against accusations he used artificial intelligence to write it, and said they stand behind him.

Orelien denied using AI tools to write C’était ça ou mourir (“It Was Either That or Die”) on Tuesday, a day after a little-known X account called “Balance ton Claude” said that running passages through AI detection tool Pangram showed the novel “was written almost entirely by artificial intelligence.”

The controversy has ignited a debate about race, literary merit and originality that has roiled the French literary establishment.

The novel, Haiti-born Orelien’s first, has been longlisted for the prestigious Goncourt prize and won several others. It tells the story of a Haitian migrant who travels north through Latin America and the United States to Canada.

Denying the accusations against him, Orelien told French daily Liberation that they had come as a surprise, even if he had faced racist attacks ever since arriving in France.

“I did not expect attacks of this kind. I am not sad, but angry,” he said. “I am in the process of putting together a dossier with my publishers in France and Quebec to prove that what I am saying is true.”

“We stand alongside Thelyson Orelien and thank the readers who continue to place their trust in him,” Canadian publisher Editions du Boreal said in a statement.

Orelien’s French publisher, Grasset, said it condemned any malicious claims over AI usage, describing them as “deeply hurtful to a writer with an exceptional career.”

“The Grasset teams stand alongside this man ... they reaffirm their absolute confidence in him,” it said.

Reuters was unable to determine who is behind the Balance ton Claude account, which said in a chat on X that its anonymity helped maintain its independence and freedom to speak out.

“We don’t see the connection between AI and skin color. Should we have stayed silent and allowed artificial intelligence to receive major literary prizes on the grounds that the official author is not white?” it said.

Pangram says it is 99.7 per cent accurate in detecting AI writing, although some experts have questioned the reliability of AI detection software.

Philippe Claudel, the president of the Academie Goncourt which hands out the top French-language literary prize, said no decision had been taken on whether to remove Orelien’s novel from the longlist.

“If, by the time of our next meeting on October 6, when we establish the second shortlist, we have information that is indisputable, then of course we will have to consider the matter carefully,” he said.

Claudel said it was “almost inevitable” that questions over AI authorship were here to stay and that a charter was needed that “makes it possible to distinguish what has been produced by AI from what has been produced by a human.”

stories.title: Poilievre rips Carney’s omnibus bill as Conservatives agonize over how to vote on it
stories.summary: Gérard Deltell said the new legislation will ‘erase’ Justin Trudeau’s legacy of inaction in getting shovels in the ground.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Ottawa — Two days after the legislation was tabled, federal Conservatives were still agonizing about their position on the Carney government’s omnibus bill that would speed up major projects but that critics say would undermine the right to strike.

While at least two Tory MPs from Quebec openly agreed with the idea of moving faster on big projects, labour critic Kyle Seeback said his party, which has been heavily courting unions, is sensitive to the labour movement’s criticism of the legislation.

On Wednesday morning, Gérard Deltell, who is the party’s critic for One Canadian Economy, raised eyebrows when he hinted that Conservatives agreed with the bill.

“We have to be careful before saying yes, no, maybe, we don’t know…”

“It’s true that, ON the principle, we agree,” he continued.

“What we know is that this bill attempts to erase the Liberal government’s ten years of inaction,” he said as he entered a caucus meeting. “That is the legacy of Justin Trudeau and of three-quarters of the people sitting across from us (in the House of Commons.)”

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s office afterwards contacted National Post to stress that Deltell was not, in fact, endorsing the Building Canada Strong Act.

In a statement received late Wednesday afternoon, Deltell said that he was supporting “the principle of reversing the anti-development policies of the last Liberal decade.”

“For us, the best way to grow our economy is for the government to get out of the way.”

His colleague Gabriel Hardy, another Conservative MP from Quebec, said he agreed with the idea that Canada needs to move faster to approve projects.

“We certainly need to take action as an economy. We must diversify and ensure that our major projects come to fruition. That is a very conservative position,” he said.

Hardy he also said, like Deltell, that the party needs to take the time to flesh out this “enormous” piece of legislation before coming to a clear position on the bill.

“But we can’t move forward with our eyes closed and without paying attention to the details. And that is precisely the danger of moving too fast. So, we’re going to take the time to analyze it thoroughly,” he added during a scrum with reporters in French.

Seeback was just as enigmatic when asked if there were enough red lines for the Conservative Party to oppose the bill based on the criticism of the labour movement. He simply said that Canadians will have “to wait and see.”

The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, tabled on Monday proposes sweeping changes to fast-track approvals for major projects across the country and curtail labour disruptions in federally regulated workplaces citing the “national interest.”

The bill has been criticized by climate activists who say it guts environmental protections, and the labour movement who say it restricts their right to strike. The government has denied that the legislation does either of these things.

“When we look at the legislation that we just tabled, it’s about being able to build projects that are really important for our country,” said Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, who noted that it includes a lot of clean energy projects.

“None of them reduces the environmental reviews that we had previously, but they do make the process more simplified in a way, I would say. That doesn’t skip the steps.”

Conservatives were conspicuously tight-lipped about the legislation after the tabling of the legislation. In the last two days, they did not ask any questions about it in question period, instead focusing on cost-of-living or crime issues affecting their constituents.

It was only on Wednesday afternoon, when the debate in second reading started on Bill C-39 in the House of Commons, that Poilievre said it’s “deja vu all over again.”

“A year and a half ago, the prime minister came storming into the Commons with a cape on his back, saying that he had a new bill, Bill C-5, that was going to bring in sweeping legislative changes to build at speeds not seen in generations,” he said.

“Today they’ve come in and they’ve announced another sweeping bill, which the media has regurgitated, unfiltered, as though it were gospel truth, and this time they’re repeating exactly the same promises.”

Poilievre said the legislation is “all talk, no results.”

“Gushing media headlines aside, there has been nothing in 18 months. The previous bill was called the Building Canada Act. It built nothing. Today we have a bill. It’s called the Building Canada Strong Act. So, in 18 months, they’ve managed to add one word.”

The sponsor of the bill, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon, described Poilievre’s speech as “yet another very Justin Trudeau-obsessed piece of rhetorical flourish.”

paragraphs: Ottawa — Two days after the legislation was tabled, federal Conservatives were still agonizing about their position on the Carney government’s omnibus bill that would speed up major projects but that critics say would undermine the right to strike.

While at least two Tory MPs from Quebec openly agreed with the idea of moving faster on big projects, labour critic Kyle Seeback said his party, which has been heavily courting unions, is sensitive to the labour movement’s criticism of the legislation.
On Wednesday morning, Gérard Deltell, who is the party’s critic for One Canadian Economy, raised eyebrows when he hinted that Conservatives agreed with the bill.
“We have to be careful before saying yes, no, maybe, we don’t know…”
“It’s true that, ON the principle, we agree,” he continued.

“What we know is that this bill attempts to erase the Liberal government’s ten years of inaction,” he said as he entered a caucus meeting. “That is the legacy of Justin Trudeau and of three-quarters of the people sitting across from us (in the House of Commons.)”
Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre’s office afterwards contacted National Post to stress that Deltell was not, in fact, endorsing the Building Canada Strong Act.
In a statement received late Wednesday afternoon, Deltell said that he was supporting “the principle of reversing the anti-development policies of the last Liberal decade.”
“For us, the best way to grow our economy is for the government to get out of the way.”
His colleague Gabriel Hardy, another Conservative MP from Quebec, said he agreed with the idea that Canada needs to move faster to approve projects.
“We certainly need to take action as an economy. We must diversify and ensure that our major projects come to fruition. That is a very conservative position,” he said.
Hardy he also said, like Deltell, that the party needs to take the time to flesh out this “enormous” piece of legislation before coming to a clear position on the bill.

“But we can’t move forward with our eyes closed and without paying attention to the details. And that is precisely the danger of moving too fast. So, we’re going to take the time to analyze it thoroughly,” he added during a scrum with reporters in French.

Seeback was just as enigmatic when asked if there were enough red lines for the Conservative Party to oppose the bill based on the criticism of the labour movement. He simply said that Canadians will have “to wait and see.”

“When we look at the legislation that we just tabled, it’s about being able to build projects that are really important for our country,” said Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin, who noted that it includes a lot of clean energy projects.
“None of them reduces the environmental reviews that we had previously, but they do make the process more simplified in a way, I would say. That doesn’t skip the steps.”

“Today they’ve come in and they’ve announced another sweeping bill, which the media has regurgitated, unfiltered, as though it were gospel truth, and this time they’re repeating exactly the same promises.”
Poilievre said the legislation is “all talk, no results.”

stories.title: Canada ratifies landmark High Seas Treaty, commits $82-million to ocean protection
stories.summary: Funding will support Arctic Ocean monitoring, underwater research and expanded efforts to track effects of climate change
stories.author: Jenn Thornhill Verma
stories.content:
Canada ratified the landmark High Seas Treaty to protect marine biodiversity on Wednesday and pledged $82-million over five years to a global ocean-monitoring alliance, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced in New York on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly.

“Canada is an ocean nation. We have the world’s longest coastline as a consequence of that. That’s our inheritance, and we recognize the obligations, the responsibilities, that come with that to help lead efforts to understand those oceans, and of course, to protect them,” said Mr. Carney, speaking at the launch of the OceanEye International Alliance , co-hosted by Canada and the European Union.

Amid shifting political winds, Canada gets more of the spotlight on the UN’s stage

The money will pay for year-round moorings in the Arctic Ocean, which is warming four times faster than the global average, said Mr. Carney. It will support autonomous underwater gliders beneath the ice, expanded monitoring of the Labrador Sea and Davis Strait. It will also more than double Canada’s contribution to the global Argo ocean climate monitoring network, and help modernize the National Oceanographic Data Centre, among other investments.

The treaty, meanwhile, which became international law in January, is the first legal framework for protected areas in waters beyond national jurisdiction, which make up nearly half the planet. OceanEye, which Mr. Carney agreed in June to co-chair with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, pays for the instruments that monitor the global ocean’s changing condition.

Both commitments, one to protect the high seas and the other to monitor the ocean as a whole, land on a tension in Canada’s ocean record. As Ottawa builds partnerships abroad, scientists say it is dismantling the monitoring and research that underpin them at home.

“As Canadian scientists, working internationally, we are watching the instruments go dark,” wrote Frédéric Cyr and Brad deYoung in a commentary published Sunday .

Dr. Cyr, a former Fisheries and Oceans Canada oceanographer now at Memorial University of Newfoundland’s Marine Institute, and Dr. deYoung, a professor emeritus at Memorial, point to significant cutbacks at the federal department, whose own plan projects spending reductions of up to $194-million by 2028-29 and about 551 fewer full-time positions. They say Ottawa has scaled back the Atlantic Zone Monitoring Program , which has tracked changing ocean conditions for more than two decades, and withdrawn support for the international program that monitors the North Atlantic currents that regulate the climate.

In their letter, they urged Mr. Carney to reverse those cutbacks and attach sustained funding to Canada’s OceanEye role. Of today’s announcement, Dr. Cyr said he was encouraged by the investments the Prime Minister had committed, but still had questions.

Most concerningly, he hopes the funds will maintain Canada’s role in monitoring the North Atlantic currents that scientists worry could be headed for collapse.

“Our oceans form one interconnected system. Canada’s leadership on protecting the high seas is much needed. At the same time, any country that is going to lead on the high seas also needs to lead at home,” said Susanna Fuller, vice-president of conservation at Oceans North, a member of the High Seas Alliance, a coalition of more than 80 conservation groups that pushed for the treaty for over a decade.

Canada signed the High Seas Treaty in March, 2024. Becoming a party now gives Ottawa a seat when countries meet for the first time in January next year. Only 1.5 per cent of the high seas is currently protected. The treaty also requires environmental assessments for high-seas activities and sets rules for sharing the benefits of marine genetic resources found there. As of this week, nearly 100 parties have joined, with Germany, Papua New Guinea and Zimbabwe among the latest to ratify .

Analysis: Trump uses UN address to threaten and deride foes and allies alike, as usual

At Wednesday’s OceanEye Alliance event , countries were invited to pledge money or in-kind support to the UN-backed Global Ocean Observing System , the network behind the ocean data used in weather forecasts and climate models. The system draws on 8,000 instruments, from floats to moored buoys, that collect some 120,000 observations a day, according to the EU, noting it remains “vulnerable to financial and geopolitical disruptions,” given just nine countries pay for 90 per cent of that monitoring effort.

The event is the latest sign of Ottawa’s push to deepen ties with the EU, weeks before a Canada-EU summit in Canada on Oct. 29-30 .

The federal nature strategy, which Mr. Carney announced in March , set aside $24.4-million over five years, plus $1.8-million in continuing funding, to ratify the treaty and carry out its commitments.

Canada will also act as host of the Our Ocean Conference in Halifax May 10-11, 2027.

Mr. Carney took a moment to acknowledge Canada’s recently named Ocean Envoy and Chair , Diana Fox Carney, his wife. “We intend to be at every table, where the future of the ocean is decided and to continue to raise our ambitions,” he said.

This story is produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Center’s Ocean Reporting Network.

stories.title: Canadians want more alternative home ownership options, survey shows
stories.summary: A new survey suggests many Canadians are open to alternative home options if it means getting easier access to the real estate market.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
As housing affordability remains a challenge for millions of Canadians amid the heightened cost of living, a new survey suggests many are open to alternative options like modular homes if it means getting easier access to the real estate market.

The survey report was released Tuesday from Meridian Credit Union, which asked 1,500 Canadian consumers as well as a national panel of 250 construction industry owners, operators and executives between May 13 and June 8, 2026, about their outlook on the housing market.

More than three-quarters (77 per cent) of consumers said housing attainability is a critical issue for Canada’s future, and nearly two-thirds (62 per cent) said they would consider non-traditional housing options such as modular, prefabricated or tiny homes for getting into home ownership.

Modular or prefabricated homes are houses or other permanent shelters that get built in factories either as individual sections or components. Those homes and are shipped to customers to be assembled relatively quickly and at a lower cost than building a home on site from scratch.

Purchasing a home that is prefabricated or modular can mean a lower purchase price for consumers, and more affordable mortgage options compared to traditional homes that may have cost more to build.

Younger survey participants may be more inclined to consider these options, with 87 per cent of Millennials and 81 per cent of Gen Z reporting ongoing stress relating to housing costs.

“Canadians are showing us that homeownership is no longer one-size-fits-all,” said Jay-Ann Gilfoy, president and CEO of Meridian Credit Union in the report.

“From co-ownership arrangements to modular housing and rent-to-own models, people are adapting to today’s realities and looking for new ways to achieve their housing goals. The challenge is ensuring those options are supported by the financing, supply and partnerships needed to make them viable.”

This comes after the federal government announced last year that it was providing funding and federal land to add 540 modular homes in Downsview Park in Toronto . The government said at the time that at least 40 per cent of those homes would be affordable and the development would provide studios and one- to three-bedroom homes.

Even though the survey suggests there is heightened demand for these alternative housing options, businesses say they are struggling to meet that demand.

Among the group of construction industry participants in the survey, nearly two-thirds (63 per cent) said they are struggling to secure financing for projects because of rising costs for materials combined with general economic uncertainty.

Even if ideal financing was available and materials were relatively cheap, 78 per cent of construction firms and 94 per cent of enterprise level employers said a shortage of skilled trades people will still delay these projects from starting.

Forty-one per cent of builders also said that because there is a dwindling pool of skilled trades talent, the cost of available labour has skyrocketed.

Among the multiple types of construction related jobs businesses said they were having a tough time filling, 28 per cent said construction labourers were the hardest roles to fill, while 18 per cent said it was carpenters or framers.

“While builders want to build, many are facing a market where rising costs, financing pressures and reduced buyer confidence make it difficult to advance new projects,” said Jason Teal, vice president of business banking at Meridian in the report.

“To create more attainable housing, we need an environment where development is economically viable and where aspiring homeowners have the confidence and means to enter the market.”

– with a file from Global News’ Isaac Callan

Modular or prefabricated homes are houses or other permanent shelters that get built in factories either as individual sections or components. Those homes and are shipped to customers to be assembled relatively quickly and at a lower cost than building a home on site from scratch.
Purchasing a home that is prefabricated or modular can mean a lower purchase price for consumers, and more affordable mortgage options compared to traditional homes that may have cost more to build.
Younger survey participants may be more inclined to consider these options, with 87 per cent of Millennials and 81 per cent of Gen Z reporting ongoing stress relating to housing costs.
“Canadians are showing us that homeownership is no longer one-size-fits-all,” said Jay-Ann Gilfoy, president and CEO of Meridian Credit Union in the report.

“From co-ownership arrangements to modular housing and rent-to-own models, people are adapting to today’s realities and looking for new ways to achieve their housing goals. The challenge is ensuring those options are supported by the financing, supply and partnerships needed to make them viable.”

This comes after the federal government announced last year that it was providing funding and federal land to add 540 modular homes in Downsview Park in Toronto . The government said at the time that at least 40 per cent of those homes would be affordable and the development would provide studios and one- to three-bedroom homes.
Even though the survey suggests there is heightened demand for these alternative housing options, businesses say they are struggling to meet that demand.

Among the group of construction industry participants in the survey, nearly two-thirds (63 per cent) said they are struggling to secure financing for projects because of rising costs for materials combined with general economic uncertainty.

Even if ideal financing was available and materials were relatively cheap, 78 per cent of construction firms and 94 per cent of enterprise level employers said a shortage of skilled trades people will still delay these projects from starting.
Forty-one per cent of builders also said that because there is a dwindling pool of skilled trades talent, the cost of available labour has skyrocketed.

Among the multiple types of construction related jobs businesses said they were having a tough time filling, 28 per cent said construction labourers were the hardest roles to fill, while 18 per cent said it was carpenters or framers.

“While builders want to build, many are facing a market where rising costs, financing pressures and reduced buyer confidence make it difficult to advance new projects,” said Jason Teal, vice president of business banking at Meridian in the report.
“To create more attainable housing, we need an environment where development is economically viable and where aspiring homeowners have the confidence and means to enter the market.”

stories.title: Canadians are flying back to the U.S. after three years of declining travel
stories.summary: Canadian resident return trips to the U.S. by air have increased for the first time in 34 months, according to the latest StatCan data.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Canadian resident return trips to the U.S. by air have increased for the first time in 34 months, according to the latest data from Statistics Canada .

The figures, which reveal travel trends between Canada and other countries in July 2026, show that return trips to the U.S. by air edged up 0.6 per cent year over year to 567,000, marking the first increase since August 2023.

Combined with 2.2 million trips by automobile (a year-over-year increase of 12.6 per cent) and 26,400 by cruise ship, total return trips to the U.S. by Canadian residents reached 2.8 million in July, up 10.1 per cent year-over-year. This marked a fourth consecutive month of year-over-year growth, following 15 consecutive months of decline.

April 2026 marked the first year-over-year increase in overall return trips from the United States since December 2024, when return trips by automobile rose by 5.8 per cent compared to a year earlier. Although return trips by air had fallen 8.1 per cent, the figures meant overall Canadian-resident return trips from the U.S. rose by 1.4 per cent that month compared to April 2025.

But despite this recent shift in travel trends, Canadian resident return trips from the U.S. remained 25.6 per cent below their July 2024 level.

Political tensions between Canada and the U.S. contributed to the drop in travel in early 2025, following tariffs imposed by President Donald Trump and his repeated suggestions that Canada could become the 51st state . Meanwhile, heightened security at the border also discouraged many from travelling south.

While the July figures suggest the decline in travel to the U.S. May be easing, the data covers a period before the latest escalation in the Canada-U.S. trade war.

In August this year, Trump threatened to impose new 50 per cent tariffs and, after talks between the two countries broke down, the levies on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods came into effect on Aug. 22.

Canada retaliated, introducing counter-tariffs on U.S. imports earlier this month. Since then, Trump and other members of his administration have aimed insults and threats at Canada , including comparing Ontario Premier Doug Ford unfavourably to his late brother and sharing a photo of a bald eagle standing on the neck of a Canada Goose from the White House’s official X account.

On Aug. 27, Trump signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to “Lake America,” ordering the Department of the Interior to update maps and databases with the new name.

These events have fuelled a renewed ‘Buy Canadian’ movement, with one Made in Canada Facebook group seeing views increase roughly 300 per cent in August compared to June this year, according to administrator Jayne Little.

That sentiment May extend to travel to the U.S., and it remains to be seen whether the recent increase in Canadians heading south will continue.

Meanwhile, travel to Canada by U.S. residents also increased in July. There were 3.5 million trips made that month, up 9.1 per cent from the same month in 2025 and marking the sixth consecutive month of year-over-year growth. Arrivals by automobile rose 7.5 per cent to 2.1 million, while arrivals by air increased 5.3 per cent to 832,100.

StatCan also highlighted the number of trips made via the Gordie Howe International Bridge , which opened on July 27 and connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, Michigan.

From July 27 to 31, 23,500 returning Canadian residents and 19,600 U.S. residents entered Canada via the Gordie Howe International Bridge by automobile, bus, motorcycle and other land vehicles.

stories.title: Why everyone wins with Kawhi Leonard-Raptors extension
stories.summary: The Raptors gave Kawhi Leonard a fully guaranteed deal that includes that player option on the second year.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Michael Grange, Sportsnet

Posted September 23, 2026 11:11 am.

It’s good to be in the NBA, and it’s especially good to be Kawhi Leonard.

Even if the contract extension the Toronto Raptors made official on Wednesday with their new/old star forward will be the last deal the 35-year-old signs, Leonard would retire after the 2028-29 season having earned nearly $500 million playing basketball. Plus, quite literally, who knows how much more via, ahem, his ‘endorsements.’

But context matters. And in the context of the Raptors signing Leonard , it matters that he signed for two years and $115 million — and not for the maximum $126-million extension he was eligible to sign on a deal that covers 2027-28 and 2028-29.

In the apron era, ever dollar saved matters.

Extended stay in the North. ???????? pic.twitter.com/6Q4khQQool — Toronto Raptors (@Raptors) September 23, 2026

The $11-million discount the Raptors got on Leonard’s contract represents $5.5 million per year of wiggle room general manager Bobby Webster will have heading into the next two off-seasons. It could be the difference in signing a veteran free agent to shore up a roster weakness or build on a strength.

The deal and the way it’s structured is also roughly comparable to a couple other contracts some older, yet highly productive, NBA stars have signed recently.

Kevin Durant, for example, signed a two-year, $90-million extension with the Houston Rockets last year that kicks in for this season. And while that’s less than Leonard got with the Raptors, Durant’s deal covers his age 38 and 39 seasons. It’s a lot of money, but like Leonard, Durant in his late 30s remains one of the NBA’s best players.

And then there’s the three-year, $96.5-million deal that James Harden signed with Cleveland this summer that will cover his age 37, 38 and 39 seasons. That matters in a different way, but we’ll get to that in a minute.

The deal is also indicative of Leonard’s determination to make things work with the Raptors.

How robust the market was for his services leaguewide is something we can’t quite know, but coming off an all-NBA season, it’s not hard to imagine a number of contenders and near-contenders believing Leonard could be the difference in winning a championship because it’s obvious to anyone who has ever seen him play at full gas that he is just that.

But Leonard put out the bat signal that he wanted to play in Toronto, that the only franchise he wanted to sign an extension with was the Raptors, and here we are. The framework of the contract remained consistent from when the Raptors first entertained the idea of acquiring Leonard back in June.

Leonard then waived his $7.5 million trade kicker to make the deal work under the Raptors’ current cap situation based on the $50.3 million he’ll earn this season — another act of faith, by NBA standards.

That all needs to be considered when evaluating the other element of the deal that raised some eyebrows around the NBA: Leonard’s deal includes a player option for its final season in 2028-29.

When I was talking with one long-time NBA executive about what the final deal might look like, he speculated that the Raptors would push to have only a partial guarantee for the second season of the deal or that the second year would only fully guarantee if Leonard — forever an injury risk — met certain thresholds for games played.

Instead, the Raptors gave Leonard a fully guaranteed deal that includes that player option on the second year, which is generally considered a concession by the team to the player.

That’s because, typically, a player option is nothing but a headache for the team. If the player underperforms or is injured or both, he picks up the last year of his deal and the team is stuck. Conversely, if the player is over-performing or has an eye on another market, the threat of him declining the option can force a team’s hand.

“I don’t understand why they would do that; there was no leverage here,” one prominent player agent said when asked about the deal. “It’s a great deal for Kawhi. Any time you get the player option it’s a win for the player.”

But again, context matters.

If we take Leonard at his word, he very much wants Toronto to be his final NBA destination.

“I’m not really championship chasing. … I didn’t want to put on a thousand jerseys,” Leonard said during the most recent episode of Open Gym , the Raptors’ in-house documentary program. “This city took a liking to my family, and I took a liking to this city … my son was born here, and he’s been asking me forever when he’s going to come back. Now he’s back, and he’s able to see it rather than me tell him the great stories that happened.”

With that in mind and given that it’s pretty unlikely that Leonard will go ring shopping heading into his age-37 season, the player option can be looked at a little differently.

Let’s presume that the Raptors, with Leonard continuing to defy the aging curve (his 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds, two steals and 62.9 true-shooting marks with the Clippers last season represented not only one of Leonard’s best but one of the best seasons ever by a player in their mid-30s), head into the 2028-29 season with championship aspirations, but in need of one more piece.

That’s where the player option could be a win for everyone concerned.

In that scenario, Leonard would opt out of his deal and sign one more for, just to pick a number, two years and $80 million. Leonard gets another $23 million in his jeans and the Raptors would head into that third off-season with an extra $17.5 million to spend, which could very well be enough to sign that missing piece.

The rough analogy here is Harden, who opted out of the final year his deal on which he was slated to earn $42.3 million with Cleveland this year and signed for three at $96.5 million, giving the Cavaliers an additional $11 million of cap space which enabled them to sign Peyton Watson, the rangy free-agent wing Cleveland hopes will vault it into Finals contention.

So sure, Leonard gains some theoretical leverage by having a player option on the final year of his new deal, but given everyone’s goal that his return to Toronto is a homecoming rather than a way station, it’s more about the potential for making the final years of his career as competitive as possible.

There are still plenty of ifs and risks, as with any NBA contract that runs into nine figures and especially so for a player in his mid-to-late 30s.

But at least with Leonard, the Raptors know exactly the player they are getting, and precisely what it costs.

Posted September 23, 2026 11:11 am.
It’s good to be in the NBA, and it’s especially good to be Kawhi Leonard.

Even if the contract extension the Toronto Raptors made official on Wednesday with their new/old star forward will be the last deal the 35-year-old signs, Leonard would retire after the 2028-29 season having earned nearly $500 million playing basketball. Plus, quite literally, who knows how much more via, ahem, his ‘endorsements.’

But context matters. And in the context of the Raptors signing Leonard , it matters that he signed for two years and $115 million — and not for the maximum $126-million extension he was eligible to sign on a deal that covers 2027-28 and 2028-29.
In the apron era, ever dollar saved matters.
Extended stay in the North. ???????? pic.twitter.com/6Q4khQQool — Toronto Raptors (@Raptors) September 23, 2026

The $11-million discount the Raptors got on Leonard’s contract represents $5.5 million per year of wiggle room general manager Bobby Webster will have heading into the next two off-seasons. It could be the difference in signing a veteran free agent to shore up a roster weakness or build on a strength.
The deal and the way it’s structured is also roughly comparable to a couple other contracts some older, yet highly productive, NBA stars have signed recently.

Kevin Durant, for example, signed a two-year, $90-million extension with the Houston Rockets last year that kicks in for this season. And while that’s less than Leonard got with the Raptors, Durant’s deal covers his age 38 and 39 seasons. It’s a lot of money, but like Leonard, Durant in his late 30s remains one of the NBA’s best players.

And then there’s the three-year, $96.5-million deal that James Harden signed with Cleveland this summer that will cover his age 37, 38 and 39 seasons. That matters in a different way, but we’ll get to that in a minute.
The deal is also indicative of Leonard’s determination to make things work with the Raptors.

How robust the market was for his services leaguewide is something we can’t quite know, but coming off an all-NBA season, it’s not hard to imagine a number of contenders and near-contenders believing Leonard could be the difference in winning a championship because it’s obvious to anyone who has ever seen him play at full gas that he is just that.

But Leonard put out the bat signal that he wanted to play in Toronto, that the only franchise he wanted to sign an extension with was the Raptors, and here we are. The framework of the contract remained consistent from when the Raptors first entertained the idea of acquiring Leonard back in June.

Leonard then waived his $7.5 million trade kicker to make the deal work under the Raptors’ current cap situation based on the $50.3 million he’ll earn this season — another act of faith, by NBA standards.
That all needs to be considered when evaluating the other element of the deal that raised some eyebrows around the NBA: Leonard’s deal includes a player option for its final season in 2028-29.

When I was talking with one long-time NBA executive about what the final deal might look like, he speculated that the Raptors would push to have only a partial guarantee for the second season of the deal or that the second year would only fully guarantee if Leonard — forever an injury risk — met certain thresholds for games played.
Instead, the Raptors gave Leonard a fully guaranteed deal that includes that player option on the second year, which is generally considered a concession by the team to the player.

That’s because, typically, a player option is nothing but a headache for the team. If the player underperforms or is injured or both, he picks up the last year of his deal and the team is stuck. Conversely, if the player is over-performing or has an eye on another market, the threat of him declining the option can force a team’s hand.

“I don’t understand why they would do that; there was no leverage here,” one prominent player agent said when asked about the deal. “It’s a great deal for Kawhi. Any time you get the player option it’s a win for the player.”
But again, context matters.
If we take Leonard at his word, he very much wants Toronto to be his final NBA destination.

“I’m not really championship chasing. … I didn’t want to put on a thousand jerseys,” Leonard said during the most recent episode of Open Gym , the Raptors’ in-house documentary program. “This city took a liking to my family, and I took a liking to this city … my son was born here, and he’s been asking me forever when he’s going to come back. Now he’s back, and he’s able to see it rather than me tell him the great stories that happened.”
With that in mind and given that it’s pretty unlikely that Leonard will go ring shopping heading into his age-37 season, the player option can be looked at a little differently.

Let’s presume that the Raptors, with Leonard continuing to defy the aging curve (his 27.9 points, 6.4 rebounds, two steals and 62.9 true-shooting marks with the Clippers last season represented not only one of Leonard’s best but one of the best seasons ever by a player in their mid-30s), head into the 2028-29 season with championship aspirations, but in need of one more piece.
That’s where the player option could be a win for everyone concerned.

In that scenario, Leonard would opt out of his deal and sign one more for, just to pick a number, two years and $80 million. Leonard gets another $23 million in his jeans and the Raptors would head into that third off-season with an extra $17.5 million to spend, which could very well be enough to sign that missing piece.

The rough analogy here is Harden, who opted out of the final year his deal on which he was slated to earn $42.3 million with Cleveland this year and signed for three at $96.5 million, giving the Cavaliers an additional $11 million of cap space which enabled them to sign Peyton Watson, the rangy free-agent wing Cleveland hopes will vault it into Finals contention.

So sure, Leonard gains some theoretical leverage by having a player option on the final year of his new deal, but given everyone’s goal that his return to Toronto is a homecoming rather than a way station, it’s more about the potential for making the final years of his career as competitive as possible.
There are still plenty of ifs and risks, as with any NBA contract that runs into nine figures and especially so for a player in his mid-to-late 30s.
But at least with Leonard, the Raptors know exactly the player they are getting, and precisely what it costs.

stories.title: Simcoe woman dies after Norfolk County house fire
stories.summary: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
stories.author: CBC News
paragraphs: Provincial police in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe on Monday afternoon.
CBC News · Posted: Sep 23, 2026 10:13 AM EDT | Last Updated: 2 hours ago
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say they're working with the offices of the fire marshal and the chief coroner to investigate the cause of Monday's fire.(Ontario Provincial Police)
X 0
Reddit 0
LinkedIn 0
Email 0
Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) in Norfolk County say a woman has died after being found inside a burning residence in Simcoe, east of London, on Monday afternoon.

At around 1 p.m. emergency crews were called to the fire at an Orchard Avenue address, police said. Firefighters were able to enter the residence and locate a 50-year-old individual. Despite life-saving efforts, she was later pronounced dead in hospital.
The Norfolk County OPP crime unit is investigating the cause of the fire along with the office of the fire marshal and the office of the chief coroner.
Anyone with information about the incident is asked to contact OPP or Crime Stoppers.

For their new documentary on the late Rush drummer Neil Peart, directors Scot McFadyen and Sam Dunn recruited four top-flight drummers to play songs from the band’s catalogue with surviving band members Geddy Lee and Alex Lifeson in a studio. The idea was to have the performances, not talking heads, speak to Peart’s virtuosity.

Neil Peart: No One’s Disciple premiered last week at the Toronto International Film Festival and makes its debut on CBC and CBC Gem this week. It succeeds as a celebration of the lyricist and musician, who died of brain cancer in 2020 , not because of the tasty jams but in the way the guest drummers were humbled by the task at hand.

Rush’s Neil Peart was revered as one of the world’s best drummers

“That beginning was tricky, man,” Tool’s Danny Carey said after a problematic run at the overture to 2112 . King Crimson’s Gavin Harrison wrote out detailed charts before even attempting Dreamline from the 1991 album Roll the Bones . “When you get into the details of it, you realize how much thought went into every drum part,” he said. “There’s no extra fat lying around. It’s all very lean.”

Stewart Copeland of the Police wrestled with the compositional complexities of 1982’s New World Man : “The drums fill aren’t challenging to play. They’re challenging to remember!” And while Red Hot Chili Peppers’ Chad Smith pounded out Working Man with no issues, he was breathing heavily after it was over.

Lee refers to the four guest timekeepers as Peart’s “drum brothers,” and compares drummers in general to baseball catchers and hockey goalies. “They see a kinship to each other,” he explains.

In a way, the film is not only a tribute to Peart but a requiem for kick-drum people overall.

“There’s a sense that people don’t really know what it means to be a great drummer,” McFadyen said during a recent video call alongside co-director Dunn. “There’s a lot of talking in documentaries. We wanted something more experiential.”

McFadyen and Dunn co-own Toronto-based Banger Films, the production company behind such rock docs as Metal: A Headbanger’s Journey , Iron Maiden: Flight 666 , Super Duper Alice Cooper and a pair of Rush films, 2010’s Rush: Beyond the Lighted Stage and Time Machine 2011: Live in Cleveland .

The documentary was conceived and the performance scenes were filmed in Los Angeles before there was any talk of the Rush reunion tour Lee and Lifeson are currently undertaking with drummer Anika Nilles and keyboardist Loren Gold. The co-directors suspected something was up, though.

Rush makes long-awaited Toronto return, with a little help from Geddy Lee’s vocal coach

“From the moment we stepped into the jam room on day one with Gavin Harrison, it was clear that Alex and Geddy had been playing a lot longer and a lot more than they’d let on,” Dunn said. “I was struck by how good the songs sounded.”

While the studio sessions are bound to be catnip for Rush fans, the soul of the film rests in the thoughtful portrait of Peart. The drummer, nicknamed the Professor, was known to be private, even standoffish. He was leery of fans and wrote about it in the song Limelight : “Cast in this unlikely role, ill-equipped to act with insufficient tact / One must put up barriers to keep oneself intact.”

In the film, Lee comments on Peart’s unapproachability. He says he spoke to the drummer about it, telling him he couldn’t have it both ways − the applause without the contact. “You live on the stage and you pay the price,” Lee said.

Lee even calls it a character flaw in Peart, which is a surprising admission in a film that very easily could have slipped into hagiography.

“The film is mostly a celebration, but it’s not all adulation,” McFadyen said.

On the other hand, through interviews with those who knew him well (such as Jethro Tull drummer Doane Perry and childhood chum Brad French), the Peart that ultimately emerges is a loyal friend and a generous colleague. Other than drummer Nilles, only people close to Peart were interviewed.

“That was intentional,” Dunn explained. “The idea was a tighter sketch of what Neil was like as a person. We felt we were giving as intimate a portrait as we could.”

stories.title: Introducing Fracette, a new sparkling wine from Niagara made using icewine
stories.summary: Fracette combines two of Niagara’s strong suits, bubbly and icewine
stories.author: Christopher Waters
stories.content:
Niagara winemakers have joined forces to create a new category of sparkling wine made using icewine as the catalyst for creating the fizz. The idea behind Fracette is to produce a fruity and frothy wine, with some of the distinctive flavours of the world-famous dessert wine but without the sweetness.

Fracette, which rhymes with cassette, was initiated by industry groups looking to give sparkling wine a regional identity by combining two of Niagara’s strong suits, bubbly and icewine. “When do you get to build a brand-new category of wine in the 21 st century?” wondered Paul Speck, president of Henry of Pelham Family Estate, one of the six wineries that helped launch Fracette this month.

“It creates a brand-new product that you can only get in Niagara, but we’re hoping to have it right across Canada. Hopefully others will join,” he added.

Provincial winemaking regulations were amended by the Ontario Wine Appellation Authority, formerly Vintners Quality Alliance, in November, 2025, to establish Fracette as a protected sparkling wine category using icewine as the sugar source for the secondary fermentation that creates the bubbles in the bottle or stainless-steel tank. The base wines must be made from vinifera grape varieties, such as riesling, chardonnay or pinot noir, and the finished wine cannot contain more than 15 grams a litre of residual sweetness, equivalent to the sugar content of champagne or prosecco made in an “extra dry” style.

Good Taste: Fostering a taste for icewine in Niagara-on-the-Lake

Speck said his winemaking team and other producers spent months conducting bench trials to determine the right amount of icewine required to create bubbles without leaving any trace of its sweetness behind. “We were after the texture and density of the icewine on the palate, but wanted to keep things really fresh,” he explains.

Sparkling wines typically feature lemon and apple flavours from grapes that are picked early to give winemakers a refreshing balance of sweetness and acidity. Icewine features richer flavours, such as apricot, pineapple and honey. Those bold flavours contribute more layers to Fracette wines.

There are other logistical considerations, which might hinder adoption of the Fracette by more wineries in Ontario and other Canadian winemaking regions. Production requires investing in specialized equipment, such as the high-pressure stainless-steel tanks that safely trap carbon dioxide while withstanding more than six-plus bars of pressure during the secondary fermentation process. There’s also the need for bottling equipment that prevents bubbles from escaping while the wine is transferred, filtered and bottled.

Fracette can also be made as a bottle-fermented sparkling wine, a more time-intensive production method that requires traditional method bubblies made in Ontario to age for at least nine months before release. (All six of the initial Fracette labels were tank fermented.)

Emma Garner, senior winemaker at Andrew Peller Limited and member of the Ontario Wine Appellation Authority’s standards development committee, explains that participating wineries worked for two years on research and development trials before making commercial volumes of the unique sparkler.

“I had never fermented two wines together like that,” she says. “It took some time to wrap my head around it, but I’m really happy with where it landed.”

When it came to establishing the winemaking rules behind the new category, Garner explains that the standards committee looked at ways to maintain an element of luxury and ensure a quality product while allowing individual wineries room to experiment with different grape varieties and approaches. Peller has introduced Fracettes from its Thirty Bench Estate, made from a base blend of riesling and chardonnay, and Peller Estates label, an aromatic rosé that blends chardonnay, gewurztraminer and gamay noir (for colour).

Peller Estates has an established traditional-method sparkling wine brand called Ice Cuvée, which adds a portion of Vidal Icewine to each bottle prior to final corking and release. The white and rosé versions of Ice Cuvée are noticeably sweet, each containing more than 20 g/litre residual sugar. The perceived sweetness of a wine is relative to the other components, most importantly acidity, in that wine as well as the taster’s sensitivity.

Fracette wines are made to balance sweetness and acidity so that the overall impression is refreshing. Garner says the expressions made at Peller are a work in progress. “We have one rendition and have learned what we might want to do differently.”

Good Taste: Three fortified wines to savour this fall

The winemaking and marketing teams at Peller, Henry of Pelham and Arterra, which owns Inniskillin, Jackson-Triggs and other wineries and brands in Ontario, worked together behind the scenes to invent Fracette.

“It has been a unique experience because not only are we launching a new category, we’re coming together as an industry to do it,” says Sandra Smith, senior marketing contractor at Arterra Wines Canada. Arterra properties, Kew, Saintly and Inniskillin, are making Fracette along with the company’s Saintly brand.

When it came time to introducing the new wines to buyers at the Lcbo, the Fracette wineries went as a group rather than individual wineries. “We showed up together, which I think was key in helping the Lcbo understand how serious we were,” she explains. “We all see the potential in bringing to light what Ontario is doing so well.”

The six labels, which range in price from $18.95 (Peller Estates Private Reserve Fracette Brut Rosé) to $34.95 (Inniskillin Fracette Rosé Sparkling 2025), are available in Ontario at the Lcbo, individual estates, the Wine Shops and the Wine Rack, and other participating retailers.

stories.title: Foreign influence watchdog ‘aware of concerns’ about Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Canadians acting on behalf of foreign nations to influence Alberta referendum question must register with new foreign influence commissioner or face penalties.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Canada’s foreign influence commissioner’s office says they’re “aware of concerns” about other states targeting the Alberta upcoming independence referendum.

In a statement Tuesday evening, Foreign Influence Commissioner Anton Boegman said his office has “proactively communicated” with both individuals and organizations that may be working with foreign governments to influence Albertans’ votes ahead of the Oct. 19 referendum.

Boegman’s office pushed any Canadian working with foreign governments to influence Canadian politics or government policy to review their website to decide whether they have to register under the Foreign Influence Transparency and Accountability Act.

So far, the registry lists just two names publicly. Anyone actively working with foreign governments must register before Oct. 3, in the case of longstanding relationships that began before Aug. 2026.

In the case of arrangements that began after Aug. 4, 2026, people working with foreign governments must register within two weeks of starting that work.

The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans if, among other things, they want to begin the constitutionally required process to hold a binding vote on separating from Canada — essentially a referendum on if they want an official independence referendum.

Alberta separatist leaders have claimed to have already met with U.S. State Department officials in attempts to secure financing for a newly independent province. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously publicly winked at the separatist cause, suggesting an independent Alberta would have allies within U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

The appeals to the Trump administration have raised concerns about U.S. foreign influence, or at least money, targeting the referendum.

Despite the concerns, public polling suggests that a strong majority of Albertans want their province to remain part of a united Canada. Poll aggregator 338Canada.com — using data from a number of different polling firms — suggests that 71 per cent of Albertans support remaining in Canada, to just 27 per cent who wish to leave the federation.

In the case of arrangements that began after Aug. 4, 2026, people working with foreign governments must register within two weeks of starting that work.

The Oct. 19 referendum will ask Albertans if, among other things, they want to begin the constitutionally required process to hold a binding vote on separating from Canada — essentially a referendum on if they want an official independence referendum.

Alberta separatist leaders have claimed to have already met with U.S. State Department officials in attempts to secure financing for a newly independent province. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has previously publicly winked at the separatist cause, suggesting an independent Alberta would have allies within U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.
The appeals to the Trump administration have raised concerns about U.S. foreign influence, or at least money, targeting the referendum.

Despite the concerns, public polling suggests that a strong majority of Albertans want their province to remain part of a united Canada. Poll aggregator 338Canada.com — using data from a number of different polling firms — suggests that 71 per cent of Albertans support remaining in Canada, to just 27 per cent who wish to leave the federation.
