This year’s shortlisted authors include Zak Jones for Fancy Gap , published by Hamish Hamilton Canada. One of the characters in the story, about three estranged generations in Appalachia, is a soldier dishonourably discharged from the military. The Toronto-based author is a U.S. Army veteran and dual Canadian-American citizen who won the Writers’ Trust of Canada’s Bronwen Wallace Award for Emerging Writers in 2023.

The jury called Fancy Gap an “exceptional, uncanny read” that brings Appalachia alive and entails beauty, despair, longing and a search for community.

Toronto-based Congo-Canadian poet and fiction writer Téa Mutonji was shortlisted for My Person , published by Random House Canada. Her debut collection of short stories, Shut Up You’re Pretty , was a finalist for the Atwood Gibson prize in 2019.

The jury praised My Person as a “witty, moving and fiercely authentic” portrait of millennial life and the complex realities of interracial relationships.

Blair Palmer Yoxall, a member of the Métis Nation of Alberta, was nominated for Treat Them as Buffalo , published by Harper Avenue. The anti-Western, about resilient Métis women and missing teenaged Indigenous boys in the late 19th century, was described by the jury as a story that “moves with high energy and suspense in an ambitious way.”

The fifth finalist is Toronto’s Ashraf Zaghal, a Palestinian-Canadian poet and novelist born and raised in Jerusalem. His Seven Heavens Away , published by House of Anansi Press, follows a Palestinian teenager who comes of age amid escalating violence in Jerusalem.

“The writing exhibits a miracle of tenderness in a harsh and perilous surround, treasuring the protagonist’s young internal voice within its larger, older cultural context of tension, loyalty and violence,” the jury said.

Among the previous Atwood Gibson winners are Austin Clarke, Helen Humphreys, Alice Munro, Joseph Boyden, Lawrence Hill, Miriam Toews, Emma Donoghue, André Alexis and last year’s prize-taker Maria Reva, for her novel Endling .

This year’s winner will be revealed at the Writers’ Trust Awards in Toronto on Nov. 10.

stories.title: Court set to hear from victims’ families in case of international poison seller, Kenneth Law
stories.summary: "It doesn't change the depth of the grief or the sadness that I've experienced," said mom Kim Prosser.
stories.author: Omar Mosleh
stories.content:
A court is set to hear victim impact statements on Wednesday from loved ones about how their lives were torn apart due to the actions of Kenneth Law, the Mississauga man who sold poisons to hundreds of people and who pleaded guilty to helping 14 Ontarians die by suicide.

The hearing is set to be the start of what will likely be a long process, with Law’s ultimate sentence to be delivered at a later date. This hearing could last up to three days, if needed. It’s expected that the Crown will go over evidence for the deaths Law took responsibility for in Ontario, and that the court will hear several victim impact statements.

Kim Prosser, whose son Ashtyn died by suicide on March 30, 2023, at age 19 through materials purchased from Law, will be attending the hearing. She has told the Star she doesn’t hold hate or resentment toward Law, but was grateful for his guilty plea.

“It doesn’t change the depth of the grief or the sadness that I’ve experienced,” she said.

But she added she’s been frustrated with how the court hearings have played out, and the overall scope of the investigation. At his last plea hearing, the court heard the stories of 79 people in the United Kingdom that authorities connected to Law, for which he accepted responsibility.

“The thing that made me so angry the first time was like, (the courts) gave a voice for 79 people. What about everyone else? Because people still have that product. And they’re using it and ending their lives,” she said.

Law’s counsel, Matthew Gourlay, said arguments on sentencing will be submitted on Nov. 27, and his sentence May be imposed after that.

Law was initially charged with 14 counts of first-degree murder in a case with vast international implications; he remains accused of selling poisons used in dozens upon dozens of suicides outside Canada.

In May, Law pleaded guilty instead to 14 charges of aiding and abetting suicide connected to 14 Ontarians, ages 16 to 36. The Crown withdrew the murder charges, explaining there was no reasonable prospect of him being convicted of murder.

At his plea, Law also took responsibility for 79 deaths in the United Kingdom.

It is not yet clear how Law’s decision to accept responsibility for the U.K. deaths will impact his Canadian sentence.

The sprawling case of poison-seller Kenneth Law

The true number of people who died through Law’s assistance is likely staggering.

He sent 1,209 packages containing a food additive that can be lethal in certain doses, as well as other materials used for self-harm, to more than 40 countries, selling the materials via four websites that operated under the guise of selling cooking materials and industrial equipment.

Many of the people he sent packages to suffered from severe mental health conditions, and some were children.

“This was an opportunity for Canada to put its foot down,” said David Parfett, whose 22-year-old

Canadian investigators say Law sent 78 shipments to Ontario recipients, with 28 people who received them dying by suicide.

Law was busiest from 2021 to 2023, and most victims purchased the product for roughly $80 (U.S.); Law admitted to making nearly $300,000 through sales, using platforms such as Shopify and PayPal.

Had Law been tried and convicted of murder, a life sentence would be automatic.

The charge of counselling or aiding suicide instead carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison, to be decided at a later date.

Criminal defence lawyers who previously spoke to the Star have said that the magnitude of his crimes suggests his sentence could land in the range of 15-20 years if the judge rules his convictions should be served consecutively.

Law has been in custody for more than three years and will likely be credited for time served.

Family members of Law’s victims have called for a public inquiry in both Canada and the U.K. to probe how Law’s websites could have operated for years before his arrest.

If you are having thoughts of suicide or are worried about a loved one, call or text 988 for suicide-prevention support at any time of day or night, or call the Talk Suicide Canada helpline at 1-833-456-4566.

stories.title: Ontario raises tire recycling target after a year of industry chaos and stockpiles across the province
stories.summary: The province is also expanding collection sites to 6,500 after a target drop in 2025 left garages and yards unable to get used tires picked up.
stories.author: Patty Winsa
stories.content:
The Ontario government is raising the recycling target for tires after more than a year of chaos in the industry caused by an earlier provincial decision to reduce the level.

The new target requires tire producers to recycle, reuse or retread 80 per cent, by weight, of the tires they sell in the province, up from 65 per cent, one of a series of amendments to the Resource Recovery and Circular Economy Act of 2016 announced by the province on Monday.

The Ontario Tire Dealers Association, which has been advocating for the increase, said it is reviewing the amendments, but that the changes by the environment ministry look positive “at a high level.”

The new target should kick-start a once-robust tire recycling industry that was hit hard when the government lowered the recycling target at the beginning of 2025. The reduction meant hundreds of garages and tire dealers couldn't get their used tires picked up because the producer responsibility organizations (PROs) that handle recycling for tire companies didn't need them to meet the lowered target.

Tire haulers were put out of work, or had to lay off staff. And processing facilities that recycle used tires into crumb operated at reduced capacity despite the fact that consumers bankroll the industry through the eco-fees they pay on new tires.

Adam Moffatt, CEO of the tire dealers association, warned that the province’s recycling capacity cannot be restored overnight and that the PROs that manage recycling for tire companies also need time to assess the new requirements and implement their collection plans.

“The question now is how quickly those plans can be put into action and how quickly the collection and processing system can respond, particularly as we enter one of the busiest times of the year for Ontario’s tire dealers,” said Moffatt.

The province’s amendments also include a requirement that PROs collect from more sites, as in garages and tire dealers, from 4,300 to 6,500 beginning in 2027.

Both the increase in the recycling target and the number of collection sites weren’t in the original amendments put out by the government earlier this year for public consultation in response to the slowdown in the industry.

Instead, the province was looking at ways to implement timelines that would encourage PROs to pick up tires more quickly.

But the environment ministry determined that a higher recycling target, and an increase in collection sites, “would be the most direct way to address backlogs and improve the reliability of tire collection services in Ontario,” said the ministry in an email.

The final amendments could be a surprise for many in the industry, including PROs, who now have to budget to meet a higher recycling target more than halfway through the year.

eTracks, the largest PRO in the province, said it was too early to comment.

The company said that it is “reviewing the changes and assessing impact on the broader tire recycling system in Ontario, as well as what it means for our producer customers, collection site partners and operations.

“We continue to operate our provincewide collection network and work with service partners to keep tires moving,” said Christopher Balestri, the company’s marketing and communications lead, in an email.

During the chaos caused by the reduced target, the environment ministry repeatedly told the media that it expected PROs to continue to pick up tires in a timely manner, an expectation that the ministry continues to repeat.

Yet, hundreds of thousands of tires were stockpiled at sites in Sudbury and Ottawa, which critics warned was a potential environmental catastrophe, but no PRO or hauler was ever publicly blamed for the problem.

“Our expectation remains that producers and producer responsibility organizations collect and manage all end-of-life tires as they become available, regardless of targets,” said the ministry on Tuesday.

But the environment ministry determined that a higher recycling target, and an increase in collection sites, “would be the most direct way to address backlogs and improve the reliability of tire collection services in Ontario,” said the ministry in an email.
The final amendments could be a surprise for many in the industry, including PROs, who now have to budget to meet a higher recycling target more than halfway through the year.

content_blocks.alt: There's actually a pretty simple solution to the risk that AI is going to 'kill all humans'

content_blocks.text: eTracks, the largest PRO in the province, said it was too early to comment.

The company said that it is “reviewing the changes and assessing impact on the broader tire recycling system in Ontario, as well as what it means for our producer customers, collection site partners and operations.

“We continue to operate our provincewide collection network and work with service partners to keep tires moving,” said Christopher Balestri, the company’s marketing and communications lead, in an email.

content_blocks.alt: Donald Trump is picking a fight on potash. Here's how Canada should respond (spoiler: not like Andrew Scheer)

content_blocks.text: During the chaos caused by the reduced target, the environment ministry repeatedly told the media that it expected PROs to continue to pick up tires in a timely manner, an expectation that the ministry continues to repeat.

Yet, hundreds of thousands of tires were stockpiled at sites in Sudbury and Ottawa, which critics warned was a potential environmental catastrophe, but no PRO or hauler was ever publicly blamed for the problem.

“Our expectation remains that producers and producer responsibility organizations collect and manage all end-of-life tires as they become available, regardless of targets,” said the ministry on Tuesday.

stories.title: Ontario must reconsider denying cancer patient access to new treatment in U.S., court rules
stories.summary: Ontario Divisional Court panel directs Ontario government to reconsider denial to fund Alex Shved’s treatment in the U.S.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
Doctors have told Alex Shved, a 37-year-old with metastatic melanoma, that a therapy exists that could extend his life.

On Tuesday, a panel of the Ontario Divisional Court agreed, directing the provincial government to reconsider its earlier denial to fund his treatment in the U.S.

The court ordered an expedited review of Shved’s case and gave the government until Oct. 2 — or earlier if possible — to make a new decision, noting Shved’s terminal diagnosis.

“The record discloses that he will likely be dead by Christmas if he does not receive the requested treatment within a few weeks,” the panel wrote in its ruling.

Shved is seeking a personalized cell treatment that was approved by Health Canada last year but is not yet covered by provincial drug plans.

Called tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, or TIL therapy, the treatment uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to find and attack cancer. The treatment is produced by a U.S. company and is marketed as lifileucel, also known by its brand name Amtagvi.

On the advice of his doctor, Shved earlier this year applied to the province for out-of-country coverage to go to a U.S. hospital for treatment. His application was denied, and Shved’s subsequent appeal to the Health Services Appeal and Review Board (Hsarb) was dismissed.

The tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to attack cancer.

Shved, who lives in Etobicoke with his wife and two young daughters, launched a judicial review of the province’s decision, representing himself at the Sept. 8 hearing.

He called Tuesday’s court decision “vindicating” and said he hopes the decision is a “wakeup call” to the province, adding that he knows of at least two Ontario patients with the same cancer who have died after being denied out-of-country access to TIL therapy.

“It makes me upset thinking about all of the people who have been wronged by this process and this system,” Shved said.

The Health Ministry did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday night but a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones previously told the Star that provinces and territories do not provide out-of-country funding for treatments that have not yet gone through Canada’s drug funding system.

That funding process, which includes price negotiations between the manufacturer and the pan-Canadian Pharmaceutical Alliance, can take more than two years.

Shved launched a judicial review of Ontario’s funding denial for his TIL treatment in June. His central argument was that the out-of-country program is in place for treatments and health services that are unavailable to Ontario patients, and that the program is most needed for patients facing terminal diagnoses with no alternatives.

Shved also argued that denying him funding disregarded expert evidence from doctors who stated the treatment was not only safe but the best available choice, offering Shved a 30 per cent chance of a sustained response. A Florida hospital quoted Shved $1.3 million for TIL therapy, which requires chemotherapy and time in hospital, in addition to producing the personalized cell treatment.

In Tuesday’s ruling, the panel stated the province provided no evidence that funding Shved’s TIL therapy would undermine drug pricing negotiations while also underscoring both Shved’s immediate need and recommendations from medical experts.

“As we have noted more than once, this presents as a life-or-death decision for Mr. Shved,” the panel wrote. “His expert physicians have recommended the treatment, which is available in the United States and is under active consideration for use in Ontario.”

A majority of the three-justice panel ordered the expedited review of Shved’s funding application through the province’s established programs, while one justice recommended an immediate recommendation to fund the treatment.

Shved, who last week had surgery to rebuild his left arm after a tumour broke through the bone, said he is hopeful the province will fund his TIL treatment. In the meantime, he said, he is focusing on regaining enough arm strength to easily cradle his five-month-old daughter.

Wednesday, September 23, 2026

The City of London, local first responders and Western University are reminding the community to prioritize safety and well-being during this weekend’s celebrations. Those celebrating are encouraged to look out for one another and avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, which can create serious safety risks.

The Unsanctioned Street Party Task Force has been preparing for anticipated gatherings this weekend, bringing together agencies from across London with a shared focus on keeping students,residents and the community safe. The task force includes representatives from the City of London, the London Police Service, the London Fire Department, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Western University and Fanshawe College, with operational support from London Health Sciences Centre and St. Joseph’s Health Care London.

Getting there

On Saturday, September 26, access to Western’s campus from Richmond Street will be closed.Additional road closures may be implemented as needed to address large gatherings and support public safety.

Safety and enforcement

First responders and enforcement agencies will be visible and active throughout the weekend in key areas to ensure community safety. Unsanctioned gatherings pose safety risks and may result in fines and/or charges. Fines can be issued for multiple infractions, and the same person can be fined multiple times in one day. Examples of fines include:

Hosting a nuisance party: $1130

Attending a nuisance party: $930

Failing to leave premises: $65

Using of a closed road: $615

Make/cause/permit noise likely to disturb inhabitants: $305

Urinating in a public place: $305

Beyond financial consequences, the top priority remains the safety and well-being of students and the wider community.

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)resources

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)can occur anywhere in the community and disproportionately affects women, gender-diverse and trans people. There is zero tolerance for any form of GBSV,including unwanted comments(such as catcalling),inappropriate gestures and unwanted physical contact.

Community members are encouraged to speak up and safely intervene if they witness sexual violence.Learn how to safely intervene and prevent sexual violence by exploringbystander intervention actions.

Those who experience GBSV can report their experience anonymously through the London Police Service’sSpeak Outwebsite, contact ANOVA’s 24/7 crisis and support line at 519-642-3000 or call 2-1-1 for 24/7 crisis counselling and referrals.Western University students can access additional resources on theGetting Help After Experiencing GBSV webpage.

“We’re looking forward to welcoming new and returning students to London,” says Amanda Pfeffer,Director, Municipal Compliance, City of London.“While Homecoming is an exciting time for students, we encourage everyone to keep safety,kindness and respect top of mind. Celebrate responsibly, look out for one another, and remember to be respectful of your neighbours and the broader community.”

"Homecoming brings a unique energy and excitement to Western’s campus. As we welcome thousands of alumni for the weekend, we want everyone to celebrate safely and responsibly,”says John Doerksen, Vice-Provost (Students), Western University. “We’re encouraging students to participate in the many sanctioned events happening on campus and to take care of themselves, their friends, and our broader community."

“As Homecoming weekend approaches, we would like to remind everyone to celebrate responsibly,” said Superintendent Bill Berg, of the London Police Service. “There will be an increased police presence in key areas of the city, with a focus on addressing nuisance parties, open alcohol consumption, underage drinking, and public intoxication. As we have in previous years, we will also be supported by additional policing partners to help ensure a safe and coordinated response throughout the weekend. While we encourage everyone to have an enjoyable weekend, we also ask that those in attendance show respect for the city, community members, and one another. Education will continue throughout the weekend; however, enforcement action will be taken when necessary.”

Wednesday, September 23, 2026

The City of London, local first responders and Western University are reminding the community to prioritize safety and well-being during this weekend’s celebrations. Those celebrating are encouraged to look out for one another and avoid large, unsanctioned street gatherings, which can create serious safety risks.

The Unsanctioned Street Party Task Force has been preparing for anticipated gatherings this weekend, bringing together agencies from across London with a shared focus on keeping students,residents and the community safe. The task force includes representatives from the City of London, the London Police Service, the London Fire Department, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, Western University and Fanshawe College, with operational support from London Health Sciences Centre and St. Joseph’s Health Care London.
Getting there
On Saturday, September 26, access to Western’s campus from Richmond Street will be closed.Additional road closures may be implemented as needed to address large gatherings and support public safety.
Safety and enforcement

First responders and enforcement agencies will be visible and active throughout the weekend in key areas to ensure community safety. Unsanctioned gatherings pose safety risks and may result in fines and/or charges. Fines can be issued for multiple infractions, and the same person can be fined multiple times in one day. Examples of fines include:

items: Make/cause/permit noise likely to disturb inhabitants: $305

content_blocks.text: Beyond financial consequences, the top priority remains the safety and well-being of students and the wider community.
Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)resources

Gender-based and sexual violence (GBSV)can occur anywhere in the community and disproportionately affects women, gender-diverse and trans people. There is zero tolerance for any form of GBSV,including unwanted comments(such as catcalling),inappropriate gestures and unwanted physical contact.
Community members are encouraged to speak up and safely intervene if they witness sexual violence.Learn how to safely intervene and prevent sexual violence by exploringbystander intervention actions.

Those who experience GBSV can report their experience anonymously through the London Police Service’sSpeak Outwebsite, contact ANOVA’s 24/7 crisis and support line at 519-642-3000 or call 2-1-1 for 24/7 crisis counselling and referrals.Western University students can access additional resources on theGetting Help After Experiencing GBSV webpage.

“We’re looking forward to welcoming new and returning students to London,” says Amanda Pfeffer,Director, Municipal Compliance, City of London.“While Homecoming is an exciting time for students, we encourage everyone to keep safety,kindness and respect top of mind. Celebrate responsibly, look out for one another, and remember to be respectful of your neighbours and the broader community.”

"Homecoming brings a unique energy and excitement to Western’s campus. As we welcome thousands of alumni for the weekend, we want everyone to celebrate safely and responsibly,”says John Doerksen, Vice-Provost (Students), Western University. “We’re encouraging students to participate in the many sanctioned events happening on campus and to take care of themselves, their friends, and our broader community."

“As Homecoming weekend approaches, we would like to remind everyone to celebrate responsibly,” said Superintendent Bill Berg, of the London Police Service. “There will be an increased police presence in key areas of the city, with a focus on addressing nuisance parties, open alcohol consumption, underage drinking, and public intoxication. As we have in previous years, we will also be supported by additional policing partners to help ensure a safe and coordinated response throughout the weekend. While we encourage everyone to have an enjoyable weekend, we also ask that those in attendance show respect for the city, community members, and one another. Education will continue throughout the weekend; however, enforcement action will be taken when necessary.”

stories.title: The value of a college education - lifelong and flexible learning
stories.summary: As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that m
stories.content:
As Fanshawe looks toward 2035, our leaders will share their perspectives on the issues that matter. This series explores the opportunities, challenges and innovations shaping the future of education, workforce development and our community.

The fall semester is now underway, and we have welcomed over 8,300 level one students beginning their full-time post-secondary studies at Fanshawe College. After a quieter summer, it’s wonderful to see the halls full of students bravely embracing this next stage of their life. We take care to thoughtfully plan events, activities and ongoing supports that provide a sense of belonging for students who are embarking on this journey from many paths.

At a time when approximately 30 per cent of our incoming students have arrived directly from high school, we are increasingly welcoming mature students seeking flexible, accessible and targeted offerings that meet the needs of diverse learners throughout their lifelong learning journey.

For decades, the post-secondary path was relatively predictable: complete a program, earn a credential and begin a career. Today, that linear journey has given way to a more dynamic reality. Our graduates are navigating a labour market that increasingly rewards skills, adaptability and experience alongside credentials. Technological advancement, economic transformation and evolving workforce needs mean that individuals will likely reskill and upskill multiple times throughout their working lives. Post-secondary education can no longer be viewed as a one-time experience. It must become a lifelong journey.

Colleges are uniquely positioned to meet this challenge. Increasingly, our role extends beyond delivering traditional post-secondary learning models, to providing continuous opportunities for career development, professional growth and lifelong learning. Fanshawe College is addressing this priority with a focus on developing and supporting more part-time, online, modular and stackable offerings that empower students with choice and remove barriers, creating new possibilities for our prospective students’ personal and professional advancement. Prior Learning Assessment and Recognition (Plar) offers academic credit that recognizes previous post-secondary studies, workplace experience, volunteer activities and other forms of experiential learning. Micro-credentials, short-duration training and flexible delivery options allow learners to access education when and where they need it most.

One example of this approach to non-traditional models is our accelerated delivery of Early Childhood Education at the Simcoe/Norfolk Regional Campus. The continuous intake and modular delivery format welcomes new students every six weeks, providing eight entry points throughout the year. Students can complete the diploma in as little as twelve consecutive months, while a combination of virtual and in-person HyFlex classes are designed specifically to meet the needs of working ECEs seeking their diploma. Through this innovative delivery model, we provide a unique opportunity for mature students balancing careers, families and financial responsibilities who require a pathway that acknowledges those realities.

Fanshawe is also focusing on the community and economic impact of the programming we offer for our students. By aligning students’ learning with local and regional workforce needs, the benefits extend well beyond the personal impact for our graduates. Employers gain access to the talent they need to grow and innovate their businesses, while communities become more resilient and regional economies become stronger and more competitive.

The skilled trades provide a powerful example of this impact. A highly skilled workforce has become central to Canada's economic future, as evidenced in Canada Strong and Protect Ontario priorities. Demand continues to grow for highly skilled trades professionals who can support infrastructure development, advanced manufacturing, housing construction and emerging technologies. Fanshawe’s programs are preparing graduates for these careers that offer meaningful work and long-term stability while addressing critical workforce shortages.

For example, Canada is experiencing a sustained shortage of Aircraft Maintenance Engineers, driven by an aging workforce, increased consumer commercial flight demand, and continued growth across the aviation sector. Fanshawe is committed to growing our enrolment to meet the ongoing need to expand Transport Canada-approved training capacity and develop a strong pipeline of qualified maintenance professionals to support Canada's aviation industry.

Success in preparing learners for these and other opportunities depend on strong employer partnerships. Close collaboration with industry through our various Program Advisory Committees help ensure curriculum remains current, practical and aligned with real-world expectations. Apprenticeships, co-operative education, applied learning and other work-integrated learning experiences prepare our graduates with both technical expertise and the professional skills employers value most.

As we support our students on their learning journey this fall, we are reminded that some are preparing for their first career, while many more are on other paths. By continuing to innovate how we deliver education and by strengthening partnerships with employers and communities, we are transforming individual and community potential into ongoing impact. Behind every enrolment is an individual taking a courageous step toward a brighter future, and we are privileged to be part of that journey.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.CA

Close collaboration with industry through our various Program Advisory Committees help ensure curriculum remains current, practical and aligned with real-world expectations. Apprenticeships, co-operative education, applied learning and other work-integrated learning experiences prepare our graduates with both technical expertise and the professional skills employers value most.

As we support our students on their learning journey this fall, we are reminded that some are preparing for their first career, while many more are on other paths. By continuing to innovate how we deliver education and by strengthening partnerships with employers and communities, we are transforming individual and community potential into ongoing impact. Behind every enrolment is an individual taking a courageous step toward a brighter future, and we are privileged to be part of that journey.

content_blocks.text: The fall semester is now underway, and we have welcomed over 8,300 level one students beginning their full-time post-secondary studies at Fanshawe College. After a quieter summer, it’s wonderful to see the halls full of students bravely embracing this next stage of their life. content_blocks.text: At a time when approximately 30 per cent of our incoming students have arrived directly from high school, we are increasingly welcoming mature students seeking flexible, accessible and targeted offerings that meet the needs of diverse learners throughout their lifelong learning journey.

For decades, the post-secondary path was relatively predictable: complete a program, earn a credential and begin a career. Today, that linear journey has given way to a more dynamic reality. Our graduates are navigating a labour market that increasingly rewards skills, adaptability and experience alongside credentials. Technological advancement, economic transformation and evolving workforce needs mean that individuals will likely reskill and upskill multiple times throughout their working lives. Post-secondary education can no longer be viewed as a one-time experience. It must become a lifelong journey.

content_blocks.text: Colleges are uniquely positioned to meet this challenge. Increasingly, our role extends beyond delivering traditional post-secondary learning models, to providing continuous opportunities for career development, professional growth and lifelong learning. Fanshawe College is addressing this priority with a focus on developing and supporting more part-time, online, modular and stackable offerings that empower students with choice and remove barriers, creating new possibilities for our prospective students’ personal and professional advancement. Prior Learning Assessment and Recognition (Plar) offers academic credit that recognizes previous post-secondary studies, workplace experience, volunteer activities and other forms of experiential learning. Micro-credentials, short-duration training and flexible delivery options allow learners to access education when and where they need it most.

content_blocks.text: One example of this approach to non-traditional models is our accelerated delivery of Early Childhood Education at the Simcoe/Norfolk Regional Campus. The continuous intake and modular delivery format welcomes new students every six weeks, providing eight entry points throughout the year. Students can complete the diploma in as little as twelve consecutive months, while a combination of virtual and in-person HyFlex classes are designed specifically to meet the needs of working ECEs seeking their diploma. Through this innovative delivery model, we provide a unique opportunity for mature students balancing careers, families and financial responsibilities who require a pathway that acknowledges those realities.

stories.title: Rock duo Angine de Poitrine wins Polaris Prize
stories.summary: The Quebec group took home the $30,000 prize, and also won the $10,000 song prize for their song ‘Fabienk’
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath
stories.content:
Angine de Poitrine has won the Polaris Music Prize for their album “Vol II.”

About 200 music industry experts selected the second album by the costume-clad rock duo for the $30,000 prize, naming it the best Canadian record of the year based solely on artistic merit.

The Quebec group also took home the $10,000 song prize for the tune “Fabienk.”

How Angine de Poitrine’s global success benefits their friends at home in Quebec

The recognition continues a breakout year for the anonymous rockers, who dress in polka-dot outfits and describe themselves as 333-year-old aliens.

The Polaris is considered one of the country’s most prestigious music awards.

A change to the voting process saw this year’s winner selected by a voting pool rather than an 11-person jury, as in previous years.

stories.title: Bennett Bridge crash brings Central Okanagan traffic to a standstill
stories.summary: The latest closure has renewed calls from local politicians and residents for a second crossing of Okanagan Lake.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Tuesday morning’s commute in the Central Okanagan was brought to a standstill following a serious multi-vehicle collision on the Bennett Bridge.

“At this time, RCMP is unable to confirm what factors May have contributed to the collision, nor the extent of injuries which May have been sustained,” said Kelowna RCMP Cpl. Steven Lang. “Further details regarding the investigation will be released when it is appropriate to do so.”

The crash happened shortly after 4 a.m., shutting down all three southbound lanes into West Kelowna and temporarily impacting one of the two northbound lanes into Kelowna.

The nearly five-hour incident caused major traffic backups in both directions and forced Mt. Boucherie Secondary School to cancel classes for the day after staff were unable to get to work.

Motorists were advised that the best alternate southbound route was to travel north to Vernon before taking Westside Road — a roughly 130-kilometre detour.

The latest closure has renewed calls from local politicians and residents for a second crossing of Okanagan Lake.

Gavin Dew, Conservative MLA for Kelowna-Mission, said incidents such as Tuesday’s crash highlight the need for additional transportation infrastructure.

“Every time there is a closure on the bridge, it’s a reminder of the fact that we are still waiting for significant traffic improvements that are overdue,” Dew said.

The idea of a second crossing has been raised by community leaders and residents for years.

However, another bridge was not included in the 20-year transportation plan unveiled by the province in 2023.

Macklin McCall, Conservative MLA for West Kelowna-Peachland, said congestion and the need for another crossing have been ongoing concerns.

“This didn’t just spring up overnight. This was an issue with the second crossing and congestion for quite some time,” McCall said. “We still haven’t had meaningful conversations. The province hasn’t said, you know, this is one of the fastest-growing areas in British Columbia and there hasn’t even been discussions on it. But I’ll tell you this, people in the region are certainly discussing it.”

West Kelowna’s Stephen Johnston, who has been acclaimed as the city’s next mayor, told Global News that a second bridge remains a long-term solution but he wants to see action now.

“The bridge should be properly six-laned, with a new pedestrian and active transportation lane cantilevered off the side,” Johnston stated in an email to Global News. “It was originally designed to accommodate this, and we need to leverage that opportunity. This would add much-needed capacity while providing greater flexibility to keep traffic moving in both directions when an accident occurs.”

McCall said transportation infrastructure is a major issue for the Okanagan region.

“If it doesn’t get addressed, it’s only going to get worse,” McCall said.

stories.title: Terry Fox foundation a major help for cancer research
stories.summary: The Terry Fox run is an annual tradition in London, where hundreds of people sign up to run in honour of the l...
stories.author: Ben Andrews
stories.content:
The Terry Fox run is an annual tradition in London, where hundreds of people sign up to run in honour of the late Terry Fox, to raise awareness of and to raise funds for cancer and cancer research. “F or our site, it was about $126,000,” said Pete Ferguson, a member of the Terry Fox run committee as well as a cancer researcher. “T he total will be close to half a million dollars by the time everybody’s [schools in London] done.”

Funds raised by the Terry Fox foundation go to a “national pot”, which is then used to help fund different cancer research laboratories. The more money that the Terry Fox foundation raises, the more laboratories can benefit from this funding, including smaller, local laboratories.

“Ri ght now, there’s over 600 projects that are funded by the foundation,” said Ferguson. “In the 46 years that it’s been going on, it’s raised over a billion dollars now.”

Despite the large amount of funds the Terry Fox run is raising, more donations are always welcome, especially since cancer research is very expensive. “ the people that do it have to be paid, that money comes from various sources, including the Terry Fox Foundation,” said Ferguson. “C hemicals, some of the machinery that we use, it has advanced cancer research greatly, but those things are expensive.”

With all these costs associated with cancer research, and with how much the Terry Fox foundation contributes to cancer research, Ferguson thinks that cancer research would be nowhere as advanced as it is now without the foundations help. “ Cancer research and a lot of research is notoriously underfunded by the government,” said Ferguson. S o other fundraisers have been so important in advancing cancer research, and Terry Fox Foundation is a major part of that.”

“C ancer research would not have advanced as much as it has today without fundraising and charity fundraising and, of course, the contribution of the Terry Fox run.”

stories.title: Alberta Premier suggests introducing health premiums for temporary residents if immigration changes pass referendum
stories.summary: The immigration questions propose a new system to access services such as education and health care
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is floating the idea of a $1,900 health premium for some temporary residents, one of the first concrete ideas she has pitched as the province prepares to vote on immigration policy proposals in October’s referendum.

Ms. Smith on Tuesday said the government is looking at charging some temporary residents between $1,400 and $1,900 per person for health care, which she suggested could be shouldered by businesses.

“This is a new conversation. I recognize that we have been generous for a long time, but it’s put too much strain on our system,” Ms. Smith told members of the business community at a Calgary Chamber of Commerce event.

While the Premier was non-committal when pressed by reporters for details, Finance Minister Jason Nixon, suggested that the government’s proposals wouldn’t be implemented until after the next provincial election in October, 2027.

It was one of the first times Ms. Smith has provided examples of how some temporary residents could be affected in the wake of Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum, which proposes a suite of reforms to provincial immigration policy.

Opinion: Alberta’s shameless attempt to scapegoat immigrants

The five immigration and citizenship proposals, and four others on constitutional issues have largely taken a back seat to the question around secession – the tenth and final item on the ballot. For that question, Albertans will pick between remaining in Canada or starting the legal process toward holding a second, binding secession vote.

The Premier has said she needs a mandate from Albertans before implementing the immigration policies. The province is spending $4-million in advertising to encourage residents to vote in favour of the government’s proposals.

The immigration questions propose introducing a yet-to-be-defined “Alberta-approved immigration status” that would make certain temporary residents eligible for services such as education and health care.

Ms. Smith is also proposing requiring non-permanent residents to live in Alberta for a year before being able to access public social-support programs and charging non-permanent migrants fees for using the health and education systems.

Ms. Smith said her government hasn’t made decisions around specifics, such as whether temporary residents currently living in Alberta would be required to pay the new fee or if it would only apply to new temporary residents.

“We have to talk about that as a cabinet,” Ms. Smith said. “I want to see if we even have a mandate to do it.”

Danielle Smith denies watering down government messaging on independence question

The Premier said a $1,900 health premium would be designed to encourage employers with low-skill labour needs, such as fast-food companies, to hire local youth.

“I guess that’s the question: Is $1,900 for a business to take on that fee, is that going to make or break your business? If it is, you’re probably hiring into a low-skilled profession, and we want those low-skilled jobs to go to youth employment.”

Mr. Nixon suggested that the United Conservative Party would likely provide precise details in the run-up to the next provincial election, scheduled for Oct. 18, 2027.

“We would need clear instructions from Albertans, which we’re asking for in this referendum, and from there we will begin the process to implement it,” Mr. Nixon said.

“I would not see it being fully implemented until post the ‘27 election,” Mr. Nixon said.

Calgary Chamber president Deborah Yedlin said such a proposal could become a drag on finding labour needed to build major projects in the province and would add costs to businesses.

“This is not necessarily going to make businesses more competitive in Alberta,” Ms. Yedlin said.

Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi said Ms. Smith’s proposal targets non-permanent residents who pay the same amount in taxes as all other provincial residents.

“If she says that every temporary worker who pays the same taxes as every other Albertan is sucking out money from the health care system, guess what? That means every Albertan is sucking money out of the health care system,” Mr. Nenshi told reporters at a news conference.

The Premier has said the province’s roughly 246,000 temporary residents annually cost the government about $1-billion. In February, staring down a $9.4-billion deficit, Ms. Smith partly pinned the shortfall on immigration, but the provincial budget did little to show how Alberta’s rapidly growing population pushed it into the red.

Ms. Smith also announced on Tuesday that her government was repealing Alberta’s 13-cent-per-litre retail gas tax on Oct. 1 in response to windfall oil revenues tied to the Iran war.

Provincial law requires the government to tie the gas tax to the average price of West Texas Intermediate over a stretch of the previous quarter. In June, however, her government opted to keep the tax and cut $100 cheques to Albertans .

Mr. Nixon said there were “a lot of challenges” with the province’s online payment system and so they decided to opt for a tax cut for the next quarter.

stories.title: Shooting at Belleville synagogue an escalation of antisemitic violence, advocates say
stories.summary: Synagogues, Jewish schools and institutions across Canada have been vandalized more than two dozen times over the past three years
stories.author: Joe Friesen
stories.content:
The shooting Sunday at the Sons of Jacob synagogue in Belleville, Ont., represents a dramatic escalation of attacks targeting Jewish institutions in Canada, one that has left many in the community shaken and has led advocates to call on authorities to tackle the issue.

Over the past three years, more than two dozen incidents of gunfire, arson, window-breaking and other types of vandalism have happened at synagogues, Jewish schools and institutions across Canada, according to a tally by the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs. These previous attacks have largely resulted in property damage rather than injury.

But Sunday’s attack, in which the suspected gunman was fatally injured and a police officer was left in critical condition, had the potential to be much worse. Witnesses to the incident said many more people could have been killed or injured if police had not stopped the attacker before he could gain entry to the synagogue.

“We’ve seen synagogues and schools subjected to firebombings and shootings before this. But typically those have taken place under cover of darkness in the middle of the night, intended to intimidate and sow terror,” said Noah Shack, chief executive officer of Cija, a Jewish advocacy organization.

“This was fundamentally different in that the gunman chose to target the synagogue at the time of peak attendance, with the objective of murdering as many Jewish people inside that building as possible.”

Suspect in Belleville synagogue shooting was removed from military service, sources say

The attack took place Sunday night, ON the eve of Yom Kippur, and targeted the congregation in the Eastern Ontario city of Belleville. About 25 people were inside the synagogue at the time; no one inside the building was injured.

The suspected gunman was prevented from gaining entry to the synagogue by a Belleville police officer, Constable Jeff Smith, who was stationed outside.

Constable Smith and other officers engaged the attacker in a gunfight that saw approximately 30 shots fired, with bullets striking the synagogue windows as well as nearby vehicles and homes. Constable Smith suffered serious injuries and is being treated in hospital.

The suspected gunman, Sean Ward, a former member of the Canadian Forces, died in hospital Monday night.

Prime Minister Mark Carney , speaking at the United Nations in New York, was asked whether he’s concerned about extremist views in the military. He declined to answer that question, but expressed gratitude for what he described as the heroic actions of Constable Smith and other police officers.

“We stand against all manifestations of hate against communities and condemn this violence, and no effort will be spared from the federal government perspective,” Mr. Carney said.

Canada has seen a documented rise in hate incidents since 2020. According to Statistics Canada, 70 per cent of the religiously targeted hate crimes logged in 2024 targeted the Jewish community.

Attack against Canadian Jewish community a ‘realistic possibility,’ federal report warns

Mr. Shack, who was in Belleville Tuesday, said the rise in incidents targeting the Jewish community in recent years must be understood as a threat to Canada’s national security.

“It underscores the fact that what my community is facing are not a series of isolated hate incidents, but a fundamental threat to our safety and security, and to Canada’s national security and public safety. And it’s important that our agencies and multiple levels of government start orienting themselves to that reality,” Mr. Shack said.

“This isn’t about a small number of people with hate in their hearts. This is increasingly a violent threat targeting neighbourhoods across this country.”

Some members of the Jewish community have launched a fundraiser on the GoFundMe website to assist Constable Smith and his family with what May potentially be a long and difficult recovery.

“When members of a vulnerable community needed protection, he put himself in harm’s way,“ the organizers wrote. “We will not forget what he did outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue.”

The campaign had raised more than $240,000 by Tuesday evening.

Norm Weddum, president of the Sons of Jacob synagogue, said the members of the congregation who witnessed the shootout are recovering from the traumatic incident. He said the community expects to be able to offer services at the synagogue again relatively soon.

“We will carry on. We will resume programming and we will rise up from the ashes,” Mr. Weddum said.

Planning for the Yom Kippur services at Sons of Jacob began more than a month ago. A rabbi from Israel was invited to lead prayers. In an online post, the synagogue said that at a time when communities across Canada were feeling the effects of rising antisemitism, it was more important than ever to express solidarity with all Jewish people. It announced it had removed the high holiday service fee for non-members in order to maintain a “barrier free open door policy.”

Shari Thorley, a long-time member of the congregation, said she would never have imagined such a violent attack would happen in Belleville. She was unable to attend the service Sunday, but had spoken with some who were present. She said on the one hand she wished she was there so she could support the others, but at the same time she feels a bit shaken.

“I’ve always been very open about being Jewish. And I said to my husband about five minutes ago, ‘I’m not so sure I want to be that open about it any more,’ ” Ms. Thorley said Monday.

“But people come together. We’ve had incidents in the past where they’ve broken windows. People come together and keep on going.”

With a report from Laura Stone

stories.title: Ottawa to clamp down on labour violations in trucking sector
stories.summary: There are more workplace complaints, including for wage theft, from long-haul trucking than any other federally regulated industry
stories.author: Sara Mojtehedzadeh
stories.content:
The federal government says it will crack down on labour violations in the trucking industry and devote additional resources to address wage theft and employee misclassification.

The measures, introduced as part of sweeping legislative changes aimed at economic reform, will strengthen compliance and enforcement in the trucking sector, as well as introduce digital tools to tackle misclassification, Ottawa said.

If passed, the measures announced in Bill C-39 will commit more resources to labour inspections and invest in “digital solutions” such as a worker complaint portal, Pamela Wotherspoon, a spokesperson for Employment and Social Development Canada, said in a Tuesday statement.

A Globe and Mail investigation published in May found that weak and disjointed regulation in the trucking industry has resulted in widespread workplace abuse.

Trucking companies deemed unsafe permitted to employ temporary foreign workers

Long-haul trucking is the largest source of workplace complaints of all federally regulated industries, The Globe’s investigation found. However, Ottawa collected less than 20 per cent of the $6-million in unpaid wages it has ordered trucking firms to pay workers since 2022, data obtained by The Globe revealed.

The Globe’s investigation also found the number of trucking workers classified in census data as self-employed significantly increased between 2011 and 2021 – reflecting mounting problems with employee misclassification.

Misclassification refers to when employers falsely treat workers as self-employed to evade minimum labour protections as well as statutory contributions like employment insurance payments.

The bill will also amend federal labour law to provide Esdc with stronger powers to enforce settlement agreements in wage theft cases – and to secure workers’ unpaid wages when there is a risk that an employer May move or dispose of their assets before the money owed can be recovered, Ms. Wotherspoon said.

The statement did not say how much money would be committed to the proposed measures.

Jonathan Blackham, director of policy and public affairs with the Canadian Trucking Alliance, the national federation of provincial trucking associations, called the proposals an “opportunity to give government better tools to identify non-compliance and recover wages that are owed.”

The CTA welcomed the prospect of additional enforcement resources, he added.

“Worker misclassification is an issue that affects both workers and the trucking companies that play by the rules,” Mr. Blackham said.

“When someone who should be an employee is improperly treated as a contractor, it can mean lost wages and protections for that worker, while giving non-compliant operators an unfair cost advantage.”

Navi Aujla, a service director with Brampton, Ont.-based non-profit Labour Community Services of Peel, said Esdc’s enforcement efforts will not be effective without stricter penalties.

Ms. Wotherspoon said in the statement that Esdc has sought to target misclassification and other workplace violations in trucking through targeted inspections, outreach and education in collaboration with provincial and territorial partners.

Ontario to standardize trucker training after audit flagged widespread issues

A publicly-available database of employers fined by Esdc shows they have penalized eight trucking employers for misclassification this year. The fines ranged from $1,500 to $24,000. None of the firms have paid their fines, according to the database.

Some 70 per cent of long-haul truck drivers in Canada have experienced wage theft on the job, according to a survey of 400 truck drivers published in February by worker advocacy groups including Toronto legal clinic Parkdale Community Legal Services and Labour Community Services of Peel.

More than 65 per cent of the drivers surveyed also reported that they were currently misclassified as independent contractors, or had been in a past job.

The federal government has already implemented tax reforms aimed at addressing employee misclassification.

Last fall, the federal government also committed $77-million for the Canada Revenue Agency to increase scrutiny of trucking firms’ payments to contractors – lifting a previous moratorium on penalizing failure to report these transactions.

The Ontario Trucking Association, which advocates on behalf of trucking firms across the province, has said the moratorium weakened oversight of the trucking sector and accelerated the “predatory use” of the misclassification model and welcomed renewed enforcement.

However, labour advocates have raised concern that the Cra’s efforts have targeted drivers who were unwillingly misclassified by their employers.

Ms. Aujla said the strategy “penalizes the victims of wage theft and does little to hold accountable the employers responsible for it.”

stories.title: Michelin Guide 2026: The surprises, shakeups and rising stars beyond Toronto
stories.summary: The Michelin Guide 2026 is recognizing five restaurants in southern Ontario for providing good bang for the buck.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted September 22, 2026 9:14 pm.

Last Updated September 23, 2026 8:51 am.

Toronto’s dining scene held steady in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide, but the story this year is about how the city’s top restaurants are evolving and how ambitious kitchens outside Toronto are reshaping the region’s culinary identity.

The latest selection, unveiled on Tuesday , features 15 Starred restaurants across Toronto and surrounding communities. While no new restaurants earned Stars, inspectors highlighted major chef changes at two One‑Star establishments, a surge of standout dining in Collingwood, Ont., and the Niagara region, and a widening embrace of diverse cuisines across the GTA.

Two Toronto favourites — Enigma Yorkville and Restaurant 20 Victoria — retained their One‑Star status despite significant shifts behind the pass.

Enigma Yorkville Chef Zachary Barnes, formerly of Restaurant Gordon Ramsay, Daniel and Alo, has replaced founding chef Quinton Bennett. Barnes has moved the restaurant toward ingredient‑focused simplicity while keeping its theatrical edge. Inspectors praised his lobster‑stuffed chicken ballotine and the reimagined Signature Tree, now a savoury canapé opener featuring short rib croquettes and salmon mille‑feuille.

Restaurant 20 Victoria New chef Rafael Covarrubias has infused the menu with bold, contemporary flavours rooted in his Mexican heritage. Dishes like tamale with salsa roja and snow crab and scallop with mole verde mark a departure from the restaurant’s previously restrained European style.

Inspectors say some of the region’s most exciting culinary developments are happening outside the city.

The Pine (Creemore) — The One‑Star modern Chinese and East Asian restaurant has expanded with LORE in Collingwood, offering seafood‑forward Canadian cuisine with playful touches like scallop nuggets and an elevated “Holiday Shrimp Ring.”

Niagara‑on‑the‑Lake — Revé is earning attention for its “farm‑to‑fire” philosophy, cooking hyper‑local ingredients over an open flame. Standouts include Lake Erie pickerel with beets and velouté, and Beverly Creek Farm beef bavette with potato crespelle and Bordelaise.

St. Catharines — Les Incompetents and oddBird continue to delight inspectors with French‑inspired bistro fare and gourmet comfort food.

Jordan Village — RPM Bakehouse, tied to Two‑Star Pearl Morissette, transforms farm‑grown produce and heritage grains into standout pastries, breads and seasonal cakes.

The 2026 Guide celebrates Toronto’s multicultural dining landscape, with new Bib Gourmand and recommended restaurants spanning:

Barbecue — Golden Horseshoe

Indian — PUNCH

Italian — Bar ARDO

Latin American — Antylia

Korean — 156 ONEFIVESIX; Takja

Vietnamese — Pho Ngoc Yen; The Lunch Lady of Saigon

Special awards include:

Best Cocktail Program — 156 ONEFIVESIX

Best Service — LORE

Best Sommelier — Restaurant 20 Victoria

Best Young Chef — Golden Horseshoe Barbecue

stories.title: Ontario court sides with patient appealing province’s refusal to cover out-of-country cancer treatment
stories.summary: Court finds justifications unreasonable and inadequately explained, orders new decision by Oct. 2
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
The Ontario Superior Court of Justice has quashed the province’s decision to refuse to cover out-of-country cancer treatment for a father of two with stage 4 melanoma, ordering a new decision by Oct. 2.

Alex Shved, a 37-year-old Etobicoke resident, had challenged the province’s decision and said Tuesday that the court’s judgment validates arguments he has put forward in his fight to see public drug coverage for tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) therapy. His physicians support Mr. Shved accessing it in Florida.

On Tuesday, justices Jean‑Marc Labrosse and Sharon Shore set aside decisions that denied funding for Mr. Shved’s potentially life-saving treatment, finding the justifications unreasonable and inadequately explained.

They also sent the matter back to the executive officer of the Ontario Public Drug Programs and requested a new decision with an expedited timeline, emphasizing that time is now “very tight.”

“The record discloses that he will likely be dead by Christmas if he does not receive the requested treatment within a few weeks,” the justices said.

A third judge, Justice David Corbett, agreed that the decisions should be quashed. However, he disagreed on the approach supported by justices Labrosse and Shore.

He said he would have directed the executive officer to recommend treatment and would have instructed Ohip’s general manager to expedite a funding decision.

Ontario parents hope son’s death can change Canada’s approach to novel cancer treatments

In August, 2025, Health Canada approved a commercial version of TIL therapy called lifileucel. But it is not available in Canada outside of clinical trials because it is still being reviewed for public funding.

Mr. Shved is one of three Ontario melanoma patients who spoke with The Globe and Mail about their fears and frustrations waiting to access TIL therapy while it makes its way through the country’s complex system for funding new medical treatments.

He applied for a provincial out-of-country program to see if it would pay for him to be treated in the U.S. But he was denied and told the program isn’t intended to be used as an interim funding route for drugs that could eventually qualify for public coverage.

A single treatment of lifileucel costs US$515,000, not including the cost of a stay at an American hospital.

So he filed for a judicial review in court in June. He said the process to review medications for funding can take years and that there is no way for a Canadian patient to access the therapy.

“What is somebody that’s got stage 4 cancer to do?” he said.

“They don’t have two years to wait for this to get approved. And I think that is exactly what the judges saw.”

Mr. Shved, who has a five-month-old baby and a two-year-old, has also appealed to legislators to help.

Days after having surgery on his left arm to remove a tumour, he continued to reach out to politicians. He e-mailed Ontario Premier Doug Ford and Health Minister Sylvia Jones on Tuesday after the court’s decision.

“The Court has made clear that Ohip cannot deny potentially life-saving treatment based on blanket internal policies, unsupported claims about harm to ‘the system’ or superficial reasoning,” he wrote.

“There is clearly something very broken in our healthcare system.”

A spokesperson for Ms. Jones did not immediately offer comment Tuesday on the court’s decision.

Mr. Shved said he has spoken directly with Ms. Jones in the past couple of months but lamented that “she has done nothing.” He said that makes the legal challenge his only available avenue.

And while he said he grows discouraged from time to time when he does not receive anything in return from politicians, he remains hopeful.

He wants to help other patients “wrongly denied this treatment for absurd and unlawful reasons.”

“That’s, I think, what keeps me going and inspires me to continue.”

With reports from Kelly Grant in Toronto

stories.title: Alberta craft whisky lands on Costco shelves as trade war looms
stories.summary: Alberta whisky appearing on Costco shelves gives distillers access to one of the province's largest retail audiences, as they head into a crucial season with U.S. tariffs looming.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Craft producers of Alberta whisky are getting a boost ahead of their busiest sales season and a looming U.S. ban on Canadian alcohol, as Costco liquor stores across the province have begun carrying a selection of locally made whiskies.

Last week, the retailer started stocking eight products from seven small Alberta distilleries at its 15 liquor stores, from Medicine Hat in the south to Grande Prairie in the north.

“If you’re into Alberta whisky, you’re gonna see it’s slightly different at each Costco,” said Bryce Parsons, president of the Alberta Craft Distillers Association and co-founder of True Wild Distilling, whose liquor is being stocked at Calgary’s Heritage Costco location.

“Every Costco is a little bit different — a bit of a treasure hunt.”

The liquor store at the Costco Tsuut’ina in southwest Calgary has whisky from Wild Life Distillery in Canmore, Bridgeland Distillery in Calgary, Anohka Distillery near Stony Plain in Parkland County, and Eau Clare Distillery in Diamond Valley.

“People know what they want but this allows them to explore something new,” said Brian Lerner, manager of Costco Tsuut’ina liquor store, who said customers are increasingly interested in supporting locally made products.

“People want to buy things that have been made and produced with care from the people around us,” Lerner added.

“They make fantastic products here in Alberta.”

Whisky from The Maligne Range distillery in Jasper and Burwood distillery in Calgary are also included in the Costco showcase.

2:53 Alberta Matters: Challenges small liquor producers face in the province

While all of the distilleries provided information for Costco staff to be able to educate customers about the products, representatives from participating producers have also been visiting stores to offer tastings and educate customers about Alberta-made whisky.

“I think overall, people find it extremely exciting and very happy that someone like Costco — who has a great reach to Albertans — that they’re supporting an initiative like this, at this time,” Parsons said.

Earlier this year, the Alberta government introduced the Alberta Whisky Act, which lays out the requirements on how products can qualify for the Alberta Whisky designation, similar to Canadian Whisky branding.

A Costco rep attended a party to unveil the association’s Alberta Whisky logo back in July, which Parsons said got the ball rolling.

5:07 U.S.-Canada trade war: The impact of Costco going local

Getting a product into Costco is no easy feat.

Costco stores carry roughly 4,000 unique items, whereas standard big box stores like Walmart have over 100,000 different products.

Because the retailer is highly selective about what it will stock, suppliers have to be able to demonstrate their product delivers exceptional value to members, can generate strong sales, and can be produced and distributed reliably at the scale the warehouse demands.

As a result, smaller brands often can’t produce the volume required to get their product a coveted space on a Costco shelf.

“I can’t imagine the challenges that some of these distilleries might have to meet — the kind of quantity requirements that we have in our buildings,” Lerner said.

He said it’s fantastic the local producers and the retail giant were able to come to an agreement.

“To get into our market, to put them on our shelves, to promote them the way that we like to promote them and provide that opportunity — it is only going to open the door for more and more of this to happen as time goes on.”

The rollout comes as the industry prepares for the United States’ planned ban on Canadian alcohol imports, scheduled to take effect Sept. 29.

2:07 Dairy, liquor, motorcycles among Canadian goods facing U.S. ban

Canadian wine, beer and spirits producers sell the vast majority of their products within Canada, but the overwhelming majority of the small amount that is exported internationally is sent to the United States.

“Whether we’re selling there or not, it’s quite important because all of us plan to sell in the U.S. So now there’s uncertainty,” Parsons said.

Inter-provincial trade barriers within Canada, coupled with Alberta’s very competitive liquor retail scene, add to the challenges for small producers.

“We have a very, very, very competitive province, our free-market nature has a lot of products in this province — which is great for the consumer, but makes it very hard for the producer here to stand out.”

The timing of the Costco deal is significant for Alberta distillers.

Parsons said the three-month period leading up to Christmas is typically the busiest season for spirits sales, making the expanded retail presence especially valuable for the province’s growing whisky industry.

“Teaming up with someone like Costco, who reaches out to Albertans very effectively, is incredibly important for us in helping that and giving us a revenue boost right when we need it.”

Despite the potential challenges posed by trade disruptions, Parsons said producers are focused on adapting.

“We’re not throwing in the towel based on trade,” he said. “We’re problem-solvers as well.”

Business leaders say the initiative reflects broader support for Canadian-made products.

Ruhee Ismail-Teja of the Calgary Chamber of Commerce said consumers and businesses have increasingly rallied around buying local.

“This moment is one of the more unique ones that we’ve seen in the last several years where people are all rallying together,” she said. “Consumers are on the same page as large businesses and small businesses that we all really need to support Canada.”

According to the Government of Canada’s Trade Commissioner Service, Canada exported $1.36 billion in alcoholic beverages in 2023 and 90 per cent of those exports were sent to the U.S., with two-thirds being for spirits alone, including rye whisky, gin and vodka.

With files from Ariel Rabinovitch, Global News

stories.title: City council votes down controversial Sarnia Road apartment proposal
stories.summary: https://youtu.be/oAA30SesXzQ The controversial eight-storey student apartment project proposed to be built on ...
stories.author: Curtis Stokman
stories.content:
The controversial eight-storey student apartment project proposed to be built on Sarnia Road has been turned down by the city of London.

City council held a meeting on Monday, during which they discussed the matter of the project, which has gained major attention recently for its proposed location, size, and cost. After a debate on the floor, the vote on the project failed by a margin of two votes for to 13 against.

The project had previously been approved on Sept. 9 after a review that saw the planned apartment’s height boosted from six storeys to eight, and today represented the vote to re-zone the area where the apartment was set to be built.

The discussion of the project saw spirited debate in favour and against it. Ward 6 councillor Sam Trosow spoke at length in opposition, objecting to the cost of the apartments (which he cited at being $1,200 per bedroom) among other things, in a speech that received praise from mayor Josh Morgan. Ward 4 councillor Susan Stevenson also voiced her disapproval for the project, stating that she believed there could’ve been more open discussions on the project.

Conversely, Ward 2 councillor and deputy mayor Shawn Lewis voiced his approval for the apartment project, saying that while “Change is hard” for neighbourhoods such as Sherwood Forest and Orchard Park where the apartment was set to be built, he believed the project needed to move forward. Mayor Morgan also voiced his support for the project.

A row of signs protesting against the Sarnia road student apartment proposal. City council voted down the project on Monday much to the approval of the protestors. Photo by: Curtis Stokman

The viewing public also made their opinions heard during the debates. Several people in the public viewing gallery brought signs urging councillors to “Vote No” on the project. When the motion failed, several of them applauded, to which mayor Morgan reminded them that the council chamber is meant to be a neutral place and that expressions such as theirs are not a part of proceedings.

With the vote, where the Sarnia Road project might go from here remains to be seen.

stories.title: Pickering nuclear station shuts down for refurbishment, raising fears of higher power prices
stories.summary: Ontario expects gas-fired plants, which generally incur higher marginal costs, will step up to provide larger portion of province’s electricity
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
Pickering Nuclear Generating Station’s Unit 5 reactor shut down Tuesday, the first step in taking Canada’s oldest nuclear power plant offline for a lengthy overhaul.

All four operational units at the station, located east of downtown Toronto, are scheduled to come offline before Sept. 30 to undergo an extensive, $26.8-billion refurbishment. The Ontario government said in a statement that construction work began Monday; the station’s owner, Ontario Power Generation, said work on Unit 5 is expected to begin early next year.

The Pickering B units, which OPG says produce about one-10th of the province’s electricity, are expected to return to service between 2031 and 2034. Until then, the provincial government expects gas-fired plants will step up to provide a larger portion of Ontario’s power.

Four Ontario nuclear reactors taken off-line ahead of Pickering station’s refurbishment

That expected increase in gas-fired generation has raised fears from some quarters that Ontario’s electricity prices are poised to skyrocket.

Unlike residential consumers, who pay fixed rates for electricity set by the Ontario Energy Board, large businesses and industrial users typically pay wholesale prices that change throughout the day. Natural gas generators generally incur higher marginal costs, which increase wholesale prices.

Brad Duguid is president of the Association of Major Power Consumers in Ontario, which counts among its members large automakers such as Ford Motor Co. and Toyota Motor Corp., and steel producers Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco. He said large industrial users experienced extraordinary price hikes last winter; Pickering’s shutdown promises to make this winter even worse.

“We are critically concerned that we’re going to see unprecedented price spikes during that period when all of the natural gas generators will have to run to fill the gap of Pickering’s generation,” he said.

“The average mortgage in Ontario was about $3,000 a month. Imagine if that increased by 165 per cent. Suddenly, you’d be paying $8,000 a month just to stay in your home. That’s what industrial consumers are experiencing.”

Ampco has lobbied the provincial government to create a new program that would lower electricity rates for large industrial consumers. In a letter to Premier Doug Ford and three of his ministers in August, Mr. Duguid urged them to introduce that program before this winter.

Mr. Duguid also recommended that Ontario’s Emissions Performance Standards be adjusted so that carbon costs associated with natural gas-fired generation would be reduced or eliminated from the electricity prices paid by industrial users.

“We are thankful that the province appears to recognize the magnitude of the problem,” he said, adding, “We’re running out of time.”

AtkinsRealis joint-venture to refurbish unit of Pickering nuclear power plant

The Pickering B units, which OPG says produce about one-10th of the province’s electricity, are expected to return to service between 2031 and 2034. Until then, the provincial government expects gas-fired plants will step up to provide a larger portion of Ontario’s power.

That expected increase in gas-fired generation has raised fears from some quarters that Ontario’s electricity prices are poised to skyrocket.

Unlike residential consumers, who pay fixed rates for electricity set by the Ontario Energy Board, large businesses and industrial users typically pay wholesale prices that change throughout the day. Natural gas generators generally incur higher marginal costs, which increase wholesale prices.

Brad Duguid is president of the Association of Major Power Consumers in Ontario, which counts among its members large automakers such as Ford Motor Co. and Toyota Motor Corp., and steel producers Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco. He said large industrial users experienced extraordinary price hikes last winter; Pickering’s shutdown promises to make this winter even worse.
